note: The approved Idea bank, with the seven materials guides folded into their cards.

cards.title: Watercolor
cards.summary: Ways to offer pan, liquid and pencil watercolor on many surfaces, from one color and water to layered paintings of what we see on our site.

items: A pan set holding only red, yellow and blue, one soft round brush, two water cups and a small sponge, set out on a clean tray in the Studio or a class atelier.
One color only, such as blue, with water and white watercolor paper, so children find every blue from the palest wash to the deepest pool.
Black paper with white liquid watercolor or white gouache and a fine brush, with white paper and colors alongside so children can compare and choose.
Liquid watercolor in small lidded jars with droppers and pipettes over thick watercolor paper, coffee filters and paper towels.
Wet paper first, brushed with clear water, so colors bloom and travel when they touch it.
A white crayon or white oil pastel drawing on white paper, painted over with a wash so the hidden lines appear.
Coarse salt sprinkled into wet paint, with a magnifier nearby for looking at the speckles once dry.
Surfaces set side by side to test, such as watercolor paper, newsprint, cardstock, brown kraft, gray paper, tracing paper and vellum.
Paper cut into circles, long strips, tiny cards and torn-edge pieces, waiting in a basket beside the paints.
Brushes of many sizes and shapes, from a wide flat wash brush to a tiny round, with sponges, droppers, a feather and a stick in a jar beside the paints.
Spray bottles of thinned liquid watercolor aimed at butcher paper clipped to the fence in the outdoor piazza.
Rain painting in the rainy season, with dots of liquid watercolor on paper carried out into a light rain.
A small easel in the garden facing the valley oaks, the willow dome or one bloom, for painting what is in front of us.
A table easel by the animal yards for painting the goats, the chickens, the rabbits or Sheldon from life.
Fallen leaves, smooth stones, shells and pieces of bark to paint on, gathered with care.
A block of ice on a tray in the sun with droppers of liquid watercolor and a pinch of coarse salt.
Masking tape shapes pressed onto paper, painted over and peeled away to find white lines.
Watercolor pencils and water brushes on clipboards for drawing outside and adding water after.
A long roll of watercolor or butcher paper on the floor for a small group to paint side by side.
Thin painted papers, tracing paper and vellum laid on the light table, so children see color glow when light comes through.

sections.text: Both. A single tray and a quiet seat let a child follow the water slowly, in the Studio or in any class atelier. A long shared sheet, a fence of spray painting or a garden easel for two invites talk about where colors meet.

Liquid watercolor stains hands, wood and fabric, so cover tables and offer smocks. Dilute liquid watercolor with one to three parts water and keep one stronger jar for small details. Heavy watercolor paper or cardstock holds water, while thin paper pills and buckles, so tape wet work to a board on all four edges. Offer two water cups, one for rinsing and one clean, and a sponge at each place. Let pans dry open after use so they do not mold, and store liquid colors in labeled lidded jars at child height. Artist-grade pans and good round brushes with a fine point last for years with care and are worth the cost.

items: Fills and carries water cups with two hands.
Wakes up each pan with a few drops of water before painting.
Mixes liquid colors into jars with droppers and decides how strong to make them.
Chooses the surface, its color and its shape from the paper shelf.
Chooses a brush or tool for the idea, from a wide wash brush to a fine point.
Rinses brushes, blots them on the sponge and lays them flat to dry.
Decides when a painting is finished or ready for another layer.
Shows a friend how to lift extra water with a sponge or tissue.
Moves wet work to the drying rack, marks a name on the back and tells the story of the painting for an educator to write down if they wish.

sections.text: Children rinse each brush in the wash bucket, blot it on the sponge and lay it on the drying rack. They leave pans open on the tray to dry, cap the liquid color jars and pour the rinse water into the waste bucket. A damp sponge at each place and a photo label for every tool mean the table is wiped and reset by the children before they move on, so nothing waits for an educator later.

Sit at the child's level beside the tray and keep your own hands still and soft while the water moves. Narrate what you see in a regular voice, such as "The blue ran into the wet part." Let puddles and buckled paper be part of the work, with a sponge nearby and a calm face when a cup tips.

items: I notice the blue is moving across the wet paper. I wonder where it will stop.
How did you make that pale part so soft?
I wonder how the white looks on the black paper and on the white paper.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one color and water so children meet how the paint moves and how water makes it paler.

For 2s, offer one strong color in a heavy jar with a fat brush and big paper. For 3s, add a second color, droppers and wet paper. For 4s, offer full pan sets, fine brushes and paintings returned to over days.
Add a second and third color and let them meet on the paper.
Offer wet and dry paper side by side to compare.
Offer black paper with white watercolor beside white paper with color, and notice what children choose.
Introduce droppers, pipettes and spray bottles with liquid watercolor.
Model a few techniques without a product, such as a flat wash, lifting color with a tissue and touching one wet color into another, then step back.
Add salt, tape and crayon resist as new questions to try.
Try new surfaces and shapes, from vellum and tracing paper to circles, strips and tiny cards.
Paint with ice, rain and fog as part of the work in their seasons.
Move the easel into the garden and paint from what children see, then carry the painting back to the plant to compare.
Paint the same tree or view across months and hang the paintings in a row.
Return to dry paintings with pens, pencils or collage.
Cut favorite painted papers for collage and handmade books.
Look at Chiura Obata's paintings of the Sierra Nevada and wonder how he painted outdoors.
Look at Albrecht Dürer's young hare and then paint one of our rabbits from life.
Look at Maria Sibylla Merian's paintings of plants with the insects that live on them, then paint a plant from the pollinator garden with the creatures children find there.
Move to open studio where watercolor is self-serve in the Studio and in every class atelier, with a travel set ready to carry outdoors and a clear routine for care.

setting.why: Watercolor is self-serve once children know the care routine. Painting at the animal yards and at a garden easel follows our ratio of one adult to six children in the garden.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer spray bottles at the fence, big wet paper on the floor and painting with hands in a wash of color. A block of ice to drip color onto adds cold and weight to carry.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small card, one color and a long brush that keeps fingers dry, at a quiet seat. Let them watch a friend first and wipe hands on a damp cloth whenever they choose.
connected: Chiura Obata on the Artists page, for watercolor and ink paintings he made outdoors in the Sierra Nevada.
Albrecht Dürer on the Artists page, for his close watercolor study of a young hare.
Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for watercolor paintings of plants with the insects that live on them, many made on vellum.

sections.text: A simple pan watercolor set, a soft brush, two cups of water, a rag or sponge, and thick paper. A sheet of black paper with a little white paint is a lovely extra. The plain inside of a cereal box, a coffee filter or a paper bag all work too.

items: Paint with only one color and water and see how many light and dark versions you can make.
Draw with a white crayon first, then paint over it to find the hidden drawing.
Wet the paper with clear water and drop color on to watch it spread.
Paint with white on black paper and with colors on white paper, side by side.
Paint a flower, a tree or the sky you can see from a window while looking at it.
Set a few drops of paint on paper outside in a light rain and see what the rain does.

sections.text: Your child can fill the water cups, wake up the paints with a few drops of water, choose the colors and the paper, rinse the brush and decide when a painting is done. Let them lay paintings flat to dry and choose where to hang them. Your child can rinse the brush, pour out the water cups and wipe the table with a damp sponge. Leave the paint box open so it dries, and let your child choose where it lives.

items: Where do you think the color will go?
I wonder what more water will do.
Tell me about your painting.

sections.text: Your child is learning how water and color move, how to make a color lighter or darker, and how to care for real tools. Holding a soft brush and controlling the water builds small hand muscles, and the slow flow of color helps many children settle.
Send a photo of a painting or the painting itself for our walls. You can also send clean flat cardboard and coffee filters for the Studio. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Liquid watercolor can stain clothes and counters, so cover the table and use an old shirt. Most watercolor washes off skin with soap and water. Let the paint set dry open after painting so it stays fresh.

cards.title: Tempera
cards.summary: Ways to offer thick, bright tempera from a palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black, at easels, on the ground, on boxes and with tools from nature.

items: An easel with red, yellow, blue, white and black in no-spill cups, one thick brush in each and a palette for mixing.
One color only with white beside it, such as red and white, so children find every pink from deep to pale.
Black paper with white tempera and a choice of brushes, with white, gray, brown kraft and colored paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Brushes of many sizes and shapes, palette knives, sponges, rollers, droppers, sticks and feathers on a tray by the paint.
Brushes made from leaves, grasses, feathers, sticks and pine needles tied with string, gathered from fallen pieces.
Pebbles or marbles rolled through paint across paper in a shallow box lid.
Paint dropped onto cardboard, covered with plastic wrap and pounded with hands or soft mallets.
Large boxes, tubes and sculptures children have built, ready for paint.
Butcher paper hung along a fence in the outdoor piazza for big standing arm work.
Window or plexiglass painting with a drop of dish soap in the paint, then washing it off together.
Paper pressed onto a painted plexiglass sheet to pull a print.
Toy vehicles rolled through paint along a long paper road on the floor.
A cup of thin paint with a small hole, swinging from a string over paper on the ground.
Paint mixed with sand for a rough texture on cardboard.
Tempera blocks with a damp brush for quick thick color, in a class atelier or carried outside.
Big brushes and big paper with music from the Song book.
Frozen paint cubes on craft sticks for painting on a hot afternoon.
The whole art table covered with a new surface each week, such as butcher paper, bubble wrap, cardboard or cloth, for one shared changing piece.
Surfaces beyond the paper rectangle, such as circles, long strips, torn shapes, wood scraps, fabric, stones and clear sheets on the light table.
A self-serve paint shelf with small jars, palettes and sponges for open studio.

sections.text: Both. An easel gives one child a place to stand and decide, in the Studio or a class atelier. Fences, floors, big boxes and the shared art table invite many hands to work on one piece.

Choose washable nontoxic tempera with the AP seal, and quality liquid tempera holds far more color than thin budget paint. Our palette is red, yellow, blue, white and black, and children mix the rest. Choose a red and a blue that mix a clear purple and test before buying, and keep more white than any other color since it goes fastest. A drop of dish soap helps paint wash out and helps it stick to glass and plastic. Thin paint with water for spray bottles and swinging cups, and thicken it with a little cornstarch for texture. Keep lids on between uses so paint does not dry or mold. Set a bucket of soapy water and towels close by and offer smocks.

items: Pours paint into cups from a small pitcher.
Mixes new colors on a palette and names them.
Adds white a little at a time and black a tiny bit at a time, and notices the difference.
Gathers fallen materials to become brushes.
Chooses tools and surfaces for the day, including paper color and shape.
Helps cover the art table with each new surface.
Washes brushes, cups and easels at the sink.
Hangs finished work to dry and decides where it goes.
Teaches a friend how to wipe a brush on the cup edge.

sections.text: Children snap lids on the paint cups, carry brushes and cups to the low sink and wash them until the water runs clear. They wipe the easel and table with the damp sponge kept beside the paint, hang smocks on their hooks and set brushes bristles up in the drying jar. The soapy bucket and towels sit at the easel from the start, so the close happens right there and an educator only checks the floor.

Stand or kneel near the easel and stay there, within arm's reach, for the whole time the easel is open. Keep your face relaxed when paint drips, lands on arms or turns brown. Describe the marks you see, such as "You swept your arm across and the line got long," and model wiping the brush without touching the painting.

items: I notice you made a color we have not seen. How did it happen?
I wonder how pale this red can get with more white.
Where will the marble go if the box tips the other way?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin at the easel with red, yellow and blue and one brush each.

For 2s, offer one or two colors, fat brushes, big paper and plenty of time to move. For 3s, add a palette and white. For 4s, offer the full palette with black and invite planned work that children return to.
Offer one primary with white to explore tints, then one with black for shades.
Offer black paper with white paint beside white paper with color, and notice what children choose.
Swap brushes for tools children gather in the garden.
Paint with the whole body at the fence, on the ground and on big boxes.
Try rolling, swinging and pounding to see what marks each makes.
Paint new surfaces such as cardboard, fabric, wood, stones and plexiglass, and new shapes such as circles and long strips.
Model a few techniques, such as wiping the brush, rinsing between colors and dabbing with a sponge, then step back.
Pull prints from painted plexiglass.
Mix colors to match something real from our site set on the easel tray, such as a pomegranate flower, a crow feather or a piece of coast live oak bark.
Look at Jacob Lawrence's Migration Series and notice flat shapes of color telling a story in many panels.
Paint a series of pictures that tell a story, with dictation.
Paint boxes, signs and props for dramatic play and the Unicorn Café.
Keep invented colors in labeled jars with names children choose.
Paint a big mural together across days on butcher paper along the hallway wall or the outdoor piazza fence.
Combine tempera with collage, oil pastel and printmaking on one surface.
Open a self-serve paint shelf where children set up and clean up on their own, in the Studio and in each class atelier.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Easel and table painting is open to everyone. Pounding paint with mallets and swinging paint cups need an educator close by, and big box and fence painting works best as a small group.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big brushes at a fence-high sheet, pounding paint under plastic with mallets, and pushing heavy boxes to paint. Finger painting with thick paint on a tabletop gives lots of touch.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a long-handled brush, a small amount of one color and a smock with long sleeves. Gloves, a quiet easel away from the busy table and time to watch first all help.
connected: Jacob Lawrence on the Artists page, for telling a long story in flat bright shapes of tempera paint.

sections.text: Washable tempera or poster paint in red, yellow, blue and white, big paper or flattened boxes, a paper plate for mixing, a few brushes, sticks and fallen leaves, and an old shirt. Black paper with white paint is a fun extra.

items: Put out just one color and white and mix every light version you can.
Paint a big cardboard box outside.
Tie grass or fallen leaves to a stick to make your own brush.
Roll a ball or pebble through paint in a box lid.
Paint a window with paint mixed with a drop of dish soap, then wash it off together.
Paint with white on black paper, or paint along with music.

sections.text: Your child can pour small amounts of paint, mix colors on the plate, choose tools and paper, wash brushes and decide where the painting goes. Your child can put the lids back on, wash the brushes in a bowl of soapy water and wipe the table with a sponge. A towel on the floor near the sink makes this easy and calm.

items: I wonder what a little white will do.
Which mark does this stick make?
Tell me how you made that color.

sections.text: Your child is learning how colors mix, how tools make different marks, and how to care for materials. Painting big at an easel or fence uses the shoulders and whole body and crosses the middle of the body, which helps the two sides of the body work together.
Send a photo of a brush your child invented, or the name of a color they mixed. You can also send clean boxes, tubes and jar lids for the Studio. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Washable paint can still mark fabric. Rinse clothes in cold water soon after painting. Put out small amounts at a time so less is wasted.

cards.title: Acrylic
cards.summary: Ways to offer acrylic paint for work that needs to last, on wood, stone, clay, canvas and murals, indoors and outdoors.

items: Smooth rocks painted as markers for each class's home beds in the garden.
A palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black squeezed onto a lidded tray, so children mix every color they need.
Wood scraps or canvas boards painted black, with white acrylic and fine brushes, and white boards alongside so children can compare and choose.
Dry clay pieces children made, ready to paint.
Wood scraps and pieces built with real tools, ready to paint.
Round wood slices from fallen branches, sanded by children and painted.
A shared canvas board that a small group returns to over many days.
A long wooden board or fence panel painted together as a mural for the garden or outdoor piazza.
Palette knives and thick paint spread on heavy cardboard.
Paint mixed with sand or fine sifted soil for texture.
Wooden signs for the garden and animal yards, with words children choose.
Fallen pinecones, shells and seed pods to paint.
Recycled sculptures painted so they can stay outside through the rain.
Fine brushes and small river rocks for close, slow work.
Plaster casts painted once dry.
A gel plate rolled with acrylic for printing with leaves and textures.
Instruments children build for the music shed, painted to last.
Small squares of canvas, cardboard, kraft paper, wood, stone, glass and fabric set out to compare how the same paint sits on each.
Clear acrylic sheets or glass jars painted thinly for the light table and windows, where the color glows.

sections.text: Both. A rock or a sign is one child's careful work. A mural or shared canvas grows from many children over weeks, in the Studio, the art shed or outdoors.

Acrylic dries fast and becomes permanent, and it will not wash out of clothes once dry. Use student-grade nontoxic acrylic with the AP seal, smocks and old clothes. Put out small amounts on a palette or lid. Thin acrylic with a little water for washes, keeping it to about a third water so it still holds. Brush a coat of white or black on cardboard first when color needs to stay bright. Keep brushes in water while working and wash them with soap right after. A palette covered with a damp paper towel and a lid keeps paint for another day. An adult brushes clear outdoor varnish on pieces that will live outside. Let rinse water settle in a bucket and put the dried sludge in the trash, away from sinks and the garden.

items: Chooses the object and plans what it needs.
Squeezes small amounts onto the palette and mixes colors there.
Sands wood slices and rocks smooth before painting.
Paints a base coat and waits for it to dry before adding detail.
Keeps brushes wet and washes them right away.
Decides where finished pieces will live outdoors.
Checks on outdoor pieces through the seasons.
Teaches a friend why acrylic brushes need water.
Writes or dictates words for garden signs.

sections.text: Children move brushes straight from the water jar to the low sink and wash them with soap before anything else, since acrylic sets fast. They cover the palette with a damp paper towel and a lid to keep it for tomorrow, wipe the table and pour rinse water into the settling bucket. Painted rocks and wood go to a labeled drying board, and an adult saves outdoor varnish for later in the week.

Sit at the table with your own hands holding a damp cloth, with no brush of your own, so the work stays the child's. Speak calmly about care, such as "The brush stays in the water so it stays soft." Notice any worry you feel about permanent paint and keep the setup small enough that you can stay relaxed.

items: Where will this rock live in the garden?
I notice the paint looks different now that it is dry.
I wonder what the rain will do to it.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with tempera so children know paint before meeting a permanent one.
For 2s, offer acrylic on one rock or block outdoors with an adult close by. For 3s, offer small objects and a few mixed colors. For 4s, offer signs, murals and work across many days.
Offer acrylic for one small object that will go outside.
Talk together about what stays and what washes away.
Paint dry clay, plaster and wood that children made.
Try palette knives and thick paint.
Add texture with sand and sifted soil.
Paint white on black boards and color on white boards, and hang them side by side.
Model layering, with a base coat first and detail once it is dry, then step back.
Plan and paint garden markers, signs and labels with children.
Mix colors to match the plants a marker will stand beside, such as lavender, yarrow or rosemary.
Paint a shared mural over several weeks.
Use acrylic on a gel plate for printing.
Look at Alma Thomas and her small dabs of bright color, inspired by gardens and trees she watched from home.
Visit outdoor painted pieces through the seasons and notice change.
Keep a small acrylic shelf in the Studio and the art shed for lasting outdoor work, with a care routine children know.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Acrylic is permanent and will not wash out, so an adult sits at the table. Varnishing outdoor pieces is adult work away from children, and the West class paints one rock or block with an adult beside them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy rocks to carry from the creek trail or garden, sanding wood slices with firm pressure, and thick paint spread with a palette knife.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small smooth rock, one or two colors and a brush with a long handle, at a quiet table. Gloves and a damp cloth close by help a child who dislikes paint drying on skin.
connected: Alma Thomas on the Artists page, for bright acrylic dabs of color inspired by gardens and trees.

sections.text: A few tubes of nontoxic student acrylic in red, yellow, blue, white and black, a jar lid for a palette, small brushes, a cup of water, old clothes, and smooth rocks or wood scraps.

items: Paint a rock to mark a spot in your garden or a pot.
Paint a wood scrap as a sign for a door or a bed of plants.
Paint one rock black and add white dots and lines, then compare it with a rock painted white.
Mix in a little sand and feel the bumpy paint when it dries.
Leave a painted rock outside and check on it after rain.

sections.text: Your child can choose the rock or wood, squeeze small amounts of paint, mix colors on the lid, and wash the brush as soon as painting ends. Your child can wash the brush with soap the moment painting ends, before it dries. They can wipe the lid palette, carry finished rocks to a drying spot and put the paint tubes back in a small box.

items: Where should this live?
I wonder how it will look after the rain.

sections.text: Your child is learning to plan a piece that lasts and to care for tools. Sanding, squeezing tubes and painting small details build hand strength and careful control.
Send smooth rocks, clean wood scraps or jar lids for palettes. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Acrylic is permanent on clothes and furniture once dry. Cover the table, wear old clothes, and wash brushes and hands with soap right away.

cards.title: Earth and plant paints
cards.summary: Ways children find, grind and mix colors from the soil, stones, charcoal and plants of our site, and paint with them on many surfaces.

items: A soil color walk with small jars to gather earth from garden beds, the Log yard and the creek trail, with an adult confirming each spot.
Trays of gathered soil drying in the sun, then shaken through screens and sieves.
A mortar and pestle or two flat stones for grinding dry earth, soft rock and chalk into powder.
Small piles of powder on a palette with water and a binder for mixing paint, such as flour paste, gum arabic or a little clear acrylic medium.
White from ground chalk and white clay, and black from charcoal, set beside the reds and browns so children have light and dark to mix.
Earth paints on black paper, white paper, brown kraft paper and cardboard side by side, to see where each color shows.
Clay slip made from our clay and water, painted with brushes and hands.
Mud painting on big paper, cardboard and the fence.
Willow charcoal we make from willow dome trimmings, ground with an adult into a soft black.
Fallen petals, grass and leaves rubbed straight onto paper to see the color they leave.
Flowers and leaves from the botanical dye bed laid between paper or cloth and pounded with mallets.
Liquid colors from botanical dye bed plants, simmered by an adult into small jars for brushes and droppers.
Ink from galls found under the valley oaks, soaked by an adult and darkened with a little iron water from rusty nails in vinegar.
A color library of jars, each labeled with where the color came from.
A map of our site with a dot of each color where it was found.
Earth paint on rocks, bark, wood, stone, fabric and paper made in the Studio.
Brushes from feathers, sticks, grasses and fingers, the tools painters used long before store brushes.
A palette of four or five earth colors on a flat stone in the garden, with a small jar of water.
A big shared painting on a roll of brown kraft paper outdoors, using only colors found that week.
Earth paints set beside store tempera for comparing.

sections.text: Mostly together. Gathering, sifting and grinding are shared work with lots of talk. A child may then sit alone with a jar of a color they found and paint slowly.

Poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site, so an adult confirms every plant and spot before anything is gathered. California pipevine is poisonous to eat, so it stays a plant to look at and draw. Berries and all food stay out of paint. Pick with purpose and leave some for others. Grind with a damp cloth nearby and never blow the dust. Mix powder and binder on a palette with a palette knife to a smooth paste. Gum arabic from an art supplier makes a watercolor-style paint, and a little clear acrylic medium makes paint that lasts on wood and stone. Flour paste spoils in a day or two, so mix only what is needed. Simmering plant colors is an adult job on a hot plate away from children, in pots kept only for the Studio, and plant colors spoil within days, so make small amounts and compost what is left. Store dry powder in labeled lidded jars.

items: Finds colors on walks and in the garden.
Decides which colors to keep and which to leave.
Sifts, grinds and mixes with real tools.
Grinds charcoal and chalk for black and white.
Tests each color on a scrap and adds a swatch to a color book.
Labels jars with where each color came from.
Returns extra soil to the garden.
Teaches a friend where a color can be found.
Cleans the mortar, screens and palettes.

sections.text: Children tap screens clean over the soil basket, wipe the mortar and pestle with a damp cloth and return color jars to their labeled shelf by place. Leftover soil goes back to the garden bed it came from and spent plant paint goes to compost, carried by the children in a small bucket. The damp cloth, the compost bucket and a home for each jar are set out at the start, so the table is clear when the painting ends.

Kneel in the dirt with the children on the color walk and show real interest in each soil. Notice your own feelings about mud and dust and let your face say the earth is welcome. Model slow grinding with steady hands, then pass the pestle and step back.

items: Where did this color come from?
I wonder what other colors are hiding on our site.
I notice this soil changed when it got wet. How did that happen?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with mud and water on paper outside.
For 2s, offer mud and slip with hands and big brushes outdoors. For 3s, add sifting and a color walk. For 4s, add grinding, binders and a labeled color library.
Go on a color walk to find different soils and stones.
Dry, sift and grind the finds together.
Mix paint with a simple binder and compare thick and thin.
Compare binders, such as flour paste, gum arabic and acrylic medium, and notice which one stays.
Start a color library with labeled jars.
Add white from chalk and black from charcoal, and mix lighter and darker earth colors.
Paint on black, white and brown paper side by side.
Add colors from fallen petals and the botanical dye bed.
Make oak gall ink with an adult when galls drop in the fall.
Map where each color was found on our site.
Paint across the seasons and notice which colors change, from wet winter soil to dry summer dust.
Compare our paint with store tempera and watercolor.
Look at Jason Logan's inks made from plants, rust and soil he gathers in the city.
Look at photos of the Chumash Painted Cave, where people painted long ago with red, black and white colors from the land, and wonder together where those colors came from.
Use our own colors for books, signs and a mural.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Gathering and grinding need an adult confirming every plant and spot, with dust kept down. Simmering plant colors on a hot plate and making oak gall ink with iron water are adult work, with children watching from a set place.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer grinding with a heavy mortar and pestle, carrying jars of soil on a color walk, and mud painting with hands on big paper.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer dry, sifted powder already in small jars with a brush and a spoon. Let them sort and label colors or watch the grinding before touching mud.
connected: Jason Logan on the Artists page, for inks he makes from plants, rust and soil he gathers in the city.
Chumash Painted Cave State Historic Park, a cultural place, for paintings made long ago with red, black and white colors from the land.

home.title: Earth and plant paints at Home

sections.text: A few jars, an old sieve, a spoon, flour and water, paper and brushes, and soil from your yard or a place where gathering is allowed. Black paper and white paper side by side are a nice extra.

items: Collect soils of different colors in jars and set them side by side.
Dry the soil, sift it, and mix a spoonful with a little flour and water paste to paint.
Grind a piece of chalk or cooled charcoal between two stones outside for white and black.
Rub fallen petals or grass on paper to see what color they leave.
Paint the same soil on black paper and on white paper.
Make a color chart and write where each color came from.

sections.text: Your child can find the colors, sift and stir, grind with stones and decide what to paint. Your child can carry extra soil back to the yard, rinse the sieve and wipe the table with a damp cloth. They can put the color jars in a basket or on a shelf they choose.

items: How many colors of dirt can we find?
I wonder why this soil is darker.
Where should we look next?

sections.text: Your child is learning that color comes from the land around us, and how to look closely at it. Grinding, sifting and carrying soil give the body heavy work, which helps many children feel calm and organized. Smelling damp earth and petals adds to what children notice.
Send a small labeled jar of soil from a place your family loves, so it can join our color library. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Only gather plants you know are safe, and skip berries and food. Wash hands after handling soil. Flour paint spoils quickly, so mix fresh each time.

cards.title: Ink and pens
cards.summary: Ways to offer pens, brushes and ink, black on white and white on black, including tools children make from sticks and feathers.

items: Fine black pens and clipboards for close looking at shells, feathers, leaves and Sheldon.
White gel pens, white paint pens and white ink on black paper, with black pens and white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
A small heavy jar of black ink with sticks, feathers and grass stems as drawing tools.
Twig pens trimmed with garden pruners by children with an adult.
A sumi ink stick and ink stone, with children grinding their own ink in a little water.
Bamboo pens and dip pens beside small jars of ink.
Brushes from wide flat to fine round with one jar of ink and big paper on the floor for long sweeping marks.
Ink in three jars, full strength, half water and mostly water, for finding grays from one black.
Ink dropped onto wet paper to watch it feather and spread.
Ink blown across paper through a straw.
Ink floated on water in a shallow tray and lifted with paper, a Japanese practice called suminagashi.
Surfaces to test, such as thin Japanese paper, newsprint, cardstock, tracing paper, vellum, brown kraft and gray paper.
Pens offered over a dry watercolor or earth paint painting.
Oak gall ink made with an adult from galls under the valley oaks.
Fine pens on tracing paper or acetate laid over a pressed plant, then set on the light table.
Long strips and tiny cards of paper for ink drawings, in a basket that travels to the garden.
Pens and paper beside the mailboxes for letters to other classes.
Washable markers dotted on coffee filters, then touched with water to watch colors separate.
Markers for maps and signs where bright color helps.
A scribbling machine built with an adult, with markers taped as legs to a cup and a small battery motor that makes it wobble and draw on its own.

sections.text: Mostly alone. Ink and fine pens ask for slow, close work. Shared ink brush paper on the floor and suminagashi trays are good for a small group, in the Studio or a class atelier.

India ink is permanent and stains, so use smocks, cover tables and pour a little into small heavy jars that do not tip. Choose nontoxic inks. Sumi and India ink can be thinned with water to make grays. White ink and gel pens show best on black or dark paper. Thin Japanese paper soaks up ink fast, so lay newsprint under it. We favor chalk, crayon and pencil for building hand strength, so pens are one choice among many. Store markers tip down with caps on. A sumi ink stick lasts for years.

items: Grinds sumi ink and decides when it is dark enough.
Mixes grays from black ink and water in small jars.
Gathers sticks and feathers to test as tools.
Makes twig pens with real tools and an adult.
Chooses black or white paper and the tool that shows best on it.
Caps pens and sorts out the dry ones.
Washes brushes and ink jars.
Uses pens for letters, maps and signs that others will read.
Shows a friend how to wipe the dip pen on the jar edge.

sections.text: Children cap every pen until it clicks, test the doubtful ones on a scrap and drop dry pens in the marked jar. They wash brushes and ink jars at the low sink, wipe the table with a damp sponge and stand jars back on the photo-labeled tray. Small heavy jars and a sponge at each place keep spills small, so the children finish the close at the table and nothing is left for later.

Sit close and quiet, matching the slow pace of ink work, and keep your voice low. Hold the ink jar steady while a child learns to dip, then let go. If ink spills, breathe, reach for the cloth and say what happened plainly, so the child borrows your calm.

items: I wonder which line a feather will make.
How did you get that gray?
I notice the white line looks bright on the black paper.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with fine pens and close looking at one object.
For 2s, offer thick markers and one brush with ink in a heavy jar. For 3s, add fine pens, sticks and feathers. For 4s, add dip pens, twig pens, sumi grinding and longer looking studies.
Offer white pens on black paper beside black pens on white paper.
Offer black ink and a single brush on big paper.
Mix three grays from one ink and paint with only those.
Gather sticks, feathers and grasses and test each as a tool.
Make twig and bamboo pens with an adult and real tools.
Grind sumi ink on an ink stone.
Try ink on wet paper, blowing ink and floating ink on water.
Make oak gall ink in the fall.
Draw with pens over dry watercolor and earth paint.
Look at Vincent van Gogh's reed pen drawings and notice dots, dashes and swirls.
Look at Chiura Obata's ink and brush paintings and try a single brush stroke for a branch.
Use pens for maps, letters, signs and books.
Build scribbling machines and compare the marks they make with our own.
Keep a shared pen journal of one plant across the season.
Keep pens and ink on a self-serve tray in the Studio and each class atelier, with a cap check routine.

setting.why: Pens are open to everyone, and permanent ink needs an educator close by. Trimming twig pens with garden pruners is one adult with one or two children, and building a scribbling machine needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer grinding a sumi ink stick on the stone with firm circles, big ink brush marks on the floor while kneeling, and blowing ink through a straw.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a fine pen and a small card at a quiet table, with no open ink. Let them watch the ink feather on wet paper before trying it.
connected: Vincent van Gogh on the Artists page, for drawings made with reed pens and ink in dots, dashes and swirls.
Chiura Obata on the Artists page, for ink and brush paintings of trees and mountains.

sections.text: A fine black pen or two, a white gel pen, a few washable markers, white and black paper, a clipboard or book to lean on, and sticks or feathers from a walk.

items: Draw a leaf, shell or houseplant while looking closely.
Draw with a white gel pen on black paper, then a black pen on white paper.
Dip a stick or feather in a little washable paint and draw with it.
Dot markers on a coffee filter, add drops of water and watch colors split apart.
Write a letter or draw a map together.

sections.text: Your child can choose what to draw and which paper to use, find sticks to test, and put caps back on pens. Your child can put every cap back on, sort out the pens that have dried up and wipe the table with a damp cloth. A small cup or basket for pens gives everything a home.

items: I notice so much when we look really close.
Which tool makes the thinnest line?
Tell me about your drawing.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely and to choose tools for an idea. Gripping a fine pen and grinding ink build hand strength, and slow, close drawing helps many children feel calm and focused.
Send a letter or map your child made for our mailboxes, or send clean feathers and sticks for drawing. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Real ink stains, so washable markers and paint are easier at home. Cover the table and keep caps on.

cards.title: Pencil
cards.summary: Ways to offer graphite, colored and white pencils on many papers for close looking, planning, mapping and revisiting ideas, everywhere on our site.

items: Clipboards with paper and sharpened pencils in every space, indoors and outdoors.
One natural object and a magnifier on the investigation table, with paper and pencils beside it.
White and light colored pencils on black paper, with graphite on white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
A cup of drawing pencils from hard to very soft for comparing light and dark lines.
Graphite sticks and chunky pencils for younger hands.
Colored pencils sorted by color in clear jars, and watercolor pencils with a water brush.
Papers to test, such as gray, brown kraft, cardstock, tracing paper, vellum and smooth white.
A standing mirror with paper and pencils for self-portraits.
A plant in the garden drawn from day to day as it grows.
Paper and peeled graphite sticks for rubbings of bark, leaves and textures around the yards.
A bench by the animal yards with clipboards for drawing the goats, chickens and rabbits.
Tracing paper laid over pressed plants to follow the edges.
Paper for drawing plans before building with blocks or wood.
Maps of the creek trail and the garden drawn after a walk.
Tiny cards for small drawings and long strips for long journeys and tall plants.
A pencil drawing on vellum or tracing paper placed on the light table.
A big roll of paper on the floor for a group pencil drawing, such as a map of the whole site.
A drawing journal for each child kept in the class atelier, open for returning to ideas.
A hand-crank sharpener and a small shavings dish that children manage.
Erasers offered as a tool for changing a drawing.

sections.text: Mostly alone, side by side. Each child follows their own looking. Plans, maps and big floor drawings become shared when children talk them through together.

Hand-crank and manual sharpeners let children do the work. Keep one cup for sharp pencils and one for pencils that need sharpening. Chunky and triangle pencils help younger hands. Quality colored pencils with soft cores lay down color with less pressing, and white pencils on black paper need a soft core, so test a few. Agree on walking with points down. Soft pencils smudge, so a scrap of paper under the hand helps.

items: Sharpens pencils and empties the shavings.
Sorts pencils into the right cups.
Chooses a pencil for a light or dark line.
Chooses paper color and size for the drawing.
Carries a clipboard to what they want to draw.
Returns to a drawing to add or change it.
Shares a drawing at meeting time.
Uses drawings to plan building and walks.
Teaches a friend how to hold a pencil on its side for rubbing.

sections.text: Children empty the sharpener into the compost bin, sort pencils into the sharp cup and the needs sharpening cup and slide clipboards back into their rack. They brush eraser crumbs into their hands and drop them in the trash. Each cup and rack has a picture label, so the drawing table is ready for the next friend in a minute.

Sit beside the child with your own clipboard and look at the same object with real interest. Describe what you notice in the drawing, such as "You made the lines close together here," and resist drawing on their page. Stay through the quiet so the child knows the looking matters.

items: I notice you are looking very closely.
I wonder what is on the other side.
How would this drawing look on the dark paper?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with free drawing and plenty of paper.
For 2s, offer chunky pencils, graphite sticks and big paper. For 3s, add clipboards and a magnifier. For 4s, add soft and hard pencils, colored pencils and drawings returned to over days.
Put clipboards in every space.
Invite close looking at one natural object with a magnifier.
Offer white pencils on black paper beside graphite on white.
Add pencils of different softness and compare.
Model pressing light and hard and using the side of the lead for shading, then step back.
Add colored pencils and watercolor pencils.
Draw the same plant, animal or tree over time.
Draw plans before building and maps after walks.
Use mirrors for self-portraits.
Look at Ellsworth Kelly's plant drawings and notice how one line can hold a whole leaf.
Draw an idea again after talking with friends, and set the drawings side by side.
Combine pencil with watercolor, ink or collage.
Gather drawings into a book or onto the wall as documentation.
Keep journals in each class atelier for drawing and returning across the year.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Pencils and clipboards are self-serve in every space. Drawing at the animal yards and in the garden follows our ratio of one adult to six children in the garden.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer pressing hard rubbings on bark and logs, turning a hand-crank sharpener, and big pencil drawings standing at a wall.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a clipboard in a quiet corner, a soft pencil that needs little pressure and time to look before drawing. An eraser and fresh paper close by remove worry about mistakes.
connected: Ellsworth Kelly on the Artists page, for simple pencil line drawings of leaves and plants.

sections.text: Pencils, a white or light colored pencil, a small sharpener, an eraser, white and black paper, and something firm to lean on.

items: Draw a houseplant, a pet or a shoe while looking closely.
Draw with a white pencil on black paper.
Lay paper on tree bark or a leaf and rub with the side of a pencil.
Draw a map of your street or your walk to school.
Draw your face while looking in a mirror.

sections.text: Your child can sharpen pencils, choose the paper and what to draw, and come back to add more later. Your child can empty the sharpener, stand pencils in a cup points up and put drawings in a folder or box. Eraser crumbs can be swept into a hand and dropped in the trash.

items: I notice so much when we look closer.
I wonder what you will add next time.
Tell me about this part.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look carefully and to share ideas on paper. Holding a pencil and steadying the paper with the other hand builds the small muscles and teamwork of the hands that writing will need later.
Send a drawing of something from home to share at meeting time, or send pencils and clipboards for our yards. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Walk with pencil points down. Keep small sharpeners away from very young siblings.

cards.title: Crayon
cards.summary: Ways to offer crayons on many surfaces, white on black and color on white, for rubbing, resisting, melting, remaking and strong mark making.

items: A basket of chunky crayons and big paper taped to the table.
White and light crayons on black paper, with dark crayons and white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Peeled crayons on their sides for rubbings of bark, leaves, logs and textures around the site.
A white crayon drawing washed over with watercolor to reveal it.
A small jar of one color family, such as every blue, with white and black beside it.
Broken crayons sorted by color and remade in silicone molds in a low oven with an adult.
Beeswax block and stick crayons for layering soft color.
Crayons on sun-warmed rocks so the wax softens as it moves.
Crayon shavings between sheets of paper, warmed by an adult with an iron.
Crayon on sandpaper, cardboard, fabric, wood, brown kraft, gray paper and tracing paper.
Paper shapes beyond the rectangle, such as circles, long strips and torn pieces.
Crayons and clipboards in a bag for walks.
Drawing to music with a crayon in each hand.
Bright crayon layers covered with dark crayon and scratched through with a stick.
Crayon on cotton fabric, pressed under paper by an adult with an iron to set it.
Paper taped to the underside of a table for drawing while lying on the floor.
Big paper on the floor or wall for a small group drawing.
A crayon drawing on thin paper held to the window or laid on the light table so the color glows.
Letter stones and texture plates for rubbing in the Writing center.
Crayons sorted in clear jars by color on the open shelf.

sections.text: Both. A rubbing walk is a shared hunt for textures. A child alone at the table can press hard and fill a page.

Choose nontoxic crayons with the AP seal. Quality crayons lay down strong color with less pressing, which helps younger hands, and beeswax crayons are softer and glow in thin layers. Peeling paper is good hand work for children. Melting and ironing are adult jobs at low heat, with children watching from a set place. Keep broken pieces in a jar for remaking. Crayon on walls lifts with a damp cloth and a little baking soda.

items: Peels and sorts crayons by color.
Saves broken pieces for remaking.
Chooses paper color and surface.
Chooses surfaces and textures to rub.
Carries the crayon bag on walks.
Decides colors to melt together into a new crayon.
Lies under the table or stands at the wall to draw, choosing how to move.
Shows a friend how to use the side of a crayon.
Returns crayons to their jars.

sections.text: Children sort crayons back into their color jars and drop broken pieces into the remaking jar. They return leaf and bark rubbing pieces to the garden basket and stack paper back on the shelf by color. A jar for each color, labeled with a real crayon mark, lets children close this themselves before they move on.

Sit at the child's level with your hands relaxed and free. Name what you see, such as "You pressed hard and the color got bright," and leave praise of the picture aside. When crayons break, show calm interest and drop the pieces in the remaking jar together.

items: I wonder what is hiding under this paper.
How does the crayon feel on the warm rock?
I notice the white crayon shows on the black paper and hides on the white.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with chunky crayons and big paper.
For 2s, offer chunky and block crayons on big paper taped to the floor and wall. For 3s, add rubbings and resist. For 4s, add scratching, remaking and layering over days.
Peel crayons and use the sides.
Offer white crayons on black paper beside dark crayons on white paper.
Go on a rubbing walk and make a texture book.
Try crayon resist with watercolor.
Draw on new surfaces such as sandpaper, wood, fabric and kraft paper.
Model pressing hard and soft and layering two colors, then step back.
Save broken crayons and remake them with an adult.
Layer colors and scratch through.
Warm crayon on sun-warmed rocks on hot days.
Compare beeswax crayons with wax crayons.
Draw under the table, up on the wall and on the floor for big body drawing.
Look at Martín Ramírez's drawings of trains, tunnels and animals in crayon and pencil.
Draw maps, signs and letters with crayon.
Combine crayon with watercolor, collage and printmaking.
Open a self-serve crayon shelf sorted by color in the Studio and each class atelier.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Crayons are self-serve for every age. Remaking crayons in a low oven and ironing shavings or fabric are adult work, with children watching from a set place.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer pressing hard rubbings on bark and logs, drawing with a crayon in each hand to music, and paper taped under a table for drawing on their back.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer chunky crayons with the paper left on, a small sheet at a quiet table and no music. Let them choose to watch a rubbing walk before joining.
connected: Martín Ramírez on the Artists page, for crayon and pencil drawings of trains, tunnels and animals made while he lived at a state hospital in Auburn, California.

sections.text: Crayons, including broken ones and a white one, white and black paper, and things with texture such as leaves, coins and bark.

items: Peel a crayon and rub its side over paper laid on a leaf or a tree.
Draw with a white crayon, then paint over with watercolor.
Draw with white and light crayons on black paper.
Tape paper under a table and draw lying on your back.
Draw on a rock that has warmed in the sun.
Save broken crayons in a jar to send to school for remaking.

sections.text: Your child can peel crayons, find textures to rub, choose the paper and sort colors. Your child can sort crayons by color into cups or a muffin tin and keep broken bits in a jar for melting later. Rubbing leaves can go back outside.

items: I wonder what will show up when we rub here.
How does it look when you press hard and soft?

sections.text: Your child is building hand strength and noticing texture. Peeling and pressing crayons builds hand strength, and drawing with both hands helps the two sides of the body work together.
Send broken crayons for our crayon remaking. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Leave melting to adults. Crayon on walls lifts with a damp cloth and a little baking soda.

cards.title: Oil pastel
cards.summary: Ways to offer soft, buttery oil pastels on black, white and many papers for blending, layering, scratching and resisting.

items: White oil pastel on black paper, with a full set and white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Oil pastels on black, gray, brown kraft and colored paper.
A small limited set, such as one color with white and black, for finding light and dark versions.
A tray of warm colors and a tray of cool colors, each with its own paper.
A soft cloth for blending two colors with a fingertip.
A cotton swab with a drop of oil for blending colors on paper.
White pastel layered over colors to make lighter versions.
Oil pastel drawings washed over with watercolor so the lines resist.
Layers of bright color covered with dark pastel and scratched through with a stick.
Flowers from the garden in a small vase to draw while looking closely.
Feathers, shells and bark from our site set on black paper to look at and draw.
Marks for feelings after a few slow breaths together.
Oil pastel on sandpaper, then warmed by an adult with an iron to transfer onto cloth.
Oil pastel on rocks, wood, cardboard and fabric.
Clear acetate and oil pastels on the light table so colors glow.
Round paper, long strips and tiny cards for small and long drawings.
Clipboards and pastels outside in the shade on warm days.
Drawing to music with big swirling marks.
A shared sheet of black butcher paper on the floor for a calm group drawing.
Small boxes of pastels on a tray for open studio.

sections.text: Mostly alone. Blending and layering ask for slow attention. A shared sheet of black paper can become a group piece on a calm afternoon.

Choose oil pastels with the AP seal. Artist-grade oil pastels are softer and blend more easily than school sets, and a small set of quality colors goes a long way. They stay soft and never fully dry, so store finished work flat with paper between. Warm days soften them, so keep outdoor sets in the shade. Store pastels in a tray with sections so colors stay clean. Wipe hands on a cloth before washing. Oil for blending is a pantry staple and only a drop is needed. Scratching sticks stay pointed down.

items: Chooses paper color and pastel colors.
Chooses a warm, cool or limited set for the drawing.
Blends with fingers, cloth or swabs.
Decides when to add watercolor.
Scratches through layers with care.
Cleans a muddy pastel by rubbing it on a scrap.
Wipes and returns pastels to their box.
Shares a feelings drawing if they wish.
Shows a friend how to make a lighter color with white.

sections.text: Children rub a muddy pastel clean on a scrap, wipe fingers on the cloth and set each stick back in its section of the tray. They slip finished drawings between sheets of paper in the flat drawer and wipe the table with a damp cloth and a drop of soap. A tray with a section for each color, labeled by a swatch, makes the reset quick and complete.

Sit close and slow, especially when pastels follow a few calm breaths. Keep your voice soft and your face open to whatever marks appear. Model blending once on your own scrap, then put your hands in your lap.

items: I notice two colors meeting under your finger.
I wonder what is under the dark layer.
How did you make it glow on the black paper?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few colors on white paper.
For 2s, offer a few thick pastels on big white paper and big black paper. For 3s, add blending and resist. For 4s, add scratching, transfers and drawing from life over days.
Offer white pastel on black paper beside colors on white paper.
Offer black, gray, kraft and colored paper.
Explore blending with fingers, cloth and a drop of oil.
Add white to make lighter versions and black to make darker ones.
Offer warm and cool sets on separate days, then together.
Try oil pastel resist with watercolor.
Layer and scratch through with sticks.
Draw garden flowers and leaves from life.
Try sandpaper drawings and transfer them to cloth with an adult.
Draw on acetate for the light table.
Use pastel marks to share feelings after calm breathing.
Combine oil pastel with tempera, collage and printmaking.
Offer pastels in open studio beside chalk pastels for comparing.
Keep oil pastels on a self-serve tray in the Studio and each class atelier, sorted by color.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Oil pastels are self-serve once children know the tray. Ironing a sandpaper drawing onto cloth is adult work, and scratching through layers with sticks needs an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer blending with whole fingers, pressing thick layers and scratching through with a stick, on big black paper on the floor.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer pastels with paper wrappers, a cotton swab or cloth for blending and a wet wipe close by. Let the child choose a small sheet and a quiet spot.

sections.text: A small box of oil pastels with a white one, white and black paper, a soft cloth and a few cotton swabs.

items: Draw with white on black paper and with colors on white paper.
Rub two colors together with a finger to make a new one.
Draw, then paint over with watercolor.
Cover bright colors with black and scratch a picture with a stick.
Draw a flower or a feather while looking at it.

sections.text: Your child can choose the paper and colors, blend and decide when the picture is done. Your child can wipe each pastel on a scrap, put it back in the box and wipe hands on a soft cloth before washing. Store drawings flat with paper between them.

items: How did you make that new color?
I wonder what the black paper does to the colors.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is learning how colors blend and layer. Pressing and blending soft color gives the fingers strong feedback, and slow drawing can help a child notice and settle their feelings.
Send a photo of a blended drawing, or send black paper or sandpaper for the Studio. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Oil pastels smear and can mark fabric. Wipe hands on a cloth, then wash with soap.

cards.title: Chalk pastel
cards.summary: Ways to offer soft chalk pastels on black, white and toned papers for blending color, drawing light and sky, and making colored dust.

items: Soft pastels on black paper for glowing color, with white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
White and light pastels only on black paper, for drawing fog, clouds, feathers and leaf veins.
Soft pastels on toned, gray, brown kraft and colored paper with tissues for blending.
A limited set of one color with white and black, for finding light and dark.
Pastels on wet paper for strong bright color.
Pastels on sandpaper, rough cardboard and pastel paper with tooth.
A standing mirror with pastels for self-portraits.
An easel in the outdoor piazza facing the sky on a foggy morning and again at midday.
Garden blooms in a small vase to draw in soft color.
Small trays of a few colors for drawing a single sunset or sky.
Long strips of paper for drawing the line of hills and sky seen from the yards.
Stencils cut from cardstock with pastel rubbed along the edge and smudged out onto paper.
Fallen leaves laid on paper with pastel smudged out from their edges, then lifted.
A water brush pulled across pastel lines to turn them into paint.
Pastels at a standing easel for big arm drawing.
Black butcher paper on the wall for a small group drawing of the night sky or the moon.
Pastels on wood, stone and fabric, compared with paper.
Pastel ends ground in a mortar into colored dust for playdough or paint.
Pastel dust sifted through a screen onto paper and pressed with a palm.
Pastels on a tray in a class atelier with a damp sponge, ready for a quiet drawing.

sections.text: Mostly alone. Each child blends and smudges at their own pace. Grinding pastel dust and big wall drawings are lovely shared work.

Pastels make dust. Choose AP seal pastels, keep dust down with damp sponges and never blow it. Harder pastel sticks are less dusty for younger children, and soft artist pastels hold the strongest color. Pastel paper with tooth holds more layers than smooth paper. Grind dust outdoors. Children wash hands after. Spray fixatives are for adults away from children, and a clean sheet of paper laid over finished work keeps it from smearing.

items: Chooses black, white or toned paper.
Blends with fingers and tissues.
Decides whether to wet the paper first.
Cuts or tears stencils for smudging.
Grinds old pastel ends into dust.
Wipes the table with a damp sponge.
Covers finished work with a clean sheet.
Teaches a friend how to blend softly.
Returns pastels to the tray by color.

sections.text: Children press a damp sponge across the table to pick up the dust, rinse it at the low sink and return pastels to the tray by color. They lay a clean sheet over finished work and carry it to the flat drawer, then wash their hands. Damp sponges sit at each place from the start, so the dust is gone before children leave the table.

Sit at the table with a damp sponge in reach and wipe dust calmly as part of the work. Describe the colors you see the child making in a regular voice. Notice if dusty hands bother you and keep your face easy so the child feels free to smudge.

items: I notice two colors becoming one where you rubbed.
I notice the sky looks different now. How does it look to you?
I wonder how the white looks on the dark paper.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few colors on toned paper.
For 2s, offer harder, chunky pastels on big paper with a damp sponge. For 3s, add blending and black paper. For 4s, add stencils, wet paper and drawing from life.
Offer pastels on black paper beside white paper.
Add blending with fingers and tissues.
Model a light touch and blending with a fingertip, then step back.
Compare dry paper, wet paper and sandpaper.
Offer one color with white and black for light and dark.
Draw the sky and fog at different times of day.
Try self-portraits with mirrors.
Try stencils and leaf edges with smudged color.
Grind pastel ends into dust to color playdough and paint.
Look at Mary Cassatt's pastel portraits of parents and children.
Look at Edgar Degas's landscapes, where he added pastel on top of printed ink.
Compare chalk pastels and oil pastels side by side.
Combine with charcoal for light and dark.
Offer pastels in open studio with a damp sponge routine.

setting.why: Drawing with chalk pastels is open to everyone with a damp sponge close by. Grinding pastel ends into dust happens outdoors with an educator nearby, and spray fixative is adult work away from children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big arm drawing at a standing easel, grinding pastel ends in a mortar and blending with the whole palm.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer harder pastel sticks, a tissue for blending and a damp sponge right beside the paper. Let the child wear a glove on the drawing hand or blend with a paper stump.
connected: Mary Cassatt on the Artists page, for soft pastel portraits of parents and young children.
Edgar Degas on the Artists page, for landscapes made by adding pastel over a printed image.

sections.text: A small set of soft pastels with a white one, black and colored paper, tissues and a damp cloth.

items: Draw the sky at sunset and smudge colors together.
Draw with white and light colors on black paper.
Draw on wet paper and see the colors brighten.
Lay a leaf on paper and smudge color out from its edges.
Draw your face while looking in a mirror.

sections.text: Your child can choose colors and paper, blend with fingers and wipe the table after. Your child can wipe the table with a damp cloth, never blowing the dust, and put the pastels back by color. Then everyone washes hands together.

items: I wonder which colors are in the sky right now.
How did these two colors blend?

sections.text: Your child is noticing color and light and how colors blend. Smudging and blending with fingers builds touch awareness and hand control.
Send a sky drawing or photo of the sky from home for our window. You can also send old pastel ends for grinding. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Pastels are dusty. Draw on a tray, wipe with a damp cloth, never blow the dust, and wash hands after.

cards.title: Charcoal
cards.summary: Ways to offer charcoal for bold dark marks, smudging, erasing, light on dark grounds, comparing willow, vine and compressed charcoal, and making our own willow charcoal.

items: Willow and vine charcoal sticks with big paper taped to a wall or easel.
Compressed charcoal for dark bold lines.
White charcoal pencils or white chalk on black paper, with black charcoal on white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Charcoal and white chalk on gray or brown kraft paper, so dark and light both show.
Fingers, tissues and paper stumps for smudging.
Paper covered in charcoal, then erasers to draw light back in.
Kneaded erasers that children stretch and shape to lift small lights.
Newsprint, cardstock, watercolor paper and textured paper set side by side to test.
Charcoal tied to long sticks for big loose drawing on a roll of paper on the floor.
Shadows of plants and toys traced in charcoal on paper in the sun.
A single object lit by a lamp in a dim corner, for drawing light and shadow.
Willow, vine and compressed charcoal side by side, for testing which is darkest and which erases best.

Willow charcoal made by an adult from willow dome trimmings, sealed in a small metal tin and heated, with children watching from a marked distance and a willow twig beside the finished charcoal to compare.
Charcoal ground to powder and mixed with water to paint.
Charcoal over a dry watercolor wash.
Charcoal on big rocks, logs and stumps outdoors, left for the rain.
The oaks or the goats drawn from life on big paper on clipboards.
Tiny cards for small studies and long strips for whole branches.
A drawing changed, erased and drawn again in steps, with a photo of each step for a short moving picture.
A lidded tin of charcoal, a damp cloth and paper on a tray in a class atelier.

sections.text: Both. Big paper on a wall invites shared bold drawing. Erasing and redrawing is slow work for one child.

Charcoal is dusty and smudges everything. Use smocks, damp cloths for cleanup and never blow the dust. Vine and willow charcoal are light and easy to erase, and compressed charcoal is darker and messier. Paper with tooth holds more charcoal than smooth paper, and newsprint is fine for big loose work. Charcoal on a long stick keeps hands cleaner and makes big marks. We make willow charcoal on purpose from willow dome trimmings. An adult seals the sticks in a small metal tin and heats it in a contained fire set up only for charcoal making, with clear agreements and children at a marked distance. We do not have campfires. The tin must cool completely before opening. We also buy willow, vine and compressed charcoal from an art supplier. Store charcoal in a lidded tin.

items: Chooses vine or compressed charcoal.
Chooses black, white or gray paper and the tool to match.
Smudges, erases and redraws.
Shapes a kneaded eraser to lift small lights.
Gathers and bundles willow trimmings from the dome for our charcoal making, then compares a twig with the finished charcoal.
Tests different kinds of charcoal and shares what they notice.
Wipes surfaces with a damp cloth.
Photographs drawing steps with an adult.
Covers finished drawings with clean paper.

sections.text: Children wipe the table with damp cloths, folding them so the dust stays inside, and rinse the cloths in the wash bucket. Charcoal sticks go back into the lidded tin by kind, erasers into their dish and finished drawings under a clean sheet in the flat drawer. Everything has a labeled place within reach, so the close is part of the drawing time.

Stand or kneel beside the big paper and stay with the noise and mess of bold drawing. Show comfort with black hands and smudged faces. When a child erases or redraws, narrate the change, such as "The light came back where you rubbed," and let the drawing keep changing.

items: I wonder where the willow went when it became charcoal.
How did the eraser find the light in the dark?
Where is the light in what you are drawing?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with vine charcoal on big paper.
For 2s, offer chunky charcoal on big paper on the wall or floor, with plenty of wiping. For 3s, add smudging and erasing. For 4s, add drawing from life, toned paper and drawings that change in steps.
Add smudging tools.
Try drawing light with erasers.
Offer white on black and black on white side by side.
Add white chalk and toned paper.
Draw with charcoal tied to long sticks.
Trace shadows in the sun.
Draw a lit object in a dim corner and notice light and shadow.
Compare willow, vine and compressed charcoal and name the differences.
Make willow charcoal together, with children gathering the willow and watching from a marked distance, then wonder how wood turns black.
Grind charcoal into paint.
Look at Käthe Kollwitz's charcoal drawings of mothers holding their children and notice how dark and light carry feeling.
Look at William Kentridge's drawings that he changes again and again to make films.
Make a drawing that changes in steps and photograph each step.
Combine charcoal with watercolor, chalk pastel and earth paint.
Offer charcoal in open studio with a damp cloth routine.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Drawing with charcoal is open to everyone. Making willow charcoal is adult work with children watching from a marked distance.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer charcoal tied to long sticks on paper taped high on a wall, big bold arm drawing and heavy erasing.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a charcoal pencil or a stick wrapped in foil, a small sheet and a damp cloth beside it. Let the child draw with an eraser into charcoal another child laid down.
connected: Käthe Kollwitz on the Artists page, for charcoal drawings of mothers and children full of dark and light.
William Kentridge on the Artists page, for charcoal drawings he erases and redraws to make animated films.

sections.text: A few sticks of vine charcoal, a piece of white chalk, big white paper and a sheet of black or brown paper, an eraser and a damp cloth.

items: Draw big on paper taped to a wall or the floor.
Smudge lines with a finger.
Cover paper in charcoal and draw light shapes with an eraser.
Draw with white chalk on black paper beside charcoal on white paper.
Trace shadows of toys or plants in the sun.

sections.text: Your child can choose the paper, decide how to smudge and erase, and wipe up after. Your child can wipe up the dust with a damp cloth, put the charcoal back in its tin and wash hands well. A sheet of paper over a finished drawing keeps it from smudging.

items: I wonder what will happen when you erase into the dark.
Where did the shadow go?

sections.text: Your child is learning about light and dark and that drawings can change. Big arm drawing on a wall uses the shoulders and the whole body, and smudging dark and light helps children notice changes they make.
Send a photo of a shadow drawing, or a box of willow or vine charcoal from an art store. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Charcoal is dusty and smudges clothes. Use old clothes, wipe with a damp cloth, never blow the dust, and wash hands after.

cards.title: Chalk
cards.summary: Ways to offer chalk on the ground, on black paper and boards, and as dust, for drawing, mapping, mixing and changing.

items: A basket of thick chalk beside open concrete, with nothing drawn first.
White chalk on black paper and chalkboards, with colored chalk and white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Chalk dipped in water for bright wet lines.
Chalk on wet black paper, where colors turn strong.
Chalk on brown kraft paper, gray paper, cardboard, wood fences and stepping stones.
Shadows of children, toys and plants traced on the outdoor piazza, then traced again later in the day.
Chalk paint from chalk dust, cornstarch and water in squeeze bottles or with brushes.
Chalk ground with salt in a mortar and layered into a shared jar.
Chalk dust kneaded into playdough to color it.
Chalk on rocks, logs and stumps in the Log yard.
Big chalk roads, paths and maps for toy vehicles.
Chalk marks on a ramp or slope to see how far balls roll.
Names, letters and signs written outdoors.
Spray bottles of water over chalk drawings to watch them change.
Chalk tied to long sticks for drawing standing up.
Chalk made by an adult from plaster and water in molds, then colored by children.
Game lines and obstacle courses children design and draw.
A chalk drawing left out in the rain and visited after.
A chalkboard wall or easel in a class atelier for drawing, erasing and drawing again.
A shared mural on the outdoor piazza across a week, added to each day.

sections.text: Both. Big surfaces invite teamwork. Paper and a small board hold a child's own thinking.

Thick sidewalk chalk suits small hands and strong pressing. Colored chalk shows strongest on black, and white chalk on black paper is a regular invitation. Chalkboard paint on a board or wall gives every class a surface for erasing and redrawing. Chalk dust is fine, so grind outside and never blow it. Store chalk dry. Outdoor drawings wash away, so photograph the ones children want to keep. An adult mixes plaster away from children.

items: Carries the chalk basket outside and back.
Decides where to draw and what to keep.
Chooses black or white paper and the chalk to go with it.
Grinds chalk and adds a layer to the shared jar.
Mixes chalk paint.
Designs games and courses for friends.
Washes drawings away or chooses to leave them.
Erases the chalkboard with a damp cloth for the next friend.
Photographs drawings to keep with an adult.

sections.text: Children gather chalk pieces into the basket, drop tiny ends into the grinding jar and carry the basket back to its shelf. They decide which drawings stay, ask for a photo of the ones they want to keep, and wash the rest away with watering cans or a wet broom. Chalkboards get a damp cloth from the children, so the close needs no educator time.

Get down on the ground with the children and stay there. Keep your voice regular and your body relaxed as drawings grow and wash away. Narrate the change, such as "The water made your line bright," and let children decide what to keep.

items: I wonder where the line went.
How did the water change your drawing?
It reminds me of a road. Where does it go?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with thick chalk on open concrete.
For 2s, offer thick chalk outdoors and big black paper on the floor. For 3s, add water, shadows and roads. For 4s, add games, maps, grinding and drawings kept by photograph over days.
Offer white chalk on black paper beside colored chalk on white paper.
Add water to chalk and to drawings.
Trace shadows at different times of day.
Grind chalk into dust and layer a shared jar.
Use dust to color playdough and make chalk paint.
Draw roads, maps and games together.
Use chalk marks with ramps and rolling.
Leave drawings for the rain and notice what stays.
Make chalk with an adult from plaster.
Look at Keith Haring's quick white chalk drawings on black paper in the New York subway and try fast white lines on black.
Draw a mural together across days on the outdoor piazza.
Combine chalk with charcoal on toned paper.
Photograph outdoor drawings and gather them into a book.
Keep chalk and a small board on a tray in each class atelier.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Chalk is open to everyone indoors and out. Grinding chalk in a mortar needs an educator nearby, and mixing plaster for homemade chalk is adult work away from children.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer drawing long roads while crawling, grinding chalk with salt in a heavy mortar, and chalk on long sticks for walking lines across the piazza.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small chalkboard and one thick chalk at a quiet table, with a damp cloth nearby. Let the child draw on paper first before joining the busy ground.
connected: Keith Haring on the Artists page, for quick white chalk drawings he made on black paper in the New York subway.

sections.text: Thick sidewalk chalk, a patch of concrete or a chalkboard, black paper, a cup of water and a spray bottle.

items: Trace each other's shadows in the morning, then again in the afternoon.
Dip chalk in water and draw.
Draw with white chalk on black paper.
Draw a road or a maze for toy cars or bikes.
Spray a drawing with water and watch it change.

sections.text: Your child can choose where to draw, invent games and wash the drawings away. Your child can pick up every piece of chalk, put the little ends in a jar and wash a drawing away with a watering can or a wet broom when they are ready.

items: I wonder why your shadow moved.
How will the rain change our drawing?
