sections.text: Your child is building strong hands and noticing how things change. Drawing on the ground while kneeling and crawling builds whole-body strength and balance, and pressing chalk builds hand strength.
Send a photo of a shadow drawing, or send sidewalk chalk for our yards. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Chalk washes off with water. Grind chalk outdoors and avoid breathing the dust.

cards.title: Color mixing
cards.summary: Ways children build their own understanding of color through limited palettes, from one primary to all three, through tints, shades, tones and neutrals, and toward the real colors of our site.

items: One primary only, such as blue tempera, with water, a palette and white paper, so children find every blue one color can give.
One color with white on a palette, for mixing tints from the deepest red to the palest pink.
One color with black in a tiny dish, for mixing shades a drop at a time.
One color with gray mixed first from black and white, for finding softer, quieter tones.
Two primaries only, such as yellow and blue, so children discover a secondary color on their own.
A primary with its neighbor, such as yellow with orange or blue with green, for mixing the tertiary colors in between.
All three primaries with white and black on a palette, once children know each one well.
Complementary pairs, such as red with green or blue with orange, mixed toward browns, grays and neutrals.
A warm palette of reds, oranges and yellows on one table and a cool palette of blues, greens and purples on another.
A whole week of one color, with that color in paint, chalk, crayon, cellophane, playdough and found objects from our site on every tray.
Long strips of paper for children's own color charts, painting one color step by step from light to dark.
Blank cards, a hole punch and rings for children to make their own swatch books of the colors they mix.
Paper circles for children to make their own color wheels, in any order that makes sense to them.

A basket of real things from our site on the easel tray, such as a valley oak leaf, a rose petal, a crow feather, coast live oak bark, a scoop of soil and a photo of today's sky, with paint to match each one.
Paint sample cards carried on a garden hunt to find matching colors.
Black paper with white and one color, beside white paper with the same colors, to see how the ground changes a color.
Colored water in clear jars or a muffin tin with droppers and an empty tin for mixing.
Color paddles, colored acetate and cellophane on the light table and in sunny windows.
Two colors of paint sealed in a zip bag taped to a window to squish together.
Paint mixed for skin colors in self-portraits and family portraits.

sections.text: Both. A child alone with a limited palette can follow one color all morning, in the Studio or in any class atelier. Color hunts on our site, a shared week of one color and comparing swatch books are full of talk and shared discovery.

Our paint palette is red, yellow, blue, white and black, and children mix every other color. Offer few colors at a time so children can go deep with each one. Add dark to light a little at a time, since a drop of black or blue changes a lot of white and a lot of white is needed to change a dark. Choose a red and a blue that mix a clear purple and test before buying. Palettes with wells, flat white trays or plates give room to mix, and a palette knife or spare brush keeps colors clean. Keep a clean water cup and a sponge at each place. Color water with liquid watercolor, paint or chalk dust, and keep food dyes and kitchen foods out of mixing. Gather real things for matching with care, confirm every plant, and return them to the garden or compost after.

items: Chooses the palette for the day from a few limited sets.
Squeezes or pours small amounts and adds dark to light a little at a time.
Mixes a color step by step and paints a chart from light to dark.
Names new colors and adds them to the color library and their own swatch book.
Brings a leaf, petal, feather or stone from our site to match and decides when the match is close.
Makes a color wheel in the order that makes sense to them.
Mixes their own skin color for a portrait.
Teaches a friend how they made a color.
Cleans palettes, knives and droppers and sets out the palette for the next friend.

sections.text: Children scrape extra paint off palettes with the palette knife, rinse palettes, knives and droppers in the wash bucket and stack them on the drying rack. Gathered leaves, petals and stones go back to the garden or the compost bucket. Each tool has a photo-labeled home, so the palette is set out for the next friend before children leave.

Sit beside the palette with real curiosity and let the colors go muddy without fixing them. Describe what you see, such as "A little blue made the yellow green," in a calm voice. Model adding a little at a time on your own swatch, then step back.

items: I wonder how you made that color. Can you show me?
I notice it changed when you added a little more white.
Where on our site can you find this color?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one primary and water, then that primary as thick paint, so children meet a single hue fully.
Add white to that one color for tints and paint a chart from dark to light.
Add black to the same color for shades, a drop at a time.
Mix gray from black and white and add it for tones.
Offer two primaries and let children find a secondary on their own.
Offer a primary with its neighbor to find tertiary colors in between.
Offer all three primaries with white and black.
Mix complements together and follow them toward browns, grays and neutrals.
Set out warm and cool palettes and paint with each.
Live a whole week with one color across mediums and spaces.

For 2s, offer one or two colors and let mixing happen on the paper and on hands. For 3s, offer two primaries and white on a palette. For 4s, offer limited sets in sequence, charts, swatch books and color wheels children design.
Model a few ways to mix, such as adding a little at a time and wiping the brush between colors, then step back.
Keep children's own color charts, swatch books and color wheels in the class atelier and add to them across the year.
Match paint to real colors from our site, such as leaves, petals, bark, soil, feathers and sky, and paint a swatch beside each thing.
Follow one plant's colors across the year, such as the Japanese maple or the pomegranate leaves, and mix each new color as it changes.
Mix with water and light, using droppers, jars, the light table, prisms in a sunny window and colored ice melting on a white tray.
Mix with hands in playdough and sealed bags.
Mix skin colors for portraits of ourselves and our families.
Look at Josef Albers's squares and notice how a color changes beside another, then test our own colors on black, white and gray paper.
Look at Claude Monet's wheat stacks in different light, Alma Thomas's paintings to find every color she used, and Wassily Kandinsky's color study of circles in squares.

setting.why: Mixing on a palette is open to everyone. A color hunt in the garden follows our ratio of one adult to six children, and an adult confirms every plant before it is picked.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer squishing paint in sealed bags, kneading colored playdough and mixing with hands in thick tempera on a tray.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one color with white, a palette knife for mixing and a small card for a swatch. Droppers and jars of colored water keep hands dry.
connected: Claude Monet on the Artists page, for painting the same stacks of wheat again in different light.
Josef Albers on the Artists page, for showing how a color changes beside other colors.
Alma Thomas on the Artists page, for bright colors set side by side in small patches.
Wassily Kandinsky on the Artists page, for a color study of circles in squares, each color beside its neighbors.

sections.text: Red, yellow, blue, white and black washable paint, a paper plate or old tray for mixing, a brush, paper, a cup of water and a rag. Things from a walk, such as leaves, petals and feathers, are wonderful for matching.

items: Put out only one color and white, and make as many light versions as you can.
Put out just yellow and blue, or red and yellow, and see what appears.
Paint a strip of paper from dark to light, one square at a time.
Bring home a leaf or petal from a walk and mix paint to match it.
Mix the color of your skin and paint your family.
Make a little book of the colors you mixed and give each one a name.

sections.text: Your child can choose the colors, add a little at a time, mix, name what they make and decide when a match is close enough. Your child can rinse the mixing plate and brush, wipe the table and carry leaves and petals back outside. A towel by the sink is enough to make this their job.

items: I wonder what these two will make.
How much black does it take to change it?
Tell me the name of your new color.

sections.text: Your child is discovering how colors combine and change, and is learning to look closely at the colors of the world around them. Mixing colors with a brush or palette knife builds hand control, and slow mixing helps many children feel calm and focused.
Send the name and a swatch of a color your child invented for our color library, or a page from their home swatch book. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Paint can stain. Cover the table, use an old shirt, and add dark colors a little at a time so less paint is used.

cards.title: Printmaking
cards.summary: Ways to offer printing with found objects, leaves, plates, stamps and cloth on many papers, from simple pressing to layered prints and white on black.

items: Spools, corks, lids, blocks and loose parts beside shallow trays of paint for stamping.
White ink or white paint rolled on plates and printed on black paper, with black ink on white paper alongside so children can compare and choose.
Fallen leaves rolled with paint and pressed onto paper or cloth.
A plexiglass sheet or gel plate rolled with paint, drawn into with fingers and sticks, then printed.
A gel plate rolled with one color, then a second color printed over it, so colors mix in layers.
Foam plates pressed with a pencil to make lines, then rolled with paint and printed.
Cardboard plates with string, lace, leaves and textures glued on, then inked and printed.
Bubble wrap, corrugated cardboard and burlap to roll and print.
Flowers and leaves laid on cloth, covered and pounded with mallets to print their color.
Stamps children make from clay or craft foam glued to wood blocks.
Rubbings of bark and textures as a print without paint.
Bare feet and hands printed on long paper outdoors, then washed in a tub.
Toy vehicle tires and pine cones rolled through paint.
A small tabletop press, a heavy roller or the back of a wooden spoon for pressing prints.
Papers to print on, such as newsprint, brown kraft, gray, colored paper, tissue, fabric and old maps.
Prints pulled on circles, long strips and tiny cards for books, garlands and mail.
Letter stamps in the Writing center for signs and letters.
String wound around a block for printing lines.
One plate printed many times to notice how each print changes.
A printing table on the outdoor piazza with a drying line strung between two posts and clothespins.

sections.text: Both. Stamping and long paper prints are lively and shared. Making a plate is one child's slow planning.

Brayers roll paint thin and even. Use water-based block printing ink, tempera or acrylic. Black, white and the three primaries in water-based ink let children mix print colors on a glass or plexiglass slab with a palette knife. Roll ink thin until the surface looks even and slightly textured, since thick ink fills fine lines. Wipe gel plates with a damp cloth and store them flat with their cover. Set up a drying rack or line before printing. Pounding needs mallets, a firm board and clear agreements. Soft carving blocks and lino cutters are for older children only, one at a time, with a bench hook, a cut-resistant glove and an adult beside them. Bare feet printing happens on a towel path with a wash tub and shoes go back on after.

items: Chooses objects and leaves to print.
Mixes ink colors on the slab with a palette knife.
Rolls paint with a brayer.
Makes their own stamps and plates.
Chooses paper color and shape for each print.
Pulls prints and hangs them on the drying line.
Decides how many prints to make.
Cleans brayers, plates and trays.
Shows a friend how to press evenly.

sections.text: Children roll brayers on scrap paper until they are nearly dry, then wash brayers, plates and trays in the wash bucket and stand them on the rack. They wipe gel plates with a damp cloth and slide them into their covers, and pin the last prints on the drying line. For bare feet printing, children walk the towel path to the wash tub, dry off and put their own shoes back on.

Stay at the printing table through the whole cycle of inking, pressing and lifting, so children feel your steady presence. Keep your face calm when a print comes out blurry or blotchy, and say what you see. Model clean brayer care with slow hands, then let children lead.

items: I wonder what will show up on the paper.
How is this print different from the first one?
I notice the white print looks strong on the black paper.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with found objects and stamping.
For 2s, offer big stamps, hands and rollers on big paper. For 3s, add leaves, brayers and gel plates. For 4s, add foam plates, texture plates, layered prints and sets of many prints.
Print leaves and natural finds.
Add brayers and rolling.
Print white on black and black on white side by side.
Try monoprints on plexiglass or a gel plate.
Layer prints in two colors and notice where they mix.
Make foam plate prints.
Build cardboard and texture plates.
Make stamps from clay and foam.
Pound flowers and leaves into cloth.
Print on fabric for banners and books.
Carve soft blocks with an adult, for older children ready for the tool.
Look at Katsushika Hokusai's woodblock prints of waves.
Look at Elizabeth Catlett's carved linocut prints and Kenojuak Ashevak's prints of owls and birds.
Look at Ruth Asawa's prints made by repeating one laundry stamp across a page, then print one stamp again and again in patterns.
Make a set of prints for a class book or for mail to other classes.
Keep a printing tray in the Studio and each class atelier with a brayer, a slab and a drying rack.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Inking, pressing and lifting go best with an adult at the table through the whole cycle. Carving soft blocks with lino cutters is one adult with one child, with a bench hook and a cut-resistant glove, and pounding flowers needs clear mallet agreements.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer pounding flowers into cloth with mallets, rolling a heavy brayer and pressing prints with the whole body weight on a press or roller.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a stamp with a handle, a small tray of paint and a quiet table. Let the child pull a print a friend has inked, or watch the first prints before trying.
connected: Katsushika Hokusai on the Artists page, for woodblock prints of waves and mountains.
Elizabeth Catlett on the Artists page, for strong carved linocut prints of people.
Kenojuak Ashevak on the Artists page, for bold printed owls and birds.
Edgar Degas on the Artists page, for one-of-a-kind printed landscapes he finished with pastel.
Ruth Asawa on the Artists page, for patterns she printed by repeating one laundry stamp across a page.

sections.text: Washable paint on a plate, white and black paper, and things to print with such as corks, lids, spools, leaves and bubble wrap.

items: Dip lids, spools and blocks into paint and stamp.
Paint a fallen leaf and press it onto paper.
Print with white paint on dark paper.
Roll toy cars through paint on long paper.
Lay leaves and flowers on an old cloth, cover with paper and tap with a hammer to print their color.

sections.text: Your child can choose what to print and which paper to use, press, and decide how many times. Your child can roll the paint off the roller onto old paper, wash the tools in a bowl of soapy water and hang prints on a string with clothespins.

items: I wonder what shape this will make.
Why is the second print lighter?

sections.text: Your child is learning about pattern, texture and cause and effect. Rolling, pressing and pounding give the body heavy work, and holding the paper while pressing helps both hands work together.
Send corks, spools, lids and bubble wrap for our printing trays. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Cover the table. Hammer printing needs an adult close by.

cards.title: Sun prints
cards.summary: Ways children use sunlight to print shapes of plants and objects on sun print paper, cloth and fading paper, across seasons and weather.

items: Sun print paper laid in the sun with leaves, feathers, flowers and loose parts on top, then rinsed in water.
Dark construction paper with objects on top, left on a sunny table or window for several days to fade.
Black, blue, red and brown construction paper faded side by side, to see which colors change most.
Sun print cloth squares joined into a shared banner.
A clear acrylic sheet on top to keep things flat in the wind.
Hands held still on large sun print paper.
Drawings made on clear acetate with black marker, then printed in the sun.
Cut and torn paper shapes laid on sun print paper for a printed collage.
Things that let some light through, such as feathers, petals, tissue and lace, beside things that block it all.
Prints made on a sunny day, a foggy day and a cloudy day for comparing.
A sand timer for counting the minutes in the sun.
Pressed plants from the garden printed on sun print paper.
Keys, mesh, washers and other loose parts printed.
The same plant printed through its life, from sprout to seed.
Old cloth left in the sun under leaves to fade.
Sun print paper cut into tiny cards, circles and long strips for books and garlands.
Finished blue prints drawn into with white pencil, white ink or a white gel pen.
Paper painted by an adult with color pressed from botanical dye bed petals, then left under leaves in the sun for many days so the sun fades the uncovered parts, a process called anthotype.
A sun print kit on a tray by a class atelier window, ready to carry into the sun.

sections.text: Both. Each child arranges their own print. Rinsing and comparing is a lively small group gathering.

Buy pre-treated sun print paper and cloth and store them in a dark bag until use. Mixing the chemicals is an adult job and is not offered to children. Shapes come out white on deep blue, so white pencils and inks add naturally to finished prints. Rinse prints in a tub of water and dry them flat. The blue deepens over a day. Bright midday sun prints in a few minutes and fog days take longer. Weigh things down in wind. Anthotypes take days to weeks and fade again if they hang in the sun, so display them away from bright windows.

items: Chooses and arranges objects.
Tests which objects let light through.
Holds still and watches the timer.
Rinses prints in the tub.
Compares prints from different days.
Gathers fallen plants with an adult.
Lays prints to dry and labels them.
Adds white drawing to a finished print.
Explains the process to a friend.

sections.text: Children slide unused sun print paper back into the dark bag and lift the weights off. Objects go back to their basket and plants to the garden or compost. They rinse prints in the tub, lay them flat on the drying rack and tip the rinse water onto bare ground, so the whole close happens where the prints were made.

Sit with the child in the sun and share the waiting with a calm body and few words. Notice warmth, light and stillness aloud, such as "The sun feels warm on our arms." Let children arrange their own objects without adjusting them.

items: I wonder what the sun will do to the paper.
I notice this side is lighter. How did that happen?
Where did the feather let the light through?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with fading paper over several days.
For 2s, offer hands and big simple objects on fading paper. For 3s, add sun print paper, rinsing and a timer. For 4s, add acetate drawings, cloth, anthotypes and prints through the seasons.
Try sun print paper with simple objects.
Print plants and feathers.
Compare objects that block light with ones that let some through.
Use a timer and compare short and long times.
Compare sunny, foggy and cloudy days.
Draw on acetate and print the drawing.
Print on cloth and make a banner.
Make anthotypes with petals from the botanical dye bed.
Draw into finished prints with white pencil and white ink.
Print the same plant through the seasons.
Look at Anna Atkins's sun prints of algae from long ago.
Combine sun prints with collage and bookmaking.
Make a class book of sun prints from the garden.
Keep a sun print kit in each class atelier for sunny days.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Sun print paper comes pre-treated, so children arrange and rinse with an educator close by. Mixing sun print chemicals is adult work and never offered to children, and an adult paints the petal color for anthotypes.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running prints out into the sun and back, carrying the rinse tub, and timing prints with a big sand timer.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small card, a few flat objects and a quiet shady spot to arrange them. Let the child watch a print rinse before trying their own.
connected: Anna Atkins on the Artists page, for her book of sun prints of algae.

sections.text: Dark construction paper or sun print paper, leaves and small objects, a sunny spot, a white pencil, and a tub of water if you use sun print paper.

items: Lay leaves and keys on dark paper in a sunny window and check after a few days.
Make a sun print with special paper and rinse it.
Try a feather or a piece of lace and see where light gets through.
Try on a cloudy day and compare.
Draw on a finished blue print with a white pencil.

sections.text: Your child can choose and arrange the objects, rinse the print and decide what to add. Your child can carry leaves and objects back to where they belong and lay prints flat to dry. If you used water, they can rinse the print and pour the tub out.

items: I wonder what the sun changed.
Why do you think the leaf shape stayed?

sections.text: Your child is noticing how sunlight changes things over time. Holding still and waiting in the sun helps children notice their own bodies and practice calm, and arranging small objects builds careful hands.
Send a sun print made at home for our window, or send leaves and flat objects for printing. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use pre-treated paper and keep it in the dark until use. Wash hands after rinsing prints.

cards.title: Clay
cards.summary: Real earthenware clay offered from a first big block with bare hands to tools, slabs, coils and shared sculptures.

items: A whole 25 lb block of clay set on a low table or a canvas cloth on the floor, with nothing else, so hands meet it first.
A big block outside on a stump in the Log yard, where children can push, punch, stand on and lean into it.
Clay beside a basket of natural tools such as sticks, acorn caps, pinecones, feathers from our chickens and smooth stones.
Small bowls of water and sponges beside the clay, so children find out what water does to it.
Clay pressed onto textured bases such as bark, leaves, burlap, bricks and the tire swing tire to see what marks stay.
Slabs rolled out flat for printing, cutting and building small walls, houses and bowls.
Clay in different states side by side, a dry chunk, a soft piece, a bowl of slip and a jar of dry powder.
A shared clay piece on one large board that a small group adds to over several days.
Clay set near a lamp or flashlights so children can watch shadows on their forms.
For the West class, a fist-sized ball for each child and lots of time just to squeeze, poke and pat.
Labeled boards on a drying shelf where finished pieces wait and children can visit them.
A color study in slip, with three small jars of white, buff and red clay slip and wide flat brushes, offered on a gray clay slab and a white tile side by side.
Leather-hard tiles carved with loop tools, forks, nails and pencil ends, so lines show as light marks on a dark surface.
Clay on a canvas-covered board, a slate tile, a mirror, a metal tray, a wooden round and a smooth river stone, so children feel how each surface grabs or releases the clay.
A tool tray with wooden paddles, a rolling pin, a fettling knife, a loop tool, a fork, a garlic press, a cut wire, a sponge on a stick and a spray bottle, offered a few at a time.
Clay in the class atelier on a low table near the window, with the same boards and tools as the Studio, so a child can return to clay any day.
A clay table under the valley oaks on a warm morning, with a bucket of water, a cloth to keep the block damp and leaves falling onto the work.
Observation clay beside a real object from our site, such as a pinecone, a snail shell, an egg from our chickens or a branch of feijoa, set on a black cloth so its edges stand out.
For the North class, short coils and balls on individual boards, with a wooden tool or two and a small dish of slip for joining.
For the South class, a slab roller or two guide sticks and a rolling pin for even slabs that become tiles, boxes, masks and story scenes.

sections.text: Both. A big block on the floor draws a group into pushing and talking together. A child alone with a small piece can follow an idea for a long time. In the Studio a small group can share one big block and one long conversation. In a class atelier a child can sit with clay beside the window during free choice time and work quietly for as long as the idea lasts.

Store clay wrapped tight in plastic in a lidded bin and reclaim dry scraps by soaking them in a bucket of water. Wipe tables and floors with a damp sponge and never sweep or brush dry clay, because the dust is not good to breathe. Pieces dry slowly on boards away from sun and can be fired by a potter in our community or left as air dried work. Wedge or knead clay before it goes out so it is soft and free of air pockets. Keep slip in lidded jars and mix it from dry scraps and water to the thickness of yogurt. A damp cloth over unfinished work and a plastic bag over the board keeps it workable for days. Air dried clay stays fragile, so we tell children it can crack and that cracks are part of the story. Wash tools in a bucket first and pour the settled water into the garden, never the sink, because clay clogs drains. Keep wet towels close for wiping hands. Keep the block out for weeks, so the work can become a thread or a project. The youngest children may bring clay toward their mouths, so stay close, name what they are doing and offer the clay again for hands, such as Clay is for our hands. You can squeeze it. Stay close whenever a clay wire is in use. Label stored pieces with the child's name and the date, and talk with children about how drying clay grows lighter and more fragile.

items: Wedge and pat the block ready with an educator.
Choose tools and decide when a piece needs water.
Name and label their own board.
Show a friend a way they found to make a coil or a hole.
Decide if a piece is finished, still growing or going back to the bucket.
Help wrap the clay, sponge the table and soak the scraps.
Tell or draw the story of their piece for documentation.
Mix slip from dry scraps and water and decide when it is thick enough.
Choose a surface for their work, such as canvas, wood, slate or stone.
Cover unfinished work with a damp cloth and check it the next day.

sections.text: Children press scraps into the reclaim bucket, sponge the boards and the table, and lay a damp cloth over unfinished work. Tools go into the wash bucket, then onto the drying rack and back to their photo-labeled tray. The settled bucket water goes to the garden later in the day, carried by children, so no clay reaches a drain and no educator stays after.

Sit at the low table with your own small piece of clay and let your hands get as wet and gray as the children's. Keep your face soft when clay reaches sleeves and floors, and narrate what you see, such as You pressed with your thumb and it made a deep hollow. Leave their forms as they are, even when a piece slumps or cracks. Notice how the youngest children poke, pat and press, and how older children use force, fists and elbows with growing intention. Watch for children beginning to work together on one form, such as digging a tunnel, and for how a child solves a problem, such as a bowl that holds things or an animal that stands up.

items: I notice the clay holds the print of your thumb.
I wonder what will happen to it by tomorrow.
How did you make it stand up?
Tell me about the slip you mixed.
What do you see that makes you say that?
I wonder what would happen if you pushed it with your elbow.
Your sculpture is a lighter gray today. How does it feel now?
How does the clay feel different from the mud in our yards after rain?
Hands only with the big block, many times over, until children know its weight and smell.
For the West class, keep clay to hands and a few natural tools for many weeks, with soft clay and plenty of water.
For the North class, add one wooden tool at a time and small boards each child can name.
Add natural tools from our garden and yards.
Add wooden tools, the wire cutter and rolling pins, one at a time with a short story about each.
Offer water and slip and let children find out how pieces join.
Explore balls, coils and slabs and the shapes children invent from them.
Press textures from around our site and make a texture wall of clay tiles.
Build up tall and hollow forms, then wonder together about balance.
Look at clay with magnifiers and a microscope to see what is inside it.
Dig a little soil from the garden, soak it and sieve it to find out if our own ground holds clay.
Offer clay with other materials such as wire, sticks and loose parts.
Make a group sculpture or a clay village that grows over many days.
Visit pottery made by Maria Martinez and Toshiko Takaezu on screen, and invite a local potter to throw on a wheel.
Watch pieces dry, change color and maybe come back from a kiln, then compare wet, dry and fired.
Paint leather-hard pieces with white, buff and red slip only, so children study how a few earth colors sit beside each other.
Model techniques without making a product, such as scoring and slipping a join, smoothing with a wet finger and hollowing a thick form so it dries without cracking.
Make observational clay from real things on our site, such as acorns, a goat's ear, a snail or a fig leaf, and keep the object beside the clay.
For the South class, plan a piece in a drawing, make it in clay and compare the drawing and the form.
Open studio, where children take clay from the shelf when an idea calls for it.
When ideas grow bigger than hands can manage, quietly set a small basket of natural tools nearby and watch.
When a child wants to keep a piece, show how to pull the clay wire taut and cut it from the block.
When children begin to shape faces and bodies, offer clay self portraits beside drawing, paint and wire, as the Seeing Ourselves module describes.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Clay is open to everyone with an educator close by to keep it damp and the dust down. The wire cutter and fettling knife are used with an adult at the table, and firing is done by a potter away from children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the whole 25 lb block on the floor to push, punch, lean on and wedge, and a wire cutter to slice thick pieces off with two hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small piece of firm clay on a board with a wooden tool or a stick, so hands stay clean, and a damp cloth close by for wiping.
connected: Maria Martinez on the Artists page, for polished black pottery made from local clay by hand.
Toshiko Takaezu on the Artists page, for round closed clay forms that hold an empty space inside.
Viola Frey on the Artists page, for huge clay figures made in the Bay Area.
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A small bag of air dry clay or earthenware clay from a craft store, a bowl of water, a sponge and an old placemat or cutting board. A spray bottle, a fork, a wooden spoon and a few smooth stones make good first tools.

items: Give a big lump and let hands squeeze, pat and pound it with no plan.
Press leaves, keys, shells or fabric into a flat piece to see the marks.
Roll snakes and balls and see what they turn into.
Make a little home for a toy or a bowl for treasures.
Make a small pinch pot by pressing a thumb into a ball and turning it slowly.
Sit outside with clay and a leaf, a pinecone or a shell and try making what you see.

sections.text: Your child decides what the clay becomes, and that it might change many times. Let them help set up, add water and wipe up. Your child can also choose what surface to work on, such as a board, a placemat or a flat stone. Your child can drop scraps back in the bag, sponge the board and table and rinse tools in a bowl of water. Pour the water outside on soil, never down the sink.

items: I wonder what happens if we add a little water.
How did you make that?
Tell me about your clay.

sections.text: Strong hands, patience and the idea that a material can change and come back again. Squeezing and pounding clay gives the hands and arms heavy work, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send a photo of a clay piece or a texture your child loved pressing. Extra clay, clay tools or wooden boards for our studio are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Wipe clay with a damp cloth and never sweep dry clay dust. Keep leftover clay sealed in a bag so it stays soft. Clay that will not be kept can go back into a bag with a splash of water to soften for next time.

cards.title: Playdough
cards.summary: Soft dough made from pantry staples, often by the children themselves, with herbs, tools and natural materials to press and shape.

items: A self-serve playdough shelf with flour, salt, cream of tartar, oil, warm water and a picture recipe children can follow.
A batch made together at meeting time, with each child measuring and stirring, and for the North class a four-step picture recipe with real cups and spoons.
Dough scented with herbs from our garden such as lavender, rosemary, spearmint and lemon balm.
Dough on a tray with acorn caps, sticks, seed pods, feathers from our chickens and small stones to press in.
Dough colored with chalk dust ground in a mortar or a few drops of liquid watercolor.
A balance scale or kitchen scale beside the dough so children can weigh and compare.
Dough in the mud kitchen or on an outdoor table for long play in the shade.
A big shared lump in the middle of the table for passing, pulling and building together.
Dough with letter stamps and name cards near the Writing center.
A cooked dough and an uncooked dough side by side, so children can feel the difference.
Cornstarch and baking soda dough cooked with an adult, for a smooth white dough that is gluten free.
Dough in the home area as part of a pretend bakery or café.
For the West class, warm dough just made and a lot of time to squeeze.
A limited palette of dough in red, yellow and blue only, plus a white dough and a black dough, so children knead colors together and discover new ones.
One color of dough for a whole week, such as yellow, with white and black dough beside it for making lighter and darker yellows.
Warm and cool dough tables, one with reds, oranges and yellows and the other with blues, greens and purples, set near matching fabric and objects.
Dough offered on different surfaces, such as a wooden board, a slate tile, a mirror, a metal tray and a round of canvas, so children notice what sticks.
A tool basket with rolling pins of several sizes, wooden stampers, a garlic press, a pizza wheel, scissors, a butter knife, a potato masher, a fork, a cheese grater, sticks and feathers.
Dough in the class atelier on a round table, with a basket of garden pieces gathered that morning by the children.
For the South class, dough recipes children write and test, changing one ingredient at a time.

sections.text: Both. Making a batch is real shared work with roles for everyone. A child alone with a soft lump can settle and think. In the Studio a group batch gives every child a real job. In a class atelier one lump on a tray lets a child knead and think at their own pace.

Store dough in lidded jars or bags and make fresh when it gets sticky, dry or smells sour. Check for wheat allergies and use the cornstarch dough when needed. Dough stays at the table and in hands and is never for tasting, which children can help remind each other. A basic cooked dough is two cups flour, one cup salt, two tablespoons cream of tartar, two tablespoons oil and one and a half cups boiling water, stirred by an adult and kneaded when cool. Color with liquid watercolor or tempera in the water, or knead powdered chalk in later. Make primaries and white first, then let children mix every other color by kneading. Black dough needs a strong black tempera and darkens hands, so offer gloves to anyone who wants them.

items: Measure, pour, stir and knead a batch.
Choose the color, the scent and what goes in.
Decide when it is too sticky or too dry and fix it.
Teach a friend how to read the picture recipe.
Keep the self-serve shelf stocked and tidy.
Store dough so it stays soft for tomorrow.
Share ideas for a new recipe to test.
Mix their own colors by kneading two doughs together.
Choose the tools and surface for the day from a labeled shelf.

sections.text: Children scrape crumbs from the table with a dough scraper, press dough into balls and seal them in their lidded jars. Tools go back on the labeled self-serve shelf, and a damp cloth wipes the table clean. Since the shelf, jars and cloth are set within reach, children close the dough table as part of playing.

Sit down at the dough table at the children's level and knead a lump of your own slowly while you talk in a quiet, regular voice. When a batch turns sticky, stay curious with your face and words, since children borrow our calm. Notice aloud what you see, such as You squeezed the blue and the yellow and now there is green.

items: I notice it feels different today.
I wonder what will happen if you knead the white into the blue.
How many greens could we make from these two?
Tell me how you mixed that color.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer warm fresh dough and plenty of open time.
For the West class, offer one color at a time, warm and soft, with hands and a rolling pin.
Add simple tools one at a time.
Add natural materials and herbs from our garden.
Make a batch together and keep the picture recipe at children's eye level.
Move to a self-serve shelf where children make dough on their own with an adult nearby.
When a batch fails, turn it into an investigation about what to change.
Test different recipes and make a chart of what children noticed.
Color dough with chalk dust or watercolor and mix colors by kneading.
Add a scale, measuring cups and numbers for weighing and comparing.
Make salt dough that dries hard, for pieces children want to keep.
Use dough as a story material with figures and natural pieces.
Offer red, yellow and blue dough only and let children knead to discover orange, green and purple.
Add white dough for tints and black dough for shades, and line up a row of every color made.
Mix a dough of each complementary pair, such as red and green, and notice how it moves toward brown.
Make observation dough beside real objects from the garden, such as a snail shell, a fig leaf or a pinecone.
Try dough on many surfaces and with many tools, and ask children to choose what fits their idea.
Move the self-serve shelf into each class atelier so dough is always within reach.
Invite families to share playdough recipes from their own homes and test them together.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Playdough is open to everyone and is never for tasting. Pouring boiling water and cooking dough are adult work, and the self-serve making shelf needs an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big, firm lump to knead, pound and roll with a heavy rolling pin, and stiff dough that takes real strength to push through a garlic press.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer smooth, dry, unscented dough in a small ball with a rolling pin and cutters, so fingers can touch it a little at a time.

sections.text: Two cups flour, one cup salt, two tablespoons cream of tartar, two tablespoons oil and about one and a half cups of warm water. A bowl, a spoon and a jar with a lid. For colors, a few drops of food coloring or washable paint in the water works well. Make red, yellow and blue and let your child mix the rest.

items: Make it together and let your child measure and stir.
Add a pinch of dried herbs or a few drops of food coloring.
Press in things from a walk such as leaves, sticks and small stones.
Use kitchen tools such as a rolling pin, a garlic press and cookie cutters.
Make three small balls in red, yellow and blue and knead two together to see a new color.

sections.text: Your child can measure, pour, knead and decide when the dough feels right. They can also help put it away so it lasts. Your child can choose the colors and mix new ones by kneading. Your child can roll the dough into a ball, put it in a jar with a lid and wipe the table. A small basket for the dough tools keeps them together for next time.

items: I wonder what will happen if we add more flour.
How does it feel today?
Tell me about the color you made.

sections.text: Measuring, strong hands and how mixing simple things makes something new. Kneading and squeezing dough gives the hands heavy work and strong touch, which many children find calming.
Send in your family's favorite dough recipe, or a jar of homemade dough for our class. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Dough is for hands, never for eating, because it is very salty. Keep it in a sealed jar and toss it when it smells sour. Colored dough can stain hands for a little while, and it washes off with soap.

cards.title: Beeswax
cards.summary: Warm modeling beeswax and beeswax sheets that children soften in their hands, shape into small forms and roll into candles.

items: A small piece of modeling beeswax for each child at meeting time, held and warmed quietly before shaping.
Beeswax sheets in a basket with a small cloth, for rolling simple candles.
Beeswax set in a sunny window or in a bowl of warm water so children find out how warmth changes it.
A seasonal table where beeswax forms join acorns, leaves and stones.
Two colors of modeling wax offered together, so children can find out what happens when they blend.
Beeswax pressed onto a window to catch light.
Beeswax with photos of honeybees and comb, and a visit to the pollinator garden to watch bees on lavender and salvias.
A real piece of honeycomb or empty comb on the Investigation table with a magnifier.
Beeswax shared outside on a warm day at a table in the shade.
Small beeswax creatures that live in a little world on a tray of moss and bark.
For older children, beeswax sheets cut with scissors into shapes before rolling.
A rest time basket of beeswax for a child who needs something calm in their hands.
A limited palette of modeling wax in red, yellow and blue, plus white, so children warm and blend two colors to find new ones.
A single color of beeswax for a whole week, with white beside it for lighter tints.
Thin pieces of colored wax pressed onto a sunny window in overlapping layers to see colors mix with light.
Beeswax pressed onto smooth stones, wood rounds and shells from our site to make small relief pictures.
A wax tray in each class atelier with a warm cloth, a small board and a few colors, so wax is ready during quiet times.
Natural undyed beeswax beside honey-colored, golden and dark comb photos, so children compare the shades.
For the South class, wax figures and tiny animals modeled while looking closely at a real photo of a bee on lavender.

sections.text: Mostly alone with others nearby. Warming wax is slow and quiet work in a child's own hands. Sharing a group candle or seasonal table brings everyone together. In the Studio a small group can make a shared seasonal table together. In a class atelier a child can hold warm wax at meeting time or rest time without needing anyone else.

Modeling beeswax stays firm until warmed in hands, warm water or sun, and never needs a stove for this work. Store pieces in a tin away from heat and keep very small pieces away from the youngest children. Candle rolling needs no flame, and the candles children roll stay unlit at school or go home with them. Warm wax in a bowl of warm tap water for a few minutes before children arrive, or keep it in a pocket or under an arm. A hair dryer is adult only. Wax leaves a light film on tables, which wipes away with a dry cloth. Keep colors separate in a tin with sections so they stay bright.

items: Warm the wax with patience in their own hands.
Choose colors and decide whether to blend them.
Roll a candle for the table or for their family.
Care for the bees by watching them gently in the garden.
Return wax to the tin so it stays clean.
Show a friend how they warmed a piece quickly.
Warm wax for a younger friend and pass it on.
Sort wax back into its colors in the tin.

sections.text: Children sort wax back into its color in the sectioned tin and press small crumbs onto the matching piece. They wipe the table with a dry cloth and tip the warm water bowl into the garden. The tin with a color in each place makes the close quick, and it happens right at the table.

Hold a piece of wax in your own hands and warm it quietly beside the children, at their level and within arm's reach. Let your breathing and voice stay slow, since this is calm work. Name what you notice about warmth and softness and leave the shaping to the child.

items: I notice the wax is softer now.
I wonder how the bees made this.
It reminds me of honey in the sun.
How did you warm it so fast?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer a single small piece and lots of quiet time to warm it.
For the West class, offer one large soft piece warmed ahead and lots of time to squeeze.
Notice together what warmth does, using hands, sun and water.
Add a second color and wonder about blending.
Shape small forms for a seasonal table.
Watch bees in the pollinator garden and look at comb with magnifiers.
Roll beeswax sheet candles to set unlit on the table at a gathering.
Offer wax with other materials such as wire, sticks and wool.
Look at the glowing Wax Room by Wolfgang Laib on screen and wonder about a room made of wax.
Invite a beekeeper from our community to bring a frame of comb to look at.
Offer only two primary colors and white and notice tints and secondary colors together.
Press thin wax onto windows and the light table and watch colors overlap.
Model small animals and plants while looking at real photos of creatures on our site.
Press wax onto stones and wood rounds and bring them to the nature table.
Make beeswax wrapped fabric together with an adult using a warm iron, for wrapping snack from home.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Modeling wax is calm, open work for every age, with very small pieces kept away from the West class. The hair dryer is adult only, and making beeswax wrapped fabric with a warm iron is one adult with one or two children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a firm cold piece to warm with strong squeezing and rolling between both palms, and a larger block to press into stones and wood.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small, already warm piece on a little board with a wooden stick to press with, and let the child hold it in a closed hand without shaping.
connected: Wolfgang Laib on the Artists page, for rooms and works made from beeswax and pollen.

sections.text: A few sticks of modeling beeswax, or beeswax sheets and cotton wick from a craft store.

items: Hold a piece in warm hands for a few minutes and see what happens.
Shape a small animal, a nest or a little bowl.
Roll a sheet of beeswax around a wick to make a candle.
Look for bees on flowers together and watch them work.
Press a thin piece of wax onto a sunny window and watch the light come through.
Blend two colors together in warm hands and see what new color appears.

sections.text: Your child warms the wax and decides what it becomes. They can roll a candle as a gift. Your child can sort the wax back by color in a tin and wipe the table with a dry cloth. Keep the tin away from heat so it is ready next time.

items: I wonder how bees make wax.
How did you make that new color?
Tell me about your shape.

sections.text: Patience, careful hands and a connection to bees and flowers. Warming wax slowly in the hands helps a child notice warmth and pressure and can be very calming.
Send a photo of something your child made, or extra beeswax sheets for our class. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep small pieces away from babies and toddlers. Grown-ups light any candles and stay nearby. Warm wax in a bowl of warm water, never on a stove.

cards.title: Plaster and casting
cards.summary: Plaster poured into impressions in clay, sand and mud to capture tracks, textures and forms from our site.

items: A slab of clay pressed with leaves, bark, seed pods and shells, then a plaster pour on top to make a relief tile.
Tracks in the mud after rain, from goats, chickens, birds and our own shoes, cast in plaster.
Wet sand in a box with handprints, objects and patterns pressed in, ready to cast.
A wall of plaster casts of textures from around our site at children's eye level.
Plaster poured into recycled containers such as yogurt cups and egg cartons to see the shapes that come out.
Small natural objects set into soft plaster in a dish for a permanent nature tile.
Plaster gauze strips dipped in water and laid over a balloon or a cardboard form.
Dry plaster casts offered with watercolor or tempera to paint.
Dry plaster blocks offered with wooden tools to carve and scrape.
Mixing plaster outdoors at a table with a bucket of water nearby, so children can watch it warm and set.
A small group mixing one batch together, with jobs for pouring, stirring and timing.
A track trail walk to the creek to look for prints in soft mud.
Casts of the same leaf in white plaster and in plaster tinted gray with a little black tempera, set side by side.
Dry casts painted with a limited palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera, mixed by the children.
White casts brushed with a thin wash of black watercolor and wiped back, so every line and vein shows.
A casting table in the outdoor piazza with cottage cheese tubs, a scale, a timer and a bucket of water for rinsing tools.
Prints of bark, tire tread, brick and oak roots pressed in clay and cast, then hung in a row as a texture map of our site.
For the South class, casting the inside of a small box or cup to see what an empty space looks like when it becomes solid.

sections.text: Together. Plaster sets quickly, so a small group works as a team with an educator. Each child can still make and keep their own cast. In the Studio casting is a small group project with a clear job for each child. In a class atelier a single tile or a track cast can be made with one or two children and an educator.

Adults handle dry plaster powder and mix it outside or near open air, adding plaster to water. Never pour plaster or plaster water down a drain, and let leftovers harden in the bucket to break out into the trash. Plaster warms as it sets, so it never goes on hands or bodies, and children wait until it is cool and hard. Mix about two parts plaster to one part water by volume, sprinkling plaster into the water until small islands form, then stir gently. It sets in about twenty minutes and is fully dry in a day or two. Use a clay wall or a cardboard strip around the impression so plaster stays in place. Wipe tools in the bucket right away and let the water settle so the plaster can be scraped into the trash.

items: Choose and prepare the impression to cast.
Pour, stir or time the setting with an educator.
Check when the plaster is hard and ready to lift.
Clean and paint their cast.
Decide where casts are displayed.
Teach a friend how to find a good track.
Build the clay wall or cardboard ring around the impression.
Mix paint colors for their cast from a limited palette.

sections.text: An adult handles plaster powder and the mixing bucket, and children keep the rest of the close. They wash cardboard strips or clay walls clean, return clay to its bag and carry hardened casts to a labeled drying board. Paint palettes and brushes go to the wash bucket and drying rack, so only the plaster bucket waits for the adult.

Stay at the casting table the whole time plaster is setting, standing or kneeling beside the children so your hands are free to steady the cup. Keep your voice even when plaster drips, and describe the change you see, such as It is getting warm and thick now. Let children lift and discover their own cast, even if an edge breaks.

items: I wonder who made this track.
How did the bumps become dents?
I notice the leaf looks different on the gray cast.
Where should the casts live?
What do you think will happen when we lift it?
Look for prints and impressions around our site.
For the West class, press hands and objects into damp sand and clay and look at the marks, with no plaster.
Press objects into clay and sand without casting, to see the marks.
Watch an educator mix and pour, then take on pouring and stirring.
Cast textures from the garden and yards.
Cast animal and bird tracks after rain.
Make relief tiles with natural objects pressed into clay.
Paint and carve dry casts.
Compare the cast with the impression and wonder about inside and outside.
Use plaster gauze over forms for bigger sculptures.
Look at the casts of empty spaces by Rachel Whiteread on screen and cast the inside of a box or a cup.
Make a track guide of animals on our site with casts and photos.
Paint casts with only red, yellow, blue, white and black and notice the colors children make.
Brush a thin wash over a white cast and wipe it back to find the hidden lines.
Cast the same texture in white and in gray plaster and compare them.
For the North class, take turns stirring and timing, with an educator pouring.
Create a cast garden path or wall made over many weeks.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Plaster warms as it sets, so casting is a small group with an adult at the table the whole time. Adults handle and mix the dry powder, and the track walk to the creek follows our walk agreements with each child holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, give the job of carrying the water bucket, stirring the plaster with a strong spoon and pressing deep tracks into wet sand with the whole hand.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, invite the child to choose the object to press and to watch the pour from a step back, then to brush the dry cast with a soft brush.
connected: Rachel Whiteread on the Artists page, for casting the empty space inside rooms and objects.

sections.text: A small bag of plaster of Paris, a disposable cup, a craft stick, a strip of cardboard and water.

items: Find an animal or shoe track in soft mud and cast it.
Press shells, leaves or keys into a flat piece of play clay and pour plaster over it.
Paint your cast when it is dry.
Paint your cast with only one or two colors plus white and see how many shades you can make.

sections.text: Your child can find the track, help stir and decide when it is ready to lift. Grown-ups handle the dry powder. Your child can carry the cast to a safe spot to dry and wash the craft stick and paint brushes. A grown-up handles the dry powder and leftover plaster.

items: I wonder who walked here.
How will it look when we lift it?
Tell me about the bumpy side.

sections.text: Careful looking, waiting and the surprise of seeing a shape turned inside out. Pressing, stirring and waiting builds strong hands and careful looking.
Bring a cast to share at school, or send in clean recycled containers for molds. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Mix plaster outside and never pour it down the sink. Plaster gets warm as it sets, so never put hands in it.

cards.title: Wire
cards.summary: Soft, bendable wire that children twist, coil and join to draw lines in the air and build light, open sculptures.

items: A spool of soft aluminum armature wire with pre-cut lengths and wooden bases with holes drilled for standing pieces.
Thin colored copper wire with beads, buttons and washers to thread on.
Wire and clay together, with the wire poking into a clay base or a clay ball.
Wire offered with sticks from our garden to wrap and join.
Wire beside a photo of a tree, a bird or a spider web, for looking and bending.
Wire sculptures hung near a lamp or window so children can find their shadows on the wall.
Wire on the light table for drawing lines that glow at the edges.
Wire and pliers at a small group table, with an educator showing how to curl the ends.
Long lengths of wire outdoors wound around fence posts and stakes to make a shared web.
Chenille stems for the West class as a first soft wire for twisting.
Wire with natural pieces such as feathers from our chickens, seed pods and leaves for a hanging mobile.
A wire drawing of a friend's profile, made while looking at them.
Black wire on a white board and silver wire on a black board side by side, so children see how a line changes on each.
A limited palette of colored wire in one family, such as reds and oranges only, or blues and greens only.
Wire drawings pinned to a gray foam board so children can bend, pin and change the line.
Wire wrapped around a pencil or dowel to make springs and spirals, with tools of different thickness to compare.
Wire in the class atelier on a small tray with a wooden base and a few beads, ready for a quiet idea.
Wire bent around fence posts and stakes in the garden to make shapes plants can climb.
For the North class, thick aluminum wire in short lengths for bending with whole hands.
For the South class, wire drawing from observation, such as the shape of a tree in the Tire swing yard or a goat's horns.

sections.text: Both. A child alone can follow one twisting line for a long time. A group web or mobile grows when many hands add to it. In the Studio a group mobile or web needs many hands and a shared plan. In a class atelier a child can sit with one length of wire and follow it for a long time.

Use soft aluminum or copper wire that bends easily, and curl or tape every cut end. Wire cutters and needle nose pliers are real tools used with an adult nearby. Store wire on spools or in labeled lengths so it stays untangled. Aluminum armature wire in 12 to 16 gauge is soft enough for young hands. Thin copper wire works for wrapping and beads. Store wire by thickness and color on labeled spools or in clear jars.

items: Choose lengths and colors of wire.
Curl the ends safely and remind friends to do the same.
Use pliers and, with an adult, wire cutters.
Decide where a sculpture hangs or stands.
Wind leftover wire back onto spools.
Show a friend a twist or loop they invented.
Choose a black or white board and decide which shows the line best.
Bend wire around a dowel and teach a friend how a spring forms.

sections.text: Children curl or tape every cut end, wind leftover wire back onto its spool and sort short lengths into jars by thickness. Pliers go back on their photo-labeled board and an adult returns wire cutters. A small magnet tray or basket catches dropped bits, so the table is safe and clear before children move on.

Sit beside the children with your own length of wire, bending slowly and saying aloud what you notice, such as Your line went up and then curled back down. Keep your hands near and still so you can steady a cut end when asked, and resist straightening a child's line.

items: Where does the line go next?
I notice a shadow on the wall. I wonder where it came from.
It reminds me of the willow dome.
How did you make that spiral?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with soft chenille stems or short lengths of aluminum wire for twisting and bending.
For the West class, offer chenille stems and a colander or wire basket for poking and twisting.
Add beads and buttons to thread on.
Add wooden bases so sculptures can stand.
Combine wire with clay, sticks and natural materials.
Introduce pliers and wire cutters with clear agreements.
Use wire to draw what children see, such as a leaf, a goat or a friend.
Hang pieces near light and explore shadows.
Look at the wire Circus figures by Alexander Calder and the looped wire forms by Ruth Asawa on screen.
Try looping wire in rows, the way Ruth Asawa did, around a dowel or a child's fingers.
Build a group mobile that balances, and wonder about weight together.
Make wire armatures and cover them with clay, papier mache or fabric.
Offer black and white boards side by side and compare wire drawings on each.
Use a limited palette of colored wire, such as warm colors only, for a shared mobile.
Draw in wire from real things on our site, such as a fig leaf or the outline of the willow dome.
Model techniques such as wrapping, coiling and looping around a dowel.
Open studio with wire on the shelf for any idea that needs a line.

setting.why: Cut wire ends and real pliers need an adult at the table. Wire cutters are used by children only with an adult beside them, and every cut end is curled or taped.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick aluminum wire to bend around a post or dowel with whole hands, and pliers that need a strong squeeze.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer soft chenille stems or thin wire in short pieces with taped ends, and a quiet corner of the table.
connected: Alexander Calder on the Artists page, for drawing in the air with wire in his Circus figures and mobiles.
Ruth Asawa on the Artists page, for looped wire sculptures made by hand in San Francisco.

sections.text: A few chenille stems or a roll of soft craft wire, some beads and a lump of play clay for a base.

items: Twist and bend wire into any shape your child invents.
Thread beads onto wire and coil it.
Stand wire in play clay to make a tree or a tall sculpture.
Hold a sculpture near a flashlight and look at its shadow.
Lay a wire shape on white paper and then on dark paper and see which you like best.

sections.text: Your child chooses how to bend the wire and what it becomes. They can help curl sharp ends. Your child can curl sharp ends, wind leftover wire around a cardboard tube and put beads back in their bowl. Check the floor together for little pieces.

items: Where could the line go next?
I wonder what the shadow will look like.
Tell me about your shape.

sections.text: Strong fingers, planning and seeing a line become a shape. Bending and twisting wire uses both hands together and builds finger strength.
Send a photo of a wire sculpture, or extra beads and craft wire for our class. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Grown-ups cut wire and curl or tape the sharp ends. Keep beads away from babies.

cards.title: Wood and tools
cards.summary: Real woodworking with hammers, saws, hand drills and sandpaper at a sturdy bench, growing from tapping nails to children's own inventions.

items: A low sturdy workbench with a vise, safety glasses, hammers, nails with big heads and soft wood offcuts.
A tree stump in the Log yard for hammering nails, where children can work with real force.
Soft wood pieces with a hand drill and a set of bits to make holes.
A pull saw used with an educator one to one, with wood clamped tight in the vise.
Sandpaper in several grits and rough blocks to smooth.
Wood glue, corks, bottle caps, spools and wire for joining and adding.
Screws and screwdrivers with a board that has pilot holes.
Fresh green sticks and vegetable peelers for peeling bark, with an educator and clear agreements.
Opening logs with wedges and mallets to look inside at grain, insects and rings.
Tree cookies and branch rounds to sand, oil and stack.
A take apart table with an old wooden chair or drawer and screwdrivers.
Wood pieces and glue for the West class to build without tools.
Drawings and plans on clipboards hanging above the bench.
Finished pieces painted, oiled or left plain on a display shelf.
Wood painted with a limited palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera or acrylic, mixed by the children on a palette.
Wood offcuts sanded and left plain beside pieces brushed white and black, so children compare how grain shows on each.
A tool board with hammers of two sizes, a hand drill, screwdrivers, a pull saw, clamps, a rasp, a file and sanding blocks.
Woodwork in the class atelier on a small low bench with one hammer, soft wood and a basket of nails.
For the North class, sanding, gluing and hammering into a stump with an educator beside each child.
For the South class, drawn plans on graph paper and a tape measure, so children measure and mark where to cut.

sections.text: Mostly alone with an educator close by, since each child needs room and attention at the bench. Bigger builds, such as a bird feeder or a goat yard sign, bring a small group together. In the Studio a woodworking bench serves a small group with an educator close. In the yards a stump and a hammer let a child work alone with real force while an adult stays near.

Begin with very few children at the bench, about one adult to three, and keep sawing one to one at all times. Use soft untreated wood such as pine, redwood offcuts or cedar, check for splinters and never use pressure treated wood. Teach each tool with its agreement, keep safety glasses on, and store tools on a shadow board that shows where each one lives. Agreements are short and clear, such as glasses on, tools stay at the bench and one person at a time on the saw. Offer real tools of good quality sized for small hands, since cheap tools slip and frustrate. Keep a first aid kit near the bench.

items: Choose wood and plan a piece.
Wear safety glasses and remind friends to wear them.
Learn each tool and then teach a friend.
Clamp wood in the vise and check it with an adult.
Return tools to the shadow board.
Sweep sawdust and sort scraps for reuse.
Decide when a piece is done.
Mix paint colors for their wood piece on a palette.
Check the first aid kit and the glasses before the bench opens.

sections.text: Children hang each tool back on its outline on the shadow board, sort usable scraps into the reuse bin and sweep sawdust with a child-sized broom and dustpan. They take off safety glasses and return them to their hooks. An adult checks the shadow board for every saw and sharp tool, and the bench is closed before anyone leaves it.

Stay at the bench the whole time it is open, standing or kneeling at the children's height with your hands ready but still. Notice your own worry about tools and let your face stay calm and confident, since children borrow it. Name what you see, such as You held the hammer near the end and the nail went in straight.

items: I wonder what is inside this log.
How could you join these two pieces?
I notice the hammer sounds different on this wood.
Tell me about your plan.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Explore wood pieces, bark and tree cookies by touch and smell.
For the West class, hammer golf tees into foam and wooden pegs into soft wood with a light mallet.
Tap nails into a stump with a hammer.
Hammer nails into soft wood at the bench, then pull them out with the claw.
Add a hand drill and screwdrivers.
Introduce sanding and smoothing.
Saw one to one with wood in the vise.
Tinker freely by joining pieces with nails, glue and screws.
Draw a plan first, build it and compare.
Make useful things for our site such as signs, bird feeders and plant markers.
Peel green sticks and make walking sticks and garden stakes.
Visit a local woodworker or invite a family member who builds.
Look at the stacked wood boxes of Louise Nevelson and the redwood sculpture of J.B. Blunk on screen.
Build a group sculpture or a box assemblage from scrap wood.
Paint wood with a limited palette and let children mix their own colors.
Make rubbings of wood grain with crayon on white paper and white crayon on black paper.
Draw wood pieces and tools from observation on clipboards hung by the bench.
Model techniques such as starting a nail with a light tap, clamping before drilling and sanding with the grain.
Keep woodwork open every day once children are confident.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Real tools need close attention and clear agreements, with about one adult to three children at the bench. Sawing is always one adult with one child, and peeling sticks and opening logs with wedges and mallets need an adult beside the child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a stump and a real hammer for driving big nails, sawing with an educator and carrying heavy logs in the Log yard.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer sanding and gluing at the end of the bench away from the hammering, with ear protection or a later turn when the bench is quiet.
connected: Louise Nevelson on the Artists page, for sculptures built from found wood pieces stacked in boxes.
J.B. Blunk on the Artists page, for large sculptures carved from redwood and cypress in Marin County.
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A real small hammer, nails with big heads, a stump or a thick piece of soft wood, sandpaper and safety glasses.

items: Hammer nails into a stump or a board.
Sand a rough piece of wood until it is smooth.
Glue wood scraps together into a sculpture.
Take apart an old wooden thing with a screwdriver.
Make a crayon rubbing of wood grain on paper.

sections.text: Your child uses real tools with you right there. They can wear the glasses, choose the wood and put tools away. Your child can put each tool back in its place, sweep sawdust with a small broom and dustpan and sort wood scraps into a box for next time.

items: How could we join these?
I wonder how this wood smells.
Tell me about what you built.

sections.text: Strength, focus and the feeling of being trusted with real tools. Hammering and sanding give strong heavy work for the arms and help many children feel steady and capable.
Send in clean, untreated wood scraps, corks or spools for our workbench, or a photo of something you built together. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Stay right beside your child, use safety glasses and keep saws for grown-up help only. Use only untreated wood.

cards.title: Found and recycled sculpture
cards.summary: Clean collected materials, sorted with care, that children join into sculptures, inventions and assemblages.

items: A materials shelf of clean recycled pieces sorted in clear jars by type, such as caps, lids, tubes, corks, spools and fabric scraps.
A box of small boxes, tape, scissors and glue, set up with children helping to choose what goes out.
Materials sorted by color on a long tray so the colors invite new ideas.
Low temperature glue guns at a small table with an adult and clear agreements.
A take apart table with an old keyboard, a clock or a radio, cords cut and batteries removed, plus screwdrivers.
An invention table where parts from the take apart table become new machines.
Bottle caps and lids for patterns on the floor or a mirror.
A large group sculpture in the outdoor piazza made from crates, tubes and fabric.
Wooden frames, boards, box lids, wood rounds and black trays as bases for flat assemblages that hang on the wall or sit on a shelf.
A materials walk with a basket to find what others left behind, such as fallen bark and lost buttons.
Robots, vehicles and creatures with wire, tape and fasteners.
A sealed mystery box of new materials opened together at meeting time.
For the West class, big tubes, boxes and lids to stack, fill and carry.
A one-color assemblage invitation where children choose pieces of only one color, or paint a whole sculpture white, black or gray to unify it.
Sculptures painted with red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera, mixed by children.
Joining tools of many kinds, such as masking tape, string, pipe cleaners, brads, clothespins, rubber bands and white glue.
A shelf in each class atelier with a few jars of found pieces, so building can happen any day.
A large outdoor assemblage on a fence panel in the garden, built from weatherproof pieces such as lids, tiles and wood.
For the North class, pieces that join easily, such as tubes with tape and lids with glue on a box base.
For the South class, planning drawings on clipboards, then building and changing the plan.

sections.text: Both. Shared sculptures grow from many ideas at once. A child alone with a tray of parts can invent something entirely their own. In the Studio a long shared sculpture can grow for weeks. In a class atelier a child with a tray of parts can invent a machine or creature alone.

Wash everything before it comes in and leave out sharp edges, food packaging with allergens and anything too small for the youngest children. Old electronics come in with cords cut off and batteries and glass removed. Sort and label materials so children can find and return them, and change what is out over time based on what children use. White paint or gesso over a finished piece lets children see shape and shadow instead of the labels on boxes. Sort by material and color in clear jars, and set a fixed day each week for children to restock.

items: Sort and label new donations with an educator.
Choose materials and decide how to join them.
Use the glue gun with an adult and teach the agreement to friends.
Take apart old objects and name the pieces they find.
Decide what to keep, display or take apart again.
Keep the materials shelf tidy and tell educators what is running low.
Ask families for materials in their own notes and letters home.
Choose one color for an assemblage and find pieces to match.
Paint a finished sculpture white or black and notice what changes.

sections.text: Children return unused pieces to their labeled jars by material and color and set finished or growing sculptures on the display shelf. An adult unplugs and puts away the low-temp glue gun once it cools, while children wipe the table and sweep stray bits with a child-sized broom. Labeled jars at child height make the shelf ready for tomorrow without an educator restocking it later.

Sit at the building table with the children and keep your own hands free of their sculptures. When a piece falls apart, stay steady and wonder aloud with the child instead of fixing it. Describe what you see, such as You used three tubes and a lid to make the top tall.

items: I wonder what this used to be.
How could these join together?
I notice it looks different now that it is all white.
Tell me about your machine.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Gather and clean materials with children and families.
For the West class, offer large boxes, tubes and lids to stack, fill and topple, with no glue.
Sort them together by type, color and texture.
Offer a few materials at a time with tape and glue.
Add the take apart table and screwdrivers.
Introduce low temperature glue guns with clear agreements.
Join pieces into vehicles, robots, houses and creatures.
Build a large shared sculpture outdoors.
Make wall assemblages on boards or in boxes.
Look at the towers built from broken tiles and bottles by Simon Rodia and the bottle cap hangings by El Anatsui on screen.
Visit a creative reuse center in the Bay Area to choose materials together.
Talk about where things come from and where they go when we throw them away.
Paint finished sculptures one color and look at shadows and shapes.
Look at the black wall pieces of Louise Nevelson on screen and make a one-color assemblage in a box.
Model joins such as tabs, slots and wrapping with string.
Draw a finished sculpture from observation and compare the drawing and the piece.
Keep an open materials shelf where children self-serve for any project.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Building with found pieces is open with an educator nearby. Low-temp glue guns are used at a small table with an adult and clear agreements, and the take apart table needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big boxes and crates to lift, stack and tape together, and stiff materials that need strong pulling and pushing to join.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray of a few smooth pieces and tape, at a quiet table with time to choose.
connected: Simon Rodia on the Artists page, for the Watts Towers built over decades from found tile, glass and steel.
El Anatsui on the Artists page, for huge hangings made from bottle caps and metal pieces.
Louise Nevelson on the Artists page, for wall sculptures built from found wood scraps.

home.title: Found and recycled sculpture at Home

sections.text: Clean boxes, tubes, lids, corks, bottle caps, tape, glue and scissors.

items: Keep a box of clean recyclables for building.
Build a robot, a car or a house from what is there.
Take apart an old clock or toy with a screwdriver, with batteries removed.
Sort caps and lids by color into patterns.
Paint a finished sculpture all one color and see how it looks different.

sections.text: Your child chooses the materials and the plan. They can help wash and sort what goes into the box. Your child can sort leftover boxes, lids and tubes back into a bin, wipe the table and choose a shelf for the sculpture. A grown-up puts away the glue gun.

items: I wonder what this used to be.
How could we join these two?
Tell me what it does.

sections.text: Inventing, planning and caring about what we throw away. Joining and building helps children plan movements and use both hands together.
Send in clean recycled materials such as corks, lids, tubes, spools and fabric scraps. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash everything and leave out sharp edges and tiny parts for little ones. Remove batteries and cords before taking anything apart.

cards.title: Cardboard
cards.summary: Boxes, tubes and sheets of cardboard that children cut, fold, join and paint into houses, vehicles, sculptures and anything they imagine.

items: A huge appliance box in the middle of the room with nothing added, so children decide what it is.
Boxes, tape and scissors in a provocation children help set up.
