A cardboard tool caddy at a small table with an educator, holding cardboard saws, safety cutters, a hole punch, brads, a blunt scoring tool and clothespins.
Cardboard screws and connectors for joining sheets without glue.
Slotted cardboard pieces in many shapes that slide together to build.
A whole table covered in cardboard for painting and pounding together.
Tubes and gutters cut from cardboard for ramps and tunnels.
Corrugated cardboard peeled to show the ridges, offered with paint for printing.
Cardboard sheets on a grassy slope for sliding, then laid flat on the grass in the Tire swing yard for chalk drawing and water painting.
Cardboard looms with notches for weaving yarn and natural materials.
Boxes for building a shop, a café, a post office or a goat barn in dramatic play.
Cardboard bricks and boxes for building big walls in the block area.
A box city or village built with a small group over many days.
For the West class, boxes to climb into, push, fill and carry.
Brown cardboard painted with white tempera only, then black only, so children see how one color changes on kraft brown.
Cardboard painted with a limited palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black, with mixing trays.
Cardboard cut into circles, long strips, arches and torn shapes for building and painting.
A cardboard construction corner in each class atelier with boxes, tape and a basket of tubes.
For the North class, boxes to paint, cut windows in and fill with toys and natural materials.
For the South class, scale models of our school made with small boxes after a walk around the site.

sections.text: Both. A big box draws a crowd and needs many hands. A child with a small box can work alone on a careful idea. In the Studio a group can build a large box city. In a class atelier a child can turn a single box into a careful world of their own.

Collect clean boxes with tape and staples removed and store them flat. Cardboard saws and safety cutters are real tools used with an adult and clear agreements. Cardboard gets soggy in rain, so outdoor builds come in or go to the recycling when they are done. Corrugated cardboard folds best along the ridges, and scoring with a blunt tool makes clean folds. Collect cardboard in many thicknesses and colors, including gray board and white mat board offcuts from frame shops.

items: Help gather, flatten and store boxes.
Choose what a box becomes.
Cut and join with real tools after learning the agreement.
Plan and draw before building.
Paint and decorate together.
Decide when a build is done or recycled.
Teach friends how to fold, score or slot.
Choose paint colors from a limited palette for a build.
Score a fold with a blunt tool and show a friend.

sections.text: Children flatten and stack leftover boxes in the cardboard rack and put saws and safety cutters back in their labeled caddy, checked by an adult. They gather scraps into the recycling bin and sweep small bits with a child-sized broom and dustpan. Builds that will keep stay on a marked spot, so the floor is clear without educator time.

Get down on the floor beside big boxes and stay there while children climb in and out. Keep a relaxed face when a box tears or collapses, and narrate the change, such as The side folded in and now there is a door. Hold a box steady only when a child asks.

items: I wonder what this box could be.
How could these two pieces hold together?
I notice the cardboard bends one way more easily.
Tell me about your plan.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer whole boxes for climbing in and pushing.
For the West class, offer boxes big enough to sit in and paint with brushes and rollers.
Add tape and scissors for joining.
Paint boxes and big sheets.
Introduce cardboard saws, cutters and connectors.
Fold, score and slot to make shapes stand.
Build vehicles, homes and shops for dramatic play.
Make ramps, tunnels and marble paths from tubes.
Draw a plan, build it and compare.
Build a group city or village over many days.
Look at the cardboard furniture designed by Frank Gehry on screen and wonder about making a chair strong enough to sit on.
Test how strong cardboard can be by stacking, folding and layering.
Paint cardboard with white only and then black only, and compare on brown.
Mix colors from a limited palette for a shared painted cardboard wall.
Make cardboard reliefs by layering shapes cut in circles, strips and torn edges.
Build models of our site after a walk and use them for maps and stories.
Keep cardboard and tools on an open shelf for any idea.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Big boxes and building are open with an educator nearby. Cardboard saws and safety cutters are used with an adult at the table, and sliding on cardboard down a slope needs an educator watching the bottom.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big boxes to push, drag, climb into and flatten, and cardboard saws that take two hands and strength.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small box with a lid to open and close, tape and crayons, in a calm corner.
connected: Frank Gehry on the Artists page, for furniture made from layered cardboard.

sections.text: Boxes of any size, masking tape, scissors and crayons or paint.

items: Let your child turn a big box into a house, car or boat.
Cut windows and doors together.
Join small boxes into a robot or a tower.
Use tubes to roll balls through.
Paint a box with white or with one color and see how it looks on brown.

sections.text: Your child decides what the box is, and that can change. They can help cut, tape and paint. Your child can flatten boxes, stack them by the door and drop scraps in the recycling. Tape and scissors can go back in their basket.

items: I wonder what this box could be.
How could we make it stand up?
Tell me about your build.

sections.text: Planning, problem solving and big imaginative play. Pushing, carrying and climbing into boxes gives the whole body heavy work.
Send in clean boxes or tubes for our class, or a photo of your box creation. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Grown-ups do any cutting with sharp blades. Remove staples and plastic tape before play.

cards.title: Blocks
cards.summary: Unit blocks, hollow blocks and natural wood blocks offered with time, space and care, from first carrying to towns, bridges and stories.

items: A full set of hardwood unit blocks on low shelves with outlines showing where each shape lives.
Large hollow blocks and planks outdoors in the outdoor piazza for building things children can climb into.
Tree blocks and branch rounds cut from our own fallen limbs, with bark still on.
Blocks with a basket of people figures, animals from our animal yards and small vehicles.
Blocks with fabric, scarves and cardboard tubes for roofs, rivers and tunnels.
Blocks beside real photos of bridges, towers, barns and homes in Sonoma County at children's eye level.
Clipboards and pencils in the block area for drawing plans and finished builds.
A work in progress sign so builds can stay overnight and grow the next day.
Blocks on a mirror or a light table to see builds from new angles.
Blocks with painter's tape roads and a map on the floor.
A small set of blocks at a table for a child who wants to build alone.
Blocks and natural loose parts such as stones, acorns and pinecones to decorate and fill.
For the West class, lighter blocks and baskets for carrying, filling, dumping and lining up.
Black and white paper with white pencils and black pencils on clipboards in the block area, for drawing builds.
Blocks on surfaces of many kinds, such as a wooden floor, a rug, a mirror, a black cloth and grass.
A small set of painted blocks in only red, yellow and blue, beside natural wooden blocks.
Colored transparent blocks on the light table and in a sunny window, so light mixes their colors.
Blocks in each class atelier and the Studio with photos of structures from our site, such as the willow dome and the art shed.
For the North class, blocks and baskets of figures, with clipboards for building plans.
For the South class, blueprints, graph paper, rulers and tape measures for measuring builds.

sections.text: Both. Block play often starts alone and side by side, then grows into shared building with plans and roles. Long uninterrupted time lets both happen. In the block area builds become shared projects. A small tray of blocks at a table lets a child build alone without interruption.

Give block play long stretches of time and a space out of walkways with a rug that softens the sound. Agree together that blocks stay low enough to be safe and that we take care of each other's buildings. Store heavy blocks low, keep each shape together and oil wooden blocks once a year. Offer enough blocks of each shape for large builds, and add blocks gradually as children grow in skill. Photographs at the end of the day help children return to their work.

items: Choose and carry blocks to their space.
Plan, build and name what they built.
Decide with friends who builds which part.
Draw or photograph a build before it comes down.
Put up a work in progress sign.
Match blocks to the outlines when cleaning up.
Teach a friend how they made a bridge or an enclosure.
Draw a build on black paper with a white pencil or on white paper with a black pencil.
Measure a build with string or a tape measure.

sections.text: Children photograph or draw a build, then lift blocks down from the top, carry them in their arms and match each one to its outline on the shelf. Heavy blocks go low and long blocks lie flat. Outlines on every shelf let children put the block area back together themselves.

Sit on the floor at the edge of the block area so you are close but out of the build. Keep a calm face when towers fall, since collapse is part of building. Describe what you see, such as You put the long block across two short ones and made a bridge.

items: I wonder how it stays up.
Who might live here?
How would it look from above?
Tell me about your building.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer blocks for carrying, filling, piling and lining up.
For the West class, offer lightweight blocks for carrying, stacking and knocking down.
Notice towers and rows, and give time to repeat them.
Wonder about bridges and enclosures as they appear.
Add people, animals and vehicles for story play.
Add photos of real structures from our town.
Add clipboards for drawing plans and finished builds.
Let builds stay overnight and grow over days.
Bring blocks outdoors and mix hollow blocks with planks and crates.
Add tree blocks and natural materials from our site.
Build a shared town or map of our school with blocks.
Measure builds with string, hands and tape measures.
Draw builds on black and white paper and compare the drawings.
Build on many surfaces, such as mirror, grass and black cloth, and notice what changes.
Build models of real structures on our site after a walk.
Make block patterns with painted primary color blocks beside natural ones.
Walk to see real bridges, barns and buildings, then build them back at school.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Blocks are open to everyone with agreements about height and care for each other's buildings. Large hollow blocks and planks outdoors that children climb on need an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer large hollow blocks and planks to carry and build big, and a safe agreed place to knock a tower down.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small set of blocks at a table away from crashing towers, and a basket to build in.

sections.text: Wooden blocks if you have them. Boxes, books and plastic containers work too. A clear patch of floor.

items: Build a tower and knock it down together.
Make a house or a garage for toy animals or cars.
Build a road and a bridge.
Take a photo of a build before it comes down.
Draw your build on paper before it comes down.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to build and how. They can also help put blocks away by shape. Your child can stack blocks back into a bin or on a shelf by shape and size. A photo of the build before it comes down helps them say goodbye to it.

items: I wonder how tall it can go.
Who might live here?
How did you make that stay up?

sections.text: Balance, shapes, planning and working with others. Carrying, stacking and balancing blocks helps children judge space and use their whole body.

Send a photo of a home build to share at school, or a photo of a bridge or building near your home. Wooden blocks or tree rounds for our class are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep tall towers away from babies and help your child choose a safe height.

cards.title: Loose parts
cards.summary: Open collections of natural and found pieces that children move, combine, sort, line up and transform in any way they choose.

items: Baskets of wood rounds, spools, rings, stones, acorns, pinecones and shells on a low shelf for self-serve.
Tinker trays with sections of small pieces for arranging patterns and pictures.
Loose parts on a mirror, a light table or a wood frame for making temporary art.
Big loose parts outdoors in the Log yard and Tire swing yard, such as crates, planks, tires, tubes, pipes, stumps and fabric.
Loose parts in the mud kitchen and sand area for cooking, filling and building.
Containers, scoops and bags for carrying and transporting pieces from place to place.
Metal pieces such as tins, lids, chains and washers for sound and shine.
Fabric pieces of many sizes for wrapping, enveloping and hiding.
Loose parts with clothespins and a rope line between two posts.
Natural pieces from our site set beside photos of where they came from.
A family loose parts collection where each family adds something from home.
Loose parts with clay, playdough or blocks.
For the West class, larger pieces to fill, dump, carry and line up.
Loose parts on black felt and on white board side by side, so children see how pieces stand out on each.
A one-color collection, such as everything blue from the garden and Studio, for a week of arranging.
Loose parts in warm colors on one tray and cool colors on another, for patterns and mixing.
Natural loose parts on gray slate and brown kraft paper to show subtle colors.
Loose parts in every class atelier in labeled jars, changed with children's interests.
For the North class, a few collections with clear trays for arranging.
For the South class, loose parts for maps, patterns and stories drawn and photographed.

sections.text: Both. A child alone can arrange the same pieces again and again. Big outdoor parts need teamwork to lift, carry and build. In the Studio a group can build a large shared arrangement. A child alone with a tinker tray can arrange and rearrange for a long time.

Check every piece for size, edges and splinters, and keep small pieces out of the West class. Sort collections into clear or natural baskets and change them over time based on what we observe so the space stays fresh. Wash shells and stones, dry wood pieces well and return natural parts to the garden when they wear out. Choose a few rich collections. Store them in clear jars and baskets, sorted by color and material.

items: Choose pieces and decide what they become.
Carry pieces between areas and return them.
Sort and organize collections by their own rules.
Photograph or draw what they made before it changes.
Help gather new pieces on walks and from home.
Teach friends a pattern or a build they invented.
Choose a black or white background and say what changes.
Gather pieces for a one-color collection.

sections.text: Children sort loose parts back into their baskets and jars by their own rules or by the photo label on each one. They carry pieces home from other areas and sweep up stray small bits with a child-sized dustpan. Each basket has a clear place on a low shelf, so the close is part of play and the area is ready for tomorrow.

Sit near the child at their level and watch for a while before you speak. Describe what you see, such as You put the round ones in a line, and leave their arrangement as it is. Stay calm when pieces travel to other areas, since carrying is part of the play.

items: I notice you lined them up. I wonder what comes next.
How do they look on the black cloth?
It reminds me of a path in the garden.
Tell me about your pattern.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer a few collections and watch how children use them.
For the West class, offer large pieces in baskets for filling, dumping and carrying.
Notice what children do, such as carrying, lining up or enclosing, and add pieces that support it.
Add containers and bags for transporting.
Add mirrors, frames and trays for temporary art.
Add large outdoor parts such as crates, tires and planks.
Combine loose parts with other materials such as clay, blocks and fabric.
Photograph creations and make a book of children's ideas.
Sort collections with children and let them name the categories.
Look at sculptures made from thousands of everyday objects by Tara Donovan on screen.
Invite families to add pieces from home with a short note about each one.
Use loose parts for counting, patterns, stories and maps.
Arrange loose parts on black and white backgrounds and photograph both.
Build one-color collections and warm or cool trays for a week at a time.
Draw arrangements from observation with pencil on clipboards.
Combine loose parts with clay, wire and paper for mixed media pieces.
Keep loose parts open across every area of the room.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Loose parts are self-serve, with small pieces kept out of the West class. Big outdoor parts such as crates, planks and tires need an educator nearby and a check for black widows by an adult first.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy outdoor parts such as stumps, tires and crates to roll and carry, and metal parts that clink and shine.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a single tray with a few smooth natural pieces on a black cloth, in a quiet spot.
connected: Tara Donovan on the Artists page, for sculptures made by gathering huge numbers of one everyday object.

sections.text: A basket of safe household and natural pieces such as lids, spools, clothespins, wooden spoons, fabric scraps, stones and pinecones. A tray or a mirror.

items: Make pictures and patterns on a tray or mirror.
Fill and dump pieces from containers.
Build a house for a toy with whatever is in the basket.
Collect pieces on a walk and add them.
Arrange pieces on a dark towel and then on white paper and compare.

sections.text: Your child decides what each piece is for. They can help collect, sort and put pieces away. Your child can sort the pieces back into their baskets and decide which basket each thing belongs in. Small baskets and a low shelf make it easy.

items: I wonder how many ways we could sort these.
How do they look on the dark towel?
Tell me about what you made.

sections.text: Creativity, sorting and problem solving with simple things. Sorting, arranging and carrying small and big pieces helps children use their hands and judge space.
Send in safe loose parts from home, such as wood spools, lids or fabric pieces, with a note about where they came from. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep small pieces away from babies and toddlers. Check for sharp edges and splinters.

cards.title: Natural materials
cards.summary: Sticks, stones, leaves, seed pods, bark and other gifts from our site gathered with purpose and used to build, arrange, weave and wonder.

items: A gathering walk with baskets, using our agreement to pick with purpose and leave some for others.
Fallen valley oak and coast live oak leaves, acorns and caps sorted on a tray.
Sticks, stones and leaves arranged into circles and spirals on the ground.
Weaving long grasses, sticks and yarn into the willow dome.
Feathers from our chickens with seed pods and bark on the Investigation table with magnifiers.
Stone and wood stacking on a stump in the Log yard.
Natural materials pressed into clay, playdough and plaster.
Sticks lashed together with string to make frames, rafts and small shelters.
Natural materials on a light table to see veins, holes and edges.
A collection that changes with the seasons, from spring blossoms to autumn leaves and winter twigs.
Natural pieces sorted by color into a rainbow on the ground.
Small homes for roly polys and lizards built with bark and leaves, then left for the creatures.
Sticks used as tools for digging, drawing in the mud and opening logs.
Natural brushes made from rosemary, lavender, grasses, feathers from our chickens and pine needles tied to sticks, for painting on kraft paper with a limited palette.
Natural materials on black paper and white paper side by side for arranging and drawing.
A one-color hunt, such as everything yellow or brown that has fallen in the garden.
Natural materials in each class atelier on a low shelf, with magnifiers and clipboards.
Leaves, bark and stones painted with a limited palette of red, yellow, blue, white and black.
For the North class, sorting trays for leaves, stones and sticks by color and size.
For the South class, natural material maps of our site laid out on the ground.

sections.text: Both. Gathering and big outdoor builds bring children together. A child alone can sort and arrange pieces with deep focus. Gathering walks and large builds bring the group together. Arranging alone on a tray or the ground gives a child a calm, focused time.

Adults confirm every plant children gather is one we know, because poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site, and we check for black widows in woodpiles. We use feathers only from our own chickens, since wild bird feathers stay where they fall. Return natural materials to the garden or compost when they are done. Return materials to the garden when they are done and replace collections with the seasons.

items: Gather with purpose and leave some for others.
Check with an adult before gathering a new plant.
Sort, name and display their findings.
Choose what to build or arrange.
Return materials to the earth when they are done.
Teach friends our agreement to be kind to all beings.
Photograph or draw their arrangements before they change.
Choose a background and compare how materials show on each.

sections.text: Children sort materials back into their baskets, set worn leaves and petals in the compost bucket and carry stones and sticks back to the garden. They brush the tray or table into their hands and take the crumbs outside. A basket for each kind of thing and a compost bucket at the table make this quick and complete.

Walk slowly with the children and pause when they pause. Crouch to their level to look at what they found and keep your voice soft. Notice your own feelings about bugs and dirt and keep your face open and curious.

items: I wonder where this came from.
I notice the leaf looks brighter on the black paper.
How might it change by tomorrow?
Tell me about your arrangement.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Go on gathering walks and talk about our agreements.
For the West class, offer baskets of large pinecones, sticks and leaves for carrying and filling.
Sort findings by children's own categories.
Arrange pieces into patterns, circles and lines on the ground.
Build with sticks and stones on stumps and in the Log yard.
Weave natural materials into the willow dome and frames.
Look closely with magnifiers and draw what children see.
Look at Wood Line by Andy Goldsworthy in the Presidio and his work with leaves and stones on screen.
Visit Wood Line together or invite families to visit it.
Leave arrangements outside and return to see how weather changes them.
Learn the names of plants on our site with iNaturalist.
Learn about Southern Pomo basket weaving and the plants it uses, such as sedge and willow, with a local Pomo weaver or cultural center.
Make a seasonal nature table that children curate.
Arrange on black and white backgrounds and photograph both.
Paint natural materials with a limited palette.
Draw natural materials from observation with pencil and white pencil.
Make natural brushes and use them with a limited palette.
Use natural materials in every area, from blocks to writing to clay.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Gathering is open with an educator nearby, and an adult confirms every plant because poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site. The garden follows one adult to six children, and an adult checks woodpiles for black widows before children reach in.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy logs and stones to carry, rough bark and pinecones to handle, and strong smelling herbs such as rosemary and lavender.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer smooth stones and leaves on a tray to look at first, and gloves for gathering.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for sculptures made from leaves, stones and wood outdoors, including Wood Line in the Presidio.
Mabel McKay on the Artists page, for Pomo baskets woven from sedge, willow and feathers.

sections.text: A basket or bag for a walk, and a tray or table at home for your findings.

items: Collect fallen leaves, sticks and stones on a walk.
Arrange them into patterns or a circle on the ground.
Build a tiny house for a bug with bark and leaves.
Sort findings by color, size or shape.
Lay leaves on dark and light paper and compare.

sections.text: Your child leads the gathering and decides what to keep. They can choose where to display findings at home. Your child can sort findings into small baskets and return what is done to the garden or yard. Leaves and petals can go into the compost.

items: I wonder where this came from.
How does it look on the dark paper?
Tell me about your favorite one.

sections.text: Noticing, caring for nature and seeing the seasons change. Handling leaves, stones and bark gives many kinds of touch and smell and is calming for many children.
Bring a special finding from a family walk to our nature table, with a note about where you found it. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Gather only plants you know, and leave mushrooms and berries alone. Wash hands after gathering.

cards.title: Ramps and moving things
cards.summary: Ramps, tubes, gutters, pulleys and wheels that children build and change to make balls, water and loads roll, slide and travel.

items: Wooden planks and cove molding with balls of different sizes on a rug or in the outdoor piazza.
Rain gutters and pipes leaning on crates, fences and the climbing structure in the yard.
Ramps in the sand area, where balls and sand travel together.
Water ramps from gutters and pipes in the garden, carrying water to the beds.
A pegboard wall with tubes and funnels that children move to make a ball path.
Cardboard tubes taped to a wall or fence for a ball run.
A pulley with a rope and bucket hung from a beam for lifting loads.
Wheelbarrows and wagons for moving soil, mulch and stones in the garden.
Dominoes, blocks and books lined up to make a chain that falls in a row.
A grassy slope for rolling bodies and balls.
For the West class, big balls and wide, low ramps for pushing and chasing.
A ramp painting tray, with a sheet of white paper in a shallow box, a short plank and balls dipped in red, yellow and blue tempera, so colors cross and mix where paths meet.
Black paper on a long plank with balls rolled through white tempera, beside white paper with balls rolled through black, so children compare the trails.
Ramps of many surfaces, such as smooth wood, corrugated cardboard, carpet, bubble wrap, a metal tray and a towel, to test what slows a ball.
A basket of things that move in different ways, such as acorns, spools, wooden eggs, toy cars, corks, pinecones, a cylinder block and a cube block.
A small ramp kit in each class atelier with two planks, three unit blocks and a basket of balls, so ramps can happen any day on a rug.
Long gutters on the slope in the Tire swing yard, where children send balls, water and leaves from top to bottom.
A rope and bucket pulley hung from a low branch in the Log yard for lifting acorns, stones and sand.
For the North class, two or three planks and many balls of one size, so children can change the height and see what happens.
For the South class, clipboards, chalk marks and a tape measure for marking where things stop, and a sand timer for racing two balls.

sections.text: Both. Long ramps need many hands to hold, catch and fix. A child alone can test one ball again and again until they are satisfied. In the yards a long gutter run needs one child at the top, one at each bend and one to catch. In a class atelier a child alone with one plank can test the same ball many times and decide when the idea is finished.

Use balls too large to swallow with the West class and check that ramps rest on stable supports. Agree where balls and catchers go so feet and heads stay clear. Store gutters, tubes and planks together outdoors in a rack where children can reach them. Planks with sanded edges and lengths of cove molding make good indoor ramps, and vinyl rain gutters and PVC pipe work well outdoors. Paint balls stay in a tray with sides, and children wash them in a bucket afterwards. Check for pinch points when planks rest on crates, and agree that bodies stay off ramps built for balls.

items: Build and change the ramps themselves.
Choose what to send down and predict what happens.
Catch, measure and mark how far things go.
Fix the ramp when something falls off.
Work out turns with friends.
Draw or photograph their best ramp.
Put tubes and planks back in the rack.
Choose ramp surfaces and predict which one is fastest.
Mix the paint colors for ramp painting and wash the balls after.

sections.text: Children carry gutters, tubes and planks back to the outdoor rack and stack them by length. Balls go into their basket, and paint balls go into the wash bucket to be scrubbed and laid on a towel. An adult lifts any long plank or crate that is too heavy, and children do the rest as part of the work.

Stand or kneel at the bottom of the ramp, where you can see the whole run and the children's faces. Stay relaxed when balls fly off or ramps fall, and describe what you see, such as You raised the top and the ball went past the rug. Let children fix the ramp themselves.

items: I wonder what will happen if we make it steeper.
Why do you think that one stopped?
I notice the colors changed where the paths crossed.
How could we make it go farther?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer one plank and some balls and watch.
For the West class, offer big soft balls and one wide, low plank to push, chase and climb beside.
Add more planks, blocks and crates for changing height.
Add things that roll, slide and stop, and wonder about the differences.
Mark how far things travel with tape and measure.
Join ramps into longer paths with turns and drops.
Build ramps for water and sand outdoors.
Add pulleys, wagons and wheelbarrows for moving heavy loads.
Build a pegboard ball wall or a cardboard tube run on a fence.
Make chain reactions with blocks, dominoes and balls.
Watch The Way Things Go by Peter Fischli and David Weiss on screen and wonder about chain reactions.
Draw plans and test them, then change the plan.
Roll balls through red, yellow and blue paint on white paper and look for new colors where trails cross.
Compare trails on black and white paper and talk about what shows best.
Cover ramps with different materials and test what speeds or slows a ball.
Draw a ramp from observation, then build it again from the drawing the next day.
Model ways to make a ramp steady, such as stacking blocks under both ends and taping joins.
Build a big shared ball machine over many days.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Ramps and balls are open to everyone, with large balls only in the West class. Pulleys lifting loads, ramps leaning on the climbing structure and long gutters in the Tire swing yard need an educator nearby.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer long heavy planks and gutters to carry and set up, and a grassy slope to roll down with the whole body.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a short ramp at a table with one quiet ball, away from busy gutters and crashing.
connected: Peter Fischli and David Weiss on the Artists page, for a film of a long chain reaction made from everyday objects.

home.title: Ramps and moving things at Home

sections.text: A board, a large book or a cardboard tube, some balls and small toy cars. Washable paint, a shallow box lid, paper and a few balls make ramp painting.

items: Lean a board on the couch and roll balls and cars down.
Tape paper towel tubes to a wall to make a ball run.
Line up blocks or books so they fall in a row.
Pour water down a ramp in the yard or bath.
Put paper in a box lid, add a paint-dipped ball and tilt it to make tracks.

sections.text: Your child builds and changes the ramp. They can decide what to roll and guess what will happen. Your child can gather the balls and cars into a basket and carry the board back to its place. After ramp painting, they can wash the balls in a bowl of water.

items: I wonder what will go fastest.
How could we make it go farther?
Tell me about your ramp.

sections.text: Predicting, testing ideas and learning how things move. Carrying ramps and chasing balls helps children judge distance and plan how to move.
Send a photo or drawing of a home ramp, or clean tubes and gutters for our class. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use balls too big to fit in a small mouth. Watch that ramps are steady and away from stairs. Paint play stays in the box lid and the balls get rinsed in a bucket afterwards.

cards.title: Magnets
cards.summary: Large, safe magnets that children use to find out what attracts, what repels and what moves through other materials.

items: A basket of large magnet wands, horseshoe magnets and bar magnets on the Investigation table.
A tray of objects from around the room to test, such as keys, spoons, washers, wooden pieces, corks and stones.
A magnet dragged in a plastic bag through creek sand or garden soil to see what clings.
Paper clips or washers on a paper plate, moved by a magnet underneath.
Ring magnets on a dowel that float above each other.
Iron filings sealed inside a clear bottle or tray for moving with a magnet.
Magnetic tiles on the light table or a window.
Magnets with a metal board, wall or cookie sheet for building pictures and stories.
A magnet on a string for fishing metal objects out of water or sand.
A compass and a magnet together for wondering about direction.
Clipboards with two columns of pictures for children to record what sticks.
For the West class, big magnet wands and large metal pieces for pulling and dropping.
A sealed tray of iron filings set over white paper and another over black paper, so children compare the patterns a magnet pulls.
Magnets on different surfaces, such as a cookie sheet, a whiteboard, a fridge door, a metal gate and a filing cabinet, to find which ones hold.
A magnet maze, where a car or a paper clip on a cardboard track is pulled by a magnet wand underneath.
Magnets tested through different materials, such as a thin book, a sheet of felt, a wooden board, a cup of water and a glass of sand.
A small magnet basket in each class atelier, beside a metal tray for building and storytelling.
A magnet walk outdoors, testing the gate, the fence, the wheelbarrow, the garden tools and the bench legs.
For the North class, big wands, a basket of large metal lids and a sort into two baskets.
For the South class, prediction charts on clipboards, where children draw what they think will stick and then test it.

sections.text: Both. Testing alone can go on for a long time. Comparing findings brings children together to argue and test again. In the Studio a small group can test the same object and argue over the result. In a class atelier a child alone can sort, chart and test again for a long time.

Use only magnets too large to swallow and leave out small strong magnets, because two swallowed magnets can cause serious harm. Seal iron filings tightly and check sealed bottles often. Keep magnets away from phones, tablets and cards, and store them in pairs so they last. Ceramic and alnico wands are sturdy and safe to drop. Check sealed filing trays each week for cracks and replace any that leak. Store bar magnets with a metal keeper or in pairs, and keep them away from the light table tablet and cameras.

items: Test objects and sort them by their own findings.
Choose new objects to test.
Record findings with drawings or pictures.
Share discoveries at meeting time.
Keep magnets in their pairs and baskets.
Remind friends where magnets should not go.
Choose a background and record the filing patterns in drawings.
Lead a magnet walk for a friend and show what they found.

sections.text: Children put magnets back in their pairs, sort test objects into the basket and set sealed filing trays flat on the shelf. They check the floor for any small metal piece and drop it in the basket. Each pair has a labeled slot, so the magnet tray is reset in a few minutes before children move on.

Sit at the investigation table beside the children and test along with them. Keep your voice even and describe what you see, such as The clip jumped when the magnet came close. Let children discover their own answers and argue them out.

items: I wonder why this one sticks and that one does not.
How does the pattern change when you turn it around?
I notice the filings look different on black.
Tell me about your chart.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer magnet wands and a few objects to test.
For the West class, offer big wands and large metal lids to pull, drop and pull again.
Hunt for what magnets stick to around the room and yards.
Notice push and pull between two magnets.
Test through paper, water, wood and fabric.
Count how many paper clips each magnet can hold.
Look for black sand in the soil and creek with a magnet in a bag.
Record findings on simple picture charts.
Build with magnetic tiles on the light table.
Make magnet games and machines, such as fishing or moving a car on a track.
Explore a compass and wonder about north.
Look at the magnetic sculptures of Takis on screen and wonder about things floating in the air.
Draw iron filing patterns with black pencil on white paper and white pencil on black paper.
Test magnets through many materials and record each result.
Build magnet mazes and tracks from cardboard and tape.
Model holding the wand still and moving it slowly, so children see the filings follow.
Keep magnets open in the Investigation table for children to come back to.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Large magnets are open to everyone, and small strong magnets never come to school. Sealed iron filing trays are checked each week, and fishing for metal in water needs an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer strong wands to pull heavy metal lids and a magnet walk around the yards to test fences and tools.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one wand and a small tray of objects at a quiet table, with time to test slowly.
connected: Takis on the Artists page, for sculptures held in the air by magnets.

sections.text: One or two large magnets, such as a magnet wand or a big fridge magnet, and a basket of household objects.

items: Walk around the house testing what the magnet sticks to.
Sort objects into two piles.
Move paper clips on a plate with a magnet underneath.
Fish for spoons and keys with a magnet on a string.
Move paper clips on white paper and then on dark paper with a magnet underneath and compare.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to test and guesses first. They can sort the results. Your child can put magnets back in pairs, sort the test objects into a basket and keep magnets away from phones and cards.

items: I wonder if it will stick.
Why do you think that happened?
Tell me what you found.

sections.text: Testing ideas, sorting and noticing invisible pushes and pulls. Moving magnets slowly and watching closely helps hands and eyes work together.
Send a drawing or list of what stuck to magnets at home. Large magnets for our class are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Never use small strong magnets or magnet pieces small enough to swallow. Keep magnets away from phones and cards. Magnet toys with small loose magnets are not safe for young children.

cards.title: Tape
cards.summary: Masking, painter's, paper and packing tape for joining, marking, sticking, peeling and building, on tables, floors, walls and outdoors.

items: A tape shelf with dispensers, small scissors, a ruler, a measuring tape and masking, painter's and paper tape in several widths.
Toys and natural objects taped to a table for children to rescue by peeling.
A web of painter's tape across a doorway, sticky side out, for tossing light things onto.
Tape roads and maps on the floor for blocks and vehicles.
Tape shapes on concrete outdoors, colored with chalk, then peeled to show the lines.
Tape resist on paper with watercolor painted over, then peeled.
Paper tape collage on cardboard, brown paper bags or the whole table.
Tape lines on the floor for jumping, hopping, balancing and measuring.
Tape for joining boxes, tubes and recycled materials into sculptures.
A strip of tape stretched between two chairs to test what sticks.
Packing tape and clear contact paper for sticky collage with leaves and petals.
Tape on a wall for building a group line drawing that grows each day.
Tape and string for marking a garden path or a bed in the garden.
Pre-torn strips on the edge of the table for the West class to peel and stick.
White paper tape on black paper and black tape on white paper, side by side, for line drawings made only from tape.
Colored painter's tape in a limited palette, such as only red, yellow and blue, for overlapping strips on a window and seeing new colors.
Tape on many surfaces, such as kraft paper, cardboard, a wood board, a window, a mirror and concrete outside.
A tape corner in each class atelier with masking tape, paper and boxes, ready for joining.
For the North class, wide masking tape and tape torn by pinching, with strips stuck to the table edge.
For the South class, tape maps of our site on the floor, with paper signs for the garden, the animal yards and each class.

sections.text: Both. A tape web or floor map is a shared project. A child alone can tear and stick for a long time and make careful decisions. In the Studio a tape mural or floor map needs many hands. In a class atelier a child can tape a careful line drawing alone.

Painter's tape peels off walls and floors without damage, and it is the best choice for walls and furniture. Teach how to tear tape by pinching, and offer dispensers and scissors for older children. Keep tape off living plants and animals, and pick up scraps so goats, chickens and rabbits never eat them. Keep rolls on a dowel or a paper towel holder so children can pull and tear. Colored tape fades in sun, so outdoor tape lines are temporary and get peeled up together.

items: Tear, cut and stick tape with their own hands.
Decide where tape goes and when it comes off.
Make lines, maps and roads for others to use.
Pick up tape scraps from the floor and yards.
Teach friends how to pinch and tear.
Tell an educator when tape is running low.
Choose tape colors and backgrounds and say what changes.
Peel up tape lines at the end and roll scraps into a ball for the trash.

sections.text: Children peel tape lines up off floors and walls, roll scraps into a ball and drop it in the trash. They walk the yards to check for tape pieces near the animal yards and plants. Rolls go back on their dowel holder, so the close is done by children before they leave the space.

Sit at the table with the children and let them tear and stick even when tape tangles. Keep a calm face when tape sticks to itself, and narrate what you see, such as You pinched the edge and pulled and the strip came free.

items: I wonder what will stick.
Where does the line go now?
I notice the white tape glows on the black paper.
How did you make the corner hold?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer pre-torn strips to peel and stick.
For the West class, stick and peel strips on a window or tabletop with lots of repeats.
Add rolls and dispensers for tearing.
Rescue toys taped to a table.
Make tape lines on the floor for moving bodies.
Build roads and maps for blocks and cars.
Join boxes and recycled materials into sculptures.
Try tape resist with chalk and watercolor.
Build a sticky web for tossing and catching.
Make a group tape drawing on a wall or window.
Look at the climbable tape installations made by the design group Numen/For Use on screen.
Make clear tape casts of small objects by wrapping them, cutting the tape open and taking the object out.
Make tape drawings on black and white paper side by side.
Overlap colored tape on a window and look for new colors.
Draw a map of our site on the floor with tape and add signs.
Model tearing by pinching and pulling, and taping a corner so a box stands up.
Keep tape on an open shelf for any project.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Tape is self-serve for every age. Packing tape with a toothed dispenser stays at a table with an adult, and tape used near the animal yards is picked up right away so animals never eat it.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer wide tape to stretch across doorways and pull off tables, and big tape webs to push through.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer pre-torn strips on the table edge and a small sheet of paper, so fingers touch only a little sticky surface.
connected: Numen/For Use on the Artists page, for huge walk-in sculptures made only from clear packing tape.

sections.text: Masking or painter's tape and some boxes, paper or toys.

items: Make a road or a hopscotch on the floor with tape.
Tape small toys to a table and let your child peel them free.
Join boxes into a sculpture.
Stick tape on paper, paint over it, then peel it off.
Make a tape drawing on dark paper with white tape, or on white paper with dark tape.

sections.text: Your child tears, sticks and decides where tape goes. They can also help peel it up afterward. Your child can peel the tape up, roll it into a ball and put it in the trash. Put the tape roll back in its basket for next time.

items: Where could the road go?
I wonder what will stick to it.
Tell me about your tape picture.

sections.text: Strong fingers, planning and joining things together. Tearing and peeling tape builds strong fingers and both hands working together.
Send a photo of a tape road or a sculpture made at home. Extra rolls of masking or painter's tape for our class are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Painter's tape comes off walls and floors without damage. Keep tape away from babies' mouths. Colored tape can leave marks on walls, so test a small spot first.

cards.title: Paper
cards.summary: Ways to offer paper itself as a material to tear, crumple, fold, roll, cut, hear and build with.

items: A paper carpet taped to the floor with many papers side by side, such as kraft, tissue, parchment, newsprint, corrugated card and foil, for hands and feet to explore.
A basket of scrap paper beside a large empty bin, with time to tear and listen.
A paper library on a low shelf with papers sorted by kind, weight and color for children to choose from.
Long rolls of butcher paper unrolled down the hallway, across the outdoor piazza or along a fence for big bodies and big marks.
Paper strips with a stapler, tape and a small glue dish for curling, looping and standing paper up into sculptures on a cardboard base.
Tissue and parchment papers on the light table to layer, fold and look through.
Paper and a few simple folds offered beside one real folded object, such as a fan, a paper boat or a paper cup.
Good scissors with papers of different stiffness, including thin strips that cut in one snip for the youngest hands.
Paper taken outdoors on a windy day to hold up, let fly, chase and weigh down with stones.
Large sheets of kraft paper for wrapping objects and guessing what is hidden inside.
Paper tubes and rolled paper for building tall, making ramps and looking through.
A tray with spray bottles so children can watch paper soften, tear, stick and dry.
Paper bags and boxes for paper houses, masks, puppets and costumes.
One sheet of paper each and the question, how many ways can we change it?
White, black, gray, brown kraft and colored papers side by side in the paper library, so children compare and choose the color of their ground.
Black paper with white chalk, white oil pastel, white pencil and white crayon, offered beside white paper with charcoal and black pencil.
Papers cut into circles, long strips, triangles and torn-edge pieces, so a drawing or fold can begin from a shape beyond a rectangle.
Papers from tiny cards the size of a palm to a floor mural on butcher paper, set out together so children choose a scale.
Watercolor paper, newsprint, cardstock, tracing paper and vellum in a tray for testing which holds paint, folds cleanly or lets light through.
A paper tool caddy with scissors of several sizes, a hole punch, a bone folder, a ruler, a stapler and paper clips.

sections.text: Both. A shared paper carpet or a long roll invites children to work side by side and notice each other's ideas. A single sheet held in one child's hands gives quiet room to fold, cut and decide alone. In the Studio a long roll invites a group to share one big surface. In each class atelier a small paper library on a low shelf lets a child choose a paper and work alone at any time.

Save and sort paper all year in labeled bins so the paper library is always full. Keep good scissors for paper only and store them blade down in a caddy. Recycle with children and save the smallest scraps for collage and papermaking. Store papers flat by kind and color in shallow drawers or labeled trays, with black and white always stocked. Buy good quality paper, since thin paper tears under young hands and frustrates. Cut circles and strips ahead with a paper cutter, which stays adult only.

items: Sorts incoming paper into the paper library by kind and color.
Chooses the paper that fits an idea and explains why.
Tears, cuts and folds with real tools and shows a friend a new fold.
Cares for scissors and returns them to the caddy.
Decides when a piece is finished or still growing.
Sorts scraps into collage, papermaking and recycling bins.
Names the sounds and textures papers make and invents words for them.
Photographs or draws their paper work for the wall.
Choose between black, white and colored paper and say why.
Cut circles and strips for others from a template with an educator.

sections.text: Children sort scraps into the collage, papermaking and recycling bins and return unused paper flat to its tray by kind and color. Scissors go back in the caddy blade down. Clearly labeled bins at child height mean the paper library is tidy without educator time later.

Sit on the floor or at the table with a sheet of your own and tear, fold or crumple slowly as the children do. Stay calm with the noise and the scraps, and narrate what you see, such as You folded it twice and now it stands up. Leave their folds and cuts as they made them.

items: I notice this paper sounds different from that one.
I wonder what this paper could become.
How does the chalk look on the black paper?
Tell me about the shape you chose.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with tearing and crumpling a few kinds of paper, with time to listen and feel.
For the West class, offer big sheets of kraft and tissue to crumple, tear and stomp on, with no tools.
For the North class, add snipping strips with small scissors and folding in half.
Build a paper carpet and change it over several days by adding new papers and taking some away.
Add light by holding papers to the window, the light table and a flashlight to see which ones let light through.
Introduce scissors with thin strips first, then wider sheets, then curves.
Offer simple folds such as halves, fans and rolls, and let children teach each other.
Move to paper sculpture with strips, tabs, slots and tape on a sturdy base.
Build big with paper by wrapping a chair, lining a tunnel or making a paper house children can enter.
Take paper outdoors to meet wind, rain and sun, and record what happens to it.
Explore papers in a small group, such as which one holds water, which one tears straight and which one stands up.
Try paper weaving with strips children cut themselves.
Connect to papermaking so children see where paper comes from and how it can be made again.
Look at large paper cut-outs by artists and cut big shapes for a shared wall.
Offer black and white paper side by side with white and black drawing tools, and talk about what each surface does.
Change the shape of the paper to circles, long strips and torn edges and notice how children's work changes.
Model techniques without making a product, such as scoring a fold with a bone folder, tearing along a wet line and cutting by turning the paper.
For the South class, plan and build paper sculptures and pop-ups from drawings.
Open the paper library for self-serve use in the Studio and class ateliers.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Paper is self-serve in the Studio and every class atelier. The paper cutter is adult only, and scissors stay at the table with an educator nearby for the youngest children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick kraft paper to crumple into big balls, tear into long strips with both arms and stomp flat on the floor.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer smooth, quiet paper such as cardstock or tissue in a small stack, with a choice to watch others tear first.
connected: Henri Matisse on the Artists page, for cutting large shapes from painted paper in his cut-outs.

sections.text: Paper you already have, such as newspaper, envelopes, paper bags, wrapping paper and tissue, plus child-safe scissors and some tape. Black or dark paper from an art store with a white crayon or chalk makes a striking first invitation.

items: Make a paper pile on the floor and let your child tear, crumple and listen.
Save a box of different papers and let your child sort them by color or feel.
Fold a paper boat or a fan together, then float it or wave it.
Wrap small toys in paper and take turns guessing what is inside.
Tape a big sheet to the floor or a wall for drawing with the whole body, and try white chalk on black paper beside crayon on white.

sections.text: Let your child choose the paper, decide how to change it and help put scraps in the recycling. Small helpers can hand you tape and sort colors. Your child can sort scraps into a box for later and a bag for recycling, and put scissors back in a cup or caddy.

items: How does this paper sound?
I wonder what this paper could become.
Tell me about the paper you chose.

sections.text: Your child is building hand strength and learning how materials change when we fold, tear and cut them. Tearing and crumpling paper uses both hands together and gives the fingers and arms strong work.
Send in clean, interesting papers such as wrapping paper, maps, envelopes or paper bags for our paper library. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Tearing is a good first step before scissors. Put scissors away after use. Stay close with little ones, since paper and thin wrappers are not for mouths. Keep a box of black, white and brown paper bags ready so your child can choose.

cards.title: Paper collage
cards.summary: Ways to tear, cut, arrange and join papers into pictures, maps, stories and shared walls.

items: A tray of torn and cut paper scraps sorted by color, with a glue dish, a brush and a sturdy base.
Contact paper taped sticky side out on a window or low wall for the youngest children to press tissue, petals and leaves onto.
Papers children paint with tempera on one day, dried and cut into collage papers on another day.
Black or white base paper with bright cut shapes, offered beside images of large paper cut-outs.
Printed photos of the garden, the animal yards and our class for children to cut into collage maps and stories.
Old magazines, maps, calendars and seed catalogs for collage portraits, with a mirror nearby.
Natural collage outdoors with fallen leaves, petals and bark pressed onto contact paper or a glue board.
Tissue collage on parchment or clear plastic, hung in the window so light passes through.
A long shared collage on butcher paper that the whole class adds to over a week.
Collage on boxes, tubes and cardboard sculptures.
A color zone tray holding one color family only, such as every blue we can find.
Texture collage with corrugated card, sandpaper, doilies, foil and fabric scraps.
Story collage, where a child tells a story and builds the pictures with cut paper.
A collage map of the creek trail or the garden beds made from torn paper.
A limited palette collage of one color family, such as only blues, cut from children's own painted papers in tints with white and shades with black.
Black and white collage, with black, white and gray papers on a black ground and on a white ground side by side.
Collage papers painted by children with red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera, using sponges, rollers, combs and feathers for texture.
Warm and cool collage trays, one with reds, oranges and yellows, the other with blues, greens and purples.
Collage on grounds of many kinds, such as kraft paper, cardboard, circles, long strips, wood boards and fabric.
A collage tray in each class atelier with sorted scraps, a glue dish and two sizes of brush.

sections.text: Both. A shared collage grows layer by layer as children respond to each other's choices. A personal collage lets a child arrange and rearrange until it feels right. In the Studio a shared wall collage grows with many hands. In a class atelier a child can collage alone on a small board for as long as they like.

Keep scrap bins sorted by color so collage paper is always ready, and invite children to fill them. White glue in small dishes with brushes goes further than squeeze bottles, and flour paste works well for large pieces. Dry work flat on a labeled rack. No glitter. Petals and leaves come only from plants adults have confirmed. Make collage papers in batches, with a week of painting papers and a week of cutting. Keep black, white and gray scraps in their own bin. Brushes for glue stay separate from paint brushes.

items: Paints the papers that later become collage papers.
Sorts scraps into the color bins.
Chooses a base and arranges pieces before gluing.
Decides when to tear and when to cut.
Mixes flour paste from a picture recipe card.
Adds to the shared collage and talks about what changed.
Hangs finished work and tells its story.
Paint collage papers in tints and shades of one color.
Choose a black or white ground and compare.

sections.text: Children sort leftover scraps into the color bins and carry finished collages flat to the labeled drying rack. They wash glue brushes and dishes in the wash bucket and wipe the table with a damp sponge. Each bin and the drying rack are set within reach, so the close is complete when the gluing ends.

Sit at the collage table within arm's reach and keep your hands in your lap or busy with sorting scraps. Notice aloud the choices you see, such as You put the dark blue on top of the light one. Let pieces stay where the child puts them, even if they hang over the edge.

items: I notice you moved that piece three times.
I wonder what would happen if this piece went on top.
How did you make the blue lighter?
Tell me about your collage.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with pressing pieces onto sticky contact paper so arranging comes before gluing.
For the West class, press pieces onto contact paper on a window, with large shapes and no glue.
Add glue dishes and brushes and notice together how much glue holds a piece.
Offer tearing first, then scissors, then shapes children draw and cut themselves.
Make painted papers with tempera and texture tools, then collage with them as picture book artists do.
Look at large cut-paper works and cut big shapes for a wall collage.
Add photographs of our site for collage maps, portraits and stories.
Try see-through collage for the window and the light table.
Add found and textured papers for collage you can feel with your eyes closed.
Look at collage that layers photographs and papers into city scenes, then make a collage of our own neighborhood.
Build collage onto boxes and sculptures.
Layer collage with drawing, paint and stitching in mixed media.
Make a collage book with one page from each child.
Make a limited palette collage from tints and shades of one color.
Try black and white collage on black and white grounds.
Make warm and cool collage and talk about how each feels.
Collage from observation, such as a fig leaf or a rooster, with the real thing or a photo nearby.
For the South class, cut detailed shapes with small scissors and layer them.
Open the collage materials for self-serve use on a shelf children keep stocked.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Collage is self-serve once the scrap bins and glue dishes are known. Natural collage outdoors uses only petals and leaves from plants an adult has confirmed.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick papers to tear with both hands, stiff card to cut and sticky contact paper to press hard with palms.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a glue stick or contact paper instead of wet glue, and a small tray with a few pieces.
connected: Eric Carle on the Artists page, for picture books built from his own painted tissue paper collage.
Henri Matisse on the Artists page, for large shapes cut from painted paper and arranged on the wall.
Romare Bearden on the Artists page, for collage that layers photographs and papers into neighborhood scenes.

sections.text: Old magazines, junk mail, wrapping paper, tissue, a glue stick or white glue, child-safe scissors and a piece of cardboard as a base. Black and white paper as a base lets your child compare how colors look on each.

items: Tear colorful pages into pieces and sort them into piles by color.
Make a picture of your family or your street from cut and torn paper.
Stick tissue scraps on a window with tape and look at the light.
Gather fallen leaves and petals on a walk and press them onto clear contact paper.
Paint a few sheets of paper one day and cut them up for collage the next day.
Make a picture from only one color, using all the blues or greens you can find.

sections.text: Your child chooses, tears, cuts and places the pieces. Let them move things around as much as they like before gluing. Your child can sort leftover paper into a box by color, wash the glue brush and wipe the table with a damp sponge.

items: Where do you want to put this piece?
It reminds me of our walk. Tell me about yours.
How did you choose the colors?

sections.text: Your child is making choices, planning and strengthening small hand muscles. Tearing, cutting and placing small pieces strengthens fingers and helps eyes and hands work together.
Send in colorful scrap paper, old maps, calendars or seed catalogs for our collage bins. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Use a small amount of glue on a dish with a brush or cotton swab. Only use leaves and flowers you know are safe, and leave some for others. Paint a few sheets in one color with a little white or black mixed in, and you have a whole family of collage papers.

cards.title: Glue
cards.summary: Ways to explore joining with white glue, homemade pastes and low-temp glue guns, and to compare them with other ways of holding things together.

items: Small dishes of white glue with brushes beside paper scraps for first gluing.
Glue sticks, glue dishes, flour paste and tape side by side to try which one holds which material.
Flour paste children mix from flour and water with a picture recipe card.
A wood scrap sculpture table with white glue and a sturdy base, left to dry overnight.
A low-temp glue gun table with one adult, a silicone mat and clear agreements, for joining cardboard and heavier natural materials.
Glue lines drawn on dark paper, left to dry, then rubbed with chalk or painted with watercolor.
Bark, seed pods, pebbles and acorn caps with a glue board at an outdoor table.
Papier-mache with flour paste and newspaper strips over a cardboard or crumpled paper form.
Glue drops on a plastic lid for the youngest children to watch dry from white to clear.
Salt sprinkled onto wet glue lines and touched with drops of liquid watercolor to watch the color travel.
A joining table where glue sits beside clips, string, slots and tape so children can choose.
A shared mosaic on cardboard with pebbles, smooth tiles and shells.
Black glue drawings, with white glue mixed with a little black tempera squeezed onto white paper, dried and then painted with watercolor between the lines.
White glue lines on black paper, dried overnight, then rubbed with white chalk or colored chalk.
Glue tinted with a limited palette of red, yellow and blue, squeezed onto clear plastic or a lid to dry and mix where colors touch.
Glue tools of many kinds, such as brushes, cotton swabs, sticks, spreaders and squeeze bottles, side by side.
Glue in each class atelier in small lidded jars, refilled by children from a larger bottle.
Gluing outdoors on a warm day with bark, leaves and seed pods on cardboard, where glue dries faster.
For the North class, glue dishes and brushes with paper and light natural materials.
For the South class, joining heavier pieces with white glue and clothespins to hold them while they dry.

sections.text: Both. Joining is often a two-person job, with one child holding while another fixes. Alone, children slow down and watch closely what the glue does. In the Studio a mosaic or papier-mache form is shared work. In a class atelier a child can glue alone and watch closely what the glue does.

Use small amounts in shallow dishes and wash brushes the same day. White glue needs a flat place and a night to dry. Glue guns are low-temp only, used with an adult on a clear surface, with cords out of the path. Flour paste keeps a few days covered in the refrigerator, then goes to compost. No glitter. Black glue is about one part black tempera to four parts white glue, mixed in the bottle and shaken. Test glue on each material before offering.

items: Fills glue dishes and decides how much is enough.
Mixes flour paste and adjusts it with more water or flour.
Chooses a joining method for each material and explains the choice.
Holds pieces for a friend while the glue sets.
Follows the glue gun agreements and reminds others of them.
Washes brushes and dishes and wipes the table.
Checks the drying rack and shares what held and what came apart.
Mix black glue in a squeeze bottle.
Refill the small glue jars.

sections.text: Children scrape extra glue from dishes back into the jar when it is clean, then wash brushes and dishes in the wash bucket and lay them on the drying rack. They wipe the table with a damp sponge and carry pieces to dry flat. An adult unplugs and stores the low-temp glue gun once it cools, and children do every other step.

Sit with the children and keep your face relaxed about sticky fingers and drips. Narrate what you see, such as You held it still and now it is staying. Let children decide how much glue to use and learn from what holds and what slips.

items: I wonder what the glue will look like tomorrow.
How did you make it hold?
I notice the white lines shine on the black paper.
Tell me about the pieces that stayed.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with glue dishes and paper only, and watch how children handle the brush.
For the West class, offer glue sticks and contact paper for pressing paper pieces.
Add flour paste that children mix, and compare it with white glue.
Offer heavier materials such as wood, bark and cardboard and notice what holds.
Set up a joining table with glue, tape, string, clips and slots side by side.
Watch glue dry over a day, from wet to tacky to hard, and record it with photos.
Introduce the low-temp glue gun with one adult and two or three children at a time.
Try glue resist drawings and salt and glue drawings.
Build papier-mache forms over several days, layer by layer.
Make mosaics and relief panels with natural materials for the garden or hallway.
Let children invent their own paste recipes from pantry staples and keep them in a class recipe book.
Draw with black glue, let it dry and paint between the lines with watercolor.
Draw with white glue on black paper and rub with chalk.
Tint glue with primaries and watch colors mix as it dries.
Model using a small amount of glue and holding pieces still while it sets.
Open the joining table for self-serve use, with children restocking it.

setting.why: Glue dishes and paste are open to everyone. Low-temp glue guns are one adult with two or three children at a small table with clear agreements.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer glue to spread with fingers and thick flour paste to mix with a big spoon.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a glue stick, a cotton swab or a brush so fingers stay dry, and a damp cloth nearby.
connected: Romare Bearden on the Artists page, for joining layers of cut photographs and paper into city scenes.
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: White school glue or a glue stick, a small dish and brush, paper scraps and cardboard. For homemade paste you need flour and water.

items: Mix a little flour and water together until it is thick and smooth, then use it to stick paper.
Try sticking paper, a leaf, a bottle cap and a piece of cardboard and see which ones stay.
Make a small sculpture from cardboard bits and glue and leave it to dry overnight.
Draw with glue on dark paper, let it dry and feel the bumpy lines.
Mix a little black paint into white glue, draw lines and paint between them the next day.
Draw lines of white glue on black paper, let them dry and rub colored chalk over the top.

sections.text: Your child can pour a little glue, mix paste, choose what to join and help wash the brush. Your child can put the cap back on the glue, wash the brush and dish and wipe the table. Flour paste can go to compost or into a covered jar in the fridge.

items: Which one do you think will hold best?
I wonder what happened to the glue overnight.
Tell me how you made it stay.

sections.text: Your child is learning how things join, how to plan and how to wait for something to dry. Spreading glue and holding pieces still builds careful hand control.
Send in cardboard, bottle caps, wood scraps or a family recipe for homemade paste. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use small amounts on a covered table. Homemade paste goes in the compost after a few days. Keep hot glue guns for grown-ups.

cards.title: Papermaking
cards.summary: Ways to turn scrap paper into new handmade paper with pulp, screens and plants from our garden.

items: A tub of soaked scrap paper for hands to squeeze and pull apart before any blending.
Pulp in a wide tub with a mold and deckle made from a frame and window screen, or an embroidery hoop and screen.
A couching tray with felt or cotton cloths and sponges for pressing water out.
Petals, leaves and grasses from plants we know, laid onto wet sheets.
Native wildflower seeds such as California poppy pressed into pulp for seed paper to plant in the garden.
Pulp colored with dye water from the botanical dye bed or with scraps of colored paper.
Pulp in squeeze bottles for pulp painting onto a wet base sheet.
Pulp pressed into molds, bowls or between hands for pulp shapes and small sculptures.
An outdoor papermaking table in the outdoor piazza on a warm day, with sheets drying in the sun.
Sheets drying on cloths laid on a rack, a board or a sunny window.
A basket of handmade papers from many places to touch and look at with magnifiers.
Paper from our class recycling bin torn by hand to start the whole cycle.
Pulp in a limited palette, with separate tubs of white pulp, black pulp from black paper scraps and pulp tinted with one dye bed color.
Black paper pulp and white paper pulp offered side by side, so children pour one over the other.
Pulp poured into round, long and torn-edge shapes by laying cookie cutters or cardboard frames on the screen.
Papermaking in each class atelier with a small hoop mold and a tub of soaked pulp.
For the North class, a small tub, a hoop mold and lots of squeezing before pulling sheets.
For the South class, sheets of many thicknesses compared by holding them to the window.

sections.text: Together. Papermaking has many jobs, from tearing and soaking to pulling, pressing and drying, and children share roles and take turns. A child may also return alone to pull sheet after sheet. In the Studio or outdoors many children share the pulp tub. In a class atelier one child can make a small sheet with a hoop mold.

Tear paper the day before and soak it overnight. An adult runs the blender while children watch and add paper and water. Avoid glossy paper. Cover tables, wear smocks and keep towels close. Strain leftover pulp through a screen and keep it out of the drain. Seeds go only in paper for our own garden and should be native or garden flowers we know. Sort scrap paper by color before soaking so pulp colors stay clear. Keep black pulp in its own tub.

items: Tears and soaks the paper.
Decides how much water the pulp needs.
Pulls sheets and presses water out with a sponge.
Chooses and places petals, leaves or seeds.
Checks drying sheets each day and peels them when ready.
Decides what the paper will become, such as books, cards or seed packets.
Teaches a new friend the steps.
Strains and saves leftover pulp.
Sort scrap paper by color before soaking.
Choose a pulp color and shape for their sheet.

sections.text: Children strain leftover pulp through a screen and save it in a lidded tub. They wring out sponges and towels, hang them on the line and wipe the table. Fresh sheets go to the drying rack and screens get a rinse in the wash bucket, so nothing waits for an educator afterward.

Stand or kneel at the pulp tub with sleeves rolled up and your own hands in the water. Keep your face relaxed when water splashes the floor, and narrate the change, such as The water is draining and the pulp is staying on the screen. Let children pull their own sheets, even thin or torn ones.

items: I wonder where the writing went when the paper got wet.
How does the pulp feel when you squeeze it?
I notice this sheet lets more light through.
Tell me what your paper will become.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with soaking and squeezing paper using only hands and water.
For the West class, offer soaked paper to squeeze and tear in a tub, with no mold.
Watch an adult blend pulp and notice how the paper changes.
Pull first sheets with a small hoop mold.
Add couching, pressing and drying, and visit the sheets each day.
Add petals, leaves and seeds and notice what shows through.
Color pulp with plant dye water and paper scraps.
Try pulp painting and pulp shapes.
Make seed paper, plant it in the garden and watch what grows.
Look closely at handmade papers from many places and at plant fibers in the garden, such as iris leaves and grasses.
Wonder together how people first made paper from plants, and share books about it.
Use the handmade paper for bookmaking, cards, mail and documentation.
Make pulp in a limited palette of white, black and one plant color.
Pour pulp into shapes beyond rectangles.
Use handmade papers for drawing with white pencil on black and black pencil on white.
Keep a papermaking area open in the Studio through a season.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Pulp tubs mean water and mess, so an adult stays at the tub. The blender is adult only, with children watching and adding paper and water.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big handfuls of wet pulp to squeeze and the job of pressing water out with a sponge and the whole body.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the job of laying petals on a sheet with tweezers or a spoon, and a dry spot to watch from first.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: Scrap paper such as old drawings, envelopes or egg cartons, a tub of water, an old picture frame or embroidery hoop with window screen, sponges and old towels. Sorting scrap paper by color before soaking gives white, gray or colored sheets.

items: Tear paper into small pieces and soak them overnight.
Squish the soaked paper with your hands until it turns into mush.
Spread the mush on the screen, press out the water with a sponge and let it dry in the sun.
Press flower petals or wildflower seeds into the wet paper.
Plant your seed paper in a pot and watch what grows.

sections.text: Your child tears, soaks, squishes, spreads and presses. They can check each day to see if the paper is dry. Your child can squeeze out sponges, hang towels to dry and help save leftover pulp in a container. Keep pulp out of the sink.

items: Where did the paper go?
I wonder what we could make with our new paper.
Tell me how the pulp feels.

sections.text: Your child is seeing how something old can become something new and following steps over several days. Squeezing wet pulp and pressing water out gives the hands strong touch and heavy work.
Send in a sheet of your homemade paper or a bag of clean scrap paper for our papermaking tub. This counts toward your family participation hours.

It is wet and messy, so work outside or on towels. Grown-ups run any blender. Pour leftover pulp in the trash or compost, never down the sink. Black paper scraps make dark pulp that looks striking with white petals pressed in.

cards.title: Bookmaking
cards.summary: Ways for children to make their own books, from simple folded pages to sewn bindings, class books and field journals.

items: Folded and stapled blank books in many sizes on a shelf in the writing center.
Accordion books from one long strip, ready to fill, fold and stand up.
Books sewn with yarn through hole-punched pages.
One sheet of paper folded and cut into a small eight-page book.
Books bound with a rubber band and a twig through two holes.
Board books children make from cardboard, with covers they choose.
