Touch books with pages of fabric, bark rubbings, handmade paper and other textures.
Photo books of our site, the animals and the garden for children to write in or dictate.
Story dictation books where a child tells, an adult writes and the child illustrates.
Flap and pop-up pages for hiding and finding.
A class book where each child adds one page about a shared experience.
Field journals carried on creek walks and garden visits with clipboards and pencils.
Wordless books told only in pictures.
Books children make for the reading nook and the lending basket.
Black paper books with white pencils, white crayons and white ink, beside white paper books with pencil and black pens.
Books in many shapes, such as circle books, long strip books, tiny palm books and big floor books.
Books of many papers, such as kraft, tracing paper, cardstock, handmade paper and vellum pages.
Bookmaking tools in a caddy, such as a long-arm stapler, a hole punch, a bone folder, yarn, a large needle and rubber bands.
A bookmaking tray in each class atelier with blank books and a few binding tools.
For the North class, two-page and four-page books with a single staple.

sections.text: Both. A class book gathers many voices into one place. A child's own book holds a private story, a collection or a question that matters to them. In the Studio a class book gathers every child's page. In a class atelier a child can make a small book of their own.

Keep blank books ready in many sizes so a story can start right away. Use a long-arm stapler or a hole punch and yarn for binding. Write exactly what a child says. Give children's books a place in the reading nook beside published books and treat them with the same care. Fold and cut black and white paper books ahead and keep them together on the shelf so both are always offered.

items: Chooses the size, paper and binding for the book.
Decides what goes on each page and in what order.
Dictates or writes the words and makes the pictures.
Punches holes and sews or ties the binding.
Designs the cover and gives the book a title and an author name.
Reads the book to a friend or at meeting time.
Places the book in the reading nook and cares for it.
Choose black or white pages for a book.
Fold and cut their own pages with a bone folder.

sections.text: Children return the hole punch, the stapler and yarn to their labeled caddy and drop paper scraps in the bins. They put finished books in the reading nook and works in progress in their own folder. A home for every tool and each child's book makes the close part of making the book.
Sit beside the child at the writing center and write their words exactly as they say them, in a regular voice. Keep your hands off their drawings. Read their book back slowly when they ask.

items: I wonder what happens on the next page.
Who would you like to read this to?
I notice you used white on the black pages.
Tell me about your cover.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with ready-made blank books and let children fill them freely.
For the West class, offer board books made from photos of their own class to hold and carry.
Add story dictation and reading books aloud at meeting time.
Offer accordion folds and simple sewn bindings children can do themselves.
Add flaps, pockets, windows and pop-ups.
Make books with handmade paper, painted papers and fabric covers.
Look at books for young children that use holes, textures and see-through pages, and make our own.
Make field journals for creek walks and the garden.
Make collection books, such as a book of leaves, feathers or bark rubbings.
Build class books that document a project in photos, drawings and children's words.
Make books to give, such as books for the class next door or for families.
Start a lending basket so books travel home and come back.
Make black paper books with white drawing tools.
Make books in shapes beyond rectangles.
Model folding with a bone folder and sewing a simple pamphlet stitch.
For the South class, plan a book with a first, middle and last page.
Open a bookbinding shelf in the writing center for self-serve use.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Blank books are self-serve in the writing center. Story dictation needs an adult sitting with the child, and sewing bindings with a large needle needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer punching holes with a strong hole punch, pressing folds with a bone folder and carrying a heavy class book to the reading nook.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small ready-made book with a few pages and a quiet seat in the writing center.
connected: Eric Carle on the Artists page, for picture books with die-cut holes and pages of many sizes.
Bruno Munari on the Artists page, for his Prebooks, small books of cloth, wood and see-through pages made for children too young to read.

sections.text: Paper, a stapler or hole punch, yarn or a rubber band, and something to draw with.

items: Fold a few sheets in half and staple them to make a blank book.
Make a long folding book from a strip of paper and draw a walk you took together.
Write down your child's story word for word and let them draw the pictures.
Make a family photo book with your child telling what is happening.
Tape leaves or tickets from a day out into a book of treasures.
Make a small book with black pages and draw in it with a white crayon or gel pen.

sections.text: Your child decides what the book is about, makes the pictures and tells the words. They can read it to you and the family. Your child can put the tools back in a box, add their finished book to the family bookshelf and keep unfinished pages in a folder.

items: Where does the story go next?
Who would you like to read this to?
Tell me about this page.

sections.text: Your child is learning that their ideas can be written down, read and shared. Folding, punching and turning pages builds careful hands, and seeing their words written gives children pride.
Send a homemade book to school to read with friends, or a photo of your child reading it. If you make blank books for our writing center, this counts toward your family participation hours.
Staplers and hole punches need a grown-up nearby. Keep books somewhere special so your child can find and reread them.

cards.title: Fabric
cards.summary: Ways to touch, drape, build, wrap, wash and make with cloth, indoors and outdoors.

items: A fabric basket with silk, cotton, wool, burlap, velvet, felt, lace and mesh to touch, drape and sort.
Large sheets, clips and clothespins outdoors for building forts and dens on fences, trees and crates.
Fabric hammocks and slings with an adult close, for enveloping and gentle swinging.
Sheer fabric on the light table and over windows to see color and light change.
A tub, a clothesline and clothespins for washing real cloth and hanging it to dry.
Fabric scraps with fabric scissors and glue for fabric collage.
A long length of fabric stretched across the yard on stakes to walk beside, hide behind and watch move in the wind.
Cloth for wrapping and tying around objects, dolls and bundles.
A parachute or big shared cloth for lifting, waving and sheltering under at meeting time.
Fabric strips beside the fence for weaving in and out.
Plain cotton for drawing on with fabric crayons or painting, then hanging as banners in the garden.
Fabric as a stage curtain or shadow screen for puppets and storytelling.
Open pieces of dress-up fabric with clips instead of costumes so children invent their own.
Tunnels and hideaways of fabric over tires and crates.
A limited palette fabric basket of one color in many textures, such as all blues in silk, denim, wool, cotton and mesh.
Black and white fabrics side by side, such as black velvet and white muslin, for wrapping, draping and drawing on.
Natural undyed fabrics in white, cream, gray and brown, beside the same fabrics dyed from the dye bed.
Fabric tools in a basket, such as fabric scissors, clips, clothespins, safety pins, rubber bands and string.
A fabric basket in each class atelier for wrapping, building and draping.
For the North class, large pieces with clips for building on fences and crates.

sections.text: Both. Building with big cloth takes many hands holding, clipping and deciding. A single soft piece of fabric offers one child comfort, privacy and calm. Outdoors a group can build a big fabric den together. In a class atelier one child can wrap and drape a small piece.

Wash fabric often and store it folded by kind in open baskets. Fabric scissors cut fabric only. Keep cords and long ties away from necks and keep hammock use close to an adult. Ask families for remnants and old sheets, and look for natural fibers at thrift stores. Store fabric by color family in open baskets. Keep black and white fabrics in their own basket.

items: Chooses fabric and decides how to use it.
Clips, ties and drapes fabric to build spaces.
Washes, hangs and folds fabric with the class.
Cuts fabric with fabric scissors and keeps them separate.
Sorts fabric by texture and kind.
Invites friends into a fabric space and makes its agreements.
Takes down and stores the fabric at the end of the day.
Choose fabric by color and texture.
Fold and sort fabric by color family.

sections.text: Children unclip fabric, fold it and sort it into the baskets by color family. Clips go back in their jar and fabric scissors into their own labeled place. Anything wet or muddy goes into the laundry basket, carried there by children, so the fabric is put away on the spot and never waits for an educator.

Sit near the fabric space at the children's level and stay there while they build. Keep your voice low and calm inside fabric dens. Notice what you see, such as You clipped it twice and now it stays up, and let children build their own walls even when they fall.

items: I notice this fabric lets the light through.
I wonder how we can make it stay up.
How does the velvet feel next to the cotton?
Tell me about your den.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a fabric basket for touching, wrapping and hiding.
For the West class, offer soft pieces to wrap, peek under and carry.
Add clips, clothespins and rope for building spaces indoors and out.
Bring fabric to the light table, the windows and the shadow screen.
Wash, hang and fold fabric as real care work.
Cut fabric for fabric collage and notice how it differs from paper.
Draw and paint on cloth and hang the banners in the garden.
Stretch a long cloth line across our yard on stakes and watch the wind move it through the day.
Look at stretchy fabric spaces people can walk inside, and build one with knotted fabric.
Look at quilts made from worn clothing and old cloth, and piece our own scraps together.
Add sewing, weaving and dyeing so children see how fabric is made and changed.
Look at where fibers come from, such as cotton bolls, flax and wool.
Offer a limited palette basket of one color in many textures.
Draw with white fabric crayon on black cloth and black on white.
Model folding and clipping fabric to make it hold.
Keep a fabric library in the Studio that children restock and sort.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Fabric building is open with an educator nearby, and cords and ties stay away from necks. Hammocks and slings need an adult close by, and fabric scissors are used at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a fabric hammock or tight wrap with an adult close, heavy blankets and a parachute to shake.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer smooth cotton or silk in a small piece, and a quiet fabric tent to rest in.
connected: Ernesto Neto on the Artists page, for stretchy fabric and crocheted spaces people walk inside.
The quiltmakers of Gee's Bend on the Artists page, for quilts pieced from worn work clothes and fabric scraps.
El Anatsui on the Artists page, for large shimmering cloths made of metal pieces joined with wire.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude on the Artists page, for wrapping buildings and landscapes in fabric.

sections.text: Old sheets, towels, scarves, pillowcases and fabric scraps, plus clothespins or clips.

items: Build a fort with sheets, chairs and clothespins.
Make a touch basket of different fabrics and feel them with eyes closed.
Wash doll clothes or washcloths in a tub and hang them on a line.
Wrap a stuffed animal in a blanket or wrap a gift in a cloth.
Hold a sheet together and wave it up and down to make wind.
Gather all the soft things of one color in the house and feel how different they are.

sections.text: Your child builds, clips, wraps, washes and folds. Let them decide how the fort is built and who gets invited in. Your child can unclip, fold and stack the fabric in a basket, and put clips in a jar. Taking down the fort is part of the fun.

items: How can we make it stay up?
I wonder how this one feels.
Tell me about your fort.

sections.text: Your child is solving building problems, using their whole body and finding cozy places to rest. Wrapping in fabric and building forts gives deep pressure and cozy places, which help many children feel calm.
Send in clean fabric remnants, old sheets or scarves for our fabric library. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep ties, cords and long scarves away from necks. Stay close when a child is inside or under heavy fabric.

cards.title: Yarn and string
cards.summary: Ways to wrap, wind, tie, connect, knot and build with yarn, string and rope.

items: Yarn for wrapping sticks, branches and cardboard shapes, with thick chunky yarn and short sticks for the North class.
Two crossed sticks and yarn for wrapping a woven diamond, known in Mexico as the ojo de dios.
A yarn web strung between table legs, chairs or trees to crawl through and add to.
Finger knitting and finger crochet chains for older children.
Cardboard rings for making yarn pom-poms.
A basket of yarn, embroidery floss, cotton string, jute twine and rope of many weights and textures to roll, unwind, compare and wind back up.
Rope outdoors for pulling, tying and lifting buckets on a pulley.
Found objects to wrap in yarn until they become new forms.
String painting, where yarn dipped in tempera is laid on paper and pulled out.
A fence post or tree trunk wrapped by the whole class over a season.
String telephones made from cups and a long string.
String for measuring a friend, a garden bed or the path to the gate.
Mobiles of sticks and string with found treasures hanging from them.
Thick cord and rope for practicing knots, bows and loops.
A limited palette yarn basket of one color with black and white, such as reds with black and white, for wrapping sticks and cardboard shapes.
Natural undyed yarns in white, cream, gray, brown and black from different sheep, beside yarn dyed in our dye bed.
Warm yarns in one basket and cool yarns in another, so a shared wrapped branch can move from warm to cool.
Yarn tools in a basket, such as small scissors, plastic needles, a wooden yarn winder, a lucet, a spool knitter, clothespins and tape.
A yarn basket in each class atelier with sticks from the garden for quiet wrapping.
For the South class, a spool knitter or lucet for making long cords.

sections.text: Both. A shared web or wrapped tree grows from many children's turns. Wrapping alone is calm, rhythmic work a child can settle into. In the yards a web or wrapped tree is shared work across many days. In a class atelier wrapping one stick alone is steady, quiet work.

Cut yarn into lengths children can manage and wrap the ends with tape for threading. String is never tied around necks, and fingers and wrists are wrapped only loosely. Take webs down before rest and at the end of the day. Wind loose yarn back into balls together so it does not tangle. Worn-out natural fibers can go in the compost. Store yarn by color family in clear jars with a hole in the lid so a strand pulls through without tangling. Keep black, white and natural yarns always stocked. Cut lengths about as long as a child's arm so they do not knot.

items: Chooses colors and textures for wrapping.
Winds yarn back into balls and stores it.
Cuts lengths and tapes the ends.
Ties knots and teaches a friend a knot.
Decides where a web goes and how it comes down.
Plans a shared wrapping project with the group.
Holds the end for a younger child.
Choose a limited palette for a wrapping and explain the choice.
Wind yarn on the winder for the next group.

sections.text: Children take webs down, wind loose yarn back into balls and return each ball to its jar. Short ends go into the scrap basket for wrapping and worn natural fibers to compost. An adult checks that no string is left at neck height, and children do the rest.

Sit with the children and wrap a stick of your own slowly, so the rhythm in the room stays calm. Keep your hands still when yarn tangles and let the child try first. Notice aloud what you see, such as You wrapped round and round and the stick turned red.

items: I wonder where this string goes.
How did you make the knot?
I notice the colors change as you wrap.
Tell me about your web.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with winding and unwinding yarn balls and wrapping sticks.
For the West class, offer big yarn balls and thick rope to roll, pull and unwind, with an adult close.
Add webs between furniture and trees.
Offer knots, ties and bows with thick cord and rope.
Try crossed-stick wrapping and wrapping cardboard shapes.
Add finger knitting for older children and let the chains grow longer each day.
Look at artists who wrap objects in yarn, and wrap our own found objects.
Look at crocheted net spaces children climb in, and build a rope and net space outdoors with an adult.
Use string to measure, map and connect things on the yard.
Add pulleys and rope for lifting buckets and baskets.
Wrap a tree or fence across a season and photograph how it changes in sun and rain.
Try string painting and string prints.
Connect to weaving, sewing and beads.
Wrap with one color plus black and white and notice how the stripes change.
Compare natural sheep colors with dyed yarns and sort them.
Model winding a ball, tying a square knot and finger knitting slowly.
Wrap sticks from observation, matching yarn colors to a bird, a flower or a lichen on our site.
Keep a yarn shelf open with children responsible for its care.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Wrapping and winding are open with an educator nearby, and string never goes around necks. Webs come down before rest, and rope pulleys and a rope and net space outdoors need an adult close by.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick rope for pulling, a tug between two friends and a pulley for lifting heavy buckets.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one soft yarn and a smooth stick to wrap at a quiet table, with the end already taped.
connected: Judith Scott on the Artists page, for wrapping found objects in yarn and fiber at Creative Growth in Oakland.
Toshiko Horiuchi MacAdam on the Artists page, for huge crocheted nets children climb and play inside.

sections.text: Yarn, string or rope, sticks from a walk, tape and a few cardboard pieces. A ball of one color plus a little black and white is enough for striped wrapping.

items: Wrap yarn around a stick until it is covered in color.
Make a yarn web between chair legs to crawl through.
Wind a messy pile of yarn into a ball together.
Make a string telephone from two cups and a long string.
Practice tying knots and bows on a thick rope.

sections.text: Your child picks the colors, winds, wraps and ties. Holding the end while you tie is a real job too. Your child can take down string, wind the yarn back into a ball and put it in a basket. Keep string off necks.

items: Where does this string go?
I wonder what happens if you pull it.
Tell me about your colors.

sections.text: Your child is building hand strength, patience and an understanding of how things connect. Wrapping and winding yarn uses both hands together and helps many children feel calm.
Send in leftover yarn, string, rope or empty spools for our yarn shelf. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Never tie string around a neck. Take down webs when play is done so no one trips.

cards.title: Weaving
cards.summary: Ways to weave over and under with fabric, yarn, paper, willow and plants, from fence weaving to small looms.

items: Fabric strips in a basket beside the fence for weaving in and out.
Cardboard looms with notches and a yarn warp, ready for weaving.
A stick frame or forked branch with a twine warp for grasses, leaves and feathers.
A milk crate or cooling rack for the youngest children to weave ribbon and pipe cleaners through.
A big rope loom strung between two trees in the garden for many children at once.
Paper weaving with strips children cut themselves.
A bicycle wheel loom hung in the outdoor piazza.
Willow prunings for weaving into the willow dome in the dormant season.
Lavender stalks, grasses, iris leaves and flowers from plants we know for nature weaving.
A basket of real woven things, such as baskets, mats, cloth and a hammock, with magnifiers.
Moving our bodies in and out through ropes and a line of chairs with a weaving song.
Garden netting or a trellis to weave ribbon and fabric through.
A frame loom or small table loom for older children who want to make cloth.
A limited palette weaving tray with yarn and strips in one color plus black and white, such as greens with black and white.
Warm and cool weft baskets beside two fence looms, one warm and one cool.
Natural undyed wool and cotton in white, gray and brown beside dye bed yarns, so children choose earth colors.
Weft of many kinds, such as yarn, fabric strips, ribbon, paper strips, raffia, grasses and feathers from our chickens.
Weaving tools in a basket, such as craft stick shuttles, plastic needles, a wide-tooth comb for beating the weft and clothespins.
A cardboard loom tray in each class atelier with weft sorted by color.

sections.text: Both. Fence and tree looms are shared work that grows over days. A small frame or cardboard loom holds a child's own pattern. In the yards fence and tree looms are shared work that grows over days. In a class atelier a small cardboard loom holds a child's own pattern.

Warp looms ahead at first, then teach children to warp. Wrap yarn ends with tape or use a plastic needle or a craft stick shuttle. Keep strips in baskets by each loom so weaving can happen any time. Gather only plants adults know and pick with purpose. Warp looms with strong cotton string, not stretchy yarn. A comb or fork pushes rows close. Keep weft sorted by color in baskets beside each loom.

items: Chooses materials and colors for the weft.
Goes over and under and notices the pattern forming.
Cuts strips and tapes yarn ends.
Gathers grasses and leaves with an adult.
Decides when the weaving is finished and how it comes off the loom.
Helps warp the next loom.
Shows a friend how over and under works.
Choose a limited palette for the weft.
Beat the rows down with a comb.

sections.text: Children slip shuttles and needles back into their cup and sort leftover weft by color into the baskets beside each loom. Natural materials go back to the garden or compost. Looms rest on their shelf with work in progress, so nothing waits for an educator later.

Sit beside the loom at the child's level and weave a row of your own slowly, saying over, under as you go. Let skipped rows and loose edges stay, since they belong to the child. Name what you see, such as You chose blue, then white, then blue again.

items: I notice the strips go over and under.
I wonder what holds it together.
How did you choose the colors?
Tell me about your pattern.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with weaving wide strips through a fence, crate or rack.
For the West class, offer ribbons and fabric strips to push through a crate or a cooling rack.
Add stick frames and forked branches with natural materials.
Offer cardboard looms with notches and thick yarn.
Try paper weaving with strips children cut.
Look closely at baskets and woven cloth with magnifiers.
Learn about Pomo basket weaving here in Sonoma County, visit a local museum collection if possible, and notice the plants and patterns.
Weave willow into the willow dome in winter.
Weave with yarn dyed from the botanical dye bed.
Warp looms with children so they come to know warp and weft.
Look at woven art made on a loom and notice lines and patterns.
Move to a frame loom or small table loom for older children.
Make a class weaving with a strip from every child.
Photograph a nature weaving as it dries and changes over days.
Weave with one color plus black and white and notice the stripes.
Weave warm and cool looms side by side.
Model going over and under and pushing rows close with a comb.
For the South class, plan a stripe pattern in a drawing and weave it.
Keep looms open in the Studio and the yard for self-serve weaving.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Fence, crate and cardboard looms are open to everyone. Gathering plants for nature weaving needs an adult confirming each plant, and the rope loom in the garden follows one adult to six children.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big fence or tree loom with thick rope and fabric strips to pull through with the whole arm.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small cardboard loom with a craft stick shuttle at a quiet table, with weft already cut.
connected: Elsie Allen on the Artists page, for Pomo baskets woven from sedge, willow and bulrush here in Sonoma County.
Anni Albers on the Artists page, for woven art on the loom built from line, color and pattern.
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A piece of cardboard, yarn or ribbon, fabric strips or paper strips, and tape.

items: Cut slits in cardboard, wrap yarn around it and weave strips over and under.
Weave ribbons or fabric strips through a fence, a laundry basket or a cooling rack.
Weave paper strips into a paper mat.
Find a forked stick on a walk, wrap string across it and weave in grasses and leaves.
Weave with only one color plus black and white strips and see the stripes.

sections.text: Your child picks the colors and materials and weaves over and under. They decide when it is done. Your child can put yarn and strips back in a basket and stand the cardboard loom somewhere safe to finish later.

items: Where else do you see weaving?
I wonder what holds it together.
Tell me about your colors.

sections.text: Your child is noticing patterns, coordinating both hands and staying with a task. Going over and under uses both hands together and crosses the middle of the body.
Send in fabric strips, ribbon or yarn for our looms, or a photo of something woven at home. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Only collect plants you know are safe, and leave some for others. Keep long yarn away from little ones' necks.

cards.title: Sewing and embroidery
cards.summary: Ways to stitch, lace, mend and embroider with real needles, from first lacing cards to class quilts.

items: Burlap stretched in embroidery hoops with plastic needles and thick yarn.
Lacing cards cut from cardboard with holes children punch themselves.
Sewing on paper with a hole punch and yarn with taped ends.
Large blunt metal tapestry needles and felt for older children.
Buttons with big holes to sew onto felt or burlap.
Plain fabric children draw on with fabric crayon, then stitch along their lines.
Fallen leaves to stitch through with a big needle and see what happens.
A mending basket for repairing dolls, cushions and dress-up clothes.
Small pillows sewn and stuffed with wool or fabric scraps.
A class quilt with one square from each child, joined by an adult and a child together.
A sewing machine with an adult, where a child guides the fabric or presses the pedal.
A big hoop hung outdoors for shared embroidery.
Running stitch patterns on cloth, with images of story quilts nearby.
A sewing tool basket as its own invitation, with plastic needles, blunt tapestry needles, needle threaders, a needle book, small scissors and a pincushion.
White thread on black felt and black thread on white muslin, side by side in hoops.
A limited palette of embroidery floss in one color family, such as only greens or only warm colors, for stitching a leaf or a flower.
Burlap, felt, muslin, cotton and black linen in hoops, so children compare how the needle moves through each.
A sewing basket in each class atelier with a few hoops already threaded.
Stitching outdoors at a table under the valley oaks with a big hoop and a leaf to look at.
For the North class, large plastic needles, burlap and thick yarn doubled and knotted.

sections.text: Mostly alone with an adult close, since stitching is focused and careful work. A class quilt or big shared hoop joins each child's stitches with others. In the Studio a class quilt joins every child's stitches. In a class atelier stitching alone is calm, focused work.

Start with plastic needles and burlap, then move to blunt metal tapestry needles. Count needles out and back into a needle book or pincushion. Tie a large knot or tape the tail to the back. Thread a doubled length so the needle stays on. One adult sits with a small group. Burlap with a loose weave is easiest for first stitching. Keep black and white threads always stocked.

items: Threads the needle and knots or tapes the end.
Chooses colors and decides where stitches go.
Returns needles to the needle book and counts them.
Mends a doll, a cushion or a dress-up piece.
Helps a friend untangle a knot.
Decides what the sewing becomes.
Stuffs and closes a pillow.
Choose black or white thread and a background.
Thread a needle with a threader.

sections.text: Children count needles back into the needle book with an adult and wind thread around its card. Hoops and fabric go into their basket, and scraps into the scrap bin. The count happens at the table, so the close is done by children and finished before they move on.

Sit beside the child at their level with a hoop of your own and stitch slowly. Keep your hands off the child's hoop unless asked. Say what you see, such as Your needle came up right beside the last stitch.

items: I wonder where the needle will come up.
How does the back look?
I notice the white thread shows on the black felt.
Tell me about your stitches.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with lacing cards and plastic needles in burlap hoops.
For the West class, offer lacing cards and a colander with chenille stems.
Add sewing on paper and cardboard with a hole punch.
Introduce buttons and big beads to sew on.
Move to blunt metal needles and felt.
Draw on fabric and stitch the drawing.
Look at story quilts and quilts made by families and communities, and invite family members who sew or quilt to visit.
Sew and stuff small pillows or soft creatures.
Mend real things from our class in a mending basket.
Make a class quilt or an embroidered banner.
Combine stitching with collage, weaving and plant-dyed cloth.
Try a sewing machine with an adult.
Stitch with white on black and black on white.
Stitch with a limited palette of one color family.
Model a running stitch and turning the hoop over to look at the back.
Stitch from observation, such as the shape of a leaf from the garden.
For the South class, embroider a drawing they made on cloth.
Keep a sewing basket open for self-serve use.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Needles are counted out and back in, so an adult sits with a small group at the table. The sewing machine is one adult with one child, and blunt metal needles are for older children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a stiff fabric and a strong needle to push and pull, and stuffing a pillow tightly.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer lacing cards or a big plastic needle and burlap, with a quiet seat.
connected: Faith Ringgold on the Artists page, for story quilts that join painting, words and stitching.
Harriet Powers on the Artists page, for her appliqued Bible Quilt that tells stories in stitched pictures.
The quiltmakers of Gee's Bend on the Artists page, for quilts pieced and stitched by generations of women.

sections.text: Burlap or felt, a large plastic or blunt needle, thick yarn, an embroidery hoop if you have one, and buttons with big holes. White yarn on dark felt or dark yarn on light burlap shows every stitch clearly.

items: Punch holes around a piece of cardboard and lace yarn through them.
Stretch burlap in a hoop and stitch in and out with yarn.
Sew big buttons onto felt.
Mend a torn stuffed animal together.
Let your child draw on cloth and then stitch over the lines.

sections.text: Your child threads, stitches and decides where to go next. You can tie the knot and help untangle when asked. Your child can count needles back into a pincushion with you and wind leftover yarn around a card. Fabric goes back in its basket.

items: Where will the needle come up?
How does the back look?
Tell me about your stitches.

sections.text: Your child is building careful hand control, patience and pride in finishing. Pushing and pulling a needle builds careful hand control and patience.
Send in buttons, burlap, felt or a family quilt story or photo to share. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep needles in a needle book and count them at the end. Stay close with blunt needles only.

cards.title: Wool and felting
cards.summary: Ways to wash, card, felt and spin wool, from raw fleece to felted balls, soap and stones.

items: Raw fleece from a local sheep farm to touch, smell and pull apart.
Tubs of warm soapy water for washing raw fleece and drying it in the sun.
Hand carders or pet brushes for carding wool into soft batts.
Wet felting with roving, warm soapy water and bubble wrap on a towel.
Wool wrapped and felted around a bar of soap.
Wool felted around smooth stones at an outdoor table.
Felted balls rolled between soapy hands.
Colored roving sorted in a basket for laying felt pictures.
A drop spindle turned by an adult while children draft and pull the wool.
A basket of fleece, roving, yarn and felt to feel and compare.
Needle felting for the oldest children, one at a time with an adult, a foam pad and finger guards.
Fibers to compare, such as sheep wool and the hair and fur brushed from our goats and rabbits.
A natural sheep color palette of white, cream, gray, brown and black roving, so children felt with only the colors sheep grow.
A limited palette of dyed roving in one color plus white and black, laid in thin wisps to make lighter and darker areas.
Wet felting on different surfaces, such as bubble wrap, a bamboo mat, a ridged washboard and a towel, to compare how fast the wool holds.
Felting tools on a tray, such as a bamboo mat, a spray bottle, a sponge, a bar of olive oil soap, a pool noodle for rolling and a bowl of warm water.
A wool basket in each class atelier with roving to pull, sort and lay on a felt board, with no water.
Felting outdoors on the outdoor piazza on a warm afternoon, with buckets of warm soapy water and towels on the ground.
For the North class, felted balls and soap felting, with an educator pouring the warm water.
For the South class, flat felt pictures laid from observation of a bird, a flower or one of our goats.

sections.text: Both. Wet felting is warm, rhythmic work children can do side by side while singing. Rolling a felted ball alone is steady and calming. On the outdoor piazza felting is warm, rhythmic shared work with a song. In a class atelier rolling one felted ball alone is calm and steady.

Use warm water and gentle soap, and work outdoors or on towels. Roll sleeves up and keep the floor dry. Wash hands after handling raw fleece. Felting needles are very sharp and are for the oldest children only, one at a time with an adult beside them. Felt takes a day or two to dry. Sort roving by natural sheep color and by dyed color in clear jars. Lay wool in thin wisps in two crossing layers for flat felt. Rinse in cool water at the end to set the felt and squeeze out the soap.

items: Pulls wool into thin wisps and lays the layers.
Pours the warm soapy water and decides how much.
Rubs, rolls and squeezes until the wool holds.
Washes and dries raw fleece.
Cards wool and sorts the colors.
Keeps the rhythm of rubbing with a song.
Rinses pieces and lays them out to dry.
Choose natural sheep colors or a dyed palette.
Lay two crossing layers of thin wisps.

sections.text: Children pour soapy water onto bare ground, wring out towels and bubble wrap and hang them to dry. They lay felt on the drying rack and return roving to its jars by color. An adult counts and puts away felting needles, and children close everything else right where they worked.

Sit or kneel at the felting table with your own hands in the warm water and sing a slow rubbing song. Keep your face easy when water runs onto the ground. Say what you see, such as You rubbed a long time and now the wool is holding together.

items: I wonder what happened to the wool.
How does it feel when you rub it longer?
I notice the gray and white are mixing.
Tell me about your felt.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with touching and pulling apart wool and fleece.
For the West class, offer dry wool to touch, pull apart and squeeze, with no water.
Wash raw fleece and watch the water change.
Card wool and sort colors.
Roll felted balls with soapy hands.
Wet felt flat pieces in bubble wrap.
Felt around soap and stones as gifts.
Dye wool with plants from the botanical dye bed.
Watch an adult spin with a drop spindle and try drafting.
Compare fibers brushed from our goats and rabbits with sheep wool and wonder which ones might felt.
Visit a sheep shearing or wool fair, or invite a spinner to visit.
Use felted pieces in puppets, books and stitched pictures.
Try needle felting with the oldest children.
Felt with natural sheep colors only and notice how many grays and browns appear.
Felt with one dyed color plus white and black for tints and shades.
Model pulling thin wisps and laying them in crossing layers.
Felt from observation of animals and plants on our site.
Keep a wool basket in the Studio for self-serve felting.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Warm soapy water and wet felting go best with an adult at the table. Needle felting is one adult with one child with a foam pad and finger guards, and the drop spindle is turned by an adult.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer rolling felt inside a bamboo mat with strong arms and rubbing hard on a ridged washboard.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer dry wool to pull apart, or felting sealed inside a zip bag so hands stay dry.

sections.text: Wool roving from a craft store, a bar of soap, warm water, a towel and some bubble wrap.

items: Pull wool into soft wisps and feel how it changes.
Wrap wool around a bar of soap, dip it in warm water and rub until it holds.
Roll a ball of wool between soapy hands until it gets firm.
Lay wool on bubble wrap, add soapy water and rub to make a small felt picture.
Use only natural wool colors such as white, gray and brown, and see how many shades appear.

sections.text: Your child pulls, lays, pours and rubs. Singing a song while rubbing helps the time pass. Your child can wring out the towel, hang it to dry and pour the soapy water outside. The wool can go back in a jar for next time.

items: How does the wool feel now?
I wonder what is happening.
Tell me about your felt.

sections.text: Your child is using steady hand strength and seeing how a soft material becomes firm. Rubbing wool in warm soapy water gives strong touch and steady heavy work, which many children find soothing.
Send in wool, felt or a felted soap your child made to share. This counts toward your family participation hours.
This is wet work, so use towels or go outside. Felting needles are very sharp and are for grown-ups.

cards.title: Botanical dyeing
cards.summary: Ways to find, make and use color from the plants on our site, from hammered flowers to sun jars and dye pots.

items: A walk through the botanical dye bed to notice which flowers, leaves and roots might hold color.
Flowers and leaves hammered onto cotton with a wooden mallet to print their color.
Sun dye jars with flowers, water and cotton or wool, set in a sunny window or the outdoor piazza.
A small dye pot on an electric hot plate outdoors, with an adult tending the heat and children adding plant material.
Bundle dyeing, where children lay petals on cloth, roll and tie it, and an adult steams it.
Yarn, wool and cotton squares ready to dip and compare.
A color wheel of dyed samples on the wall, each labeled with its plant.
Acorn caps and oak galls gathered from under our oaks for brown and gray tones.
Plant dye water used as paint on paper.
Rubber bands and string for tying patterns into cotton before dyeing.
Fresh and dried flowers from the same plant side by side to compare.
A dye journal with a swatch, a drawing and the plant name for each dye.
A limited palette dye week of one color, such as yellows from several dye bed flowers, on white wool and white cotton side by side.
One dye bath used on white, cream and gray fiber, so children see how the ground color changes the result.
A dye bath split into two pots, one plain and one with iron water added by an adult, for lighter and darker versions of the same color.
A dilution row of jars with strong dye, half dye and a little dye, so children dip squares and see tints from one plant.
Overdyeing, where a yellow dyed square goes into a second dye bath to find out what new color appears.
Dye tools on a tray, such as a wooden mallet, tongs, a wooden spoon, a strainer, rubber bands, clothespins and a drying line.
A sun dye jar in each class atelier window, checked each morning and drawn in the dye journal.
For the North class, hammering petals onto cotton with a mallet and watching the color appear.

sections.text: Together. Gathering, tearing, stirring and waiting are shared work across several days. Each child may also dye their own piece and watch how it changes. In the garden and the outdoor piazza dyeing is shared work across several days. In a class atelier one child can watch a sun dye jar change and record it.

Use only plants adults have confirmed, and use fallen material and the dye bed before picking anywhere else. Adults handle heat, hot water and any mordant, and children stay a safe distance from the hot plate. Keep dye pots and utensils for dyeing only. Pre-wash fabric and use natural fibers. Colors shift with light and washing, which becomes part of the story. Use only dye bed flowers, fallen leaves, acorn caps and oak galls, and never kitchen produce. Keep a dye journal with a swatch, the plant, the fiber and the date for every bath. Iron water and alum are adult only and stay in labeled jars on a high shelf.

items: Gathers plant material with an adult and picks with purpose.
Tears and pounds plant material.
Prepares fiber by washing and wetting it.
Dips and lifts fabric with an adult guiding.
Keeps the dye journal with swatches.
Decides what the dyed yarn or cloth will become.
Plants, waters and cares for the dye bed.
Choose a limited palette of plants for the week.
Dip squares in a dilution row and lay them in order from light to dark.

sections.text: An adult empties and cleans hot pots, mordant jars and the hot plate. Children rinse dyed fabric in cool water, hang it on the line and carry spent plant material to the compost. They add the last swatch to the dye journal and return it to its shelf, so the close is finished in the dye area and nothing waits for later.

Stay beside the dye pot the whole time heat is on, with your body between the children and the pot. Keep your voice slow and curious, and narrate what you see, such as The water turned gold when the flowers went in. Let each child unroll their own bundle and see the surprise.

items: I wonder what color this flower will give.
How did the color change on the gray wool?
I notice this square is lighter than that one.
Tell me about your swatch.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by noticing color in the garden and gathering fallen petals and leaves.
For the West class, smell and touch dye bed flowers and watch a sun jar change color.
Hammer flowers and leaves onto cloth.
Set sun dye jars and check them each day.
Make a dye pot with an adult outdoors and compare colors on wool and cotton.
Try bundle dyeing and unroll the bundles together.
Keep a dye journal and build a color wheel of samples.
Compare the same plant in different seasons.
Try oak galls and acorn caps, and watch an adult add iron water to change the color.
Plant, tend and harvest the dye bed with children across the year.
Use dyed yarn and cloth for weaving, sewing and felting.
Learn from natural dyers in the Bay Area and invite one to visit.
Dye a whole week of one color and lay the swatches in a row.
Make tints with a dilution row and darker shades with iron water.
Overdye a square to make a new color from two plants.
Model tying a bundle tightly and unrolling it slowly.
For the South class, plan a dye test in the journal and compare results.
Paint with plant dye water and make plant inks.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Dyeing uses heat and plants that must be confirmed, so it is small group work. An adult tends the hot plate with their body between children and the pot, and iron water and alum are handled only by adults.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer hammering flowers hard with a wooden mallet and wringing wet cloth with both hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a sun dye jar to watch and gloves and tongs for dipping, away from the steam and smells.
connected: Sasha Duerr on the Artists page, for plant-based color made from Bay Area gardens and plants.

sections.text: Fallen flowers and leaves you know are safe, a white cotton cloth or old t-shirt, a hammer or smooth rock, and a jar with water.

items: Lay flowers on cotton, cover with paper and gently hammer to print the color.
Put petals and water in a jar with a scrap of cotton and leave it in the sun for a few days.
Make a color chart of everything you try, with the plant name.
Notice colors in your yard or on a walk and wonder which ones might dye cloth.
Try the same flower on a white cloth and a gray or cream cloth and compare.

sections.text: Your child gathers, hammers, checks the jar each day and decides what to do with the cloth. Your child can carry the used flowers to compost, rinse the cloth and hang it to dry. A grown-up handles anything hot.

items: Which color do you think it will make?
I wonder if it changed overnight.
Tell me about your color.

sections.text: Your child is noticing color in nature and seeing that plants can change other things. Hammering, wringing and smelling plants gives strong touch and smell and helps children notice small changes.
Send in a swatch from your dye jar with the plant name, or cuttings and seeds from a dye plant in your yard. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Only use plants you are sure are safe, and leave some for others. Keep any hot dye work for grown-ups, and keep dye jars and pots for dyeing only.

cards.title: Beads and threading
cards.summary: Ways to thread, string and make beads from wood, clay, paper, felt and natural materials.

items: Large wooden beads and stiff laces for the youngest children.
Pipe cleaners and a colander for threading through holes.
Spools, rings and cardboard tubes threaded onto a thick rope outdoors.
Clay beads made from Studio clay, pierced with a stick, dried and threaded.
Paper beads rolled from strips of old magazines and drawings with glue.
Felt beads rolled from wet felted wool.
Acorn caps and seed pods with holes drilled by children using a hand drill and an adult.
Fallen leaves threaded onto string with a big needle for garlands.
Garden flowers threaded into garlands for café tables.
Dowels standing in clay or playdough for stacking beads up and down.
Buttons and washers on string or wire.
A bead tray with beads sorted by color, material and size, kept in the Studio and in each class atelier with a small bowl for each child.
Beads threaded onto wire to make shapes that hold.
A one-color bead tray, such as only blues in wood, glass, clay and felt, for a week of threading.
Black and white beads on a black and white tray, for patterns of two colors.
Clay beads painted with red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera, mixed by the children.
Threading materials of many kinds, such as shoelaces, cord, yarn, wire, pipe cleaners and dowels.
Threading tools such as bodkins, big plastic needles, a hole punch and a hand drill with a clamp.
For the North class, medium beads on stiff laces with a knot already tied at the end.
For the South class, small beads in lidded trays for patterns children plan and draw first.

sections.text: Mostly alone, since threading is quiet and focused work. A long shared garland or class strand lets everyone add a turn. In the Studio a long class strand grows from everyone's turns. In a class atelier threading alone is quiet, focused work.

Use large beads only with two year olds and any child who still mouths objects, and keep small beads in a lidded tray with an adult close. Tape lace ends or use stiff laces. Thread only materials that are not food. Dry natural materials first and check them for cracks and mold. Hand drills are used with an adult and a clamp. Sort beads by color and size in clear lidded trays. Keep small beads to the South class with an adult close.

items: Sorts beads by color, size or material.
Makes beads from clay, paper and felt.
Drills holes in natural materials with an adult.
Chooses patterns and repeats or changes them.
Ties off strands and helps friends with knots.
Cares for the bead tray and gathers stray beads.
Gives a strand as a gift or adds it to the shared garland.
Paint clay beads from a limited palette.
Draw a pattern and then thread it.

sections.text: Children sort beads back into the tray by color and size and gather stray beads from the floor. Laces go back in their basket and an adult puts away the hand drill. The tray with its labeled sections makes the close quick and done by children.
Sit beside the child with a lace of your own and thread slowly. Keep your hands off their strand, even when beads slip off. Say what you see, such as You chose black, then white, then black again.

items: I notice you chose these colors again.
I wonder how long it could grow.
How did you make the pattern?
Tell me about your strand.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with big beads, pipe cleaners and colanders.
For the West class, offer big wooden beads, spools and a thick rope or dowel.
Add laces and thinner strings.
Make beads from clay and dry them.
Roll paper beads with glue.
Gather and drill natural beads.
Thread leaves and flowers into garlands.
Look at beads from many places, including clamshell disc beads made by Pomo people, and notice how they were made.
Look at art made by joining many small pieces with wire, and join our own small found pieces.
Use beads in sewing, weaving and wire work.
Make a long class strand that grows across the year.
Sort and organize a bead library with children.
Thread a one-color strand with many materials.
Make black and white patterns.
Paint clay beads from a limited palette.
Model holding the lace near the tip and pulling the bead down.
Keep threading open for self-serve use.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Large beads and laces are open to every age. Small beads stay with the South class in lidded trays with an adult close, and drilling natural beads with a hand drill is one adult with one or two children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy wooden beads on a thick rope, and rolling and pinching clay beads.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a few large smooth beads and a stiff lace at a quiet table.
connected: El Anatsui on the Artists page, for joining thousands of small metal pieces with copper wire into large hangings.

sections.text: Large wooden beads, buttons, spools, cut paper straws or homemade paper beads, plus shoelaces, yarn with a taped end or pipe cleaners. A small bowl for each color helps your child choose and sort.

items: Thread big beads onto a shoelace.
Push pipe cleaners through the holes of a colander.
Roll paper strips around a pencil with glue to make paper beads.
Thread fallen leaves onto string to make a garland.
Sort a jar of buttons by color, then thread them.

sections.text: Your child chooses, sorts and threads. Let them make patterns or no patterns at all. Your child can sort beads back into bowls by color and check the floor for any that rolled away.

items: How long could it grow?
I wonder which colors you will choose.
Tell me about your strand.

sections.text: Your child is building focus and the small hand control used later for writing and buttoning. Threading builds careful hands and steady attention.
Send in buttons, spools or interesting beads for our bead library. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Small beads are choking hazards, so use big ones with little children and stay close. Keep food for eating.

cards.title: Concoctions
cards.summary: Mixing safe pantry staples, soap, chalk and color so children can watch materials change and invent their own recipes.

items: A concoction table with small jars of baking soda, cornstarch and salt, squeeze bottles of vinegar and water, and spoons, pipettes and bowls.
Baking soda in a muffin tin with droppers of vinegar tinted with liquid watercolor, so each cup fizzes a different color.
A tall jar inside a deep tray for a slow fizzing eruption, with children deciding how much of each to add.
Cornstarch and water in a wide tub so hands can squeeze it solid and feel it melt away again.
Foamy soap whisked from dish soap and a little water with egg beaters and whisks, then tinted with a few drops of watercolor.
Shaving cream spread on a tray with pipettes of liquid watercolor for swirling, then paper pressed on top to lift the pattern.
Sidewalk chalk ground with salt in a mortar and pestle, then spooned into a shared clear jar in colored layers.
Chalk dust kneaded into fresh playdough to see where the color goes.
A salad spinner with paper inside and drops of watercolor, spun and opened to see what happened.
Glue and our slime activator mixed slowly into a stretchy slime that children adjust until it holds together, with an adult adding the activator.
Oil and water in clear bottles with watercolor drops, shaken and left still to watch them part.
A nature soup tub at the mud kitchen with water, fallen petals, leaves and seed pods.
Salt water painted on dark paper and left in the sun to see what stays behind.
Outdoor potion pots on the outdoor piazza with pitchers of water, droppers and fallen flowers from the garden.
A primary-only concoction tray, with droppers of red, yellow and blue liquid watercolor only, so every orange, green and purple is mixed by a child.
A one-color week of concoctions, such as blue only, with white from cornstarch or chalk dust for paler mixtures and a drop of black for darker ones.
Concoctions on a white tray and on a black tray side by side, so children see how fizz, foam and color look on each.
A tool tray with pipettes, eyedroppers, turkey basters, measuring spoons, a whisk, a mortar and pestle, a funnel and clear test tubes in a rack.
A small concoction shelf in each class atelier with three labeled jars and a waste bucket.
For the North class, two ingredients and one color at a time, with big pipettes and a deep tray.

sections.text: Both. One child alone can run a long private experiment and repeat it many times. A shared jar or tub becomes a conversation where children compare recipes and build on each other's ideas. In the Studio or on the outdoor piazza a shared jar becomes a long conversation. In a class atelier one child can run a private experiment and repeat it many times.

Use only pantry staples, soap, chalk, glue and watercolor, and never fresh food or produce. Set clear agreements that concoctions are for looking, smelling and touching and never for tasting. Offer child safety glasses for fizzing and keep vinegar and shaving cream away from eyes. Small amounts in small containers keep the focus on the change. Store dry ingredients in labeled lidded jars and pour used mixtures into a waste bucket, never down the garden beds. Baking soda and salt water can harm plants. Liquid watercolor goes a long way, so offer a few drops in a small jar of water. Keep the palette to red, yellow and blue at first so children discover secondary colors themselves.

items: Choose ingredients and decide the amounts.
Measure, pour, grind and stir with real tools.
Name their concoctions and write or draw the recipe in a shared concoction book.
Predict what will happen and notice what really happens.
Teach a friend a recipe that worked.
Refill jars, wipe trays and carry used mixtures to the waste bucket.
Decide which concoctions to keep on a shelf to watch over days.
Mix secondary colors from primaries and name them.
Choose a white or black tray and say what shows best.

sections.text: Children carry used mixtures to the waste bucket, rinse cups, spoons and droppers in the wash bucket and set them on the drying rack. They wipe trays with a damp sponge, refill jars and record recipes in the concoction book. Every tool has a labeled home on the shelf, so the close happens as part of the work.

Sit at the concoction table within arm's reach and keep your face curious and calm when a mixture spills or fizzes over. Narrate what you see, such as You added two drops of yellow and the blue turned green. Leave the recipe to the child, even when it turns brown.

items: I notice it changed.
I wonder what would happen if you added more of one thing.
It reminds me of the fog this morning.
How could we make it happen again?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one ingredient and water so children can feel and watch it alone.
For the West class, offer water, one powder and a big pipette in a deep tray, with lots of repeats.
Add a second ingredient and give time for many repeats of the same mix.
Offer droppers, pipettes and squeeze bottles so small hands control the amount.
Introduce color with liquid watercolor and let children mix their own tints.
Start a concoction book where children draw or dictate each recipe and its name.
Add a mortar and pestle and chalk so children make their own powders.
Set up a self-serve concoction shelf with labeled jars children refill themselves.
Leave a few concoctions on a windowsill and draw what changes each day.
Add magnifiers to look at crystals left after salt water dries.
Invite children to sort ingredients into ones that fizz, dissolve, sink or stay.
Use a clear jar of layered chalk salt as a shared piece the whole class adds to over weeks.
Carry the concoction trays outdoors so concoctions meet water, mud and fallen petals.
Invite children to plan a concoction for a purpose, such as a slow eruption or the foamiest foam.
Offer only red, yellow and blue and record every new color in the concoction book.
Spend a week with one color and add white or black for tints and shades.
Model squeezing a pipette slowly and adding one drop at a time.
For the South class, plan a concoction in a drawing, test it and compare.
Hold a small group concoction share at meeting time where makers explain their recipes.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: The concoction table is open with an educator nearby and an agreement that nothing is tasted. Fizzing mixtures need safety glasses, and slime with activator is mixed with an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick cornstarch mixtures to squeeze with both hands and big fizzing bowls to stir hard.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer pipettes and spoons so hands stay dry, unscented ingredients and a small cup instead of a tub.

sections.text: Baking soda, vinegar, cornstarch, salt, dish soap, water, a few drops of food-safe watercolor or paint, and small cups, spoons and a tray. An old muffin tin and a medicine dropper help a lot.

items: Put spoonfuls of baking soda in a muffin tin and let your child drip colored vinegar into each cup.
Mix cornstarch and a little water in a bowl and squeeze it.
Whisk dish soap and water into a tall foam in the sink or bath.
Stir salt into warm water, paint it on dark paper and check it the next day.
Give a tray of leftover ingredients and let your child invent a recipe.
Use only red, yellow and blue drops and see how many new colors appear.

sections.text: Let your child choose, pour and stir. They can name the concoction and tell you the recipe while you write it down. Your child can pour used mixtures into a bucket, rinse the cups and spoons and wipe the tray. A towel under the tray keeps spills easy.

items: How did it change?
I wonder what would happen if we added more.
Tell me your recipe.

sections.text: Your child is noticing how materials change and trying ideas again and again. That is the start of real science. Squeezing pipettes and stirring builds strong fingers, and watching slow changes can be very calming.
Send in a drawing or photo of a favorite home recipe for our concoction book. You can also send a box of baking soda, cornstarch or salt. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Concoctions are for looking and touching and never for tasting. Keep vinegar away from eyes. Work on a tray or outside and pour leftovers down the sink, never on plants.

cards.title: Water
cards.summary: Pouring, moving, painting and caring with water indoors and out, from the sensory table to the garden beds.

items: A sensory table of clear water with pitchers, ladles, funnels, clear tubing and metal measuring cups.
Rainwater collected in buckets for pouring with metal utensils in the rainy season.
Gutters, pipes and funnels clipped to a fence to build a water wall children rearrange.
Sink and float baskets of found objects, from acorns and corks to keys and stones.
Big brushes and buckets of water for painting the fences, walls and paths and watching the marks fade.
Boats made from recycled materials and tested in a tub or the long yard sink.
Squeeze bottles, droppers and turkey basters for moving small amounts of water.
A washing tub for dolls' clothes, play dishes, bikes or garden tools with soap and scrub brushes.
Watering cans for the class home beds and the strawberry beds as real care work.
Clear jars of water with liquid watercolor drops to watch color drift and spread.
A water xylophone of glass jars filled to different heights for tapping with a wooden spoon.
Tubing and a bucket set higher than a tray so children can discover how a siphon pulls water along.
Hand pumps, spray bottles and sponges for squeezing, spraying and soaking.
Filling the water dishes for the rabbits, chickens and Sheldon with an educator.
Three clear jars of water tinted red, yellow and blue, with pipettes and empty jars, so children mix their own orange, green and purple.
Water painting on many surfaces, such as concrete, a black slate, the wooden fence, brown kraft paper, a stone wall and a chalkboard, to see where marks last longest.
Water tools of many sizes, such as house painting brushes, rollers, sponges, squeeze bottles, basters, pipettes, ladles and a watering can with a rose.
A water tub in each class atelier with clear cups, a pitcher, a funnel and a towel, for quiet pouring on a tray.
For the North class, a low tub of warm water with cups, pitchers and sponges for squeezing.
For the South class, a water wall they design and draw first, then build with gutters and clips.
A basket of leaves, flowers, twigs and stones from the garden beside the water, so children guess whether each will float or sink and then test it.
Ice in the water, so children feel the cold and watch it melt.
Petals and leaves from the dye garden frozen into ice cubes in winter, so children hunt for colors as they melt.
Sponges, whisks and a small amount of soap for making bubbles.

sections.text: Both. Pouring alone is calming and lets a child repeat an idea many times. A water wall or channel invites children to plan together and hand water along from one to the next. On the yards a water wall or channel needs many hands passing water along. In a class atelier pouring alone from cup to cup is calm and lets a child repeat an idea many times.

Always have an adult close to any standing water, and empty tubs at the end of each day. Offer smocks or rain gear and keep towels and a change of clothes ready. Reuse play water on garden beds when it holds no soap, since we live in a dry climate. Wipe spills quickly indoors so floors stay safe. Warm water in the cool months keeps hands comfortable. Tinted water goes into a waste bucket and never onto garden beds. Every container stays shallow, since even a small amount of water needs an educator's attention. Change the water for each long session and avoid water that has been standing. Keep floors dry and covered with mats so no one slips.

items: Fill and carry buckets and pitchers to where water is needed.
Build and change pipe and gutter paths.
Choose objects to test and sort them after.
Water plants and fill animal dishes as their own job.
Mop, wipe and hang towels to dry at clean-up.
Notice where water could be saved and decide how to reuse it.
Show a friend a way to make water move.
Mix colored water from primaries and line up the jars.
Choose a surface for water painting and check how long the marks last.

sections.text: Children empty tubs onto garden beds when the water holds no soap or color and pour tinted water into the waste bucket. They mop with child-sized mops, hang towels on the line and stack tools in their basket. An adult tips any tub that is too heavy, and children do the rest before they leave the water.

Stay at the water the whole time, kneeling or sitting at the children's level within arm's reach. Keep your face easy about wet sleeves and puddles, and narrate what you see, such as You tipped the pitcher slowly and the cup filled to the top. Notice the predictions a child makes about floating and sinking and what the child says when a test surprises them. Watch how a child's pouring, squeezing and carrying change over days, and when children begin to work together, such as holding a funnel for a friend. Record a child's theory as a Notice and Wonder observation, and link it to the Garden page when it involves plants or stones from our site.

items: I wonder where the water will go next.
How does it move down the tube?
It reminds me of the creek after rain.
How could we get the water over there?
What do you see that makes you say that?
How many small cups do you think it will take to fill the big pitcher?
I wonder where the water goes when a water painting dries.
I wonder which leaves from our garden will float the longest.
Begin with plain water and a few pouring tools so children can feel weight and flow.
For the West class, offer a low tub of warm water with cups and sponges and plenty of time to pour.
Add clear tubing and funnels so children can see water travel.
Offer sink and float objects and invite children to bring their own to test.
Build a water wall on a fence with gutters and pipes that children move.
Add color with liquid watercolor drops and watch it mix.
Collect rainwater together and compare it with tap water.
Make boats from recycled materials and test which ones carry a load of stones.
Explore siphons and pumps as children ask how to move water uphill.
Tune a water xylophone and play it with songs from the Song book.
Paint with water on warm and shady surfaces and notice which marks stay longer.
Take water to the garden and decide together which plants need it most.
Map the path of rain as it runs across our site after a storm.
Visit the creek trail with an educator who holds a water safety certificate to watch real moving water.
Tint water with red, yellow and blue only and mix secondary colors in clear jars.
Paint with water on black slate, concrete, wood and kraft paper and compare.
Model pouring slowly with the spout close to the rim.
Draw the water wall from observation and change it from the drawing.
Invite children to design a water system across the outdoor piazza with channels, dams and pools.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: An adult stays at any standing water the whole time, within arm's reach. Creek visits leave campus with an educator who holds a water safety certificate, and filling the animals' water dishes is done with an educator.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy buckets to carry, a hand pump to work and a hose to direct into channels with an adult.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small cup and pitcher on a tray, warm water, a smock and a towel close by, with a choice to watch first.
connected: Ned Kahn on the Artists page, for sculptures that make the movement of water and wind visible.
Katsushika Hokusai on the Artists page, for showing the shape and force of a wave.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for working with rain, rivers and the way water changes his sculptures.

sections.text: A dish tub or the bath, plastic cups, a small pitcher, a funnel, a sponge, a baster or squeeze bottle, and a towel. A bucket of water and an old paintbrush work outside.

items: Pour from cup to cup in the sink or bath.
Paint the fence, steps or sidewalk with plain water and watch it dry.
Gather small objects and guess which ones will float.
Let your child water the house plants or garden with a small can.
Wash plastic dishes or toy cars together with soapy water.
Tint three jars red, yellow and blue and mix new colors with a dropper.

sections.text: Your child can fill, carry, pour and clean up. Real jobs with water, such as watering plants, help them feel capable. Your child can pour water onto plants, wipe spills with a towel and hang it to dry. Cups and pitchers can go back in a basket.

items: Where did the water go?
I wonder which will float.
How could we move the water over there?

sections.text: Your child is learning how water moves and how much a cup can hold. Pouring also builds strong, steady hands. Carrying and pouring water gives arms heavy work, and slow pouring helps many children feel calm.
Send in clean plastic bottles, funnels or old kitchen ladles for our water play. This counts toward your family participation hours. You can also share a photo of your child watering at home.
Stay close any time there is water, even a shallow tub, and empty it when you finish. Play outside or on towels and expect wet clothes.

cards.title: Ice
cards.summary: Freezing, melting, carving and coloring ice so children can feel cold and watch water change form.

items: Large blocks of ice frozen in tubs, set in a tray with salt shakers and droppers of liquid watercolor.
Fallen leaves, petals and seed pods frozen in shallow pans with a loop of string to hang as ice suncatchers.
Small treasures frozen in ice for children to free with pipettes of warm water, spoons and small wooden mallets.
Ice cubes and chunks in the sensory table with tongs, scoops and metal bowls.
Ice painting with liquid watercolor brushed on cubes over thick paper.
Ice boats frozen in yogurt tubs with a stick mast, then floated in a tub of water.
Colored ice bricks frozen in recycled cartons for building a short wall outdoors.
Two ice blocks placed in sun and shade so children can check them through the morning.
Ice on the light table so light shines through bubbles and cracks.
A frosty morning walk to find frost on the grass, the log yard and the cars in the parking lot.
Children fill trays with water and their own chosen natural objects to freeze for the next day.
Ice cubes with salt laid on a string so the string can lift the cube.
Ice blocks frozen with red, yellow and blue water, set on a white tray so colors run together and mix as they melt.
Ice on a black tray and a white tray side by side, so frost, bubbles and cracks show differently on each.
One-color ice week, such as blue ice in many shades from pale to dark, built into a short wall.
Ice painting with liquid watercolor on watercolor paper, newsprint and paper towels, to see how each surface takes the melt.
Ice tools such as pipettes, salt shakers, wooden mallets, spoons, tongs, brushes and squeeze bottles of warm water.
An ice tray in each class atelier with one block and a few tools on a towel.
For the North class, cubes in a sensory tub with tongs, scoops and mittens.
For the South class, ice sculptures planned in a drawing and built by stacking colored blocks with salt to stick them.

sections.text: Both. Freeing a frozen treasure together needs many hands and turns. Painting one ice cube alone lets a child slow down and watch closely. Outdoors a big block brings a group together to free a treasure. In a class atelier one child can watch a cube melt on a tray.

Freeze blocks two or three days ahead in the staff room freezer and label each tray. Offer gloves or mittens for children who want them and short sessions so hands warm up. Use child safety glasses with mallets. Never freeze food or fruit into ice for play. Never offer dry ice. Salt on ice is fine and can be rinsed off trays. Freeze colored ice in primaries first so children discover secondary colors as the melt meets. Keep salt in shakers and rinse trays after.

items: Gather natural objects to freeze and choose where they go in the tray.
Fill trays with water and carry them to the freezer with an educator.
Decide where to place ice to melt and check on it.
Use real tools to chip, drip and free frozen objects.
Draw or photograph the ice as it changes.
Pour meltwater onto garden beds at the end.
Choose colors to freeze and plan the order of layers.
Choose a black or white tray and compare.

sections.text: Children pour meltwater onto garden beds, rinse salt from trays in the wash bucket and stack them on the rack. Tools go back in their basket and freed objects to their homes. Trays sit within reach, so the close is complete before children leave.

Kneel at the ice tray at the children's level and keep your own hands in the cold with them. Stay calm when water pools and blocks crack. Narrate what you see, such as You dripped warm water and a tunnel opened in the ice.

items: I notice the ice is changing.
I wonder where the ice goes.
It reminds me of a frosty morning.
How could we make it last longer?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with plain ice cubes to hold, slide and watch melt.
For the West class, offer large cubes to hold with mittens and push around a tray.
Add warm water, droppers and salt to change how fast ice melts.
Offer liquid watercolor so color runs into cracks and tunnels.
Freeze small treasures and give real tools for freeing them.
Invite children to choose and gather what to freeze from the garden floor.
Hang ice suncatchers in a tree and watch them drip and fall.
Compare ice in sun and shade and keep a simple drawing record through the day.
Freeze water in many shapes of recycled containers and build with the blocks.
Put ice on the light table and look through it with magnifiers.
On cold mornings look for frost and ice on our site and photograph it.
Freeze colored water in layers over several days to make a striped block.
Make a slow melting sculpture together and photograph it each hour.
Freeze primaries and watch secondary colors appear as they melt.
Look at ice on black and white trays and draw what you see.
Model dripping warm water slowly with a pipette.
Look at photos of artists who work with ice and invite children to plan their own ice piece.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Ice play is open with an educator nearby and short sessions for cold hands. Freeing treasures with wooden mallets needs safety glasses and an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big blocks to lift, chip with a mallet and slide across a tray, with bare hands for short times.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer mittens or tongs, a small cube on a warm towel and time to watch before touching.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for sculptures of ice and icicles that melt and change.
Olafur Eliasson on the Artists page, for Ice Watch, large blocks of glacial ice left to melt in a public square.

sections.text: Ice cube trays or plastic containers, water, a tray or baking dish, salt, a spoon, a medicine dropper and some leaves or small toys to freeze.

items: Freeze a small toy in a container of water and free it with warm water and a spoon.
Sprinkle salt on a big ice chunk and drip colored water on top.
Freeze leaves and flowers from your yard in a shallow dish and hang it outside.
Put one ice cube in the sun and one in the shade and check them later.
Make ice boats in small tubs and float them in the bath.
Freeze red, yellow and blue water in a tray and watch colors mix as they melt on white paper.

sections.text: Let your child pick what to freeze, fill the containers and decide where to put the ice to melt. Your child can pour meltwater onto plants, rinse the trays and put the tools away. Salty water goes away from the garden.

items: Where did the ice go?
I wonder which one will melt first.
How could we make it last?

sections.text: Your child is seeing water change from solid to liquid and noticing how warmth and time make a difference. Feeling cold and noticing when hands need warming helps children listen to their own bodies.
Send in clean yogurt tubs, milk cartons or silicone molds for freezing. This counts toward your family participation hours. You can also share a photo of what your child froze.
Short play times keep hands from getting too cold. Play on a tray or outside. Never use dry ice.

cards.title: Sand
cards.summary: Digging, pouring, building and drawing with wet and dry sand indoors and outdoors.

items: A dry sand tray with sieves, funnels, scoops and a sand wheel for pouring and watching sand fall.
A wet sand tray with buckets, molds, trowels and spray bottles for building.
Ramps, gutters and balls in the sand area so sand can slide and roll.
A deep sand pit outdoors with real shovels, wheelbarrows and buckets for big digging.
Rakes, sticks and combs for drawing lines and patterns across a smoothed patch of sand.
A thin layer of sand on the light table for drawing with a finger or a feather.
A small world in the sand with stones, bark, shells, pinecones and figures.
A sand pendulum, a cup with a small hole hung from a frame, swinging to draw paths in the sand below.
