Hiding and finding treasures with sieves and brushes, as archaeologists do.
Pressing shells, pinecones and hands into damp sand to make molds for plaster casting.
Sand timers in many sizes beside the sand table to watch time pass.
Moldable sand mixed from sand, cornstarch, water and a little dish soap for indoor shaping.
Heavy buckets of sand to haul, weigh and tip as real work.
Black sand and white sand in two shallow trays side by side, for drawing with a finger, a feather, a comb or a brush and comparing the lines.
Colored sand that children make by shaking white sand with powdered chalk in a lidded jar, in red, yellow and blue only, then layering it in clear bottles.
Sand tools of many kinds, such as sieves of several meshes, funnels, scoops, rakes, wide-tooth combs, pastry brushes, molds, trowels and real shovels.
A small sand tray in each class atelier with a feather, a brush and a smoothing board, for quiet drawing.
Sand on surfaces of many kinds, such as a mirror, black felt, a wooden board and the light table, so children see grains and lines differently.
For the North class, damp sand and molds in a tub, with spray bottles to change how it holds.

sections.text: Both. A big sand pit invites shared rivers, castles and roads. A small tray holds one child's quiet patterns and stories. In the yards a big sand pit invites shared rivers, castles and roads. In a class atelier a small tray holds one child's quiet patterns and stories.

Cover outdoor sand at night to keep animals out and rake it before play to check for anything unsafe. Use clean play sand bought for children and never take sand from the creek. Keep sand low and away from eyes, and agree that sand stays in the sand area. Brush off and wash hands after play. Dampen dry sand outdoors on windy days. Colored sand is made only from chalk, never from food coloring mixed with rice or salt. Store black, white and colored sand in labeled lidded jars. Sweep indoor trays over a sheet so spills can be poured back.

items: Choose tools and decide whether sand should be wet or dry.
Carry water and sand to where the project needs it.
Plan and build with friends.
Rake and smooth the sand for the next group.
Sweep spills back into the tray and put tools back where they live.
Photograph or draw a build before it changes.
Make colored sand from chalk and choose its color.
Choose black or white sand and say which shows the line best.

sections.text: Children sweep spills back into the tray, rake the sand smooth and hang tools on their hooks. Outdoors they help pull the cover over the sandbox. Every tool has a labeled place, so the area is ready for the next group.

Sit at the edge of the sand pit or tray, low and close, and let your hands rest in the sand. Keep your face calm when sand spills, and narrate what you see, such as You added water and now the tower stands. Let collapses happen without rushing to rebuild.

items: I notice the wet sand holds its shape.
I wonder where the sand goes when it falls through.
It reminds me of the creek bank.
How did you build that?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with dry sand and hands only to feel it pour and settle.
For the West class, offer dry sand and big scoops in a low tub, with hands welcome and time to pour.
Add scoops, sieves and funnels for filling and sifting.
Add water so children can feel the change from dry to wet.
Offer molds and recycled containers for building and stacking.
Add ramps, gutters and balls to send sand and objects downhill.
Hang a sand pendulum and let children change the swing.
Smooth a large patch and draw giant patterns with rakes and sticks.
Bring in magnifiers to look at grains of sand from different places.
Press natural objects into damp sand and pour plaster to keep the shapes.
Add small world pieces so building turns into stories.
Make maps in the sand of places children know, such as our site or the creek trail.
Invite children to collect sand samples from home and compare color and grain.
Draw on black and white sand side by side and compare the lines.
Make and layer chalk colored sand in red, yellow and blue and watch where colors meet.
Model raking slowly in long lines and smoothing the tray with a board.
For the South class, plan a river system in a drawing and build it in the pit.
Plan a long shared project such as a river system that runs across the whole sand pit.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Sand trays and the sand area are open to everyone with agreements that sand stays low. Big digging with real shovels in the deep pit needs an educator nearby, and plaster for casting sand molds is mixed by an adult.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy buckets of wet sand to carry and tip, real shovels for deep digging and a wheelbarrow to push.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray of dry sand with a spoon and a brush, and a quiet spot at the edge of the pit.
connected: Jim Denevan on the Artists page, for drawing huge patterns in sand with a stick and a rake.

sections.text: A bin or sandbox of clean play sand, cups, spoons, a sieve, a funnel and a spray bottle of water. A baking dish of sand works indoors.

items: Pour dry sand through a funnel and a kitchen sieve.
Wet the sand and build with cups and containers.
Draw in smooth sand with a finger or a stick.
Hide small objects and dig for them.
Press shells or toys into damp sand to make prints.
Put a thin layer of sand on a dark tray and draw lines with a finger or a feather.

sections.text: Your child can choose the tools, decide when to add water and help cover the sand when play ends. Your child can rake the sand smooth, put tools in their bucket and help cover the sandbox.

items: How does the sand change with water?
Where did the sand go?
Tell me about your build.

sections.text: Your child is learning how materials change and building strong hands and arms. Digging and carrying sand gives the arms heavy work, and pouring dry sand can be very calming.
Send in a small labeled bag of sand from a beach or place you visited so we can compare. This counts toward your family participation hours. Old sieves, funnels and molds are welcome too.
Keep sand out of eyes and cover outdoor sand at night. Brush off and wash hands after playing.

cards.title: Mud
cards.summary: Mixing, squishing, building and painting with real mud in the mud kitchen, the mud pit and beyond.

items: The mud kitchen stocked with real pots, pans, muffin tins, ladles and sieves for mud soup and mud pies.
Flower-petal mud soup with fallen petals and leaves stirred into pots of mud.
A mud pit made with soil and water where children dig, squish and stomp in rain boots.
A gentle mud slide on a slope during the rainy season.
Mud paint in buckets with big brushes for painting the fence, cardboard or butcher paper.
Mud tiles shaped on wax paper and pressed with leaves, bark and seed pods, then dried in the sun.
Mud bricks packed into wooden or recycled molds with straw, then dried for building.
Toy trucks and diggers in a mud patch with stones and sticks for building roads.
Thick mud balls thrown at a hung white sheet for big splatter marks.
Shaker jars of soil and water to watch layers settle over a day.
Soils from different places on our site, such as the garden, the oak roots and the log yard, mixed with water and compared.
A washing spot with buckets of warm soapy water and brushes for cleaning tools and boots.
An earth palette of mud paints from soils on our site, from pale garden soil to dark oak-root soil, mixed with water in jars and brushed on white paper and kraft paper.
Mud paint on white paper and black paper side by side, so children see how earth colors look on each.
Mud paint tinted with a little white tempera for paler tints, beside plain mud.
Mud tools of many kinds, such as trowels, ladles, potato mashers, sieves, wide house painting brushes, sticks and wooden spoons.
A small mud tray in each class atelier, with a lidded jar of soil, a pitcher and a brush, for mud painting on a covered table.
For the North class, mud in a tub with spoons and pots and plenty of washing water.
For the South class, mud brick molds and a plan for a small wall.

sections.text: Both. Mud kitchens and mud pits invite cooking, serving and building together. A child alone can spend a long time squeezing and shaping one mud ball. In the mud kitchen and pit children cook and build together. In a class atelier mud painting alone can be quiet and slow.

Use garden soil from places animals do not use, and never soil from the animal yards. Children wear rain boots or old shoes in the garden and mud areas. Tell families ahead so children come in clothes that can get dirty, and keep spare clothes ready. Build handwashing into the end of every mud time. Agree that mud food is pretend and never tasted. Sieve soil before mixing mud paint so it brushes smoothly. Label each jar with where the soil came from.

items: Carry water and soil to make mud.
Decide how thick or runny the mud should be.
Cook, serve and invent mud recipes.
Shape and dry mud tiles and bricks.
Rinse pots, scrub boots and hang wet clothes.
Teach a friend how to make the mud just right.
Show a new or unsure child a way to start with one finger or a spoon.
Gather soil from different places and mix mud paints.
Label mud paint jars by place.

sections.text: Children rinse pots and pans in the yard sink or wash tub, scrub boots on the brush and hang wet clothes on the line. They wash hands at the low sink. Brushes, buckets and a line sit beside the mud area, so the close happens on the spot.

Notice your own feelings about mud and keep your face open and easy. Crouch at the mud kitchen with the children and touch the mud yourself. Narrate what you see, such as You added water and the mud got runny.

items: I notice this mud is different.
I wonder what happens when it dries.
It reminds me of the garden after rain.
Tell me about your mud recipe.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with mud in a tub and tools so cautious children can start with a spoon.
For the West class, offer mud in a tub with spoons and cups and plenty of warm washing water.
Open the mud kitchen with real pots and pans and let children make the first mud.
Add fallen petals, leaves and seed pods for mud soup and decoration.
Compare dry soil, wet mud and runny mud and let children name the differences.
Shape mud tiles and bricks and dry them in the sun.
Offer mud as paint for big surfaces and big brushes.
Make shaker jars and watch soil settle into layers.
Look for worms and roly polys in the soil and return them gently.
Collect soils from around our site and make a row of mud color samples.
Look at photos of mud cloth from Mali and adobe buildings to see how people use mud.
Build a small mud and straw wall or bench together over several weeks.
Add ropes, pulleys and buckets so children can move heavy mud as a team.
Make an earth palette of mud paints from soils on our site.
Paint with mud on white and black paper and compare.
Model sieving soil and mixing mud to a smooth paint.
Paint from observation with mud, such as the oaks or the goats.
Visit after rain to see how puddles and mud change on our site.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: The mud kitchen is open with an educator nearby and an agreement that mud food is never tasted. The mud slide, thrown mud balls and hauling mud with pulleys need an adult close by, and the garden follows one adult to six children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer stomping in the mud pit in boots, carrying heavy buckets and squishing mud with both hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a spoon, a stick or gloves, a small bowl of mud and a washing bucket right beside them.
connected: Kazuo Shiraga on the Artists page, for Challenging Mud, a work he made by wrestling his whole body through mud.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for walls and works made from clay and earth.

sections.text: A patch of garden soil or a bin of soil, water, old pots, pans, spoons and muffin tins, and clothes that can get dirty.

items: Set up a mud kitchen with old pots and a bucket of water.
Make mud soup with fallen leaves and petals.
Paint a fence or cardboard with mud and a big brush.
Shape mud pies and leave them in the sun to dry.
Shake soil and water in a jar and watch the layers settle.
Mix soils from different spots into mud paints and paint on white paper.

sections.text: Your child can carry the water, mix the mud, cook and serve, and help scrub the pots and boots afterward. Your child can rinse pots in a bucket, scrub boots with a brush and hang wet clothes on the line.

items: How does it feel?
I wonder what happens when it dries.
Tell me what you are making.

sections.text: Your child is exploring with all their senses and building strength. Mud play is also calming for many children. Squishing, stirring and carrying mud gives strong touch and heavy work, which helps many children feel calm.
Send in old pots, pans, ladles or muffin tins for our mud kitchen. This counts toward your family participation hours. A photo of your mud kitchen at home is welcome too.
Use soil from places pets do not use. Mud food is pretend and never eaten. Wash hands well after play.

cards.title: Bubbles
cards.summary: Making bubble mixes, wands and foams so children can chase, hold and wonder at bubbles.

items: A tub of homemade bubble mix with wands bent from wire and pipe cleaners in many shapes.
A giant bubble wand made from two sticks and cotton string for long floating bubbles outdoors.
A hula hoop in a shallow pool of bubble mix so a child can stand inside a bubble.
Found tools to test as wands, such as funnels, slotted spoons, cookie cutters, berry baskets and plastic rings.
Bubble foam whisked in the sensory table with whisks, egg beaters and scoops.
A wet tabletop where children blow a dome bubble with a straw and try a bubble inside a bubble.
Wet hands and gloves for trying to hold a bubble without popping it.
A wire frame shaped as a cube or pyramid dipped to see what shape the bubble makes.
A bubble machine on the outdoor piazza for the youngest children to chase and catch.
Bubbles blown on a still day and a windy day to see where they travel.
Bubble snakes from a cut bottle and an old sock dipped in mix.
Bubble prints made by catching tinted bubbles on paper.
Bubble prints in a limited palette, with bubble mix tinted only red, yellow and blue, blown in cups and caught on white paper so colors overlap.
Bubble prints on white paper and black paper side by side, with white tempera bubbles on the black.
Bubble wands of many shapes and sizes, such as circles, squares, triangles, long loops, a slotted spoon, a berry basket and a funnel.
A bubble spot in each class atelier with a wet tray, straws and a small dish for dome bubbles.
Bubbles watched against a black cloth hung outdoors, so their colors show clearly.
For the North class, wands to dip and wave on the outdoor piazza.
For the South class, bubble frames bent from wire into cubes and pyramids that children design.

sections.text: Both. Giant bubbles need a partner to dip and a group to watch. A small dish and one wand let a child test idea after idea alone. On the outdoor piazza giant bubbles need partners. In a class atelier one child can test wands quietly.

Mix dish soap, water and a little glycerin and let it rest overnight for stronger bubbles. Bubble mix makes floors slippery, so play outdoors or on a towel. Teach blowing out before offering straws, and offer wands or a bubble machine to younger children. Rinse eyes with clean water if soap gets in. Pour used mix away from garden beds. A strong mix is about one part dish soap to ten parts water with a small splash of glycerin. Tinted bubbles stain, so use smocks and wash paper prints outdoors.

items: Measure and stir the bubble mix.
Bend and design their own wands.
Choose tools to test and share what worked.
Partner with a friend to dip and pull giant bubbles.
Notice where bubbles go and tell others.
Rinse wands and carry tubs at clean-up.
Tint bubble mix with primaries.
Bend and test a wand shape.

sections.text: Children rinse wands in a bucket of clean water, carry tubs to pour away from garden beds and lay wands on a towel to dry. They wipe or rinse the slippery ground with a watering can. The bucket and towel sit beside the bubbles from the start, so the close happens on the spot.

Kneel at the children's level and blow slowly yourself so your breath shows the pace. Keep your voice soft and your face pleased when bubbles pop. Name what you see, such as You blew slowly and the bubble grew big.

items: I notice colors on the bubble.
I wonder what shape a square wand will make.
Where do you think the bubble will go?
How could we make it bigger?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a bubble machine or adult blowing so young children can chase and watch.
For the West class, offer a bubble machine and big wands to wave, chase and pop.
Offer simple wands and a shallow dish for children to blow their own.
Make bubble mix together and test small changes to the recipe.
Bend wire and pipe cleaners into new wand shapes.
Test found objects to see which ones make bubbles.
Try giant string wands outdoors with a partner.
Blow dome bubbles on a wet table and look for colors and reflections.
Try shaped frames and notice the bubble shapes inside.
Watch bubbles to see which way the wind blows.
Make bubble foam and build towers of foam.
Look closely at bubbles with magnifiers and photograph the colors.
On a cold morning try blowing bubbles outdoors and watch what happens.
Make bubble prints with primary colors and look for new colors where they overlap.
Print on black and white paper and compare.
Model blowing out slowly before straws come out.
Look at paintings of bubbles and invite children to draw what they saw.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Wands and bubble mix are open to everyone, played outdoors or on a towel. Straws come out only after children know how to blow out, and standing inside a hula hoop bubble on a slippery pool needs an adult beside the child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running and jumping to catch bubbles and giant wands with long strong arm sweeps.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one small wand and slow blowing at a quiet table, or watching from a bench.
connected: Jean Siméon Chardin on the Artists page, for Soap Bubbles, a painting of a young person carefully blowing a bubble.

sections.text: Dish soap, water, a shallow dish, and wands from pipe cleaners, a funnel, a slotted spoon or a plastic ring. Two sticks and some string make a giant wand.

items: Mix soap and water and let your child test kitchen tools as wands.
Make a giant wand from two sticks and string and try it outside.
Whisk soapy water into foam in the sink.
Try to catch a bubble on a wet hand.
Watch where bubbles float on a windy day.

sections.text: Your child can stir the mix, bend wands and decide what to try next. Your child can rinse the wands, pour the mix away from plants and lay wands on a towel to dry.

items: Which colors can you see?
Where will it go?
How could we make a bigger one?

sections.text: Your child is testing ideas and watching closely. Slow bubble blowing is also a calm breathing practice. Slow bubble blowing helps children control their breath, which is calming.
Send in a favorite homemade wand or a bottle of dish soap for our bubble mix. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Bubbles make floors slippery, so play outside or on a towel. Rinse eyes with water if soap gets in.

cards.title: Wind and air
cards.summary: Feeling, seeing and using moving air with streamers, sails, fans, breath and the real wind on our site.

items: Ribbons, strips of fabric and crepe paper tied along a fence to show the wind.
A basket of scarves and ribbon wands for running and dancing in the wind.
A wind tube made from a clear plastic sheet rolled over a floor fan, with feathers, coffee filters, paper cups and scarves to test.
Pinwheels and windsocks made by children and planted around the garden.
Simple kites from paper bags, sticks and string flown in the tire swing yard.
Paper boats with sails pushed across a tub by breath or a hand fan.
Feathers, leaves and seeds dropped from a height to see how each one falls.
Small parachutes made from fabric squares and string with a clothespin weight.
Wind chimes made from found objects, shells and sticks hung in the trees.
A wind watch at meeting time, looking out the window at trees, flags and clouds.
Straws and watercolor drops for blowing paint across paper.
Hand fans folded from paper for cooling down and moving light objects.
A feather breath practice of slow breathing to make a feather sway.
Watching seeds that travel by wind, such as dandelion and other fluffy seeds, in the garden.
Streamers in one color family, such as only blues from pale to dark, tied along the fence so children watch shades move together.
Windsocks and pinwheels painted by children with red, yellow, blue, white and black tempera mixed on palettes.
Black and white streamers side by side on a line, to watch how each catches light and shadow as it moves.
Air movers of many kinds, such as hand fans, straws, a bicycle pump, a bellows, a turkey baster and a folded paper fan.
A wind basket in each class atelier with feathers, straws, tissue and a fan for quiet breath play on a tray.
For the South class, weather vanes they build from sticks and cardboard, and a wind chart they keep each morning.

sections.text: Both. Kites, parachutes and a wind tube invite turn taking and shared cheering. Breath and feather play can be a quiet time alone. In the yards kites and the wind tube invite turn taking and shared cheering. In a class atelier feather breath on a tray can be a quiet time alone.

Keep fan guards on and cords taped down, and an adult beside any fan. Test what flies before children arrive. Teach blowing out before offering straws. Fly kites only in open space away from trees and power lines. Skip latex balloons with the West class because they are a choking risk. Light tissue and feathers move with gentle breath, and heavier paper needs a fan. Check streamers each week and take down any that fray.

items: Choose objects to test and sort what flies and what falls.
Make and decorate their own windsocks, pinwheels and parachutes.
Decide where to hang streamers to catch the wind.
Report the wind at meeting time.
Fix a kite or parachute that does not work.
Lead a friend in slow feather breathing.
Mix paint colors for windsocks and pinwheels.
Record the wind on the chart each morning.

sections.text: Children unclip streamers, wind kite string and return pinwheels and parachutes to their basket. An adult unplugs and stores any fan. Each thing has a labeled place, so the close is done by children.

Stand out in the wind with the children and let your hair and clothes blow too. Breathe slowly and visibly when you play with feathers, since children borrow our pace. Narrate what you see, such as The ribbon flew straight out when you ran.

items: I notice the ribbons are moving.
I wonder where the wind is coming from.
How could we catch the wind?
It reminds me of the fog moving in.
What will float and what will fall?
Begin with scarves and ribbons outdoors on a breezy day.
For the West class, offer scarves and ribbons on a breezy day and chase them with the children.
Hang streamers around our site and check them at different times.
Drop feathers, leaves and seeds from a height and compare.
Make windsocks and pinwheels and place them in the garden.
Build a wind tube with a fan and test many materials.
Invite children to design a creature that floats in the wind tube.
Make parachutes and change the size or weight to see what happens.
Make sails for boats and test them with breath and fans.
Fly simple kites and repair them together.
Keep a wind chart with drawings of the trees on calm, breezy and windy days.
Make a weather vane and find where the wind comes from on our site.
Make wind chimes and listen for wind sounds in the music shed and garden.
Look at photos and films of sculptures that move in the wind and invite children to build their own.
Paint pinwheels and windsocks from a limited palette and watch the colors spin together.
Hang black and white streamers and draw how they move.
Model slow breath, in through the nose and out through the mouth, with a feather on the palm.
Draw the trees on our site on calm and windy days and compare the drawings.
Notice fog moving in and out on a still morning and talk about air we can and cannot feel.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Wind play is open with an educator nearby. An adult stays beside any fan, kites fly only in open space with two adults on the large yards, and latex balloons stay away from the West class.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running into the wind with a kite or streamer, spinning with ribbons and pumping a bicycle pump hard.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a feather on a tray to move with slow breath, in a sheltered corner away from the fan noise.
connected: Ned Kahn on the Artists page, for walls of small hinged panels that ripple when the wind passes.
Theo Jansen on the Artists page, for Strandbeests, large walking creatures powered only by wind.
Alexander Calder on the Artists page, for mobiles that turn in moving air.

sections.text: Ribbons or strips of fabric, a paper bag and string, paper, straws, feathers and a small fan or a folded paper fan.

items: Tie ribbons to a stick or fence and watch the wind.
Make a paper bag kite and run with it.
Drop a feather, a leaf and a paper scrap and see which lands first.
Blow a feather across the table with slow breaths.
Make a small parachute from a cloth napkin, string and a clothespin.

sections.text: Your child can build, test and fix their own kites, parachutes and streamers. Your child can wind up kite string, put streamers and pinwheels in a basket and hang the windsock somewhere safe.

items: Where is the wind coming from?
I wonder which will float.
How can you tell the wind is here?

sections.text: Your child is noticing something they cannot see and finding ways to show it. Slow breathing also helps the body feel calm. Running in the wind moves the whole body, and slow breathing with a feather helps children feel calm.
Send in ribbons, fabric strips, feathers or paper bags for our wind play. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Fly kites in open space away from trees and power lines. Keep small children away from fans without guards. Balloons are a choking risk for young children.

cards.title: Light and shadow
cards.summary: Playing with sun, lamps and flashlights to make, change and follow shadows and colored light.

items: A white sheet hung in the Studio with a single lamp behind it for shadow play with bodies and objects.
An overhead projector with natural objects, lace, combs and colored transparent shapes to project on the wall.
Three lamps with red, green and blue covers so children can discover colored shadows.
A shadow box from cardboard with a tracing paper screen and a flashlight behind it.
Flashlights in a fabric tent or under a table for exploring a dark space.
Chalk tracing of children's shadows on the outdoor piazza in the morning and again after lunch.
Small animals or blocks placed on paper in the sun so children can trace their shadows.
Cardboard and stick shadow puppets made by children for their own shadow stories.
A basket of materials to sort by how much light passes through, such as fabric, mesh, bubble wrap, clear cups and cardboard.
Prisms and crystals hung in a sunny window to send rainbows across the room.
Lying under the willow dome or the valley oaks to watch moving leaf shadows.
Shadows of plants traced on paper clipped to a board in the garden.
Hand shadows on the wall during a quiet story time.
A tall stick in the ground outdoors with stones marking where its shadow falls through the day.
Shadow tracing on white paper with black pencil, and on black paper with white chalk or white pencil, side by side.
A limited palette of colored transparent shapes in red, yellow and blue only on the overhead projector, overlapping to make new colors.
Shadows cast onto many surfaces, such as a white sheet, a brick wall, a black board, grass, sand and kraft paper.
Light sources of many kinds, such as flashlights, a lamp, a projector, a headlamp, battery candles and the sun.
A shadow corner in each class atelier with a small lamp, a white screen and a basket of objects.
For the South class, shadow puppet shows with planned scenes and taped marks for where the light goes.

sections.text: Both. A shadow screen invites shared stories and bodies working together. A flashlight and a small box hold one child's careful experiments. In the Studio a shadow screen draws a group into shared stories. In a class atelier one child with a flashlight and a small box can experiment alone.

Check lamps and projectors for heat and keep cords taped down. Test colored films near bulbs so they do not melt. Remind children never to look straight at the sun or shine lights into eyes. Store small transparent pieces in clear lidded boxes. Darken the space with curtains or a fabric canopy for indoor shadow play. Keep black and white paper and chalk with the shadow tracing basket. LED lights stay cool and are safest for children to move.

items: Choose and arrange objects to project.
Move the light and the object to change shadow size.
Make puppets and run their own shadow shows.
Trace and record shadows through the day.
Sort materials by how they let light through.
Set up and turn off the lights with care.
Teach a friend how to make a shadow grow.
Choose black or white paper for tracing.
Overlap colored shapes and name the new colors.

sections.text: Children turn off lights and lamps with care, sort transparent pieces into their clear boxes and return puppets to their basket. An adult unplugs any projector that is hot. Tracing papers go into the shadow basket, so the space is ready for the next day without educator time.

Sit inside the shadow space at the children's level and keep your voice low and steady. When the dark worries a child, stay close and keep the light within their reach. Narrate what you see, such as You moved closer and your shadow grew.

items: I notice your shadow changed.
I wonder where the shadow will be after lunch.
It reminds me of the oak leaves moving.
How could we make it bigger?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with bodies and one strong light so children can find their own shadows.
For the West class, offer a flashlight and a lamp on a wall and chase shadows together.
Add objects with holes, lace and mesh to project patterns.
Add transparent colored pieces and notice colored shadows.
Offer flashlights so children control the light source.
Trace shadows outdoors at different times and talk about the changes.
Sort materials into ones that block, let some or let all light through.
Build shadow boxes from cardboard and tracing paper.
Make shadow puppets and hold shadow stories with music.
Add a second and third light to make many shadows from one object.
Use red, green and blue lights together and look for new colors.
Look at artists who make pictures from shadows and invite children to build a shadow sculpture.
Put objects on a slow spinning turntable in front of the light to make moving shadows.
Mark the shadow of one tall stick across the year to see the seasons.
Trace shadows on black and white paper and compare.
Overlap red, yellow and blue shapes and look for new colors.
Model moving the light closer and farther slowly.
Make a simple sundial in the garden.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Shadow play is open with an educator nearby and cords taped down. Lamps and the overhead projector get warm and need an adult close, and children never look straight at the sun.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big body shadows to jump, stretch and chase across the outdoor piazza.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small flashlight and a box in a quiet, dim corner with a choice to leave the dark at any time.
connected: Kumi Yamashita on the Artists page, for sculptures that cast shadow portraits when lit from one side.
Lotte Reiniger on the Artists page, for The Adventures of Prince Achmed, a film made with cut-paper silhouette puppets.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for rain shadows made by lying on the ground as rain begins to fall.

sections.text: A flashlight or lamp, a blank wall or a sheet, sidewalk chalk, and small toys, kitchen tools or cut paper shapes. White chalk on dark paper is good for tracing shadows.

items: Make hand shadows on the wall at bedtime.
Trace your child's shadow with chalk in the morning and again later.
Shine a flashlight through a colander, lace or a strainer.
Make paper shadow puppets on sticks and tell a story.
Stand a toy in the sun and trace its shadow on paper.

sections.text: Your child can hold the light, move the objects and tell the shadow story. Your child can turn off the flashlight, put shapes and toys back in a basket and fold up the sheet.

items: How can we make the shadow bigger?
Where did your shadow go?
Tell me about your shadow story.

sections.text: Your child is learning how light travels and how shadows change through the day. Moving the body to make shadows helps children judge space, and quiet dim places can help them settle.
Send in a photo of a shadow you found or clear and colored plastic lids, lace or mesh for our shadow play. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Never look at the sun or shine a light into eyes. Keep lamps away from fabric and paper.

cards.title: Light table
cards.summary: Using a glowing surface to see color, pattern and inner structure in natural and transparent materials.

items: Pressed leaves and petals from the garden laid out to show their veins.
Transparent colored tiles and shapes for overlapping and mixing colors.
Petri dishes of water with droppers of liquid watercolor for color mixing.
A thin layer of salt or sand in a tray for drawing with fingers, brushes and feathers.
Sea glass, glass gems, shells and clear stones for arranging patterns.
Feathers from the chickens, skeleton leaves and seed pods to look through.
Tracing paper and pencils over pressed leaves and transparent photos of our site, which the South class can use for careful drawing.
Tissue paper on clear contact paper for a light-catching collage.
Clear and colored cups, bottle caps and lids for stacking towers.
Bubble wrap, lace and netting laid flat to show patterns.
Ice blocks and frozen leaves to watch light move through them as they melt.
A mirror tile beside the light table so arrangements double.
A small portable light pad taken outdoors under shade for looking at found objects.
Old film negatives or x-ray style photos of plants for wondering.
A limited palette of transparent tiles in red, yellow and blue only, so every overlap makes a secondary color children discover.
A one-color week on the light table, such as everything green from pale to dark, with green tissue, cellophane and leaves.
Black paper cut-outs and white tracing paper on the light table side by side, so children see solid and see-through.
White pencil drawing on black paper held over the light, beside black pencil on tracing paper.
Light table tools such as pipettes, tweezers, magnifiers, a feather, a soft brush and petri dishes.
A portable light pad in each class atelier on a low table with a basket of leaves.

sections.text: Both. Arranging pieces alone can be calm and focused. A shared light table becomes a collaborative pattern that changes as children add to it. In the Studio a shared arrangement grows across a week. In a class atelier a child alone at a light pad can look and sort calmly.

Keep water small and contained on trays and wipe the surface dry after use. Check that glass gems and small parts suit the age of the class. Do not use water beads. Store transparent pieces sorted by color in clear containers so children can choose. A darker corner makes the glow stronger. Keep transparent pieces sorted by color in clear boxes, with red, yellow and blue first. A darker corner makes the glow stronger.

items: Choose and gather materials to bring to the table.
Arrange, sort and pattern pieces.
Press and dry leaves and petals to add later.
Photograph or draw what they made.
Wipe the surface and return pieces to their colors.
Invite a friend to add to a shared design.
Overlap primary tiles and name the new colors.
Gather a one-color collection for the week.

sections.text: Children wipe the glowing surface dry with a soft cloth kept beside the table, then sort each transparent piece back into its color box. We set a photo label on every clear box and a small tray for water so nothing spills past the edge. The close happens at the table as part of the work, so the light table is ready for the next child without an educator stepping in later.

Sit at the light table at the child's height and keep your hands still and your voice low. Let arrangements stay as they are. Narrate what you see, such as The yellow went over the blue and made green.

items: I notice the light shows something new.
I wonder what happens when two colors overlap.
It reminds me of the window in the morning.
Tell me about your design.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one material such as leaves so children can look closely.
For the West class, offer large transparent shapes and leaves to lay, slide and lift.
Add transparent colored shapes and notice overlapping colors.
Offer liquid watercolor and droppers for mixing on the table.
Add a tray of sand or salt for drawing.
Bring natural objects children found and compare what light shows inside them.
Add magnifiers to look at veins, feathers and wings.
Offer tracing paper for drawing over pressed plants.
Make tissue paper and contact paper pieces to hang in the window.
Place a mirror beside the table for reflected patterns.
Move light play to the overhead projector so small designs fill a wall.
Invite children to design an arrangement for others to add to over a week.
Look at stained glass and colored light in artworks and wonder how light passes through.
Offer only red, yellow and blue tiles and record every new overlap color.
Spend a week with one color and sort it from light to dark.
Model laying pieces gently and looking from above and from the side.
Draw from observation over the light, such as a leaf's veins.
Take a light pad outdoors to the garden for looking at found things right where they grew.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: The light table is open to everyone. Small parts and glass gems are matched to the age of the class, and water on the light table stays in small trays with an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy glass gems and stones to stack and slide, and sand to push with whole hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a dim corner with a few calm pieces of one color and lowered light.
connected: Louis Comfort Tiffany on the Artists page, for stained glass windows that glow as light passes through colored glass.

sections.text: A clear plastic storage bin with a string of lights or a flashlight inside, or a sunny window. Add leaves, colored plastic lids, tissue paper and clear containers. Red, yellow and blue cellophane or plastic lids are enough to discover new colors.

items: Put leaves on the lid of the glowing bin and look at the veins.
Tape tissue paper to a window and overlap the colors.
Stack clear and colored cups on the bin.
Spread a thin layer of salt in a tray on top and draw with a finger.
Hold sea glass or shells up to the light.

sections.text: Your child can gather things to try, arrange them and tell you what the light shows. Your child can wipe the bin lid or window dry with a towel and drop each colored lid back into its own jar. A photo or color dot on each jar makes it easy for them to do alone.

items: How does it look with the light behind?
I wonder what happens when colors overlap.
Tell me about your design.

sections.text: Your child is looking closely and noticing color and pattern. Looking closely at glowing color and pattern helps eyes and hands work together and can be calming.
Send in sea glass, clear colored lids or pressed leaves for our light table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use battery lights that stay cool. Keep small pieces away from children who still put things in their mouths.

cards.title: Mirrors
cards.summary: Using safe mirrors to see ourselves, double patterns, bounce light and look at the world from new angles.

items: A low mirror in the home and dramatic play area with scarves, hats and real objects.
Hinged book mirrors with loose parts set between them to make repeating patterns.
Acrylic mirror tiles on the floor of the block area for building on top.
A mirror with paper and pencils for self-portraits, kept private and never shared publicly.
A half leaf, half flower or half shell placed against a mirror to find the whole.
A small mirror on the fence in the garden to look behind and around plants.
Handheld mirrors held under the chin while walking, so the sky and trees seem underfoot.
Mirrors in the sun to bounce spots of light onto a wall, never into eyes.
A mirror box with three sides for building small worlds that seem to go on and on.
Mirror tiles under the light table pieces or beside the light table.
Washable markers or paint on a mirror for drawing over a reflection.
Simple periscopes from milk cartons and mirror pieces for peeking over walls.
Bent shiny spoons and metal bowls to see faces stretch and shrink.
A mirror at meeting time passed around for making feeling faces.
Mirror self-portraits with black pencil on white paper beside white pencil and white oil pastel on black paper, so children choose and compare.
Book mirrors with a limited palette of loose parts, such as only red, yellow and blue pieces, to see repeating color patterns.
Mirrors of many shapes and sizes, such as round mirrors, long strips, palm-sized hand mirrors and a large floor mirror.
A mirror tray in each class atelier with a book mirror, a hand mirror and a small basket of loose parts.
Mirror drawing, where children draw half a leaf, a face or a shape and set a mirror on the line to find the whole.
For the North class, hand mirrors and a floor mirror with scarves and hats for faces and bodies.

sections.text: Both. A child alone at a mirror often talks and tries faces quietly. Book mirrors and mirror tiles invite friends to build shared patterns. In a class atelier a child alone at a mirror often talks and tries faces quietly. In the Studio book mirrors and tiles invite friends to build shared patterns.

Use acrylic or safety mirrors with smooth edges and never glass for handling. Check edges and replace cracked tiles. Keep sun reflections away from eyes and faces. Self-portraits and mirror photos stay private and children's faces are never shown publicly. Wipe mirrors with a soft cloth to avoid scratches. Keep mirror drawings and self-portraits in each child's portfolio, never on public walls or online. Store hand mirrors face up in a padded basket.

items: Choose where to place mirrors and what to reflect.
Build patterns and small worlds with mirrors.
Draw self-portraits and decide what to show.
Bounce light with care and agreement.
Clean mirrors and store them flat.
Notice and talk about how they and their friends look with respect.
Choose black or white paper for a self-portrait.
Draw half a shape and check it in the mirror.

sections.text: Children wipe each mirror with the soft cloth that lives in the mirror basket and lay hand mirrors face up in the padded basket. Small objects used for reflecting go back to their labeled trays. We keep the cloth and the basket right beside the invitation so the close is part of the work and nothing waits for an educator.

Sit beside the child at the mirror rather than behind them, so your face is beside theirs. Keep your voice warm and describe what you see without praising looks, such as Your eyebrows go up when you smile. Let the child decide what to show and what stays private.

items: I notice there are more now.
I wonder what the mirror can see that you cannot.
How did you make so many?
Tell me about your face.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a low wall mirror for faces and bodies.
For the West class, offer a low floor mirror with scarves and soft hats, and time to wave, peek and smile.
Add handheld mirrors for looking up, down and behind.
Offer hinged book mirrors with a few loose parts.
Change the angle of book mirrors and count what appears.
Use half objects against a mirror to explore symmetry.
Add mirror tiles under blocks and small world play.
Take mirrors outdoors to look at trees, sky and hidden places.
Bounce sunlight with mirrors and send light to a target.
Make periscopes and kaleidoscopes from recycled materials.
Draw self-portraits with a mirror and return to them over the year.
Look at artists who build with mirrors and invite children to make a mirror mosaic from safe acrylic pieces.
Talk at meeting time about skin, hair and eye colors with care, using real photos and mirrors.
Draw self-portraits on black and white paper and return to them across the year.
Build repeating patterns in book mirrors with a limited palette of loose parts.
Model looking at the mirror, then the paper, then the mirror again, slowly.
For the South class, draw half of something from our site and complete it with a mirror.
Build a three-sided mirror room for small figures and stories.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Safety mirrors are open to everyone. Bouncing sunlight outdoors needs an educator nearby so light never goes into eyes, and self-portraits stay private.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer dancing and moving in front of a big floor mirror and walking with a hand mirror under the chin.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small hand mirror the child can hold, turn away and put down whenever they like.
connected: The Image of the Child lens
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian on the Artists page, for mosaics made from many small pieces of cut mirror.
Yayoi Kusama on the Artists page, for Infinity Mirror Rooms where mirrors repeat lights without end.

sections.text: A safe unbreakable mirror, a hand mirror, shiny spoons and some small objects such as buttons, leaves or blocks. Plain paper and a pencil let your child try a mirror drawing.

items: Make silly, happy and sleepy faces together in a mirror.
Hold a hand mirror under your chin and walk slowly to see the ceiling or sky.
Put half a leaf against a mirror and find the whole leaf.
Look at your faces in the back and front of a spoon.
Catch sunlight with a small mirror and move the spot on a wall.

sections.text: Your child can choose what to reflect and lead the faces or the walk. Your child can polish a safe mirror with a soft cloth and tuck it face up into a basket with a towel at the bottom. They can also sort the buttons, leaves and blocks back into their own containers.

items: Where can the mirror see?
I wonder why there are two now.
How do you feel when you make that face?

sections.text: Your child is learning about themselves and their feelings, and noticing shape and pattern. Looking in a mirror helps children notice their own faces and feelings.
Send in old shiny spoons, metal bowls or small acrylic mirrors for our mirror play. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use unbreakable mirrors. Never shine sunlight into anyone's eyes. Walk slowly with a mirror under the chin.

cards.title: Magnifiers and microscopes
cards.summary: Looking closely at the living and found world with hand lenses, bug viewers and simple microscopes.

items: A tray of sturdy hand lenses beside feathers, bark, acorn caps, shells and seed pods on the investigation table.
Two-way bug viewers for gently watching roly polys, ladybugs and worms before returning them.
A magnifier hunt in the log yard, looking under logs and on bark.
A digital microscope connected to a screen so a small group can look at the same thing together.
A large magnifying sheet over a tray of soil or sand.
Magnifiers and clipboards in the pollinator garden for drawing flowers and visitors.
Looking at our own fingertips, skin and hair through a hand lens.
Shed goat hair, rabbit fur and chicken feathers to compare up close.
Lichen and moss on the valley oaks and coast live oak, looked at where they grow.
A drop of rain or creek water under a simple microscope with an educator.
Fabrics, paper and thread under a magnifier to see how they are made.
Nature slides made by pressing tiny found things under clear tape on cardboard.
Binoculars for watching crows, hawks and finches from a distance.
A tablet camera zoomed in to photograph tiny things children found.
Specimens set on a black tile and a white tile side by side, so pale seeds, feathers and lichen show on black and dark ones on white.
Observation drawing from a magnifier with black pencil on white paper and white pencil on black paper.
Looking tools of many kinds, such as hand lenses, a stand magnifier, a magnifying sheet, bug viewers, binoculars, a jeweler's loupe and a digital microscope.
A looking tray in each class atelier with one lens and one treasure that changes each week.
For the North class, a stand magnifier so both hands stay free.
For the South class, field journals with a lens tied to the cover.

sections.text: Both. A single magnifier lets a child look slowly at their own treasure. A shared screen microscope invites a group to point, notice and talk together. In a class atelier one child can look slowly at a treasure. In the Studio a shared screen microscope invites a group to point and talk.

Choose sturdy lenses around three to five times magnification for young hands. Show children how to bring the lens to the object and move it slowly. Never use a lens to focus sunlight. Be kind to all beings and return living creatures where they were found. Wipe lenses with a soft cloth and store them in a padded basket. A stand magnifier helps young children who cannot yet hold a lens steady. Keep black and white tiles in the looking basket.

items: Find and bring objects to look at.
Choose the tool that helps them see best.
Draw what they see in a field journal.
Photograph tiny details with an educator.
Care for creatures and return them gently.
Clean lenses and put tools back.
Show a friend what they found and how to look.
Choose a black or white tile for a specimen.
Draw what they see with white pencil on black paper.

sections.text: Children carry any small creature back to the spot where it was found, then wipe each lens with a soft cloth and nest it in the padded basket. Specimens return to the investigation tray or the compost, and the black and white tiles slide back into the looking basket. Every tool has a photo-labeled home on the shelf at child height, so children finish the whole cycle themselves.

Get down low beside the child and look through your own lens in silence for a while. Keep your voice slow and soft near living creatures. Narrate what you see, such as You held the lens still and the tiny hairs showed up.

items: I notice you are looking very closely.
I wonder what we would see even closer.
It reminds me of the oak bark.
Tell me about what you found.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one sturdy hand lens and one interesting object.
For the West class, offer a stand magnifier over a tray of big leaves and feathers.
Add a basket of natural objects children found themselves.
Offer bug viewers on walks and in the garden.
Draw what children see with pencils on clipboards.
Compare the same object with eyes, a hand lens and a microscope.
Add a digital microscope with a screen for shared looking.
Make nature slides and build a class slide collection.
Use magnifiers to watch change over time, such as a seed sprouting or ice melting.
Look for small creatures and plants in different places on our site.
Use iNaturalist with children to learn about something they found.
Photograph tiny details and print them large for the wall at children's eye level.
Look at artists and naturalists who drew insects and plants up close.
Look at specimens on black and white tiles and compare.
Draw from a magnifier with white on black and black on white.
Model looking with the eye close and moving the lens slowly.
Invite children to lead a looking walk for another class.
Once children have looked closely, an educator photographs the find where it lives and adds it to iNaturalist with an obscured location, as the Photography card describes.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Hand lenses and the looking tray are open to everyone. On a log yard hunt an adult rolls each log first because black widows live on site, and the microscope and digital microscope are used with an educator at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer turning logs in the Log yard to look underneath and carrying a heavy field bag of tools.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a stand magnifier over a quiet tray, with the choice to look at creatures from a distance.
connected: Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for close drawings of insects and the plants they live on.
Georgia O'Keeffe on the Artists page, for painting flowers so large and close they fill the whole canvas.

sections.text: A magnifying glass, a clear jar with holes in the lid, paper and a pencil, and a phone camera with zoom. A dark cloth and a white plate make good backgrounds for looking.

items: Look at leaves, bark and flowers in your yard or a park.
Gently watch a roly poly or ladybug in a jar and let it go.
Look at your fingertips and a strand of hair.
Zoom in with a phone camera and take a close photo together.
Draw something you looked at closely.

sections.text: Your child can choose what to look at, hold the magnifier and tell you what they see. Your child can return a bug or a rock to where it was found and wipe the magnifying glass with a soft cloth. A small box or basket that is just for looking tools gives everything a place to go.

items: How does it look up close?
I wonder what it is made of.
Tell me what you found.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look slowly and carefully and to care for small living things. Looking slowly and closely helps children settle their bodies and focus their eyes.
Send in a close-up photo or a found treasure, such as a feather or seed pod, to look at under our microscope. Spare magnifiers are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Never use a magnifier to focus sunlight. Return bugs to where you found them.

cards.title: Sound and instruments
cards.summary: Ways to listen closely, make sound with real instruments and found objects, and follow children's questions about how sound is made and how it travels.

items: A basket of real instruments in the music shed, such as hand drums, a wooden xylophone, rain sticks and a ukulele, with open space to play.
A sound wall on a garden fence, hung at different heights with pot lids, metal bowls, old baking tins, wooden spoons and short lengths of pipe.
A listening walk on the creek trail or around the garden, where the group stops, closes eyes and counts the sounds they hear.
A sound map on a clipboard, with the child drawn in the middle and a mark for each sound and the place it came from.
Shaker making with recycled containers and small pebbles, acorn caps, gravel, shells or wooden beads, then comparing how each one sounds.

Sound riddles, where children record familiar sounds on our site, such as a goat calling, a gate closing, rain on the shed roof or the chickens at feeding time, and the group guesses where each one was made.
Glass jars filled with different amounts of water and tapped gently with a wooden stick or a metal spoon.
Rubber bands of different widths stretched over open boxes and tins for plucking.
A long garden hose with a funnel at each end for talking and listening across the yard.
Big buckets turned upside down for a drum circle in the outdoor piazza.
Listening to birds with Merlin Bird ID, then answering a bird with a voice or a whistle.
Rain on different surfaces in the rainy season, with buckets, metal trays, wood and leaves set out under the drip line.
Stethoscopes and cardboard tubes for listening to our hearts after running, to the trunk of a valley oak and to the ground.
Drawing sounds on long paper, then playing the drawing back as a score.
Graphic scores drawn with white chalk and white oil pastel on long black paper, beside black crayon on white paper, then played as music.
A limited palette score, with three colors of crayon standing for three instruments, such as red for drums, yellow for shakers and blue for chimes.
Beaters and strikers of many kinds, such as felt mallets, wooden sticks, metal spoons, brushes, chopsticks and fingers, tried on the same drum.
A listening basket in each class atelier with one instrument, a pair of ear muffs and a small rug for a quiet sound corner.
For the North class, two contrasting instruments at a time, such as a drum and a chime, for loud and soft play.
For the South class, homemade instruments planned in a drawing, built, tested and changed.

sections.text: Both. A drum circle or a sound wall gathers many players at once. A quiet corner with a shaker, a xylophone or a recorder lets one child listen closely to their own sound. In the music shed a drum circle gathers many players. In a class atelier a quiet sound corner holds one child listening to their own sound.

Keep a few instruments of good quality rather than many broken ones, and store them on open shelves with photo labels so children can return them. Offer loud instruments outdoors or in the music shed, and keep a quiet listening spot nearby for children who need less noise. Seal homemade shakers with strong tape or a low-temp glue gun, since small fillers are a choking risk for younger children. Shakers are filled with pebbles, shells, acorn caps or beads, and food such as rice or beans is never used as a filler. Glass jars are used with an adult close by. Ear muffs or headphones without sound help children who find noise too much. Store mallets by kind in a labeled basket next to each instrument.

items: Children choose which instruments come out each week and help set them up.
Children care for instruments, carry them with two hands and return them to their shelf.
Children test their homemade instruments and decide what to change.
Children lead a rhythm or a song for the group to echo.
Children record sounds around our site and play them back for others.
Children teach a friend how an instrument works.
Children document their sounds with drawings, marks and their own words.
Draw a graphic score and conduct the group.
Choose a beater and compare the sounds it makes.

sections.text: Children carry each instrument with two hands back to its photo-labeled spot on the open shelf and drop each mallet into its basket by kind. Homemade shakers go into their own bin, and a child checks that every lid is still sealed. Because the shelf and baskets sit right beside the play space, children close it themselves and the educator only notices anything that needs repair.

Sit in the circle at the children's level with an instrument of your own and play softly. Keep a relaxed face during loud play, and notice your own wish for quiet without showing it as worry. Narrate what you hear, such as You played slowly and then very fast.

items: I notice the sound changed when you moved your hand.
Where do you think that sound is coming from?
It reminds me of rain on the shed roof.
How did you make it so soft?
What do you hear that makes you say that?
Begin with a single real instrument at meeting time, passed hand to hand so each child can explore it slowly.
For the West class, offer a single drum and shakers that fit in a hand, with lots of time to bang and shake.
Open the music shed with a few instruments at a time and add more as children show care.
Take a listening walk and make a group sound map of the yard or the creek trail.
Record sound riddles around our site and play them back at meeting time.
Invite children to build instruments from found and recycled materials, testing and changing them over several days.
Hang a sound wall on a fence that children help design and add to.
Explore vibration with tuning forks touched to water and with a few pinches of sand on a drum head.
Draw sounds on long paper and play the marks as a group score, with children taking turns to conduct.
Compare high and low, loud and soft, long and short sounds, and let children invent their own names for them.
Invite families to share instruments and songs from their homes and cultures.
Listen to recordings of natural soundscapes made in Sonoma County, then record our own at different times of day and in different seasons.
Look at and listen to California Native instruments, such as split elderberry clapper sticks, at the Jesse Peter Multicultural Museum, and notice the elderberry growing on our site.
Build a hanging sound sculpture of metal rods or tubes that children set ringing with their hands and the wind.
Draw graphic scores in white on black and black on white and play them.
Use a limited palette of three colors for three instruments in a score.
Model playing softly and stopping, so children see quiet as part of music.
Gather children's sound maps, recordings and scores into a documentation panel or a book for the music area.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Instruments and the listening basket are open to everyone. Tapping glass jars needs an adult close by, and a listening walk on the creek trail leaves campus with each child holding an adult's hand.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big buckets and drums to pound with strong arms outdoors, and heavy rain sticks to turn.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer ear muffs, a quiet corner with one soft instrument and the choice to listen from outside the music shed.
connected: Harry Bertoia on the Artists page, for metal rod sculptures that ring when they are touched or moved by wind.
Bernie Krause on the Artists page, for recording the natural soundscapes of Sonoma Valley and many wild places.
Pauline Oliveros on the Artists page, for listening pieces that ask everyone to listen deeply and answer with sound.
Jesse Peter Multicultural Museum at Santa Rosa Junior College, for California Native clapper sticks and other instruments.

sections.text: Pots, lids, wooden spoons, empty containers with lids, small pebbles or shells, rubber bands, a few glasses of water and a phone for recording sounds.

items: Go on a listening walk around your block or yard and count the sounds you hear.
Make shakers from containers and pebbles, shells or buttons, then compare how they sound.
Set out pots, lids and spoons for a kitchen band.
Fill a few glasses with different amounts of water and tap them gently.
Record sounds around your home and let your child guess what made each one.
Draw sounds on paper with lines and dots, then play the drawing back with a pot and a spoon.

sections.text: Let your child choose the sounds, build and fix their own instruments and lead the band. They can decide when it is time for loud sounds and when it is time for quiet ones. Your child can carry pots, lids and spoons back to the kitchen and stack them where they belong. A basket for homemade shakers keeps them together for next time.

items: I wonder what made that sound.
How could we make it louder or softer?
Tell me about your instrument.

sections.text: Your child is learning to listen closely and to notice how sounds are made. They are also finding rhythm and trying out their own ideas. Drumming and shaking give the arms strong work, and quiet listening helps children notice sound and calm their bodies.

Send us a recording of a sound from your home for our sound riddles, or teach us a song from your family. Clean lids, tins and containers for our sound wall are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Seal shakers tightly with strong tape, since small fillers can be a choking risk for little ones. We keep food for eating, so we fill shakers with pebbles, shells or buttons. Glasses need a grown-up close by, and loud play goes outside when you can.

cards.title: Music and movement
cards.summary: Ways for children to move, dance and sing with their whole bodies, indoors and outdoors, alone and together.

items: A basket of silk scarves and ribbon wands beside open floor space and a speaker with music from many places and times.
A dance party in the indoor piazza, with children choosing the music and the lights.
Songs from the Song book sung at meeting time, with children adding their own movements.
Freeze dance, where the music stops and bodies hold still, with children taking turns stopping the music.
Watching a heron, a goat or a fence lizard, then trying the way it moves with our own bodies.
A large stretchy fabric or a parachute held by everyone, lifted and lowered with the music.
Moving across the yard in many ways, such as tiptoeing, stomping, sliding, rolling, crawling and leaping.
Mirror dancing with a partner, one leading and one following, then switching.
Long paper on the floor and crayons in both hands for drawing while the music plays.
Dancing with our shadows on a sunny wall in the outdoor piazza, or in the light of a projector indoors.
Live music from a drum or a guitar played by an educator or a family member, with children changing speed as the music changes.
Dancing in light rain in rain gear during the rainy season.
Slow swaying with quiet music for calm moments and before rest.
Ribbons tied to sticks for running into the wind in the Tire swing yard.
Drawing to music with a crayon in each hand, with white chalk on long black paper beside black crayon on white butcher paper.
Scarves and ribbons in one color family for a week, such as all blues from pale to dark, so children watch shades move together.
Black and white scarves for a shadow dance in front of a lamp and a white sheet.
Movement tools of many kinds, such as scarves, ribbon wands, hoops, sand-filled cloth bags, a parachute, a low balance beam and stretchy bands.
A small music and movement basket in each class atelier with a few scarves, a hand drum and a speaker.
For the South class, dance paths drawn on paper and then danced across the outdoor piazza.

sections.text: Both. Moving together builds belonging and lets children feel the rhythm of a group. A child dancing alone with a scarf is exploring their own body, space and feelings at their own pace. In the indoor piazza and the yards moving together builds belonging. In a class atelier a child dancing alone with a scarf explores their own body and space.

Clear the space of tripping hazards and agree on boundaries before the music starts. Offer a spot nearby for children who want to watch first, since watching is a way of taking part. Listen to songs with words before playing them for children. Wash scarves often and store them folded in a basket. Shoes stay on in the piazzas, the hallway and the garden. Sand-filled cloth bags are sewn shut, checked often and washed with the scarves. Hoops and bands stay in their own basket and come out with a clear agreement about space.

items: Children choose the music and the props.
Children lead movements for the group to follow.
Children invent new dances and teach them to friends.
Children decide when to join and when to watch.
Children care for scarves and ribbons and put them away.
Children notice how their bodies feel, fast or slow, tired or calm.
Children watch video of their dancing and decide what to try next.
Choose the color family of scarves for the week.
Draw a dance path and lead friends along it.

sections.text: Children fold scarves and ribbons into their basket by color, drop sand bags into the wash bag if they need a wash, and return hoops and bands to their own basket. A few children walk the space to check for anything left on the floor. The baskets sit at the edge of the movement space so the close happens as the music ends, with nothing left for later.

Dance with the children and let your body be loose and unhurried. Keep a soft face for children who watch, since watching is taking part. Narrate what you see, such as You lifted your scarf high and let it float down.

items: I notice your arms are moving slowly.
How else could you move across the yard?
It reminds me of the way the goats jump.
Tell me about your dance.
What do you hear that makes you say that?
Begin with one scarf for each child and a single piece of music, exploring how scarves float and fall.
For the West class, offer scarves, slow music and an educator moving on the floor beside them.
Add ribbon wands, then stretchy fabric, then hoops, one at a time.
Invite children to bring a favorite song from home to share at a dance party.
Watch how animals on our site move, then dance those movements and talk about what we noticed.
Move to music from many cultures and invite families to teach a dance from their traditions.
Play with opposites such as fast and slow, high and low, heavy and light, big and small.
Use body percussion with claps, stomps and pats, then add instruments from the music shed.
Draw while listening and moving, then look at the marks together and wonder about them.
Dance with light and shadow, using a projector, a hanging sheet and colored gels.
Record children's dances and watch them back with the dancers so they can reflect and change their dance.
Create a circle dance for the whole school, with children walking or running together in rings outdoors.
Draw dance paths on paper and then dance the paths across the yard.
Invite children to plan a performance for families, deciding the music, the costumes and the program.
Draw to music with both hands on black and white paper and look at the marks together.
Dance with one color family of scarves for a week.
Model moving slowly and stopping still, so children feel the difference in their bodies.
Move outdoors with the seasons, dancing with falling leaves, wind, rain and long summer shadows.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Dancing is open with an educator nearby and boundaries agreed before the music starts. Running with ribbons in the Tire swing yard follows two adults on the large yards, and the parachute needs an educator holding it with the group.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer spinning, jumping, stomping and rolling dances, carrying sand bags across the room and pulling on stretchy bands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a cushion to watch from, quieter music, one scarf and the choice to join when ready.
connected: Anna Halprin on the Artists page, for dances made outdoors with whole communities moving together.
Pauline Oliveros on the Artists page, for pieces that invite everyone to listen and respond with voice and body.

sections.text: Music you love, a few scarves or light cloths and some open space inside or outside. A crayon in each hand and a big sheet of paper make drawing to music easy.

items: Have a dance party in your kitchen or living room with music your child chooses.
Play freeze dance and take turns stopping the music.
Dance with scarves or dish towels and watch how they float.
Take a walk and try moving the way a bird, a cat or a squirrel moves.
Sing songs your family knows and add movements together.
Sway slowly to quiet music before bed.

sections.text: Let your child pick the music, lead the moves and invent new dances for you to follow. It is fine if they want to watch first. Your child can fold the scarves or cloths and lay them in a basket when the music stops. They can also walk the room to pick up anything that ended up on the floor.

items: How else could we move?
I wonder how this music makes your body want to move.
How do you feel after dancing?

sections.text: Your child is learning how their body moves and how to share space with others. They are also finding joy and calm through music. Moving to music builds balance and coordination, and slow swaying helps the body calm down.

Send us the name of a song your family loves, or come teach us a dance from your family's traditions. Old scarves and light fabric for dancing are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Clear away rugs and toys that could trip someone. Choose songs with words that suit young children. Stop when your child shows they are tired.

cards.title: Photography
cards.summary: Ways for children to use real cameras to notice, frame and share what matters to them, and to look closely at photographs.

items: A sturdy camera with a wrist strap kept on a low shelf in the Studio and in each class atelier, beside cardboard viewfinder cards, ready for children to use without asking.
Empty cardboard frames and slide mounts for looking at the garden through a frame before any camera comes out.
A photo walk on the creek trail or around the garden, with each child choosing what to photograph.
Photographing a block building or a clay piece before it is taken apart or dried, so the work is remembered.
Close-up photos of textures such as oak bark, goat hair, a feather or lichen, then guessing what each one is.
The same tree or garden bed photographed each week and laid out in order to compare.
A clip-on close-up lens on a tablet for looking at tiny things such as roly polys, flower centers and seeds.
Children's photos printed and hung at children's eye level with their own words beside them.
Real photographs of the animals and plants on our site in baskets for sorting, drawing from and storytelling.
A camera obscura made by darkening a room and letting light in through a small hole, showing the yard upside down on the wall.
Photos projected large on a wall for children to step into, trace or draw over.
A small group documenting a day in the animal yards, from feeding to cleaning.
Family photos in a basket or on a wall near the children's cubbies.
Photos taken by children from very high and very low places, such as the top of the climbing structure or flat on the ground.
Black and white photos and color photos of the same place on our site printed side by side, so children notice what changes.
A camera set to black and white mode for a week, then color, with children choosing which to print.
A one-color photo hunt, such as everything red on our site, printed as a grid.
Photos printed on many surfaces, such as matte paper, transparency film for the light table and fabric.
Cameras of many kinds, such as a sturdy digital camera, a tablet with a clip-on close-up lens and a cardboard pinhole camera.
For the South class, a photo project of their own over a week, chosen and printed by them.
Birds and plants noticed first with eyes, ears, hands and journals, and only then an educator's phone with Merlin Bird ID or iNaturalist to learn a name together.
A bird song, with the educator holding up Merlin Bird ID Sound ID quietly, then sharing the bird's name and how it lives.

sections.text: Both. One child with a camera chooses their own view and shares it. A small group can plan a photo walk together and look back at the pictures to talk about what each person saw. In the yards a small group can plan a photo walk together. In a class atelier one child with a camera chooses their own view.

Offer real cameras with a wrist strap and show children how to carry, hold and switch them on and off. Charge batteries and clear memory cards on a set day each week. Children ask a friend before taking a photo of them, and photos of children stay within our school. We never show children's faces publicly, so photos shared beyond school show hands, work and the backs of heads. Sort and delete photos together so children are part of choosing. Print on transparency film for the light table and on fabric with iron-on sheets, adult only. With Merlin Bird ID and iNaturalist, the phone belongs to the educator and stays in a pocket until the children's own noticing is complete. Photograph a plant, insect or other living thing where it lives and leave it be. Every iNaturalist record made at school uses an obscured location, set before saving, and photographs only the plant, bird or animal, never children. Poison hemlock, poison oak, black widows, and deathcap and destroying angel mushrooms are found on or near our site. Adults remove each one as it is found and help children learn to recognize them. Children never pick or taste a mushroom, and they only taste what an adult has named edible. Record each find as a Notice and Wonder observation and add plant finds to the Garden page.

items: Children decide what to photograph and why.
Children care for the camera, wear the strap and return it to its place.
Children choose which photos to print and where to hang them.
Children write or dictate captions for their photos.
Children document their own work and the work of their small group.
Children teach a friend how to use the camera.
Children ask before photographing another person.
Children sort and delete photos with an educator.
Choose black and white or color for a print.
Choose a one-color photo hunt and lead it.
Talk about how their noticing helps people who study and care for birds and plants.

sections.text: Children switch the camera off, wrap the strap around it and return it to its labeled spot, and they plug the charging cord in where the photo label shows. On the weekly sorting day they sit with an educator to choose and delete photos. The camera home is low and labeled, so children close the work on their own and it is ready for the next photographer.

Walk at the child's pace and stop when they stop. Keep your hands off the camera unless asked. Narrate what you see, such as You lay down to take that one, so the tree looks tall. Notice the details a child names first, such as a color, a spot pattern, a sound or a way of moving, and write down how a child describes a song exactly as the child says it.

items: I notice you got very close.
I wonder what you wanted us to see.
Where is the edge of your photo?
Tell me about this picture.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Listen. What does its song sound like?
I wonder why it is tapping on the tree.
Begin by looking through empty frames and cardboard viewfinders, choosing what to keep inside the frame.
For the West class, offer cardboard frames to look through and photos of their own class to hold.
