Introduce one camera to a small group, practicing holding it steady and pressing the button.
Keep a camera available every day in the class and outdoors.
Print a few children's photos each week and talk about them at meeting time.
Go on a theme walk, looking for circles, lines, shadows or a single color.
Photograph the same place across the seasons and make a timeline.
Use children's photos as references for drawing, painting and clay.
Look on screen at photographs by artists who photographed plants up close, then try close-ups of plants on our site.
Try a camera obscura or a pinhole box camera to see how light makes a picture.
Make photograms with objects laid on sun print paper.
Let children take turns bringing a camera home for a weekend and share the photos at school.
Use children's photos with iNaturalist to learn about plants and creatures together.
Invite children to make a book or a documentation panel from their own photos and words.
Compare black and white and color photos of the same place.
Go on a one-color photo hunt and print a grid.
Model holding the camera with two hands and breathing out before pressing.
Look on screen at black and white photographs of Yosemite by Ansel Adams and wonder about light, dark and gray.
Have children photograph their own project from start to finish and use the photos to tell its story to families.
After a name is found, bring it back to the children and look again together, wondering why an insect is on a certain plant.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Cameras with wrist straps are self-serve, and photos of children stay within our school. A photo walk on the creek trail leaves campus with each child holding an adult's hand, and photographing from high places follows our climbing agreements.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer photo walks that climb, crouch and lie on the ground to find high and low views.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet camera job at a table, such as photographing one object on a black cloth.
connected: Karl Blossfeldt on the Artists page, for close-up photographs of seed heads, buds and stems.
Imogen Cunningham on the Artists page, for close photographs of flowers and plants made in the Bay Area.
Ansel Adams on the Artists page, for black and white photographs of California light and land, such as Moon and Half Dome.
John James Audubon on the Artists page, for life-size paintings of the birds of America.

sections.text: A phone or an old camera, some time outdoors and a way to look at the photos together afterwards.

items: Hand your child the camera on a walk and let them choose what to photograph.
Look for a shape or a color together, such as circles or green things, and photograph what you find.
Photograph the same tree or plant each week and look at the changes.
Get very close to something small, such as a flower or a bug, and look at the photo together.
Print a few favorites and let your child tell you about them.
Take the same photo in black and white and in color and compare them.

sections.text: Let your child hold the camera with the strap on, choose what to photograph and pick their favorites. Let them tell the story of each picture. Your child can turn the camera or phone off and set it back in its place with a strap or case. Looking through the photos together and choosing which to keep is part of finishing too.

items: How did you choose this?
I wonder what is just outside the photo.
Tell me about your favorite one.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely and to share what matters to them. They are also learning to care for a real tool. Choosing a view and holding a camera still helps children slow down and judge space.
Send us a photo your child took with a few words about it, or a family photo for our walls. Photos stay within our school.
Use a wrist strap and a soft case. Ask before photographing other people, and keep photos of children private.

cards.title: Puppets and storytelling
cards.summary: Ways for children to tell, act and retell stories with puppets, story stones, shadows and their own voices.

items: A basket of hand puppets of real local animals, such as a goat, a crow, a heron and a hawk, beside a low puppet theater.
A puppet theater made from a large cardboard box, a table turned on its side or a sheet hung between two chairs.
Story stones with small drawings or real photos sealed onto them, kept in a cloth bag and pulled out one at a time.
Story dictation, where a child tells a story, an educator writes every word and the group acts it out on a taped stage at meeting time.
Stick puppets children make from cardboard, fabric scraps, feathers, leaves and twigs.
Shadow puppets cut from card and held between a lamp and a sheet or a wall.
A story basket holding a book and real objects from the story, ready for retelling.
Finger puppets sewn from felt or made from old glove fingers.
A tabletop small world of natural materials, blocks and small figures for building a story scene.
Puppets made from socks, paper bags or wooden spoons with yarn hair.
Storytelling in the willow dome or the Log yard, where the place becomes part of the story.
A felt board with pieces children cut themselves.
A puppet that visits meeting time to wonder aloud about a problem the group is working through.
Retelling a walk or a garden morning with puppets and things found along the way.
Black card silhouette puppets on a white screen beside puppets cut from colored transparent film, so children compare solid and colored shadows.
A limited palette for puppet making, with fabric, paper and yarn in one color family, so a whole cast of characters shares one color.
Puppet making with materials of many kinds, such as socks, wooden spoons, felt, paper bags, sticks, feathers from our chickens and fabric scraps.
Puppet tools in a basket, such as brads for joints, dowels, clothespins, tape, a hole punch and low-temp glue guns with an adult.
A small puppet basket in each class atelier with two puppets and a cloth for a stage.
Storytelling outdoors in the willow dome with puppets and objects found on the way.

sections.text: Both. Puppets give a quiet child a voice and invite friends to play out a story together. A child alone with a story basket can retell a story many times in their own way. At meeting time a story acted out on a taped stage gathers everyone. In a class atelier a child alone with a story basket can retell a story many times.

Store puppets on hooks or in open baskets where children can see each one. Wash cloth puppets and wipe hard ones often. Choose animal puppets that are true to the real animals, and use real photos on story stones. Use a light that stays cool, such as an LED lamp or a projector, and tape cords down. Keep buttons and small pieces off puppets for the youngest children. Black card makes the sharpest silhouettes, and colored film makes colored shadows. Joints made with brads let figures move.

items: Children make their own puppets and decide how they look and move.
Children tell stories for an educator to write down, then choose the actors.
Children build the theater and the scenery.
Children decide the roles and take turns as actors and audience.
Children care for the puppets and return them to their place.
Children retell familiar stories and change the endings.
Children use puppets to show how they feel or to work through a problem with a friend.
Cut a silhouette puppet from black card.
Choose a color family for a puppet cast.

sections.text: Children hang each puppet on its hook or lay it in its open basket, stack the story stones in their tray and slide shadow figures into a flat folder. An adult unplugs and coils the lamp cord. Every puppet has a photo-labeled home at child height, so the theater is reset by the children as the story ends.

Sit at the children's level in the audience and give your full attention. Use a regular voice and laugh with them, never at them. Write their words exactly and let their story go where it goes, even when it is scary or has no ending.

items: I wonder what the goat puppet would say about that.
How did you make it move?
It reminds me of our walk to the creek.
Tell me what happens next.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a single puppet at meeting time that wonders aloud and listens to children.
For the West class, offer soft animal puppets of real local animals to hold, hug and wave.
Add a basket of puppets and a simple theater for open play.
Offer story dictation and acting on a steady rhythm so every child who wants a turn gets one.
Make story stones with children from smooth stones and their own photos or drawings.
Invite children to design and build their own puppets over several days.
Explore shadow puppets on a sheet, with children moving the light to change the size of the shadow.
Add story baskets for familiar books, with real objects in each one.
Retell a book many times and invite children to move the story to our own site.
Use a taped stage on the floor for acting out stories, with the audience sitting around its edges.
Watch silhouette films made with cut paper figures, then try jointed shadow puppets held together with paper fasteners.
Record children's stories and play them back as audio stories in the reading nook.
Invite families to share stories told in their homes and in their home languages.
Plan a puppet show for another class or for families, with children making the tickets and programs.
Make black silhouette and colored film puppets and compare their shadows.
Build a puppet cast in one color family.
Model moving a puppet slowly and giving it a quiet voice, then hand it over.
For the South class, write a program and tickets for a puppet show.
Collect dictated stories into a class book that children illustrate and keep in the reading nook.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Puppets and story baskets are open to everyone, with small pieces kept off puppets for the youngest. Shadow puppet lamps need an educator nearby, and low-temp glue guns for puppet making are used with an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big body puppets, large stick puppets to hold up high and acting stories with jumping and stomping.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small finger puppet and a quiet place behind the theater to speak from.
connected: The Image of the Child lens
Lotte Reiniger on the Artists page, for silhouette films made with jointed cut paper figures.

sections.text: Old socks, paper bags, wooden spoons, fabric scraps, yarn, a cardboard box or a sheet and a flashlight. Black paper cut into shapes and taped to sticks makes strong shadow puppets.

items: Make puppets together from socks, paper bags or spoons.
Turn a box or a table on its side into a puppet theater.
Make shadow puppets on a wall with a flashlight after dark.
Write down a story your child tells you, word for word, and act it out together.
Retell a favorite book with toys and objects from around the house.

sections.text: Let your child tell the story, choose the characters and give the directions. You can be the audience or an actor. Your child can put each puppet to bed in a basket or on a hook and fold the sheet used as a stage. A shoebox works well for flat shadow puppets.

items: Where does the story go next?
I wonder how the puppet feels.
Tell me another ending.

sections.text: Your child is learning to tell stories in their own words and to imagine how others think and feel. Moving puppets with both hands and telling stories helps children plan movements and share their feelings.

Send in a story your child told you, written word for word, and we can act it out at school. Old socks, fabric scraps and yarn for puppet making are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep buttons and small pieces away from little ones. Use a flashlight that stays cool.

cards.title: Books
cards.summary: Ways to bring books into every part of the day, indoors and outdoors, so children become listeners, readers, makers and keepers of books.

items: A small basket of books in the garden, the Log yard and near the animal yards, changed with the seasons.
Field guides to birds, oaks, insects and wildflowers beside the nature table and on clipboards outdoors.
The same picture book read many times over a week, so children notice more each time and begin to retell it.
Wordless picture books for children to tell in their own words.
A story basket holding a book and real objects from it.
Books in the home languages of our families, with family members invited to read them aloud.
Children's own handmade books shelved beside published books in the reading nook.
A book hospital with tape and a bone folder, where children repair torn pages.
Books placed in every area, such as building books in the block area and cookbooks in the piazza.
A reading spot under the willow dome or on a blanket under a valley oak.
Reading aloud near the animal yards during a quiet visit.
A lending basket so children can take a book home and bring it back.
Information books paired with real things, such as a book about feathers beside a basket of feathers.
A walk or a family trip to the public library to get library cards and choose books.
High contrast black and white books, such as White on Black and Black on White by Tana Hoban, in a basket for the West class.
Books whose pictures use a limited palette, such as books in black ink only, set beside full color books to compare.
Picture books made with many mediums, such as collage, watercolor, woodcut, photographs and pencil, beside the same materials in the Studio.
Books on many surfaces and shapes, such as board books, cloth books, accordion books and tiny palm books.
A small book basket in each class atelier with one information book linked to the medium on the table.
For the South class, field guides and their own field journals side by side.

sections.text: Both. Reading together at meeting time builds shared stories and words. A child alone with a book in a cozy spot can look, wonder and return to favorite pages as often as they like. At meeting time reading together builds shared stories. In a class atelier or reading nook a child alone can look and wonder.

Display books with covers facing out at children's height and change them often. Keep a mix of stories, poems, information books and wordless books, with people and places that reflect our families. Choose animal books with real photos or true-to-life art. Repair books as soon as they tear. Outdoor books live in a covered bin and come inside before rain. Pair a book with the medium it uses, such as a collage picture book beside the collage tray.

items: Children choose books for meeting time and for the reading nook.
Children read to friends by telling the story from the pictures.
Children care for books and repair torn pages.
Children make their own books and add them to the class library.
Children suggest books to look for when a question comes up.
Children carry books outdoors and back again.
Children sort and shelve books in ways they decide together.
Choose a book that matches the medium on the table.

sections.text: Children carry outdoor books back to the covered bin, set any torn book in the book hospital basket, and return the rest face out to the low shelf. A child can check the shelf for books standing upside down. With a return basket and a repair basket close at hand, books find their way home during the work and an educator only handles the bigger repairs.
Sit low and close, and read slowly in a regular voice with pauses to look. Let the child turn the pages and skip ahead. Follow their pointing and name what they notice.

items: I notice something new in this picture.
I wonder why the story ended this way.
It reminds me of our garden.
How do you think the artist made this picture?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a small set of books chosen with care and read many times.
For the West class, offer high contrast black and white books and board books with real photos.
Read the same book across a week, adding new wonderings each time and inviting children to retell it on the last reading.
Add field guides when children bring questions about birds, bugs or plants, and look things up together.
Pair books with real objects, story baskets and puppets.
Invite children to dictate stories and illustrate them, then bind them into books.
Set up a book hospital where children repair books with tape and glue.
Take books outdoors in small baskets for each yard and season.
Invite families to read in their home languages and to share favorite books.
Start a lending library so books travel home and back.
Visit the public library and invite children to choose books for the class.
Look closely at how illustrators make their pictures, such as painted paper, collage or mixed media, then try those ways in the Studio.
Make a class book about a project with children's photos, drawings and words.
Make a book about our site for new families, written and illustrated by children.
Compare books with a limited palette and books in full color.
Look at how a picture book was made and try that medium in the Studio.
Model turning pages slowly and pausing on a picture.
Gather children's favorite books into a list to share with families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Books are open to everyone indoors and out. Reading near the animal yards happens with an educator, and a walk to the public library leaves campus with each child holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer carrying heavy book baskets outdoors and reading while rocking or swinging in a hammock with an adult.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet nook with a soft light and one familiar book.
connected: Yuyi Morales on the Artists page, for Dreamers, a picture book about finding home in a public library, made in mixed media.
Tana Hoban on the Artists page, for White on Black and Black on White, high contrast photo books for the youngest readers.

sections.text: A few books, a cozy spot and some time. A free public library card opens up many more. High contrast black and white books are lovely for the youngest children.

items: Read the same favorite book many times and let your child tell parts of it.
Visit the library and let your child choose books.
Read outside on a blanket, at the park or in the yard.
Look at wordless picture books and tell the story together.
Make a small book together with folded paper, drawings and your child's words.
Read in the languages your family speaks.

sections.text: Let your child choose the book, turn the pages and tell you what they notice. Pause and let them fill in words they know. Your child can put books back on a low shelf with the covers facing out and set a torn one aside for you to fix together. A small basket by the bed makes a good home for this week's books.

items: Where do you think this story happens?
I wonder what will happen next.
Tell me about this picture.

sections.text: Your child is learning that books bring joy and answers to questions. They are building words and a love of reading. Reading together calms the body and builds words and listening.

Send in a favorite book for a few days, or a book in your family's language, and we will read it together. You are also welcome to come read to the class. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep books where your child can reach them. Tape torn pages together with your child so the book can keep being read.

cards.title: Real objects for dramatic play
cards.summary: Ways to stock pretend play with real tools and everyday objects so children can try out the work and life they see around them.

items: Real dishes, metal pots, wooden spoons, cloth napkins and a teapot in the home area.
A café with menus, order pads, aprons and a small chalkboard, connected to our Unicorn Café in the piazza.
A shop with a real scale, baskets, paper bags, coins, a cash box and price tags children write.
An office with an old keyboard, phones with batteries and cords removed, clipboards, envelopes, stamps and a hole punch.
A vet clinic with real stethoscopes, bandages, clipboards and realistic animal figures or puppets.
A garden shop with empty seed packets, small pots, child size garden tools and watering cans.
A post office with mailboxes, envelopes, rubber stamps and a mail bag.
Real objects from our families' homes, such as a tortilla press, a steamer basket, chopsticks, a mortar and pestle, a teapot or woven baskets, lent and labeled by families.
A building site near the block area with hard hats, measuring tapes, levels, safety goggles and clipboards.
An outdoor camp with a tent, sleeping bags, lanterns, maps and a pretend fire ring of logs and stones.
A baby care corner with real baby clothes, cloth diapers, a small tub and blankets.
A repair shop with screwdrivers and old appliances with the cords cut off.
A bus or a train made from chairs, with tickets, maps and a steering wheel.
A farm stand with empty egg cartons, baskets and signs, connected to our chickens and garden.
Real tools of many kinds for each play setting, such as a whisk, a ladle, a measuring tape, a stapler, a stethoscope, a level and a watering can.
Natural, unbranded objects in calm colors, such as white dishes, linen napkins, wooden bowls and woven baskets, so children's own signs and props stand out.
Sign-making supplies in every play setting, such as black markers on white card, white chalk on a small chalkboard and kraft paper tags.
A small set of real objects in each class atelier home corner, changed as the play changes.
For the West class, a few real objects to fill, carry and empty, such as a basket, a purse, a pot with a lid and a cloth.
For the South class, play settings children plan, list and build, with a shopping list for what they need.

sections.text: Both. Dramatic play draws children into roles, talk and shared plans. A child alone stirring a real pot or sorting a wallet is trying out the grown-up world at their own pace. In the home area and outdoors play draws children into shared roles. In a class atelier a child alone with a real tool tries out grown-up work at their own pace.

Real objects need safety checks. Remove batteries, cut off cords and plugs, check for sharp edges and glass, and keep small parts away from younger children. Ask families to lend or give objects, and label anything that must go home. Real food stays for eating, so pretend food is made by children from clay, felt, cardboard or found materials. Change objects as interests change and keep a few well-chosen things so shelves stay uncrowded. Choose real objects with calm, natural colors so the space feels warm and homey, and children's own work is what stands out.

items: Children decide what the play space will become next.
Children make signs, menus, tickets and price tags.
Children set up, care for and put away the real tools.
Children bring ideas and objects from their own homes.
Children take on roles and invite others in.
Children solve problems in the play, such as running out of tickets.
Children teach friends how a real tool works.
Make signs with black on white or white on black.
Write a list of what a new play setting needs.

sections.text: Children wipe dishes and tools with a damp cloth, return each real object to its photo-labeled spot and sort the signs, tickets and menus they made into a paper basket. Anything that must go home goes into the labeled family bag. Shelves stay uncrowded and every object has a home, so children reset the play space themselves as play ends.

Sit inside the play space at the children's level and take a small role only when invited, such as a customer. Keep your voice regular and follow the children's script. Notice your own wish to tidy and let the play be busy and full.

items: I wonder what this is for.
How does your shop work?
It reminds me of the café in the piazza.
Tell me what your shop needs.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a small set of real home objects children know well, such as dishes, pots and cloth napkins.
For the West class, offer a basket of real objects to fill, carry and empty, with doubles so turns are easy.
Watch and listen for what children are playing, then add real objects that fit their play.
Ask children what the space needs and make a list together.
Invite families to lend objects from their homes and cultures, with a family member sharing how each one is used.
Visit real places such as a shop, a post office, a library or a bakery, then bring the ideas back to play.
Invite children to make their own props, signs and pretend food from clay, cardboard and fabric.
Connect play to real work on our site, such as the café, egg collecting and the garden.
Add writing tools to every play setting so children can make lists, menus, tickets and maps.
Take play outdoors with a camp, a farm stand or a shop under the oaks.
Offer real screwdrivers for taking apart old appliances with cords removed, with an adult close by.
Let a play theme grow over weeks, with children deciding when it changes.
Photograph the play and look at the photos together to plan what comes next.
Add sign-making supplies to every setting and let children choose their own lettering.
Model using a real tool slowly and carefully, then hand it over.
For the North class, add one new real object at a time and talk about how it is used.
Invite people with real jobs, such as a vet, a baker or a mail carrier, to visit and bring their tools.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Real objects that pass a safety check are open to everyone. Taking apart old appliances with real screwdrivers needs an adult close by, and small parts stay away from younger children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy real jobs in play, such as carrying a full laundry basket, pushing a loaded cart and moving furniture for a new setting.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet corner of the play space with one familiar object, such as a teapot and two cups.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

home.title: Real objects for dramatic play at Home

sections.text: Everyday things from around your home, such as old pots, spoons, bags, envelopes, keys, an old phone with the battery removed, paper and pencils.

items: Set up a café with real cups, napkins and a menu your child writes or draws.
Make a shop with bags, a box for money and price tags.
Give your child a real job alongside you, such as setting the table or sorting the mail.
Build a camp with blankets, a flashlight and a map.
Share objects from your family's culture and tell your child how they are used.

sections.text: Let your child set up the play, choose the roles and make the signs. Follow their lead and ask them what you should do. Your child can wipe the pots and spoons with a sponge and put each one back on its shelf or in its basket. A bag by the door for borrowed things helps them remember what goes back.

items: How does this tool work?
I wonder who uses this at our house.
Tell me about your café.

sections.text: Your child is learning about the people and the work in their world, and how to plan and share play with others. Real jobs and play with real tools give children strong hands and the feeling of being trusted and capable.

Lend us an everyday object from your home or culture for our play spaces, with your name on it so we can return it. Empty boxes, bags and envelopes are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Remove batteries and cut the cords from old electronics. Check for sharp edges and small parts. We keep real food for eating.

cards.title: Seeds
cards.summary: Ways to find, open, save, sort, plant and wonder about seeds across the year on our site.

items: A seed hunt in the garden with small paper envelopes, looking for seed heads on California poppies, salvias, yarrow and lavender.
Magnifiers and a tray of seeds from our seed library, with small dishes for sorting by size, shape and color.
Dry seed pods and seed heads from the garden, opened by hand to see what is inside.
Large seeds from the seed library or seed packets, soaked overnight and gently opened to look inside.
Seeds tucked against damp paper towel in a clear jar, so roots and shoots can be watched each day.
Japanese maple seeds dropped from a height to watch them spin, then paper spinners children design and test.
A sock walk, where a child wears an old fuzzy sock over a shoe through dry grass, then plants the sock to see what grows.
Acorns from the valley oaks and the coast live oak, gathered, sorted and planted in deep pots.
Seed balls made from clay, compost and native wildflower seeds, then tossed onto a bare patch of ground.
Seeds found in fruit at snack, such as apple seeds, rinsed, dried and planted to see what happens.
A seed journal where children draw a seed each day as it sprouts.
Planting seeds in each class's home beds and in pots children choose.
Seed packets children design, fill and label for the seed library.
Seed heads left standing in the garden so children can watch finches come to eat.
Seeds from the seed library set on a black tray and a white tray side by side, so pale and dark seeds show clearly.
Observation drawing of seeds with black pencil on white paper and white pencil on black paper, with a magnifier beside each.
A one-color seed study, such as all the brown or all the black seeds from our garden, sorted from light to dark.
Seed tools of many kinds, such as tweezers, small spoons, paper envelopes, sieves, a magnifier and a mortar for opening dry pods.
A seed tray in each class atelier with a few large seeds, a magnifier and a small notebook.
Seeds offered on many surfaces, such as damp paper towel, cotton, soil, sand and moss, to see where roots appear.

sections.text: Both. Seed saving and planting are shared garden work in small groups. A child alone with a magnifier and a few seeds can look closely for a long time. In the garden seed saving is shared work in small groups. In a class atelier one child with a magnifier and a few seeds can look closely for a long time.

Seeds for study come from our garden, our seed library or seed packets. Seeds sold as food, such as dried beans and rice, stay in the kitchen and are never used for collage or sensory play. Some seeds are poisonous, including annual morning glory and poison hemlock seeds, so adults confirm every seed children gather and children wash hands afterward. Small seeds are a choking risk for younger children, so keep them in lidded jars and use them with an adult close by. Dry seeds fully before storing them in labeled paper envelopes in a cool, dry place. Keep a black tray and a white tray in the seed basket so seeds can always be seen clearly.

items: Children search for and gather seeds with purpose, leaving some for the birds and the garden.
Children sort, label and store seeds in the seed library.
Children choose which seeds to plant and where.
Children water and care for seedlings.
Children draw and record how seeds change.
Children share seeds with families and other classes.
Children decide how to test their own questions, such as whether a seed grows in the dark.
Choose a black or white tray to show a seed best.
Draw a seed with white pencil on black paper.

sections.text: Children brush loose seeds from the trays into labeled envelopes, set wet paper towels and soil cups in the drying spot, and return lidded jars to the seed library shelf. Everyone washes hands at the sink afterward. Envelopes, a small brush and the seed library sit beside the work so children close it themselves.
Kneel in the garden at the children's level and move slowly near the plants. Keep your voice quiet and curious. Narrate what you see, such as You shook the poppy head and the seeds rattled out.

items: I wonder what is inside.
How do you think this seed travels?
It reminds me of the spinning maple seeds.
Tell me what changed since yesterday.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few large seeds and magnifiers, looking and drawing before any names are offered.
For the West class, offer large seed pods and pinecones to hold and shake, and plant big seeds in pots with an educator.
Go on a seed hunt in the garden and gather seed heads in paper bags.
Open pods and seed heads together and sort what is found.
Plant seeds in clear containers so the roots can be seen.
Notice how seeds travel, by wind, by spinning, by sticking to fur and socks and by animals, and test children's ideas.
Make seed balls with clay and native wildflower seeds and plant a bare patch.
Plant acorns and watch for oak seedlings over many months.
Save seeds from the garden at the end of a season and label them for the seed library.
Invite children to design seed packets and share seeds with families.
Look on screen at close-up photographs of seeds and seed heads, then photograph and draw our own seeds up close.
Follow one plant from seed to seed across the year and make a book about its life.
Invite families to share seeds their families have grown and saved, and the stories that go with them.
Set up children's own tests, such as seeds planted in sun and in shade.
Draw seeds on black and white paper and compare.
Sort a one-color seed study from light to dark.
Model opening a dry pod over a tray and looking before naming.
Visit a seed library at a public library or a community garden.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Seed looking and planting are open with an educator nearby, and small seeds stay in lidded jars for younger children. An adult confirms every seed gathered because annual morning glory and poison hemlock seeds are poisonous, and the garden follows one adult to six children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer digging deep holes for acorns, carrying watering cans and shaking dry seed heads into a bag.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a single seed on a tray with tweezers and a magnifier at a quiet table.
connected: Karl Blossfeldt on the Artists page, for close-up photographs of seed heads, pods and buds.

sections.text: A few seed packets, seeds saved from fruit you eat, small pots or cups of soil, a clear jar, paper towels and a magnifying glass if you have one. A dark plate and a white plate help you see small seeds clearly.

items: Save seeds from fruit after you eat it, rinse and dry them, and plant a few.
Tuck a seed against a damp paper towel in a clear jar and watch it sprout.
Look for seeds on a walk, such as acorns, maple seeds that spin and dandelion puffs.
Plant seeds in a pot on a windowsill and care for them together.
Open a dry seed pod and count what is inside.

sections.text: Let your child choose, plant and water the seeds. They can check each day and draw what they see. Your child can brush stray seeds into an envelope, write or draw a label and put the cups of soil on a sunny sill. Washing hands together is the last step.

items: I wonder what is inside.
How do you think it grows?
Tell me what changed since yesterday.

sections.text: Your child is learning that living things grow and change, and how to care for them over time. Picking up tiny seeds builds careful fingers, and caring for seedlings over time is calming.
Send in seeds your family has saved, with a note about the plant and where it grew, for our seed library. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Some seeds are poisonous, such as annual morning glory and wisteria seeds, so check what your child gathers. Small seeds can be a choking risk for toddlers. Seeds from the pantry stay for eating.

cards.title: Pressed plants
cards.summary: Ways to gather, press, study and create with leaves and flowers from our garden through the seasons.

items: A flower press made from two boards, cardboard and paper, with straps or wing nuts children tighten themselves.
A gathering walk with a basket in the garden, each child choosing one flower or leaf with purpose and leaving plenty for the pollinators.
Pressed leaves and petals on the light table to see veins and color.
Herbarium pages with one pressed plant on each sheet, marked with the date, the place and the child's own name for it.
Pressed flower pictures arranged on card and set in place with thinned glue.
Pressed plants sealed between clear contact paper and hung in a window.
Hammered flower prints, where children tap fresh petals and leaves onto cotton cloth or watercolor paper with a mallet.
Pressed plants laid into handmade paper while it is still wet.
Leaves and flowers pressed into playdough or clay to leave prints, then cast in plaster.
A seasonal pressed plant calendar, with one plant from the garden added each month.
Pressed petals sorted into a color wheel on a tray.
Pressed plants under clear sleeves as placemats for the café tables in the piazza.
Heavy books with paper between the pages for a quick press in any class.
Pressed plants carried back to the garden to match with the living plant they came from.
Pressed plants arranged on black paper and white paper side by side, so children notice how petals and leaves show on each.
A one-color pressing week, such as all the yellows in the garden from California poppies to yarrow, arranged from pale to deep.
Pressed plants on many grounds, such as kraft paper, watercolor paper, tracing paper, handmade paper, gray card and plain cotton.
Pressing tools on a tray, such as a flower press, blotting paper, tweezers, a soft brush, a small dish of thinned glue and clear contact paper.
A small press in each class atelier with a basket for gathering on the way back from the garden.
For the North class, pressing with heavy books and a few big, flat leaves such as redbud and Japanese maple.

sections.text: Both. Gathering and pressing for a class herbarium is shared work. A child alone can arrange, study and draw pressed plants with full attention. In the garden and the Studio gathering and pressing for a class herbarium is shared work. In a class atelier a child alone can arrange and draw pressed plants with full attention.

Adults confirm every plant before it is picked, since poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site. Gather on a dry day after the dew is gone, and choose thin, flat leaves and flowers such as clover, California poppies, rose petals, yarrow, lamb's ear and Japanese maple and redbud leaves. Herbs we grow for tea and cooking stay for the kitchen. Lay plants between paper in the press and check after one to two weeks. Store pressed plants flat in labeled folders away from sun. Pick with purpose and leave some for others. Tweezers and a soft brush move fragile pressed petals without tearing. Black paper shows pale petals well and white paper shows dark leaves and veins, so keep both with the collection.

items: Children choose which plants to gather and pick with care.
Children layer the press and tighten the straps.
Children check the press and decide when plants are ready.
Children label herbarium pages with their own marks and words.
Children arrange and create with pressed plants.
Children care for the class collection and decide how to sort it.
Children share pressed plants as gifts for families and other classes.
Choose a black or white ground for an arrangement and say why.
Lift and place pressed petals with tweezers.

sections.text: Children tighten the press straps, carry the press to its flat shelf and slide pressed pieces into labeled folders with tweezers and a soft brush. Scraps of leaves and stems go to the compost bucket. The press, folders and compost bucket all live beside the work table, so the close is done by children before they move on.

Walk slowly through the garden at the children's pace and crouch to look at each plant they point to before anyone picks. Keep your voice calm and your hands still while they arrange. Narrate what you see, such as You placed the poppy petals in a ring.

items: I notice the color changed in the press.
How is this pressed leaf different from the ones on the tree?
I wonder where else this plant grows.
Tell me about your arrangement.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with heavy books and a few leaves, opening the book together a week later.
For the West class, press big leaves in a heavy book with an educator and open it together a week later.
Build a flower press with children using boards, cardboard and straps.
Go on gathering walks with agreements about picking with purpose.
Start a class herbarium with one plant on each page, adding to it each season.
Use iNaturalist and field guides to learn plant names together.
Explore pressed plants on the light table and under magnifiers.
Create pressed plant pictures, window hangings and cards.
Try hammered flower prints on cloth and paper.
Add pressed plants to papermaking, clay and plaster.
Look on screen at a herbarium of pressed plants kept long ago, then talk about what we would keep in our own book.
Look on screen at pictures made entirely from pressed leaves and petals, then try arranging our own.
Make a pressed plant calendar of our garden across the whole year.
Compare pressed plants gathered in the rainy season and in the dry season.
Arrange pressed plants on black and white paper and compare.
Press one color across a week and lay the collection from pale to deep.
Model lifting petals with tweezers and laying them down without pressing.
For the South class, draw a pressed plant with pencil and white pencil beside the real one.
Make a book of our site's plants for families with pressed plants, drawings and children's words.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Pressing and arranging are open with an educator nearby. Gathering needs an adult confirming every plant before it is picked because poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site, and the garden follows one adult to six children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer tightening the press straps or wing nuts with strong hands and stacking heavy books on top.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer tweezers and a few already pressed plants on a quiet tray, with no gathering needed.
connected: Emily Dickinson on the Artists page, for the herbarium of pressed plants she made and labeled as a young person.
Helen Ahpornsiri on the Artists page, for pictures of birds and animals made entirely from pressed leaves and petals.

sections.text: A few heavy books, plain paper or paper towels, and leaves or flowers from your yard or a walk. Dark paper makes pale petals glow, and white paper shows dark leaves.

items: Pick a few flowers or leaves on a walk, choosing with care and leaving plenty.
Press them between paper inside a heavy book and check after a week.
Arrange pressed plants on paper to make a picture or a card.
Make a small book with one pressed plant on each page and your child's words.
Gently tap fresh petals onto cloth or paper with a hammer to see the color print.

sections.text: Let your child choose what to gather, place it in the book and decide when to check. They can arrange and name their own pressed plants. Your child can stack the heavy books back on top of the press and slide finished flowers into a folder. Leftover stems can go in the compost or the yard.

items: How did it change after pressing?
I wonder where this plant came from.
Tell me about your picture.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely at plants and to wait for and care for something over time. Pressing and arranging plants builds careful fingers and patience, and quiet sorting helps many children feel calm.
Send in pressed plants from your yard or a family trip, with a note about where you found them, for our class collection. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Check every plant before picking, since some plants such as poison oak can hurt skin. Ask before picking in parks or neighbors' yards. Hammering needs a grown-up close by.

cards.title: Obstacle courses
cards.summary: Indoor and outdoor obstacle courses built with children from logs, crates, planks, tires and tunnels, changing over weeks to meet the body's need to climb, balance, crawl, jump and carry.

items: A pile of crates, planks, tires, stumps and spools left at the edge of the Log yard with one question at meeting time, Where could our bodies go today?
A plank laid from a stump to a crate, a tire to step through, a log to straddle and scoot along, and a woodchip patch to land in, set out as a start for children to change.
An indoor course in the class atelier or the indoor piazza from cushions, a low bench, a fabric tunnel, carpet squares as stepping spots and a table to crawl under.
Tape lines on the floor that zigzag, curve and spiral, for walking heel to toe, hopping along or walking sideways.
A course with an over, an under, a through, an around and an across, so the body has to change its shape at each part.
A carrying course, where each child takes a beanbag, a small log or a bucket of woodchips from one end to the other.
A course that ends with heavy work, such as pushing a full wheelbarrow back to the start or stacking the crates at the finish.
A course that crosses the middle of the body, with a ball to pass from one hand to the other around a post or a rope to pull hand over hand.
A long course that runs from the Log yard toward the small hill, with a roll down the slope and a crawl through the tires at the bottom.
Two children building a short course for each other and then trading.
A partner course where two children carry one long plank or one heavy crate together.
A clipboard and pencils by the start for drawing a map of the course before or after it is built.
Photographs of the course printed and posted at children's eye level so children can rebuild it another day.
For the West class, three or four low parts close to the ground, such as a wide plank on the grass, a tire to sit in and a short tunnel, with plenty of time to repeat.
For the North class, five to seven parts with a low beam, a step up onto a crate and a jump into woodchips.
For the South class, a course children plan, draw, build, try, change and name, with real choices about height and order.
A rainy day course in the indoor piazza with mats, a balance board, a crawl under a cloth and a pillow pile at the end.
A slow course, walked as quietly as possible, after a loud morning.

sections.text: Both. Building a course is shared work that needs many hands to carry crates and planks and many voices to decide the order. Each child tries it in their own way and at their own pace, while friends watch, cheer or join in. A child may also build a small course alone and use it again and again.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Children help build, and an educator checks every plank end sits flat and stable and every crate stands on level ground before the course opens. Planks over about knee height go on two supports with no gap to slip into. Leave clear space around each part so a child who comes off lands on soft ground and away from other parts. Keep the flow going one way and agree with children where to wait. Indoors, push furniture to the walls, lay mats under any step down, and keep the course out of walkways. Change the course a little at a time over weeks so children meet something new while the rest feels known. Store planks and crates flat and dry so they do not warp or rot, and retire any split board. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose the materials and decide where each part goes.
Carry, drag and set crates, planks and tires in place with friends.
Try a part, notice what happens and change it.
Draw a map of the course and post it at the start.
Make and remind others of the agreements, such as one at a time on the beam.
Show a younger child a way through.
Decide when the course needs something new.
Take the course apart and store each piece where it lives.
Photograph the course for the wall and tell how it changed.

sections.text: Children take the course apart in reverse, carrying crates, tires and light planks to their stacks and laying them flat and dry. An adult moves anything too heavy to lift and checks for split boards as pieces come in. Every piece has a marked place, so the course is put away by the children who built it and the yard is clear for the next group.

Stand at the side of the course where you can see every part, with hands at your sides and a relaxed face, and stay there. Narrate what bodies are doing, such as You stepped over the log with one foot and then the other. When a part collapses, keep your voice even and ask the builders what they want to try next.

items: I notice you went under the plank this time.
I wonder where the course could go next.
How did you decide the order?
Tell me about the hardest part for your body.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few low parts set out by educators and let children move freely through them.
Invite children to add one piece each day and talk about where it should go.
Add a map at the start and let children draw the course as they see it.
Introduce the words over, under, through, around, across and between as children move.
Add a carrying part so the course holds heavy work.
Add a part that needs both hands together, such as pulling along a rope or climbing a cargo net.
Raise one part a little, with children judging if they want to try it.
Let children run the course in a new direction, backwards or sideways.
Add a partner part where two children carry or balance together.
Invite the South class to plan a course on paper first and then build it from the plan.
Invite children to build a course for the West class and watch how the younger children use it.
Move the course to a new place on the site, such as the small hill, the Tire swing yard or the indoor piazza, and notice what changes.
Add a calm ending, such as lying on a mat or walking slowly back.
Keep a photo book of the courses through the year and return to it at meeting time.
Let a long-running course become a project, with signs, rules children write and an opening day.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stands where they can see every part of the course, with two adults on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. An adult checks logs, crates and tires for black widows first, and planks above knee height need an educator close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add a heavy part such as dragging a tire or carrying a full bucket between each part, and a jump into woodchips at the end.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a short course of two or three low parts away from the line, with time to watch first and a choice to walk beside it holding nothing.
connected: An obstacle course from what is out

sections.text: Cushions, a blanket, chairs, a low step or stool, a broom handle, painter's tape, a laundry basket, pillows and some open floor. Outside, a log, a board, a garden hose laid in a line and a patch of grass.

items: Build a living room course together with a crawl under the table, a step over pillows and a walk along a tape line.
Lay a hose or rope in a wiggly line in the yard and walk along it.
Carry a basket of socks or toys from one end of the course to the other.
Let your child build a course for you and follow it the way they show you.
Change one part each day and see what your child does with it.

sections.text: Your child can plan the course, carry the cushions, decide the order and show you the way through. They can also put it all away. Your child can carry the cushions, pillows and basket back where they belong and peel up the tape lines. Putting the course away together is part of the game.

items: I wonder where the course goes next.
How did you get over that part?
Tell me about the part you made.

sections.text: Your child is planning movements, judging space and using their whole body with strength and balance. Climbing over, crawling under and carrying things gives the body heavy work and movement, which helps many children feel calm and organized.

Draw or photograph your home course and send it to school so your child can show friends. If you have crates, planks or tires to give, send a note first, and this counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep courses low and away from sharp corners and glass. Put pillows under any step down. Expect some furniture to move and plan a cleanup together.

cards.title: Jumping and landing
cards.summary: Jumping from stumps, logs, crates and platforms of rising height into soft landing zones, where children choose their own height and learn to land.

items: A row of stumps of rising height leading to a deep woodchip landing zone in the Log yard.
A low crate, a medium crate and a log beside a raked woodchip pile, so children choose where to jump from.
A tire laid flat as a target to land inside, and later two or three tires in a row to hop between.
Jumping off the small hill onto soft ground, and down the slope in long strides.
Jumping into a pile of raked leaves in autumn.
Jumping over a stick, a rope laid on the ground, a narrow line of woodchips and then a wider one.
Jumping across stepping stumps set further and further apart.
Jumping into the mud pit in rain boots on a wet day.
Indoors in the class atelier, jumping from a low step onto a thick mat, or from carpet square to carpet square.
Jumping on two feet, then one foot, then landing on the other foot.
Jumping and freezing on landing, holding still before the next jump.
Jumping to touch a leaf on a low branch or a ribbon hung from a valley oak.
Jumping in place to music in the indoor piazza or the music shed.
For the West class, jumping off a low wide step or a curb-high log onto grass, with lots of repeats and two feet together.
For the North class, jumping from a stump of knee height into woodchips, and jumping over a rope on the ground.
For the South class, jumping from higher stumps and crates they reach by themselves, jumping for distance with a marker stick, and hopscotch drawn in chalk.

sections.text: Both. Each child jumps alone and judges their own height. Friends wait their turn, watch each other land, cheer and invent new ways to jump together, such as jumping at the same moment from two stumps side by side.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Landing zones are loose woodchips about nine inches deep, raked into a soft pile each morning, or thick mats indoors. Keep the landing zone clear of other children, logs and tools, and agree with children that the landing spot is empty before anyone jumps. Children jump only from heights they reach by themselves, and adults never lift a child onto a stump or crate. Check that stumps and crates are steady and do not roll or tip. Soft knees on landing protect the body, and children find this by doing it again and again. Wet woodchips and wet stumps are slippery, so we look together at the surface on rainy days. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose a height to jump from.
Check that the landing spot is clear before jumping.
Rake woodchips back into a soft pile with an educator.
Move stumps and crates to make new jumping places.
Mark how far a jump went with a stick or a stone.
Make and remind others of the agreement of one jumper at a time.
Show a friend how they land with soft knees.
Decide when they are ready for a higher spot, or when they want to stay low.

sections.text: Children rake the woodchips back into a soft pile with child-size rakes and roll small stumps and crates back to their spots. An adult moves any stump too heavy to roll. Rakes hang on low hooks at the edge of the landing zone so children reset it themselves before they leave.

Stand beside the landing zone at a little distance, hands down and still, and let your face stay calm when a child chooses a high spot. Notice your own worry and keep it out of your voice. Name what you see, such as Your knees bent when you landed, and leave the choice of height with the child.

items: I notice you looked down before you jumped.
I wonder how it feels in your legs when you land.
Where will you jump from next?
How did you know you were ready?
Tell me about that landing.
Start with low, wide places to jump from and a deep, soft landing.
Let children jump the same spot many times before anything changes.
Add a second stump of a different height and let children choose.
Add a landing target such as a tire or a circle of rope.
Invite jumping over things, from a stick to a wider line.
Invite one-foot hops and landing on the other foot.
Add stumps in a row that children jump between.
Invite jumping for distance, with children marking their own landing with a stick.
Add jumping and freezing on landing to build control.
Raise heights slowly over weeks while children judge their own readiness.
Draw the jumping place on a clipboard and talk about which spot is highest.
Bring jumping indoors on rainy days with mats and low steps.
Notice with children how the body feels after many jumps, such as a fast heart and warm cheeks.
End jumping time with a slow walk or lying in the woodchips to rest.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stands beside the landing zone and children jump only from heights they reach by themselves. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard, and jumping in the mud pit needs an educator close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer many repeats from a slightly higher spot they reach alone, a deep pile to crash into, and carrying a log back to the start between jumps.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a low step and a wide soft mat away from the line, a hand to hold on the way down if they ask, and time to watch others first.

sections.text: A sturdy low step, a curb, a pile of pillows or a folded comforter, a rope or a stick, and sidewalk chalk.

items: Jump off the bottom stair onto a pillow pile.
Lay a rope on the ground and jump over it, then make it wider.
Draw hopscotch squares with chalk and hop through them together.
Jump into a pile of raked leaves in the fall.
Jump and freeze, and see who can stay still the longest.

sections.text: Your child chooses where to jump from and when they are ready. They can set up the pillows and check the landing is clear. Your child can pile the pillows back on the couch and fold the comforter. Outside, they can sweep away chalk marks with a broom or leave them for next time.

items: I wonder how far that jump went.
How did your legs feel when you landed?
Where else could you jump from?

sections.text: Your child is learning to judge height and distance and to land with control. Jumping and landing gives the body strong pressure and movement, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Tell us about a favorite jumping spot near home, or send a photo of your child mid-jump with their face turned away.
Let your child climb to jumping spots by themselves instead of lifting them up, so they jump from heights their body is ready for. Keep landings soft and away from furniture edges.

cards.title: Climbing
cards.summary: Climbing trees, cargo nets, ladders, logs, ropes and crates, where children climb only as high as they can get by themselves.

items: Low, sturdy branches of a valley oak, checked by an educator, with woodchips spread beneath.
A cargo net hung low between two posts or on a frame, for climbing up, across and over.
A wooden ladder leaned at a gentle angle against a sturdy platform, tied at the top, for climbing up and down.
A big log or a stack of logs to climb onto, walk along and climb off.
A knotted rope hung from a sturdy beam or branch for climbing a little way up and coming back down.
Crates and spools set in steps of rising height to climb up and over.
A rope tied to a post on the small hill for pulling up the slope hand over hand.
The willow dome branches for low climbing and holding on.
A tree climbing morning where children look closely at the bark, the branches and the birds above.
Indoors in the class atelier, a climbing triangle or a low ladder between two sturdy frames over a mat.
Climbing up the slide or a ramp of planks and sliding back down.
For the West class, climbing onto low crates, a short log, a wide ramp and a low step frame, with lots of time on hands and knees.
For the North class, climbing a low net, a few steps of crates and the lowest oak branches.
For the South class, climbing higher in the tree where they get by themselves, a knotted rope, and building their own climbing set-up from crates and planks.
Binoculars or a small magnifier left at a lookout so a climber can stop and look.

sections.text: Both. Climbing is a child's own body and own judgment, so each child climbs alone and decides how high to go. Friends climb side by side, show each other a foothold and wait at the bottom. Building a climbing set-up from crates is shared work.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Children climb only as high as they can get by themselves. Adults never lift a child up into a tree or onto a structure, because a child who climbs alone knows how to come down. If a child is stuck, an educator stands close and talks them through each foot and hand. Trees for climbing are checked for dead branches, splits and poison oak, and branches are limbed up or marked so children know which ones we climb. Soft woodchips cover the fall zone and are raked back daily. Licensing playground safety rules ask that equipment is safe and in good repair, so we check ropes, nets, knots and ladder rungs every day and take anything worn out of use. Children climb in shoes. Wet bark and wet nets are slippery, and we look at them together after rain. Agree on how many children can be on a branch or net at once. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose where and how high to climb.
Check a branch or rung with a hand before trusting it with their weight.
Help an educator look for dead branches and splits.
Make agreements about how many climbers fit on a branch.
Show a friend a foothold or handhold they found.
Talk a friend down by naming where the next foot can go.
Build a climbing set-up from crates and planks.
Draw the tree or net and mark their favorite spot.

sections.text: Children carry the crates and planks they used for climbing set-ups back to their stacks and hang ropes on their hooks. An adult handles anything too heavy and takes a worn rope out of use. With every piece stored at the edge of the space, children close it as part of the climb.

Stand below and a little to the side within reach, hands relaxed at your sides and never on the child, and keep your face calm even when a child is higher than you like. Notice your own worry about heights and breathe it out. Narrate what you see, such as Your left foot is on the thick branch, and let the child find the next move.

items: I notice you checked that branch with your hand.
Where will you put your foot next?
I wonder what you can see from up there.
How did you get down?
Tell me about the way you climbed.
Begin with low wide climbs such as logs, crates and ramps, with plenty of repeats.
Add a low cargo net for climbing with hands and feet together.
Open the lowest branches of a valley oak after checking it with children.
Add a ladder at a gentle angle, tied at the top.
Add a knotted rope for climbing a little way with both hands.
Invite climbing down as well as up, and talk about how the body feels going down.
Invite children to build their own climbing set-ups with crates and planks.
Make a map or drawing of the climbing tree with its branches and favorite spots.
Add looking work at the top, such as binoculars to watch crows and hawks.
Invite climbing in a new way, such as across the net sideways or up with eyes on the next hold.
Talk at meeting time about how each climber decides how high to go.
Follow the climbing tree through the seasons, noticing leaves, acorns and birds.
Notice with children how their arms and hands feel after climbing.
Let a child who knows a climb teach a newer child where the footholds are.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stands below and a little to the side of climbers, with two adults on the large yards. Tree climbing and the knotted rope need an educator within reach, and a stuck child is talked down by an educator standing close.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer climbing ropes and nets that need pulling with the arms, many repeats, and carrying something up in a bag on the back.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a low wide log or a ramp near the ground, time to watch others climb, and an educator close by who talks them through each move.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A safe low tree, a playground climbing frame, a sturdy log, a low ladder, or a stack of firm cushions indoors.

items: Visit a park or tree with low branches and let your child climb as high as they get by themselves.
Climb on a fallen log on a walk and walk along it.
Build a climbing mountain of firm cushions on the floor.
Climb up the slide at the park when no one is coming down.
Climb down as well as up, and let your child find the way down.

sections.text: Your child decides where to climb and how high to go. They can check a branch with their hand before trusting it. Your child can stack the cushions back on the couch or carry a small ladder back with you. Coiling a rope and hanging it on a hook is good work too.

items: Where will you put your foot next?
I wonder what you can see from up there.
How did you find your way down?

sections.text: Your child is learning to plan movements, use both hands and both feet together and judge their own body. Climbing gives arms and legs strong work, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send a photo of a favorite climbing tree or log near home, with your child's face turned away, so we can talk about it at meeting time.

Please let your child climb only as high as they get by themselves and avoid lifting them up. Stay close and talk them through each move if they feel stuck. Check branches for dead wood and avoid poison oak.

cards.title: Balancing
cards.summary: Balancing on beams, logs, stepping stones, stumps and low slacklines, where children feel their center and find their own way across.

items: A long log laid flat and steady in the Log yard for walking along, forward, backward and sideways.
A row of stumps set as stepping stones, close together at first and further apart later.
A plank resting on two low supports, wide at first and narrower over weeks.
A slackline tied low between two trees in the Tire swing yard, a few inches off the ground over woodchips, with a hand line above.
Flat stones or carpet squares set as stepping spots across the grass or the indoor piazza floor.
A wobble board or a balance board in the class atelier on a mat.
A rope laid on the ground in curves to walk along heel to toe.
Walking along the edges of tires laid in a row.
Carrying something while balancing, such as a beanbag on the head, a basket in two hands or a cup of water.
Standing on one foot on a stump to look at something above.
Balancing on the edges of the garden beds only where educators and children agree they are steady and wide.
A seesaw made from a plank over a short round log, low to the ground, for two children to find the balance together.
Walking across the small hill sideways, where the ground tilts.
Bare feet on mats indoors, so feet feel the surface.
For the West class, wide planks flat on the ground, low stumps close together and a hand to hold when a child asks.
For the North class, a log or a plank on low supports and stepping stumps a short stride apart.
For the South class, the low slackline, narrower beams, stepping stumps of different heights and balancing while carrying.

sections.text: Both. Each child balances in their own body, slowly and at their own pace. Two children can cross a log from each ends and find a way to pass, or hold hands across a slackline. A plank seesaw needs two children who work out the balance together.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Logs and planks sit firm on the ground or on supports that do not roll. Stepping stumps are dug in or set on level ground and checked for rot. Slacklines for young children hang only a few inches above deep woodchips, with a hand line or a friend's hand, and an educator stays near whenever the slackline is up. Take the slackline down at the end of the day. Wet logs and boards are slippery, so we look and feel together after rain and fog. Leave clear soft ground on both sides of every beam so a child who steps off lands safely. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose a beam, log or line and a way to cross it.
Decide when to hold a hand and when to go alone.
Set stepping stumps closer or further apart.
Help tie and check the slackline with an educator.
Make an agreement about passing on a log.
Show a friend a way to cross, such as sideways or with arms out.
Carry something across and decide what to carry.
Draw the balancing path on a clipboard.

sections.text: Children carry planks and light stepping stumps back to their places and stack them flat. An educator unties and coils the slackline with children helping hold the line. Planks and stumps have marked spots at the edge of the yard, so the balance path is reset by children as play ends.

Stand at the side of the beam a step away, still and quiet, and offer a hand only when a child reaches for it. Keep your breathing slow and your face soft so the child borrows your calm. Narrate what you see, such as Your arms went out wide when the log wiggled.

items: I notice your arms help you balance.
Where will you put your foot next?
How did you get across without stepping off?
I wonder how it feels to go backward.
Tell me about the wobbly part.
Begin with wide flat logs and planks on the ground.
Add stepping stumps close together and let children cross many times.
Raise a plank onto low supports.
Narrow the beam over weeks while children judge their own readiness.
Invite walking backward, sideways and on tiptoe.
Invite carrying a beanbag, a basket or a cup of water across.
Add a balance board indoors on rainy days.
Add a low slackline with a hand line for older children.
Invite two children to cross from each end and find a way to pass.
Add a plank seesaw for two children to balance together.
Invite stopping in the middle on one foot to look up at the oaks.
Invite children to draw their balancing path and design a new one.
Notice with children which muscles feel tired after balancing.
End with a slow walk across a beam with eyes on a far tree, then rest.

setting.why: Low beams and stepping stumps are open with an educator nearby. An educator stays near the slackline the whole time it is up, and the plank seesaw for two needs an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add a balance board, a wobbly crossing over deep woodchips, carrying a heavy basket across, and crossing again and again.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a wide plank flat on the ground, a hand to hold when they reach for it, and time to watch first or cross on hands and knees.

sections.text: A curb, a long piece of tape or rope on the floor, a fallen log on a walk, a low wall, a few pillows or flat cushions.

items: Walk along a tape or rope line on the floor, forward, backward and sideways.
Step across pillows set on the floor as stepping spots.
Walk along a curb or a fallen log on a walk while holding a hand if your child wants one.
Stand on one foot together and see what helps you stay up.
Carry a small basket across the line without dropping anything.

sections.text: Your child chooses where to balance, how to cross and when they want a hand. Your child can roll up the rope, peel up the tape line and stack the flat cushions back in place. A basket for the rope keeps it ready for next time.

items: I notice your arms went out.
Where will you put your foot next?
How did you stay on?

sections.text: Your child is building balance and learning where their body is in space. Balancing gives the inner ear and the body steady movement input, which helps many children feel calm and steady.
Send a photo or a drawing of a favorite balancing spot from your walks, and your child can tell us about it.
Keep balancing spots low and on soft or flat ground. Wet logs and curbs can be slippery after rain.

cards.title: Swinging, spinning and hanging
cards.summary: The tire swing, rope swings, hammocks and low branches, offering strong movement input while children lead how fast and how long.

items: The tire swing in the Tire swing yard, for one child alone or two or three together, pushing and spinning.
A rope swing with a wooden seat hung by an adult from a sound branch, for swinging and twisting.
Lying belly down on a swing and walking feet back and forth.
Hanging from a low branch of a valley oak with hands and lifting the feet.
Hanging upside down by the knees from a low bar, only for children who climb into it by themselves.
A trapeze bar or a stout stick hung low for hanging and swinging feet.
Spinning slowly in place outside with arms out, then stopping to notice the world.
A spinning seat or a turntable board where children push with their feet.
Twisting the rope swing around and around and letting it unwind.
Pushing a friend on the tire swing, which gives the pusher heavy work too.
Swinging to a song from the Song book, slowing as the song slows.
Indoors in the class atelier, a fabric hammock or a lycra swing low over a mat where we have one.
For the West class, low swinging with feet near the ground, gentle pushing and a short hang from a low bar.
For the North class, the tire swing with a friend, short hangs from branches and slow spinning.
For the South class, longer hangs, crossing bars hand over hand, twisting swings and spinning they control.

sections.text: Both. A child alone on a swing can rock and think for a long time. The tire swing brings two or three children together to pump, push and spin. Pushing a friend is shared work with its own agreements.

Swinging feeds the vestibular system in the inner ear, which tells the body where it is in space and supports balance, posture, coordination, eye control for tracking and later reading, body awareness and attention. Slow, steady, back and forth swinging (linear movement) tends to calm and organize, and fast, spinning or start and stop movement (rotary movement) tends to alert. Too much can overwhelm, so we watch for a flushed face, pale skin, nausea or dizziness and let the child decide when to stop. Many children today get less of this movement than their bodies need, which can show up as trouble sitting still or seeking movement all day. We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Effects of spinning can show up later, so the child leads the speed and the stopping, and adults never spin a child who has not asked. We also watch for sweating, yawning or a sudden quiet and rest if we see them. Every swing has a clear fall zone of soft woodchips in front, behind and around it, and children agree to walk around the swing instead of in front of it. Educators check ropes, chains, knots, branches, hooks and the tire every morning, and take anything worn out of use. Tires have drainage holes so water does not collect and no steel showing. Children hang only from bars and branches they reach by themselves. Adults never lift a child up to a bar. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose how fast and how long to swing or spin.
Say when to stop, and stop a friend when asked.
Push a friend on the tire swing.
Make agreements about how many on the tire swing and where to wait.
Help check ropes and the tire with an educator.
Count, sing or take turns for swing time.
Notice and tell an adult how their body feels after spinning.
Show a friend how to pump with their legs.

sections.text: Children stop the tire swing gently, carry any loose balls or crates back to their stacks and rake woodchips back under the swing with child-size rakes. An adult handles ropes, chains and anything too heavy. Rakes and stacks sit beside the swing, so the yard is reset by children before they move on.

Stand at the side of the swing outside its arc, with your weight settled and your hands free, and watch the child's face more than the swing. Keep your voice regular and let the child say when to slow and stop. Narrate what you notice, such as You leaned back and the swing went higher.

items: I notice you closed your eyes on the swing.
How does your body feel when you stop spinning?
