I wonder what the sky looks like from upside down.
Tell me about how you made it go higher.
Start with gentle swinging where feet can touch the ground.
Invite pumping with the legs instead of being pushed.
Invite lying belly down on a swing and walking with the hands.
Add the tire swing with two or three children together and agreements about pushing.
Invite short hangs from a low branch or bar.
Invite slow spinning the child controls, then stopping to notice the body.
Add twisting and unwinding on a rope swing.
Invite hanging and swinging the feet, then crossing bars hand over hand.
Talk at meeting time about how swinging and spinning feel in the body.
Swing to a song that gets slower at the end.
Watch the leaves and clouds from the swing and draw what was seen.
Invite children to push friends and notice how their own arms feel.
End swinging with a calm body, such as lying on the grass or pressing hands together.

setting.why: An educator stands outside the arc of every swing and watches faces, with two adults on the Tire swing yard. Hanging upside down, twisting rope swings and the spinning seat need an educator close by, and adults never spin a child who has not asked.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer long swinging they pump themselves, pushing friends for heavy work, and hanging from a branch, and watch their body closely after spinning.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer slow rocking with feet on the ground, a swing with a low seat, a hand on the rope beside them, and a choice to only push a friend.

home.title: Swinging, spinning and hanging at Home

sections.text: A park swing, a sturdy low branch, a playground bar, an office chair that spins, or a blanket for gentle rocking.

items: Swing at the park and let your child pump their own legs.
Hang from a low bar or branch and swing the feet.
Spin slowly in the yard with arms out and then lie on the grass to watch the sky move.
Rock your child gently in a blanket held by two adults low to the floor.
Let your child push you or a sibling on a swing.

sections.text: Your child decides how fast, how long and when to stop. They can say stop and know you will listen. Your child can slow the swing to a stop and help put away anything you brought, such as a blanket or a water bottle. At home, they can roll a chair back to the desk when spinning is done.

items: How does your body feel when you stop?
I wonder what the sky looks like upside down.
Tell me how you made it go higher.

sections.text: Swinging feeds the balance sense in the inner ear (the vestibular system), which helps your child know where their body is, sit and stand steady, move with coordination, follow things with their eyes and later read, and pay attention. Slow, steady, back and forth swinging tends to calm the body, and fast spinning or stop and start swinging tends to wake it up. Too much can make a child dizzy or queasy, so watch for a flushed or pale face and let your child decide when to stop. Many children today get less of this movement than their bodies need, and swinging at home helps. Hanging builds grip and arm strength too.
Tell us what kind of swinging or spinning your child loves at home, so we can offer it at school.
Let your child lead the speed and never spin a child who has not asked. Stop if your child looks pale, sweaty or quiet. Let them reach bars by themselves.

cards.title: Hammocks
cards.summary: Hammocks in the yards for swinging, resting, being alone, two children bumping together and wrapping in, hung low and checked every day.

items: A canvas hammock clipped low to the cattle panel arch, with soft woodchips below, ready for swinging or resting.
A hammock with a basket of books beside it for reading alone in the shade.
Lying in a hammock looking up through the arch at clouds, birds and the oak leaves.
A hammock as a quiet spot a child can choose to be alone, with an agreement that friends ask first.
Two children in one hammock together, with agreements about bumping and swinging.
Pushing a friend in the hammock with two hands, slow and steady.
Wrapping in the hammock fabric with the sides pulled around, for a snug cocoon.
Swinging side to side and then front to back, noticing how each feels.
A hammock with a small blanket on a cool foggy morning.
Binoculars or a clipboard in a hammock for watching crows, hawks and finches above.
Lying belly down in a hammock and reaching down to touch the woodchips.
Rocking to a quiet song from the Song book.
Indoors in the class atelier, a low fabric hammock or a hammock chair over a thick mat where we have one.
For the West class, a hammock hung very low with gentle rocking and an educator close by.
For the North class, a low hammock for one child or two friends with simple agreements.
For the South class, hammocks children help clip on and check, with agreements they write and post on the arch.
Slow back and forth swinging after a busy morning, and faster swinging a child leads when their body asks for more.

sections.text: Both. A hammock is one of the few places on our yards a child can be alone in a soft, held space, and we protect that. Two children together can swing and bump with agreements. A friend pushing is shared work that gives the pusher heavy work too.

Our hammocks hang from an arch made of a 16 foot cattle panel bent into a curve and held by a T-post at each corner. The hammocks are canvas and clip to the arch with load-rated carabiners, the kind marked with a weight rating. We hang them low, with the lowest point of the canvas about knee height of a standing child, so children climb in and out by themselves and a tumble out lands on soft woodchips. Every morning before children arrive an educator checks the panel for bent or broken welds and sharp wire ends, the T-posts for leaning or loosening, the carabiners for closed gates and wear, and the canvas for tears, thin spots and frayed seams, and takes any hammock with a worn part out of use. Fall zones around and under the arch are kept clear and soft. Swinging feeds the vestibular system in the inner ear, which tells the body where it is in space and supports balance, posture, coordination, eye control for tracking and later reading, body awareness and attention. Slow, steady, back and forth swinging (linear movement) tends to calm and organize, and fast, spinning or start and stop movement (rotary movement) tends to alert. Too much can overwhelm, so we watch for a flushed face, pale skin, nausea or dizziness and let the child decide when to stop. Many children today get less of this movement than their bodies need, which can show up as trouble sitting still or seeking movement all day. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Two children together agree on how much bumping, and either one can say stop and the swinging stops at once. No standing in hammocks, no ropes around necks, and hammock fabric never covers a face. We protect a child's alone time. A child in a hammock may say they want to be alone, and friends ask before joining. Educators watch from nearby instead of pulling the child back into play. Hammocks come down or get tied up out of reach when no adult is outside and after rain until dry. Two adults are always on the large yards.

items: Choose to rest, swing, read or be alone.
Say they want to be alone, or invite a friend in.
Make agreements with a friend about bumping, and use the stop word.
Push a friend slowly and stop when asked.
Help an educator check the carabiners, the canvas and the T-posts.
Wrap in the canvas and decide how snug it feels.
Bring a book or binoculars and put them back after.
Write or draw the hammock agreements to post nearby.

sections.text: Children take out any books or binoculars they brought and return them to their basket, then shake woodchips out of the canvas and smooth it flat. An adult ties hammocks up out of reach or unclips them when no adult is outside or after rain, with children helping fold the canvas. The book basket hangs near the arch so children finish the close themselves.

Stay nearby and settled, within sight, without hovering over the hammock. Let your face and body say this rest is welcome. When a child asks to be alone, protect it with a quiet word to friends who come close. When two children bump together, watch their faces and step closer only if one says stop.

items: I notice you are very still in there.
I wonder what you can see above you.
How does it feel when the hammock is wrapped around you?
Tell me about the agreement you and your friend made.
Begin with one low hammock for one child at a time and lots of time to rest.
Add books and binoculars nearby.
Talk at meeting time about using a hammock to be alone and how friends ask first.
Invite gentle swinging side to side and front to back.
Invite pushing a friend slowly with two hands.
Make agreements with children for two in a hammock, with a stop word everyone honors.
Invite wrapping in the fabric for snug pressure.
Invite watching the sky and drawing what was seen.
Invite children to help check the arch, carabiners and canvas each morning.
Invite children to notice which kind of swinging makes their body feel calm and which makes it feel awake.
Add a second hammock in another yard and notice how each is used.
Hang a hammock indoors over a mat on rainy days where we have a safe place.
Invite children to write the hammock agreements and post them near the trees.
Notice the oaks and sky around the arch through the seasons.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator stays where they can see every hammock. Two children together need agreements and an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer two in a hammock with bumping agreements, pushing a friend for heavy work, and longer front to back swinging they lead.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a still hammock alone in a quiet corner of the yard, a light blanket, slow rocking they control with one foot on the ground, and friends asked to wait.

sections.text: You can build the same arch we use at school. You need one 16 foot cattle panel and four T-posts from a farm supply store, a T-post driver, fence clips or heavy wire, a canvas hammock or a two-person camping hammock, and load-rated carabiners. A simpler way is a two-person camping hammock, which any outdoor store sells, hung low between two strong trees with tree straps.

items: Build the arch by driving two T-posts on each side, bending the cattle panel into a curve between them and clipping it firmly to all four posts.

Clip a canvas hammock to the top of the arch with load-rated carabiners so it hangs low, about knee height on your child, or hang a two-person camping hammock low between two strong trees with wide straps.
Lie together in the hammock and watch the leaves and clouds, or read a book.
Wrap your child snugly in the hammock and rock slowly, back and forth.
Let your child push you or a sibling gently and stop when asked.
Let your child have quiet alone time in the hammock.

sections.text: Your child chooses when to rest, swing or be alone, and can say stop. They can help check the knots. Your child can shake out the hammock, carry books back inside and help you fold it if it comes down. A basket by the door for outdoor books keeps things together.

items: I wonder what you can see from there.
How does it feel when it is wrapped around you?
Tell me when you want to swing or rest.

sections.text: Your child is learning to notice what their body needs and to rest. Swinging feeds the balance sense in the inner ear (the vestibular system), which helps your child know where their body is, sit and stand steady, move with coordination, follow things with their eyes and later read, and pay attention. Slow, steady, back and forth swinging tends to calm the body, and fast spinning or stop and start swinging tends to wake it up. Too much can make a child dizzy or queasy, so watch for a flushed or pale face and let your child decide when to stop. Many children today get less of this movement than their bodies need, and swinging at home helps. Being wrapped gives snug pressure, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Tell us if a hammock is a favorite resting spot at home, so we can offer it when your child needs quiet. A photo of your home arch helps other families build one too.

Hang the hammock low over soft ground such as grass, woodchips or mulch, so your child climbs in and out alone. Keep an adult nearby, keep cords, straps and clothing ties away from necks, and never let fabric cover a face. Check the panel, posts, carabiners and fabric before each use, and use only carabiners marked with a load rating. One example of a two-person camping hammock is at wiseowloutfitters.com/products/two-person-hammock.

cards.title: Crawling, tunnels and squeezing through
cards.summary: Crawling, tunnels and tight spaces that give the whole body pressure and ask it to change shape.

items: A fabric tunnel laid across the grass, straight at first and then curved.
A line of crates turned on their sides to crawl through, end to end.
Tires stood upright and half buried in the sand or woodchips for crawling through.
A big barrel or a large cardboard box open at both ends.
Crawling under a table draped with cloth in the class atelier.
Crawling under a rope or a branch tied low between two stumps.
Squeezing through the gaps between logs in the Log yard.
Wriggling on the belly across the grass, pulling with the arms.
Walking on hands and feet with hips high, and on hands and feet with the belly up, across the yard.
Crawling through the willow dome openings in the garden.
Squeezing between two firm cushions or mats on the floor, with the child choosing how snug.
A stretchy fabric tube or body sock to push against from the inside, on a mat indoors.
Crawling under a parachute held low by friends.
Moving the way our rabbits hop or the goats climb, after watching them in the animal yards.
For the West class, short wide tunnels, crawling across mats and a box to climb in and out of.
For the North class, longer tunnels with a turn, crawling under ropes and squeezing through crates.
For the South class, tunnels children design and build from crates, cloth and tires, and dark tunnels with a flashlight.

sections.text: Both. A tunnel is a private place for one body at a time, and many children like the quiet inside. Building tunnels is shared work, and friends wait at each end to greet the crawler. Crawling side by side across the grass brings children together.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Look inside tunnels, tires, barrels and crates before children crawl through, since spiders and wasps like dark shelters. Tunnels are open at both ends so a child can always see light and leave. Keep tunnels short enough that an educator can see and reach in at each end. Children choose how snug a squeeze is, and pressure games such as squeezing between mats happen only when the child asks and stop the moment they say stop. Faces stay uncovered. Wash fabric tunnels and covers often. Shoes stay on outside, and we brush woodchips off knees together after.

items: Build tunnels from crates, cloth and tires.
Check inside a tunnel for spiders with an educator and a flashlight.
Choose how snug a squeeze feels and say when to stop.
Wait at the end to greet a friend coming through.
Make agreements such as one at a time in the tunnel.
Show a younger child a way through.
Shake out and fold the fabric tunnel at the end of the day.

sections.text: Children carry crates and tires back to their stacks, take down the cloth, shake it out and fold it into its basket. Fabric that needs a wash goes in the wash bag. An adult moves barrels and anything too heavy, and children brush woodchips off knees and mats on the way out.

Get down at the tunnel's end at the child's level, with a calm face where the child can see it as they come out. Stay put and let the quiet inside the tunnel be theirs. Narrate the body, such as You pulled with your elbows to get through.

items: I notice you went through on your belly this time.
How did it feel inside the tunnel?
I wonder where the tunnel could go next.
Tell me about the tight part.
Begin with a short wide tunnel and lots of time to go in and out.
Add crawling across mats and grass in many ways.
Lengthen the tunnel and add a turn.
Invite children to build tunnels from crates, tires and cloth.
Add crawling under low ropes and branches.
Add squeezing through narrow gaps between logs.
Invite walking on hands and feet in different ways after watching our animals move.
Add a dark tunnel with a flashlight for older children.
Add squeezing games with mats and cushions where the child chooses the pressure.
Bring a tunnel into an obstacle course.
Invite children to draw a map of the tunnels.
Use tunnels as a quiet place after big movement.
Notice with children how arms, shoulders and knees feel after crawling.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Tunnels stay short enough that an educator nearby can see and reach in at each end. Squeezing games and the body sock need an adult beside the child, and dark tunnels with a flashlight are for older children with an educator at the opening.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer belly crawling across the grass, a snug squeeze between firm mats they ask for, and pushing a heavy ball through the tunnel.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a short wide tunnel with light at both ends, time to look in first, and an educator's face waiting at the other end.

home.title: Crawling, tunnels and squeezing through at Home

sections.text: Chairs and a blanket, a big cardboard box, couch cushions, a laundry basket, or a play tunnel.

items: Build a tunnel from chairs and a blanket and crawl through.
Open both ends of a big box for a tunnel.
Crawl across the floor on bellies, pulling with arms.
Squeeze between couch cushions while your child chooses how snug.
Move the way animals you have watched move.

sections.text: Your child can build the tunnel, decide how snug a squeeze feels and say stop. Your child can take the blanket off the chairs, shake it out and fold it, then push the chairs back to the table. Flattening a big box for next time is good work too.

items: How did it feel inside?
I wonder where the tunnel could go.
Tell me about the tight part.

sections.text: Your child is learning to move their body in many shapes. Crawling and squeezing give strong pressure, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in large clean cardboard boxes for tunnels, and this counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep both ends of a tunnel open and never cover a face. Stop squeezing games when your child says stop.

cards.title: Pushing, pulling and hauling
cards.summary: Wagons, wheelbarrows, sleds of logs, ropes and pulleys, where children move real loads with their whole bodies.

items: Wagons and wheelbarrows beside the woodchip piles, with shovels, for moving woodchips to paths and landing zones.
A sled or a sheet of heavy tarp with a rope, for dragging logs and stumps across the Log yard.
A thick rope for tug of war on the grass, with a line drawn in the middle and soft ground behind each team.
A pulley hung from a sturdy beam or branch with a bucket, for hauling woodchips, stones or water up and lowering them down.
Pushing a big ball or a tire up the small hill and letting it roll down.
Pulling a friend in a wagon along the path, and then trading.
Hauling buckets of water from the spigot to the garden beds and the mud kitchen.
Rolling a heavy log with two or three friends to a new place.
Raking leaves into big piles and pulling the tarp of leaves to the compost.
Pushing a loaded cart of crates or blocks across the indoor piazza.
A rope tied to a post for pulling the body up the slope hand over hand.
Pushing against a wall or a tree trunk with both hands as hard as possible, then letting go.
Carrying hay or feed with an educator in the animal yards.
For the West class, small wagons and buckets with light loads, pushing a laundry basket of blocks and pulling a toy on a rope.
For the North class, wheelbarrows with woodchips, a short tug of war and the pulley with a small bucket.
For the South class, sleds of logs, real hauling jobs across the site, planning a route and teams that share a heavy load.

sections.text: Both. Heavy loads draw children together to lift, pull and steer. A child alone with a wheelbarrow can fill and dump again and again, deep in their own rhythm. Tug of war is a group effort with agreements everyone keeps.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Check wagon wheels, wheelbarrow handles and tires, and ropes for fraying every day. Children choose loads they can move, and we talk about lifting with bent knees and holding a load close to the body. For tug of war, ropes have no loops or knots around hands or bodies, everyone holds with open hands along the rope, players stand on soft grass or woodchips, and an agreed word stops the pull for everyone at once. Pulleys hang from beams or branches an educator has checked, and no one stands under a raised bucket. Keep wheelbarrow paths clear and agree on which way they go.

items: Choose a load and decide how much to carry.
Fill, push, steer and dump the wheelbarrow.
Plan a route with friends and clear the path.
Make the tug of war agreements and use the stop word.
Work the pulley and call out before lowering a bucket.
Check the wagon wheels and the ropes with an educator.
Put tools, wagons and ropes back where they live.
Notice and tell how their arms and legs feel after the work.

sections.text: Children empty the last load, park wagons and wheelbarrows in their spots and hang ropes and pulley buckets on their hooks. An adult handles any load too heavy to move and checks wheels and ropes as they come in. Parking spots are marked with photos so children close the work themselves.

Work beside the children with your own hands on a shovel or rope, at their pace, and let your face show you enjoy the effort. Hold back from taking the heavy end. Narrate the work, such as You leaned back and the log moved.

items: I notice you leaned your whole body into it.
How did you get the log to move?
I wonder how many buckets the path needs.
Tell me about how your arms feel.
Begin with small wagons and buckets with light loads.
Add wheelbarrows and the woodchip piles with real places that need woodchips.
Add dragging sleds and tarps of logs and leaves.
Add a pulley with a bucket.
Invite tug of war with agreements children make together.
Invite teams to move one heavy log together.
Add hauling water to the garden and the mud kitchen.
Invite children to plan and draw a route for a hauling job.
Invite counting loads, such as how many wheelbarrows it took to fill a landing zone.
Add pushing heavy things up the small hill.
Connect hauling to real care of the site, such as mulching beds and carrying hay to the goats.
Notice with children how the body feels after hauling and before a quiet time.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Hauling is open with an educator nearby and paths agreed. Tug of war needs an adult at the rope who can call the stop word, pulleys need an adult watching that no one stands under the bucket, and hay in the animal yards is carried with an educator.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the heaviest safe load, a sled of logs to drag across the yard and back, and a real job such as filling a whole landing zone.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small wagon or a single bucket, a quiet path away from busy hauling, and the choice to work beside an educator.

home.title: Pushing, pulling and hauling at Home

sections.text: A wagon, a laundry basket, a rope, a bucket, a toy box on a towel, or a wheelbarrow if you have one.

items: Pull siblings or toys in a wagon around the yard.
Push a laundry basket full of books or laundry across the room.
Haul a bucket of water to the plants.
Play tug of war with a rope on soft grass, with a stop word.
Help move mulch or soil in the garden.

sections.text: Your child can choose the load, push and pull, and decide how much is enough. Real jobs give real pride. Your child can pull the wagon or carry the laundry basket back to its spot and coil the rope. Finishing with one last real load, such as carrying shoes to the closet, makes a good end.

items: How did you get it to move?
I wonder how many loads it will take.
Tell me how your arms feel.

sections.text: Your child is building strength and learning to plan and steer. Pushing and pulling give the body heavy work, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in an old wagon, a sled or a rope in good shape, and this counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep loads small enough to manage. Never wrap rope around hands or bodies, and stop tug of war when anyone says stop.

cards.title: Rough and tumble play
cards.summary: Wrestling, chasing and play fighting with agreements children make, where both players say yes, the stop word is honored at once and an adult stays near.

items: A wrestling place on thick mats in the indoor piazza or on soft grass in the Log yard, marked with a rope circle.
Wrestling agreements made with children at meeting time and posted with photographs at their eye level.
Both players say yes before wrestling starts, and either player can say no.
A clear stop word chosen with children that everyone honors at once.
Open hands only, with pushing and holding and no hitting.
No heads and no necks, with hands on shoulders, arms and backs.
Wrestling on knees first, which keeps bodies low and falls short.
Back to back pushing, where two children sit back to back and push.
Hand to hand pushing, standing on a line, palms together.
Chasing games on the grass with a safe base under a valley oak.
Superhero and animal chases where children decide who chases and who runs, and trade.
A check in after each round, with a thumbs up or a word from each player.
Pillow pushing on the mats, where children push with big pillows held in two hands.
For the West class, rolling on mats beside a friend, gentle pushing and chasing in a small space with an educator close.
For the North class, back to back pushing and knee wrestling with simple agreements.
For the South class, agreements children write and change, a stop word they choose and wrestling on knees and standing.

sections.text: Together. Rough and tumble play needs a partner who says yes, and it builds trust when players read each other's faces and bodies. A child may watch from the edge before joining, and that watching is welcome.

Rough and tumble play is one of Ellen Sandseter's six kinds of risky play, and Frances Carlson calls it big body play. Children learn strength, self-control and how to read a friend. Play fighting looks different from real fighting. Players smile and laugh, take turns being on top or being chased, and come back for more. If faces tighten, a child stops laughing or one child is always on the bottom, we pause and check in. Our wrestling agreements are made with children and can change when children decide together. Both players say yes. A clear stop word is honored at once by everyone. Open hands only. No heads or necks. Wrestling happens on soft ground or mats in a marked space. An adult stays nearby. Players check in with each other after each round. Clear the space of furniture, logs and tools. Children take off anything hard or sharp such as clips. Two adults are always on the large yards, and an educator stays within a few steps of the wrestling place.

items: Make the wrestling agreements together and change them when needed.
Choose the stop word and use it.
Ask a friend if they want to wrestle and accept a no.
Stop at once when anyone says the stop word.
Check in with a partner after each round.
Set out the mats and the rope circle, and put them away.
Remind friends of the agreements.
Tell an adult when a game stops feeling like play.

sections.text: Children drag the mats to their stack and coil the rope circle into its basket. Partners check in with each other one last time as they put things away. The mats and rope live at the edge of the wrestling place, and an adult helps only with a mat too heavy to lift.

Stay close to the mats, on your knees or sitting, with a relaxed body and a soft face that shows this play is welcome. Watch faces more than bodies. When you step in, use a regular voice and describe what you see, such as I see his face is not smiling, and ask the players to check in.

items: I notice you both stopped right away when you heard the stop word.
How did you know your friend still wanted to play?
I wonder what agreement might help this game.
Tell me about how your body feels after wrestling.
Begin by talking about big body play at meeting time and making agreements together.
Offer back to back pushing and hand to hand pushing first.
Add a marked wrestling place on mats or soft grass.
Add wrestling on knees with the agreements posted.
Practice the stop word in many games until everyone stops at once.
Practice checking in after each round.
Add chasing games with a safe base and trading roles.
Invite children to change an agreement when a game shows the need.
Invite children to draw or photograph the agreements for the wall.
Talk with families about why we welcome this play and how we keep it safe.
Follow superhero and power play into stories and building.
End rough and tumble time with a calm body practice.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: The wrestling place holds one pair at a time, with an educator within a few steps watching faces. Chasing games on the grass are open with two adults on the large yards.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer back to back pushing, pillow pushing and knee wrestling with a partner who also wants big pressure, then heavy work after.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer watching from the edge, hand to hand pushing with an adult, and the right to say no to any invitation.

home.title: Rough and tumble play at Home

sections.text: A soft rug, a mattress on the floor, couch cushions or soft grass, and room to move.

items: Agree on a stop word together and practice it.
Sit back to back and push.
Wrestle on knees on a soft rug with open hands and no heads or necks.
Play a chasing game with a safe spot and trade who chases.
Check in with each other after each round.

sections.text: Your child can make the agreements, say yes or no, choose the stop word and stop right away when anyone says it. Your child can stack the couch cushions back and straighten the rug. Saying thank you to their play partner is a nice way to end.

items: How did you know I still wanted to play?
I wonder what rule would help.
Tell me how your body feels.

sections.text: Your child is learning strength, self-control and how to read another person. Big pushing and pulling play gives the body strong pressure, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Tell us the stop word your family uses at home so we can talk about it at school.
Play on soft ground away from furniture. Stop at once when anyone says the stop word, and check that everyone is still smiling.

cards.title: Rolling and tumbling
cards.summary: Rolling down the small hill, in barrels and on mats, and rolling logs and tires, for strong movement through the whole body.

items: Log rolls down the small hill on grass, arms overhead or by the sides.
A thick mat on a gentle wedge or slope in the indoor piazza for rolling down.
Forward rolls on mats for children who tuck their chin and choose to try.
Rolling inside a big barrel on the grass with a friend pushing slowly.
Rolling logs and stumps across the Log yard with hands and feet.
Rolling tires down the small hill and chasing them.
Rolling a big ball up the slope and letting it go.
Rolling across the grass side to side and then lying still to feel the ground.
Rolling in the leaves after they have been raked into a pile.
Rocking on the back holding the knees.
Rolling a friend slowly in a blanket on the mat, only when they ask, with the face always outside the blanket.
Rolling a big log across the yard and then walking along it.
Rolling down the slope holding a ball against the belly.
For the West class, rolling across a mat on the floor, rocking and rolling down a very gentle slope.
For the North class, log rolls down the hill, barrel rolling and rolling tires.
For the South class, forward rolls on mats, rolling in pairs and designing rolling races down the hill.

sections.text: Both. Rolling down the hill is one body at a time, and friends gather at the bottom laughing. Rolling a heavy log or barrel takes a group. A child alone on a mat can roll and rock for a long time.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Walk the small hill with children before rolling to look for rocks, sticks, ant nests and holes, and keep the bottom clear. One roller at a time, and the next waits until the bottom is clear. Rolling is strong input to the inner ear, so we let children stop when they choose and rest if they feel dizzy. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Forward rolls happen only on thick mats with the chin tucked, and adults never push a child over. Barrels are rolled slowly on flat grass. Check tires for exposed steel and drain water out.

items: Walk the hill to check for rocks and holes.
Choose how to roll and how fast.
Wait at the top until the bottom is clear.
Push a friend slowly in the barrel and stop when asked.
Roll logs and tires to new places with friends.
Set out and fold the mats.
Tell how their body feels after rolling.
Say when they want to stop and rest.

sections.text: Children fold the mats and drag them to their stack, and they roll tires and the barrel back to their places with friends. An adult drains water from tires and handles anything too heavy. A last walk of the hill to pick up anything left behind closes the space.

Sit at the bottom of the hill on the grass, low and easy, and greet each roller with a calm face. Be comfortable with grass stains and leaves in hair. Name what you see, such as You kept your arms close and rolled straight.

items: I notice the world kept turning after you stopped.
How did you roll so straight?
I wonder what the hill feels like under you.
Tell me about the dizzy feeling.
Begin with rocking and rolling across a flat mat.
Add rolling down a gentle slope.
Add log rolls down the small hill.
Add rolling logs, tires and balls.
Add the barrel on flat grass.
Invite forward rolls on mats with a tucked chin.
Invite rolling in pairs side by side.
Invite children to design rolling races and starting lines.
Notice with children how rolling feels in the body and when they want to stop.
Roll in the leaves through the fall.
Add rolling with a ball held against the belly.
Invite children to try the same roll slow and fast and tell how each feels.
End rolling with lying still on the grass and watching the sky.

setting.why: Rolling is open with an educator at the bottom of the hill and one roller at a time. Forward rolls on mats, barrel rolling and a blanket roll a child asks for need an adult beside the child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer many log rolls down the hill, rolling heavy logs, and the barrel, while watching their body closely for dizziness.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer rocking on the back or a slow roll across a flat mat, with the choice to stop and watch others first.

sections.text: A grassy slope, a soft rug or mattress, a big ball, or a pile of raked leaves.

items: Roll down a grassy hill at the park.
Roll across a soft rug and then lie still.
Rock on your backs holding your knees.
Roll a big ball up a slope and let it go.
Roll in a pile of raked leaves.

sections.text: Your child chooses how to roll and when to stop. Your child can fold the blanket, carry the ball inside and rake the leaf pile back together. A quick look around for anything left on the grass ends the play.

items: I notice the world kept spinning after you stopped.
How did you roll so straight?
Tell me about the dizzy feeling.

sections.text: Your child is building balance and body awareness. Rolling gives the inner ear and body strong movement, which helps many children feel alert and then calm.
Tell us about a good rolling hill near home.
Check slopes for rocks and holes first. Let your child stop when dizzy, and never push a child over in a roll.

cards.title: Speed and running
cards.summary: Running, races, slopes and bikes on the dirt, where children feel speed and learn to start, stop and turn.

items: Open grass for running as fast as possible, from the oak to the fence and back.
Running down the small hill and up again.
Races children design, with a starting line and an ending line drawn with chalk or a stick.
Bikes on the dirt, with agreements about direction.
Running and stopping to a drum, a bell or a song.
Chasing games with a safe base.
Running with streamers or scarves in the wind.
Running backwards slowly on soft grass.
Chasing a rolling tire or ball down the slope.
Running in rain boots through puddles after rain.
A relay where children carry a stick or a beanbag and hand it to a friend.
Pulling a friend in a wagon fast across flat grass, then trading.
Running in zigzags around stumps and tires, then in a straight line, and noticing the difference.
A sand timer or a song as a way to see how long a run takes, with children deciding what to do with it.
Running to the willow dome and back, or to a named tree, as a place to turn around.
For the West class, running in a small open space and stopping at a sound.
For the North class, races down the slope and bikes on the dirt.
For the South class, races with rules they write, bikes on the dirt and running courses they design.

sections.text: Both. Running fast alone gives a child the feel of their own speed. Races and chases bring children together with rules they agree on. Bikes share the dirt and need agreements.

We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. High speed is one of Ellen Sandseter's six kinds of risky play. Running paths and the dirt where bikes ride are kept clear of logs, tools and loose parts, and we agree on which way bikes go. Bikes stay on the dirt. Look at the ground together after rain, since wet grass and mud are slippery. Children wear closed shoes. On hot dry late summer days, run in the morning shade and drink water often. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Design races with starting and ending lines.
Make agreements about bike direction and safe bases.
Choose how fast to go and when to stop.
Clear the path before running.
Hand off a stick in a relay.
Notice and tell how fast their heart is beating.
Park bikes where they live and check the wheels.
Invite a friend who is watching to join in.

sections.text: Children park bikes in their marked spots and check the wheels, then carry cones, sticks and start lines back to their basket. A few children sweep chalk lines or leave them for tomorrow. Parking spots and the basket sit at the edge of the dirt path, so the close is quick and done by the riders.

Stand at the edge of the running space where you can see the whole path, relaxed and smiling, and let the noise be. Notice any worry about collisions and keep it out of your face. Name what you see, such as You leaned forward and your legs went faster.

items: I notice your heart is beating fast.
How did you stop so quickly?
I wonder how it feels going down the hill.
Tell me about the race you made.
Begin with free running on open grass.
Add running and stopping to a sound.
Add running down and up the small hill.
Add races children design with starting lines.
Add bikes on the dirt with agreements about direction.
Add relays where children hand off a stick.
Invite running backwards and sideways slowly.
Invite children to feel their heartbeat before and after running.
Invite children to draw a map of the running paths.
Run in different weather and notice what changes.
Add zigzag running around stumps for turning at speed.
Invite children to choose a turning tree and a route and draw it.
Add bike routes on the dirt with signs children make.
End running with a slow walk and a drink of water.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Running on open grass is open to everyone, with two adults on the large yards. Bikes on the dirt and fast wagon pulling need an educator watching the paths and the agreed direction.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running up the hill many times, pulling a wagon at speed on grass, and long chases with a safe base.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer running alone in a quiet part of the yard, a slow walk beside an educator, or watching first.

sections.text: Open grass, a park, chalk, a bike for a dirt path, and closed shoes.

items: Run as fast as you can across a park and back.
Draw a starting line with chalk and make a race together.
Run down a grassy hill.
Play a chasing game with a safe spot.
Feel your heartbeat before and after running.

sections.text: Your child can make the race rules, choose how fast to go and decide when to stop. Your child can park the bike in its spot and bring the chalk back inside. Hanging the helmet on a low hook keeps it ready for next time.

items: I notice your heart is beating fast.
How did you stop so quickly?
Tell me about the race you made.

sections.text: Your child is learning to start, stop, turn and feel speed. Running gives the body big movement, which helps many children feel alert and then ready to rest.
Tell us about a race your child made up at home.
Run in open spaces away from streets and cars. Wear closed shoes and drink water on hot days.

cards.title: Heights and lookouts
cards.summary: High places children reach by themselves, from stumps and crates to low branches and the top of the small hill, for looking out and feeling height.

items: The top of the small hill as a lookout, with binoculars for watching hawks, crows and herons.
A tall stump or crate tower that children climb onto by themselves.
A low platform of planks and crates built with children.
The low branches of a valley oak as a lookout.
A sturdy platform at the top of a climbing structure.
A clipboard at a lookout for drawing what can be seen from up high.
A lookout on the hill facing the creek trail or the orchard.
Standing on a stump to look over the garden beds.
Looking down at the yard from high and finding friends.
A lookout spot with a basket holding a spyglass made from a cardboard tube, a compass and a small field guide to local birds.
Lying on the ground under the lookout and looking up at the child above, then trading places.
Calling down and passing messages or a bucket on a rope from a lookout to friends below.
Watching fog lift from the hilltop on a gray morning and the sky change through the day.
Indoors in the class atelier, a sturdy loft or a step platform with a rail, a window view and a mat below.
For the West class, low lookouts on a wide crate or the top of a gentle slope.
For the North class, stumps, the hill and low branches.
For the South class, higher lookouts they reach by themselves and lookout maps they draw.

sections.text: Both. A lookout can hold one child alone watching the sky, or a few friends looking out together and pointing. Building a lookout is shared work.

Great heights is one of Ellen Sandseter's six kinds of risky play, and children feel the scary and fun mix of being high. We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Children climb only as high as they can get by themselves, and adults never lift a child up. A child who climbs up alone can come down, and an educator stays close to talk them through. Every high place has soft ground below. Platforms are wide and steady and checked each day. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Choose a lookout and how high to go.
Build a lookout with friends.
Bring binoculars and a clipboard up.
Make agreements about how many fit on a lookout.
Draw what they see from high up.
Talk a friend down by naming where to step.
Check the platform and the ground below with an educator.
Decide when to come down and find their own way.

sections.text: Children carry binoculars and clipboards down and return them to their basket, then carry crates and light planks from a built lookout back to their stacks. An adult handles anything too heavy. The basket waits at the foot of the lookout so children put things away as they come down.

Stand below a lookout within reach, hands still, and look out where the child is looking. Notice your own worry about heights and breathe slowly. Name what you see, such as You found a way up with your knee first.

items: I wonder what you can see from up there.
Where will you put your foot next?
How did you get up?
Tell me about what looks different from high up.
Begin with low wide lookouts.
Add binoculars and clipboards at lookouts.
Build a lookout with children from crates and planks.
Open low branches of a valley oak as a lookout.
Invite drawing what can be seen from high up.
Invite children to make a map of all the lookouts.
Watch birds from a lookout through the seasons.
Talk at meeting time about the scary and fun feeling of being high.
Add a bucket on a rope for sending things up and down from a lookout.
Invite children to photograph the yard from a lookout and from the ground and compare them.
Invite children to find the highest place they can get to by themselves and tell how they decided.
Let older children help younger children find a low lookout and a way up.
End with lying low on the grass and looking up.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Children reach lookouts by themselves with an educator below within reach. Higher lookouts, the indoor loft and a bucket on a rope need an educator close by, and no one stands under a raised bucket.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer climbing up to a lookout many times, carrying binoculars up in a bag, and building a new lookout with crates.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a low lookout on a wide crate or the hilltop, time to watch others, and an adult close by.

sections.text: A hill, a sturdy low wall, a park platform, binoculars and a notebook.

items: Walk up a hill and look out together.
Climb onto a park platform your child reaches alone.
Bring binoculars to look for birds.
Draw what you see from up high.

sections.text: Your child chooses how high to go and finds their own way up and down. Your child can carry the binoculars and notebook home in their own bag and hang it on a hook. A small basket just for outdoor looking tools makes the next trip easy.

items: I wonder what you can see.
Where will you put your foot next?
Tell me what looks different from up here.

sections.text: Your child is learning to judge height and space. Being up high gives the body balance work, which helps many children feel steady and brave.
Send a photo of the view from a favorite high place with no faces shown.

cards.title: Risky play set-ups
cards.summary: Ellen Sandseter's six kinds of risky play, great heights, high speed, real tools, dangerous elements, rough and tumble and going out of sight, and how we set each up as safely as necessary.

items: Great heights. Stumps, crates, low branches and lookouts children reach by themselves, with soft woodchips below.
High speed. Running down the small hill, bikes on the dirt, the tire swing and rolling down the slope.
Real tools. A woodworking bench with real hammers, nails, saws and clamps, offered with one adult and a small group and clear agreements.
Real tools outside. Hammering golf tees and then nails into a stump, sawing branches held in a clamp, and whittling with a peeler for older children.
Dangerous elements, water. Creek walks with educators who hold water safety certificates, the mud pit and hauling water in buckets.
Dangerous elements, more water. Balancing along wet logs, pouring from heavy jugs and stomping through deep puddles in the rainy season, with dry clothes ready.

Dangerous elements, pretend fire. A pretend campfire ring of logs and stones with fabric flames, where children make fire agreements, practice stop, drop and roll and learn about fire from books and real photos.
Rough and tumble. Wrestling on mats and soft grass with agreements children make, a stop word and an adult nearby.
Going out of sight. Hiding places in the willow dome, behind the logs or under a cloth, where children feel hidden while an educator can still see and hear them.
A meeting time where children name what feels scary and fun and what helps them feel safe.
Photos of children's own risky play, faces turned away, posted with their words about it.
A risk benefit walk with children before a new set-up, looking for what could hurt and what we can change.
For the West class, low heights, short speed on gentle slopes, hammering with a mallet into soft clay or a stump, and hiding under a cloth near an adult.
For the North class, stumps and the hill, hammering golf tees, water play in the mud pit and hide and seek in a small space.
For the South class, woodwork with saws and nails, longer creek walks with water agreements and higher climbing they reach by themselves.

sections.text: Both. Risky play is personal, and each child judges their own risk. Children also make agreements together, cheer each other on and keep each other safe.

Ellen Sandseter, a Norwegian researcher, described six kinds of risky play children seek on their own, great heights, high speed, dangerous tools, dangerous elements, rough and tumble play and disappearing or getting lost. She found children feel a mix of scared and thrilled, and her later work suggests this play may help children manage fear. Tim Gill writes about risk benefit thinking, where we weigh what children gain against what could go wrong, and Rusty Keeler and Angela Hanscom write about the value of real challenge outdoors. We aim for as safe as necessary. Pete Moorhouse shows how real woodworking tools can be offered to young children with clear agreements and close adults. We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Children climb only as high as they can get by themselves, and adults never lift a child up. We never have real fire with children. Children explore fire as a dangerous element through pretend campfires, stories, books and real photos, and water is the dangerous element they meet for real. Water play near deep water happens only with educators who hold water safety certificates, and buckets are emptied after play. Going out of sight means hidden from friends and never out of an adult's watch. Licensing playground safety rules ask that equipment is safe and in good repair, and we check it daily. We watch first and let children judge their own risk. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and offer a question such as Where will you put your foot next?

items: Name what feels scary and fun.
Help make agreements for each set-up.
Walk a space with an educator to look for hazards.
Choose their own level of challenge.
Care for real tools and put them away.
Remind friends of agreements.
Tell an adult when something feels too risky.
Document their risky play with drawings and words.

sections.text: Children carry the crates, planks and loose parts they can lift back to their stacks, return real tools to the tool tray for an adult to count, and tip out water buckets. An adult carries saws and any part too heavy to lift. Each piece has a photo-labeled home, so children close every set-up themselves.

Before a risky set-up, notice your own fear and settle it with a slow breath, because children read our faces. Stand close enough to help and far enough to let children judge, with hands still. Use plain descriptions of what you see instead of warnings.

items: I notice you stopped and looked before you went.
Where will you put your foot next?
How did you know you were ready?
I wonder what helps you feel safe up there.
Tell me about the scary and fun feeling.

Make agreements with children for each set-up.
Add real tools with one adult and a small group.
Add heights and speed slowly as children show readiness.
Add deeper water play and creek walks with full agreements and educators who hold water safety certificates, and add a pretend campfire with fire safety practice.
Add hiding places where adults still see and hear.
Talk at meeting time about scary and fun.
Invite children to help with risk benefit walks.
Document children's risky play and their words about it.
Share our risk benefit thinking with families.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Each set-up has an educator close enough to help and far enough to let children judge, with two adults on the large yards. Real tools are small group only and sawing is one adult with one child, and creek walks leave campus with educators who hold water safety certificates and each child holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer real tools, real hauling jobs and higher climbing they reach by themselves, with agreements and an adult close.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the lowest level of each set-up, time to watch first, and an adult beside them who names what is happening.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A park, a stump, a hammer and golf tees, a hill, a bucket of water and a backyard hiding spot.

cards.title: Heavy work
cards.summary: Real jobs that use big muscles, carrying, digging, moving soil and mulch and stacking, offered as open invitations children choose and return to as they need.

items: Shovels, buckets and wheelbarrows waiting by the woodchip piles.
A digging spot in the garden with real shovels and trowels.
Compost to move to the garden beds with buckets and a wheelbarrow.
Crates, spools and logs to stack and restack.
Buckets for hauling water to the garden.
Real brooms in the piazza for sweeping.
Logs to carry from one pile to another.
Hay to carry in the animal yards with an educator.
Indoors, heavy books or blocks to move to shelves.
Indoors, wiping and scrubbing tables with real sponges.
A mulching job, spreading woodchips around the fruit trees in the Tire swing yard orchard with rakes and buckets.
Stones to carry from a pile to build a border around a garden bed.
A refill job for the landing zones, where children shovel woodchips back under the stumps and swings.
Pushing the full compost cart or carrying the chicken bucket to the animal yards with an educator.
Watering the garden with full watering cans held in two hands.
A job board at children's eye level with real photos of each job, where children choose one.
Heavy work offered before meeting time or a quiet time, so bodies arrive ready to settle.
For the West class, small buckets, light logs and sweeping.
For the North class, wheelbarrows, digging and stacking crates.
For the South class, real jobs across the site that children plan.

sections.text: Both. Heavy jobs bring children together to share loads. A child alone can dig or carry in a steady rhythm.

Heavy work means pushing, pulling, carrying, lifting and digging against real resistance. It sends strong messages through muscles and joints (proprioception), which helps many children feel calm, organized and ready to focus, and occupational therapists often build it into a child's day as part of a sensory diet. The input tends to settle a child for a while after the work, so we offer it before transitions and quiet times. We think in risk and benefit and set things up as safe as necessary. Educators check fall zones and soft landing surfaces every morning before children arrive, and rake woodchips back where they have been kicked away. Two adults are always on the Log yard and the Tire swing yard. Before children use logs, boards, crates, spools or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Check shovels, rakes, wheelbarrows, wagons and brooms each day for loose heads, splinters and flat tires, and use real tools sized for children. Children choose loads they can manage, lift with bent knees and hold loads close. Gloves are on hand for woodchips, stones and compost, and hands are washed after soil and compost. Keep paths clear and agree on where wheelbarrows go. Adults confirm every plant children gather or move is one we know, since poison hemlock and poison oak occur on site.

items: Choose a job and where to do it.
Decide how much to carry.
Care for tools and put them away.
Work with friends to move heavy things.
Notice when a job is finished.
Tell how their body feels after.
Choose a job from the job board and move their photo to show it.
Notice what the site needs, such as a thin landing zone or a dry bed.
Teach a friend how to use the shovel or the wheelbarrow.

sections.text: Children finish the last load, rinse shovels and rakes in the wash bucket and hang them on their hooks, and park wheelbarrows and wagons in place. Gloves go back in their basket and hands get washed. Tool hooks have photo labels at child height, so the heavy work ends with children putting it away.
Work alongside with real effort, at the children's pace, and let your face show the job matters. Leave the heavy end to the children. Name the work, such as You carried four logs to the pile.

items: I notice you bent your knees to lift.
How did you know where it should go?
I wonder how many loads it will take.
Tell me how your arms feel.
Begin with one invitation and one real job.
Add more jobs over weeks as children show what their bodies seek.
Connect jobs to real needs on the site.
Invite children to plan the jobs.
Add a job chart children make.
Invite counting loads.
Notice how the body feels before and after.

Invite teaching a friend how to use a tool.

Notice with the team which children seek heavy work and offer it on purpose through the day.
Let a long job, such as building a stone border, become a project over weeks.

Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the heaviest safe jobs, such as dragging logs or filling a wheelbarrow many times.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small bucket and a quiet job beside an educator.

Dig in the garden with a real shovel.
Sweep the porch or kitchen.
Move a basket of laundry.
Stack firewood or blocks.

sections.text: Your child chooses a job and does it with real tools. Your child can rinse the shovel with a hose, hang the broom on its hook and stack the bucket. Putting tools away is heavy work too.

items: How did you lift that?
I wonder how many loads it will take.
Tell me how your arms feel.

sections.text: Your child is building strength and pride in real work. Heavy work gives the body deep pressure, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in child-sized tools in good shape, and this counts toward your family participation hours.

cards.title: Calm body after big movement
cards.summary: Cooling down after big movement with slow walking, pressure, breathing, rest and heavy blankets with an adult near.

items: A slow walk around the yard after running.
Lying on the grass under a valley oak watching the leaves.
Pressing hands together or pushing against a wall.
A heavy blanket over the legs with an adult near.
Breathing with a hand on the belly to feel it rise.
Blowing a feather across a table slowly.
Hugging knees and rocking on the back.
A drink of water in the shade.
Feeling the heartbeat with a hand on the chest.
Humming a quiet song from the Song book.
Resting in the willow dome or a hammock.
Lying on the back on a mat with a beanbag or a small heavy pillow on the belly, watching it rise and fall.
Cold water on the hands and face at the long yard sink, and noticing the cool.
Sitting with the back against a valley oak and feeling the bark.
Slow stretching up to the sky and folding down to touch the ground.
A basket of calm tools near the yard door with a heavy lap blanket, a pinwheel, a feather, a soft ball to squeeze and a sand timer.
Listening for the sounds of the yard with eyes closed, then naming them.
For the West class, an adult lap or a blanket and a quiet song.
For the North class, wall pushes and breathing with a feather.
For the South class, choosing their own calm tools and noticing their body.

sections.text: Both. Some children calm best alone in a quiet spot. Others calm together with a friend or an adult nearby.

After big movement, bodies need time to come back to calm. Slow steady movement, deep pressure through muscles and joints (proprioception) and long slow breaths out help many children settle, and noticing the heartbeat and breath builds awareness of body signals (interoception). Fast or spinning movement can leave a child alert for a while, so a calm routine after it helps before meeting time, lunch and rest. Heavy blankets go only over the legs and body, never over the head or face. A child can push the blanket off alone, it is light enough for that child to move, it is never used at nap or for sleep, and an adult stays near the whole time. Pressure games such as a blanket roll happen only when a child asks and stop the moment they say stop. Offer water and shade after movement, especially on hot dry late summer days. Calm tools are offered and never required, and a child is never sent away to calm alone.

items: Choose a calm tool.
Notice their heartbeat and breathing.
Find a quiet spot.
Tell an adult what helps.
Help a friend find calm.
Put calm tools away.
Decide how heavy a blanket feels right and take it off when ready.
Lead a friend in a slow breath.

sections.text: Children fold the heavy blanket and lay it in its basket, return the feather and calm tools to their tray and set water cups at the sink. A child can straighten the cushions in the quiet spot. Everything lives in one low basket nearby, so children put it away at their own pace.

Sit down low near the child, breathe slowly yourself, and let your voice drop soft and slow. Co-regulate a child who is struggling before offering anything new. Name what you notice, such as Your breathing is getting slower.

items: I notice your heart is slowing down.
How does your body feel now?
Where do you feel calm in your body?
Tell me what helps you feel calm.

Add breathing with a hand on the belly.
Add wall pushes and hand presses.
Add heavy blankets with an adult near.
Add a quiet spot in the willow dome or hammock.
Invite children to notice their heartbeat before and after.
Invite children to choose their own calm tools.
Make a calm tools basket with children.
End big movement times with a calm routine.
Invite children to draw how their body feels after running and after resting.
Add slow stretching and slow walking along a log.
Add a listening rest with eyes closed under the oaks.
Notice with the team which calm tools each child reaches for and offer them through the day.
Invite children to teach the calm routine to the West class.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Calm tools are open to every child and never required. A heavy lap blanket needs an adult near the whole time, and a blanket roll happens only when a child asks, with an adult beside them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer wall pushes, a heavy blanket on the legs and squeezing hands together before resting.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet spot alone, a light blanket and time with an adult nearby.

home.title: Calm body after big movement at Home

Put a heavy blanket over your child's legs while you sit near.
Breathe with a hand on the belly.

I notice your heart is slowing.
Tell me what helps you feel calm.

sections.text: Your child is learning to notice and settle their body. Pressure and slow breathing help many children feel calm and organized.

cards.title: Studio and class ateliers
cards.summary: How to set up our Studio and each class atelier so they are open, beautiful and ready for children to choose, make and return to their work.

items: Low open shelves with materials in clear jars, baskets and trays so children can see every choice.
Materials grouped by kind and by color zones, with the same home for each thing every day.
Paint offered as red, yellow, blue, white and black so children mix their own colors and hues.
Real tools at child height, such as scissors, brushes of many widths, palette knives, clay tools and a wire cutter used with an adult.
A clear work surface with room for two to six children and space to leave work in progress.
A drying rack, labeled boards for clay and a shelf for work that is not finished yet.
Natural light where possible, plus a light table, a projector or a lamp for light and shadow.
Mirrors at child height and a mirror tile under a tray so work can be seen from new angles.
One or two quiet provocations, such as a branch in a jar beside pencils or a seed pod beside charcoal.
Real photographs of artists at work and of children's past processes at eye level.
A sink or water spot with sponges, cloths and a small broom that children can reach.
Clipboards, pencils and a basket of sketchbooks so plans can happen before making.
Natural and found materials collected with children and sorted in labeled trays.
A smaller atelier in each class, so anything offered in the Studio can also live in the West, North or South class.
Some empty space on shelves and tables on purpose, so the room feels calm and each material stands out.
Paints and dyes made from garden plants, from the botanical dye bed with marigold, calendula, coreopsis, Japanese indigo and black hollyhock, for painting paper and dyeing fabric and wool.
Mirrors with fine black pens and paints children mix to match their own skin, for self portraits, as the Seeing Ourselves module describes.
Burlap with large needles and simple weaving looms beside fabric scraps, yarn and wool.
Large paper taped to the floor or the table for the North and South classes, and beginner scissors used with an educator close by.

sections.text: Both. Shared tables and long sheets of paper invite collaboration and conversation. A personal sketchbook and a small tray of chosen materials give a child room for their own idea.

Begin the year with a few mediums offered slowly so children learn care and respect for materials, then move toward open studio where children self-serve. Keep sharp tools, wire cutters and low-temp glue guns in an adult zone with clear agreements. Change what we offer over time based on what we observe, refreshing what is out more often than adding new things, and store paint and clay sealed so they stay ready. Give three-dimensional work a base to sit on, and display finished pieces with care at children's eye level. Label each piece on the back or a corner with the child's name, the date and any words the child wants written. Stay close when scissors and needles are out, and keep setups for the youngest children simple and contained in a tray. Plant dyes and natural materials come from our garden and our site, and food is never an art material. Record a standout process as a Notice and Wonder observation, link it to a thread, and share it as a Proud Moment without comparison.

items: Choose materials from open shelves and return them to their homes.
Help mix paint, wedge clay and prepare trays for the next group.
Care for brushes, wash palettes and wipe tables.
Plan with a drawing before making and revisit the plan after.
Teach a peer how to use a tool they know well.
Decide when a piece is finished or needs another day.
Sort and label new found materials.
Photograph their own work in progress with a shared camera.
Help set up a provocation for others to find.

sections.text: Children wash brushes in the wash bucket and lay them on the drying rack, wipe the table with the damp sponge, slide wet work onto the drying rack and return each tool to its photo-labeled home. A child sweeps under the table with the small broom while an adult puts away the low-temp glue gun and wire cutter. With a wash bucket, sponge and labeled shelves within reach, the atelier is reset by children and needs no time from an educator later.

Sit at the table at the children's height and stay for a while. Keep your hands busy caring for brushes and jars, and leave the children's work to them. Name what you see in a regular voice, such as "The blue spread into the wet part." Model a technique on your own paper and leave the outcome to the child, so you never draw on or fix a child's work. Notice how a child moves from the feel of a material toward planning an idea across several days, and write down the child's words and color choices exactly as the child says them.

items: I notice you went back to that blue three times. I wonder what you are looking for.
Tell me about what this material can do.
What do you see that makes you say that?
How could we make this easier for the next person?
I wonder what would happen if you used the side of the chalk.
What materials might be strong enough to hold it up?
I wonder what colors we will find in the flowers of our dye bed.
Offer one medium at a time at the start of the year with time to notice how it moves and feels.
Add care routines children lead, such as washing brushes and closing jars.
Introduce tools in pairs, such as a wide brush and a fine brush, so children can compare marks.
Open the shelves for self-serve once routines feel steady.
Bring in a medium that follows the current class inquiry.
Add a long-term work space where a group piece can stay for weeks.
Cover a whole table with a new surface each week, such as butcher paper, cardboard or cloth, for one shared evolving piece.
Set up a light and shadow corner with a projector, transparent colored objects and a hanging sheet.
Offer mixed media trays that combine two mediums children already know.
Show an artist's work on screen or in print beside the same materials.
Add a tinkering zone with cardboard, tape, wire, string and simple real tools.
Take the atelier outside with a portable cart, easels under the oaks or a clay board in the garden.
Invite children to redesign one shelf and explain their choices.
Start a materials library where families send in clean recycled and natural finds.
Keep a small documentation board by the door showing the current exploration in children's words.
Plan atelier work in small group, and bring finished pieces to meeting time so children can talk about their process.
Paint the same flower on different days and look at the paintings side by side.
Children walk in, look around and walk out.
Work looks the same from child to child.
Materials are mixed together, missing lids or hard to find.
Children ask an adult for every item.
Shelves are full and nothing has changed in weeks.
Children rush to finish and leave work behind.
Conflict gathers around one crowded tool.

sections.text: Sit in the space at child height and notice what calls to you and what feels tired. Ask children what they wish the Studio had, then sort, clear and arrange the shelves together. Add one strong provocation tied to their questions and document what happens so the space keeps growing with them.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Open studio is the goal, with children self-serving from open shelves. Wire cutters, low-temp glue guns and tinkering zone tools stay in an adult zone and are used with an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a 25 lb block of clay to pound, wedge and tear, or a standing easel with big brushes and a large sheet. Heavy, wet and resistant materials give the hands and arms more to push against.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray with one material and a tool such as a brush, sponge or clay stick so hands can stay clean. A seat at the edge of the table and the choice to watch first also help.

cards.title: Writing center
cards.summary: How to set up a writing center full of real reasons to make marks, from names and letters to mail, signs, menus, maps, journals and books.

items: A low table near good light with seats for two to four children.
Pencils, crayons and chalk offered first, since they build hand strength, with markers as an occasional choice.
Paper in many sizes, colors and weights, plus envelopes, cards, sticky notes and small notebooks.
A basket of small smooth stones with letters written or painted on them for building names and words.
Letter stamps with a washable ink pad and scrap paper to test them.
A mailbox with a slot, and a pocket or cubby for each child, each educator and each class.
Name cards for every child and educator with a photo, kept in a basket children can borrow from.
A sign-making basket with card stock, tape, clothespins, string and stakes for outdoor signs.
Blank menus, order pads and receipts for the café and for play shops.
Maps of our site, the creek trail and the neighborhood, plus blank paper for new maps.
A journal for each child that lives in the area.
Bookmaking supplies, such as folded paper, a stapler, a hole punch, yarn and ribbon.
Real tools of writing, such as clipboards, a date stamp, a pencil sharpener and a calendar.
An alphabet strip at child height in a font with single-story letters.
A shallow tray of sand or salt for drawing letters with a finger or a stick.
Tools presented in wooden trays, clear jars and low baskets, so children choose and return them on their own.
Big surfaces for the North and South classes, such as butcher paper on the floor or wall and cardboard boxes, where the whole arm can move.
Shells, leaves, feathers, bark and keys from our site set out for observational drawing.

sections.text: Both. Letters, mail and signs are written to someone, so writing pulls children together. A journal or a quiet page lets one child follow their own marks and stories.

Every mark counts, so scribbles, shapes and invented letters are all early writing. Sharpen pencils daily, keep ink pads moist and refresh the paper so the area looks cared for. Offer letter stones only to children past the mouthing stage. Offer markers rarely, since crayons, chalk and pencils give the resistance that builds dexterity and grasp. Display a single mark with the child's own words as proudly as a detailed drawing, at children's eye level. Write children's words onto the work or on a separate label exactly as they say them, and enter them in the noticed field of an observation so the team can follow the thread.

items: Sign in each day by finding their name card.
Write letters and send them through the mailbox to friends, families and other classes.
Deliver the day's mail to pockets and classes.
Make signs for block buildings, the café, garden beds and the animal yards.
Dictate stories to an educator and illustrate them.
Write menus and order slips for the Unicorn Café.
Make maps of places they know and places they imagine.
Bind their own books and add them to the Reading nook.
Show a friend how to find a name card or build a word with letter stones.

sections.text: Children return pencils and crayons to their jars, close the ink pad, stack paper back by size and sort letter stones into their basket. A child sharpens any dull pencils at the end. Each tool has a labeled tray or jar, so children put the area back together as they finish.

Sit beside the writer within arm's reach and write your own list or letter nearby. Read back marks as the child tells them, and keep your pen off the child's page. A relaxed face tells children that any mark is a real start. Notice how a child's marks change, from dots and long lines toward circles and letter-like forms, and when a child uses writing for a purpose, such as a list, a sign, a map or a message in the mailbox.

items: I notice these marks go all the way across the page. I wonder what they say.
Who could this letter be for?
What do you see that makes you say that?
How will the reader know where to go?
I notice you are telling a story while you draw.
I wonder what this person is saying.
Could you teach me how to make that letter?
Start with name cards, pencils and paper so children find their own names first.
Add letter stones and stamps beside a tray for building names and words.
Open the mailbox with a pocket for each child and a slot for each class.
Write letters to other classes, to the animals, to the kitchen and to families.
Offer real stamps, envelopes and postcards and walk together, hand in hand, to mail a letter in the neighborhood.
Add the sign basket and invite signs for buildings, garden beds and the lost and found.
Carry menus and order pads into dramatic play and the café.
Start a map basket with site maps, the creek trail and blank paper.
