Begin individual journals and invite children back to them each week.
Open bookmaking with folded books, accordion books and simple sewn spines.
Add an old typewriter or a keyboard with no cord for letter play.
Offer brushes, dip pens or chicken feather quills with ink for a slower line.
Read dictated stories aloud at meeting time and let children act them out.
Place a writing basket in every area, from blocks to the garden.
Write outside with sticks in dirt and sand and with water on warm concrete.
Keep the writing center and the Studio or class atelier linked, so a story can become a sculpture and a drawing can become a poem.
Invite the older children to make maps of our garden with the beds, the greenhouse and the compost.
Make handmade books that retell a read-aloud, such as The Enormous Turnip or Stone Soup.
Paper sits unused and pencils are dull.
Children copy one model and stop.
The mailbox stays empty for days.
Writing happens only when an adult asks.
Children say they cannot write.
Signs and lists around the room are all made by adults.

sections.text: Writing grows when it has a real reader and a real reason. Ask children who they want to tell something to, and build the mailbox, signs and menus they need together. Hang their own writing around the room so every child sees their marks read and used.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Children write and draw here freely. Letter stones are offered only to children past the mouthing stage, and walking to mail a letter in the neighborhood means each child holds an adult's hand.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick chalk on a chalkboard or paper taped to the wall, a heavy letter stamp to press hard, or clay to carve letters into. Working upright and pressing firmly gives the arm and shoulder more input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a chunky crayon or a short pencil and a small card instead of a big page. A quiet corner of the table, a stamp in place of drawing, or telling words to an educator who writes them down are all ways in.
connected: Corita Kent on the Artists page, for bold screenprints built from words, letters and signs.
Xu Bing on the Artists page, for Book from the Sky, a whole book of invented characters.

sections.text: A small box or basket with pencils, crayons, paper, envelopes, old cards, tape and a shoebox mailbox.

items: Make a family mailbox and leave notes and drawings for each other.
Write a grocery list together while your child makes a list of their own.
Make signs for a bedroom door, a pretend shop or a plant pot.
Draw a map of your home, your street or the way to a favorite park.
Fold and staple paper into a small book for your child to fill.
Write to a grandparent or friend and mail it together.

sections.text: Your child decides what to write and who it is for. Scribbles and invented letters are real early writing, so ask your child to read them to you. Your child can close the box, put pencils and crayons in their cup and stack paper back in the basket. Sharpening a pencil for next time is a good last step.

items: Who would you like to send a letter to?
Tell me what this sign should say to people.
Can you read me your list?

sections.text: Your child is learning that marks carry meaning and that writing connects us with people we care about. Pressing with chalk and crayon builds the small hand muscles that make writing comfortable later.
Send a letter or postcard to your child's class mailbox. Clean envelopes, cards and old maps are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Pencils and crayons build hand strength. Keep it relaxed and skip correcting letters or spelling.

cards.title: Block area
cards.summary: How to set up a block area with room, real materials and time for children to build, test, enclose, knock down and build again.

items: Plenty of wooden unit blocks so children can build big and still share.
Low open shelves marked with the outline or photo of each block shape so blocks have a home.
A large rug or open floor out of the main walkway so buildings stay safe.
Hollow blocks, planks and boards for big building.
Loose parts nearby, such as spools, tree cookies, branches, stones, cylinders, fabric and baskets.
Real photos at eye level of bridges, towers, homes and buildings from many cultures and from our own town.
Small people figures and realistic animal figures in baskets.
Clipboards, pencils and tape for plans and signs.
A camera to photograph buildings before they come down.
A mirror along the edge of the rug so children can see a structure from another side.
Ramps, tubes, gutters and balls for testing movement.
A sign children can place that says a building is still in progress.

sections.text: Both. Large builds invite negotiation, shared plans and real teamwork. A child alone with blocks can test balance, length and pattern at their own pace.

Block play moves through stages, from carrying and stacking to bridges, enclosures, patterns and named buildings, so offer what fits where children are now. Agree with children on how high is safe and how knocking down happens, such as only your own building and only after checking. Leave time and space for buildings to stay more than one day.

items: Choose blocks and return them by shape to the shelves.
Plan a building with a drawing or with friends.
Decide whether a building stays for another day.
Make signs and labels for their buildings.
Photograph and draw what they built.
Agree on rules for knocking down together.
Show a peer how to make a bridge or a strong base.

sections.text: Children carry blocks back and match each one to its outline or photo on the shelf, then sort loose parts and figures into their baskets. A building that is staying gets its in-progress sign. The shelf labels make sorting a real job children can finish on their own, and a basket for tape and clipboards closes the area.

Sit on the floor at the edge of the building with relaxed shoulders. When a tower falls, keep your face and voice calm and describe what happened, such as "It leaned and then it dropped." Step in with your body only when a build becomes unsafe.

items: I notice the tower leans this way. I wonder what it needs.
How did you get the bridge to stay up?
What do you see that makes you say it is strong?
Who might live in or use this place?
Offer unit blocks alone at first so children find balance, length and pattern.
Add shelf outlines so children sort and care for the blocks.
Bring in natural loose parts, such as tree cookies, branches and stones.
Add fabric, cardboard sheets and baskets for roofs, walls and enclosures.
Hang real photos of buildings from around the world and our neighborhood.
Offer clipboards for plans and a camera to keep each build.
Introduce ramps, tubes, gutters and balls.
Add a lamp and transparent blocks for colored shadows on the wall.
Carry blocks outside, or offer big outdoor parts such as crates, planks, spools and tires.
Walk together, hand in hand, to look closely at a nearby building, bridge or fence, then build what was seen.
Begin a long-term group build, such as our school, the creek trail or our town.
Invite children to draw maps of their buildings and keep them in a book.
Add tape measures, string and rulers to compare heights.
Add real building tools, such as a level, a plumb line and blueprint paper.
Blocks are thrown or dumped more than built with.
The same small tower appears every day.
Buildings are knocked down by others often.
Few children choose the area.
Blocks are mixed in bins and hard to find.
There is no room to build big.

sections.text: Watch what children are trying to do with blocks, such as enclosing, rising high or knocking down, and offer materials that serve that need. Bring in photographs, plans and words so buildings are seen, named and remembered. Let a build stay and grow over days while children decide its story.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Children build here on their own with agreements about height and knocking down. Very tall builds and big hollow block towers need an educator nearby, and walks to look at nearby buildings mean holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the largest hollow blocks, long planks and full crates to carry across the room and stack. Building something big enough to sit inside adds even more heavy work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small mat or tray with a basket of unit blocks set a little apart from the busy building. A warning before towers fall and the choice to build low and wide help the noise feel predictable.
connected: Louise Nevelson on the Artists page, for wall sculptures built by stacking wooden boxes and found wood.

sections.text: A set of wooden blocks or a mix of clean boxes, cardboard tubes and small cartons, plus a few toy animals or people.

items: Build tall towers and take turns deciding when to knock them down.
Make a house or a zoo for toy animals with walls and doors.
Use cardboard tubes and books to make ramps for balls.
Take a photo of a building before it comes down.
Add a paper sign your child makes for the building.

sections.text: Your child is the builder and decides what to make and when it is done. You can hand over blocks and ask questions. Your child can stack blocks or boxes back by size and put animals and people into their basket. A bin with a photo of what lives there helps them sort alone.

items: How did you make it stand up?
I wonder what would happen if we added one more.
Who lives here?

sections.text: Your child is learning about balance, size, shape and planning, and about working with others. Lifting and carrying blocks is heavy work for muscles and joints, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send a photo of a home building to share at meeting time, or clean tubes and boxes for our block area. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Build away from walkways and agree on knocking down rules. Keep small parts away from very young children.

cards.title: Home and dramatic play area
cards.summary: How to set up a home and dramatic play area with real objects, open fabrics and room to grow into shops, cafés, clinics and other places children know.

items: Real kitchen items, such as metal pots, wooden spoons, measuring cups, a kettle, cloth napkins and sturdy dishes.
A child-size table, chairs, a stove and shelves that children can rearrange.
Dolls with many skin tones and features, with cloth slings, blankets and a bed.
Open fabrics, scarves and clips that become capes, roofs, baby wraps and tents.
A few dress-up clothes on low hooks, including work clothes such as aprons, boots and hats.
Natural loose parts in baskets for cooking and serving, such as acorns, pinecones, stones, shells and tree cookies.
Real tools of home and work, such as a broom, a dustpan, a phone, a calendar, a clipboard and a calculator.
A mirror at child height.
Real photos of families from our community and around the world.
Writing materials for lists, recipes, menus, tickets and appointments.
A prop basket that changes with the inquiry, such as a shop, café, clinic, vet or post office.
A plant, a small rug and soft light so it feels like a home.
A place right beside the block area, so blocks can become counters, walls and fences inside the story.
Edges marked with low open shelving or a rug, so ideas and materials can still move between areas.
Fabrics such as silk, burlap, felt and lace, with wood slices, smooth stones and shells, and large play silks for wrapping and hiding.
Real objects with weight, such as old keyboards and telephones, measuring tapes, maps and blueprints.
Props, photos and family pictures that reflect the children's own skin tones, hair and families, as the Seeing Ourselves module describes.
Loose parts such as buttons, wire and tubes for building control panels and inventions.
A light panel or an overhead projector for translucent fabrics.
Clipboards, paper and mark-making tools for menus, plans, signs and prescriptions.

sections.text: Mostly together. Dramatic play is where children try on roles, negotiate stories and practice caring for others. A child may also rock a doll alone and replay a moment from home.

Keep props real, sturdy and few, such as metal, wood and enamel dishes, and teach careful handling. Natural loose parts stand in for food, and fresh food stays out of pretend play. Wash fabrics and dolls often and check for small parts with the 2s. Fasten mirrors securely at children's height. Offer only real objects that are safe for the youngest children in the class, and check small loose parts before they come out. Pretend food comes from fabric, wood, stones and empty containers. When a deeper idea appears, record it as a Notice and Wonder observation, bring it to a team inquiry, and plan new provocations in small group.

items: Decide roles and build the story together.
Rearrange the furniture to make a new place.
Make the props they need, such as tickets, money, signs and menus.
Care for dolls by dressing, bathing, feeding and putting them to bed.
Wash dishes in a tub of soapy water and set the table.
Return items to their labeled places.
Bring stories and traditions from home.

sections.text: Children wash dishes in the soapy tub and set them on a drying rack, fold fabrics and scarves into their basket and tuck dolls into bed. Natural loose parts go back to their baskets and dress-up clothes go on low hooks. Every item has a labeled spot, so children reset the home as part of the play.

Sit low at the table and wait to be invited into the play. Take a small role such as a guest when asked, and follow the children's story. Notice your own reactions to loud or messy play and keep your voice warm and even. Join as a co-player to extend an idea, and leave the direction of the story to the children. Watch for the deeper idea underneath a theme, such as rescue, bravery, care for animals or how water moves, and for how a child uses blocks, fabric or writing tools to make the story larger.

items: I notice the baby is wrapped up tight. I wonder how she is feeling.
Tell me what this place needs next.
What do you see that makes you say the shop is open?
How do people in your home get ready for dinner?
What is on the menu today?
I notice you used the blue silks to make a river on the floor. I wonder how the animals will get across.
I notice the three of you are setting the table together. I wonder who is coming for dinner.
Start with a simple home with real dishes, dolls and fabric.
Add a basket of natural loose parts for cooking and serving.
Invite families to share photos, recipes and everyday objects from home.
Add a tub of soapy water for washing dishes and doll clothes.
Follow children's play into a new setting, such as a shop, café, vet, clinic, post office, campground or train.
Have children make the props, such as money, tickets, signs and menus.
Add a phone book, a calendar and appointment cards for planning and writing.
Welcome real objects from a family's culture, with the family showing how they are used.
Carry the home outside to the mud kitchen or the outdoor piazza.
Visit a real place in the neighborhood and rebuild it together afterward.
Add puppets and a small stage so stories can be told to an audience.
Connect café play to real cooking in the culinary atelier.
Change props as interests grow, such as gauze, cotton balls and craft sticks for a doctor's office, or envelopes and stamps for a post office.
Bring the care of our goats, chickens, rabbits and Sheldon into play, with fresh water and feeding as a daily routine.
Play repeats the same script every day.
Items are scattered, broken or missing.
Children argue over a single prop.
Only one group of children ever plays there.
Play turns rough because there is little to do.
The families and cultures in our community are not reflected.

sections.text: Listen to the stories children act out and ask what would make them richer. Build the new setting with children, using real objects, their own signs and family contributions. Return to the play at meeting time so children reflect on the roles and ideas they explored.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Children play here freely with real, sturdy props. Check for small parts with the 2s, keep an educator near the tub of soapy water, and neighborhood visits mean holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy basket of laundry to carry and fold, a big pot to stir, a baby doll to rock or a crate to push as a cart. Dress up with snug vests and heavy coats adds body pressure too.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small table set for two in a corner with fewer props. Soft fabrics without scratchy trims and the choice to play a quiet role such as a guest or a sleeping baby help.
connected: Carl Larsson on the Artists page, for watercolors of everyday family life at home in A Home.
Faith Ringgold on the Artists page, for story quilts about family, home and dreams.
The Image of the Child lens

home.title: Home and dramatic play area at Home

sections.text: A basket of real kitchen items, a few scarves or old sheets, a doll or stuffed animal, clean empty boxes and paper for signs, menus and tickets.

items: Let your child help with real chores, such as washing dishes or folding cloths, then play them.
Build a pretend shop with clean empty boxes and jars and paper money.
Make a café with cloth napkins and take turns ordering and serving.
Use sheets and chairs to make a house, a camp or a vet clinic.
Keep a dress-up basket with old work clothes, hats and bags.

sections.text: Your child leads the story and chooses the roles. Join in when invited and follow their lead. Your child can wash pretend dishes in a tub, fold the scarves and put the doll to bed. A towel on the counter and a basket for each kind of thing make it easy.

items: Who are you today?
Tell me what happens next in the story.
I wonder what the baby needs.

sections.text: Your child is learning to take turns, see other points of view, use words to work things out and care for others. Pretending to be hungry, sleepy or cold helps children notice those same signals in their own bodies.
Share a family photo, a recipe or an everyday object that could visit our home area. Clean empty boxes and dress-up clothes are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use unbreakable dishes for younger children and keep cords and small parts out of reach. Clean up together as part of the play.

cards.title: Reading nook
cards.summary: How to make a reading nook that is soft, calm and full of books children care about, including the books they make themselves.

items: A soft rug, cushions and a low bench or couch where children can settle.
Books displayed face out on low shelves so covers invite a choice.
A small set of books that changes with the season, the current inquiry and children's questions.
Books that reflect many families, languages, abilities and cultures, including Indigenous Californian authors.
Nonfiction with clear real photographs of the animals, plants, bugs and birds on our site.
Books made by children and class books of our own experiences.
Natural light and a warm lamp.
A basket of puppets or story props beside a favorite book.
Field guides for looking up what children find.
A clipboard or notebook for drawing about a story.
A return basket so books find their way back.

sections.text: Both. Sharing a book with a friend or an educator builds language and closeness. A child alone with a book can rest, revisit and imagine.

Fewer, well chosen books work better than packed shelves, so change them often and repair torn pages with children. Check books for stereotypes and dated images and replace them. Keep the nook away from the busiest paths so children can settle.

items: Choose books and read alone, with friends or with an adult.
Retell a story to a friend, a doll or a puppet.
Repair books with tape at a book hospital.
Suggest books for the nook and help choose which ones leave it.
Add their own handmade books.
Act out a story with props.
Return books face out to the shelves.

sections.text: Children drop books in the return basket or shelve them face out, plump the cushions and fold any blanket. A torn book goes to the book hospital. With the return basket at the door of the nook, children close the space as they leave.

Sit on the floor or cushions at the children's level and stay through the whole story. Read in your natural voice and slow down at the pictures. A child who wanders off can come back to the same calm adult.

items: I notice you keep coming back to this page. I wonder what you see here.
Where do you think the story goes next?
What do you see that makes you say she is worried?
Does this story remind you of something?
Start with a few familiar books and add new ones slowly.
Add books tied to children's current questions.
Add class books made from photos and children's words.
Open a book hospital with tape and a small sign.
Set story props, puppets or small figures beside a favorite book.
Add recordings of family members reading or telling stories in their home languages.
Invite families to visit and read in their own language.
Add field guides and nonfiction with real photographs.
Carry a basket of books outside under the oaks or into the willow dome.
Visit the public library together and bring back borrowed books.
Let children design a borrowing system with library cards they make.
Read aloud to the rabbits or to Sheldon the tortoise.
Books stay untouched for days.
Books are often thrown or torn.
Children use the nook to run or tumble.
Shelves are crowded with spines facing out.
The books feel unrelated to what children care about.

sections.text: Notice which books children carry around and which stories they act out, then build the nook around those. Ask children what would make the space cozy and which books are missing. Add books children make about their own lives and our site so the nook holds their stories too.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Children settle and choose books on their own. Reading to the rabbits or Sheldon happens with an adult in the animal yards, and library visits leave campus with hand holding.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy cushion or lap pad to hold, a bean bag to sink into, or a rocking chair. Books with textures to touch, flaps to lift and sounds to make together add input while the child still listens.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, keep the nook dim and quiet with one or two books facing out and a soft spot for one. Let the child listen from nearby before joining, and offer headphones for a recorded story.
connected: Faith Ringgold on the Artists page, for Tar Beach, a story quilt that also became a picture book.

sections.text: A basket of books, a pillow or blanket and a corner with good light.

items: Make a cozy reading spot with cushions in a corner or under a table.
Keep a few books facing out where your child can reach them and change them often.
Visit the library together and let your child choose.
Make a family book with photos and your child's words.
Read in your home language and tell stories from your own childhood.

sections.text: Your child chooses the books and can tell you the story from the pictures. Follow their pace and their favorite pages. Your child can shelve the books face out and fluff the pillow. A small return basket helps on busy days.

items: I wonder what will happen next.
Which picture do you keep looking at?
Does this remind you of anything?

sections.text: Your child is learning to love stories, build words and understand feelings and ideas. Curling up close for a story helps the body slow down, and listening to words builds attention.
Lend a favorite family book for a week, or record a story in your home language for our nook. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Short, cozy reading times every day matter most. Keep sturdy board books for younger children.

cards.title: Sensory table
cards.summary: How to set up a sensory table with water, sand, soil, ice and pantry mixtures, real tools and room for children to pour, mix and discover.

items: A table at a comfortable height for the children who use it, with room on all sides.
One base material at a time, such as water, sand, soil, mud, clay slip, ice, stones, wood chips, shredded paper or fabric scraps.
Real tools, such as metal scoops, ladles, funnels, sieves, pitchers, tongs, droppers, whisks and measuring cups.
Clear jars, bottles and tubes so children can see what happens inside.
Smocks on low hooks, a towel, a dustpan and a small broom.
Natural additions gathered with children, such as fallen leaves, fallen petals, bark, pinecones, shells and smooth stones.
Mixtures from pantry staples, such as dish soap foam, cornstarch and water, or baking soda with vinegar.
A small photo or sign showing what is in the table this week.

sections.text: Both. Side by side pouring and scooping invites quiet company and shared discoveries. A child alone at the table can settle and focus through the hands.

Food is never a sensory material, so leave out rice, beans, pasta and fresh produce and use water, sand, soil, ice and pantry staples instead. Check every material for choking hazards with the 2s, change water daily and wipe spills quickly. Agree with children on how many can play and where materials stay.

items: Fill, measure and mix the base material.
Help choose and gather what goes in next.
Prepare pantry mixtures, such as whipping dish soap foam or stirring cornstarch goop.
Wash tools, sweep spills and dry the floor.
Decide how many friends can play and make a sign.
Draw or describe what they notice.

sections.text: Children wash tools in the wash bucket and set them on the drying rack, sweep spills with the child-size broom and dustpan and dry the floor with a towel. Smocks go back on their hooks. With a damp cloth, broom and labeled tool basket beside the table, the whole close is done by children during the work.

Stand or kneel at the table with your own hands in the material, moving slowly. Notice any discomfort you feel about spills or wet sleeves and let your face stay easy. Describe what you notice, such as "The water ran through the holes."

items: I notice the sand holds its shape when it is wet. I wonder why.
Where does it go when you pour it faster?
What do you see that makes you say it is sinking?
How does it feel on your hands now?
Start with water or sand and a few tools.
Add clear tubes, funnels and pipes so children can watch things travel.
Try sink and float with natural and found objects.
Freeze fallen leaves, petals and stones in ice blocks and offer warm water and droppers.
Offer cornstarch and water or dish soap foam that children whip themselves.
Make baking soda and vinegar eruptions colored with liquid watercolor.
Add garden soil with a short visit from worms and magnifiers, then return the worms.
Add mud or clay slip with brushes and stones.
Build boats from recycled materials and test them.
Add water wheels, pumps, basters and a hand whisk.
Offer shredded paper or fabric for hiding and finding.
Mix primary colors of liquid watercolor in clear water.
Move the table outdoors and connect it to rainwater, the mud kitchen or the long yard sink.
Let children design the next week's table and make the sign.
Material leaves the table more than it stays.
Children dump and walk away.
Crowding and pushing at the table.
The same material has been out for weeks.
No one talks about what is happening.

sections.text: Watch for what children are exploring, such as pouring, transporting, enclosing or mixing, and add tools that serve it. Ask children what they want to try next and let them prepare the mixtures. Place photos and their words beside the table so findings are remembered.

setting.why: An educator stays near the table to watch water, choking hazards with the 2s and how many children share the space. Worm visits and baking soda and vinegar eruptions need an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer wet heavy sand, cold water with ice blocks, or thick cornstarch and water mixtures, with full buckets to lift and pour. Standing to scoop and dump from a height adds more.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer scoops, tongs, ladles and a small tub of dry or warm material set beside the main table. The child can watch first, wear gloves or start with a single finger and come closer in their own time.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for works made from ice, water, leaves and stone that melt and change.

sections.text: A large plastic bin or baby bath, towels, cups, spoons, a funnel, a sieve and a base such as water, sand, soil or bubbles.

items: Fill a tub with water and cups for pouring at bath time or outside.
Freeze small toys or leaves in ice and free them with warm water.
Mix cornstarch and water into goop.
Whisk dish soap and water into a mountain of foam.
Give your child a patch of soil or sand with spoons and pots.

sections.text: Your child can help fill, mix and clean up. Let them explore at their own pace and get messy. Your child can rinse cups and spoons, set them on a towel to dry and wipe up spills with a sponge. A small broom and dustpan just for them makes sweeping their own job.

items: Tell me how it feels.
I wonder what happens if you pour from up high.
Where did the ice go?

sections.text: Your child is learning how materials behave and finding calm through their hands. Pouring, scooping and squeezing give hands rich touch, which helps many children settle and focus.
Send in clean funnels, sieves, cups or scoops for our sensory table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Stay close whenever there is water. We save food for eating and use water, sand, soil, ice and a few pantry basics like cornstarch for play.

cards.title: Investigation table
cards.summary: How to set up an investigation table with one strong object, real tools for looking closely and room for children's questions and theories.

items: A table near natural light with one focus at a time, such as a seed pod, a gall, a bone, a shed snakeskin, a fallen branch or a chicken feather.
Hand lenses, a magnifying sheet, a digital microscope, tweezers and specimen trays.
Clipboards, pencils and colored pencils for close observation drawings.
Field guides and printed real photos of what is being studied.
A tablet with iNaturalist and Merlin Bird ID for looking things up together.
Rulers, tape measures, a balance scale and a magnet.
Clear bug viewers for short visits from small creatures.
A small mirror to see the underside of things.
A light table or lamp for looking through leaves, shells and seeds.
A card holding children's questions and words about the object.
A tinkering tray with old clocks, locks or radios and small screwdrivers.

sections.text: Both. One object at the center invites shared talk and many points of view. A child may also sit alone and draw what they see for a long time.

Wild bird feathers, nests and eggs are protected by law, so use feathers from our own chickens and leave nests in place. Return small creatures to where they were found the same day, and adults confirm every plant before it comes inside. Cut off cords and remove batteries before anything is opened.

items: Bring found objects and tell where they came from.
Choose the next thing to investigate.
Use real tools carefully and show others how.
Draw, measure and photograph what they observe.
Record questions and theories on a shared card.
Look up a finding together in a field guide or on iNaturalist.
Care for small visitors and return them home.

sections.text: Children return small creatures to where they were found, put lenses and tweezers back in their tray and set the focus object back in its place. Drawings go to the clipboard folder, and an adult puts away the small screwdrivers on the tinkering tray. Every tool has a photo-labeled spot so children close the table themselves.
Sit across from the child and look at the object with real interest before you speak. Hold the magnifier steadily and model gentle handling of living things. Let silence stay while the child looks.

items: I notice there are tiny holes here. I wonder who made them.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Tell me what you would like to know about it.
How could we find out?
Start with one strong object and a magnifier.
Add drawing materials for close observation.
Add a second, similar object to compare.
Build a collection over time, such as seed pods, bark, rocks or shells, and sort it.
Connect a digital microscope to a screen so the group can look together.
Use iNaturalist or Merlin Bird ID together.
Add measuring tools and a scale.
Open old machines with screwdrivers on the tinkering tray.
Open a seed pod or a gall with an adult and look inside.
Watch a change over days, such as a chrysalis, a sprouting seed, a melting ice block or a decaying leaf.
Invite children to bring findings from home and walks.
Invite a family member or a visiting expert who knows about the object.
Make a class museum with labels children write.
Follow a lasting question into a project documented over weeks.
Objects sit untouched and dusty.
The table is crowded with too many things.
Questions stop coming.
Tools are lost or broken.
Children glance and move on.

sections.text: Choose objects that come from children's own findings and questions. Leave room for theories, record their words and return to them days later. When a question keeps coming back, follow it out the door to the garden, the creek or an expert.

setting.why: Looking, drawing and magnifying are open to everyone. The tinkering tray with screwdrivers needs an adult at the table, opening a pod or gall is adult work, and small creature visits need an educator nearby.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy rocks to sort and weigh, rotting logs to pry open with a small pry bar, or a mortar and pestle to grind chalk or dry leaves. Real tools that take effort add pressure to the hands and arms.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one object on a small tray with a magnifier, tweezers and a seat at the quiet end of the table. Looking without touching is a full way to take part.
connected: Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for paintings of insects and plants drawn from close study in Metamorphosis of the Insects of Suriname.
Albrecht Dürer on the Artists page, for Great Piece of Turf, a close study of grasses and weeds.

sections.text: A tray or small table, a magnifying glass, paper, pencils and something from outside, such as a rock, a leaf, a pinecone or a shell.

items: Put one found treasure on a tray each week and look closely together.
Draw what you see with a pencil.
Look up a bird, bug or plant together with a free app such as iNaturalist or Merlin Bird ID.
Open an old broken clock with a screwdriver after removing batteries and cords.
Watch something change over days, such as a seed sprouting in a jar.

sections.text: Your child finds, chooses and studies. Let their questions lead and look for answers together. Your child can put the magnifying glass in its box and return the rock or leaf to the yard or a treasure tray. Keeping the drawing in a folder saves it for next time.

items: I notice this part is rough. Tell me what you notice.
I wonder what it is.
How could we find out?

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely, ask questions and test ideas. Using tweezers and a magnifier builds careful hands and steady eyes.
Send a found treasure with a note about where it came from for our investigation table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash hands after handling natural finds. Leave nests and wild bird feathers where they are, since they are protected, and return bugs where you found them.

cards.title: Music area
cards.summary: How to set up a music area with real instruments, found and natural sound makers and room to listen, play and move.

items: Real instruments of good quality, such as hand drums, a xylophone, a glockenspiel, rain sticks, shakers, bells, a ukulele and a thumb piano.
Instruments from many cultures, each with a real photo of how it is played.
Found sound makers, such as pots, lids, metal bowls, wooden spoons, bamboo and tubes.
Natural sound makers, such as stones, sticks, seed pods and dried gourds.
Scarves and ribbons for moving.
A simple way to play recorded music children choose.
A mirror for seeing bodies move.
A low shelf or hooks where each instrument has a home.
Space to move, set away from quiet areas.
Paper and crayons for drawing sound.
Photos of musicians playing, including family members.

sections.text: Both. Making music together builds rhythm, listening and belonging. A child alone can test sounds, loud and soft, fast and slow.

Offer a few instruments at a time and show care for each one. Agree on loud and quiet times and places, since sound travels into calmer areas. The music shed holds bigger instruments and outdoor sound play.

items: Choose instruments and return them to their homes.
Lead a rhythm for others to echo.
Make new instruments from found and natural materials.
Choose music to share at meeting time.
Draw or record the sounds they make.
Decide how loud the music area can be and make a sign.

sections.text: Children carry each instrument back to its photo-labeled home on the shelf or hook and fold scarves into their basket. Drawings of sound go in the paper folder. The shelf sits right in the area so children close it as the music ends.

Sit on the floor among the instruments and play softly yourself before inviting others. When the sound gets loud, keep your shoulders loose and your face calm, and use your agreed signal for quiet. Describe what you hear, such as "Your drum got faster."

items: I notice it gets quieter when you tap softly. I wonder why.
It reminds me of footsteps. Tell me what it reminds you of.
What do you hear that makes you say that?
How could we make the sound of rain?
Start with a few drums and shakers.
Add instruments with pitch, such as a xylophone or bells.
Make shakers and drums from recycled materials, stones and seed pods.
Build a sound wall outside with pots, pans, lids, tubes and wooden spoons.
Listen to music from many cultures and from our families.
Invite family members to play an instrument for the group.
Record children's music and play it back.
Draw sounds with crayons and play the drawings as music.
Add scarves, ribbons and a dance party.
Listen for the sounds of our site, such as wind, water, birds and goats.
Use Merlin Bird ID to record and name bird songs.
Sing songs from the Song book all year and let children add verses.
Build a hanging sound sculpture from found metal and wood that sounds in the wind.
Visit a musician or a performance in our community.
Instruments are banged roughly or broken.
Noise overwhelms other areas.
Children play briefly and leave.
The same few songs are sung every day.
Instruments are tangled together in bins.

sections.text: Notice the sounds children seek, such as booming, tapping or soft rattling, and offer instruments that answer. Bring in family music and real musicians, and record children's own compositions. Let children shape the space, the agreements and the sound.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Children choose and play instruments on their own with agreements about loud and quiet. A visit to a performance in our community leaves campus with hand holding.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big floor drum to play with both hands, heavy shakers, and space to stomp, jump and spin to the beat. Loud then soft games give strong input with a clear stop.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer ear defenders, a soft instrument such as a rain stick or finger cymbals, and a spot at the edge to listen first. Agreeing on a quiet signal before playing helps the sound feel predictable.
connected: Harry Bertoia on the Artists page, for Sonambient sculptures of metal rods that ring when touched or moved by air.

sections.text: A basket of pots, lids, wooden spoons, a homemade shaker and a scarf or two.

items: Make shakers from clean bottles with small stones and tape the lids tight.
Play a kitchen band with pots and spoons.
Dance with scarves to music from your family's culture.
Go on a sound walk and listen for birds, wind and cars.
Sing family songs at bath time and bedtime.

sections.text: Your child can lead the beat, choose the music and invent songs. Follow their rhythm and echo it back. Your child can put pots and lids back in the cupboard and fold the scarf into a basket. A spot just for the shaker keeps it ready.

items: How can we make it louder or quieter?
Tell me what this sound reminds you of.
Which sounds did you hear outside?

sections.text: Your child is learning to listen, keep a beat, move their body and share feelings through sound. Shaking, drumming and dancing to a beat help the body organize movement and find a calm rhythm.
Share a family song or instrument with the class, or send in clean pots, lids and containers for our sound wall. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Tape shaker lids securely and keep small fillings away from children who still mouth things. Pick a time and place for loud music.

cards.title: Meeting time
cards.summary: How to make meeting time a short, warm gathering where children share findings, revisit their work and plan together.

items: A gathering place where everyone can see each other, such as a circle rug, cushions or a ring of stumps.
A short, steady rhythm children can predict.
A centerpiece that invites talk, such as a found object, a photo, a plant or a child's work.
Recent photos and documentation from the class's work.
A talking object to pass so each voice is heard.
Songs from the Song book.
A visual plan of the day with real photos.
A moment for children to share news, findings and questions.
Room to move before and after sitting.
Chart paper and a clipboard to record children's ideas.

sections.text: Together. Meeting time builds belonging and lets children hear each other's ideas. Children who need to move can stand, rock or hold something and still be part of it.

Keep it brief for the 2s and let it lengthen as children grow, watching bodies for when it is time to move. Use it to plan, revisit documentation, share findings and solve problems together. A child not ready to join can stay nearby with an adult and a quiet role.

items: Share news, finds and questions.
Lead a song, a movement or a greeting.
Revisit photos and tell what happened.
Propose ideas and help decide plans.
Help solve problems that come up in play.
Pass the talking object and listen.
Bring an insect, a plant or a found object to share.

sections.text: Children carry cushions or sit-upons back to their stack, return the talking object to its place and set shared objects back on the display. The chart paper stays up for the next meeting. Cushions have a basket at the edge of the rug, so the gathering place is reset by children as they leave.

Sit in the circle at the same height as the children and arrive settled before you begin. Use a regular speaking voice and slow your pace when energy rises. If a child is struggling, move close and help them calm before asking anything of the group.

items: I notice many of you were digging today. I wonder what you were looking for.
Where should we go with this idea next?
What do you see in this photo that makes you say that?
How could we solve this together?
Start with greeting songs, names and a short story.
Add a centerpiece object and invite I notice, I wonder and It reminds me of.
Revisit photos of yesterday's play and let children tell the story.
Use the meeting to plan small groups and projects.
Bring a real problem from play, such as sharing the tire swing, and solve it together.
Invite children to lead parts of the meeting.
Share insects, plants and finds in a clear viewer.
Read aloud stories children dictated and let them act them out.
Hold some meetings outdoors under the oaks or in the garden.
Invite families or visitors to share a skill or a story.
Close the day with a short reflection meeting.
Record children's theories on chart paper and return to them later.
Many children wiggle, leave or poke friends.
Adults do most of the talking.
Meeting runs long for the group.
Children rarely refer back to it.
The same few voices are always heard.

sections.text: Make meeting time about the group's real life, its findings, questions and plans. Shorten it, add movement and let children lead pieces of it. Bring documentation to the center so children see their thinking valued and carried forward.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Meeting time welcomes every child in the class with an educator leading. Insects passed in a clear viewer need an adult holding the viewer, and a child who needs a break stays nearby with an adult.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, begin with a movement song, wall pushes or a big stretch, and offer a wiggle cushion or something to hold and squeeze. A job such as passing the talking stone keeps the body moving with purpose.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a seat at the edge of the circle or just outside it with a clear view. Keep the meeting short and predictable, use a quiet signal for turns, and let the child listen without being asked to speak.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A table or a spot on the floor where the family can gather, and a few minutes each day.

items: Have a short family talk at dinner where everyone shares one thing they noticed today.
Plan the weekend together and let your child add ideas.
Look at photos from your day and tell the story.
Sing a family song before bed.
Solve a family problem together, such as how to share a toy.

sections.text: Your child shares, listens and helps decide. Every voice counts, including the youngest. Your child can push in the chairs and carry plates or a candle back to their place after your family gathers. Choosing what to put out next time can be their job.

items: Tell me something you noticed today.
I wonder what we could do tomorrow.
How could we solve this together?

sections.text: Your child is learning to listen, take turns speaking and feel part of the family team. Sitting together, taking turns and noticing how the body feels help children stay with the group a little longer each time.
Send a photo or a small object from home for your child to share at meeting time.
Keep it short and cozy. Little bodies can wiggle and still listen.

cards.title: Entry and nature table
cards.summary: How to set up a welcoming entry with a nature table that follows the seasons on our site and invites children and families to look, draw and add.

items: A low table or wide shelf by the entry where everyone passes.
Fallen leaves, seed pods, acorns, branches, bark, pinecones and stones gathered on our site and on walks.
Orchard fruit and garden produce on display to look at, smell and draw, which afterwards goes to snack or the chicken bucket.
A cloth or tray in the colors of the season.
Clipboards, pencils and colored pencils for drawing what is on the table.
Magnifiers and a small mirror.
Labels in children's words and real photos of the tree or plant each finding came from.
A vase of garden flowers or branches in bloom.
The name basket for sign-in and a welcome space for families.
A basket where children and families can add their findings.
A small card with a question for families about the season.
Documentation of current class work for families to read at drop-off.

sections.text: Both. The entry is where families and children meet each day and share findings. A child can also stand alone and draw a seed pod before the day begins.

Adults confirm every plant brought in is one we know, since poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site. Fruit on the table is for looking and drawing and goes to snack or the chicken bucket afterwards, never to art. Refresh the table weekly so it follows the season, and compost wilted plants with children.

items: Gather with purpose and leave some for others.
Add findings and tell where they came from.
Draw and describe what is on the table.
Arrange the table and choose what stays.
Carry fruit to snack or the chicken bucket when its time on the table ends.
Write or dictate labels.
Welcome families and show them new finds.

sections.text: Children compost wilted plants, carry fruit to snack or the chicken bucket when its time ends and return magnifiers and clipboards to their basket. A child wipes the tray with a damp cloth. The compost bucket and baskets sit by the table so children refresh it themselves each week.

Be at the entry as children arrive, standing still with a calm face and open hands. Pause at the nature table with a child and look together. Notice what a child brings in and name it without judging it.

items: I notice this leaf is changing color from the edges. I wonder why.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Where do you think it came from?
How might it look next week?
Start with a few findings from our own site.
Add drawing tools and invite close observation.
Set out one orchard fruit to look at, smell and draw, then send it to snack or the chicken bucket.
Keep one object for weeks and draw it as it changes.
Make a color line of fallen leaves arranged from green to brown.
Add field guides and photos of the trees each finding came from.
Invite families to add findings from home and walks.
Make a seasonal book from children's drawings at the table.
Add a year wall showing the orchard and the oaks through the seasons.
Arrange findings into patterns and circles that stay for a day.
Press leaves and flowers to keep.
Compare findings from different places, such as the creek, the Log yard and home.
Add a small card where families can write their own questions.
The table has looked the same for weeks.
Items are dry, dusty or broken.
Children walk past without stopping.
Families do not notice or add to it.
It is crowded and hard to see any one thing.

sections.text: Let children decide what belongs on the table and why, and keep their words beside each finding. Follow the year so the table tells the story of our site. Invite families to look, add and wonder alongside their child at drop-off.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Everyone can look, touch and draw at the table. Adults confirm every plant that comes in, and small seeds and pods stay out of reach of the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy basket of rocks, pinecones or small logs to carry to the table and arrange, and rosemary or lavender to crush and smell. A rough piece of bark and a smooth stone side by side invite strong touch.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, keep the table uncluttered with a few objects in small dishes and a magnifier. Arrival can begin with simply looking at the table before joining the class.
connected: Albrecht Dürer on the Artists page, for Great Piece of Turf, a close watercolor study of plants as they grow.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for arranging fallen leaves, stones and sticks outdoors by color and pattern.
Mabel McKay on the Artists page, for Pomo baskets woven from plants gathered with care and knowledge.

home.title: Entry and nature table at Home

sections.text: A small shelf, windowsill or tray near your door, and treasures from walks and your yard.

items: Collect fallen leaves, seed pods and stones on walks and display them.
Change the display with the seasons.
Draw something from the tray together.
Set a piece of fruit out to look at and draw before you eat it.
Keep a magnifying glass nearby.

sections.text: Your child gathers, arranges and decides what stays. Let them tell you the story of each find. Your child can take wilted flowers to the compost and wipe the tray with a cloth. Choosing what stays on the shelf is part of their job.

items: Where did you find it?
How has it changed?
I wonder what we might find next season.

sections.text: Your child is learning to notice the seasons, care for nature and look closely. Touching, smelling and looking closely at nature wakes up the senses gently and calms many children.
Send a seasonal find from home or a walk, with a note about where it was found, for our entry table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Pick with purpose and leave some for others. Wash hands after collecting and check any plant before bringing it inside, since some are poisonous.

cards.title: Clipboards everywhere
cards.summary: How to keep a clipboard with paper and a pencil in every area, indoors and out, so children can draw and document whatever they notice.

items: A clipboard with paper and a pencil in every area, indoors and out.
Clipboards on low hooks or in baskets so children can grab one anytime.
Plain paper, plus some sheets with a box for drawing and space for words.
Sharpened pencils, tied on with string for outdoor clipboards.
Colored pencils or crayons in some areas.
Weatherproof clipboards or a lidded box outdoors to keep paper dry in the rainy season.
Clipboards at the garden beds, animal yards, block area, nature table, sensory table, mud kitchen and in the creek walk bag.
A folder or basket by each area for finished drawings.
Educators with clipboards too, noting children's words.

sections.text: Both. A child may draw a bug alone for a long time. Children also draw side by side, compare what they see and plan builds together.

Clipboards make drawing part of every place, so children document what they see while it is happening. Keep a refill routine so paper and pencils are always ready. Bring pages to meeting time and to the walls so children see their records used.

items: Draw and document what they see, where they see it.
Make plans, maps and lists for their play.
Write signs and keep tallies, such as eggs collected.
Record observations of animals and plants.
Refill paper and sharpen pencils.
Share drawings at meeting time.
Decide where their drawings go next.

sections.text: Children hang clipboards back on their hooks or drop them in the area basket, file finished drawings in the folder and refill paper. A child sharpens pencils at the end. Paper and the sharpener live by the clipboard basket so children keep the system running.

Carry your own clipboard and draw beside the children, at their level, with unhurried hands. Keep your marks on your own page. Describe what you see in their drawing, such as "You gave the beetle six legs."

items: I notice you drew the legs very carefully. I wonder what you saw.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Tell me what you want to remember about this.
How might you change it next time?
Start with clipboards in two or three areas.
Add one to every area indoors and out.
Draw and take notes alongside children.
Add simple observation sheets for animals, the garden or the sky.
Count and tally, such as eggs collected or birds seen.
Draw the same thing over time, such as a plant growing.
Carry clipboards on walks and creek walks.
Draw plans before building or making.
Add a camera beside the clipboard for drawing and photo pairs.
Use drawings to start conversations and projects.
Make books and walls from the collected drawings.
Add new tools, such as charcoal or watercolor pencils.
Clipboards stay empty.
Paper is wet, torn or missing.
Pencils are dull or gone.
Drawings are left behind and never revisited.

sections.text: Clipboards matter most when drawings are used. Look at them with children, ask what they saw and carry their ideas into the next day.

setting.why: Clipboards are open to every child in every area. Clipboards on walks and creek walks follow those rules, with each child holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy clipboard to carry on a long walk, drawing while lying on the belly, or pressing hard with chalk on a big board. Lying on the belly gives the arms and shoulders weight to push against.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small clipboard with a short pencil and a quiet spot such as the reading nook or a bench. The child can watch an educator draw first or begin with a single line.
connected: Beatrix Potter on the Artists page, for careful watercolor studies of fungi drawn from life.
Leonardo da Vinci on the Artists page, for notebooks of drawings made while watching plants, water and animals.

sections.text: A clipboard or a piece of cardboard with a binder clip, paper and a pencil.

items: Keep a clipboard by the door for walks.
Draw birds, bugs or plants you see.
Make a list or a map before an outing.
Draw a building before taking it apart.
Keep drawings in a folder to look back on.

sections.text: Your child decides what to draw and remember. Their marks are their own record of what they noticed. Your child can clip fresh paper on the clipboard and hang it by the door. Putting drawings in a folder or box keeps them safe.

items: Tell me what you noticed.
I wonder what you want to remember.
Where would you like to draw next time?

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely, plan and share ideas through drawing. Holding the board with one hand and drawing with the other helps both hands work together.
Send a drawing from home or a walk to share at meeting time.
Tie the pencil to the clipboard with string for walks. Every way of drawing is welcome.

cards.title: Walls and documentation
cards.summary: How to use walls for documentation that makes children's thinking visible, at their eye level, with photos and their own words.

items: Documentation of children's process at their eye level, with photos and their words.
Fewer things on the walls so each piece can be seen.
Calm wall colors and natural backing, such as cork, wood or burlap.
Children's work framed, mounted or hung with care.
Panels that show a story over time, from questions to theories to discoveries.
Real photos of our site, animals and plants.
Space for children's current drawings and plans.
A family-facing board near the entry.
A belonging wall with children's names and family photos.
Laminated documentation outdoors.
Photos that keep children's faces out of anything shared publicly.

sections.text: Both. Shared panels show a group's thinking. A single drawing on the wall honors one child's idea.

Documentation shows learning in progress and is shared with children, families and colleagues. Keep children's faces out of anything shared publicly, mark portfolio pieces with the child's age in years and months, and keep printouts clean with few words. Change panels as work grows so the walls stay current.

items: Choose what goes on the wall.
Revisit documentation and add new words.
Help hang and arrange work.
Photograph their own process.
Explain the wall to families and visitors.
Decide when a panel is done.

sections.text: Children take down a finished panel with an educator, sort the pieces into portfolios and return pins and clips to their box. Tape and clothespins have a labeled box so children can help hang and take down work themselves.

Stand at children's eye level when you look at the walls together and give each piece your full attention. Hang work with care while children watch and help. Speak about what the work shows and leave praise words aside.

items: I notice you are looking at this photo for a long time. I wonder what you remember.
What do you see that makes you say that?
How should we show what happened next?
Who should see this?
Start with a few photos and children's words at eye level.
Add children's drawings and plans in progress.
Build a panel that tells a project's story over weeks.
Invite children to revisit the panel and add comments.
Add a family question card that invites responses.
Create a belonging wall with names and family photos.
Take documentation outside with laminated panels.
Make a class book from the panels.
Bring documentation to meeting time to plan next steps.
Host a family evening to walk through the walls together.
Place an artist's work beside children's work on the same idea.
Clear and refresh the walls each season with children.
Walls are crowded and faded.
Store-bought posters and cartoon images fill the space.
Children never look at the walls.
Every piece of work looks the same.
Documentation hangs too high for children to see.

sections.text: Clear the walls with children and ask what they want others to see. Put up the process of the current inquiry, with photos and children's words, at their eye level. Return to the wall often so it sparks new thinking.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Children look, revisit and add their words freely. Hanging panels with tools or ladders is adult work, and children's faces stay out of anything shared publicly.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite the child to carry the step stool, lift frames, press pushpins and reach high to hang work with an adult. A large wall panel to add to while standing gives more movement.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, keep walls calm with neutral backgrounds, plenty of empty space and a few pieces at eye level. A small personal panel or book the child can look at alone offers a quieter way to revisit work.
connected: DRDP the Foundations and Our Interpretations
The Image of the Child lens
Ruth Asawa on the Artists page, for a San Francisco fountain built from figures modeled by children and neighbors.

sections.text: A wall, a corkboard, a string with clothespins or the fridge, plus a few photos and your child's drawings.

items: Hang your child's drawings at their eye level on a string with clothespins.
Make a family photo wall with everyone's names.
Write your child's words about a drawing beside it.
Change the display each month together.
Make a book of saved drawings at the end of the year.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to display and tells you about it. Your child can take down old drawings, choose which to keep and put them in a folder or box. Clothespins go back in their jar.

items: Which one should we hang?
Tell me what you were thinking when you made it.
I wonder what you remember about this day.

sections.text: Your child is learning that their ideas are seen and valued. Calm, uncluttered walls help eyes rest and make it easier to find what matters.
Send a family photo for our belonging wall or a drawing from home to share.
Use wall-safe tape and keep displays low and simple.

cards.title: Quiet and cozy space
cards.summary: How to make a quiet and cozy space where children can choose to rest, calm their bodies and feel safe in a busy day.

items: A small enclosed spot away from busy paths, such as a fabric canopy, a nook under a loft or a corner with a low divider.
Soft cushions, a rug, blankets and a small mattress with washable covers.
Soft warm light from a lamp or a window.
A few calming objects, such as a weighted lap pad, a smooth stone, a sand timer or a breathing ball.
Books about feelings and a basket of familiar comfort items.
A family photo book children can hold.
Headphones with quiet music or recorded sounds of our site.
Room for one or two children.
Real photos of calm places, such as the creek, the oaks or the ocean.
Pastels and paper for marking feelings after deep breaths.
A plant to care for.

sections.text: Mostly alone or with one friend. Children need a place to rest and feel safe from the busy room. An educator may sit nearby to help a child calm.

The cozy space is a choice for comfort and never a punishment or time out. Keep it visible for supervision while it still feels private, and wash fabrics often. Agree with children on how to use it and how many fit inside at once.

items: Choose to go when they need a break.
Decide when they are ready to return.
Help choose calming objects and books.
Care for the space and fold blankets.
Invite a friend to rest together.
Draw feelings with pastels after deep breaths.

sections.text: Children fold the blanket, return the calm objects to their basket and straighten the cushions as they leave. A child can water the plant. Everything has a place inside the space so children reset it on their own.

Sit near the entrance of the space within reach, and keep your own breathing slow and steady. Use a quiet voice and few words. Stay with a child who is upset until their body settles before offering a book or a choice.

items: I notice your breathing is slowing. How does your body feel now?
Tell me what helps you feel calm.
What do you see in this picture that makes you feel quiet?
How could we make this space cozier?
Start with soft cushions, a blanket and a few books.
Add family photos and comfort items.
Add breathing tools, sand timers and smooth stones.
Offer pastels for marking feelings after deep breaths.
Add quiet music or recorded sounds from our site.
Make a feelings book with children's drawings and words.
Create a cozy spot outdoors in the willow dome or under the oaks.
Add fabric to hide in, such as a hammock or a covered crate.
Invite children to redesign the space.
Breathe slowly while smelling lavender or lemon balm from the garden.
Add a plant children water.
Make a small book of calm places on our site.
Children avoid the space or use it to hide from adults.
It is crowded or noisy.
Cushions are dirty or worn.
Children use it for rough play.
It feels too open to feel safe.

sections.text: Ask children where they feel calm and what helps them. Build the space with them, using their ideas for light, softness and objects. Name it together so it feels like their own.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator keeps the space in view and stays near a child who is upset until their body settles. A hammock or covered crate added inside needs an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy cushions to pile on, a weighted lap pad, a blanket to roll up in with an adult nearby, and a ball to squeeze. Deep pressure gives strong input that also calms.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, keep the space dim, quiet and for one, with a soft blanket, ear defenders and a few calm picture cards. The child decides when to come and go.
connected: Agnes Martin on the Artists page, for quiet paintings of soft lines and pale color.

home.title: Quiet and cozy space at Home

sections.text: A corner, a few pillows, a soft blanket, a book or two and a small lamp.

items: Make a cozy corner with pillows and a blanket.
Drape a sheet over a table for a quiet hideaway.
Add a family photo book and a favorite soft toy.
Practice slow breaths together, such as smelling a flower and blowing out a candle.
Offer crayons and paper for drawing feelings.

sections.text: Your child decides when to go and when to come back. The space is a comfort they choose. Your child can fold the blanket, put the book back and turn off the lamp. Keeping the corner ready is their job.

items: Tell me what helps you feel calm.
How does your body feel now?
How could we make this spot cozier?

sections.text: Your child is learning to notice feelings and find ways back to calm. Snuggling under a heavy blanket or squeezing a pillow gives deep pressure, which helps many children feel calm and safe.
Share a family photo or tell us what helps your child feel calm, so we can support them here too.
Keep it a place of comfort and never a punishment. Wash blankets and pillows often.

cards.title: Piazza and culinary atelier
cards.summary: How our indoor piazza works as a shared meeting place and a real kitchen studio, home of the Unicorn Café, where children cook, serve and eat together across classes.

items: Low open shelves with real dishes, glasses, small pitchers and cloth napkins that children can reach and put away.
A self-serve snack table with a picture menu, small serving tongs and spoons, and a clear place for used dishes.
A child-height counter or sturdy table for cooking, with a step stool, aprons on hooks and a handwashing routine posted in photos.
A self-access baking shelf with labeled jars of flour, oats, baking soda and salt, plus measuring cups, spoons and whisks.
Real kitchen tools sorted in clear bins, including peelers, graters, a citrus juicer, mortar and pestle, salad spinner and a timer.
Child-safe knives to start, then small real knives and cutting boards with a clear agreement about how we hold and pass them.
Small vases, clippers and a basin of water for flowers children cut from the garden and arrange for the tables.
A menu board and blank menus near the café sign, with chalk, pencils and clipboards for children to write and draw the day's offering.
A recipe stand holding the day's picture recipe, and a growing binder of family and class recipes.
A compost bucket and a chicken bucket, each labeled with a real photo, for peels and scraps.
A display table where garden harvests and fruit sit to be looked at, smelled and drawn before they go to snack or the chicken bucket.
Tables set for small groups with a centerpiece, so the piazza feels ready to welcome guests from any class.

sections.text: Both. Cooking, serving and eating are deeply shared, and the piazza is where children from West, North and South meet as buddies. A single child can also take quiet ownership of one job, such as folding napkins, arranging flowers or writing the menu.

Our kitchen is vegetarian and nut free, so every ingredient and every label is checked, and allergies are posted where adults prepare food. Adults run any heat source and hot surfaces, and we do not use a slow cooker in the piazza. Wash hands before and after cooking, keep knives on a tray when not in use, and clean as you go. Food here is for cooking and eating with respect, so produce never becomes an art or sensory material. The educator leading the piazza is responsible for cleaning every tool. Children may wash, dry and sweep as part of the work, and the educator finishes and checks each tool before it is put away. Every session starts with handwashing with soap and water, tied hair and sleeves pushed up. Tools are set out on the rolling cart before children arrive, and only the tools for that recipe come out. All plugging, unplugging and hot surfaces stay with the educator, and children stand back behind a marked line while anything heats. A recipe step that stays with the educator begins with An adult and carries the adult hand on its demonstration sheet. One adult works with no more than two children cutting at once, while the others wash, tear, scoop or watch, then they trade. Child knives are a serrated tomato knife for our youngest and a mini santoku for older children, one child per knife, always seated at the board. We teach the bridge grip, with fingers arched over the food, and the claw grip, with fingertips tucked under, starting with soft foods such as banana and cucumber. Cherry tomatoes and grapes are cut in quarters lengthwise for our youngest children. A cut resistant glove goes on the hand holding the food, never the knife hand, and a damp cloth under each cutting board keeps it from sliding. The educator's knife for hard or round foods such as squash, cabbage, onions and whole apples, the knife sharpener, the food processor, the oven, the kettle and the blenders are adult only, with children watching from their seats. Children add ingredients to a mixer or a food processor only while it is off and unplugged. Popcorn is eaten seated, with an educator close beside the children, and an adult checks the lid of every jar. Knives are washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with blades covered. Cast iron, rolling pins and the flour sifter are wiped clean and never soaked, the pasta roller is brushed clean when dry, and scales are wiped with a damp cloth and never submerged. Whisks and beaters are washed right away, since egg and batter harden, and every pan and pot cools before it is washed and dried fully.

items: Set the tables with real plates, cups and cloth napkins, counting places for each guest.
Cut, arrange and refresh flowers for the tables, and decide where each vase goes.
Serve themselves at snack and pour from small pitchers, then clear and scrape their own dishes.
Read the picture recipe aloud with friends, choose a cooking job and do the real steps.
Write, draw and post the menu, and take orders from guests at the Unicorn Café.
Taste as they cook and decide together if a dish needs more lemon, herbs or salt.
Wash, dry and put away dishes, and fold and sort cloth napkins for the laundry.
Invite and host a buddy from another class, showing them how our café works.
Carry scraps to the chicken bucket and the compost, and explain which goes where.
Wash hands with soap and water, tie back hair and push up sleeves before every session.
Scrub FEED bin and garden produce in a basin of cool water, and spin washed greens dry in the salad spinner.
Peel carrots and cucumbers away from the body, with the vegetable resting on the board.
Snip herbs, green onions and greens with culinary scissors over a bowl, tips pointing down.
Turn the crank of the apple peeler, the rotary grater, the flour sifter or the food mill while an educator holds the base.
Press our lemons and mandarins on the citrus juicer and watch juice and seeds separate.
Scoop and level each measure with a flat knife, count each cup aloud, and crouch to read the line on the liquid measure.
Weigh food before and after, such as apples before and after drying, on a digital or balance scale.
Count the turns of the hand egg beater until foam forms.
Roll dough from the middle out, turning it a quarter turn each time, and press masa in the tortilla press.
Pour batter with a measuring cup, ladle it into the waffle maker and lay fruit and herbs on the dehydrator trays before it is switched on.
Add washed vegetables and beans to the soup pot from a bowl before the heat is on.
Fill a tea strainer with dried herbs and steep their own cup once it has cooled.
Pack cabbage into the fermentation vessel with their hands and check the brine each day.
Carry the harvest from the garden in the hod and rinse it right in the basket.
Wash bowls and spoons at the sink caddy as the last step, and sweep their own space with the dustpan and brush.

sections.text: Children scrape their own dishes into the compost or chicken bucket, wash bowls and spoons at the sink caddy, set them on the drying rack and sweep their space with the dustpan and brush. Cloth napkins go in the laundry basket. Knives stay with the educator, who washes them one at a time and checks every tool before it goes back on the rolling cart. Because only the tools for that recipe come out and each has a photo-labeled spot, children carry most of the close themselves.

Work at the table alongside the children, using real tools with calm, careful hands. Keep your voice even when something spills or burns and invite the children into the cleanup. Name what you see, such as "The dough got smoother after you pushed it."

items: I notice the dough changed after we added water. Tell me what you notice.
I wonder how we will know when it is ready.
It reminds me of a smell from home. Does it remind you of something?
Who should we invite to the café, and how will they know?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with the self-serve snack routine, real dishes and cloth napkins, so children learn the rhythm of serving, eating and clearing.
Add flower cutting and arranging, with children choosing vases and placing them on each table.
Open the Unicorn Café with a sign, menus and simple roles such as host, server and cook.
Cook simple recipes from the garden, such as mint and lemon balm tea, citrus squeezing for lemonade and herb toast.
Hold a short chef meeting before cooking, where the group reads the picture recipe together and each child chooses a job.
Introduce a check-in question while the group sits at the table, then wait until everyone is served before eating together.
Invite families to send a recipe from home and cook one each month, adding it to the Recipe library with the family's name.
Offer taste tests of garden varieties, such as three kinds of apples or tomatoes, and invite children to draw and describe each taste.
Keep a sourdough starter that children feed and watch, noticing bubbles, smell and rise over days.
Use a dehydrator for fruit leather or dried apple rings, and track the change over a day.
Set up a self-access baking shelf for pancakes or muffins, where small groups measure and mix with growing independence.
Pair buddies across classes, with older children guiding younger ones through a recipe or the café routine.
Host a harvest meal where each class brings something from its home bed and the piazza becomes a shared table.
Make class cookbooks or recipe cards with children's drawings and dictated steps to send home.
Children wait for adults to hand out every cup and plate.
Snack feels rushed and the dishes come back half eaten and unnoticed.
The café sign is up and no one takes orders or writes menus.
Flowers on the tables are wilted and no child seems to notice.
Children from different classes pass through without speaking.
Cooking only happens when an adult does most of the steps.

sections.text: A tired piazza becomes a place for inquiry when children take real roles in it. Ask children what a café needs, and build it together over weeks with menus, roles, flowers and invitations to other classes. Notice the questions that come up while cooking, such as why bread rises or where a lemon comes from, and follow them into the garden, the Recipe library and the books we read.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Cooking with real tools needs an adult at the table, and knife work happens in a small group with an adult beside each new cutter. Self-serve snack and flower arranging are open to all, and every heat source stays with an adult.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer bread dough to knead, citrus to squeeze in a hand press, a mortar and pestle for herbs, and heavy pots and trays to carry. Real kitchen work gives the hands and arms plenty to push against.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a job done with tools such as stirring with a long spoon, washing dishes or setting tables with cloth napkins. A child may smell or look first, and tasting is always a choice.
connected: Wayne Thiebaud on the Artists page, for painting rows of cakes, pies and café counters with care
Rachel Ruysch on the Artists page, for painting arranged flowers with every petal studied
The Image of the Child lens

home.title: Piazza and culinary atelier at Home
