sections.text: A low shelf or drawer with a few real plates, cups and cloth napkins, a small pitcher, a step stool, an apron, and simple kitchen tools such as a whisk, measuring cups and a citrus juicer.

items: Let your child set the table each night, counting places and folding napkins.
Cook one simple recipe together each week, such as pancakes, lemonade or herb tea, reading the steps aloud.
Invite your child to cut or gather a few flowers and arrange them for the table.
Make a family menu together on paper and post it on the fridge.
Let your child pour their own water from a small pitcher and clear their own plate.
Taste two kinds of the same fruit side by side and talk about how they differ.

sections.text: Your child can do real kitchen work, including washing, stirring, pouring, measuring and serving. Give them a job they can finish on their own and let small spills be part of learning. Your child can scrape their plate, wash it in a tub of soapy water and set it on a towel to dry. Folding napkins and sweeping under their chair with a small broom finishes the meal.

items: I wonder what will happen when we mix these.
How does it smell now? How did it smell before?
Who should we share this with?

sections.text: Your child is learning to care for others, follow steps, measure and wait, and to feel at home in a real kitchen. Kneading, squeezing and stirring give the hands heavy work, and noticing hunger and fullness helps children listen to their bodies.

Send in a family recipe, written or as a photo, so we can cook it in the Unicorn Café and add it to our Recipe library. You might also send in cloth napkins or small vases for our tables. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep hot pans, stoves and sharp knives with an adult. Our school is nut free and our kitchen is vegetarian, so recipes you send for school should be too. Expect a little mess and keep a towel nearby.

cards.title: Garden
cards.summary: How our garden works as a place where children dig, plant, tend, harvest and wonder, with each class caring for its own home bed.

items: Each class has its own home bed with a sign children make, so they know which bed is theirs.
Child-size real tools in a reachable spot, including trowels, hand forks, rakes, small shovels, buckets, wheelbarrows and harvest baskets.
A dig spot left unplanted, where children may dig deep and freely.
Clear paths and narrow beds so children can reach the middle without stepping on plants.
Clipboards, pencils, magnifiers and a field guide or phone with iNaturalist ready in a garden basket.
A place to sit and look, such as a log, a bench or the willow dome.
Permanent strawberry beds, the botanical dye bed and the pollinator garden marked with real photos so children know each place.
Plants grown for the senses near the path, such as lamb's ear, lavender, spearmint, lemon balm, rosemary and salvias.
A clear sign or photo marking the plants we may taste, kept separate from those we only look at.
A garden journal or chart where children record what they plant, what grows and what they harvest.
Buckets for weeds and prunings that go to the goats after an adult checks them.

sections.text: Both. Garden work often takes many hands, such as turning compost, moving soil or harvesting a bed. A child alone can also find calm in weeding a small patch, watching a bee or checking a seedling each day.

We keep one adult to six children in the garden, and children wear shoes. Poison hemlock and poison oak grow on our site, and black widows hide in dark corners, so adults confirm every plant children gather and check under boards and pots first. We use no herbicides or pesticides. Our beds are irrigated, so children help by noticing drips and dry spots for adults to fix. Garden tools live in the Barn and Garden shed, and seeds live in the seed library.

items: Choose what their class plants in its home bed, and help plan where it goes.
Prepare beds by digging, raking and spreading finished compost from our pile.
Sow seeds, transplant seedlings and label rows with signs they make.
Pull weeds and carry them, after an adult checks, to the goats.
Harvest with purpose, leave some for others, and carry the basket to the piazza.
Watch for pollinators, ladybugs, roly polys and worms, and add them to iNaturalist with an adult.
Save seeds from flowers and vegetables and return them to the seed library.
Cut flowers for café tables and stems for the botanical dye pot.
Teach a younger buddy how to use a trowel or where the strawberries hide.

sections.text: Children rinse trowels and hand forks in the wash bucket and hang them in the shed, carry weeds to the goats after an adult checks them and set harvest baskets by the piazza door. Seeds go back to the seed library. Tools have photo-labeled hooks at child height so children close the garden themselves.

Kneel or sit on the ground at the children's level within arm's reach. Notice how you feel about dirt, bugs and worms, and let your face show calm curiosity. Model gentle handling of plants and creatures and slow the pace so children can look.

items: I notice the leaves on this side are bigger. I wonder why.
Tell me what might be under the soil right now.
Who has been visiting these flowers?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with daily garden walks so children learn the paths, the beds and the plants we may taste.
Introduce real tools one at a time, with agreements about carrying, using and putting them back.
Give each class its home bed and invite children to decide what to grow, using seed packets and photos.
Set up garden jobs that children choose, such as composting, digging, sowing, harvesting, mulching and sign painting.
Plant a five senses corner, with herbs to smell, lamb's ear to touch, berries to taste, tall grasses to hear and bright flowers to see.
Grow a bean or gourd teepee or a sunflower house that children can sit inside as it grows.
Plant a soup bed with the herbs and vegetables from family soup recipes, then cook the harvest in the culinary atelier.
Hang a colander on a nail by the hose bib so children can rinse a harvest right in the garden.
Make wind chimes from old metal spoons and keys to hang near the pollinator garden.
Start a worm bin and harvest worm castings to feed the home beds.
Keep a class garden journal with drawings, photos and measurements of one plant across weeks.
Notice which flowers open and close through the day, such as California poppies closing in the evening and on foggy days.
Save seeds at the end of a season, sort them in small envelopes, and decorate the envelopes for the seed library.
Invite families with garden knowledge to lead a planting or share a plant from their culture.
Children walk past the beds without stopping.
Tools stay in the shed because children do not know where they live.
Only adults harvest, and children see the food first at snack.
Home beds are bare or overgrown for weeks.
Children pick everything at once and leave nothing for others.
No one has drawn, photographed or written about the garden in a while.

sections.text: A garden becomes a place for inquiry when children decide what it holds and follow what happens there. Ask a class what they want to grow and why, then plan, plant and watch together over a full cycle from seed to seed. Return to the same plant each week to notice change, and let one surprise, such as a chewed leaf or a strange sprout, open a longer investigation.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: We keep one adult to six children in the garden. Real tools are introduced one at a time with an adult, and adults confirm every plant children gather.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer real shovels for digging new beds, full watering cans and wheelbarrows of compost or mulch to move. Pulling up spent plants with a firm grip adds strong input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer garden gloves, a trowel and a small pot or one bed to tend. Watering, gathering seeds or sitting on a bench to watch the pollinators are gentle ways in.
connected: Claude Monet on the Artists page, for painting his own garden at Giverny again and again
Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for drawing plants with the insects that live on them in every life stage
Patrick Dougherty on the Artists page, for weaving living saplings into shelters children can walk inside

sections.text: A small patch of soil, a large pot or a window box, a trowel, a watering can, a few seeds or seedlings, and a notebook for drawings.

items: Plant fast-growing seeds such as beans, peas or radishes and check them each morning.
Grow herbs your family cooks with, such as mint, basil or parsley, in a pot by the door.
Leave a small corner just for digging.
Draw or photograph the same plant each week and line up the pictures.
Go on a slow walk in your yard or block and look for bees and butterflies on flowers.
Save seeds from a flower or a vegetable you ate and plant them again.

sections.text: Your child can choose what to plant, dig, sow, water, pull weeds and harvest. Let them be the one who checks on the plants and tells you what changed. Your child can rinse the trowel and hang it up, coil the hose and put seed packets back in their box. Carrying weeds to the compost is good work too.

items: I wonder what this seed needs.
How has it changed since yesterday?
Who else lives in our garden?

sections.text: Your child is learning patience, care for living things and how food grows. Digging, carrying and watering give the whole body heavy work, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in seeds you saved, a cutting, extra pots or a photo of what you grew. You might also share a plant or recipe from your family. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Check that every plant your child may touch or taste is one you know. Use gardening gloves for thorny plants, wash hands after digging, and skip chemical sprays.

cards.title: Mud kitchen
cards.summary: How our mud kitchen offers a real place to mix, pour, cook and invent with soil, water and plants, deepening over months.

items: A sturdy counter at child height with a basin or sink, near a water source children can reach.
Real metal pots, pans, muffin tins, ladles, whisks, sieves, funnels, spoons and old china dishes.
Containers of many sizes, including jugs, bottles, jars and measuring cups, for pouring and comparing.
Bins of soil, sand and gravel with scoops, kept covered when not in use.
Herbs planted nearby in pots or tires so children can pick a few leaves for their mud recipes.
Hooks and shelves so each tool has a home and children can put things away.
A low table or plank for serving, and a chalkboard for menus and recipes.
Aprons or old shirts, and a rinse bucket and towel close by.

sections.text: Both. The mud kitchen invites shared stories of cafés, restaurants and potions, with children taking orders and serving each other. A single child can also stir, pour and mix for a long time, absorbed in how mud changes.

Children wear shoes here and wash hands well after mud play. Use only plants adults have confirmed, and check bins and the underside of the counter for black widows. Produce from the garden and snack stays out of the mud kitchen, so children use soil, water, sand, petals, leaves, sticks, seed pods and stones. Old flowers past their best and spent herbs from pruning are fine. Plan for wet clothes and keep spares.

items: Fill, carry and pour water to make mud as thick or thin as they choose.
Gather petals, leaves, pods and stones with purpose, leaving some for others.
Invent recipes and write or draw them on the chalkboard.
Run a mud café and take orders from friends and adults.
Compare amounts by pouring between containers of different sizes.
Care for the tools by rinsing them and hanging them back up.
Decide what the mud kitchen needs next and help gather it.

sections.text: Children rinse pots and tools in the rinse bucket, hang each on its hook and put the covers on the soil and sand bins. Aprons go to the wash basket and hands get washed. Hooks and bins with photo labels sit right at the counter, so children reset the kitchen themselves.

Wear clothes that can get muddy and put your own hands in the mud. Notice any dislike you feel about mess and let your face and voice stay relaxed. Describe the changes you see, such as "The mud got thicker when you added soil."

items: I notice this mud is runny and that mud is stiff. How did you make them different?
I wonder what will happen if it sits in the sun.
Tell me what your recipe needs next.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with soil, water, a few pots and spoons, so children meet mud itself.
Add real metal utensils and china dishes so the kitchen feels serious and real.
Add funnels, jugs, sieves and gutters so water can travel to the kitchen.
Plant herbs and flowers near the kitchen for children to pick for their recipes.
Offer a chalkboard and clipboards for menus, recipes and orders.
Add sand and gravel bins so children can compare how each mixes with water.
Introduce muffin tins and molds, then leave mud cakes in the sun and notice what happens over a day.
Build with mud as mortar, stacking bricks or stones together and testing how strong the wall is.
Make mud paint with brushes on paper, boards or fence panels in the art shed.
Bring in a familiar story about building homes and let children build small mud houses for it.
Mix flower-petal mud soup and compare colors as petals are crushed and soaked.
Visit the mud kitchen in rain and notice how puddles, flow and texture change.
Invite children to photograph and describe their best recipe for a mud kitchen recipe book.
Children grab tools and leave quickly.
Tools pile up dirty because no one knows where they go.
The same play repeats every day without new language or ideas.
There is no water, so the mud is either dust or dried crust.
Children ask for food from snack to put in the mud.

sections.text: A bare mud kitchen becomes a place for inquiry when educators notice what children are already testing and add tools for it. If children are mixing thick and thin, add measuring cups and a chart. If they are serving, add menus and a sign. Ask children what a real kitchen has that ours lacks, and gather it together.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Children play here freely with an educator nearby who checks bins and the counter for black widows first. Picking herbs for recipes needs an adult to confirm each plant.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer full buckets of water to haul, heavy pots of thick mud to stir and a mud pit to stomp through in boots.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer long spoons, ladles and gloves, a dry spot at the edge, and dry sand or plain water before mud. Washing dishes in clean water is a gentle way to join in.

sections.text: A corner of the yard or a patio, a bucket of soil, a jug of water, and old pots, pans, spoons, muffin tins and jars from the kitchen or a thrift store.

items: Set up a crate or low table as a counter with a tub of water beside it.
Mix mud with your child and notice how it changes with more or less water.
Gather fallen petals, leaves and seed pods for mud recipes.
Make mud cakes in a muffin tin and leave them in the sun to dry.
Draw a menu for the mud café and take orders.

sections.text: Your child can mix, pour, invent, serve and clean up. Let them choose the recipe and decide when it is ready. Your child can rinse the pots with a hose or bucket, stack them in a basket and cover the soil bucket. Washing hands is the last step.

items: How did this mud get thicker?
I wonder what happens if we leave it overnight.
What should we call this recipe?

sections.text: Your child is learning how materials change, how to measure and pour, and how to tell a story through play. Stirring thick mud and carrying water give the hands and arms heavy work, and the cool, squishy feel helps many children settle.
Send in old metal pots, pans, ladles or china dishes for our mud kitchen. You might also send a photo of your mud recipe. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Dress for mess, keep a towel nearby and wash hands well afterwards. Use soil from your yard or plain bagged topsoil, and avoid potting mixes with added fertilizer.

cards.title: Animal yards
cards.summary: How children help care for our goats, chickens, rabbits and Sheldon the tortoise, learning their needs, habits and how to be kind to all beings.

items: A handwashing spot at the gate with soap, water and a photo sign of our hygiene routine.
Real photos of each animal at children's eye level, with their names and something about them.
A task chart with real photos for jobs such as feeding, watering, collecting eggs and refreshing bedding.
Child-size buckets, scoops and egg baskets kept just outside the yards.
A clear place to stand and watch, such as a low bench or a marked spot by the fence.
Clipboards, pencils and a magnifier for drawing animals and their tracks, feathers and droppings.
A bucket for weeds and prunings for the goats, and a chicken bucket for kitchen scraps, each labeled.
A simple chart for each species of what they like and do not like, made with children.

sections.text: Both. Caring for animals is shared work, and children learn to take turns, move slowly and speak quietly together. One child sitting still beside the rabbit yard or watching Sheldon eat can find deep calm.

Children wear shoes in the animal yards and follow our hygiene protocol for the chickens and goats, washing hands before and after every visit. Children feed and watch Sheldon and do not touch him. Goats eat only plants, so only weeds and prunings an adult has checked go to them, and animals never eat the food we grow for people. Chickens get kitchen scraps from the chicken bucket. Rabbits feel safest with all four feet on the ground, so children sit low and let rabbits come to them. Rabbits get only plants an adult knows are safe for rabbits, offered in small amounts. Usually safe are mint, basil, parsley, cilantro, dill, lemon balm, clover, dandelion, plantain, nasturtium, calendula, rose petals, strawberry leaves, raspberry and blackberry leaves, carrot tops and chard. Kept from rabbits are the onion family (chives, garlic, leeks), nightshade leaves (tomato, tomatillo, pepper, potato), azalea and rhododendron, lilies, foxglove, sweet pea, lupine, daffodils and other bulbs, ivy, yew, milkweed and pipevine.

items: Feed and water animals following the task chart, and check off each job.
Collect eggs gently, count them and sort them by color.
Carry weed and pruning buckets to the goats after an adult checks the plants.
Carry the chicken bucket from the piazza and empty it for the hens.
Watch and record what each animal does, eats and avoids.
Lead a younger child through the handwashing and quiet approach.
Notice when an animal seems unwell or different, and tell an adult.
Help name new animals and add them to the photo wall.

sections.text: Children rinse feed buckets and scoops, hang them just outside the yards and check off each job on the task chart. Everyone washes hands at the gate. Buckets and scoops have labeled hooks, so children finish animal care without an educator coming back later.

Move slowly and keep a quiet voice inside the yards so animals and children can settle. Crouch at the children's height to watch together. Your calm hands with the animals show children how to be gentle.

items: I notice the goats all went to the shade. I wonder why.
Where do you go when you feel too hot?
How can we tell what Sheldon likes?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with short, calm visits where children only watch and listen, learning each animal's name.
Teach the handwashing routine and the quiet approach, with children practicing them together.
Introduce one care job at a time, such as egg collecting, then feeding, then refreshing bedding with an adult.
Make a task chart with real photos and let children sign up for jobs each week.
Build a likes and dislikes chart for the rabbits by offering safe plants and recording what they choose.
Watch Sheldon over the year and notice when he is active, when he eats and when he hides away.
Sort and count eggs by color and size, and keep a tally across weeks.
Collect shed feathers and fur with an adult to look at under magnifiers and in the Studio.
Draw animals from life with clipboards, returning to draw the same animal again weeks later.
Notice molting, broodiness and seasonal changes in coats, and record them with photos.
Map the animal yards with children, marking food, water, shade and favorite spots.
Invite a veterinarian or a family who keeps animals to visit and answer children's questions.
Talk openly and gently when an animal is sick or dies, and let children ask questions and remember the animal together.
Make a book about each animal, with children's drawings, real photos and their own words, for the Book collection.
Children run, shout or chase near the yards.
Visits are a quick look with no job or question.
Children cannot name the animals or say what they eat.
Handwashing gets skipped or rushed.
Animal care has become an adult chore that children only watch.

sections.text: The animal yards become a place for inquiry when children hold real care and real questions. Notice what children wonder about, such as why one hen lays blue eggs or why the goats climb, and follow it with observation over weeks. Let children decide how to share what they learn with other classes and families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An adult is with every small group in the yards, and handwashing comes before and after each visit. Refreshing bedding and collecting shed feathers and fur happen with an adult beside the child, and Sheldon is never touched.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer real chores such as carrying hay, hauling water buckets, raking the yard and pushing the wheelbarrow of bedding. These jobs give strong heavy work with a real purpose.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a spot outside the fence to watch first, gloves for gathering eggs and a gentle job such as filling a water dish for Sheldon. Smells and sounds can be talked about before going in.
connected: Rosa Bonheur on the Artists page, for painting farm animals from close study in the field
Albrecht Dürer on the Artists page, for drawing a young hare with every hair observed
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A pet, a backyard visitor or a nearby farm, plus a notebook, a pencil and a place to sit quietly and watch.

items: Give your child one daily pet care job, such as filling the water bowl.
Sit quietly with your child and watch birds, squirrels or lizards in the yard.
Visit a local farm and notice what each animal eats and how it moves.
Draw an animal while watching it, then draw it again another day.
Keep a chart of what your pet likes and does not like.

sections.text: Your child can feed, water, watch and notice. Let them be the one who reminds the family about the animal's needs. Your child can rinse the pet bowl, hang up the leash and wash hands after caring for an animal. A small chart of jobs helps them remember each step.

items: How can we tell how this animal feels?
I wonder what it needs today.
Tell me something you noticed that you never saw before.

sections.text: Your child is learning gentleness, responsibility and how to read the needs of another living being. Carrying feed and water is heavy work for growing muscles, and noticing what an animal needs helps children notice their own needs too.

Send a photo or drawing of an animal your family cares for or met on a walk. You might also send clean straw, wood shavings or a sturdy bucket for our animal yards. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash hands after touching any animal or its space. Teach your child to move slowly and let animals come to them.

cards.title: Log yard
cards.summary: How our Log yard under the valley oaks offers logs, stumps, sticks and planks for climbing, building, balancing and discovering what lives inside wood.

items: Logs and stumps of many sizes, some fixed for climbing and some light enough to move.
Planks, crates and spools for children to build bridges, ramps and balance paths.
A basket of sticks sorted by length, and rope for tying and lashing.
Tree cookies and wood rounds for stacking, counting rings and building towers.
Magnifiers, bug boxes and a field guide nearby for creatures found under logs.
A rotting log left in place so children can watch it change.
A tool area with hammers, nails, a hand drill and a small saw, used with an adult and clear agreements.
Shade from the valley oaks, with acorns, leaves and bark to gather.

sections.text: Both. Moving big logs and building forts takes many hands and shared planning. A child alone may balance across a log again and again, or sit quietly peeling bark and watching roly polys.

Adults check logs and stumps before each use for rot, splinters, loose bark and black widows, and lift logs first so children can look underneath safely. Children wear shoes and gloves when moving rough wood. Watch first, then step in only when a risk is beyond what children can judge. Children learn to judge their own reach and balance. Real tools are always used with an adult beside them. Put logs back where creatures live, gently and in the same spot.

items: Move, roll and stack logs to build their own structures.
Decide on a balance path and test it with a friend.
Lift logs with an adult and look for roly polys, worms and beetles, then roll the log back gently.
Saw branches and hammer nails into stumps with an adult beside them.
Use sticks as tools to pry, dig and open old wood.
Count rings on tree cookies and compare thick and thin rounds.
Make agreements about how many children can stand on a log at once.
Tidy the yard by returning loose parts to their places.

sections.text: Children roll and carry logs, sticks and tree cookies back to their places and return the rotting log gently to its spot. Real tools go back to the tool tray for an adult to count, and an adult carries the saw. Loose parts have marked spots so children tidy the yard themselves.

Stand close enough to help and keep your hands at your sides unless help is asked for. Notice any worry about heights or falls and keep your face steady. Describe what you see, such as "You tested the log with one foot first."

items: I notice this log feels softer than that one. I wonder why.
Who do you think lives under here?
How did you decide where to put your foot?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with fixed logs and stumps for climbing and balancing, so children learn how wood feels underfoot.
Add planks and crates so children can build their own bridges and ramps.
Introduce lighter logs and rounds for carrying and stacking.
Bring out sticks and rope for lashing, tying and building frames and dens.
Offer hammers, nails and stumps for real hammering with an adult.
Add a small saw, a vise and branches for sawing with an adult.
Leave a log to rot in place and visit it each month to see who moves in.
Open old logs with sticks and hand tools to find what is inside.
Collect acorns and oak leaves and compare valley oak and coast live oak.
Build a shared fort or shelter over several days, adding to it each visit.
Draw plans for a structure before building, then compare the plan with what was made.
Bring in larger loose parts, such as wooden spools and tubes, for new kinds of building.
Photograph and display each structure before it is taken apart, with children's words about it.
Children walk the same log in the same way every day.
Loose parts lie scattered and unused.
Children ask for help to move things they could move together.
There is little talk about what lives in and under the wood.
Building ends quickly because nothing can be added.

sections.text: The Log yard becomes a place for inquiry when children shape it. Ask what they want to build and what they need, then add materials in response. Leave structures standing over days so ideas can grow, and follow questions about rot, creatures and trees into longer investigations.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Children climb and build here with an educator close enough to help, and two adults are on the large yard. Hammering and drilling need one adult with one or two children, and sawing is always one adult with one child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer rolling and carrying heavy rounds with a partner, balancing along higher logs, jumping from a stump onto soft ground and building with long branches. Each gives strong input to muscles and balance.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer low logs close to the ground, an adult hand to hold while balancing, and the job of looking for creatures under logs with a magnifier. Sitting on a stump to watch is a fine first step.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for building with sticks, stone and wood found on site
Patrick Dougherty on the Artists page, for building huge woven structures from sticks and saplings
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: Fallen branches, a few logs or stumps, some boards, rope, and a place outside where your child can build.

items: Set out a log or plank low to the ground for balancing.
Build a small fort with branches and a sheet.
Lift a log or stone together to see what lives under it, then put it back gently.
Count the rings on a cut stump or a slice of wood.
Hammer nails into a stump with your child beside you.

sections.text: Your child can lift, carry, balance, build and decide. Let them test their own balance and ask for help when they need it. Your child can stack sticks and boards in a pile and put the rope in a bucket. Rolling a log back gently keeps homes safe for bugs.

items: Who do you think lives in this log?
How can we make it stronger?
Where will you step next?

sections.text: Your child is learning strength, balance, planning and care for small creatures. Balancing on logs and carrying heavy pieces help the body know where it is and move with confidence.
Send in tree rounds, clean branches or a photo of something your child built. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Check wood for splinters, rot and spiders before play. Wear gloves when moving rough logs, and stay close when real tools are out.

cards.title: Tire swing yard
cards.summary: How our Tire swing yard, our orchard of plum, apricot, apple, fig and nectarine under the valley oaks, offers spinning, swinging, shade and a full year of fruit.

items: A sturdy tire swing with space around it and a clear waiting spot.
Orchard trees with real photo labels showing leaf, blossom and fruit for each one.
Shady places to sit, lie down and look up into the branches.
Baskets for gathering fallen leaves, blossoms and fruit with adult guidance.
Clipboards and pencils for drawing trees across the seasons.
Ribbons or scarves on a branch to show which way the wind blows.
Loose parts such as tires, balls and ramps for rolling and spinning.
A sand timer or a turn list on a clipboard hung near the swing.
A low ladder or step stool kept for adults so children can watch harvests up close.
An orchard calendar on a weatherproof board where children add drawings and photos each month.
Blankets or sit-upons for resting under the trees on hot days.

sections.text: Both. The tire swing invites taking turns, pushing a friend and riding together. One child can also lie under a fruit tree and watch the leaves move, or spin slowly alone.

Check the swing ropes and fittings regularly. Talk with children about how many can ride, where to stand while waiting and how to push safely. Fallen fruit can draw bees and wasps, so check before children gather, and send fallen fruit to the chicken bucket. Ripe fruit we pick goes to the culinary atelier. Adults confirm every plant children gather.

items: Take turns on the swing and decide together how to share it.
Push friends and count pushes or spins.
Watch the orchard through the year and notice blossoms, fruit and falling leaves.
Gather ripe fruit with an adult and carry it to the piazza.
Collect fallen fruit for the chicken bucket.
Draw the same tree again each season.
Notice pollinators visiting blossoms in spring.
Make and keep the agreements for the swing, and remind friends of them.
Roll tires and balls down slopes and decide which path is fastest.
Carry winter prunings to the goats after an adult checks them.

sections.text: Children stop the swing gently, gather balls and tires back to their spot and fold blankets and sit-upons into their basket. Fallen fruit goes to the chicken bucket. Baskets sit near the trees so the yard is reset by children before they go in.

Stay close to the swing with a relaxed stance and follow each child's signals for faster, slower and stop. Notice your own worry about spinning and heights and let your voice stay calm. Watch faces closely and slow the swing at the first sign a child has had enough.

items: I wonder what makes the swing spin faster.
Which tree do you think will bloom first?
Tell me what you notice when you look up from here.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with the swing and simple agreements about turns, pushing and waiting.
Add a sand timer or a song for turns so children can manage waiting together.
Introduce the orchard trees by name with real photo labels.
Lie under the trees and draw what you see above.
Watch blossoms in late winter and spring and count bees and other visitors.
Measure the fruit as it grows and keep a chart.
Harvest ripe fruit together and cook it in the culinary atelier, such as stewed apricots or dried apple rings.
Taste different orchard fruits side by side and draw each taste.
Watch winter pruning and send the prunings to the goats.
Compare the deciduous orchard trees with the evergreen oaks through the year.
Offer other spinning tools, such as tops and spinning seats, to explore how things turn.
Make a big orchard calendar that children add to each month.
Tie ribbons and wind socks on low branches and watch how wind and the swing move them.
Press orchard leaves and blossoms and compare their shapes across the five fruit trees.
Notice which birds and insects come for ripe and fallen fruit, and record them with Merlin and iNaturalist.
Invite children to choose one tree as a class tree and visit it as an old friend all year.
Turns on the swing cause conflict every day.
Children never stop to look at the trees.
Fruit falls and rots without anyone noticing.
The yard is used only for running through.
Children seek spinning elsewhere, such as twirling into others indoors, and need more chances here.
No one can name the trees or say what they give us.

sections.text: The Tire swing yard becomes a place for inquiry when the orchard and the swing are both noticed. Ask children what they notice about the trees and follow their questions through the seasons. Use the swing to wonder about speed, spinning and turns, and let children make the agreements that keep it fair.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator stays close to the tire swing and watches each rider's face. Gathering fallen fruit waits until an adult checks for wasps, and the ladder is for adults only.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer longer spins and higher swings with an adult pushing, pumping the legs, and pushing a friend on the swing. Pushing a swing is heavy work too.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer slow straight swinging with feet near the ground, a gentle stop when asked, and the choice to lie under the trees and watch the leaves. The child says when to start and stop.
connected: Vincent van Gogh on the Artists page, for painting fruit trees in blossom
Alexander Calder on the Artists page, for mobiles that turn and spin in moving air

sections.text: A swing at home or at a park, a nearby fruit tree, a blanket and a notebook.

items: Take turns pushing each other on a swing and count the pushes.
Lie on a blanket under a tree and look up together.
Visit the same fruit tree each month and notice how it changes.
Gather fallen leaves and sort them by color or size.
Pick fruit together from a tree you know is safe.

sections.text: Your child can push, take turns, notice and gather. Let them decide how fast and how high feels right. Your child can fold the blanket, carry the notebook in and gather any fallen fruit for the compost. A basket for outdoor things makes it easy.

items: How has the tree changed this month?
How does it feel when you spin?
Who else visits this tree?

sections.text: Your child is learning balance, turn taking and how trees change through the year. Swinging and spinning give strong movement input, and many children feel calmer and more focused afterwards.
Send a photo of a fruit tree your family loves, or a recipe made with fruit from a home or neighborhood tree. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Check swing ropes and seats regularly. Watch for bees and wasps near fallen fruit.

cards.title: Art shed
cards.summary: How our art shed holds materials children can carry outside to paint, draw, sculpt and print in the open air, in every season.

items: Low open shelves with clear labeled bins so children can see and choose materials.
Outdoor easels, fence easels and clipboards ready to carry to any spot.
Large paper, cardboard and fabric for working big on the ground or on a fence.
Paint in primary colors plus white and black, so children mix their own colors.
Brushes of many sizes, sponges, rollers and natural brushes made from grasses and feathers.
Chalk, crayon, charcoal, oil pastel and pencils in sorted containers.
A drying rack and clips so work can dry safely outdoors.
Buckets of water, rags and a clear clean up routine posted in photos.
Smocks or old shirts on hooks at child height.
A clay bin with boards and simple wooden tools for working at an outdoor table.
A basket of natural surfaces such as smooth stones, bark strips, tree cookies and shells.
A low table or tarp that can be carried to any spot in the yards.
Real photos of artists at work outdoors, posted inside the shed door.

sections.text: Both. Large shared pieces on a fence or the ground bring children together. A child alone at an easel under a tree can work for a long time.

Keep materials sorted and protected from rain and sun. Check the shed for spiders before children reach in. No glitter. Produce stays out of art, and children use leaves, flowers, sticks, stones and mud from the site. Wash brushes and return them so the shed stays ready for the next group.

items: Choose materials and carry them to where they want to work.
Set up easels, paper and water for themselves and friends.
Mix their own colors from primaries, white and black.
Gather natural materials as brushes, tools and surfaces.
Clean brushes and return materials to their bins.
Decide how to display finished work outdoors.
Show a younger child where things live in the shed.
Help sort, label and restock bins at the start of each week.
Choose where to work, such as under the oaks, in the garden or beside the animal yards.
Photograph their own work and tell an adult what to write beside it.

sections.text: Children rinse brushes in the water bucket and lay them on the drying rack, clip wet work to the drying line, wipe tables with rags and return materials to their labeled bins. A child carries the tarp back to the shed. Clean up steps are posted in photos so children carry the whole close themselves.

Stand or sit at the easel beside the children and stay through the painting. Keep your own hands busy rinsing brushes and refilling paint. Meet drips and mixed colors with a calm face and describe them.

items: I notice the color changed when it dried. I wonder why.
Which colors do you see out here that we do not have yet?
Where should this piece live while it dries?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few materials, such as chalk and watercolor, and teach how to carry and return them.
Add fence easels and clipboards so children can work anywhere outside.
Paint the colors you see outdoors, mixing to match a leaf, a sky or a flower.
Make bark and leaf rubbings on trees and stones.
Paint with mud and earth pigments ground from soil and soft rocks.
Pound leaves and flowers onto cotton muslin to see the colors they hold.
Paint rocks, tree cookies and bark strips.
Make a sound map by choosing a color for each sound heard outdoors.
Work big on rolls of paper on the ground with rollers and long brushes.
Bring clay outside and press in leaves, seeds and bark.
Make sun prints with leaves and flowers on sunny days.
Leave each place as we found it, with no paint in the soil and no tools left behind.
Cover a whole outdoor table with a new surface each week, such as butcher paper, cardboard or cloth, for a shared piece that grows.
Paint in the rain and watch drops change the marks.
Draw the same view from the art shed in each season and line the drawings up.
Build a weaving frame on the fence and weave grasses, ribbons and fabric strips through it.
Paint with natural brushes children make from pine needles, feathers and grass tied to sticks.
Children wait for adults to bring out materials.
Bins are mixed up or empty.
Outdoor art always looks the same.
Work is left in the rain or blowing away.
Children only draw indoors and say there is nothing to make outside.
Brushes come back stiff with dried paint.

sections.text: The art shed becomes a place for inquiry when children know it is theirs. Organize it with them, notice which materials they reach for, and add new ones in response. Take art out to where children's questions are, such as the garden, the creek trail or the animal yards.

setting.why: Children choose and carry materials out on their own once routines are steady. Pounding leaves with mallets and grinding earth pigments need an adult at the table, and sun print paper is handled with an adult.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big brushes on a large outdoor easel or wall panel, sponges and rollers, and heavy buckets of water to carry for cleanup. Painting standing up with the whole arm adds movement.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small board with a brush, a smock and a cloth close by, and a quiet corner away from the busy table. Drawing with pencil or crayon is another gentle choice.
connected: Jackson Pollock on the Artists page, for painting on canvas laid on the floor of a barn with whole body movement
Alma Thomas on the Artists page, for paintings built from the colors of her garden and the trees outside her window

sections.text: A basket or box of art supplies you can carry outside, such as chalk, crayons, paper, a clipboard, a few brushes and a water jar.

items: Take paper and crayons outside and draw what you see.
Make rubbings of bark, leaves and stones.
Paint with water on a fence or sidewalk and watch it dry.
Mix mud and paint with it on cardboard.
Paint the colors of the sky at different times of day.

sections.text: Your child can choose materials, carry them outside, set up and clean up. Let them decide what to make and where. Your child can rinse brushes in a jar, lay them on a towel to dry and pack the art basket. Carrying it back inside finishes the job.

items: Which colors do you see out here?
I wonder what happens when it dries.
Where should we hang it?

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely and to share ideas with color and line. Painting big with the whole arm helps the body cross the middle and builds strong shoulders for later drawing and writing.
Send in old paintbrushes, clipboards or a large roll of paper for our art shed. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Expect some mess and dress for it. Use washable paints, and keep food in the kitchen and out of art.

cards.title: Music shed
cards.summary: How our music shed offers real instruments and sound makers outdoors, where children can play loud, move big and listen closely.

items: Real instruments on low shelves and hooks, such as drums, shakers, rain sticks, xylophones, a ukulele and bells.
A sound wall made from pots, pans, lids, metal bowls and spoons hung where children can play them.
Scarves, ribbon wands and streamers for moving to sound.
A space in front of the shed for dancing and performing.
A small speaker and recordings of music from many cultures, including families' music.
Photos of each instrument with its name so children can return it to its spot.
Clipboards and paper for drawing sounds and writing songs.
Buckets, tubs and plastic barrels turned over as drums, with wooden beaters.
Pipes, tubes and lengths of gutter children can sing and tap through.
A basket of found sound makers, such as seed pods, shells, stones and sticks.
A rug or mat in the shade for listening and quiet play.

sections.text: Both. Playing together builds rhythm and listening. A child alone may spend a long time exploring how one drum sounds when struck in different places.

Show children how to hold and care for each instrument. Keep instruments dry and out of the sun. Check the shed for spiders before children reach in. Loud play is welcome outside, and quiet listening matters too.

items: Choose instruments and return them to their places.
Lead a song or a rhythm for others to follow.
Invent new instruments from found and recycled materials.
Dance and move to music with scarves and ribbons.
Draw or record sounds and play them back.
Plan and perform a show for another class.
Teach a friend a rhythm by playing it and waiting for an echo.
Tune and test sounds, deciding which pot, lid or bar sounds highest.
Care for instruments by wiping them, hanging them up and reporting anything broken.

sections.text: Children hang instruments back on their photo-labeled hooks, wipe any wet ones with a cloth and fold scarves into their basket. Anything broken goes on the repair shelf for an adult. Every instrument has a place, so children close the shed themselves.

Play along at a gentle volume and keep your body loose when the shed gets loud. Use the agreed signal for stop and model it with your whole body. Name what you hear without judging it, such as "That beat was slow and heavy."

items: I wonder how to make this drum sound softer.
Which sounds can you hear when we all stop?
It reminds me of thunder. Tell me what this sound reminds you of.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a few real instruments and agreements about care.
Add a sound wall of pots, pans and lids.
Offer scarves and ribbons for movement and dance.
Sing songs from the Song book outdoors and add instruments.
Listen for sounds outdoors, such as birds, wind and rain, and try to match them with instruments.
Make shakers and drums from recycled materials with seed pods and pebbles inside.
Make wind chimes from old silverware and keys.
Record children playing and let them listen back.
Draw sounds as lines and shapes and play the drawing as a score.
Invite family musicians to play and share instruments from their culture.
Hold a dance party or a performance on the outdoor piazza.
Build a long sound path children can play as they walk along it.
Listen to rain on different surfaces, such as metal, wood, plastic and leaves, and choose favorites.
Fill glass jars with different amounts of water and tap them to compare high and low.
Use long tubes as talking pipes between two places in the yard.
Take instruments to the garden, the animal yards and the creek trail and play in response to what we hear there.
Keep a class song collection with children's own songs added to the Song book.
Instruments are piled in a heap or broken.
Children bang loudly and then leave.
The shed stays closed for days.
The same songs and instruments are used for months.
Children drum on tables and walls indoors and need a place outside to be loud.
No one stops to listen.

sections.text: The music shed becomes a place for inquiry when children explore how sound works and what it can say. Follow their questions about high and low, loud and soft, and how to make new sounds. Invite them to build instruments and compose together.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Children play the instruments freely with agreements about care. Tapping glass jars of water needs an adult at the table, and taking instruments to the creek trail follows our walk rules.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big drums to play hard with both hands, dancing and stomping to the beat, and carrying instruments out and back. Loud and fast followed by slow and soft keeps a clear rhythm.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer ear defenders, a soft instrument and a seat by the door to listen first. Playing one instrument at a time with a clear start and stop helps.
connected: Harry Partch on the Artists page, for building his own instruments from wood, glass and metal

sections.text: Pots, pans, wooden spoons, containers with lids, seeds or pebbles for shakers, and a scarf or two.

items: Make a kitchen band with pots and spoons.
Fill containers with different things and listen to the sounds they make.
Dance with scarves to music from your family's culture.
Go outside, close your eyes and listen together.
Make up a song about your day.

sections.text: Your child can play, sing, dance and lead. Let them choose the instruments and the rhythm. Your child can put pots, pans and spoons back in the cupboard and fold the scarves. A box for homemade instruments keeps them ready.

items: Which sounds can you hear right now?
How can we make it louder or softer?
I wonder what song we could make up.

sections.text: Your child is learning to listen, keep a beat and express feelings through sound and movement. Drumming and dancing give strong input to the hands and whole body, and quiet listening helps them settle again.
Send in a song your family loves, a recording or an instrument to share. You might also send in old pots, lids or metal spoons for our sound wall. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep small items for shakers sealed tight so they do not spill. Save loud play for times and places that work for everyone.

cards.title: Outdoor piazza
cards.summary: How our outdoor piazza works as a shared gathering place under the trees, where classes meet, perform, celebrate and eat together.

items: Open space for meeting time in a circle, with sit-upons or logs.
Tables for shared meals, small group work and buddies across classes.
Trees, including Asian pear, cherry, redbud and Black Lace elderberry, labeled with real photos.
Laminated documentation at children's eye level telling the stories of what happens across our school.
Chalk for drawing on the pavement.
A small stage space or a marked area for performances.
A message board for notices, invitations and maps made by children.
Mailboxes for each class so children can send letters and invitations across our school.
Shade, water and a place to set down cups and baskets.
A basket of large loose parts, such as fabric, crates and cardboard tubes, for building a stage, a market stall or a café.
A low display table for things children bring to share, such as a nest, a feather or a seed pod.

sections.text: Mostly together. The outdoor piazza is where classes meet and our community gathers. A quiet bench or corner can still hold a child who wants to watch.

Children wear shoes in the outdoor piazza. Adults confirm every plant children gather, and Black Lace elderberry leaves, stems and raw berries stay off limits. Keep documentation laminated and refresh it often.

items: Gather for meeting time and take turns sharing.
Plan and host performances, markets or celebrations.
Invite buddies from other classes to join them.
Draw with chalk and leave messages for others.
Choose documentation to share and explain it to visitors.
Help set up and clear tables for shared meals.
Deliver letters and invitations to other classes through the mailboxes.
Notice and report changes in the trees, such as redbud blossoms or ripe cherries.
Make signs and tickets for shows, markets and gatherings.

sections.text: Children clear tables, wipe them with a damp cloth and carry cups and baskets inside. Large loose parts go back to their basket and sit-upons stack by the logs. With a damp cloth and baskets nearby, children reset the piazza as part of the gathering.

Stay in the piazza with a grounded stance where you can see the whole space. Join gatherings at the children's level and keep a regular speaking voice. Narrate what you notice the group doing together.

items: I notice the redbud has changed. Tell me what you notice.
Who do you think will come here today?
How can we share what we did with everyone?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with outdoor meeting time and shared meals under the trees.
Add chalk for pavement drawing and messages.
Post laminated documentation of class work for others to see.
Invite buddies across classes for shared lunches or games.
Host a market where children trade drawings, seeds or garden flowers.
Hold performances of songs, dances and stories.
Make a map of our whole site with children and post it here.
Watch the trees through the year and record blossoms, leaves and fruit.
Hold celebrations with families, such as a harvest gathering.
Invite children to plan what the outdoor piazza needs next.
Hold a picnic snack with real dishes and cloth napkins carried out from the culinary atelier.
Play circle games and singing games from many cultures, including those families teach us.
Stretch long paper across the pavement for a shared drawing every class adds to over a week.
Open a weekly market of garden flowers, seeds, drawings and handmade books, with tickets children make.
Look closely at a painting of children playing in a town square and compare their games with ours.
The space is used only for passing through.
Documentation is old and faded.
Classes rarely meet each other here.
Children do not have a voice in what happens here.
Younger and older children rarely play side by side.
Families pass through at pick up without stopping to look.

sections.text: The outdoor piazza becomes meaningful when children see it as the heart of our community. Invite them to plan gatherings, share their work and welcome others. Notice how they use the space and add what supports those uses.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: The outdoor piazza is open to everyone, with an educator able to see the whole space. Black Lace elderberry stays off limits, and adults confirm any plant children gather here.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer chalk for big drawings made on hands and knees, carrying chairs and tables to set up gatherings, and running and chasing games in the open space.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a bench at the edge of the piazza with a clear view, a small job such as handing out napkins, and time to arrive before the group gathers.
connected: Pieter Bruegel the Elder on the Artists page, for painting a town square full of children at play

sections.text: A front step, a porch, a park bench or a corner of the yard where your family can gather.

items: Eat a meal outside together.
Invite neighbors or friends for a simple gathering.
Draw with chalk and leave messages for passersby.
Put on a family show.
Make a map of your street.

sections.text: Your child can help plan, invite, set up and host. Let them welcome guests and share what they made. Your child can wipe the table with a damp cloth, carry cups inside and stack the cushions. Sweeping the step with a small broom finishes it.

items: Who should we invite?
Tell me what you want to share.
I wonder what you noticed about our neighbors.

sections.text: Your child is learning to belong to a community and to share ideas with others. Big open space for moving, carrying and gathering helps children use their whole bodies and then settle together.
Send a photo of a family gathering or a chalk message from home to share in our outdoor piazza. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Check plants nearby are safe before children pick them. Bring water and shade on hot days.

cards.title: Creek walks
cards.summary: How we walk the creek trail next door to notice water, plants, birds and creatures through the seasons, with clear agreements and real tools.

items: Walk agreements made with children and posted with real photos, including holding an adult's hand until the group returns.
A field bag with clipboards, pencils, magnifiers, a small net, a clear bucket or viewer, and a first aid kit.
A phone with Merlin Bird ID and iNaturalist for identifying birds and plants with an adult.
A map of the creek trail that children add to on each walk.
A familiar sit spot along the trail where the group stops each time.
Sturdy shoes, layers and rain gear in the rainy season.
A small collecting bag for fallen leaves, feathers and seed pods we may bring back, after an adult checks them.
Water, a small towel and a change of socks in the field bag.
Real photos of the birds, plants and creatures of the creek trail posted in each class before and after walks.
A roll call and head count routine children help with at the start, at the sit spot and on return.

sections.text: Mostly together. Walking the creek is a shared journey. Once the group is settled at the sit spot, a child may find quiet time to watch the water alone with an adult nearby.

Our educators hold water safety certificates. A child holds an adult's hand on the walk until the group returns. Check the weather and creek level before going, and skip creek walks after heavy rain when water rises fast. Poison oak and poison hemlock grow along trails, so adults confirm every plant. Children look at creatures and put stones back where they found them. Leave plants on the bank undisturbed.

items: Help make and review the creek walk agreements.
Carry the field bag and tools.
Notice and point out birds, plants, creatures and changes in the water.
Draw and add to the creek map.
Float leaves or sticks to see how fast the water moves.
Look under stones with an adult and put them back gently.
Record what they find with drawings, words and photos.
Help count the group at each stop.
Pick with purpose and leave some for others, gathering only fallen things an adult confirms.
Share findings with their class at meeting time on return.

sections.text: Before we leave the sit spot, children pack the clipboards, magnifiers, net and viewer back into the field bag, each in its photo-labeled pocket. Back at school they rinse the net and viewer in the wash bucket and hang them on the low drying rack, then set fallen finds on a tray for the nature table. Children carry the field bag to its hook so it is ready for the next walk, and nothing waits for an educator later.

Walk at the children's pace with a steady, calm stride and a hand held in yours. Notice any worry you feel near the water and let your voice stay even. Stop often, crouch low and look and listen together in silence.

items: I notice the water is higher today. I wonder why.
Where do you think the water is going?
Who lives here that we cannot see?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with short walks to the creek trail, focusing on agreements and noticing.
Choose a sit spot and visit it each time, listening and looking for five quiet minutes.
Start a creek map that children add to on each walk.
Bring clipboards and draw what children see.
Float leaves and sticks and watch how the water carries them.
Use a clear bucket or viewer to look into the shallows.
Look for herons, egrets and other birds and use Merlin to listen for calls.
Notice plants along the creek, such as willow and sedge, and learn how Pomo weavers have gathered them for baskets.
Return in each season and compare the creek in the rainy season and in late summer.
Make a creek book with drawings, photos and children's words.
Walk to a new part of the trail and compare it with our sit spot.
Invite families to join a creek walk.
Turn around and walk back upstream to see the same creek from the other direction.
Look for tracks in the mud along the bank and draw them on clipboards.
Build small leaf and stick pieces on the bank, photograph them and leave them for the water and wind to change.
Play a listening game where children raise a finger for each new sound they hear.
Bring sound recorders and record the creek in different seasons to play back in class.
Follow a bug hunt from our own yards to the creek and compare who lives in each place.
Make a big collaborative creek map in the Studio from all the small maps children drew.
Walks feel rushed with no time to stop.
Children cannot say what they noticed.
Agreements are often forgotten.
The same route is walked without new questions.
Children collect handfuls of plants and stones without thought.
Nothing from the walk comes back into the class.

sections.text: Creek walks become meaningful when children return to the same place and notice change. Follow their questions about water, creatures and plants, and let the map, the sit spot and the creek book grow with them across the year.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.level: One adult with one or two children
setting.why: Each child holds an adult's hand from leaving until the group returns, so each adult walks with one or two children. Educators with water safety certificates stay closest to the water, and adults confirm every plant.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer walking on uneven ground and gentle banks while holding an adult hand, carrying a small backpack, and dropping stones into the water to hear the splash where it is safe.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a shorter walk on the flat part of the trail, a look at the route on a map first and a quiet listening stop. Holding the same adult hand the whole way helps.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for leaf and stick works made on rivers and left for the water to change
Elsie Allen on the Artists page, for Pomo basketry woven from sedge and willow gathered along creek banks

sections.text: A safe creek, river or stream nearby, sturdy shoes, a small notebook and a magnifier.

items: Visit the same spot by water each season and notice changes.
Float a leaf and follow it downstream.
Sit quietly and listen to the water and birds.
Draw a map of your walk.
Look under a stone together and put it back gently.

sections.text: Your child can lead the walk, notice, draw and share. Let them choose what to look at closely. Your child can carry the walk bag home, shake sand out of shoes over the garden and rinse a bucket or net at the hose. A towel by the door and a small basket for found treasures give every walk an easy ending.

items: Where do you think the water goes?
How has it changed since last time?
Who lives near the water?

sections.text: Your child is learning to observe closely and care for wild places. Walking on uneven ground builds balance, and the sounds of water and birds help many children feel calm.
Send a drawing, photo or map from a family walk by water. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Stay close and hold hands near water. Avoid creeks after heavy rain, and learn to recognize poison oak before you go.

cards.title: Kinesthetic lab
cards.summary: How we build and use the outdoor space beside the music shed as a kinesthetic lab, with body areas that are always open, where children come and go by choice and find the balance, movement, pressure and calm their bodies ask for.

items: Begin with a few strong body areas and open ground between them. Every area is open at the same time, and children move in and out freely, stay as long as their body needs and invent their own paths. Each area below names the body sense it feeds in plain words with the term.

Balance area. A low balance beam or a long log set firmly on the ground, a row of stepping stumps at different heights and spacing, a low slackline strung a hand's width above soft woodchips, and two or three wobble boards. Balance feeds the sense of movement and balance from the inner ear (vestibular) and the sense of where the body is from muscles and joints (proprioception).

Swinging and spinning area. Canvas hammocks hung from a cattle-panel arch, with a clear soft fall zone and room to walk around them, and a note pointing to the tire swing in the Tire swing yard. Back and forth swinging and slow spinning feed the movement and balance sense (vestibular).

Heavy work area. A wagon or wheelbarrow, buckets with handles, short logs, a pile of woodchips or sand to haul, a digging patch with real shovels, and sewn canvas weighted bags filled with sand in a few sizes. Pushing, pulling, lifting and carrying feed the sense of body pressure and effort from muscles and joints (proprioception).

Crash and landing area. A thick outdoor crash pad or a deep bed of woodchips, with a row of rising stumps beside it so a child chooses how high to jump from. Jumping and landing feed body pressure (proprioception) and movement and balance (vestibular).

Climbing and crawling area. A low A-frame with rungs, a cargo net pegged at a gentle slope, and a fabric or culvert tunnel to crawl through. Climbing and crawling feed body pressure (proprioception) and touch (tactile), and ask the body to plan each move (motor planning). We do not add monkey bars.

Rhythm and movement area. The open ground nearest the music shed, with drums, rhythm sticks and shakers carried out from the shed, so children drum while they move, march, freeze and use body percussion. Moving to a beat feeds listening (auditory) and movement and balance (vestibular), and helps the body plan and time its moves (motor planning).

Body awareness area. A smooth patch of pavement or a board for life-size body maps traced in chalk, an unbreakable outdoor acrylic mirror fixed low on the shed wall, and narrow gaps between posts or under a low rope to squeeze through. These feed body pressure (proprioception), seeing (visual) and the sense of what is happening inside the body (interoception).

Crossing the middle and two hands area. Ribbon wands for big figure eights, a figure-eight path painted or laid in rope on the ground, and a thick rope tied to a post for pulling hand over hand. These feed both hands working together (bilateral coordination) and crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing).

Eye tracking area. Balls to roll down a plank or gutter, a soft ball hung on a rope from a beam as a pendulum to tap and follow, and light chiffon scarves to toss and catch. Following a moving thing with the eyes feeds seeing and judging space (visual-spatial).

Calm-down corner. A shaded, sheltered nook at the edge of the lab with a hammock, cushions, a heavy lap blanket in a basket with an adult near, and a few smooth stones or a soft object to hold. Any child can choose it at any time. Deep, steady pressure and slow rocking feed body pressure (proprioception) and touch (tactile), and help many children come back to calm (self-regulation).
Loose parts such as planks, crates and short logs left between areas, so children can link areas their own way, such as a balance walk that ends in a jump.
Soft, raked woodchips under every area where a child could fall, and clear walking lanes between areas so moving children do not cross into a swing or landing zone.
A weatherproof board at the entrance with real photos of each area and a blank space for the map of the lab children draw.
A shady spot with water bottles, because big movement makes bodies hot and thirsty, and a place to sit and rest whenever a child wants.

sections.text: Both, and children choose. The hauling area, the hammock arch, rhythm and figure eights often draw friends to work and move together. Balance, crash and the calm-down corner also give a single child a place to find exactly the input their body needs, at their own pace and for as long as they need.

We think in risk and benefit and build the lab as safe as necessary. Two adults are on the lab whenever it is open, as on our large yards. Educators check every area each morning, rake woodchips back under landing and fall zones, test the slackline, hammock and pendulum ropes and knots, and take anything worn out of use. Before children use logs, stumps, boards, crates or tires, an adult with gloves turns them and looks underneath and in the gaps for black widows. Children wear shoes in the lab, climb only as high as they get themselves, and jump only from a stump they climbed onto alone. There are no monkey bars, and bikes stay on dirt paths away from the lab. Weighted bags stay light, about a tenth of a child's body weight or less. Heavy blankets are offered only with an adult right there, rest across the lap or shoulders, never cover the head or face, are never tucked or used to hold a child still, and a child takes them off any time. Adults never spin a child who has not asked, and we watch for a flushed or pale face, sweating, yawning or a sudden quiet after spinning and rest if we see them. Children are never sent to an area, moved along or given a set order. Each child follows their own body's need. Instead of saying be careful, we describe what we see and ask a question such as Where will you land? We describe what an area feeds and never label or diagnose a child.

items: Help design the lab by drawing ideas, testing set-ups and saying what their bodies want more of.
Haul stumps, roll logs, carry planks and set out loose parts to build and rebuild areas with adults.
Draw and redraw the map of the lab, and help decide where a new area goes.
Come and go as their body needs, staying in one area a long time or moving between many.
Combine areas their own way, such as hauling woodchips to the landing zone or drumming while they balance.
Check the landing zone and rake woodchips back before jumping, and look over ropes with an educator.
Make agreements together, such as how many on the slackline, where to walk around the hammocks and how we wait for the crash pad.
Carry instruments from the music shed and return them, and lead a freeze dance or a marching beat.
Trace a friend's body map in chalk and add what they notice about their own body.
Tell an educator which area helps them feel calm and which helps them feel awake, so it can go in their documentation.
Teach a younger child how to step across the stumps or pull the rope hand over hand.

sections.text: At the end of lab time, children carry back the loose parts, crates, planks and small stumps they can lift and stack them in their marked places. They rake woodchips back under the landing zones and hang the wobble boards and ropes on low hooks. An adult handles only the heavy logs and anything too big for children to move, so the lab is reset on the floor as part of the play.

Stand where you can see the whole lab, with your weight settled and your hands free, and move close to an area without hovering over it. Let each child choose where to go, how long to stay and when to leave. Keep your face calm when a child jumps higher or swings faster than you like, and notice your own worry and breathe it out. Narrate what you see, such as You landed with both feet and bent your knees, and in the calm-down corner sit low and quiet beside a child before offering anything.

items: I notice you went back to the stumps three times. Tell me about the stumps.
I wonder how your body feels after the hammock compared with after the crash pad.
Where do you feel it in your body when you pull the rope?
How did you find your balance on the wobble board?
I wonder what your body wants to do next.
It reminds me of the way you marched to the drum yesterday. Where could the march go next?
What do you see that makes you say that?

Start with an empty space and a question at meeting time. Ask children where in their bodies they love to feel movement, and walk the space together, noticing slopes, shade, sun and the sound from the music shed.
Invite children to draw what they wish the lab had, and gather the drawings on the board at the entrance. Return to them each time the lab grows.

Build the first areas with children doing real work. Haul stumps for stepping and jumping, roll a long log for balancing and spread woodchips with wheelbarrows and shovels. The building is the first heavy work.
Move or add the canvas hammocks on a cattle-panel arch, and agree together on where we walk and how many share one hammock.
Add the crash pad and set stumps of rising height beside it, so each child chooses a jump that feels right and climbs onto it alone.
Bring the music shed outside. Children carry drums and shakers into the lab for marching, freeze dances, moving fast and slow to a beat and body percussion with claps, pats and stomps.
Add the climbing and crawling area with a tunnel first, then a low A-frame, then a cargo net, testing each one with children before it opens.
Add a low slackline a hand's width above the woodchips, with a guide rope overhead to hold, and lower or raise it as children ask.
Add the eye tracking area with a ball run down a gutter, a pendulum ball on a rope and scarves to toss and catch.
Add the crossing the middle area with ribbon wands, a rope figure eight on the ground and a thick rope to pull hand over hand from a post.
Build the calm-down corner with children, choosing the shady spot, the hammock, cushions and the basket with the heavy lap blanket, and agree on how we use it quietly.
Invite children to draw a map of the lab, then redraw it each time the lab changes. Post the newest map at the entrance and keep older maps in a binder so children can see how their lab grew.

Change what we offer over time based on what we observe. Every few weeks, turn the balance log into a bridge between stumps, move the pendulum or swap the tunnel for a squeeze-through gap, and ask children what should change next.

Notice how children combine areas on their own, such as hauling woodchips to the crash pad or balancing to a drumbeat, and offer planks, crates and loose parts so they can link areas into paths and courses they plan, draw and test.

Document what each child seeks. Over several visits, note which areas a child chooses and returns to, how long they stay and how they seem afterwards, and share it with the team as a description of what the body seems to ask for, never a label.
Bring those notes to team inquiry about behavior, linking a child's return to the crash pad or the heavy blanket to the needs they may be meeting.
Ask families what their child loves to do with their body at home, and add ideas from home to the lab.
Revisit the lab each season. Add shade cloth for late summer heat, cover and drain the crash pad in the rainy season and test wet surfaces together before using them.
Children walk past the areas and gather at the gate.
The same few children use the lab and others watch from the edge.
Children wait to be told where to go next.
Children crash, climb or spin indoors at times when the lab could meet that need.
An area has not changed in weeks and children use it the same way each time.
The calm-down corner is empty or used only when an adult sends a child there.
Children no longer mention the map of the lab or ask to change anything.

sections.text: A bare yard becomes a kinesthetic lab when children help imagine it, build it with their own hands and keep changing it. Ask children what their bodies want, watch closely where they choose to go and return, and let their drawings, maps and words decide what is offered next. Over time the lab becomes a place where children learn to read their own bodies and choose the movement or the calm they need.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Two adults are on the lab whenever it is open, and an educator stays where they can see every area. The slackline, the pendulum ball and the crash pad jumps need an educator close by, and the heavy lap blanket is offered only with one adult right beside one or two children.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer longer hauling jobs with a full wagon of woodchips, repeated jumps from a stump they chose onto the crash pad and pulling hand over hand on the thick rope. Keep heavy work close by after big movement so the body has a way to settle when the child is ready.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the calm-down corner or the eye tracking area as gentle places to begin, with a choice to watch first. Offer the lowest stump, a slow sway in the hammock, the lab at a quieter time of day and as much time as the child needs.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A bit of open floor or yard, couch cushions or an old mattress for landing, a few sturdy boxes or low stools, a laundry basket, a blanket, a pillowcase, scarves or ribbons, a soft ball and a pot or bucket to drum on.

items: Lay a strip of tape or a rope on the floor to walk heel to toe, forward and backward.
Pile cushions for jumping and landing, and let your child choose a low step to jump from.
Give real heavy jobs, such as carrying the laundry basket, pushing a box of books or pulling a friend on a blanket.
Make a quiet nook with a blanket, pillows and a soft light for resting after big play.
Drum on a pot while you march, then freeze when the drum stops.
Wave ribbons or scarves in big figure eights in front of the body, and toss and catch a scarf.

sections.text: Your child can help build the course, choose what to try and in what order, and decide when they need to move and when they need to rest. Let them draw a map of the course and change it. Your child can carry cushions, balls and stepping stones back to a basket or corner after moving play. Give each thing a home they can reach so putting it away is part of the game.

items: I notice you feel calmer after carrying the basket. How does your body feel now?
I wonder where you could jump from next.
Where in your body do you feel the drum?

sections.text: Your child is learning to move with skill and to notice what their body needs. Swinging, jumping, carrying and pushing give the body movement and heavy work, which helps many children feel calm, steady and ready to focus.

Tell us what your child loves to do with their body at home, or send a photo of a course or nook you built, so we can add your ideas to our kinesthetic lab. You might also send in sturdy fabric, old pillows or a canvas bag for weighted bags. This counts toward your family participation hours.
