Check that landings are soft and away from furniture corners. Let your child climb only as high as they get by themselves, and keep blankets off the face and never tuck them in. Stop spinning when your child asks or looks flushed or pale.

cards.title: Sensory garden
cards.summary: How we build and care for a sensory garden outside the art shed, planted by sense with children across the seasons, with highly toxic plants left out and a clear caution on every other plant.

items: Begin with a few beds, one or two paths and a calm place to sit, with room left to plant with children over the year. Plant by sense so children can find a touch bed, a smell bed and a tasting bed.
Touch. Lamb's ear, soft clumping native grasses such as California fescue, smooth stones, a slab of oak bark and a shady patch of moss kept damp. Touch feeds the skin sense (tactile).

Smell. Lavender, rosemary, spearmint, lemon balm, pineapple sage, catnip, salvias and scented geranium, planted along the path edge so a child brushes them in passing. Smell feeds the nose sense (olfactory).

Taste. A separate, clearly marked tasting bed with strawberries, spearmint, lemon balm, chives, nasturtium leaves and flowers and calendula petals. Children taste only from this bed and only with an adult.

Sound. Clumping grasses that rustle in wind, wood or bamboo chimes hung in the breeze, dried hard-shell gourds and seed heads an adult has confirmed, a short gravel path that crunches underfoot and a shallow water bowl for birds. Sound feeds hearing (auditory).

Sight. Color and form that change through the seasons, with California poppies, yarrow, hummingbird sage and sunflowers, and a flat acrylic mirror set low to show the garden from a new angle. Sight feeds seeing and judging space (visual-spatial).
Underfoot. A textures path of stepping stones, oak bark, sand and smooth river stones, edged so materials stay in place, for walking in shoes and feeling each change through the soles.
A calm place to sit, such as a low bench or a ring of stumps in the shade, where a child can stop, breathe, listen and smell.

A main loop path at least three feet wide with a firm, level surface such as compacted decomposed granite, with a wider turning spot, so a wheelchair, a walker and small bodies can move along it together. The gravel and textures paths branch off this loop.
Raised beds at different heights, some high enough to reach from a seat or wheelchair and some low for the smallest children to kneel beside, with wide, smooth edges to sit on.
Low baskets, magnifiers, clipboards and pencils near the art shed door, so children can carry the garden into drawing and painting.
A small tool shelf with child-size trowels, watering cans, gloves and a hand rake.

sections.text: Both. Planting, watering and making labels are shared work, and small groups explore one sense at a time together. The calm seat and the slow paths also give a single child a quiet place to be alone with smell, sound and touch.

Only highly toxic plants stay out of the sensory garden, such as oleander, castor bean, foxglove, lily of the valley, yew, datura, angel's trumpet, azalea and rhododendron. Every other plant comes with a caution card children and families can read. For example, scented geranium, lupine and wisteria are for looking, touching and smelling, never for children to eat. Sweet pea seeds and the seeds of annual morning glories are never eaten. Our Blue Dawn morning glory is sterile and makes no seeds, so it is welcome. Our goats may eat garden plants except the highly toxic ones. Rabbits get only plants an adult knows are safe for rabbits, offered in small amounts. Usually safe are mint, basil, parsley, cilantro, dill, lemon balm, clover, dandelion, plantain, nasturtium, calendula, rose petals, strawberry leaves, raspberry and blackberry leaves, carrot tops and chard. Kept from rabbits are the onion family (chives, garlic, leeks), nightshade leaves (tomato, tomatillo, pepper, potato), azalea and rhododendron, lilies, foxglove, sweet pea, lupine, daffodils and other bulbs, ivy, yew, milkweed and pipevine. An adult confirms every plant before it goes in the ground and knows which plants carry a caution. Poison hemlock and poison oak occur on our site, so adults walk the garden and its edges and pull or report any they find. Grasses with sharp seeds, such as foxtails, are pulled because they hurt eyes, ears and paws. We use no herbicides or pesticides. Children taste only from the tasting bed and only with an adult, and we keep one adult to six children here as in the whole garden. Change the bird water every day and scrub the bowl weekly. Set the mirror so it never bounces sun into eyes or onto the animal yards. Children wear shoes on every path. Garden plants and flowers are drawn and painted, and herbs grown for tasting go to the culinary atelier, never into sensory bins.

items: Help decide what the garden needs by walking the space, smelling and touching, and drawing a plan.
Dig, plant, water and mulch with real tools alongside adults.
Make plant labels with drawings, names, dictated words and the sense each plant offers.
Bring a plant they want to grow and wait while an adult confirms it is safe.
Care for the garden by watering, pulling weeds an adult has checked, refilling the bird bowl and raking the paths.
Gather fallen petals, leaves and seed heads to draw or press, picking with purpose and leaving some for others.
Guide a friend or a visiting family through the garden, sharing a favorite smell or a soft leaf.
Carry clipboards and paints from the art shed to draw and paint what they notice.
Notice and document changes through the seasons with drawings and photographs.

sections.text: Children close each visit by hanging trowels and small forks on the photo-labeled tool board and stacking watering cans by the spigot. They sweep the paths with a child-sized broom, refill the bird bowl and set gathered petals and seed heads on a drying tray. Gloves go into the glove basket, and hands are washed, so the garden is ready for the next group with no educator work afterward.

Move slowly through the garden and sit low on the path or the bench, with your hands open and still, so children see there is no hurry. Keep your voice soft and regular, and narrate what you notice, such as You rubbed the rosemary and smelled your fingers. Stay with a child who pulls back from a texture or smell, and let them watch or use a glove without urging.

items: I notice you keep coming back to the lamb's ear. Tell me about it.
I wonder how the lavender smells in the fog compared with in the hot sun.
Where is the quietest sound in the garden?
How did you know which leaf was the mint?
It reminds me of something. Does this smell remind you of somewhere?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with a walk at meeting time. Visit the space outside the art shed and ask children how a garden can be touched, smelled, heard, seen and tasted. Record their ideas on the board in the art shed.
Invite children to draw a plan of the garden, with paths, beds and a calm seat, and build the plan with them over weeks.
Lay the main loop path first, with children hauling and raking decomposed granite and testing it with a wheelchair, a wagon and their own feet.

In autumn, when the rains begin, plant the smell and touch beds with lavender, rosemary, lamb's ear, salvias, hummingbird sage and native grasses, and scatter California poppy seeds where children choose. Autumn planting lets roots grow through our rainy season.
In winter, plant bare-root strawberries in the tasting bed, set the textures path with stepping stones, bark, sand and river stones, and watch the rain soak each one.
In early spring, add spearmint, lemon balm, pineapple sage and catnip from cuttings, and begin labels with children.
In mid spring, after the cold nights pass, sow nasturtiums, calendula and sunflowers and measure the sunflowers with children each week.
Hang chimes made with children from bamboo, wood or found metal, and grow a few hard-shell gourds on a fence to dry for shaking.
Add the bird water bowl and keep a list with Merlin Bird ID of the birds that visit.
Add the low mirror and invite children to look for the garden in it.
In summer, water deeply in the morning, mulch to keep roots cool and notice which plants handle our hot dry late summer best. Harvest lavender with children after it blooms.
In late summer and autumn, collect seeds from poppies, sunflowers, calendula and nasturtiums, dry and store them in labeled jars, and plan the next planting.
Bring the garden into the art shed. Children draw and paint the sunflowers, poppies and lamb's ear from life, mix colors to match a leaf and return to the same plant each season.
Press flowers and leaves, make earth and plant paints and dye with plants from the garden, using only plants an adult has confirmed.
Make a sensory map with children, marking where each sense lives, and update it each season.
Offer one-sense walks, such as a smell walk, a listening walk or a touch walk with hands along the bed edges, and record what children notice.
Brew herb tea from the tasting bed and the smell bed in the culinary atelier with an adult, using only herbs grown for tasting.
Invite families to help with a planting day each season, bringing cuttings an adult checks and labels with any caution.
Children pass the garden on the way to the art shed without stopping.
Labels have faded and no child has added a new one.
Plants are dry, overgrown or the same as last season.
The calm seat is empty or used for storage.
Children pick leaves without noticing them, or adults are unsure which plants are in the beds.
No drawings or paintings from the garden have appeared in the art shed lately.

sections.text: A plain strip of ground becomes a sensory garden when children plan it, plant it and care for it through every season. Return often with one sense at a time, follow the questions children ask about smell, sound and change, and carry their noticing into the art shed. Over time children come to know each plant by touch and smell and feel the garden belongs to them.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: We keep one adult to six children in the garden, and adults confirm every plant. Tasting happens only from the tasting bed with an adult right there, and digging and planting with real tools are introduced with an adult beside each child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer rubbing and crushing herbs between the fingers, walking the textures path slowly, hauling soil and mulch and pressing hands into damp moss. A smell jar of crushed rosemary or mint carried around the garden adds strong input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer garden gloves, a stick to touch with, or looking and smelling from the calm seat first. Start with one gentle plant such as lamb's ear, visit at a quiet time and let the child choose when to touch, smell or taste.

sections.text: A few pots or a small bed, potting soil, a trowel, a watering can, and safe plants such as lavender, rosemary, mint, lemon balm, lamb's ear and strawberries. Smooth stones, a small chime and a bird bowl are lovely extras.

items: Plant a smell pot with mint, lemon balm and rosemary, and rub a leaf together each day.
Grow a soft leaf such as lamb's ear for touching.
Lay a short path of stones or pavers to walk across slowly.
Hang a wind chime and listen for it on breezy days.
Grow strawberries in a pot and pick and taste them together when they ripen.
Make plant labels together with drawings and names.

sections.text: Your child can choose plants, dig, water, make labels and care for the garden each week. Let them be the guide who shows you their favorite smell or soft leaf. Your child can rinse a trowel, hang it up, sweep a path and tip the last of the watering can onto a thirsty plant. A small hook and a basket by the door help them finish the garden visit on their own.

items: I wonder which leaf smells the strongest.
How does this one feel compared with that one?
Where is that sound coming from?

sections.text: Your child is learning to notice with every sense and to care for living plants. Touching soft leaves, smelling herbs and listening in a quiet garden help many children feel calm and connected to the world around them.

Send in a cutting, seeds you saved, smooth stones or a photo of your sensory garden, and we will check each plant and label any caution before it is planted. This counts toward your family participation hours.

Leave out highly toxic plants such as oleander, castor bean, foxglove and lily of the valley. Learn which of your other plants are for looking and smelling only, and keep those away from pets. Taste only plants grown for eating, always together. Skip chemical sprays and wash hands after gardening.

cards.title: Building tall
cards.summary: Ideas for when children stack, reach and build higher and higher, with real buildings, architects and walks to look up.

sections.text: Children stack blocks, crates, stones and boxes as high as they can reach, then stand on tiptoe to add one more. They may say "Mine is taller than me" or "It goes all the way to the sky." Some children build the same tower again and again, testing which base holds. Others count the levels, compare heights, or call the tower a building, a lighthouse or a rocket. Falling towers often bring as much delight as standing ones.

items: Real photos of tall buildings, towers, bridges and cranes hung on the wall at children's eye level, beside the block area.
Photos of tall things from many places and cultures, including pagodas, minarets, stupas, cliff dwellings, lighthouses, water towers and skyscrapers.
A walk to look up, holding hands, to find the tallest things near us, from the valley oaks to power poles, rooflines and the water tower.
Lying on our backs under a valley oak or in the willow dome and looking straight up, then drawing what we saw from below.
Unit blocks in quantity, with room to build in an open floor space that stays up overnight with a "Still building" sign.
Big building materials outdoors, including crates, cardboard boxes, wood rounds and planks, for towers taller than the children.
Stacking stones and wood rounds in the Log yard, finding which sides sit flat and which rock.
Cardboard tubes, paper cups, wood spools and lids for tall, light towers that wobble and lean.
A wall of butcher paper and a long ribbon so children can mark how tall their tower got next to their own height.
Books about architects and buildings, such as Dreaming Up by Christy Hale, Iggy Peck, Architect by Andrea Beaty and Young Frank, Architect by Frank Viva.
Photos and stories of real architects and builders, including Julia Morgan, who designed many buildings across California, Zaha Hadid and the structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan.
Photos of the Watts Towers in Los Angeles, built by Simon Rodia by hand from steel, cement, tile and broken dishes.
Clipboards and pencils in the block area to draw plans before building and to draw the tower once it is done.
Clay and sticks, or playdough and toothpick-sized twigs, for small tall structures on the investigation table.
A plumb line made from string and a heavy washer, so children can see whether a tower stands straight up.
A visit from a family member who builds, designs or works on tall things, bringing real tools, plans or hard hats to look at.

sections.text: Both. One child alone can test and retest the same tower. Tall structures beyond one child's reach invite partners who hold, pass and steady pieces together.

Agree with children on how tall a tower can go indoors and who may knock it down. A common agreement is that only the builder decides when it falls. For very tall builds, children stand on the floor and use a sturdy step only with an adult beside them. Keep the area clear of walking paths so towers have room to fall safely. Photograph towers before they come down so the work is held.

items: Choose materials and gather them from the shelf or yard.
Draw a plan or a picture of the finished tower.
Decide how tall is tall enough and when the tower is finished.
Measure the tower with their bodies, string, blocks or a tape measure.
Make a sign to protect a tower that is still being built.
Teach a friend which base holds the most.
Photograph the tower and help choose the photo for the wall.
Take the tower down with care and return pieces to the shelf.

sections.text: When the builder decides a tower is finished and the photo is taken, children take it down piece by piece and carry each block to its silhouette on the shelf. Tubes, cans and loose parts go into their labeled baskets, and string or tape measures roll back into their tin. Shelf outlines and baskets at children's height make the reset part of the building time.

Sit on the floor at the edge of the building space, within arm's reach, with your hands in your lap. When a tower falls, keep your face soft and your voice regular, and narrate what you saw, such as "The top block slid and the whole side came down." Notice any urge to steady the tower and let the children find the next fix.

items: I notice the bottom is wider than the top. I wonder why.
Tell me how you chose the bottom block.
How will we know which tower is taller?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer blocks and open floor space and watch how children stack.
Hang real photos of tall buildings at children's eye level near the blocks.
Take a walk to look up and photograph the tallest things we find.
Invite children to measure towers against their own bodies and mark them on a paper strip.
Add clipboards for plans, and compare the plan with the tower afterwards.
Bring in stories of architects and engineers and ask what problems they solved.
Move outdoors to crates, boxes and planks for towers taller than an adult.
Try towers from new materials, such as paper only, cups, sticks and clay, and compare what holds.
Test towers with wind from a fan or a breath, the way real buildings face wind.
Build a shared city or skyline over many days with roads, bridges and signs.
Invite a builder or architect family member to share plans and tools.
Gather drawings, photos and children's words into a book or wall panel about how we build tall.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Building and stacking are open to everyone with agreements about height and knocking down. Standing on a step for a very tall build needs an adult beside the child, and walks to look up mean holding hands.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy building outdoors with full crates, wood rounds and big hollow blocks that need two hands and a strong lift to stack. Let them carry each piece from across the yard before it goes on the tower.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small stack of wooden cubes or flat stones on a tray at a quiet table, away from falling towers. They can watch a group build first and choose when to add a piece.
connected: Simon Rodia on the Artists page, for building tall towers by hand from found tile, glass and steel.
Julia Morgan on the Artists page, for designing many of California's buildings and towers.
Zaha Hadid on the Artists page, for tall buildings with curving, surprising shapes.

sections.text: Things that stack, such as boxes, plastic cups, wooden blocks, books, pillows, cans from the pantry shelf and clean empty containers. A tape measure or a long piece of string helps too.

items: Stack cups or boxes as high as your child can reach, then measure the tower against them.
Take a walk and look up together. Count the tallest things you see on your street.
Lie under a tree and look straight up, then draw what you saw.
Build a tower from things in a drawer and see which shapes stay up best.
Look at photos of tall buildings from around the world together and choose a favorite.

sections.text: Your child picks the materials, builds, and decides when the tower is done or when it falls. You can hold pieces when asked and ask questions. Your child can take a tower down with care and sort blocks, cups or boxes back into a basket or bin. Tracing block shapes on a shelf or using one bin per kind of thing makes it quick for small hands.

items: I wonder how tall it can get.
How could we make the bottom stronger?
Tell me what you will use next.

sections.text: Your child is learning about balance, size, measuring and solving problems, and is building patience and confidence. Lifting and stacking heavy things gives the body strong work, and lining up each block helps eyes and hands work together.
Send a photo of a tower your child built, or a photo of a tall building you saw together. Clean cardboard tubes, boxes and spools are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Build away from walkways and away from anything that could break. Agree that only the builder knocks it down. Keep stacks on the floor rather than on furniture.

cards.title: Opening things
cards.summary: Ideas for children who open, unwrap, unscrew and peek inside everything, with boxes, locks, seed pods and things to take apart.

sections.text: Children open every door, drawer, lid and bag. They unscrew caps, unzip pockets, unwrap packages and peel things apart. They may ask "What's inside?" again and again, crack open seed pods and acorns, or pry open logs to find what lives underneath. Some take apart toys and pens to see how they work.

items: A sealed box placed at meeting time with no explanation, as a question to wonder about together.
A latch board with real hardware, including hook and eye, sliding bolt, hasp, chain lock, cabinet catch and hinges.
A basket of jars and bottles with screw-top lids of many sizes, to match and open.
Padlocks with keys, combination locks for older children, and a ring of old keys to try.
Purses, wallets, coin pouches and bags with zippers, snaps, buttons, buckles and clasps.
Nesting boxes, nesting cups and boxes inside boxes, each wrapped in fabric or paper.
A take-apart table with real screwdrivers and old small appliances, such as a clock radio, keyboard, toaster or phone, prepared by an adult first.
Seed pods to open and sort, including redbud pods, iris pods, California poppy pods and acorns.
Opening logs and lifting bark in the Log yard with stick tools, then putting things back the way we found them.
Peeling and opening real food in the culinary atelier, such as mandarins, peas, pomegranates and fava pods, then sharing it at snack.
Envelopes, folded letters and lift-the-flap books in the writing center.
Photos at children's eye level of things opened up, such as a cut geode, a seed in its pod, a nest, and the inside of a clock.
Real geodes and a hammer with safety glasses, opened with an adult.
Joseph Cornell boxes on screen, with small boxes and found objects so children can make their own box worlds.

sections.text: Both. Opening is often a private, focused task that a child repeats many times. A sealed box or a take-apart project draws a small group who share tools and discoveries.

For take-apart work, an adult removes cords, batteries and anything with glass, springs under tension or stored charge. Old screens, microwaves and anything with capacitors stay out. Children wear safety glasses with hammers and geodes. Small parts stay with older children and away from the West class. Agree which things in the class are for opening and which belong to someone else.

items: Choose what to open and the tool to open it with.
Sort the parts into trays as they come apart.
Draw what they see inside before and after.
Teach a friend how a latch or lock works.
Close things back up and put lids on for the next child.
Bring a mystery object from home to open at meeting time.
Decide what the take-apart parts become next.

sections.text: Children close take-apart work by sorting screws, springs and small parts into the labeled muffin tin or trays, then hanging screwdrivers and pliers back on the outlined tool board. They wipe the work mat with a damp cloth and put the half-opened object in its own tub for tomorrow. An adult checks the tool count and puts away anything sharp, and the table is clear before the group moves on.

Sit beside the child at the latch board or take-apart table and slow your own hands down, so your body shows patience with a stiff lid. Narrate the effort you see, such as "You turned it three times and it moved." Keep your hands off the work unless a tool needs a safety check.

items: I wonder what is inside.
How do you think this was put together?
Tell me what you noticed when it opened.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer jars, lids and bags with many kinds of closures and watch which children return to.
Present a sealed box at meeting time and gather children's guesses before it opens.
Build a latch board with children and add new hardware over time.
Gather seed pods across the seasons and open them together.
Open logs and lift bark, then draw the creatures and patterns found inside.
Begin a take-apart table with one prepared object and real screwdrivers.
Sort and label the parts, and wonder together what each part did.
Use take-apart parts in sculptures and found object art.
Look at Joseph Cornell's boxes and make our own boxes of treasures.
Wrap gifts or mystery objects for another class to open.
Make a book of insides, with drawings of what we found inside pods, rocks, logs and machines.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Jars, latches, bags and seed pods are open to everyone. The take-apart table needs an adult at the table, opening geodes with a hammer is one adult with one or two children, and small parts stay away from the West class.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer stiff screw-top jars, tight clothespins, padlocks and a log to pry open with a stick tool, so hands push, twist and pull hard. A take-apart table with real screwdrivers adds strong turning work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, start with a few large easy lids, a zipper bag and a box with a soft hinge on a quiet tray. They can watch a friend open the sealed box first and choose to touch it when ready.
connected: Joseph Cornell on the Artists page, for small boxes that open onto worlds of found objects.

sections.text: Clean jars with lids, old purses and bags with zippers and clasps, envelopes, boxes inside boxes, and an old broken gadget with the cord cut off.

items: Put a small surprise inside a jar or box for your child to open.
Make a basket of containers with different lids to open and close.
Take apart an old broken toy, clock or keyboard together with a screwdriver.
Open seed pods, pine cones or peas from the garden or market.
Wrap boxes inside boxes for your child to unwrap.

sections.text: Your child does the opening, unscrewing and unwrapping, and chooses what to open next. You prepare anything with sharp edges or hidden parts first. Your child can put lids back on, sort small parts into an egg carton and return a screwdriver to its box. One tray for opened things keeps the work safe and easy to come back to.

items: I wonder what is inside.
How do you think this opens?
Tell me what you found.

sections.text: Your child is building hand strength and finding out how things are made and fit together. Twisting, pulling and prying gives small hands strong work and helps both hands learn to work as a team.
Send in clean jars with lids, old keys, locks, purses or a broken gadget with the cord, batteries and glass removed. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Remove batteries, cords and glass before taking anything apart. Keep small parts away from younger siblings. Agree on which drawers and cupboards are for opening.

cards.title: Hiding and enclosing
cards.summary: Ideas for children who build dens, wrap things up, climb into boxes and hide, with fabric, crates, willow and wrapping.

sections.text: Children crawl under tables, into boxes and behind curtains. They build fences around toy animals, wrap dolls and objects in cloth, fill bags with bags, and cover a whole paper with paint. They play peekaboo and hide and seek, bury treasures in sand, and ask for the small space to themselves. A child may say "Nobody can find me" or "This is my house."

items: Large fabric, sheets, clips and clothespins near tables and low branches for building dens.
Big cardboard boxes indoors and outdoors to climb into, cut windows in and live inside.
Crates, tires and hammocks outdoors for enclosing and enveloping, with fabric to drape over them.
The willow dome in the garden as a hiding place, with baskets of cushions or books carried in.
Blocks and small fences with real-photo animal figures, to build pens, barns and yards.
Fabric scraps, paper, string and tape for wrapping objects, stones and dolls.
Envelopes, bags, purses, baskets and boxes with lids for hiding small treasures.
Burying and finding treasures in the sand area with scoops and brushes.
Peekaboo with scarves for the West class, and lift-the-flap books.
Real photos at children's eye level of dens and shelters, such as nests, burrows, tents, yurts and tule houses.
Photos of Do Ho Suh's see-through fabric houses, full-size rooms sewn from thin cloth that people walk inside.
Photos of Patrick Dougherty's woven stick houses, and willow to weave into our own den.
Painting over a whole paper or covering an object fully with paper collage.
A quiet, enclosed spot inside each class, such as a tent or a canopy with soft light.

sections.text: Both. A child often seeks a space alone or with one friend for calm. Building a big den brings a group together to plan, carry and drape.

Educators keep sightlines into dens and hiding spots and know where every child is. Leave gaps or open sides, use only breathable fabric, and keep plastic bags and cords out of den play. Hiding places stay inside our boundaries, and children agree on where hiding is welcome. Being enclosed is often how a child finds calm, so protect these spaces.

items: Choose the spot and the materials for a den.
Drape, clip and tie fabric with help as needed.
Decide who is invited in and how many fit.
Wrap objects and present them to others.
Make signs or doors for the den.
Take the den down and fold the fabric together.
Find a quiet enclosed space when they need it.

sections.text: Children close a den by unclipping the clips into their basket, then folding each sheet or cloth with a partner, corner to corner. Folded fabric goes onto the low shelf by color or size, and crates and cushions go back to their marked spots. Taking the den down together is part of building it, so the space is reset on the floor.

Stay close by and let the den belong to the children, sitting at the opening at their level when invited. Use a quiet, regular voice and resist peeking in or pulling the cloth back. A child who has gone inside to settle needs your steady presence nearby more than conversation.

items: I wonder how it feels inside.
How will people know this is your house?
Tell me what you could wrap next.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Leave fabric and clips out and notice who builds and who hides.
Add big boxes and let children decide what they become.
Build pens and enclosures for animal figures in the block area.
Offer wrapping with fabric, paper and string, and wrapped mystery objects.
Look at photos of real shelters and wonder who lives in each.
Look at Do Ho Suh's fabric houses and wrap something big together in cloth, such as a chair, a crate or a stump.
Weave willow or sticks into a den in the garden, with Patrick Dougherty's work as inspiration.
Make maps of the best hiding places on our site.
Create small worlds in boxes, with rooms, doors and windows.
Build a class den that stays up for many days and is cared for by the group.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator keeps sightlines into every den and knows where each child is. Hammocks and dens built with fabric over crates need agreements and an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a snug box or tunnel to squeeze into, a heavy blanket to roll up in with an adult close, or cushions piled on top of their den. Building the den with crates and big fabric adds lifting and stretching.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small calm den with a light cloth, one opening they can see out of and a soft cushion in a quiet corner. They can keep the opening wide and decide who comes in.
connected: Do Ho Suh on the Artists page, for sewing full-size houses and rooms from thin, see-through fabric.
Patrick Dougherty on the Artists page, for weaving sticks into houses people can walk inside.
Christo and Jeanne-Claude on the Artists page, for wrapping whole buildings in fabric and for Running Fence, which crossed Sonoma and Marin counties in 1976.

sections.text: Sheets, blankets, clothespins, pillows, a big cardboard box, scarves and paper for wrapping.

items: Build a fort with sheets over chairs or a table.
Turn a big box into a house with a door and window.
Wrap small toys or stones in paper or cloth and take turns unwrapping.
Play peekaboo or hide and seek.
Make a cozy corner with pillows for reading or resting.

sections.text: Your child plans and builds the hiding space, chooses who comes in, and decides what to wrap. You can help with the heavy parts. Your child can unclip a blanket fort, fold the sheets with you and carry the cushions back to the couch. A basket just for clips and cloths makes the next den quick to build and quick to close.

items: Who could live in here?
How can we make it darker or lighter?
I wonder what we could wrap next.

sections.text: Your child is learning about space, size and shape, and is finding ways to feel calm and safe. Squeezing into small spaces and wrapping up snugly gives the body gentle pressure, which helps many children settle.
Send a photo of a fort or den your child built. Old sheets, scarves and big boxes are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use breathable fabric and keep plastic bags and cords away from hiding play. Keep hiding spots where you can see or hear your child.

cards.title: Throwing and launching
cards.summary: Ideas for children who throw, drop, kick and launch, with targets, catapults, ramps and splatter painting in places made for it.

sections.text: Children throw sand, toys, balls and blocks. They drop things from high places to watch them fall, kick everything, and swing sticks. They may fling paint, squirt water and run and jump. A child may say "Watch how far!" Throwing is often a child exploring force, distance and how things move through the air.

items: A throwing place outdoors with a clear line to stand behind and things made for throwing.
Soft balls of many sizes and weights, fabric throwing bags and rolled socks.
Targets to aim for, such as buckets, tires, hoops hung from branches and chalk circles on the ground.
Wet sponges thrown at a wall or fence on a hot day, leaving marks that dry and disappear.
Splatter painting outdoors on huge paper, flicking brushes, shaking pine branches and squeezing bottles of tempera.
Catapults from a spoon taped to a block, or a board on a log, launching pom poms and pine cones.
Paper airplanes and paper helicopters, flown and changed and flown again.
Ramps, gutters and tubes for rolling balls, with a drop zone at the bottom.
A drop spot at a safe height, testing chicken feathers, leaves, scarves and balls to see which falls first.
Seed launching in nature, such as Japanese maple seeds that spin down and pods that snap open.
Water squirters and spray bottles for aiming at painted targets on the fence.
Stomp rockets and a long open space to chase where they land.
Real photos at children's eye level of throwers, jugglers, divers and birds diving, and of arrows and arcs.
Hammering nails into stumps in the Log yard, with an adult and safety glasses.
Jackson Pollock's flung paintings on screen, then painting on the ground with whole-arm motion.

sections.text: Both. Throwing at a target can be a long, solo practice. Launching and splatter painting become shared experiments where children take turns, fetch and compare.

Agree together on what we throw, where we throw and when we look first. Things made for throwing go to places made for throwing, and never at people or animals. Rocks and sand stay low to the ground. Set throwing zones away from paths and the animal yards. Throwing is a child meeting a need to move things through the air, and our job is to give it a place.

items: Help choose and set up the throwing place and its line.
Make and test their own targets and launchers.
Fetch and return balls for the next thrower.
Decide on and remind each other of the agreements.
Measure distances with string, sticks or steps.
Record which things flew farthest or landed first.
Clean up the splatter area with brushes and water.

sections.text: Children gather every ball, beanbag and launcher into the basket for each kind, then carry targets back to their spot on the shelf or fence. Where there was splatter, they scrub with brushes from the wash bucket and rinse brushes before hanging them to dry. The throwing line comes up last, so the zone is closed by the throwers themselves.

Stand at the throwing line with a relaxed body and an easy face, so the space feels safe for strong arms. Narrate distance and force, such as "That one went past the tire." Notice your own tension about things flying and stay with the children through the noise.

items: I wonder which one will go the farthest.
How could you throw it softer?
Where do you think it will land?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Set up a throwing place outdoors and notice how children use it.
Add targets of different sizes and distances.
Measure throws with string or steps and mark landing spots with flags.
Build catapults with blocks and spoons, and change the length of the arm.
Fold and fly paper airplanes and helicopters, and test changes.
Try drop tests from a height with many materials.
Splatter paint outdoors on a huge shared sheet.
Watch seeds, leaves and chicken feathers fly, and wonder how plants move their seeds.
Look at Jackson Pollock's paintings and paint with whole-body motion.
Invite a family member who juggles, plays ball or flies kites to share.
Gather photos and drawings into a book about how things fly and fall.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays at the throwing place so throwing goes only where it is welcome. Hammering nails is one adult with one or two children in safety glasses, and drop tests from a height are set up by an adult.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy throws such as beanbags, wet sponges or a weighted ball pushed at a big target, and soft balls thrown hard at a fence. Carrying the full bucket of balls back to the line adds more strong work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet drop spot where they let go of scarves and feathers from a low step and watch them float down. They can stand back from the throwing line and choose when to join.
connected: Jackson Pollock on the Artists page, for flinging and dripping paint across huge canvases on the floor.

sections.text: Soft balls, rolled-up socks, paper, a laundry basket or buckets for targets, and a spray bottle.

items: Set up a target game with a basket and rolled socks.
Fold paper airplanes and see whose goes farthest.
Drop a feather, a leaf and a ball at the same time and watch.
Throw wet sponges at a fence or wall outside on a warm day.
Fly a kite or throw a ball in a park.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to throw, sets up targets and decides how far to stand. Together you agree on safe things and safe places for throwing. Your child can collect balls into a bucket, bring the target in and rinse any messy spots with a sponge and water. A bucket that lives by the door means the game ends with everything back in one place.

items: How far do you think it will go?
I wonder what happens if you throw it a different way.
Tell me which one fell first.

sections.text: Your child is learning about force, distance and aim, and is building strong arms and coordination. Throwing hard and aiming gives arms strong work and helps eyes and body work together.
Send a photo or drawing of a throwing game your child invented. Old socks, soft balls and clean squeeze bottles are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Agree that soft things are for throwing indoors and that we never throw at people or pets. Give your child a place to throw so they can meet this need.

cards.title: Carrying and transporting
cards.summary: Ideas for children who fill bags, load wagons and move things from place to place, with real carrying work around our site.

sections.text: Children fill bags, purses, buckets and wagons and move them across the room or yard. They may carry all the blocks to the home area, push loaded wheelbarrows, or move sand to the mud kitchen one scoop at a time. They pile things into pockets and deliver them to friends. A child may say "I'm moving house" or "Special delivery."

items: Bags, baskets, backpacks, purses and buckets of many sizes within easy reach.
Wagons, wheelbarrows, carts and sleds outdoors, with heavy and light things to move.
Real carrying jobs, such as carrying water to the garden beds, compost to the bins and feed to the chickens.
Harvest baskets in the garden and the orchard, carried to the culinary atelier.
Moving wood rounds and planks in the Log yard with partners and dollies.
Pouring and carrying water from the long yard sink to the mud kitchen in buckets and watering cans.
Delivery play with mail bags, boxes and a delivery route between classes.
Real photos at children's eye level of people carrying things in many cultures, such as baskets on heads, babies in slings and goods on bicycles.
Photos of Pomo burden baskets and the work of Pomo basket weavers such as Mabel McKay and Elsie Allen.
Pulleys and a rope over a branch with a bucket, to lift and lower loads.
A rule that materials may travel between areas, with return baskets so they come home.
Trucks and trains with real loads of stones, acorns and sand in the block area.
Tote bags children decorate and use to carry treasures home.

sections.text: Both. A child carrying alone is often deep in their own plan. Heavy loads, long routes and real jobs bring children together to share the weight.

Ask whether our rules let children move materials from one area to another. Offer that freedom with return baskets and a clean-up song so materials come home. Children lift with bent knees and share heavy loads. Carrying is heavy work that often calms and organizes a busy body.

items: Choose what to carry and the best container for it.
Take on real jobs that move things around the site.
Plan routes and decide where things are going.
Ask a friend for help with a heavy load.
Return materials to their homes at clean-up time.
Teach younger children how to push a wheelbarrow.

sections.text: Children who love to carry do the close. They load wagons and baskets with the materials they moved and roll them back to each area, where photo labels show where everything lives. Wheelbarrows and wagons are parked in their marked spots, and the clean-up song ends with everything home and no adult hauling later.

Walk alongside the load at the child's pace and keep your hands free unless a partner is asked for. Narrate the work, such as "You leaned back to pull the wagon up the slope." A spill along the way is part of the job, so let your face stay calm and offer a broom alongside them.

items: Where is this load going?
I wonder how many it can hold.
How could we make this easier to carry?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Add more bags and containers and notice where children carry things.
Allow materials to travel and add return baskets.
Offer wagons and wheelbarrows with heavy loads outdoors.
Give children real carrying jobs in the garden and animal yards.
Look at photos of how people carry things around the world.
Weigh loads with a scale and compare full and empty.
Build pulleys and ramps to move heavy things.
Look at Pomo burden baskets and wonder how they were made and carried.
Create a delivery service between classes.
Map the routes children use most when they carry.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Carrying bags, baskets and buckets is open to everyone. Heavy wood rounds, wagons on slopes and pulleys over a branch need an educator nearby, and carrying jobs in the garden keep one adult to six children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer full watering cans, buckets of sand or compost, a wagon loaded with wood rounds, or a wheelbarrow to push up a slope. Give real jobs with a destination, such as moving mulch to a garden bed.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small basket or bag with a few light things and a short, quiet route. They can walk beside a partner pulling the wagon first and choose a load when ready.
connected: Mabel McKay on the Artists page, for Pomo baskets made to gather and carry.

sections.text: Bags, baskets, a backpack, a small wagon or laundry basket, and things to carry, such as groceries, books and laundry.

items: Let your child carry a bag of groceries in from the car.
Fill a wagon or laundry basket with toys and move them to a new place.
Carry water in a watering can to plants.
Pack a bag for a trip with things your child chooses.
Carry laundry from room to room together.

sections.text: Your child chooses what to carry, how to pack it and where it goes. You can share heavy loads. Your child can carry laundry baskets, groceries in a small bag or toys in a wagon back where they belong. Heavy work at tidy-up time is a real job they can feel proud of.

items: How much can you carry?
Tell me the best way to carry this.
Where should it go?

sections.text: Your child is building strength and learning about weight, size and planning. Carrying heavy loads gives muscles and joints strong work, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in old bags, purses, backpacks or baskets for our carrying play. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep loads light enough for your child to carry safely. Bend knees to lift. Have a place for things to come back home.

cards.title: Knocking down and crashing
cards.summary: Ideas for children who knock down, crash, smash and tear, with towers built to fall, pendulums, pounding and taking apart.

sections.text: Children build towers just to knock them down, crash cars together, stomp on sandcastles and tear paper into pieces. They may push over a friend's blocks, kick piles of leaves or bang objects together to hear the sound. A child may shout "Crash!" or "Earthquake!" and laugh as things fall. Knocking down is often a child exploring change, force and cause and effect.

items: Towers built only to be knocked down, from cardboard boxes, foam blocks, cups and tubes, in an open space.
Bowling with wood rounds, cardboard tubes or stacked cups and a heavy ball.
A pendulum wrecking ball, a weighted ball or sock on a rope hung from a branch, swung at a box tower.
Car crash ramps in the block area, where cars race down and knock over a target at the bottom.
Sandcastles built and washed away with buckets of water, or waves made in a long tray.
Ice blocks with tools, small hammers and warm water to break them open.
Pounding clay with fists and mallets, and smashing playdough flat.
Tearing paper, cardboard and newspaper into pieces, then using the pieces in collage.
Crushing chalk with salt in a mortar and pestle to make powder for a layered jar.
Stomping on bubble wrap and crunching dry leaves in fall.
A paper wall or screen stretched on a frame to run through or punch through.
Take-apart work with screwdrivers on old machines prepared by an adult.
Real photos at children's eye level of demolition, waves breaking, avalanches, trees falling and old buildings coming down.
On screen, Jean Tinguely's machine that broke itself apart, Cornelia Parker's exploded shed hung in the air, and Saburo Murakami running through paper screens.

sections.text: Both. A child alone may knock down the same tower many times. Group crashing needs an agreement on who knocks down what, and when, and children often enjoy rebuilding together.

A common agreement is that only the builder decides when their own work falls, and everyone can ask the builder. Set crash zones away from other building and from paths. Use materials that fall softly indoors. Knocking down is a child meeting a need to change things and see what happens. Give it a place and a time, so it can happen safely.

items: Build structures with the plan to knock them down.
Decide when and how the crash happens.
Ask builders before knocking down shared work.
Set up and reset bowling pins and targets.
Use the broken pieces to make something new.
Clean up and sort pieces after the crash.

sections.text: After the crash, children sort the fallen blocks, pins and boxes into their labeled baskets and stack crash-zone pieces on their shelf outline. A child-sized broom and dustpan stay close for any crumbs of cardboard. Resetting the pins is part of the game, so the area closes on the floor while the play is still going.

Stay in the space at the child's level with a calm, open face when things fall, since children borrow our ease with collapse. Speak in a regular voice and narrate cause and effect, such as "The ball hit the bottom and the top came down last." If a crash lands on a friend's work, come close first and help both children breathe before talking it through.

items: Where do you think the pieces will land?
I wonder which part fell first.
How could you make it fall a different way?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer soft building materials in a crash zone and notice how children use them.
Agree together on who can knock down what.
Add bowling and pendulum swinging to test force and aim.
Build ramps and see what crashes and what stays standing.
Pound and smash clay, ice and chalk with real tools.
Run through a paper wall and use the torn paper for art.
Look at artists who broke things to make art and wonder why they did it.
Take apart old machines and build new sculptures from the parts.
Watch videos of real demolition and building, and wonder what comes next.
Gather photos of before and after into a book about change.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays near the crash zone so only agreed work comes down. The pendulum ball and pounding ice need an adult close by, and take-apart work needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big cardboard box towers to push over with the whole body, a weighted wrecking ball swung at a stack, and clay to pound with fists and mallets. Stomping on bubble wrap and crunching dry leaves add strong pressure and sound.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer small soft towers of foam blocks or paper cups, knocked down with one finger or a slow rolled ball. They can watch from a set spot a few steps away and hear a countdown before each crash.
connected: Jean Tinguely on the Artists page, for a machine built to break itself apart.
Cornelia Parker on the Artists page, for a blown-up shed whose pieces hang in the air.
Saburo Murakami on the Artists page, for running through paper screens to make art.

home.title: Knocking down and crashing at Home

sections.text: Empty boxes, plastic cups, paper towel tubes, a soft ball, newspaper, ice cubes and a sandbox or tray of sand.

items: Stack cups or boxes and knock them down with a ball.
Build sandcastles and wash them away with water.
Freeze small toys in ice and break them free with warm water and a spoon.
Tear newspaper into strips and use it for a collage.
Crunch dry leaves or stomp on bubble wrap.

sections.text: Your child builds, decides when it falls and invents new ways to knock things down. You agree together on what is okay to knock down. Your child can pick up every piece after a crash and sort them into a basket or bin. Setting up the pins again for the next round makes cleaning up part of the fun.

items: Where will the pieces land?
How can we build it back?
I wonder how else we could knock it down.

sections.text: Your child is learning about force, cause and effect, and how things change. Pushing, pounding and crashing give the body strong work, which helps many children feel steady after big energy.
Send a photo of a crash game your child made up, or donate boxes and tubes for building and crashing. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use soft and light things indoors. Agree that your child's own builds can be knocked down, and others' work only with permission.

cards.title: Spinning and rolling
cards.summary: Ideas for children who spin, twirl, roll and turn wheels, with tops, wheels, spin painting and rolling down hills.

sections.text: Children twirl in circles until they are dizzy, roll down slopes, spin on the tire swing and watch wheels turn. They draw circles and spirals, roll balls, turn knobs and unscrew lids, and spin tops and coins. A child may lie on the floor to watch a car's wheels go round. Spinning and rolling are often a child meeting a need for movement and balance.

items: The tire swing in the orchard, with children deciding how fast and how long to spin.
Rolling down a grassy slope, and rolling in the leaves in fall.
Spinning tops of many kinds, including wooden tops, string tops and tops children make from spools and pencils.
A lazy susan or turntable with paper and paint for spin painting.
A salad spinner kept in the Studio as an art tool, with paper and a few drops of paint.
Pinwheels and whirligigs in the garden, and paper helicopters to drop and watch spin.
Scarves, ribbons and ribbon wands for twirling and dancing at music time.
Wheels, gears, pulleys and spools on the investigation table, with nuts, bolts and axles to build moving things.
Rolling marbles and pebbles in paint in a tray, and rolling balls down ramps.
A banding wheel or turntable for clay, to coil and turn.
Real photos at children's eye level of things that spin, such as windmills, water wheels, Ferris wheels, potter's wheels and dancers.
Spirals in nature to look for and draw, such as snail shells, fern fronds and sunflower centers.
Alexander Calder's mobiles on screen, and hanging our own mobiles that turn in the breeze.

sections.text: Both. Spinning alone lets a child feel their own body and decide when to stop. Spinning games, wheels and rolling races invite friends to take turns and share.

The spinning child decides how fast and when to stop, and adults stop the tire swing when asked. Watch for children who seem unwell after spinning and give them time to rest. Keep spinning space clear of hard edges. Some children spin and roll to calm and organize their bodies, so offer it freely.

items: Decide how fast and how long they spin.
Make their own tops and test them.
Set up spin painting and choose colors.
Teach friends how to wind a string top.
Build wheels and moving things with real tools.
Take turns and count turns on the tire swing.

sections.text: Children carry tops, wheels and rolling things back to their baskets and wipe the spin painting tray with a damp sponge. Brushes go into the wash bucket, then onto the drying rack, and paper goes to the drying rack too. An adult handles anything heavy, so the space closes as part of the spinning time.

Stay near the tire swing or slope, low and within reach, and watch faces and bodies closely. Keep your voice slow and even, and let the child choose speed and stopping. When a child seems dizzy or wound up, sit with them on the ground and breathe together before offering anything new.

items: I wonder how your body feels when you stop spinning.
How did it slow down?
Tell me what happens to the colors when it spins.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Notice when and where children spin and roll, and give it space and time.
Offer tops, wheels and pinwheels to test.
Spin paint on a turntable or in a salad spinner.
Make tops from spools, lids and sticks.
Build carts and vehicles with real wheels and axles.
Look for spirals in nature and draw them.
Dance and twirl with scarves to different music.
Hang mobiles inspired by Alexander Calder.
Compare things that roll and things that do not.
Gather photos and drawings of spinning things into a book.

setting.why: An educator stays near the tire swing and slope and watches each child's face. Marbles and small wheels stay away from the 2s, and spin painting with the salad spinner works best with an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the tire swing with them choosing the speed, rolling down the grassy slope again and again, and log rolls across a mat. Watch for signs they have had enough, and offer heavy work such as pushing a wagon afterward.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer small spinning things to watch, such as tops, a salad spinner or pinwheels, while their own body stays still. They can sit on the tire swing with feet on the ground and rock gently.
connected: Alexander Calder on the Artists page, for mobiles that turn and move with the air.

sections.text: Tops, a lazy susan or turntable, paper, washable paint, balls, a hill or soft grass, and scarves.

items: Spin tops on a smooth table and watch them slow down.
Roll down a grassy hill together.
Spin paint on paper on a turntable.
Twirl with scarves to music.
Look for wheels and things that spin around your home.

sections.text: Your child chooses how and when to spin and roll, and decides when to stop. You can join in and watch together. Your child can gather tops and balls into a basket and wipe a spin painting bowl with a sponge. A towel and a small bucket of water nearby make the mess easy for them to handle.

items: How do you feel when you stop?
I wonder which one spins the longest.
Where do you see spinning in our house?

sections.text: Your child is building balance and body awareness and learning about motion. Spinning and rolling feed the body's sense of balance, and many children feel more settled when they choose how fast to go.
Send in old tops, spools or wheels, or a photo of your child spinning or rolling. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Clear space around your child and give time to rest after spinning. Let your child decide when to stop.

cards.title: Climbing and high places
cards.summary: Ideas for children who climb everything and seek high places, with real challenge, safe heights and the view from above.

sections.text: Children climb onto tables, shelves, fences and anything they can reach. They seek the highest point in the yard and jump off. They may hang upside down, balance on logs or climb trees, and say "Look how high I am!" Climbing is often a child testing their body, building confidence and seeing the world from a new place.

items: Crates, spools, planks and ladders outdoors for children to build their own climbing structures.
Stumps and logs in the Log yard for stepping, balancing and jumping.
Trees with low, strong branches that adults have checked for climbing.
Balance beams and stepping stones at different heights.
Obstacle courses children design and change.
Rope ladders, cargo nets or knotted ropes hung from strong branches.
Binoculars and spyglasses to look out from high places.
Drawing the yard from above after climbing up high, and drawing it from below.
Photos taken from high places, and wondering what birds see from above.
Real photos at children's eye level of climbers, mountains, trees, bridges and rooftops.
Books about climbing and high places, and Faith Ringgold's Tar Beach, where a girl flies over the city.
Tomás Saraceno's climbable net sculptures on screen, and a net or web of rope to climb in our yard.
Climbing in place for indoor days, such as a sturdy step stool, a climbing triangle or a ladder with mats.

sections.text: Both. A climber often works alone to find the next foothold. Building climbing structures and taking turns on a ladder brings children together.

Children climb as high as they can get themselves. Adults stay close without lifting children up or placing them on high things. Use words that help children notice their bodies, such as "Where will your foot go next?" and "Is that branch strong?" Check surfaces below for softness and clear them of hard objects. Climbing is a child meeting a need for height and risk, so offer places made for climbing.

items: Choose where to climb and how high to go.
Build and change their own climbing courses.
Check that branches, crates and planks are steady.
Help friends find the next foothold with words.
Decide when they need help and ask for it.
Take turns at the top and wait at the bottom.

sections.text: Children carry back the crates, small planks and cushions they can lift and stack them in their marked places, checking each one is steady. They rake woodchips back under the climbing spots with a child-sized rake. An adult moves only the long planks and heavy frames, and the course is reset by the climbers before the next group.

Stand close with soft knees and quiet hands, ready to spot without lifting a child up to a place they cannot reach alone. Notice your own worry about heights and keep your face and voice calm, since children read our fear. Narrate what you see, such as "Your foot found the knot," and let them plan the way down.

items: Tell me what you can see from up there.
I wonder how you will get down.
Where will your foot go next?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Notice where children climb and offer places made for climbing.
Add crates, planks and ladders for children to build climbing structures.
Look out from high places with binoculars and draw what we see.
Talk together about how to climb safely and what to check first.
Add rope ladders and nets in strong trees.
Design obstacle courses and change them often.
Look at photos of climbers and mountains and wonder how they did it.
Read Tar Beach and imagine flying over our town.
Map our yard from above after looking down from high places.
Gather photos and children's words about climbing into a book.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays close enough to spot without lifting, and two adults are on the large yards. Climbing trees and rope ladders in branches needs an adult right beside the climber.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer rope ladders, cargo nets and checked tree branches where they pull up their whole weight, plus crates and planks they move to build higher routes. Hanging from a bar and jumping onto a crash mat add strong input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer low stumps, stepping stones and a wide balance beam a few inches off the ground, with an adult's hand offered. They can watch from the ground first and choose the next step themselves.
connected: Faith Ringgold on the Artists page, for a story quilt where a girl flies above the rooftops.
Tomás Saraceno on the Artists page, for huge nets people climb high in the air.
The Image of the Child lens

home.title: Climbing and high places at Home

sections.text: A safe place to climb, such as a park, a tree with low branches, or cushions and a sturdy step stool indoors.

items: Visit a park with climbing structures or rocks.
Find a tree with low branches to climb together.
Build an obstacle course with cushions and chairs.
Look out from a high place and talk about what you see.
Climb stairs and count the steps together.

sections.text: Your child chooses where to climb and how high to go. You stay close and help with words more than hands. Your child can drag cushions back to the couch and stack step stools or small crates where they live. Ask them to look over the space and decide when it is ready for the next climb.

items: Tell me what you can see from up there.
Where will your foot go next?
How will you get down?

sections.text: Your child is building strength, balance and confidence in their own body. Climbing and hanging give muscles strong work and help the body learn balance and where it is in space.
Send a photo of your child climbing or of a view from a high place. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Let your child climb only as high as they can get by themselves. Check that what they climb is steady and that the ground below is soft.

cards.title: Power, superheroes and good guys
cards.summary: Ideas for children who play heroes, good guys and bad guys, with capes, powers, stories and real helpers.

sections.text: Children run and chase as heroes and bad guys. They wear capes, make shields and swords, and shout "I'm the strongest!" They build jails and traps, rescue friends and invent powers. They may tell stories of good and bad, and argue over who is the hero. This play is often a child exploring power, fairness, fear and being capable.

items: Open fabric for capes, masks children design, and shields from cardboard.
A wide outdoor space for chasing, with agreements made together.
Story dictation and story acting at meeting time, where children's own hero stories are acted out by the group.
Blocks and loose parts for building jails, traps and hero bases.
Small world figures made from wooden pegs, fabric and paper for children to make their own heroes.
Heavy work as real power, such as carrying full watering cans, moving logs and pushing wheelbarrows.
Real helpers on our site and in our town, such as firefighters, nurses, gardeners and animal caretakers, with real photos at children's eye level.
Real photos of everyday people doing brave and kind things.
Drawing and naming their own powers, and wondering what their power is for.
Hero songs and chants children invent for meeting time.
An emergency helpers area with first aid kits, real bandages and uniforms.
Faith Ringgold's Tar Beach, where a girl flies over the city, and Kehinde Wiley's portraits of everyday people painted in heroic poses.
Books about bravery and fairness, and books where children are the heroes.

sections.text: Both. Hero play is often a big group game with roles to share and negotiate. Drawing powers, building figures and telling hero stories can be quiet and solo.

Pretending to be powerful is different from hurting. Agree together on chasing rules, such as "Stop means stop" and "Everyone in the game chose to play." Decide as a group how sticks and swords are used. Stay close, comment on what you see, and join only when invited. Watch for children left out and help them find a way in. Hero play often meets a deep need to feel strong and capable.

items: Make their own capes, masks and shields.
Invent heroes, powers and stories.
Agree together on game rules and remind each other.
Act out stories at meeting time.
Decide who is in the game and help others join.
Use their power to help in real ways around the school.

sections.text: Heroes close the play by hanging capes on low hooks and setting masks and shields in their basket. Children check that sticks and swords go back to the agreed bin, and they gather any fabric or tape used for costumes. Putting the gear away is part of the game, so nothing waits for an educator later.

Stay in the play space with a steady body and a regular voice, ready to step in close before a game tips into hurt. Narrate strength and care, such as "You carried your friend's bag all the way to the base." Notice any discomfort with loud power play and let curiosity about the story lead your face.

items: Tell me what makes someone a hero.
I wonder what your power is for.
How does the story end for the bad guy?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Watch and listen to hero play before making rules.
Make agreements together and post them with children's drawings.
Offer fabric, cardboard and tape for making hero gear.
Begin story dictation and story acting at meeting time.
Invent hero figures for small world play.
Give heroes real jobs, such as helping in the garden and caring for animals.
Invite real helpers to visit or visit them.
Wonder together about fairness, power and kindness.
Look at artists who show everyday people as heroes.
Make a book of our heroes, their powers and their stories.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Chasing and power play need an educator nearby who can step in before a game tips into hurt. Sticks used as swords follow group agreements with an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer hero training with real strong work, such as carrying full watering cans, pushing a loaded wheelbarrow, or a rescue course of crawling, climbing and dragging a heavy bag to safety. Chasing in a wide outdoor space with agreed boundaries gives room to run.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer small world heroes made from wooden pegs and fabric at a quiet table, where the story happens in their hands. They can design a power or a shield in the Studio and join the bigger game when they choose.
connected: Faith Ringgold on the Artists page, for a story quilt where a girl flies and claims the city.
Kehinde Wiley on the Artists page, for portraits of everyday people in heroic poses.

home.title: Power, superheroes and good guys at Home

sections.text: Old fabric for capes, cardboard, tape, paper and markers, and a safe place to run.

items: Make a cape or mask together.
Draw your child's hero and their power.
Talk about real helpers in your family and neighborhood.
Play chase with agreements about stopping.
Tell a hero story together and act it out.

sections.text: Your child invents heroes, powers and stories and makes their own gear. You help make agreements about safe play. Your child can hang capes on a hook and sort masks and props into a basket of their own. Give it a name together, such as the hero box, so tidying is part of the story.

items: Tell me about your power.
Who helps people in our family?
I wonder what makes someone brave.

sections.text: Your child is exploring power, fairness and feelings, and building confidence and imagination. Running, lifting and rescuing give the body strong work, which helps many children feel calm and in charge of themselves.
Send in old fabric for capes, or a photo or drawing of your child's hero. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Agree together that stop means stop and that pretend play does not hurt. Keep capes short and not tied around the neck.

cards.title: Family and babies
cards.summary: Ideas for children who care for babies and play family, with real baby things, family photos, baby animals and lullabies.

sections.text: Children feed, rock, wrap and bathe dolls. They play mother, father, grandparent, sibling and baby, and talk about new babies at home. They may want to be the baby, crawl and use baby talk. A child may say "I'm the big sister" or "Shh, the baby is sleeping." This play is often a child exploring care, belonging and their own place in a family.

items: Baby dolls of many skin tones, sizes and genders, with real cloth diapers, blankets, slings and carriers.
A doll bath outdoors with warm water, washcloths and towels.
Real baby items from families, such as small clothes, booties, rattles and a baby carrier.
Family photos on the wall at children's eye level, sent in by families.
Books about many kinds of families, new babies and growing up.
Lullabies and songs from families' home languages.
Baby animals on our site, such as goat kids and chicks, with care and quiet watching.
A visit from a family with a new baby, with family permission.
Photos of each child as a baby, with guesses and stories.
Measuring and comparing hands and feet with babies and with grown-ups.
Real photos at children's eye level of families caring for babies around the world.
Mary Cassatt's paintings of children being bathed and held, and Elizabeth Catlett's sculptures of mothers and children.

sections.text: Both. Caring for a doll can be quiet, focused and solo. Family play often grows into a group game with roles to share.

Families come in many shapes. Include every family in photos, books and talk. A new baby at home can bring big feelings, and a child may want to be the baby again. Welcome that play. Keep faces of children and families off any public display. Ask families before sharing photos.

items: Care for dolls and decide what they need.
Choose roles and change them during play.
Bring family photos and stories from home.
Help care for baby animals with adults.
Sing lullabies from home.
Make books about their own family.

sections.text: Children close family play by tucking dolls into their beds, folding baby clothes and blankets and setting bottles and dishes back on the shelf. They wipe the little table with a damp cloth and push chairs in. Photo labels on the shelves show where each thing lives, so the area is reset by the families who played there.

Sit at child level in the home area with a gentle voice and slow hands. Model care for the dolls and real baby things without taking over the story. A child who wants to be the baby may need your warm, calm presence close by.

items: Tell me what the baby needs.
I wonder what you were like as a baby.
Who takes care of you?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Add real baby items and notice how children care for dolls.
Invite families to send photos for a family wall.
Read books about many families and new babies.
Bathe dolls outdoors with real water and towels.
Watch baby animals grow and draw the changes.
Invite a family with a new baby to visit.
Look at baby photos and wonder how we have changed.
Learn lullabies from families' home languages.
Look at Mary Cassatt and Elizabeth Catlett and draw our own families.
Make All About Me and family books.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Doll care and family play are open to everyone. The outdoor doll bath needs an educator nearby, and visits with baby animals and new babies happen with an adult and family permission.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavier doll carried in a sling, a doll bath with warm water and washcloths to wring out, and snaps, buttons and buckles on real baby clothes. Rocking a doll in a rocking chair adds gentle movement.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one doll, a soft blanket and a quiet corner with a basket of lullaby books. They can care for the baby on their own terms and choose whether others join.
connected: Mary Cassatt on the Artists page, for paintings of children bathed and held by caregivers.
Elizabeth Catlett on the Artists page, for sculptures of mothers holding their children.

sections.text: A doll or stuffed animal, a small blanket, a washcloth, a tub of water and family photos.

items: Bathe a doll in a tub of warm water.
Look at your child's baby photos together.
Sing lullabies you know from your family.
Make a family book with photos and drawings.
Let your child help care for a younger sibling or pet in small ways.

sections.text: Your child cares for dolls, chooses roles and tells family stories. You share stories, songs and photos. Your child can put dolls to bed, fold small blankets and wash play dishes in a tub of soapy water. A towel to dry them on helps the care play carry right through to the close.

items: I wonder what you liked when you were a baby.
Who is in our family?
How can we help the baby feel better?

sections.text: Your child is learning about care, kindness and belonging. Wrapping, rocking and buttoning give hands careful work, and caring for a baby is a soothing kind of play for many children.
Send a family photo for our family wall, a lullaby in your home language, or outgrown baby clothes for our dolls. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Your child may want to be the baby sometimes, especially with a new sibling. This is a normal way to explore big changes.

cards.title: Shops, money and trading
cards.summary: Ideas for children who play shop, count money and trade treasures, with real registers, a café, a farm stand and walks to real markets.

sections.text: Children set up shops and sell everything in the room. They make money from paper, count coins, write tickets and receipts, and bargain over prices. They may trade stickers, stones and treasures with friends, or take orders in a café. A child may say "That will be five dollars" or "I'll trade you."

items: A shop or market in the home area with a real register, a scale, bags and a basket of coins.
The Unicorn Café in the piazza, with menus, order pads, cloth napkins and real dishes.
A farm stand where children sell eggs, herbs and flowers from our site to families.
Paper, pencils and stamps for making money, tickets, price tags, signs and receipts.
Natural treasures to trade, such as stones, shells, acorns and seed pods.
A walk to a nearby farmers market or shop, holding hands, to watch real buying and selling.
Real photos at children's eye level of markets from around the world.
Scales and weights for weighing goods and comparing.
Books about markets, shops and money from many cultures.
Coins and bills from many countries to look at and sort.
A shop children design together, deciding what to sell and who works there.
Wayne Thiebaud's paintings of cakes in shop windows and Claes Oldenburg's The Store, with clay and paper to make our own goods for sale.

sections.text: Mostly together. Shops need sellers and buyers, and trading needs a partner. Making money and signs can be a quiet, solo task.

Real coins are a choking risk for younger children. Use large tokens or paper money with the West class. Food in the shop is pretend or made from clay and paper, and real food stays in the culinary atelier. Trading can bring big feelings when a child wants something back. Agree together on fair trades.

items: Plan and set up the shop.
Make money, tickets, signs and price tags.
Choose roles as sellers, buyers and helpers.
Weigh and count goods.
Make fair trades and work out problems.
Sell real things at the farm stand with adults.

sections.text: Shopkeepers close the shop by counting the money and tokens into the till, sorting goods back into their labeled baskets and turning the sign to closed. They wipe the counter with a damp cloth and stack the scale and baskets on the shelf. The shop is ready for tomorrow, and an educator has nothing to put away.

Join the shop as a customer at the child's level, using a regular voice and letting the shopkeepers lead the prices and rules. Narrate what you notice, such as "You counted four coins into my hand." Step back once the play is flowing.

items: How do you decide what it costs?
I wonder what makes a trade fair.
Tell me what you will do with the money.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Add a register, scale and bags and watch how children play shop.
Make money, tickets and signs together.
Visit a real market or shop.
