Open a shop children design and run.
Trade natural treasures and talk about fairness.
Run the Unicorn Café with real menus and dishes.
Sell eggs, herbs or flowers at a farm stand for families.
Look at coins and money from many countries.
Look at Wayne Thiebaud and Claes Oldenburg and make goods for our shop.
Make a book of our shop, prices and stories.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Shop and café play are open to everyone. Real coins stay away from the 2s, a farm stand with real eggs needs an adult at the table, and walks to a market mean holding hands.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a busy market with heavy goods to stock, such as bags of acorns or pine cones weighed on a scale, crates carried to the farm stand, and a real register with buttons and a drawer. Calling out prices to customers adds sound and movement.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small quiet shop for one or two children, with a few treasures, a coin purse and a simple sign. They can be the shopkeeper behind a table, where customers come one at a time.
connected: Wayne Thiebaud on the Artists page, for paintings of cakes and pies lined up in shop windows.
Claes Oldenburg on the Artists page, for a store full of sculpted goods.

home.title: Shops, money and trading at Home

sections.text: A small box for a register, coins or paper money, bags, paper for signs and things to sell, such as toys or books.

items: Set up a shop with toys and price tags.
Let your child pay for something at a store.
Make paper money together.
Visit a farmers market and talk about what you see.
Trade small treasures, such as stones or shells.

sections.text: Your child plans the shop, makes signs and money and plays seller or buyer. You can be a customer. Your child can count the play money back into a box, sort shop items into baskets and wipe the counter with a sponge. Closing the shop each day can be as much fun as opening it.

items: How much does it cost?
Tell me what you would like to buy.
I wonder if this is a fair trade.

sections.text: Your child is learning about numbers, counting, fairness and how people work together. Counting coins, stamping tickets and stocking shelves give hands busy work and help eyes and hands work together.
Send in coins from other countries, old wallets, receipts or shopping bags for our shop. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep real coins away from babies and toddlers. Use paper money or large pretend coins with young children.

cards.title: Mail and letters
cards.summary: Ideas for children who write notes, fill envelopes and deliver mail, with mailboxes, real stamps and letters that travel.

sections.text: Children write notes and stuff them into envelopes. They deliver letters to friends and families and ask "Did I get mail?" They make marks, scribbles and letters on paper and call them messages. A child may carry a bag of mail all morning. This play is often a child exploring writing, connection and how messages travel.

items: Mailboxes for each class, with letters to other classes and replies.
Envelopes, paper, cards, postcards, stamps, stickers, pencils and crayons in the writing center.
Used postage stamps from many countries to look at, sort and glue.
Mail bags, a scale and a sorting tray for a post office in the home area.
A walk to a real mailbox to mail letters home, holding hands.
A visit to a real post office, or a visit from a mail carrier.
Postcards to send to families and to other schools.
Letter stamps, letter stones and name cards for children who want to write names.
Letters to the goats, the chickens or Sheldon, answered by children in another class.
Real photos at children's eye level of mail carriers, post offices and mailboxes around the world.
Books about mail and letters, such as The Jolly Postman by Janet and Allan Ahlberg, A Letter to Amy by Ezra Jack Keats and Dear Juno by Soyung Pak.
Mail art by Ray Johnson on screen, and decorated envelopes and postcards of our own.

sections.text: Both. Writing a letter is often quiet and solo. Sorting and delivering mail invites partners and a whole class.
Every mark is a message. Welcome scribbles, drawings and letters equally. Chalk, crayon and pencil build hand strength. Ask families before mailing letters to home addresses. Keep addresses private.

items: Write, draw and decorate letters and envelopes.
Sort and deliver mail.
Read and share letters at meeting time.
Decide who to write to and why.
Walk letters to a real mailbox.
Answer letters from other classes.

sections.text: Children close the post office by sorting letters into class mailboxes, capping pens, putting pencils back in their cup and stacking envelopes and paper in the tray. Stamps and ink pads go into the stamp box with the lids snapped on. Each tool has a labeled home on the shelf, so the writing table is reset by the writers.

Sit beside the child at the writing center and keep your own pencil still, so their marks stay their own. Treat every scribble as a real message and narrate it, such as "You folded it twice so it fits." Walk the delivery route with them without hurrying.

items: Who would you like to send a letter to?
I wonder how a letter gets to its place.
Tell me what you will say.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Add envelopes, paper and stamps and notice who writes.
Set up mailboxes for each class.
Start letters to other classes and wait for replies.
Mail letters home from a real mailbox.
Visit a post office or invite a mail carrier.
Set up a post office with scales and sorting trays.
Collect used stamps and look at them closely.
Write to the animals on our site.
Make mail art inspired by Ray Johnson.
Begin pen pals with another school.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Writing and sending mail are open to everyone. Walks to a real mailbox or post office leave campus with each child holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy mail bag to carry on a delivery route between classes, packages to wrap and tape, and a big rubber stamp to press hard on each envelope. Pushing thick letters through a tight mailbox slot adds hand work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet seat at the writing center with a few envelopes, stickers and one letter to one friend. They can choose to mail it themselves or ask a friend to deliver it.
connected: Ray Johnson on the Artists page, for art made to travel through the mail.

sections.text: Paper, envelopes, stamps, crayons and a box or bag for mail.

items: Write a letter to a grandparent or friend.
Make a family mailbox from a box.
Walk to a mailbox to mail a letter.
Send a postcard from a trip.
Leave notes for each other around the house.

sections.text: Your child writes, draws, decorates and delivers letters. You can help with addresses and stamps. Your child can sort letters into a family mailbox, put pencils in a cup and stack paper in a tray. A small box for envelopes and stamps keeps the mail ready for tomorrow.

items: Who could we write to?
Tell me what you want to say.
How do you think the letter will get there?

sections.text: Your child is learning that marks and words carry messages and connect people. Folding, stamping and carrying the mail give hands and arms good work, and a quiet letter can be a calm way to feel close to someone.
Send a postcard to the class, or send in used stamps, envelopes and old greeting cards. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Every mark your child makes is writing. Celebrate scribbles, drawings and letters equally.

cards.title: Maps and journeys
cards.summary: Ideas for children who draw maps, plan routes and go on journeys, with our site, the creek trail and the view from above.

sections.text: Children draw maps of their homes, the yard or treasure hunts. They plan routes, follow paths and lead friends on journeys. They talk about trips, where family lives and how to get places. A child may say "X marks the spot" or "This is the way to my house." Maps help children make sense of the places they know.

items: A large map of our site on the wall at children's eye level, with photos of each place.
Mapping the creek trail on walks, with clipboards and pencils, holding hands.
Aerial photos of our school and neighborhood to look at and find places.
Treasure maps and treasure hunts children design for friends.
Tape on the floor for roads and paths in the block area.
Compasses, magnifiers and binoculars for journeys.
Real maps of many kinds, including town maps, trail maps, globes and old maps.
Drawing the yard from above after climbing up high.
Journey stories at meeting time, with children's own maps of where they went.
Books about maps and journeys, such as Me on the Map by Joan Sweeney and As the Crow Flies by Gail Hartman.
A map of where our families come from, if families wish to share.
Jasper Johns' Map paintings and Joyce Kozloff's map art, with paint and paper for our own maps.

sections.text: Both. Drawing a map is often quiet and solo. Following maps and journeys invites friends to plan together.

Maps hold meaning for children even when they look different from adult maps. Families share where they come from only if they wish. On walks a child holds an adult's hand until the group returns. Long before roads, Southern Pomo and Coast Miwok people knew paths through this land, and that history can be part of mapping our place.

items: Draw maps of places they know.
Plan and lead journeys for friends.
Hide treasures and make maps to find them.
Use real maps and compasses.
Add places and photos to the site map.
Tell stories of journeys at meeting time.

sections.text: Children roll or fold maps and slide them into the map tube or basket, and return compasses and magnifiers to their pockets in the explorer bag. Treasures used for hiding go back to their tin, and any new place is added to the site map before the group moves on. Everything has a photo-labeled home, so the journey closes with the journeyers.

Walk the route at the child's pace and let them lead, holding hands on walks with a calm, unhurried body. Narrate the choices you see, such as "You turned at the big oak." Wrong turns are part of the journey, so keep your face curious.

items: How would you get there?
I wonder what this place looks like from above.
Tell me what you would put on your map.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Notice children's maps and routes and offer paper and pencils.
Make a map of our site together.
Map the creek trail on walks.
Look at aerial photos and find places.
Design treasure hunts with maps.
Build roads and paths in the block area.
Look at real maps of many kinds.
Make a map of where our families come from.
Look at Jasper Johns and Joyce Kozloff and make map art.
Make a book of our journeys and maps.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Map making and treasure hunts are open to everyone. Mapping the creek trail means each child holds an adult's hand, and drawing from high places needs an educator close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer journeys with lots of movement, such as an obstacle route children map and then run, a treasure hunt across the whole yard, or a backpack of tools carried on a creek trail mapping walk. Taping long roads across the floor on hands and knees adds more.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small map of one familiar place, such as their class or the garden, drawn at a quiet table. They can follow a friend's map with a finger before walking the route.
connected: Jasper Johns on the Artists page, for painting the map of the United States in loose bold brushstrokes.
Joyce Kozloff on the Artists page, for paintings and tiles built from maps.

sections.text: Paper, pencils, crayons, a map of your town and a small treasure to hide.

items: Draw a map of your home or street together.
Hide a treasure and make a map to find it.
Look at a real map before a trip.
Take a walk and draw the route afterwards.
Look at photos of your neighborhood from above.

sections.text: Your child draws maps, plans routes and leads journeys. You can follow their maps and ask questions. Your child can fold a map, put the compass back in its pouch and unpack the walk bag. A basket for maps and a hook for the bag make every journey end in the same easy place.

items: How do we get there?
Tell me what you would put on your map.
Where have we been?

sections.text: Your child is learning about space, direction and the places they belong. Following routes and climbing up to look down help children judge space and plan how their body will move.
Send a map your child drew, or a map or postcard from a place your family has been. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Your child's map may look different from yours and still hold real meaning.

cards.title: Bugs and small creatures
cards.summary: Ideas for children who hunt for bugs and small creatures, with magnifiers, log rolling, kind care and close watching.

sections.text: Children turn over rocks and logs to find roly polys, worms and beetles. They carry ladybugs on their hands, watch ants for long stretches and ask what bugs eat. They may want to keep bugs in jars or be afraid of some. A child may say "Look, a baby one!" or "Is it sleeping?"

items: Magnifiers, bug viewers and clear jars with air holes and leaves for short visits.
Log rolling and rock lifting in the Log yard and garden, putting each one back as we found it.
A worm bin or compost to watch worms at work.
A bug hotel in the garden made from sticks, bark and hollow stems.
Watching pollinators in the pollinator garden and on the salvias and lavender.
Western fence lizards on sunny rocks and logs, watched quietly.
Real photos at children's eye level of the bugs and small creatures on our site.
iNaturalist to photograph and learn the names of creatures we find.
Drawing bugs with magnifiers and clipboards.
Clay, sticks and natural materials for making bugs.
Moving our bodies the way the creatures we watch move, crawling, wiggling and flying.
Insects at meeting time, passed carefully in a clear viewer.
Bug hunts on creek walks, looking under leaves and stones.
Books about bugs and small creatures with real photos.
Maria Sibylla Merian's paintings of insects and their life cycles, and Jennifer Angus's wall patterns of real insects.

sections.text: Both. Watching a bug is often quiet and solo. Bug hunts and caring for a bug hotel invite a group.

Black widows live on our site. Adults lift boards and logs first, and children look at spiders in dark corners with their eyes only. Be kind to all beings. Bugs visit for a short time and go back where we found them the same day. We use no pesticides. Some children feel afraid of bugs, and watching from a distance is welcome.

items: Find and watch bugs with care.
Return bugs to where they were found.
Draw and photograph bugs.
Learn names with iNaturalist.
Care for a bug hotel or worm bin.
Teach friends how to hold a bug gently.

sections.text: Children close a bug hunt by returning every creature to where it was found and setting boards and logs back gently with an adult. They rinse bug viewers and magnifiers in the wash bucket and set them on the drying rack, then hang the field bag. Hands are washed, and the hunt ends with nothing left for an educator later.

Kneel or sit low and very still beside the log or viewer, with gentle hands and a soft voice that shows care for the creature. Notice your own feelings about bugs and spiders, since children read our faces. Narrate what you see, such as "Its legs curled when the light came in."

items: How does it move?
I wonder where it lives.
Tell me what you think it eats.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer magnifiers and bug viewers and go on a bug hunt.
Roll logs and lift rocks and put them back.
Watch worms in a worm bin or compost.
Build a bug hotel in the garden.
Watch pollinators in the garden across the seasons.
Learn names with iNaturalist.
Draw bugs closely with magnifiers.
Make bugs from clay and natural materials.
Look at Maria Sibylla Merian and Jennifer Angus.
Make a book of the creatures on our site.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator stays nearby because black widows live on our site and adults lift boards and logs first. Insects passed at meeting time stay in a clear viewer an adult holds.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer log rolling and rock lifting in the Log yard with a partner, digging for worms in the compost with a trowel, and crawling and wiggling the way the creatures move. Holding a roly poly gently on an open palm adds touch.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a clear bug viewer to look into, with the creature inside and their hands outside. They can watch from a set distance, use a magnifier or iNaturalist photos, and choose if and when to hold.
connected: Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for paintings of insects and their changes on the plants they eat.
Jennifer Angus on the Artists page, for patterns made from real insects on gallery walls.

home.title: Bugs and small creatures at Home

sections.text: A magnifier, a clear jar with holes in the lid, a notebook and pencil.

items: Go on a bug hunt in your yard or park.
Lift a rock or log and look underneath, then put it back.
Watch ants or a spider web for a few minutes.
Draw a bug you found.
Look up a bug's name together with a phone app.

sections.text: Your child finds, watches and cares for bugs and decides when to let them go. You can help look and learn names. Your child can let bugs go where they found them, rinse the jar and hang the magnifier on a hook. Washing hands together is the last step.

items: Where does it live?
How does it move?
I wonder what it eats.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look closely, be gentle with living things and wonder about nature. Watching quietly helps many children slow down and settle, and lifting logs and digging give the body strong work.
Send a drawing or photo of a bug your child found, or share its name and where you found it. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Look at spiders with eyes only. Put bugs back where you found them the same day. Wash hands after.

cards.title: Birds
cards.summary: Ideas for children who watch birds, collect feathers and build nests, with our own birds, nests and Merlin Bird ID.

sections.text: Children point at crows, hawks and finches. They flap their arms and fly. They collect feathers, look for nests and listen to bird calls. They may care for the chickens, look for eggs and ask where birds sleep. A child may say "That bird is talking" or "Where is its mommy?"

items: Watching crows, hawks, herons, egrets and finches on our site and on creek walks.
Merlin Bird ID to listen to bird calls and learn names.
Binoculars and a bird blind or quiet spot for watching.
Nest building with sticks, grass, mud and leaves, after looking at real nests.
Caring for the chickens and collecting eggs.
Chicken feathers to look at with magnifiers and to paint with.
Safe nesting materials left out in spring, such as small twigs, straw, leaves and untreated grass clippings.
Real photos at children's eye level of the birds on our site.
Drawing birds with clipboards and pencils.
Clay birds and nests with natural materials.
Moving our bodies the way birds move, flying, hopping, diving and pecking.
Bird songs and calls to listen to and copy.
Books about birds with real photos.
Ohara Koson's woodblock prints of birds on branches, with ink and paper for our own bird prints.

sections.text: Both. Watching birds is often quiet and solo. Building nests and caring for chickens invites a group.

Feathers of most wild birds are protected by law, so we look, draw and photograph them and leave them in place. Chicken feathers from our own flock can come inside. Leave yarn, string, hair and dryer lint out of nesting materials, since they can harm birds. Do not touch sick or dead wild birds. Wash hands after handling chickens or their feathers.

items: Watch and listen for birds.
Learn names with Merlin Bird ID.
Build nests with natural materials.
Care for the chickens and collect eggs.
Draw and photograph birds.
Leave safe nesting materials in spring.

sections.text: Children close bird watching by putting binoculars back in their cases and returning bird cards and clipboards to their basket. They empty and refill the bird bath or water dish, and nest materials go back into their bin. Chicken feathers go to the feather jar, and hands are washed before the group goes in.

Sit low and quiet with the children, letting your stillness and slow breathing set the pace for watching. Use a hushed but regular voice and point slowly. Wait with them through the long pauses, since birds come back when we stay still.

items: How does it fly?
I wonder where it sleeps.
Tell me what you think it is saying.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Watch and listen for birds on our site.
Learn names with Merlin Bird ID.
Look at real nests and build our own.
Care for the chickens and collect eggs.
Look closely at chicken feathers with magnifiers.
Leave safe nesting materials in spring.
Draw birds from life with clipboards.
Make birds from clay and natural materials.
Look at Ohara Koson's prints and make our own.
Make a book of the birds on our site.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Watching, listening and drawing birds are open to everyone. Caring for the chickens happens in a small group with an adult and handwashing, and dead or sick wild birds are left to adults.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer bird moves with the whole body, such as flapping, hopping and diving across the yard, and nest building with big armloads of sticks and mud. Carrying the feed bucket to the chickens adds strong work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet bird blind with binoculars, a cushion and Merlin Bird ID turned low. They can watch the chickens from outside the fence before going in.
connected: Ohara Koson on the Artists page, for woodblock prints of birds perched on branches and flowers.

sections.text: Binoculars if you have them, a notebook, pencils and a phone with a bird app.

items: Watch birds from a window or in a park.
Listen to bird calls and try to name them with an app.
Look for nests in trees and bushes.
Draw a bird you see.
Leave small twigs and straw out for nesting birds in spring.

sections.text: Your child watches, listens, draws and names birds. You can help with the app and look together. Your child can put binoculars away, fill the bird bath and stack bird books on a low shelf. A basket for bird things by the window keeps watching easy to start and to finish.

items: How does it fly?
Where do you think it lives?
I wonder what it is saying.

sections.text: Your child is learning to look and listen closely and to care for living things. Listening for birdsong helps many children grow calm and focused, and flapping and hopping give the whole body good movement.
Send a drawing or photo of a bird your child saw, or share its name and where you saw it. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Leave wild feathers where you find them, since most are protected by law. Do not touch sick or dead birds. Keep yarn and string away from nesting birds.

cards.title: Rainbows and color
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who chase rainbows, sort by color and mix colors of their own.

sections.text: Children may point at a rainbow spot on the floor and try to catch it. They line up blocks or crayons in color order, name a favorite color for everything, or say "I made purple!" at the paint table.

items: A glass dish of water with a small mirror leaning in it, set in a sunny window with white paper nearby to catch the rainbow.
Hanging prisms and old CDs in the windows of each class, low enough for children to turn and move.
A garden hose set to a fine mist on a sunny afternoon, with children standing with the sun at their backs to look for a rainbow in the spray.
Real photos of rainbows over hills, waterfalls, fog and city streets posted at children's eye level, with space for children's drawings beside them.
Rainbow concoctions in clear jars with liquid watercolor, droppers, baking soda, vinegar and foamy dish soap, so colors bubble and blend.
Chalk ground with salt in a mortar and pestle, each color poured in layers into one shared jar.
A color hunt in the garden with paint chip strips, matching each chip to a petal, leaf or bark without picking.
A light table with colored acetate, translucent tiles and cellophane for layering colors.
Three primary colors only at the easel for many days, with an empty palette to mix every other color.
A tray of fallen petals, leaves, feathers and seed pods gathered with purpose and arranged into a color wheel on the ground.
Bubbles blown outside in sunlight so children can look closely at the moving colors on each bubble.
Shaving cream or foamy soap on a tray with droppers of liquid watercolor for marbled color.
A visit to the botanical dye bed to see which plants give which colors, then a small dye bath with the atelierista or educator.
Rainbow books from the Book collection set beside a basket of prisms and flashlights.
The work of Sonia Delaunay or Wassily Kandinsky shown on screen from a museum site, with paint ready to answer it.

sections.text: Both. Catching a rainbow on the wall is a shared thrill that brings children together. Mixing a color and naming it is often private and quiet work.

Rainbows come with direct sun, so check where morning and afternoon light falls in each room and outdoors. Use liquid watercolor and pantry staples for color concoctions, never food or produce. Keep glass prisms on soft surfaces with an adult nearby, and use acrylic prisms with the 2s.

items: Find and mark the windows where rainbows appear and at what time of day.
Mix colors and name them with their own words.
Choose which colors go on the palette each day.
Care for prisms and mirrors and return them to their place.
Sort found objects by color and decide where each one belongs.
Teach a friend how to make a rainbow with the mirror and water.
Record color recipes in a shared book with drops and marks.
Clean brushes and droppers and set the table for the next group.

sections.text: Children close color work by setting prisms and mirrors back on their soft cloth, rinsing droppers and brushes in the wash bucket and laying them on the drying rack. They cap the liquid watercolor jars and wipe the table with a damp sponge. Color sorting objects go back to their color baskets, and the space is ready for the next group.

Sit at the window or concoction table at the child's level with relaxed hands and an easy face about drips and foam. Narrate what you see, such as "The blue went down and the yellow went up." Slow down to watch the light move together.

items: I wonder where the rainbow goes when the sun moves.
Tell me about the colors at the edge.
How do you think a rainbow is made?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one prism in one sunny window and notice who comes.
Ask children to find rainbows around the school and mark each one with a small flag or tape.
Track the window rainbow at different times of day with chalk lines on the floor.
Add a mirror in water, then a flashlight in a dim room, and compare the rainbows.
Offer primary colors only and invite children to mix every color they see in the garden.
Start a shared color recipe book where children record drops and names.
Name new colors after places and things on our site, such as goat brown or fog gray.
Collect and sort colors from nature into a seasonal color wheel each month.
Visit the botanical dye bed and dye wool or cloth in a small group.
Build a rainbow out of loose parts across the outdoor piazza as a whole class.
Bring in an artist such as Sonia Delaunay and let children answer her color circles in paint.
Invite families to send photos of rainbows they find at home and post them on the wall.
Make a class book of rainbow theories in children's own words and drawings.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Prisms, color mixing and color hunts are open to everyone. Glass prisms need an adult nearby, the hose mist needs an educator watching, and the dye bath is small group work with an adult handling heat.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer grinding chalk with salt in a heavy mortar and pestle, big foamy rainbow concoctions with full squeeze bottles, and running through the hose mist to find a rainbow. Kneading chalk dust into playdough adds strong hand work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a prism in a quiet sunny window and white paper to catch the light, with nothing to touch but the paper. Droppers and small cups let them mix color without wet hands.
connected: Sonia Delaunay on the Artists page, for circles of bright color that seem to move.
Wassily Kandinsky on the Artists page, for rings of color set side by side in squares.
Olafur Eliasson on the Artists page, for rainbows made from mist, light and colored glass.

sections.text: A sunny window, a glass of water or a shallow dish with a small mirror, white paper, a flashlight, and any paints or crayons you already have.

items: Set a glass of water in a sunny window and look for a rainbow on the floor or wall.
Spray a fine mist from the hose with the sun behind you and look for a rainbow in the water.
Go on a color walk and find something of every color on your street.
Mix two paint colors on a plate and give the new color a name together.
Blow bubbles in the sun and look closely at the colors swirling on them.

sections.text: Your child can find the sunny spot, hold the mirror, choose the colors, name what they make and show you how they did it. Your child can rinse brushes, cap paints and wipe the table with a damp cloth. A towel for drying and a cup for brushes make the close part of the painting.

items: I wonder where the rainbow went.
Tell me the colors you see.
How could we make another one?

sections.text: Your child is noticing light, color and change, and putting their discoveries into words. Grinding, squeezing and mixing give hands strong work, and watching light and color can be a calm, quiet time.
Send a photo or drawing of a rainbow you found at home for our wall, or send old CDs or small mirrors for our windows. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep glass and mirrors on a towel and stay close. Never look straight at the sun. Paint and water can spill, so an old shirt and a towel help.

cards.title: Volcanoes and eruptions
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who build mountains that erupt, talk about lava and want to know what is under the ground.

sections.text: Children may pile sand into a peak and pour water down the top, shouting that the lava is coming. They ask whether lava is hot, whether a volcano lives near them, and they make things bubble up and spill over again and again.

items: A sand or mud mountain in the sandbox or mud kitchen with a cup buried in the top for baking soda, vinegar and dish soap eruptions.
A clay volcano built by a small group, dried, and used for eruptions all week.
Real rocks to hold and compare, such as pumice, obsidian, basalt and scoria, with magnifiers and a bowl of water to test which floats.
Real photos and short video of eruptions, lava flows and new land cooling at the sea, shown at children's eye level and on a screen.
A volcano concoction tray with liquid watercolor in red, orange and yellow, droppers, vinegar and baking soda in small pitchers.
Oobleck from cornstarch and water in a deep tray, so children can feel something that flows and then holds.
Large paper and red, orange and black tempera, charcoal and oil pastel for drawing eruptions.
Layers of colored sand or soil in a clear jar to wonder about what is under the ground.
Maps and a globe with volcano spots marked, including those in California.
Dramatic play with clipboards, hard hats, binoculars and walkie talkies for volcano scientists.
Hokusai's views of Mount Fuji and Frederic Edwin Church's Cotopaxi on screen, with paint ready.
A field trip or family outing idea to the Petrified Forest in Calistoga, where trees were buried in volcanic ash.
Nonfiction books about volcanoes from the Book collection placed beside the rocks.

sections.text: Both. Eruptions draw a crowd and children love to count down together. Building a mountain and testing how much to pour can be careful solo work.

Baking soda and vinegar can sting eyes, so offer safety glasses and keep eruptions at the table or ground level. Use pantry staples only, never food. Some children feel real fear about volcanoes and earthquakes, so answer plainly and calmly and let children set the pace. Our county sits on old volcanic rock, and Pomo and Miwok people shaped local obsidian into tools, which can be shared with care and accuracy.

items: Build the mountain and decide where the crater goes.
Measure baking soda and vinegar and test what makes the biggest eruption.
Sort and test rocks for weight, texture and floating.
Draw and record each eruption on a clipboard.
Set up and clean the eruption tray for the next group.
Ask questions and add them to a wall of wonderings.
Teach a friend the eruption recipe they worked out.

sections.text: Children close an eruption by tipping the foamy tray into the outdoor drain with an adult and rinsing it in the wash bucket. They wipe the safety glasses, cap the baking soda and vinegar and put the measuring spoons back on their outlines. The tray and tools rest on the drying rack, so the next eruption is ready with no educator time later.

Stay at the tray or mud mountain within arm's reach, with a calm face when the foam spills over the edge. Keep your voice regular even when the children are loud, and narrate what changed, such as "More vinegar made it rise faster." Notice your own feelings about mess and keep a towel nearby.

items: Tell me what you think is inside the mountain.
I notice this rock has holes. I wonder why.
How could we make it go higher?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with one sand mountain and a cup of concoction outdoors.
Collect children's theories about volcanoes in words and drawings.
Offer real volcanic rocks and the floating pumice test.
Build a lasting clay volcano and keep a journal of each eruption.
Try changes such as more soap, warm water or a narrower crater, and record what happens.
Compare how lava might flow with oobleck, mud and thick paint, and watch each one move down a slope.
Look at maps to find volcanoes near us and around the world.
Invite a family member or local geologist to bring rocks and answer children's questions.
Paint a volcano many times from photos, then from imagination.
Build a big shared volcano from cardboard and papier mache in the Studio.
Turn the block area into a volcano research lab with children's own signs.
Make a class book of volcano theories and discoveries.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Baking soda and vinegar can sting eyes, so eruptions happen with an adult at the table and safety glasses. Looking at rocks and drawing eruptions are open to all, and the lasting clay volcano is small group work.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer building a huge sand or mud mountain with shovels and buckets, oobleck in a deep tray to punch and squeeze, and full squeeze bottles of vinegar for big eruptions. Pounding a clay volcano into shape adds strong work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small eruption in a clear cup on a tray, made with a dropper, so the bubbling stays small. They can stand back from the big eruptions, use a spoon in the oobleck, or hold real rocks such as pumice instead.
connected: Katsushika Hokusai on the Artists page, for showing Mount Fuji, a volcano, again and again in many views.
Frederic Edwin Church on the Artists page, for his painting of the Cotopaxi volcano smoking over the land.

sections.text: A tray or baking dish, baking soda, vinegar, a squirt of dish soap, a cup, and sand, dirt or playdough to build a mountain.

items: Build a mountain of dirt or sand outside around a cup and pour in baking soda, then vinegar.
Add a drop of dish soap and see what changes.
Collect rocks on a walk and look for ones with holes or shiny sides.
Drop rocks in a bowl of water and see if any float.
Draw or paint a volcano together.

sections.text: Your child can build the mountain, measure, pour, count down and decide what to try next. Your child can rinse the eruption tray outside, wipe the table with a sponge and put the baking soda and vinegar back in their place. Doing it in the sink or yard makes the mess easy.

items: Tell me what you think will happen.
I wonder what made it bubble.
How could we change it?

sections.text: Your child is testing ideas, noticing cause and effect, and asking big questions about the earth. Squeezing oobleck and digging mountains give hands and arms strong work, and making something bubble over again and again can help release big energy.
Send a rock you found together, or a photo of your volcano, for our rock table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Do eruptions outside or on a tray. Vinegar stings eyes, so keep faces back and rinse hands after.

cards.title: Weather, rain and wind
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who want to be out in the rain, chase the wind and watch the sky.

sections.text: Children may run into the wind with arms out, jump in every puddle, or stand under the eaves to listen to rain. They ask where the wind comes from, why it is foggy, and announce the weather at meeting time.

items: Rain gear for every child so we can go out in the rain and feel it.
A clear rain gauge in the garden that children check and mark each morning in the rainy season.
Watercolor paper set out in a light rain with dry liquid watercolor dots, so the rain paints.
Pots, pans and metal bowls upside down under the drip line to listen to rain as music.
Wind socks, ribbon streamers and flags tied to fences and the willow dome to show which way the wind blows.
Pinwheels and paper spinners made in the Studio and tested in the yards.
A homemade wind tube with a box fan, clear plastic and light things such as scarves, coffee filters and feathers.
Real photos of rain, storms, fog, frost and wind posted at eye level, with children's own weather photos added.
Puddle investigations with sticks, chalk outlines around a puddle and a return visit to see how it changed.
A weather window with clipboards for children to draw what the sky looks like today.
Gutter and downspout watching, following where rainwater goes across our site.
Kites and parachutes from tissue paper and string on a windy day.
Weather books and songs from the Book collection and Song book shared at meeting time.
Hiroshige's Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge shown on screen, with ink and watercolor ready for rain lines.

sections.text: Both. Splashing and wind running are joyful together. Watching a puddle or listening to rain can be a calm solo moment.

Our rainy season runs from November to March, and fog comes in many mornings. Dress for the weather, keep dry clothes ready and bring children in during lightning or strong wind with falling branches. On red flag and smoke days, wind becomes a fire topic, so speak plainly and calmly. Shoes stay on in the yards and garden.

items: Check and record the rain gauge and wind sock each day.
Choose rain gear and help friends with zippers and boots.
Share the weather at meeting time in their own words and symbols.
Design and test pinwheels, kites and parachutes.
Care for wet gear by hanging it to dry.
Photograph the weather and add to the wall.
Decide where to put the next wind flag to test an idea.

sections.text: Children close weather time by emptying the rain gauge after recording it and hanging wet rain gear on low hooks over a drip tray. Pinwheels, kites and wind flags go back to their basket, and muddy boots are set in the boot rack. A towel and mop at child height let them dry the floor by the door themselves.

Go out in the rain and wind with the children, dressed for it, so your body shows the weather is welcome. Notice any dislike of cold or wet in yourself and keep your face open. Narrate what you feel and see, such as "The wind pushed my hood back."

items: Where do you think the rain goes?
I wonder how we know the wind is here.
How does your body feel in the cold?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Go out in the first rain and simply notice together.
Start a daily weather check at meeting time led by children.
Set up a rain gauge and keep a long paper strip of rain marks across the season.
Paint with rain and compare light rain and heavy rain paintings.
Tie wind flags around the site and map which ones move most.
Build and test spinners, pinwheels and kites over several windy days.
Follow rainwater from roof to gutter to garden to creek.
Make rain music in the music shed and record it.
Look at fog in the morning and wonder where it goes by noon.
Keep a weather book for the whole year and compare seasons.
Invite families to send weather photos from their homes and compare.
Link to the creek walks to see the creek after rain.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Going out in the weather and watching the sky are open to everyone. The box fan wind tube needs an adult at the table, and we bring children in for lightning or strong wind.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running into the wind with streamers, jumping in puddles in rain gear, and standing in the rain with faces up. Carrying full buckets of rainwater to the garden beds adds heavy work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a sheltered spot under the eaves to watch and listen to the rain, with a hood up and a dry towel close. They can check the rain gauge or weather window and go out for a short time when they choose.
connected: Utagawa Hiroshige on the Artists page, for drawing sudden rain as fine lines over people on a bridge.
John Constable on the Artists page, for painting the sky and clouds again and again outdoors.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for his rain shadows, dry outlines left where his body lay as rain fell.
Ned Kahn on the Artists page, for large walls of small panels that move and shimmer in the wind.

home.title: Weather, rain and wind at Home

sections.text: Rain boots, a raincoat, a clear jar for rain, ribbons or a plastic bag on a string, and paper and crayons.

items: Put on rain gear and go puddle jumping, then draw a chalk line around a puddle and check it later.
Set a clear jar outside to catch rain and mark the level each day.
Tie a ribbon to a fence or stick to watch the wind.
Listen to rain on different things, such as an umbrella, a bucket or the car roof.
Look out the window each morning and draw the weather.

sections.text: Your child can check the jar, choose their gear, report the weather and decide what to test. Your child can hang up their own raincoat, set boots on a mat and wipe the floor by the door with a towel. A low hook for wet gear makes it their job every rainy day.

items: Where do you think the wind comes from?
Tell me what you hear.
I wonder where the puddle went.

sections.text: Your child is noticing patterns in the world and finding words for what they feel and see. Noticing cold hands, wet hair or warm sun helps children learn their body's signals, and puddle jumping gives big movement.
Send a weather photo or drawing from home, or extra rain boots in good shape for our spares bin. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Dress for the weather and bring dry clothes. Come inside if there is lightning or strong wind.

cards.title: Life, death and change
cards.summary: Ways to follow children's questions about living, dying and changing with honesty, care and real things from our site.

sections.text: Children may find a dead bird or bug and want to look closely, bury it or ask if it will wake up. They talk about a pet, a grandparent or a chicken that died, play dying and coming back in pretend play, and notice leaves falling, fruit rotting and seeds sprouting.

items: A respectful look at a dead bug, bird or animal found on site, with an adult using gloves or a shovel and children watching from close by.
A small burial in a chosen corner of the garden with children deciding on a stone, a song or a few words.
A decomposition tray outdoors with orchard fruit that has already fallen and spoiled, leaves and twigs, checked and drawn over weeks.
Real photos of life cycles at children's eye level, such as seed to plant, egg to chick and caterpillar to butterfly.
Our own cycles to watch, such as eggs and chicks, the goats through the year and compost turning to soil.
Pipevine on site to look for pipevine swallowtail caterpillars and their chrysalises in season.
Shed skins, empty snail shells, eggshells, bones and feathers on the investigation table with magnifiers.
A memory table where families may share photos of a loved person or pet who died, by invitation only.
Ephemeral art in the garden from leaves, petals and sticks, revisited over days to see it change.
Books about dying and remembering from the Book collection, read when the moment calls.
Maria Sibylla Merian's paintings of insects changing through each stage, shown with magnifiers and paper.
Seasonal walks to the same tree to notice buds, leaves, fruit and bare branches.
Drawings and clay to give shape to feelings about someone who died.

sections.text: Both. A group burial or a shared look at a dead animal builds belonging. Some children need quiet one to one time with an adult to ask their questions.

Use the words dead and died, and explain that a body stops working and does not come back. Avoid words such as sleeping or lost. Leave questions about spirit and afterlife to families, and say that families believe different things. Adults handle dead animals with gloves or a tool, and children wash hands after. Let directors and families know when a child is grieving.

items: Decide how to care for a dead animal they find.
Plan and lead a small burial or goodbye.
Watch and record changes over time with drawings and photos.
Ask hard questions and share their own theories.
Care for living animals and plants on site.
Choose how they want to remember, through a drawing, a song or a stone.
Comfort a friend in their own way.

sections.text: After a goodbye or burial, children return trowels and gloves to the garden tool board and wash their hands with soap. Drawings and photos for the memory book go into its folder, and any stone or marker is placed with care. The close is quiet and gentle, and children decide when the space feels finished.

Come close and kneel beside the children, slowing your body and lowering your voice to a calm, regular tone. Let your face show respect and openness, and leave room for silence and questions. Notice your own feelings about death, and comfort a child who is upset before talking about anything new.

items: Tell me what you notice about this bird.
I wonder what is happening to the fallen fruit.
How would you like to remember it?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Respond plainly and calmly the first time a dead animal is found, and follow children's lead.
Gather children's questions and theories about dying in their own words.
Set up a decomposition tray and draw it weekly.
Follow one life cycle closely, such as eggs to chicks or a pipevine caterpillar.
Mark one plant or tree to visit through the year and photograph each change.
Turn compost with children and look at what was food scraps becoming soil.
Make ephemeral art and photograph it as it changes.
Offer clay, drawing and storytelling for children to work through feelings.
Create a remembering place in the garden with a stone or a plant children choose.
Share books about dying and remembering when the moment is right.
Invite families to share their own traditions for remembering, only where they wish to.
Make a class book about change in our garden across the seasons.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: An educator stays close when a dead animal is found and handles it with gloves or a tool while children look. The memory table is by invitation only, and a grieving child needs an adult beside them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer turning the compost with a fork, digging a burial place with a real shovel, and handling bones, shells and shed skins with magnifiers. Smelling the decomposition tray each week adds strong input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer photos of the life cycle or a clear covered container to look into, with a choice to stay a few steps back. They can draw, choose a stone or sing from a quiet place instead of touching.
connected: Maria Sibylla Merian on the Artists page, for painting insects at every stage, from egg to wings.
Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for art from leaves, ice and stones that changes and fades.
The Image of the Child lens

home.title: Life, death and change at Home

sections.text: Gloves, a small shovel, a magnifier, paper and crayons, and patience for questions.

items: If you find a dead bug or bird, look closely together without touching, and talk about what you see.
Plant a seed in a cup and watch it change each day.
Put a fruit scrap or a fallen leaf in a jar outside and check it every few days.
Visit the same tree each month and notice how it changes.
Look through family photos and tell stories about people you love, including those who have died.

sections.text: Your child can ask questions, choose how to say goodbye, take care of plants and pets, and draw what they notice. Your child can help put the trowel away, wash hands and choose where a drawing or stone of remembering goes. A quiet close gives them time to feel what they feel.

items: Tell me what you notice.
I wonder what happened.
How would you like to remember?

sections.text: Your child is learning that living things grow, change and die, and that feelings and questions are welcome. Big feelings show up in the body, and naming where we feel them helps children notice and calm their own signals.
If your family has a loss, let your child's educator know so we can support your child. You may send a photo or a story to share if you wish.
Use simple true words such as died and dead. Wear gloves and wash hands after touching anything found outside.

cards.title: Our bodies and growing
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who are curious about how bodies work, grow, move and feel.

sections.text: Children may listen to each other's hearts, compare hand sizes, talk about a lost tooth, a scraped knee or a new baby. They play doctor, ask what is inside them and test how fast they can run and how their breath changes.

items: Real stethoscopes in a basket for listening to hearts before and after running.
Life-size body tracings on butcher paper that children fill in with what they think is inside.
Old x-ray films from families or clinics on the light table, with magnifiers and paper for drawing bones.
A full-length mirror and hand mirrors for looking at teeth, eyes, tongues and how faces move.
Real photos of bodies of many ages, sizes, abilities and skin colors at children's eye level.
A clinic in dramatic play with real bandages, gauze, slings, clipboards, a scale and a measuring tape.
Yarn cut to each child's height and hung side by side, with no ranking, revisited later in the year.
Baby photos from home beside current photos, with children guessing who is who.
A skeleton model and a basket of animal bones to compare with our own.
Obstacle courses, crawling, climbing and balancing in the yards with talk about which muscles are working.
Handprints and footprints in clay or paint compared across the year.
Comparing our bodies with the goats, chickens, rabbits and Sheldon, such as feet, teeth and how each one breathes.
Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man and Henri Matisse's Dance shown on screen, with children stretching into the shapes.
Books about bodies, babies and growing from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Listening to a friend's heart or tracing each other is a close shared moment. Drawing one's own body or looking in a mirror can be private discovery.

Use the real names of body parts. Respect each child's privacy and body autonomy, and ask before touching or tracing. Many children have bodies or health needs that differ, so speak with care and include every body. Wipe stethoscope earpieces between uses. Photos of children's faces and bodies stay inside our walls and never go public.

items: Trace, measure and draw their own bodies.
Listen to hearts and count beats with a friend.
Run the clinic and care for patients in play.
Ask before touching a friend and listen to their answer.
Share their own stories about teeth, scrapes and growing.
Compare their bodies with animals on our site.
Choose what goes into a class book about bodies.

sections.text: Children close the clinic by wiping stethoscope earpieces, folding bandages and gowns and returning tools to the doctor's bag. Tape measures roll back into their tin, and tracing paper is stacked in the tray. Photo labels on the shelf show where each tool goes, so the clinic is ready for its next patients.

Sit at the child's level with a calm, matter-of-fact voice, using real words for body parts. Narrate what you notice, such as "Your breath got faster after the run." Respect each child's choice about being touched, traced or listened to.

items: I wonder what is happening inside when we run.
Tell me about your hands.
How do you think bones help us?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with stethoscopes and listening to hearts.
Trace bodies and invite children to draw what is inside.
Add x-rays, a skeleton and animal bones to the light table.
Run and rest, then listen again, and record what changed.
Measure each child with yarn and revisit later to see growth.
Set up a clinic in dramatic play with real materials.
Compare our bodies with the animals in our animal yards.
Invite a family member who is a nurse, doctor or dentist to visit.
Look at baby photos and talk about how we grew.
Explore movement through dance, yoga and climbing.
Make clay figures and wire bodies in the Studio.
Build a large shared body from cardboard and recycled materials with children's ideas for each part.
Make a class book answering children's own questions about bodies.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Mirrors, stethoscopes and clinic play are open to everyone. Body tracing needs an adult who asks first, and x-rays and bones on the light table go best with an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer running, jumping and climbing, then listening to their heart with a stethoscope and feeling their breath. Being traced on butcher paper while lying flat, with firm pressure from the crayon, adds strong body input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer tracing their own hand on paper instead of being traced, and a stethoscope they try on a doll or a friend first. They can explore at a mirror or with x-rays on the light table at their own pace.
connected: Leonardo da Vinci on the Artists page, for drawing a body stretched inside a circle and a square.
Henri Matisse on the Artists page, for painting bodies moving together in a ring.

home.title: Our bodies and growing at Home

sections.text: A mirror, a ruler or tape measure, string or yarn, big paper and crayons, and family baby photos.

items: Trace your child's body on big paper and let them draw what they think is inside.
Run around, then put a hand on your chest and feel your heartbeat together.
Look at baby photos and talk about how your child has grown.
Measure your child with a piece of yarn and save it to compare later.
Look in a mirror at teeth, eyes and tongues and talk about what you see.

sections.text: Your child can trace, measure, ask questions and teach you what they know about their body. Your child can wipe the play stethoscope, fold bandages and put the doctor kit back in its box. A labeled basket keeps the clinic ready to open again.

items: Tell me what you think is inside your arm.
How does your heart feel now?
I wonder how you have changed.

sections.text: Your child is learning about their body with real words and growing pride in what their body can do. Feeling a fast heartbeat or a big breath helps children notice what their body is telling them.
Send a baby photo or a family story about growing up for our wall. Old x-ray films are welcome for our light table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use real names for body parts. Ask before touching and teach your child they can say no.

cards.title: Vehicles and machines
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who love trucks, wheels, engines and how machines work.

sections.text: Children may push trucks along every path, make engine sounds, line up cars, or stop to watch a garbage truck or a digger. They ask how things work, want to open machines and turn every round thing into a wheel.

items: A take-apart table with old clocks, radios, keyboards and toasters, cords and batteries removed, and real screwdrivers, pliers and trays for parts.
Real photos of trucks, tractors, diggers, trains and bikes at work, posted at children's eye level.
Watching real machines on our street or nearby, such as the garbage truck, a tractor or a delivery van, with clipboards for drawing.
Ramps, gutters and tubes in the yards with trucks, balls and wheels to roll.
Wheelbarrows, wagons and carts to haul mulch, compost and logs as real work in the garden.
A car and bike wash with buckets, sponges and real water in the yards.
Cardboard boxes, bottle caps, spools, dowels and low-temp glue guns for building vehicles with wheels that turn.
Pulleys, gears and a rope and bucket on the climbing structure to lift loads.
A tire track painting invitation with old toy trucks rolled through tempera on long paper.
Simple hand tools to explore, such as a hand drill, an egg beater, a bike pump and a crank.
Pieces of a found machine rebuilt into a new sculpture with wire and glue.
The chain reaction film by Peter Fischli and David Weiss or Jean Tinguely's moving machines shown on screen for ideas.
Books about how things work and about vehicles from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Hauling and building vehicles is great teamwork. Taking apart a clock with a screwdriver can hold a child alone for a long time.

Remove cords, batteries, glass and springs under tension before a machine goes on the take-apart table. Never offer televisions, screens or anything that stores charge. Loosen screws ahead of time so children can finish them. Real tools come with an adult and clear agreements. Watch vehicles from behind a fence or the curb.

items: Use real screwdrivers and pliers to open machines.
Sort parts into trays and name them in their own words.
Haul real loads with wheelbarrows and wagons.
Design, build and test vehicles that roll.
Draw machines from life and from memory.
Wash and care for the bikes and wagons.
Teach a friend how a tool works.

sections.text: Children sort screws and parts into the labeled trays and hang screwdrivers and pliers back on their outlines, while an adult checks the tool count. They wash the bikes and wagons with sponges and buckets and park them in their marked spots. Toy vehicles go back to their basket, and the area is closed on the floor as part of the work.

Sit beside the take-apart table or ramp with your hands still, offering tools only when a child asks or needs a safety check. Narrate what you see, such as "You turned the screw the other way and it came loose." Stay steady when parts scatter or a truck crashes.

items: Tell me what you think is inside.
I wonder what makes the wheels turn.
How could you change it so it goes farther?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with real vehicles on site such as wagons, wheelbarrows and bikes.
Watch and draw a real truck or tractor at work.
Open a take-apart table with one old machine and a few real tools.
Sort and display parts, and ask children what each part does.
Build vehicles from boxes and test which wheels roll best.
Add ramps of different heights and compare how far vehicles travel.
Add pulleys and gears to lift loads in the yards.
Invite a family member who drives or fixes vehicles to visit with tools.
Rebuild found parts into new machine sculptures.
Make a chain reaction across a table or yard as a class.
Paint with tire tracks and compare the patterns.
Make a class book of how children think machines work.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Ramps, wagons and building vehicles happen with an educator nearby. The take-apart table and low-temp glue guns need an adult at the table, and watching street vehicles means staying behind a fence or curb with adults.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer real hauling with wheelbarrows and wagons full of mulch or logs, a heavy truck pushed up a long ramp, and real screwdrivers on the take-apart table. A car and bike wash with full buckets and big sponges adds strong work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer small cars on a quiet tape road or a tray ramp, and watching big machines from a window or a far spot. Ear defenders can help when a garbage truck or tool is loud.
connected: Peter Fischli and David Weiss on the Artists page, for a film of everyday things knocking each other in a long chain.
Jean Tinguely on the Artists page, for sculptures made from wheels and scrap that move and rattle.
Arthur Ganson on the Artists page, for small machines with gears and wire that move in slow, surprising ways.

sections.text: An old machine such as a broken clock or radio with cords and batteries removed, a screwdriver, a tray, boxes and bottle caps for wheels.

items: Take apart an old clock or radio together and sort the parts into a tray.
Watch the garbage truck or a digger from a safe spot and talk about what each part does.
Build a car from a box with bottle cap wheels.
Let your child carry real loads in a wagon or wheelbarrow in the yard.
Roll toy cars down a board and see which goes farthest.

sections.text: Your child can hold the screwdriver, sort parts, haul loads and design their own vehicles. Your child can wash a bike or toy truck with a bucket and sponge and park it in its spot. Sorting cars into a basket afterward is a real job they can finish on their own.

items: Tell me what this part does.
How could we make it go faster?
I wonder where it is going.

sections.text: Your child is figuring out how things work, using real tools and solving problems. Pushing heavy wheelbarrows and turning screwdrivers give arms and hands strong work and help both hands work together.
Send old machines with cords cut off and batteries removed, such as clocks, radios and keyboards, for our take-apart table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Remove cords, batteries and glass first. Stay close when real tools are out. Never open screens or televisions.

cards.title: Castles, houses and homes
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who build houses, forts and castles and wonder where people and animals live.

sections.text: Children may build walls and towers with blocks, drape fabric over tables, or claim a corner as their house. They talk about kings and queens, draw their own homes, and ask where the goats, birds and bugs live.

items: Real photos of homes from many places, such as adobe houses, yurts, stilt houses, apartments, castles and tule houses, at children's eye level.
A walk around the neighborhood to look at roofs, doors, windows and walls, with clipboards for drawing.
Large fabric, clips, crates and tires for building dens and forts in the yards and under the willow dome.
Unit blocks with castle and house photos taped in the block area.
Cardboard boxes, tape, scissors and low-temp glue guns for building homes big enough to sit in.
Small houses built from sticks, bark, clay and stones for bugs and fairies in the garden.
A look at animal homes on our site, such as the chicken coop, the rabbit hutch, Sheldon's burrow, bird nests and roly poly hiding spots.
Mud bricks made in molds in the mud kitchen and dried in the sun for building small walls.
Drawing our own homes from memory and from family photos.
A dollhouse with real tiny furniture made by children from found materials.
Mapping where each child lives on a big shared map.
Do Ho Suh's fabric houses, Simon Rodia's Watts Towers and Antoni Gaudí's Casa Batlló shown on screen for ideas.
Books about homes and castles from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Building a fort together needs negotiation, roles and shared plans. Drawing one's own home or making a tiny house holds a child's personal story.

Homes are tender for children. Some move often, live in more than one home or are without stable housing, so honor every kind of home. Check that large builds are stable and that fabric dens have an open side for supervision. Build bug houses so creatures can come and go freely.

items: Plan, build and name houses and forts.
Negotiate who lives where and what the rules are.
Draw and map their own homes.
Choose materials and solve problems when walls fall.
Care for animal homes on site by cleaning and adding bedding.
Take down and put away large builds as a team.
Teach a friend how to make the walls stand.

sections.text: Builders take their houses and forts down as a team, carrying blocks, crates and planks they can lift to their marked places and folding fabric walls with a partner. Clips go into their basket, and roofs and doors are stacked by size. An adult moves only the heaviest pieces, so the space is reset by the people who built it.

Stay near the building at the children's level, ready to hold a corner only when asked. Keep your voice regular and your face calm when walls fall. Let the children decide who lives inside and how it changes.

items: Tell me what a home needs.
I wonder who lives here.
How could we make the wall stronger?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with fabric, crates and clips for a den.
Ask what a home needs and record children's ideas.
Walk the neighborhood to look at real houses and draw them.
Add photos of homes from many places to the block area.
Build big cardboard houses and add doors, windows and signs.
Look closely at animal homes on our site and help care for them.
Build bug, bird and fairy houses from natural materials in the garden.
Make mud bricks and build small walls.
Invite families to send a photo of their home or a story about where they come from.
Draw a big map of where everyone lives.
Build a castle as a whole class with blocks, cardboard and loose parts.
Make a class book of homes in children's own drawings and words.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Den and block building are open to everyone. Low-temp glue guns need an adult at the table, large builds need an educator checking they are stable, and neighborhood walks mean holding hands.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer building forts with heavy crates, tires and big fabric, and making mud bricks packed hard into molds. Moving boxes big enough to sit in adds lifting and pushing.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small house of sticks, bark and stones for bugs on a quiet garden bed, or a cozy corner with one blanket. They can sit inside a finished den before helping to build one.
connected: Do Ho Suh on the Artists page, for full-size houses sewn from thin fabric you can see through.
Simon Rodia on the Artists page, for towers built by hand from steel, cement, tile and broken dishes in Los Angeles.
Antoni Gaudí on the Artists page, for houses with curving walls and roofs covered in broken tile.

home.title: Castles, houses and homes at Home

sections.text: Blankets, chairs, clothespins or clips, cardboard boxes, tape and crayons.

items: Build a fort with blankets and chairs and decide together what it needs.
Walk your street and look at doors, roofs and windows.
Turn a big box into a house with windows your child cuts and draws.
Build a tiny house for bugs from sticks and leaves outside.
Draw your home together and add the people and pets who live there.

sections.text: Your child can plan, build, decorate and decide who is invited in. Your child can take apart a fort, fold the sheets and carry cushions back to their places. Doing it together makes building the next home just as easy.

items: Tell me what a home needs.
Who lives in our home?
How can we make it stand up?

sections.text: Your child is planning, building, solving problems and telling their own story of home. Lifting, packing and building give the body strong work, and a cozy space of their own helps many children feel calm.
Send a photo or drawing of your home or a story about where your family comes from. Large clean boxes and old sheets are welcome for building. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Keep forts low and stable. Leave a side open so you can see in.

cards.title: Collecting and treasure
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who fill their pockets, hoard treasures and sort what they find.

sections.text: Children may arrive with pockets full of rocks, acorns or feathers and want to keep them all. They hide treasures, trade them, make piles and sort them, and talk about what is special and why.

items: A personal treasure box or labeled drawer for each child.
A shared cabinet of curiosities with many small drawers in the class or outdoor piazza.
Collecting walks with small bags or egg cartons and the agreement to pick with purpose and leave some for others.
Sorting trays, muffin tins, ice cube trays and bowls on a low table for grouping finds.
Magnifiers, a light table and clipboards for looking closely at each treasure.
Real photos of museum collections, such as shells, rocks, feathers and seeds, posted at children's eye level.
A small museum children build and label for families to visit.
Treasure hunts with simple picture maps children draw for each other.
Buried treasure in the sandbox with shovels and sieves.
The iNaturalist app opened with children to learn the names of what they find.
Trading and shop play with collected treasures.
Joseph Cornell's boxes and Mark Dion's collection cabinets shown on screen for ideas.
Shadow boxes made from cardboard trays to display one collection.

sections.text: Both. Each child's treasure is personal and worth honoring. Shared collections, museums and trading build community and conversation.

Adults confirm every plant children gather is one we know, because poison hemlock and poison oak grow on site. Do not collect live animals, nests or bird eggs. Feathers from most wild birds are protected by law, so children look and draw, then return them to the ground. Feathers from our own chickens are fine to keep. Leave some for others and for animals.

items: Choose what to collect and why it matters.
Sort, count and group treasures by their own rules.
Label collections with marks, words and drawings.
Care for the cabinet and keep drawers in order.
Build a museum and guide visitors.
Decide what goes back to the garden.
Trade and share treasures with friends.

sections.text: Children close collecting time by sorting treasures into the cabinet drawers and labeling anything new with a mark or word. Magnifiers and tweezers go back to their tray, and a damp cloth wipes sand and dust off the sorting table. Things that belong outside go back to the garden with the child who found them.

Sit beside the child with interest in each treasure, holding finds with care and giving them back. Narrate what you see, such as "You put all the smooth ones together." Let the child decide what is special and where it goes.

items: Tell me what makes this one special.
I wonder how you decided where it goes.
Where did you find this one?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Honor what children bring by giving each one a place to keep treasures.
Offer sorting trays and let children make their own groups.
Go on collecting walks with agreements about picking with purpose.
Add magnifiers and the light table to look closer.
Start a shared cabinet of curiosities.
Draw and label treasures in a class field guide.
Use iNaturalist to learn names together.
Build a class museum and invite families or another class.
Make shadow boxes for one favorite collection.
Draw treasure maps and hide treasures for friends.
Visit a museum with collections, such as the California Academy of Sciences.
Return treasures to the garden at the end of a season with a small ceremony.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Collecting, sorting and displaying are open to everyone. Adults confirm every plant gathered on collecting walks, and small treasures stay away from the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer sieving and digging for buried treasure in the sandbox, carrying a full bag of finds back from a collecting walk, and sorting heavy stones into muffin tins. Rough bark, smooth stones and prickly seed pods add touch.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small egg carton with a few smooth, dry treasures to sort at a quiet table. Tongs or a spoon can move things without touching, and they can keep their own treasure box close.
connected: Joseph Cornell on the Artists page, for small wooden boxes holding found treasures arranged with care.
Mark Dion on the Artists page, for cabinets filled with things he collected, sorted and displayed.

sections.text: A shoebox or egg carton, small bags, a magnifier and a muffin tin or bowls for sorting.

items: Go on a walk and collect a few small treasures, leaving some for others.
Sort treasures by color, size or how they feel.
Give your child a box of their own for treasures.
Make a little museum on a shelf and let your child give a tour.
Draw a treasure map and hide something for each other to find.

sections.text: Your child can choose, sort, label and decide what to keep and what to return. Your child can sort treasures into an egg carton or small box and decide what goes back outside. A shelf or drawer of their own gives every collection a home.

items: Tell me why this one is special.
How could we sort these?
I wonder where it came from.

sections.text: Your child is sorting, counting, noticing details and learning to care for what they find. Sorting small treasures gives fingers careful work, and arranging them can be a calm, settling time.
Send a small collection from a family walk to share at school, such as shells, rocks or seed pods. Egg cartons and small boxes are welcome too. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Only collect plants you know are safe. Leave nests, eggs, wild bird feathers and live animals where they are. Small items can be a choking risk for babies and toddlers.

cards.title: Monsters and fear
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who play monsters, talk about scary things and test their own courage.

sections.text: Children may roar and chase, hide from a pretend monster, or ask if monsters are real. They talk about the dark, bad dreams or a scary story, build traps, and make plans to be brave.

items: Clay, wire and found materials for making monsters children can hold in their hands.
Story dictation and story acting at meeting time, where children tell monster stories and act them out together.
Puppets and fabric for monster shows in a puppet theater.
Flashlights and a dark tent or covered table to explore the dark at their own pace.
Shadow monsters made with hands and cutouts on a sheet or wall.
Drawing fears with oil pastels and charcoal, then choosing what to do with the drawing.
A monster trap building invitation with boxes, string, tape and loose parts.
Masks made from paper plates, cardboard and fabric, with mirrors to see the faces they make.
Real photos of masks and creatures from many cultures at children's eye level.
Mexican alebrijes by Pedro Linares and Japanese yokai drawings by Toriyama Sekien shown on screen for ideas.
Books about monsters and brave feelings from the Book collection, such as Where the Wild Things Are.
Chase games in the yards with clear agreements about stop, safe zones and who wants to play.

sections.text: Both. Monster play is often a group game with roles and rules. Drawing or talking about a personal fear may need a quiet moment with a trusted adult.

Monster play helps children practice power and fear in a safe frame. Agree together on how to start and stop a chase, and that everyone in the game wants to be in it. Never dismiss a fear. Listen first and ask what would help. Keep scary images gentle for the 2s and let children leave any game at any time.

items: Invent monsters and give them names, homes and rules.
Tell and act out their own monster stories.
Make agreements for chase games and remind friends of them.
Choose when to face a fear and when to step back.
Build traps, shields and brave plans.
Comfort a friend who is scared.

sections.text: Children close monster play by putting masks, capes and props back in their basket and taking down traps or shelters together. Fabric is folded with a partner and stacked on its shelf. The game ends when everyone agrees, and the space is put back by the players.

Stay close and grounded with a warm face and a calm, regular voice, so children can borrow your steadiness. Let them control the scary part and play along with interest. If a child becomes truly frightened, come to their level and breathe with them before anything else.

items: Tell me what this monster wants.
I wonder what helps you feel brave.
How does your body feel when you are scared?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Listen to monster talk and play without stopping it.
Make chase agreements with the children who play.
Offer clay and found materials for making monsters.
Start story dictation and story acting with monster tales.
Explore the dark with flashlights in a tent.
Play with shadow monsters on a sheet.
Invite children to draw a fear and decide what to do with it.
Make masks and puppets for a monster show.
Look at creature art from many cultures, such as alebrijes and yokai.
Build monster traps and test them.
Write a class book of monsters with each child's creature and its story.
Turn monsters into friends or guardians if children choose that.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Chase games and monster play need an educator nearby who helps children start and stop. The dark tent needs an adult close by, and a truly frightened child needs an adult at their side.
