cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big monster roars and stomps in the yard, building monster traps with heavy boxes and string, and squeezing and pounding clay into a monster. A dark tent with flashlights adds new things to see.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small monster of clay or wire that fits in their hand, and a flashlight they control in a tent with the door open. They can watch a puppet show from the back and choose when the lights go down.
connected: Maurice Sendak on the Artists page, for drawing wild creatures that are scary and kind at once.
Pedro Linares on the Artists page, for bright paper creatures, called alebrijes, that came to him in a dream.
Toriyama Sekien on the Artists page, for ink drawings of Japanese yokai, creatures from old stories.
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: Playdough or clay, paper, crayons, a flashlight, a blanket and some favorite stories.

items: Make a monster from playdough or clay and give it a name.
Tell a monster story together and let your child decide how it ends.
Make shadow monsters on the wall with a flashlight.
Draw a scary thing together and talk about what would help.
Read a monster book and talk about how the characters felt.

sections.text: Your child can invent the monster, lead the story, choose when to stop and tell you what helps them feel brave. Your child can put the monster masks to bed in their basket and fold the blankets from the trap. A clear ending helps scary play feel safe and finished.

items: Tell me what your monster likes.
What helps you feel brave?
I wonder what could happen next.

sections.text: Your child is practicing being brave, telling stories and handling big feelings in play. Noticing a fast heart or a tight tummy and then breathing slowly helps children learn to calm their own body.
Send a monster drawing or a story your child told for our class book.
Listen to fears without brushing them off. Let your child stop the game at any time.

cards.title: Time and clocks
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who ask how long, when and what time it is.

sections.text: Children may ask how many sleeps until a birthday, wear a toy watch, or set a sand timer for turns. They talk about yesterday and tomorrow, notice the sun moving and ask what clocks are for.

items: Sand timers of different lengths for turns and for watching sand fall.
Real wind-up clocks, watches and an old alarm clock to look at, wind and listen to.
A take-apart clock with screwdrivers and trays for gears.
A sundial on the outdoor piazza, made from a tall stick and stones children place at each hour.
Chalk tracings of a child's shadow in the morning and again at noon in the same spot.
An illustrated daily schedule with photos children help take and arrange.
A long paper timeline of the year along a hallway, with seasons and birthdays added.
Plants grown from seed and photographed each week to see time pass.
The sourdough starter in the culinary atelier fed and watched as it rises over hours.
Real photos of clocks, sundials, hourglasses and calendars from many places at children's eye level.
Claude Monet's haystacks painted at many times of day shown on screen beside paint and paper.
Rhythm and steady beat with drums, shakers and a metronome in the music shed.
Books about time, days and seasons from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Sand timers and turn-taking are about time with others. Watching a clock or a sundial can be calm private looking.

Young children understand time through routines and the sun more than clock numbers. Use time words that link to our day, such as after snack or before pickup. Remove batteries and glass from clocks for taking apart. Glass sand timers stay where an adult can see them.

items: Set and watch sand timers for turns.
Help make and arrange the daily schedule.
Mark the sundial and shadow tracings.
Take apart clocks with real tools.
Track plant growth with photos and drawings.
Keep a countdown chain for an event they are waiting for.
Remind friends of what comes next in the day.

sections.text: Children close by turning sand timers on their side on the soft mat, sorting clock parts into labeled trays and hanging small screwdrivers back on their outlines. They move the schedule card to show what comes next. An adult checks the tool count, and the table is clear before the group goes on.

Sit beside the child with a slow, unhurried body as you watch the sand fall or the shadow move. Keep your voice soft and regular, and let waiting be part of the experience. Narrate the change, such as "The sand is half gone now."

items: I wonder how the shadow moved.
How do you know it is almost time?
Tell me what you think is inside the clock.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Offer sand timers for turns and for watching.
Make the daily schedule with children's photos.
Trace shadows at different times of day.
Build a sundial with a stick and stones.
Take apart an old clock and sort its gears.
Grow seeds and photograph them weekly.
Feed and watch the sourdough starter rise over a day.
Make a countdown chain for an event.
Build a class timeline of the year along the hallway.
Play steady beat and fast and slow rhythms in the music shed.
Look at Monet's paintings of the same place at different times of day and paint one place at morning and afternoon.
Make a class book of how children think time works.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Sand timers, schedules and shadow tracing are open to everyone. Taking apart a clock needs an adult at the table, and glass sand timers stay where an adult can see them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer winding real clocks and holding them close to hear the tick, taking apart an old clock with screwdrivers, and racing a sand timer across the yard. Tracing their shadow with chalk on the piazza adds movement.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a sand timer to watch in a quiet corner and a picture schedule to check whenever they wish. Knowing what comes next helps many children settle.
connected: Claude Monet on the Artists page, for painting the same haystacks at many times of day and year.
Salvador Dalí on the Artists page, for painting soft, melting clocks.

sections.text: A sand timer or kitchen timer, an old clock or watch, chalk, a calendar and paper.

items: Use a timer for taking turns and watching.
Trace your child's shadow with chalk in the morning and again in the afternoon.
Make a paper chain to count down to a special day.
Take apart an old clock with batteries and glass removed.
Draw the steps of your morning together in order.

sections.text: Your child can set the timer, mark the calendar, tear a link from the chain and tell you what comes next. Your child can put the timer back in its spot, sort clock parts into a tray and move a picture card to show what comes next. A small basket for time things keeps them easy to find.

items: How do you know it is morning?
Tell me what comes next.
I wonder where your shadow went.

sections.text: Your child is learning about order, waiting and change through daily routines. Watching a timer and knowing what comes next helps many children feel calm, and winding clocks gives fingers strong work.
Send old clocks or watches with batteries removed for our take-apart table. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Remove batteries and glass before taking clocks apart. Small parts can be a choking risk for little ones.

cards.title: Faces and feelings
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who study faces, make expressions and want words for big feelings.

sections.text: Children may make faces in the mirror, ask why a friend is crying, or say they are mad, sad or happy over and over. They draw faces on everything, notice who looks different and ask about skin, eyes and hair.

items: A mirror with paper, pencils and fine black pens for self-portraits, offered many times through the year.
Paints mixed with children to match their own skin, eyes and hair, with each child naming their color.
Real photos of faces of many ages, cultures and feelings at children's eye level, with children's own feeling words beside them.
Family photos in a small album or on a wall at the entry, chosen and sent by families.
Clay faces built from a ball with loose parts for eyes, mouths and hair.
Faces made from natural materials on the ground in the garden and photographed.
Feeling marks with oil pastels after a few deep breaths, with children choosing colors for how they feel.
A cozy space with a soft mirror, photos of the class, and calm tools such as a breathing stone or a weighted lap pad.
Puppets with faces that change for acting out what happened and what could help.
Masks and face painting with mirrors to see one's own face change.
Portraits of a friend, drawn while sitting across from each other.
Vincent van Gogh's self-portraits, Frida Kahlo's self-portraits and Edvard Munch's The Scream shown on screen for talk about faces and feelings.
Books about feelings and faces from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Drawing a friend's face or reading feelings together builds connection. A self-portrait at the mirror is quiet personal work.

Photos of children's faces stay inside our walls and never go online or in public. Honor every skin color, feature and family structure, and answer questions about differences plainly and warmly. Self-portraits may not take off early in the year, so offer again later. Feelings are always welcome, and adults help children find safe ways to show them.

items: Draw and paint themselves and friends.
Mix and name paint colors for their own skin.
Choose feeling words and colors for what they feel.
Notice a friend's feelings and offer help.
Choose calm tools in the cozy space.
Decide which portraits go on the wall and what to say about them.
Teach a friend a breathing or calming idea.

sections.text: Children close portrait work by rinsing brushes in the wash bucket, wiping mirrors with a soft cloth and laying paintings on the drying rack. They cap the paints and wipe the table with a damp sponge. Calm tools go back into the cozy space basket, so the area is ready for whoever comes next.

Sit at eye level within arm's reach, letting your own face stay open and calm. Name feelings plainly without fixing them, such as "Your fists are tight." When a child is upset, co-regulate first with breath and closeness before offering any material.

items: Tell me about your face when you feel that way.
I wonder how your friend is feeling.
Where in your body do you feel that?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Set out a mirror and simple drawing tools.
Mix skin color paints together with each child.
Add real photos of faces and feelings at eye level.
Build clay faces with loose parts.
Offer feeling marks with oil pastels after deep breaths.
Draw a friend's portrait sitting face to face.
Act out feelings with puppets and masks.
Look at self-portraits by artists and talk about the feelings in them.
Create a family photo wall with photos families choose.
Return to self-portraits later in the year and look at both together.
Make a class book of feelings in children's words and drawings.
Build a calm corner with the children, choosing what goes in it.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Mirrors, portraits and feeling marks are open to everyone. Face painting needs an adult at the table, and a child who is upset needs an adult close for breathing and calm first.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big faces in the mirror with strong stretches and squeezes, pounding clay into a face, and a weighted lap pad or a firm hug when they want one. Feeling marks with oil pastels pressed hard on paper add strong hand work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the cozy space with a soft mirror and class photos to look at alone. They can point to a feeling photo instead of talking, and choose a pencil drawing over paint.
connected: Vincent van Gogh on the Artists page, for painting his own face many times with bold brushstrokes.
Frida Kahlo on the Artists page, for self-portraits that show her feelings, animals and plants around her.
Edvard Munch on the Artists page, for The Scream, a face and sky full of a big feeling.
Art of Presence and Language PD module
The Image of the Child lens

sections.text: A mirror, paper, pencils or crayons, family photos and some calm time.

items: Draw faces together while looking in a mirror.
Make silly, sad, surprised and angry faces in the mirror and name each one.
Look at family photos and talk about how each person feels.
Mix paint to match your skin colors and give each one a name.
Breathe together, then draw how you feel with colors.

sections.text: Your child can choose the colors, name the feelings and tell you what helps them feel calm. Your child can rinse brushes, wipe a mirror and lay a drawing somewhere safe to dry. A small towel and cup of water make the close part of the painting.

items: How do you think they feel?
Tell me what your face does when you are happy.
What helps you feel better?

sections.text: Your child is learning words for feelings and seeing themselves and others with care. Noticing where a feeling sits in the body helps children understand their own signals and find their way back to calm.
Send a family photo for our family wall or your child's self-portrait from home. This counts toward your family participation hours.
All feelings are okay. Stay close and calm when feelings are big.

cards.title: Cooking and food
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who play kitchen, want to help cook and care about where food comes from.

sections.text: Children may stir mud soup, serve pretend meals, ask to help chop, or talk about what their family cooks. They notice harvests in the garden, smell herbs, and want to taste what they grew.

items: Real cooking in the culinary atelier with real knives, crinkle cutters, peelers, graters and citrus squeezers, an adult beside each small group.
A self-access baking shelf with labeled jars, measuring cups and picture recipes children follow.
Harvest from the garden and orchard, such as strawberries, lemons, figs, herbs and greens, washed and prepared by children.
Tea from mint, lemon balm and hibiscus, and lemonade from our Meyer lemons, made and poured by children.
The Unicorn Café with real dishes, cloth napkins, menus children write and flowers from the garden on each table.
Family recipes collected for the Recipe library and cooked together in the culinary atelier.
Taste tests of garden varieties, such as different apples, citrus or tomatoes, with children's own words recorded.
Real photos of markets, farms, kitchens and family meals from many places at children's eye level.
A visit to a farmers market or a local farm.
Real fruit set on a display table to look at and draw, then shared at snack or given to the chicken bucket.
Food scraps carried to the chickens and the compost so children see where scraps go.
Paul Cézanne's apples and Wayne Thiebaud's cakes and pies shown on screen beside observational drawing.
Cookbooks and books about food and farms from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Cooking is small group work with shared tasks and a meal to share. Washing, peeling or squeezing can hold a child's own steady focus.

Our kitchen is vegetarian and nut free. Check every allergy and family food practice before cooking. Food is for eating and is never used as art or sensory material. Everyone washes hands first. Teach knife grips and the claw hand slowly, and keep hot surfaces with an adult. Share what we cook simply.

items: Wash, peel, cut, squeeze, measure and stir.
Harvest from the garden and decide what is ripe.
Read picture recipes and follow the steps.
Set tables, serve friends and clear dishes.
Write menus and signs for the café.
Carry scraps to the chickens and compost.
Teach a friend how to use a tool safely.
Bring family recipes and stories to share.

sections.text: Cooks close the kitchen work by carrying scraps to the chicken bucket or compost, scraping bowls and washing dishes in a low tub of soapy water. They dry tools with a towel, set them back on the labeled self-access shelf and wipe the counter with a damp cloth. An adult handles knives and hot pans, and the culinary atelier is reset by the children who cooked.

Stand or sit beside each child in the small group, close enough to guide a knife or grater, with calm hands and a regular voice. Model care for food and tools, and let the children do the real work even when it is slower. Spills are part of cooking, so keep your face easy and a cloth nearby.

items: Tell me how it smells now.
I wonder what would happen if we cooked it longer.
How do you think it grew?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with simple tasks such as washing, tearing and squeezing.
Introduce one real tool at a time with clear agreements.
Harvest and prepare one garden food from bed to bowl.
Make tea or lemonade from our own plants.
Set up the self-access baking shelf with picture recipes.
Collect family recipes and cook one each week.
Run the Unicorn Café with menus, signs and real dishes.
Hold taste tests and record children's words.
Draw fruit and vegetables from life, then share them at snack.
Follow scraps to compost and back to the garden.
Visit a farm or farmers market.
Make a class cookbook with children's drawings and steps.
Grow, harvest, cook and save seed from one plant across a whole year.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Real cooking happens in a small group with an adult close enough to guide each knife and grater. Hot surfaces stay with an adult, and children new to knives cut with an adult right beside them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer kneading bread dough, squeezing citrus by hand, grating, and stirring thick batter with a wooden spoon. Carrying harvest baskets from the orchard and smelling crushed mint and rosemary add strong input.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a job with tools instead of hands, such as a crinkle cutter, a citrus squeezer or a spoon, in a quieter corner of the culinary atelier. They can smell from a small jar, watch first, and choose when to taste.
connected: Paul Cézanne on the Artists page, for painting apples and fruit on a table again and again.
Wayne Thiebaud on the Artists page, a Sacramento painter, for rows of cakes and pies in thick, rich paint.

sections.text: A child-safe knife or crinkle cutter, a cutting board, a bowl, measuring cups, a step stool and a simple recipe.

items: Let your child wash, tear and stir for a family meal.
Squeeze lemons or oranges together for a drink.
Teach your child to cut soft fruit with a child knife and a claw hand.
Make a picture recipe together and follow it step by step.
Let your child set the table and serve.

sections.text: Your child can choose the recipe, measure, cut, stir, serve and help clean up. Your child can wash bowls in a low tub, dry spoons with a towel and carry scraps to the compost. A step stool at the sink lets them finish what they cooked.

items: Tell me what you smell.
How did it change when we cooked it?
Where do you think this grew?

sections.text: Your child is using real tools, following steps and feeling proud to feed others. Kneading, squeezing and stirring give hands strong work, and smelling herbs and food lets children try new senses at their own pace.
Send a family recipe for our Recipe library, ideally vegetarian and nut free, or come cook it with us. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash hands first. Keep hot pans and sharp knives with an adult. Our school is nut free.

cards.title: Fire and campfires
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who play campfire, wonder about fire and want to know how to stay safe.

sections.text: Children may build a pretend campfire from sticks, roast pretend marshmallows, or talk about fire trucks, smoke and evacuation. They ask what makes fire hot, why it is orange and what to do if there is a fire.

items: A pretend campfire in the Log yard or outdoor piazza with real logs, stones in a ring and red, orange and yellow fabric flames.
Campfire stories, songs and a pretend camp with tents, sleeping bags, lanterns and flashlights.
A pretend fire ring of logs and stones with a marked way in and out, where children make their own campfire agreements.
Battery tea lights and flashlights under orange and yellow fabric in a dark tent, for a glowing pretend fire.
Fire safety practice with stop, drop and roll, crawling low and our fire drill route.
A visit from the fire department or a walk to a fire station, with real gear to touch.
Real photos of campfires, candles, fireplaces, lanterns and firefighters at children's eye level.
Willow charcoal we make on purpose from willow dome trimmings, with children watching from a marked distance, for drawing on paper and stones.
Sorting sticks by size into tinder, kindling and logs for building pretend fires.
Talk about cultural burning and how Pomo and Miwok people have cared for land with fire, shared with care and accuracy.
Firelight colors explored with red, orange and yellow cellophane on the light table.
Georges de La Tour's candlelight paintings shown on screen beside charcoal and dark paper.
Books and real photos about what fire needs and why it glows, set beside the pretend fire so children can bring their own theories into play.
A pretend fire station with real hoses, boots, helmets and a cardboard fire truck children build.
Real photos of our county's hills turning green again after wildfire, for wondering about change over time.
Books about fire safety, campfires and firefighters from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Pretend campfires and fire drills are shared and build safety together. A child may quietly need to talk about a fire or smoke that frightened them.

We do not have campfires with children. The one intentional fire is a small contained fire an adult tends for making willow charcoal, with children watching from a marked distance. Otherwise children explore fire through pretend play, stories, songs, books and real photos. Matches and lighters stay out of children's spaces. Many families in our county have lived through wildfire, evacuation and smoke, so listen first and speak calmly. Practice our fire drill and let children know firefighters are helpers. On smoke days we follow local air quality guidance.

items: Build and tend pretend campfires.
Sort sticks by size and name each pile.
Make agreements for the pretend fire ring and walk in and out by them.
Lead stop, drop and roll for friends.
Tell campfire stories and choose campfire songs.
Draw with charcoal and wonder where it came from.
Share what they know about staying safe.

sections.text: Children close the pretend fire ring by sorting sticks back into their size piles and returning stones to the ring's edge. Charcoal drawings go to the drying rack, and charcoal sticks go back to their tin with a damp cloth to wipe hands and table. The close follows the same walk-in and walk-out agreements as the play.

Stay close and grounded, with a steady body and a calm voice whenever fire is the topic. Notice your own feelings about fire and smoke, since children read our worry. Keep agreements clear and spoken simply, and welcome every question, even the hard ones.

items: Tell me what you think fire needs.
I wonder where the smoke goes.
How can we keep safe?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Build a pretend campfire with logs, stones and fabric flames.
Add a pretend camp with tents, lanterns and flashlights.
Practice fire drills and stop, drop and roll.
Mark a pretend fire ring and practice walking in and out by children's agreements.
Sort sticks into tinder, kindling and logs.
Look at books and real photos about what fire needs and talk about what we see.
Make willow charcoal together and draw with it, wondering how wood turns black.
Invite firefighters to visit with their gear.
Build a pretend fire station with hoses, boots and a cardboard fire truck.
Learn campfire songs and tell stories around the pretend fire.
Learn about cultural burning and land care with care and accuracy.
Make a class book of fire safety in children's own words.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Pretend campfires, stories and fire drills are open to everyone. Making willow charcoal is adult work with children watching from a marked distance, and visits to a fire station leave campus with hand holding.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer carrying real logs and stones to build the pretend fire ring, practicing stop, drop and roll and crawling low, and pressing charcoal hard on paper and stones. Sorting a big pile of sticks by size adds hand work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a pretend campfire of fabric flames and a lantern in a quiet tent, with campfire songs. They can look at photos and talk about safety at their own pace, and watch the group's pretend fire from as far back as they like.
connected: Georges de La Tour on the Artists page, for paintings lit only by one candle flame in the dark.

sections.text: Sticks, stones, red, orange and yellow fabric or paper, a flashlight and a plan for where to meet if there is a fire.

items: Build a pretend campfire indoors or out and tell stories around it.
Practice stop, drop and roll together.
Make a family fire plan and walk to your meeting spot.
Find the smoke alarms in your home and test one together.
Sort sticks into small, medium and big piles.

sections.text: Your child can build the pretend fire, lead the safety practice and help make your family plan. Your child can sort sticks into piles by size, stack them in a basket and wipe charcoal from hands with a damp cloth. A clear end helps fire play stay calm and safe.

items: Tell me what you think fire needs.
Where would we meet?
How do we keep safe?

sections.text: Your child is learning how to stay safe and how to talk about fire with confidence. Carrying logs and practicing stop, drop and roll give the body strong work, and knowing the plan helps many children feel calm.
Send a photo of your family's meeting spot or your child's fire safety drawing.
Keep matches and lighters out of reach. Real fire is only for adults. Talk calmly if your child is worried about fire.

cards.title: Space, sun and moon
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who look up and ask about the sun, the moon, stars and planets.

sections.text: Children may spot the moon in the morning sky and call everyone to see. They play rockets and astronauts, ask where the sun goes at night, and wonder how far away the stars are.

items: A morning moon watch, since the moon is often visible in our sky during the day.
A moon journal where children draw the moon's shape when they see it, at school and at home.
Shadow tracing in the outdoor piazza at different times of day to follow the sun.
Sun prints on sun print paper with leaves and loose parts.
A dark tent or room with flashlights, a ball and a lamp to wonder about day and night.
Real photos of the moon, the sun, planets and Earth from space at children's eye level.
Rockets and space stations built from boxes, tubes and tape.
Craters made by dropping stones into a deep tray of flour dusted on top with colored chalk dust.
Constellation patterns poked into dark paper and held up to light.
Galileo's ink drawings of the moon and Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night shown on screen beside ink and paint.
A family evening at the Robert Ferguson Observatory in Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, or Chabot Space and Science Center in Oakland.
Books about space, the sun and the moon from the Book collection.
Night sky songs from the Song book at meeting time.

sections.text: Both. Spotting the moon together and building a rocket are shared joys. A moon journal is a child's own record over time.

Never look straight at the sun, even with sunglasses. Use the light table, shadows and sun prints to explore sunlight safely. The moon's shape changes over about a month, so keep the journal going long enough to notice. Many families see the night sky from home, so invite them in.

items: Spot and announce the moon when they see it.
Draw the moon's shape in the journal.
Trace shadows and mark the sun's path.
Build rockets and decide who does each job.
Make sun prints and choose the objects.
Share sky findings from home at meeting time.

sections.text: Children close sky work by returning the moon journal to its shelf and putting chalk back in its tin after shadow tracing. Sun print papers go to the drying rack, and rocket parts are sorted into their labeled baskets. Everything has a photo-labeled home, so the space closes as part of the work.

Look up alongside the children with a slow, curious face and a quiet voice. Lie down on the grass or sit low together to watch the sky. Let wondering hang in the air, since big questions do not need fast answers.

items: I wonder where the moon goes during the day.
Tell me about its shape today.
Where do you think the sun goes at night?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Notice the moon in the morning sky together.
Start a moon journal and invite families to add to it.
Trace shadows through the day.
Make sun prints with leaves and loose parts.
Explore day and night with a lamp and a ball in a dark space.
Build rockets and a space station in dramatic play.
Make craters by dropping stones into flour dusted with chalk dust.
Poke constellations into dark paper.
Look at Galileo's moon drawings and draw the moon from life.
Visit an observatory with families.
Make a class book of sky theories.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Moon watching, shadow tracing and space play are open to everyone. Sun print paper is handled with an adult, and dropping stones for craters needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer orbit games where children circle around a child playing the sun, carrying heavy stones to drop into the crater tray, and blasting off with jumps from a low stump. Building rockets from big boxes adds lifting and pushing.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet dark tent with one flashlight and a moon book, or a moon journal to draw in at their own pace. They can watch shadow tracing from the side before standing in the sun.
connected: Galileo Galilei on the Artists page, for ink wash drawings of the moon he made while looking through his telescope.
Vincent van Gogh on the Artists page, for The Starry Night, a sky of swirling stars and a bright moon.
Olafur Eliasson on the Artists page, for The weather project, a huge glowing sun inside a museum.
Robert Ferguson Observatory in Sugarloaf Ridge State Park
Chabot Space and Science Center in Oakland

home.title: Space, sun and moon at Home

sections.text: A window or yard, paper and crayons, a flashlight and a ball.

items: Look for the moon each night or morning and draw its shape.
Trace your child's shadow in the morning and afternoon.
Lie on a blanket and look at the stars on a clear night.
Use a flashlight and a ball in a dark room to make day and night.
Build a rocket from a box.

sections.text: Your child can spot the moon, draw it, lead the shadow tracing and tell you their ideas. Your child can put the moon journal back on its shelf and gather chalk into a tin after tracing shadows. A small sky basket keeps everything in one easy place.

items: Tell me the moon's shape tonight.
Where did your shadow go?
I wonder what is out there.

sections.text: Your child is noticing patterns in the sky and wondering about big questions. Circling like planets and jumping like rockets give the body big movement, and looking at the night sky together can be a calm way to end a day.
Send a moon drawing from home for our moon journal.
Never look straight at the sun.

cards.title: Water travel and boats
cards.summary: Ways to follow children who build boats, test floating and wonder how people travel on water.

sections.text: Children may float leaves and bark in puddles and the long yard sink, build boats from blocks, or play pirates and sailors. They ask why boats float, what sinks and how people cross the sea.

items: Boats built from recycled materials, cork, wood, foil and fabric sails, tested in the long yard sink and water tables.
A foil boat test where children add stones one at a time and count until it sinks, then try a new shape.
Sink and float trays with natural and found objects and a chart children make.
Leaf and bark boats floated in puddles and, with adults close, at the edge of the creek on creek walks.
Real photos of boats from many places, such as canoes, ferries, sailboats, cargo ships and tule boats, at children's eye level.
Talk about Coast Miwok and Southern Pomo tule boats, shared with care and accuracy, with real tule or reeds to bundle and try.
Sails tested with a fan or the wind in the yards.
Big cardboard boats children can sit in, with oars, maps and telescopes for dramatic play.
Knots and ropes for tying boats and sails.
Gutters and channels in the sand area to send boats downstream.
Katsushika Hokusai's The Great Wave and Winslow Homer's Breezing Up shown on screen beside watercolor.
A family outing idea to the Hyde Street Pier at San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park or a harbor in Bodega Bay.
Books about boats and water journeys from the Book collection.

sections.text: Both. Building a big boat or testing sails is lively teamwork. Making and testing a small boat can be a long, quiet solo project.

Water play always has an adult watching closely. On creek walks, children stay at the edge with adults and follow creek agreements, and educators hold water safety certificates. Empty water tables and buckets after use. Use stones, washers or pebbles as boat cargo, never food.

items: Design, build and test boats.
Predict, count and record what floats and sinks.
Change a design after a boat sinks.
Tie knots and rig sails.
Fill and empty the water tables.
Follow creek agreements and remind friends of them.
Teach a friend a boat design that worked.

sections.text: Children close boat play by draining the water tables with a cup or plug, rinsing boats and setting them on the drying rack. Stones, washers and pebbles go back to their cargo jars, and a child-sized mop dries the floor or deck. Emptying the water is part of the play, so nothing waits for an educator.

Sit or kneel at the water's edge within arm's reach, with calm hands and an easy face about splashes. Narrate what happens, such as "It tipped when the stones went on one side." At the creek, stay closest to the water with a steady body.

items: I wonder what will help it float.
How many stones can it hold?
Tell me what you could change.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Start with leaf and bark boats in puddles and the long yard sink.
Offer sink and float trays with many objects.
Build boats from recycled materials.
Try the foil boat test and redesign.
Add sails and test with wind and a fan.
Build gutters and channels in the sand area.
Build a big cardboard boat for dramatic play.
Learn and practice knots.
Look at tule boats and bundle reeds to make small ones.
Float boats at the creek edge on creek walks.
Visit a harbor or historic ship with families.
Make a class book of boat designs and what happened.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Water play always has an adult watching closely. Floating boats at the creek edge is one adult with one or two children, with educators who hold water safety certificates.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer carrying buckets of water to fill the boat channels, rowing a big cardboard boat with real oars, and pulling a loaded boat on a rope through the sand. Squeezing big wet sponges and pumping water add strong work.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray of water with one boat and a few stones, and long sleeves or a smock to stay dry. They can move the boat with a stick or tongs and watch the creek from a dry spot first.
connected: Katsushika Hokusai on the Artists page, for The Great Wave, with small boats riding a huge wave.
Winslow Homer on the Artists page, for painting a small sailboat with children leaning into the wind.
San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park

home.title: Water travel and boats at Home

sections.text: A tub or sink of water, foil, corks, sticks, string, small stones and recycled containers.

items: Build a boat from foil and see how many stones it can carry.
Float leaves and sticks in a puddle or tub.
Test which things float and sink in the bath.
Add a paper sail and blow on it.
Visit a pond, lake or harbor and look at real boats.

sections.text: Your child can design, test, count and change their boat until it works. Your child can tip out the tub, set boats on a towel to dry and mop up drips. A towel and basket nearby make bath or yard boat play easy to close.

items: I wonder what will float.
How could we make it hold more?
Where do you think this boat could go?

sections.text: Your child is testing ideas, solving problems and learning from what happens. Carrying water and rowing give the body strong work, and floating boats gives hands careful practice.
Send corks, foil, clean containers and small wood scraps for our boat building. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Always stay with children near water, even a tub or bucket. Empty containers after play.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: The orchard through the year
cards.summary: Following the Tire swing yard orchard and our other fruit trees from bare winter branches to blossom, fruit and falling leaves.

items: December to January. The plum, apricot, apple, fig and nectarine trees stand bare. Winter pruning happens between leaf fall and bloom, and buds sit tight on the branches.
February to March. Plum, apricot and nectarine blossoms open first, often between rainstorms. Bees work the flowers on any warm afternoon.
March to April. Cherry and Asian pear bloom in the outdoor piazza. Apple blossoms follow in April, and new leaves unfold on every tree.
May to June. Tiny green fruits swell. Extra fruit is thinned so the rest can grow. Cherries and blueberries ripen, and the fig may give an early June crop.
June to July. Apricots and plums ripen. Raspberries and currants are ready in the garden. Fallen fruit draws ants, wasps and birds.
July to September. Nectarines, thornless blackberries, the main fig crop, Asian pears, table grapes and the first apples ripen.
September to November. Later apples, pomegranates and grapes ripen. Feijoas drop to the ground when ready, from October into December.
November to December. Leaves turn yellow and fall. Fig leaves drop large and whole, and the yard opens to the winter sky again.
Fig flowers grow hidden inside the fig, so the fig tree never shows a blossom. Our olive is a non-fruiting tree and stays green all year.
Each small group adopts one orchard tree and visits it each month with clipboards, drawing from the same spot every time.
A photo of the same branch taken at the start of each month, hung in a long row at children's eye level so the whole year can be read at once.
A fallen blossom on the light table with a magnifier, to look closely at petals, stamens and the tiny green center that becomes fruit.
A bud watch in late winter. Children choose a bud, tie a soft ribbon near it and check it every few days.
Bark rubbings of each orchard tree with crayon and thin paper, compared in winter and in summer.
Pruning day in winter. Children watch an adult choose cuts with real loppers, then help carry branches to the right piles.
Picking ripe fruit with an adult and a low basket, then washing it and sharing it at snack.
Fruit on the display table for close observational drawing, then cut open together to see the seeds and pits before it goes to snack.
Cooking in the piazza culinary atelier with orchard fruit, such as stewed plums, applesauce or fruit leather in the dehydrator.
A fig cut open at snack to wonder about the hundreds of tiny flowers inside.
Watching fallen fruit from a calm distance to see who comes to eat it, then adding sketches of those visitors to the orchard journal.
A walk or visit to Luther Burbank Home & Gardens in Santa Rosa, where the Santa Rosa plum was developed.

sections.text: Adults pick anything above children's reach, and in late summer we check the ground for wasps on fallen fruit before groups settle. iGrow Sonoma (igrowsonoma.org) and the UC Master Gardeners of Sonoma County offer local timing for pruning and harvest.

items: Choose which tree their small group adopts and give it a name.
Track changes in the orchard journal with drawings, photos and dictated notes.
Decide when fruit looks ready and help test it gently with a thumb.
Carry harvest baskets and prunings to where they belong.
Wash, cut and serve fruit with real knives and adult support.
Teach younger children which fallen fruit is for the chicken bucket and which is for us.
Help choose what to cook with the harvest.

sections.text: Children close orchard work by carrying harvest baskets and prunings to where they belong and returning loppers and gloves to the tool board. Fallen fruit for the chickens goes into the chicken bucket, and the orchard journal goes back in its bag. An adult carries ladders and pole pickers, so the orchard is reset before the group leaves.

Stand under the tree with the children and look up slowly before saying anything. Touch the bark and blossoms with the same gentle hands you hope children will use. When a child climbs a low branch or drops fruit, keep your face calm and narrate what you see, such as You found a branch that holds you.

items: I notice the buds look different today. I wonder what is happening inside.
Tell me about what the tree is doing in winter.
Where do you think the fruit comes from on the branch?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with one tree and one visit, letting children notice anything they choose.
Return monthly to the same spot and keep drawings in order in a shared orchard book.
Add the photo row on the wall and invite children to point out changes.
Follow one blossom to fruit with a ribbon tag and regular sketches.
Compare two trees, such as the early plum and the late apple, across the same months.
Invite children to predict when the first blossom or first ripe fruit will come and record their guesses.
Cook with each fruit in its season and add the recipe to a class cookbook.
Gather seeds and pits after cooking, dry them, and wonder about planting one.
Make a circle calendar of the orchard year with children's drawings for each month.
Share the orchard book with families and the next year's class so the story carries on.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Each small group adopts a tree and visits it with an adult. Pruning with loppers and picking above children's reach are adult work, and fallen fruit is checked for wasps first.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry the full harvest basket or the pruned branches to the compost, and to press both palms flat against the rough bark.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one fallen blossom or leaf on a tray with a magnifier to look at first. Gloves for gathering and a spot at the edge of the group to watch from are fine.
connected: Recipe library, for stewed fruit, applesauce and fruit leather in the dehydrator
Vincent van Gogh on the Artists page, for his 1888 paintings of fruit trees in blossom made outdoors in one spring
Book collection, for The Seasons of Arnold's Apple Tree by Gail Gibbons
Luther Burbank Home & Gardens in Santa Rosa, for the story of the Santa Rosa plum

home.title: The orchard through the year at Home

sections.text: A fruit tree you can visit often, at home, on your street, at a park or at a farm stand orchard. Paper, a pencil and a phone camera help.

items: Pick one tree and visit it once a month together.
Take a photo from the same spot each time and look at them side by side.
Look for buds in winter, flowers in spring and fruit in summer and fall.
Visit a local U-pick farm or farmers market and talk about which fruits are ready now.
Cook something simple with fruit in season, such as baked apples or stewed plums.

sections.text: Your child can choose the tree, take the photos, decide what is different and help wash and cut the fruit. Your child can carry the fruit basket in, set fallen fruit aside for compost and hang their gloves on a hook. A basket by the door makes harvest an easy job to finish.

items: Tell me what you think the tree will look like next month.
I wonder where the flowers go.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is noticing how living things change over time and that our food grows through the seasons. Carrying baskets and smelling blossoms and fruit gives the body steady work and gentle sensory input, which helps many children feel settled.

Send in a photo of your tree, a drawing or a family fruit recipe for our recipe collection. If you have extra fruit from your own trees, send it in for snack. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash fruit before eating and watch for bees and wasps around fallen fruit. Fruit pits are not for chewing.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: The rainy season
cards.summary: Living outdoors through our Mediterranean rainy season, from the first storm in fall to the last puddle in spring.

items: Late September to October. The first rain often arrives. Dust turns to mud, and the smell of wet earth returns after the long dry summer.
November. The rainy season settles in. Grass turns green in the yards and on the hills, and mushrooms push up after storms.
December to February. Our wettest months. Storms can stack up for days, puddles last, the creek runs high and fast, and clear nights can bring frost.
January to February. Earthworms come up onto paths after heavy rain. Snails, slugs and frogs are out in the wet garden.
March. Showers and sunshine take turns, rainbows appear, and fruit trees bloom between storms.
April to May. Rain tapers off and the last puddles shrink a little more each day.
June to September. Almost no rain falls. Hills turn gold, soil cracks, and we watch the sky for the first clouds of fall.
Most of our year's rain falls between November and March, so the whole rhythm of the garden turns on these months.
A rain gauge made with children from a straight-sided clear jar, read at meeting time after each storm, with a long paper strip on the wall to mark every rain.
Rain walks in boots and rain gear, stopping to listen to rain on the metal roof of the music shed, on leaves, on umbrellas and on buckets.
Pots, pans and metal bowls set under the drip line so the rain can play them.
Chalk drawn around a puddle in the morning and again later, to see how it grows or shrinks.
Buckets to catch rain, then rainwater used for pouring with metal utensils at the long yard sink or for washing pots in the mud kitchen.
Paper with dots of liquid watercolor set out in a light rain so the drops can move the color.
Boats made from recycled materials floated along runoff channels and puddles.
Dams and channels built in the mud with sticks, stones and small shovels.
A tarp shelter children help tie up between posts, or time inside the willow dome, to sit and listen to a storm.
Worm rescue after storms, gently moving worms from paths back onto soil.
A sky drawing before, during and after a storm, kept together on one page.
A recording of the rain on a tablet, played back at meeting time with eyes closed.
Soup cooked together in the piazza culinary atelier on a cold wet day.

sections.text: Rain gear and a full change of clothes for every child make outdoor time possible all season, and a drying rack near the door helps. We stay off the creek trail when water runs high and fast after storms, and we move indoors for thunder or strong wind. Wet soil in the garden beds stays unworked so it keeps its structure.

items: Read the rain gauge and mark the paper strip.
Predict rain at meeting time from clouds, wind and smell.
Set out and empty catch buckets and decide where rainwater goes.
Hang their own gear to dry and help a friend with zippers and boots.
Lead the worm rescue and teach gentle hands.
Choose where to build dams and channels and test their ideas.

sections.text: Children close rainy days by emptying catch buckets, hanging their own rain gear on low hooks and setting boots in the boot rack. They mop drips by the door with a child-sized mop and towel. Dam tools and shovels are rinsed in the wash bucket and stood up to drain, so rain play closes with the children.

Dress for the rain yourself and stay out in it with the children, so your body says this weather is good. Notice any wish to stay dry or keep things clean, and set it aside. Squat at puddle level and narrate in a regular voice, such as The water climbed up your boot.

items: I notice the puddle changed. I wonder where the water went.
Where do you think the rain comes from?
Tell me about the sounds you can hear right now.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a short walk in the first rain to smell, listen and feel.
Make the rain gauge and start the paper strip on the wall.
Add the rain instruments and recordings for a rain sound collection.
Track one puddle over a week with chalk lines and photos.
Build dams and channels and test how water moves across the yard.
Follow where rain goes after it lands, from roof to gutter to soil to creek.
Compare the wet season photos with the dry summer photos of the same spot.
At the end of spring, count the storms on the paper strip and wonder about the dry months ahead.
Share a rain book of drawings, recordings and photos with families.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Children play in the rain and puddles with an educator nearby. Cooking soup needs an adult at the table, and the creek trail is skipped when water runs high.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer deep puddles to stomp and jump in, full buckets of rainwater to carry, and a walk through a light rain with face turned up.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a dry spot under the eaves to watch and listen first, a hood and gloves, and one bowl at the drip line to hold. Going out can wait until the rain is light.
connected: Recipe library, for soups on cold wet days
Utagawa Hiroshige on the Artists page, for Sudden Shower over Shin-Ohashi Bridge, where rain is drawn as many fine lines
Gustave Caillebotte on the Artists page, for Paris Street, Rainy Day and its wet reflections
Song book, for rain and weather songs
Book collection, for Come On, Rain! by Karen Hesse and Water Is Water by Miranda Paul

sections.text: Rain boots, a rain jacket, a clear jar, a few pots and pans, and a towel by the door.

items: Take a short walk in the rain and listen to it on different things.
Set a clear jar outside and check how much rain fell.
Put pots and pans under a drip and listen.
Float a leaf or a small homemade boat in a puddle.
Look at the same puddle in the morning and again later.

sections.text: Your child can choose the path, check the jar, pick what to float and help hang wet clothes to dry. Your child can hang up their raincoat, line up boots on a mat and wipe the floor with an old towel. A low hook and a towel by the door make it their job every wet day.

items: Where do you think the puddle goes?
Tell me about the sounds you can hear.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is noticing weather and water and feeling comfortable outside in every season. Stomping in puddles and carrying water gives the body strong input, and listening to rain helps many children slow down and feel calm.
Send in a photo of your rain jar or a drawing of a rainy day. Spare clothes and old rain boots for our shared supply are always welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Stay well away from fast moving creeks and storm drains after heavy rain. Warm dry clothes afterward make the next rain walk a happy one.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Seed to seed
cards.summary: Following plants from the seed we sow to the seed we save, across a full year in our garden beds and seed library.

items: October to November. With the first rains we sow fava beans, peas, garlic, cover crop and California poppy seed, and plant strawberries.
December to January. Seeds sit quietly in cold soil. We look through our seed library and seed catalogs such as Baker Creek and choose with children what to grow.
February to March. Tomato and pepper seeds start indoors in trays on a sunny sill. Peas, lettuce, radishes and potatoes go into the beds.
April. After the last frost, around the middle of April, summer starts go into the beds.
May to June. Beans, squash, pumpkins, corn and sunflowers go straight into warm soil. Lettuce and radishes bolt and flower in the heat.
June to August. Poppies, lettuce, radishes, peas and fava beans dry and set seed. Pods turn brown and rattle.
August to October. Sunflower heads, bean pods, squash and calendula ripen seed for saving. Finches and sparrows come for what we leave.
Year round. Saved seeds dry in labeled envelopes and jars and return to our seed library for next season.
A soaked fava seed opened with fingers on a tray, with a magnifier to find the tiny new plant inside.
A clear jar lined with damp paper towel and seeds pressed against the glass, so roots and shoots can be watched each day.
A seed sorting tray of seeds children harvested themselves, with small bowls, tweezers and spoons.
Seed travelers. A collection of seeds that fly, spin, float or hitch a ride, with a fan, water tray and a felt square to test them.
A bean and sunflower house planted in a circle in spring, which grows into a hiding place by summer.
Dibbers, trowels and seed packets on a low tray so children can plant at the right depth with an adult.
One plant per class left to go all the way to seed, with a photo taken each week.
A seed saving table with paper envelopes, pencils and stamps where children label what they gathered.
Children's own drawings made into seed packet art for our seed library.
Seed balls made from garden clay, compost and California poppy seed, tossed onto bare ground before rain.
Taste tests of different garden varieties at harvest, then a vote on which seeds to save.
A circle drawn large on paper where children add seed, sprout, plant, flower, fruit and seed again in their own way.

sections.text: Some seeds are toxic to eat, including sweet pea and annual morning glory seed, and coated seeds in bright colors are never used, so adults choose every seed and seeds stay out of mouths. Raw fava beans can cause a serious reaction in children with G6PD deficiency, so check health notes before fava is cooked or tasted. iGrow Sonoma (igrowsonoma.org) has local planting timing, and Harmony Farm Supply and Baker Creek carry the seed, starts and cover crop seed we use.

items: Choose what to grow from the seed library and catalogs.
Plant, label and water seed trays and beds.
Check the sprout jar daily and record what they see.
Decide when a pod or seed head is ready to harvest.
Clean, sort, dry and label saved seeds.
Share seeds with families and teach younger children how to plant.
Return seeds to the seed library and keep its records.

sections.text: Children close seed work by sweeping spilled soil into the dustpan, rinsing the watering can and putting trays on the growing shelf. Seed envelopes go back into the seed library by label, and trowels hang on their outlines. Hands are washed, and the planting table is ready for the next group.

Sit at the planting tray at children's height and keep your hands slow and light with the seeds. Let a child spill soil or plant too deep without fixing it, and narrate what happened instead. Return to the bed through the long waiting weeks with the same quiet interest each visit.

items: I wonder what is inside the seed.
Where do you think this seed would like to grow?
How do you think it got here?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by opening a soaked seed and wondering about what is inside.
Start the sprout jar and keep daily drawings beside it.
Plant one fast seed and one slow seed and compare.
Collect seeds on walks and sort how they travel.
Leave one plant to go all the way to seed and document the whole journey.
Harvest, dry and save seed from that plant.
Make seed packets with children's drawings and planting notes.
Plant the saved seed the next season and close the circle.
Open a family seed swap so seeds go home and come back.
Pass the seed library story to the next year's class.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Planting and harvesting happen in the garden with one adult to six children. Adults choose every seed because some are toxic, and fava tasting waits until health notes are checked.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big tub of soil to scoop into pots, dry seed heads to rub firmly between the palms to free the seeds, and full watering cans to carry.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer tweezers or a small spoon for moving seeds and a dibber for the soil so hands stay clean. Sorting dry seeds alone on a small tray is a quiet way in.
connected: Recipe library, for fava beans, peas and harvest cooking
Karl Blossfeldt on the Artists page, for his close-up photographs of seed heads and young plants
Book collection, for A Seed Is Sleepy by Dianna Hutts Aston and Sylvia Long

sections.text: A packet of easy seeds such as beans, sunflowers or peas, a pot or a patch of soil, a clear jar and a paper towel.

items: Sprout a bean in a clear jar with damp paper towel and look each day.
Plant a few seeds in a pot and keep them by a sunny window.
Collect seeds on a walk and wonder how each one travels.
Let one plant flower and go to seed, then save the seeds in a paper envelope.
Open a fruit at snack and look for its seeds.

sections.text: Your child can choose the seed, plant it, water it, check on it and decide when the seeds are ready to save. Your child can sweep spilled soil, put seed packets in a box and hang the trowel. A small tray for planting keeps the mess in one place.

items: I wonder what is inside a seed.
How do you think this seed got here?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is seeing that plants have a whole life and that care helps things grow. Pinching tiny seeds and pressing soil builds hand strength, and the slow, careful work helps many children feel calm.
Send in seeds you saved at home in a labeled envelope for our seed library, or a photo of your sprout jar. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Some seeds are not safe to eat, so seeds are for planting and looking. Wash hands after handling seeds and soil.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Eggs and chicks
cards.summary: Following our flock through the year, from winter rest to the full spring egg basket and the fall molt.

items: November to January. Short days slow laying, and some hens stop for a while. The egg basket is light.
February to March. Longer days bring the hens back to laying, and the basket fills again.
March to June. Our busiest laying months. Some hens go broody and sit tight on the nest. Spring is the traditional season for chicks.
July to August. Heat can slow laying. Hens dust bathe, pant in the shade and drink more water.
September to November. Many hens molt. Feathers drop all over the yard, laying pauses, and new pin feathers grow in.
Year round. Our large flock lays eggs in many colors, from white and cream to brown, speckled, blue and green.
A daily egg walk with a soft basket and an egg carton, and a tally chart children keep by the coop door.
An egg color line-up in a clear carton, from lightest to darkest, with children deciding the order.
Real photos of each hen at children's eye level, with the colors of egg each one lays.
A feather collection during the fall molt, sorted on a tray, with magnifiers to see how the parts hook together.
Feathers used as tools in the Studio, for painting, printing and drawing with ink.
A quiet watch of a dust bath from outside the run, then wondering together why hens do it.
Nest building with straw, grass and feathers in a basket, to wonder how a hen makes a nest.
A broody hen watched from a respectful distance, with a calendar to count days if eggs are under her.
A cracked egg opened in a clear bowl at the piazza to look at shell, membrane, white and yolk before it is cooked.
Cooking with our eggs in the piazza culinary atelier, such as scrambled eggs or pancakes.
If we choose to hatch eggs in an incubator, a calendar of 21 days and egg candling with a flashlight in a dark room.

sections.text: Chickens and eggs can carry salmonella, and children under five are more at risk, so we follow our hygiene protocol every time. Hands are washed with soap right after any coop, chicken or egg contact, and chicks are watched more than held. Eggs from our flock are cooked fully, and cracked or dirty eggs go to the compost.

items: Collect, count and record eggs each day.
Carry the egg basket with care and set eggs gently in the carton.
Help refill water and feed, and spread clean bedding.
Notice which hens are molting, broody or resting.
Teach new children the handwashing routine and coop agreements.
Crack, whisk and cook eggs with adult support.

sections.text: Children close egg time by setting eggs gently in the carton and carrying the basket to its shelf. They rinse the water dish, hang the scoop and feed cup back on their hooks and put gloves in the glove basket. Hands are washed with soap before anything else, so the coop routine ends with the children.

Move slowly and speak softly in the run, since the hens and the children both read your body. Crouch beside a child reaching for an egg and keep your hands open and still unless they ask for help. If an egg breaks, stay calm and wonder together about what is inside.

items: I notice the basket is lighter this week. I wonder why.
Where do you think the color of the egg comes from?
Tell me what you think the hen is doing on the nest.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a short egg walk and the tally chart.
Add the egg color line-up and hen photos.
Graph the egg count across the months and wonder about the changes.
Collect molt feathers in fall and compare them with spring feathers.
Follow a broody hen with a calendar and drawings.
Look closely inside an egg before cooking and draw its parts.
Cook with our eggs and add the recipes to a class book.
If hatching, care for eggs across 21 days and document the change from egg to chick.
Make a flock book with a page for each hen and share it with families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Egg walks and coop visits happen in a small group with an adult and our hygiene protocol. Opening an egg needs an adult at the table, and chicks are watched more than held.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry the water jug and the feed scoop to the run, rake the old bedding, and spread fresh straw by the armful.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a quiet watch from outside the run first, and let them hold the egg carton while a friend lifts the eggs. A feather on a tray is a gentle first touch.
connected: Recipe library, for scrambled eggs, pancakes and baking with our eggs
Ito Jakuchu on the Artists page, for his detailed paintings of roosters and hens drawn from birds he kept
Book collection, for An Egg Is Quiet by Dianna Hutts Aston and Sylvia Long and Chickens Aren't the Only Ones by Ruth Heller

sections.text: A carton of eggs, a bowl and a whisk. If you can, a visit to a friend's backyard flock or a farm.

items: Line up eggs from a mixed carton and talk about the colors.
Crack an egg into a clear bowl and look closely before cooking it.
Cook eggs together for breakfast.
Visit chickens at a farm or a friend's yard and watch what they do.
Look for feathers on a walk and look at them closely without picking up wild bird feathers.

sections.text: Your child can choose eggs, crack them, whisk them and help cook with you close by. Your child can set eggs gently in the carton, rinse a bowl and wash hands with soap. Giving the egg basket a home makes the routine easy for them to finish.

items: I wonder what is inside the egg.
Why do you think eggs come in different colors?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is learning where food comes from and how animals live through the year. Carrying eggs with careful hands and listening to the hens helps children practice gentle, steady movement and calm attention.
Send in a family egg recipe for our recipe collection or a photo of chickens you visited.
Wash hands with soap after touching raw eggs or chickens. Cook eggs all the way through. Feathers of wild birds are protected, so look and leave those.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: The goats through the year
cards.summary: Following our goat herd through the seasons, from winter coats and rainy days to spring shedding and summer shade.

items: September to November. The goats grow a soft winter undercoat. Fallen leaves, weeds and prunings from the garden become goat browse once an adult checks them.
December to February. Goats avoid getting wet, so on rainy days the herd stays under shelter. Hay is the mainstay while fresh browse is thin.
March to May. Fresh green browse returns. The goats shed their winter fluff in clumps, and brushing season begins.
June to September. Goats seek shade in the heat and drink more water. Flies are busy and the yard dries out.
Year round. Hooves grow and are trimmed every several weeks. The goats chew cud, climb, butt heads and sort out their herd order.
Our herd has several breeds. Saanen are large and white, LaMancha have tiny ears, Mini Nubians have long drooping ears, and Nigerian Dwarfs are small and come in many colors.
A herd wall of real photos at children's eye level, with each goat's name and breed, which children help keep current.
An ear and coat comparison, looking at the LaMancha, Nubian, Saanen and Nigerian Dwarf goats side by side.
Spring brushing with soft brushes, and the shed fluff collected in a basket.
Shed goat fluff tucked into a wire suet cage hung in a tree in spring, so birds can take it for nests.
A browse basket. Children gather pulled weeds and leaves, an adult checks each one, and children offer it on a flat palm.
A cud chewing watch, counting chews and noticing the bump that travels up the neck.
Observational drawing at the fence with clipboards and charcoal, returning to the same goat across the seasons.
A goat care task chart with jobs children choose each week, such as water, hay, sweeping and brushing.
Recordings of goat calls played back at meeting time, wondering who is calling and why.
Climbing structures in the goat yard that children help plan and adults build, with logs, stumps and planks.
Goat droppings carried with a shovel and bucket to the compost, then wondering how it helps the soil.
Shed goat fluff felted with warm soapy water in the Studio, to see what goat fiber can do.

sections.text: We follow our hygiene protocol with the goats, and every child washes hands with soap after the goat yard. Goats eat only plants an adult has checked, never people food or bread. Children offer food on a flat open palm, stay calm and quiet, and an adult is in the yard during every visit.

items: Choose and carry out goat care jobs from the task chart.
Gather browse and ask an adult to check it before offering.
Brush goats, collect fluff and decide what to do with it.
Keep the herd wall current with photos and notes.
Teach younger children the flat palm, calm voice and handwashing.
Notice and report when a goat seems different.

sections.text: Children close goat time by putting brushes in their bucket and hanging the scoop and browse basket on their hooks. They tip fluff into the fluff bag and check the gate with an adult. Every child washes hands with soap after the yard, and the jobs are marked on the task chart.

Notice your own feelings about the goats, such as worry about butting or nibbling, because children borrow your calm or your fear. Stand relaxed at the fence with soft knees and a quiet voice, within arm's reach of the youngest. Narrate what the goats do and step back when a child is ready to brush alone.

items: I notice this goat's ears are different. I wonder why.
Where do you think the goats go when it rains?
Tell me what you think the goats are saying to each other.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with visits to the fence to watch and listen.
Learn each goat's name with the herd wall.
Add goat care jobs a few at a time.
Follow one goat across the seasons with drawings and photos.
Brush and collect fluff in spring and try felting it in the Studio.
Hang fluff for birds and watch for nest builders.
Track what the goats eat across the year and why it changes.
Make a herd book with a page for each goat and share it with families.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An adult is in the goat yard during every visit, and handwashing follows. Brushing and feeding by hand need an adult within arm's reach, and felting with warm water needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to brush with long firm strokes, carry hay flakes or the browse basket across the yard, and push the wheelbarrow of bedding.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, watch the herd from outside the fence first, then offer a long-handled brush so there is space between hands and goat. A small bag of shed fluff to hold is a soft first touch.
connected: Rosa Bonheur on the Artists page, for drawing and painting farm animals closely from life
Book collection, for The Goat Lady by Jane Bregoli

home.title: The goats through the year at Home

sections.text: A visit to goats at a farm, a petting zoo or a county fair. Paper and a pencil for drawing.

items: Watch goats and notice how they eat, climb and talk.
Look at the shapes of goats' ears and coats.
Draw a goat while watching it.
Ask the farm if your child can help with a small job such as filling water.

sections.text: Your child can watch, draw, ask questions and help with a simple care job when the farm allows. Your child can rinse a pet bowl, hang up a brush and wash hands with soap after caring for an animal. Ending with clean hands is part of the care.

items: I wonder what the goats are saying.
How are their eyes different from ours?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is learning to care for animals with calm, gentle hands. Brushing and carrying hay gives the body heavy work, and calm time near animals helps many children feel settled.
Send in a drawing or photo of goats you visited. Clean, dry hay or straw for the animal yards is welcome if we ask for it. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wash hands with soap after touching any farm animal. Offer food only when the farm says it is okay, and only on a flat hand.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Compost and soil
cards.summary: Watching old plants, leaves and animal bedding become rich soil, and caring for the ground our garden grows in.

items: October to November. Fallen leaves pile up as dry browns. The first rains wet the piles, and finished compost goes onto beds before fall planting.
December to February. Piles cool and slow down. Worms rise toward the surface after rain. Wet soil stays unworked so it keeps its crumbly structure.
March to April. Compost and mulch go onto beds before summer planting. Cover crops of fava beans or clover are cut and laid on the soil.
May to September. Piles heat up fast and dry out, so they need water. Mulch keeps soil cool and damp. Bare soil cracks in the heat.
Year round. Roly polys, worms, beetles, fungi and coop bedding turn old plants into new soil in our large compost pile.
Weeds, prunings and old plants go first to the goats, food scraps go to the chickens, and what they leave behind feeds the compost.
Soil sieves with screens of different sizes over a tub, so children can separate stones, roots and fine soil.
A soil jar. Soil and water shaken in a clear jar with a lid, then set on a sill to watch layers settle over a day.
A worm tray of damp soil with magnifiers and a spray bottle, with worms returned to the pile after a short visit.
A compost thermometer read each week, with a chart children keep on the pile.
Turning the pile with real garden forks and wheelbarrows, with clear agreements about space and tools.
A buried cotton cloth and a plastic square in the same bed, dug up each month to see which one changes.
Leaf litter under the oaks lifted with hands and trowels to find roly polys, fungi and worms.
Soils from around our site collected in small jars to compare color, smell and feel, then mixed with water to paint.
A clear-sided worm bin in the class, fed with plant scraps and checked by children.
A small compost pile built by children in layers of browns and greens, with signs they write.
Spreading finished compost on a class bed before planting, using buckets and small shovels.

sections.text: Black widows can hide under boards, in piles and in tool stacks, so adults check and lift first, and children wear gloves when moving compost. Hands are washed after soil and compost work, and coop bedding is aged in the pile before it goes onto beds. Meat, dairy and oily foods stay out of our compost.

items: Decide what goes in the compost and what goes to the goats or chickens.
Turn, water and check the temperature of the pile.
Sieve soil and sort what they find.
Care for the worm bin and return worms gently.
Spread compost on beds and decide where it is needed.
Teach younger children the difference between soil, compost and mulch.

sections.text: Children close compost work by brushing soil off the sieves and hanging them up, and returning forks, shovels and gloves to the tool board. They sweep spilled soil back into the pile with a child-sized broom and dustpan. Hands are washed, and an adult lifts only the heavy boards, so the compost area closes on the floor.

Kneel in the soil with the children and let your own hands get dirty. Check your face when the smell or the worms arrive, since children read it quickly. Narrate what they find, such as You found three worms under that leaf, and stay in the space while the digging goes on.

items: I wonder where the leaves went.
Tell me what you think is happening inside the pile.
Who do you think lives in the soil?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by digging and holding soil from different spots.
Sieve and sort to see what soil is made of.
Make soil jars and watch the layers settle.
Visit the compost pile and read the thermometer each week.
Bury cloth and plastic and dig them up monthly.
Build a class compost pile or worm bin and care for it.
Spread finished compost on beds and follow what grows.
Make earth paints from site soils and paint with them.
Share a soil book of findings, photos and drawings with families.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Compost and soil work happens in the garden with one adult to six children. Adults lift boards and check piles for black widows first, and turning the pile with garden forks needs clear space and an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to turn the pile with a real garden fork, push a loaded wheelbarrow, and dig deep with both hands in the sieved soil.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer gloves, a trowel and a small sieve over a tray, and a worm to watch on a leaf with a magnifier. Stepping back from the smell is always fine.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for works made from leaves, earth and stone that change and return to the ground
Book collection, for Compost Stew by Mary McKenna Siddals and Up in the Garden and Down in the Dirt by Kate Messner

sections.text: A spot of soil, a trowel, a bucket and a clear jar with a lid. A small compost bin or a pile in a corner of the yard if you have room.

items: Dig a little soil and look for worms and roly polys.
Shake soil and water in a clear jar and watch the layers settle.
Start a small compost pile with leaves and fruit and vegetable peels.
Bury a cotton rag and dig it up a month later.
Look under a log on a walk and put it back gently.

sections.text: Your child can dig, sort, add to the compost, check on it and decide what belongs. Your child can rinse the scrap bucket, sweep spilled soil and wash hands after compost work. A small bucket with its own spot keeps the job clear.

items: Where do you think the leaves go?
I wonder who lives down there.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is seeing that nothing is wasted in nature and that soil is alive. Digging, sieving and carrying soil gives the body heavy work and lots of touch, which helps many children feel calm and organized.
Send in a photo of your soil jar or something you found while digging. Bags of dry fall leaves for our compost are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Wear gloves and wash hands after digging. Check under boards and piles for spiders before reaching in.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: The botanical dye bed
cards.summary: Growing color in our botanical dye bed and turning flowers, leaves and roots into dyed wool and cloth across the year.

items: December to January. The bed rests. Flowers dried last summer, acorn caps, oak galls and fallen leaves make winter dye pots. Madder roots keep growing underground.
February to March. We look at last year's dye samples and choose seeds with children. Japanese indigo and other seeds can start indoors.
April. After the last frost, seedlings and seeds go into the bed. Yarrow and California poppies are already blooming.
May to July. Marigolds, coreopsis, cosmos and calendula begin to bloom. Picking flowers often keeps more coming.
July to September. Peak color. Japanese indigo leaves are ready to pick before the plants flower. Flowers are picked daily and dried for later.
October to November. Flowers slow with cooler nights. Last harvests are dried and stored, seed is saved, and madder roots are dug in their third fall.
Year round. Fallen eucalyptus leaves, oak galls, acorn caps and yarrow can be gathered from our site and neighborhood for the dye pot.
A daily flower harvest into a flat drying basket, with children deciding which flowers are ready.
Pounding flowers and leaves onto cotton cloth with wooden mallets on a hard board to print their color and shape.
