Solar dye jars. Flowers, water and wool yarn in clear jars set on a sunny wall for several weeks, with children checking the color change.
Bundle dyeing, where children lay petals on damp cloth and roll it tight with string, then an adult steams it.
A swatch board where each dye test is stapled beside a real photo of the plant it came from.
Iron water in a small jar that shifts a dyed sample darker, so children can see one plant give many colors.
Dyed wool yarn taken to the Studio for weaving, wrapping and felting.
Fresh indigo leaves rubbed into silk with a little salt by children's hands, turning blue as it meets the air.
A dye plant garden map children draw, marking what grows where.
Dye seeds saved by children and added to the seed library.
Winter dye pots with acorn caps and oak galls gathered from under the oaks.

sections.text: Adults handle all heat, steam, alum and iron, and dye pots and tools are kept only for dye and never used for food. Fresh food and produce never go into our dye pots, so we dye with flowers, leaves, roots, bark and galls. Some dye plants, such as marigold and yarrow, can irritate skin, so we wear gloves for long sessions and wash hands afterward.

items: Choose what to plant and help sow seeds.
Harvest, sort and dry flowers.
Predict what color a plant will give and test it.
Pound, roll and wrap bundles for dyeing.
Record results on the swatch board.
Use their dyed yarn and cloth in weaving, sewing and felting.
Save seed and plan next year's bed.

sections.text: Children close dye work by hanging dyed yarn and cloth on the drying rack and sorting flowers and leaves into labeled baskets to dry. They rinse mortars, pestles and rollers in the wash bucket and wipe the table with a damp cloth. An adult carries the dye pots and handles heat, alum and iron, so the children close the rest.

Stand at the pounding board at child height and let the loud work happen without hushing it. Keep your own hands off the cloth so the marks stay the children's. Handle jars and flowers with slow care, and meet a dye test that turns brown with the same interest as a bright one.

items: I wonder what color this flower will make.
I notice the yarn changed. How do you think that happened?
I wonder what will happen if we leave it longer.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by walking through the bed and noticing colors.
Pound a single flower onto cloth and look at the print.
Start a solar dye jar and check it each week.
Build a swatch board of every dye test.
Compare the color of the flower with the color it gives.
Add iron water and see how colors shift.
Dye wool for a class weaving or a shared hanging.
Dry flowers for winter dyeing and try the winter pot.
Save seed, map the bed and plan next year with children.
Share a color book with families showing each plant and its color.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Pounding flowers with mallets and setting up dye jars need an adult at the table. Harvesting keeps one adult to six children in the garden, and heat, steam, alum and iron are adult only.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer pounding flowers onto cloth with a wooden mallet, wringing dyed wool with both hands, and rolling bundles very tight.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer gloves for wet dye and a flat basket of dry petals to sort first. Watching a solar dye jar change color on a sunny sill is a quiet way in.
connected: Sasha Duerr on the Artists page, for growing and gathering plants in the Bay Area to dye cloth and yarn by season
Book collection, for Weaving the Rainbow by George Ella Lyon

home.title: The botanical dye bed at Home

sections.text: Flowers from your yard such as marigolds or coreopsis, a clear jar with a lid, white wool yarn or cotton cloth, and a wooden mallet or rolling pin.

items: Put flowers, water and wool yarn in a jar and set it in the sun for a few weeks.
Lay a flower on cotton cloth, cover it with paper and tap it with a mallet.
Gather fallen leaves on a walk and wonder what color they might give.
Dry extra flowers in a paper bag for later.

sections.text: Your child can pick flowers, tap the cloth, check the jar and decide when the color is done. Your child can rinse bowls, hang dyed cloth to dry and sort flowers into a basket. Doing it outside at the hose makes the close easy and colorful.

items: I wonder what color this flower will make.
How is it different since yesterday?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is learning that color comes from plants and that waiting brings change. Pounding petals and wringing cloth gives hands and arms strong work, which helps many children feel calm and focused.
Send in dried flowers, a sample of your dyed yarn or a photo of your jar. White wool yarn or cotton fabric for our dye bed is welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Use dye jars and tools only for dye and keep them away from kitchen dishes. Wash hands after handling flowers.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Oaks and acorns
cards.summary: Following our valley oaks and coast live oak through the year, from catkins and new leaves to acorns, galls and falling leaves.

items: September to November. Valley oak acorns ripen and drop in the Log and Tire swing yards. Coast live oak acorns in the North yard follow from October into December.
Fall. Scrub jays carry and bury acorns, and acorn woodpeckers store them in holes they drill in trees and posts.
November to January. Valley oak leaves turn brown and fall, and the dry tan oak apple galls show on bare twigs. The coast live oak stays green.
December to February. Acorns that were missed split and send a root down into wet soil.
March to April. Valley oaks leaf out in soft new green and hang long yellow catkins that shed pollen. The coast live oak drops last year's leaves as new ones come in.
May to August. Deep shade. Oak apple galls swell green on valley oak twigs, and tiny green acorns form.
Acorns have been and still are an important food for the Southern Pomo and Coast Miwok people whose land we are on.
Acorns and caps gathered into baskets and offered as loose parts for sorting, lining up, building and counting.
A cap whistle. Children hold an acorn cap between their thumbs and blow across it to find the sound.
A float test in a tub of water, then floaters cut open by an adult to look for weevil holes and grubs.
Fresh valley oak acorns planted in deep pots of soil in fall, watered and watched as the root comes first.
Valley oak and coast live oak leaves side by side on the light table, comparing shape, edges and feel.
Oak apple galls looked at closely with magnifiers, then cut open by an adult to see the inside.
Trunk hugs. How many children does it take to reach around a valley oak, measured again with a string and kept on the wall.
Bark rubbings and clay pressed onto bark to keep its texture.
Real photos of acorn woodpecker granaries and scrub jays at children's eye level, then a walk to look for them.
A catkin collection in spring, with magnifiers to see the pollen.
Acorn caps and galls gathered for the winter dye pot.
A visit to a museum or cultural place where Pomo or Miwok people share their own acorn and basket traditions, or a visiting Native educator.

sections.text: We are a nut-free school, so acorns are natural materials that are never eaten, ground or cooked. Poison oak grows near oaks on our site and along the creek, so adults confirm every place children gather. We learn about Pomo and Miwok acorn traditions from Native people and their own museums and books, and we do not act them out.

items: Gather, sort and count acorns and caps.
Plant acorns and care for the pots through winter.
Measure and compare the oaks over the year.
Look closely at galls, catkins and leaves and record what they see.
Share findings at meeting time and teach the cap whistle.
Decide which acorns go back to the ground for the jays and woodpeckers.

sections.text: Children close acorn work by sorting acorns and caps into their labeled baskets and returning magnifiers and rulers to their tray. Acorns for the jays and woodpeckers go back under the oak with the children who chose them. Potted acorns are watered and set back on their shelf, so the space is ready again.

Sit with your back against the oak and let children come to you with what they gather. Keep your voice regular and your hands open to receive an acorn or a gall. Narrate what you notice and leave long quiet spaces for children to wonder first.

items: I wonder who else needs these acorns.
Tell me what you think is inside the gall.
How old do you think this tree is?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by gathering acorns and caps under the valley oaks.
Sort, count and build with them as loose parts.
Float acorns and look for weevils.
Plant acorns and watch the root and shoot through winter and spring.
Compare the valley oak and coast live oak across seasons.
Watch for jays and woodpeckers and map where acorns go.
Follow a gall from green to tan across the summer and fall.
Return the oak seedlings to a good spot or share them with a local planting group.
Learn from Native educators and museums and share what children learn with families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Gathering, sorting and building with acorns are open to everyone. Acorns stay away from the 2s as a choking risk, adults cut open acorns and galls, and adults confirm each gathering spot for poison oak.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry full baskets of acorns, blow a loud cap whistle, and wrap both arms around the wide trunk of a valley oak.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small basket and a few smooth acorns to hold and sort in a quiet spot. Watching the cap whistle before trying it is a fine start.
connected: Julia Parker on the Artists page, for her Coast Miwok and Kashaya Pomo basketry and decades of teaching about acorns and baskets
Book collection, for Because of an Acorn by Lola M. Schaefer and Adam Schaefer
Jesse Peter Multicultural Museum at Santa Rosa Junior College, for Native California baskets and materials
Kule Loklo at Point Reyes National Seashore, a Coast Miwok cultural site

sections.text: A walk to an oak tree in a park or neighborhood, a small bag or basket, and a pot of soil.

items: Gather acorns and caps and sort them by size.
Try an acorn cap whistle between your thumbs.
Plant a fresh acorn in a deep pot and keep it outside and damp.
Visit the same oak in each season and notice the changes.

sections.text: Your child can collect, sort, plant and care for the acorn pot. Your child can sort acorns into a basket, water the acorn pot and carry the rest back outside. A small bowl for treasures keeps the table clear.

items: I wonder who eats acorns.
How old do you think this tree is?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is getting to know a tree that matters to many animals and people here. Gathering, sorting and carrying acorns uses small hand muscles and steady body work, which helps many children feel calm.
Send in a photo of your oak or your acorn pot. Clean acorn caps for our loose parts are welcome. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Acorns are not for eating. Watch for poison oak near oak trees and wash hands after gathering.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Fog, sky and clouds
cards.summary: Watching our coastal fog, changing skies and clouds across the seasons in Sonoma County.

items: June to September. Cool ocean fog flows inland through the Petaluma Gap on many nights, so mornings start gray and damp. The sun usually burns through by late morning, and afternoons turn warm and clear.
September to October. Clear blue days, warm afternoons and the first tall clouds that bring rain. Some years wildfire smoke hazes the sky.
November to February. Storm clouds roll in low, gray and fast. On cold still mornings after rain, valley fog settles in low spots and dew or frost covers spider webs.
March to May. Puffy white clouds build on warm afternoons, showers come and go, rainbows appear, and afternoon wind picks up.
Year round. Crows, hawks and turkey vultures ride the air, the moon shows in the daytime sky, and airplane trails cross overhead.
Cloud watching lying on blankets in the outdoor piazza or Log yard, with clipboards for drawing.
A sky photo taken from the same spot at the same time each morning, hung in a long strip along a wall.
Hand mirrors laid flat on the ground so children can look down and see the sky.
A fog walk on gray mornings, noticing what disappears, what sounds carry and how the air feels on skin.
Dew on spider webs in fall and winter mornings, looked at with magnifiers and photographed without touching.
A weather chart children keep, choosing words and drawings for the sky each day.
A cloud in a jar. An adult pours warm water in a clear jar and sets ice on top, and children watch the mist form.
Wet paper and watercolor in grays and blues for painting skies as they change.
Cardboard viewfinders for framing one piece of sky at a time.
Wind socks and streamers hung where children can see which way the fog and wind move.
Breath on a cold mirror or window on winter mornings, wondering where the mist went.

sections.text: Children never look straight at the sun, and on bright days hats and sunscreen go on even after a foggy morning. On days with wildfire smoke or poor air quality we follow local air quality guidance and stay indoors. Fog mornings can be cold and damp, so layers that come off by midday help.

items: Take the morning sky photo and add it to the strip.
Choose words and symbols for the weather chart.
Predict whether the fog will lift and check later.
Lead the fog walk and name what they notice.
Share cloud drawings and ideas at meeting time.

sections.text: Children close sky work by putting the camera or tablet back in its place, returning weather symbols to their pocket chart and hanging clipboards on their hooks. Cloud drawings go into the shared folder. Each tool has a labeled home, so the morning sky routine closes with the children.

Lie down on the blanket beside the children and look up, so your body shows that slow looking matters. Speak little and softly in the fog and let the quiet stay. Notice if the cold makes you want to hurry inside, and stay a little longer than feels easy.

items: I notice the hills disappeared. I wonder where they went.
Where do you think the fog comes from?
Tell me what that cloud is doing.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with cloud watching on blankets and open talk.
Start the daily sky photo strip.
Add the weather chart and children's own symbols.
Take fog walks and record sounds and feelings.
Make a cloud in a jar and wonder about fog.
Paint skies across the seasons and compare them.
Compare summer fog mornings and winter fog mornings.
Make a sky book of the year with photos, paintings and words to share with families.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Cloud watching, sky drawing and weather charts are open to everyone. The cloud in a jar needs an adult pouring warm water at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a walk through the fog waving a long scarf, slow spins while looking up at the clouds, and cold dew to feel on bare hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a blanket to lie on close to an adult, a hat or hood on cold mornings, and the window as a place to watch the sky first.
connected: John Constable on the Artists page, for his cloud studies painted outdoors again and again
Fujiko Nakaya on the Artists page, for sculptures made of real fog, including her fog work at the Exploratorium in San Francisco
Book collection, for The Fog by Kyo Maclear and Little Cloud by Eric Carle

home.title: Fog, sky and clouds at Home

sections.text: A window or a spot outside where you can see the sky, a blanket and a phone camera.

items: Lie on a blanket and watch clouds move.
Take a photo of the sky from the same spot each morning for a week.
Go outside on a foggy morning and listen.
Look for dew on spider webs on cold mornings.

sections.text: Your child can choose the spot, take the photos and describe what the sky is doing. Your child can hang up a jacket, put away a cloud drawing and set the weather picture for the day. Small routines like these let the morning sky stay a daily habit.

items: Where do you think the fog goes?
Tell me what that cloud is doing.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is noticing weather and learning to slow down and look closely. Lying on the ground to watch clouds and feeling cool fog on the skin helps children notice their bodies and slow down.
Send in a sky photo or a cloud drawing for our sky wall.
Never look straight at the sun. On smoky days check local air quality before going outside.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Birds through the seasons
cards.summary: Noticing which birds live on our site all year, which arrive for winter, which come to nest in spring and what each is doing season by season.

items: Late September to October. White-crowned and golden-crowned sparrows arrive to spend the winter in our yards and shrubs. Scrub jays and acorn woodpeckers are busy with acorns.
November to February. Winter flocks move through, including yellow-rumped warblers, and cedar waxwings can visit berry shrubs. More hawks hunt from open perches in winter.
December to March. Anna's hummingbirds nest in the rainy season, and males climb high and dive with a sharp chirp to court.
February to March. Allen's hummingbirds return. Tree and violet-green swallows arrive in March to nest.
March to May. Nest building everywhere. Finches, crows, phoebes and swallows carry grass, mud and fluff. Black-headed grosbeaks and warblers arrive in April. Winter sparrows leave by May.
June to August. Fledglings beg loudly and follow their parents. Herons and egrets hunt along the creek and in open grass.
August to September. Swallows gather and head south, and we wait for the winter sparrows to return.
Year round. Crows, red-tailed hawks, house finches, Anna's hummingbirds, scrub jays, herons and egrets.
Merlin Bird ID sound recording at meeting time or on a walk, then listening again to the bird it heard.
A bird watching window with child-size binoculars, a clipboard and real photo cards of the birds we see most.
A bird bath children fill, clean and watch each day, with a log of who visits.
Spent sunflower heads left standing in fall so finches and sparrows can feed.
Nesting material in spring, with short natural fibers such as goat fluff, wool and dry grass in a wire cage.
Real photos of birds' nests and eggs on the wall, then a slow walk looking up for nests in trees and eaves.
Observational drawing of birds from photos and from life, with pencil and watercolor.
A seasonal bird list on the wall that children add to, marking which birds are here now.
Joining the Great Backyard Bird Count each February, counting birds in our yards for a short time.
Crow watching. Noticing how crows call, gather and work together.
A hawk or heron watch from a quiet spot, waiting together with no talking for a few minutes.
Hummingbird watching at the salvias, pineapple sage and hummingbird sage.

sections.text: Feathers, nests and eggs of wild native birds are protected by federal law, so we look, photograph and leave them, while chicken feathers can come inside. Nests in use are watched from a distance so parents keep coming back. Bird baths are scrubbed and refilled often, and we skip long string or dryer lint for nesting, which can tangle birds.

items: Record birdsong with Merlin and decide which birds to look for.
Fill and clean the bird bath and keep the visitor log.
Add birds to the seasonal list and notice who is missing.
Set out nesting material in spring.
Teach friends to move slowly and use quiet voices near birds.
Share sightings and drawings at meeting time.

sections.text: Children close bird time by scrubbing and refilling the bird bath with a brush and watering can, then hanging the brush to dry. Binoculars go back in their cases, and the visitor log goes on its clipboard hook. Nesting material is put away in its bin, so the space closes with the children.

Settle in one spot and sit low with the children so the birds stay and the group calms. Use a voice only as quiet as the moment needs, and point with an open hand. Name what you notice, such as That bird flew to the same branch again, and leave room for children to say more.

items: I notice that bird is back. I wonder where it was.
Tell me what you think that bird is saying.
Where do you think the swallows go?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by listening outside with eyes closed and counting songs.
Add Merlin recordings and photo cards.
Set up the bird bath and visitor log.
Start the seasonal bird list on the wall.
Look for nests in spring and offer nesting material.
Notice who leaves and who arrives as seasons change.
Join a community bird count.
Make a bird book of the year to share with families and the next class.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Listening, watching and drawing birds are open to everyone. Cleaning the bird bath needs an educator nearby, and walks to look for nests beyond our yards mean holding an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry and fill the bird bath, scrub it clean with a stiff brush, and hop and flap the way a bird they just saw moved.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the bird watching window with binoculars and a soft cushion away from the group. Listening to one bird song on Merlin Bird ID at a low volume is a gentle way in.
connected: John James Audubon on the Artists page, for The Birds of America, life-size paintings of birds
Ito Jakuchu on the Artists page, for his close paintings of birds and plants
Book collection, for About Birds by Cathryn Sill and Mama Built a Little Nest by Jennifer Ward

home.title: Birds through the seasons at Home

sections.text: A window or a spot outside, a phone with the free Merlin Bird ID app, and a shallow dish for water.

items: Sit outside quietly for a few minutes and listen for birds.
Record a bird with Merlin and see what it finds.
Set out a shallow dish of water and watch who comes.
Look up for nests in spring.
Keep a list of birds you see each season.

sections.text: Your child can listen, record, fill the water dish and keep the list with drawings. Your child can scrub and refill a bird bath and put binoculars back in their case. A hook for the brush by the bird bath makes it their job.

items: I wonder what that bird is saying.
Where do you think it sleeps?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is learning to be still, listen closely and notice who shares our neighborhood. Sitting still to listen for birds helps children practice calm attention and careful listening.
Send in a photo or a Merlin recording of a bird you found for our bird list.
Look at wild bird feathers and nests and leave them where they are. Clean water dishes often.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Strawberries
cards.summary: Caring for our permanent strawberry beds through the year, from planting and runners to flowers, berries and sharing.

items: October to November. New plants can go in. Rooted runners are dug and moved to fill gaps or start new plants.
December to February. Plants rest low and green. Old brown leaves are tidied away and straw or pine needle mulch goes down. Bare root plants can go in during January.
March to April. White flowers open and bees visit. Each flower's center slowly swells into a hard green berry.
May to July. Our main harvest. Berries turn white, then pink, then red. Birds, snails and roly polys find some too.
July to October. Everbearing and day-neutral plants keep fruiting in smaller waves. Runners stretch out in every direction.
Every few years, the oldest plants are replaced with young runners to keep the beds strong.
A flower watch. Children tie a soft ribbon by one flower and visit it each day until it becomes a ripe berry.
A daily berry check with a small basket, picking only red berries with a gentle twist.
Berries looked at closely with magnifiers before snack, wondering about the tiny seeds on the outside.
Observational drawing of a whole strawberry plant, with roots, runners, flowers and fruit, then the berries go to snack.
Runner pots. Children set a small pot of soil under a runner and pin it down, then cut it free once it roots.
A roly poly and snail check under the leaves, moving visitors to the compost area.
Netting or berry cages children help plan to share with the birds a little less.
A taste test of different varieties side by side, with children's words recorded.
Cooking in the piazza culinary atelier, such as strawberry lemonade or sliced berries over pancakes.
Mulching the beds with straw in winter, carried in buckets and spread by hand.
A strawberry bed map where children mark the ripest spots each week.

sections.text: Berries are rinsed before eating and shared at snack or cooking time, and berries are never used for painting, stamping or sensory play. Children step only on paths between beds so the plants and shallow roots stay safe. iGrow Sonoma (igrowsonoma.org) and Harmony Farm Supply are good local sources for timing and new plants.

items: Check, pick and carry the harvest.
Decide which berries are ready and which need more time.
Root runners and replant them.
Mulch and tidy the beds.
Wash, cut and share berries at snack.
Teach younger children to pick only red berries and walk on paths.

sections.text: Children close the harvest by carrying baskets to the sink, rinsing berries for snack and returning trowels and gloves to the tool board. They rake straw mulch back over bare spots and put the harvest basket on its shelf. Green tops go to the chicken bucket, so nothing waits for an educator later.

Kneel at the bed within arm's reach of the children and pick slowly yourself, so your hands show care for the plant. When a child picks a green berry, narrate what you see instead of correcting, such as This one is white inside. Stay at the bed and let the work take as long as it takes.

items: I wonder how a flower turns into a berry.
Tell me about the outside of the strawberry.
Who else do you think is eating our strawberries?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a slow walk through the strawberry beds, noticing leaves, flowers and runners.
Tie a ribbon on one flower and follow it to a berry.
Start a daily harvest routine and tally chart.
Root runners and give new plants to another class or to families.
Taste test varieties and record children's words.
Cook with the harvest and add recipes to a class book.
Mulch and care for the beds through winter.
Make a strawberry year book with photos from bare winter beds to summer harvest.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Picking and caring for the beds happen in the garden with one adult to six children. Cooking with the harvest needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry watering cans to the beds, spread straw mulch by the armful, and dig holes for new plants with a trowel.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small basket and one berry to look at with a magnifier first. Gloves for reaching under leaves and the choice to watch a friend pick are fine.
connected: Recipe library, for strawberry lemonade and fresh berries with pancakes
Jean-Simeon Chardin on the Artists page, for his still life painting of a basket of wild strawberries drawn from life
Book collection, for Strawberries Are Red by Petr Horacek

sections.text: A strawberry plant in a pot or a patch, or a visit to a U-pick farm or farmers market in spring and summer.

items: Grow a strawberry plant in a pot on a sunny step.
Watch one flower turn into a berry.
Pin a runner into a small pot of soil and grow a new plant.
Pick berries together at a local farm.
Wash and slice berries together for breakfast.

sections.text: Your child can water, watch, pick, wash and help slice berries with a butter knife. Your child can carry the berry basket in, rinse berries for snack and take tops to the compost. A basket with its own spot makes picking easy to finish.

items: How do you think the flower turns into a berry?
Tell me about the outside of the strawberry.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is watching food grow from flower to fruit and learning to care for a plant. Picking ripe berries gently and carrying water to the beds builds hand control and gives the body steady work.
Send in a strawberry runner from your garden or a family recipe that uses berries. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Rinse berries before eating. Strawberries are for eating and sharing, so save play for other materials.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Falling leaves
cards.summary: Following leaf color and leaf fall on our site, from the first dry oak leaves in fall to spring leaf drop on the evergreen oak.

items: September to October. The first dry valley oak leaves drop in the heat. Grape and Asian pear leaves start to change color.
October to November. The Japanese maple in the West yard turns red and orange. Grape leaves go gold and red, and redbud, fig and cherry leaves turn yellow. Windy first storms bring leaves down.
November to January. Valley oaks drop their brown leaves. Most fruit trees and vines stand bare, and leaves pile on paths and soften with rain.
February to March. Old leaves break down into leaf mold under the oaks as buds swell on bare branches.
April to May. The coast live oak in the North yard drops last year's leaves while new ones grow, so evergreen trees have a leaf fall too.
June to August. Leaves are full and green, giving shade. Some trees drop a few leaves early in long hot spells.
Child-size rakes, a big tarp and an open space for raking leaf piles to jump into and carry.
A large cloth on the ground where children lay leaves in a line of color from green to brown.
Leaf rubbings with crayon and thin paper, comparing leaves from different trees.
Leaves pressed in a flower press or heavy books, then used for collage and the light table.
Leaf catching on windy days, wondering which leaves fall fast and which drift.
Leaf threading on yarn with a large blunt needle for hanging garlands and crowns.
Land art in the Log yard with leaves, sticks and stones, photographed before the wind changes it.
Tempera printing with leaves on paper and cloth.
The same tree photographed every week in fall, hung in a row at children's eye level.
Leaf mold investigation under the oaks, lifting layers with trowels to see how leaves change below.
Leaves gathered into the compost as browns, carried in buckets and wheelbarrows.
Japanese maple seeds collected and dropped from a height to watch them spin.

sections.text: Adults decide which leaves go to the goats. Poison oak drops its red leaves in fall too, so adults confirm every gathering spot. Check leaf piles for black widows and other creatures before children jump in, and rake away from tree trunks and roots.

items: Rake, carry and pile leaves for play and for compost.
Sort and arrange leaves by color, size and shape.
Choose leaves to press and use in the Studio.
Photograph and record the class tree each week.
Decide where leaves go, to the compost, the paths or the beds as mulch.
Teach younger children which leaves to leave alone.

sections.text: Children close leaf play by raking leaves back into a pile and carrying them in wheelbarrows to the compost or beds. Rakes and child-sized brooms go back to their hooks, and leaves chosen for pressing go between the press boards. An adult moves only the full heavy loads, and the yard is reset by the children.

Rake alongside the children, then step back once the pile is ready. Keep your face relaxed when bodies jump and crash in, and stay close enough to check the pile is clear. Narrate the big moments in a regular voice, such as You landed on your back and the leaves flew up.

items: I notice this leaf is many colors. I wonder why.
Where do you think the leaves go after they fall?
How do you think some trees keep their leaves all winter?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with raking, piling and jumping.
Collect leaves and sort them by color on a cloth.
Rub, press and print leaves in the Studio.
Photograph one tree weekly through fall.
Catch falling leaves and spinning seeds on windy days.
Make land art and photograph how it changes.
Follow leaves into the compost and the leaf mold.
Notice spring leaf fall on the coast live oak and compare.
Make a leaf book for families with rubbings, pressed leaves and photos.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: An educator checks leaf piles for black widows and stays close while children jump. Adults confirm gathering spots because poison oak drops red leaves too.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to rake one huge pile, drag the full tarp across the yard, and jump and roll in the leaves.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a single leaf to look at on the light table, or a small basket to fill one leaf at a time. Gloves and a spot at the edge of the pile are fine.

Utagawa Hiroshige on the Artists page, for Maple Trees at Mama, with red maple leaves framing the view
Book collection, for Leaf Man and Red Leaf, Yellow Leaf by Lois Ehlert

sections.text: A rake, a basket or bag, some heavy books and paper and crayons.

items: Rake a leaf pile and jump in.
Collect leaves on a walk and sort them by color.
Press leaves in a heavy book for a week.
Make leaf rubbings with crayon and thin paper.
Watch one tree in your neighborhood change through fall.

sections.text: Your child can rake, collect, sort, press and decide what to make with the leaves. Your child can rake leaves into a pile, carry them to the compost and hang the rake. Raking up after jumping in is part of the fun.

items: I wonder why leaves change color.
Where do you think the leaves go?
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is noticing seasons change and using strong muscles while raking and carrying. Raking, carrying and jumping in leaves gives the body big movement and heavy work, which helps many children feel calm afterward.

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Blooms and pollinators
cards.summary: Following what blooms on our site month by month and the bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and beetles that visit.

items: December to February. Rosemary, salvias and early citrus blossoms feed Anna's hummingbirds and early bees. The California pipevine hangs small curved flowers from January into February.

February to March. Plum, apricot and nectarine blossoms open. The western redbud in the outdoor piazza turns magenta, California poppies begin, and pink jasmine perfumes the front fence. Pipevine swallowtail butterflies fly and lay eggs on the pipevine.

March to May. Peak bloom. Cherry, Asian pear and apple blossoms, hummingbird sage, irises, catnip, yarrow and honeysuckle. Pipevine swallowtail caterpillars feed on the vine, and ladybugs show every life stage.
May to July. Lavender, salvias, yarrow, roses and the pink flowers of the Black Lace elderberry. Pomegranate, feijoa and passionfruit flowers open. Bees need water on hot days.
August to October. Pineapple sage blooms red for hummingbirds, Blue Dawn morning glory covers the fence, and salvias keep going. Late native bees work the last flowers.
November. Few flowers, so the ones that bloom matter more. Rosemary and salvias carry pollinators into winter.
A pollinator count. Children choose one plant, sit for five minutes and tally every visitor with marks on a clipboard.
A bee water dish, shallow with stones to land on, filled and cleaned by children.
A fallen or spent flower taken apart on a tray with tweezers and magnifiers, laying out every part.
A bloom calendar on the wall where children add a drawing or photo each time a new flower opens.
A pipevine watch in spring, looking for the red-orange eggs and dark caterpillars with magnifiers.
Ladybug life stages found on our plants and matched to real photos, from eggs to larvae to pupae to adults.
Hummingbird watching at the salvias, noticing which flowers they choose.
Hand pollinating squash flowers with a small soft paintbrush, then watching for fruit.
Garden flowers cut and arranged by children for café tables in the piazza.
Flowers used as paintbrushes and pressed for collage and the light table.
Observational drawing of a flower with watercolor pencils, returning to the same plant across the year.
Movement with scarves at meeting time after a bee watch, as children show how the bees moved from flower to flower.

sections.text: Children stay still and calm around bees and never swat, and we know which children have allergy plans before any pollinator walk. The California pipevine is poisonous to eat, as are its caterpillars, so we look closely and wash hands after touching the vine. Adults confirm every flower children pick, and we pick with purpose and leave plenty for the pollinators.

items: Count and record pollinators with tally marks.
Keep the bee water dish clean and full.
Add new blooms to the bloom calendar.
Search for eggs, caterpillars and ladybug larvae and share findings.
Cut and arrange flowers for the café tables.
Teach friends to stay still near bees.

sections.text: Children close bloom work by rinsing and refilling the bee water dish and returning clippers to an adult and vases to the shelf. Tally clipboards go back to their hook, and picked stems not used go to the compost. Hands are washed after touching the pipevine, so the garden closes with the children.

Sit low and still near the flowers, showing with your body that bees are safe to watch. Notice any fear of bees in yourself and breathe slowly, because children read your face. Narrate in a calm voice, such as The bee went in and came out with yellow legs.

items: I wonder why the bee chose that flower.
Tell me about the middle of the flower.
Where do you think the caterpillar will go next?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin by sitting quietly by a flowering plant and watching.
Start the bloom calendar on the wall.
Add the pollinator count and compare plants.
Take apart a flower and draw its parts.
Follow the pipevine swallowtail from egg to caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly.
Follow ladybugs through their life stages.
Hand pollinate squash and follow the fruit.
Plant more flowers where children found the fewest pollinators.
Share a bloom and pollinator book of the year with families.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Garden time keeps one adult to six children, and an adult knows each child's allergy plan before a pollinator walk. The pipevine watch needs an adult close by because the vine is poisonous to eat.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry water to the bee dish, follow a butterfly along the paths with big flapping arms, and dig spaces for new salvias.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a five minute pollinator count from a cushion a little away from the bees, and tweezers for taking a spent flower apart on a tray.

Georgia O'Keeffe on the Artists page, for painting flowers so large and close that we see their centers

Book collection, for The Reason for a Flower by Ruth Heller

items: Sit by a flowering plant for five minutes and count the visitors.

sections.text: Your child can choose the plant, count visitors, keep the water dish full and help plant. Your child can fill a shallow water dish for bees, rinse a vase and wash hands after the garden. A small water can by the door makes it an easy daily job.

items: I wonder why the bee picked that flower.

What do you see that makes you say that?

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: The creek through the year
cards.summary: Returning to the creek trail next door across the seasons to see how the water, plants and animals change.

items: July to October. The creek runs low, with a trickle or still pools. Stones, cracked mud and animal tracks show in the creek bed.
October to November. The first rains wash leaves into the water. Flow begins again and the creek smells different.
December to February. The creek runs at its highest. After storms the water is fast and brown, and high water lines of leaves and sticks show on the banks.
February to April. Water runs clearer between storms. Willows leaf out, Pacific chorus frogs call, and tadpoles gather in still edges.
May to June. Flow slows. Pools warm and turn green with algae, and dragonflies, damselflies and water striders hunt.
Year round. Herons and egrets fish along the water. Poison oak grows along the banks, bare in winter and still able to cause a rash.
A photo taken from the same safe spot on the trail each month, hung in a row at children's eye level.
A listening stop where children close their eyes and count the sounds of water, birds and wind.
Leaf boats dropped on one side of a small footbridge or bend and watched as they float away.
A marked stick an adult sets at a fixed safe point so children can see the water rise and fall across the year.
Clipboard sketching from the bank, drawing the same view in each season.
A clear viewing tub where an adult scoops a little water to look at tadpoles and water bugs, then returns them right away.
A creek trail map made with children and added to after each walk.
Animal tracks in summer mud, photographed and matched to real photos.
Collecting a few fallen leaves along the trail to compare in each season.
Back in class, a long blue fabric and stones for retelling the creek walk with small figures and loose parts.
A creek book of photos, drawings and children's words for each walk.

sections.text: On creek walks a child holds an adult's hand until the group returns, educators hold water safety certificates, and we stay on the trail and off the banks when the water is high or fast. Adults confirm every plant before children touch it because poison oak grows along the creek, and tick checks after spring walks are a good habit. We look under stones and put them back the way we found them, and we leave creatures in the creek.

items: Help plan creek walks and review the agreements together.
Take the monthly photo and add to the map.
Read the marked stick and compare with last time.
Sketch and describe the creek in their own words.
Remind friends to hold hands and use gentle hands with living things.
Share findings at meeting time and in the creek book.

sections.text: Children close the creek walk by packing the camera, clipboards and magnifiers into the field bag before we leave. Back at school they rinse muddy tools in the wash bucket, set them on the drying rack and add the monthly photo to the creek book. Wet shoes go on the boot rack, so the walk closes with the children.

Hold a child's hand with a calm, steady grip and walk at the pace of the slowest child. Stop often and crouch at the water's edge with the group so your body sets a slow rhythm. Notice any worry you feel near water, breathe, and keep your voice regular and clear.

items: I notice the water is different today. I wonder why.
Where do you think the water comes from?
Tell me where you think it goes.
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a short walk and a listening stop.
Start the monthly photo from one safe spot.
Make the creek map and add to it each walk.
Set the marked stick and follow the water level.
Compare summer pools and winter flow side by side.
Watch for frogs and tadpoles in spring.
Follow rain from our roofs and yards to the creek.
Retell creek walks with blocks, fabric and loose parts in class.
Share the creek book of the year with families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.level: One adult with one or two children
setting.why: Each child holds an adult's hand on the creek trail, so each adult walks with one or two children. Scooping water into the viewing tub and setting the marked stick are adult work.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to walk the bumpy and sloped parts of the trail while holding an adult's hand, and to carry the group's bag of clipboards and the viewing tub.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a listening stop with eyes closed on a dry spot close to an adult, with a hand to hold the whole time. Looking at the creek from the trail first is enough.

Book collection, for A River by Marc Martin and Water Is Water by Miranda Paul

home.title: The creek through the year at Home

sections.text: A safe trail by a creek or stream near you, good shoes and a phone camera.

items: Visit the same creek in different seasons and take a photo from the same spot.

sections.text: Your child can choose the spot, take the photo and tell you what changed. Your child can rinse muddy boots, hang the walk bag and set treasures on a tray by the door. An easy end makes the next walk easy to begin.

items: Where do you think the water goes?
Tell me about the sounds you hear.
What do you see that makes you say that?

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Shadows through the year
cards.summary: Tracing our own shadows and the shadows of trees and buildings across the seasons to see how the sun moves.

items: Around December 21. The shortest day of the year. The sun stays low in the south and noon shadows are at their longest, close to twice as long as a child is tall.
Around March 20. Day and night are close to equal. Noon shadows are mid length and getting shorter each week.
Around June 21. The longest day of the year. The sun climbs high, noon shadows are at their shortest and sit close around our feet.
Around September 22. Day and night are close to equal again, and shadows grow longer each week.
The sun is highest around 12:15 pm in winter and around 1:15 pm during daylight saving time, so midday shadows are shortest a little after clock noon.
In summer the valley oaks and orchard trees cast deep shade. In winter bare branches let sun reach the ground and draw lacy shadows on the yard.
Shadow tracing. A child stands on the same chalk mark at the same time each month while a friend traces the shadow in chalk, with a photo kept each time.
A shadow stick in the outdoor piazza, with stones set at the tip of the shadow each hour of a morning.
Shadow length strings, where a string cut to the length of a child's shadow is hung on the wall each month.
Shadow tag and shadow dancing on sunny afternoons.
Small objects and animal figures set on paper outdoors so children can trace their shadows and return later to see the change.
A tree shadow map, drawing where the shade falls in the yard in summer and again in winter.
Shadow puppets made from cardboard and sticks, played outdoors in sun and indoors with a lamp.
A light table and flashlights indoors on rainy days, with natural objects to cast shadows on the wall.
Photographs of the same yard spot at the same time in each season.
A sundial children design from a stick and stones, checked across the year.

sections.text: Children never look straight at the sun, and on bright days hats and sunscreen go on. Winter is the best season for long dramatic shadows, and early fall and spring change fastest, so monthly tracing shows the most. Chalk marks fade in rain, so a painted dot or a fixed stone keeps the standing spot.

items: Stand on the mark and trace each other's shadows.
Set stones at the tip of the shadow stick.
Cut and hang the shadow strings each month.
Predict how long the shadow will be next time.
Teach younger children how to find and trace a shadow.

sections.text: Children close shadow tracing by gathering chalk into its tin and coiling the shadow strings back onto their cards. Stones from the shadow stick go back to their basket unless they mark today's tip. The tracing tools have a labeled home, so the close is as quick as the set-up.

Stand on the concrete with the children and let your own shadow join the play. Hold out the chalk to a child and step back so they trace and decide. Narrate changes plainly, such as Your shadow reaches the bench now, and return at the same time to look again together.

items: I notice my shadow is longer today. I wonder why.
Where do you think your shadow goes on a cloudy day?
How do you think the shadow will look by lunch?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with shadow play on a sunny day.
Trace shadows with chalk and come back an hour later.
Start the monthly shadow tracing at the same spot and time.
Add the shadow stick and hour stones.
Hang shadow strings each month and compare lengths.
Map tree shade in summer and winter.
Bring shadows indoors with lamps, puppets and the light table.
Build a sundial and test it across the year.
Make a shadow book with photos and strings to share with families.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Shadow play, tracing and sundials are open to everyone. Children never look straight at the sun, and adults remind them on bright days.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer shadow tag, shadow dancing with big jumps and spins, and long chalk lines traced around a friend's whole shadow.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer tracing the shadow of a small object on paper at a table in the shade. Standing still while a friend traces their shadow is another quiet way in.

Kumi Yamashita on the Artists page, for artworks made from light and the shadows objects cast
Book collection, for Shadow by Suzy Lee and What Makes a Shadow? by Clyde Robert Bulla

home.title: Shadows through the year at Home

sections.text: A sunny spot, sidewalk chalk and a piece of string.

items: Trace your child's shadow in chalk, then trace it again later in the day.
Cut a string as long as their shadow and save it to compare next month.
Play shadow tag in the yard or at the park.

sections.text: Your child can stand, trace, measure and predict what will happen to the shadow. Your child can gather chalk into a tin after tracing shadows and rinse chalky hands. A small basket for chalk by the door makes the next shadow hunt easy.

items: I wonder why your shadow changed.
Where does your shadow go on a cloudy day?
What do you see that makes you say that?

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Citrus in winter
cards.summary: Harvesting our Meyer lemon, mandarin and finger limes through the cold months, when the citrus trees are at their brightest.

items: July to December. Finger limes ripen a few at a time, from late summer to the end of the year.
October to November. Meyer lemons turn from green toward yellow and mandarins begin to color.
December to March. The main citrus harvest. Mandarins sweeten through winter and Meyer lemons hang ripe and plentiful. Frost cloth goes over the trees on nights a freeze is forecast.
February to April. Sweet smelling white blossoms open, often while ripe fruit still hangs on the same tree.
May to August. Tiny green fruits form, and many drop in early summer. The rest grow slowly through the heat.
Citrus does not ripen after picking, so tasting is how we know when fruit is ready.
A citrus harvest with a basket and child-size clippers, cutting fruit with a short stem.
A taste test of Meyer lemon, mandarin and finger lime side by side at snack, recording children's words.
Fruit cut across on a board to look at segments, seeds and the oily peel with a magnifier, then squeezed or eaten.
Hand reamers and squeezers in the piazza culinary atelier for fresh juice and lemonade for the Unicorn Café.
A finger lime opened at snack so children can see and taste the tiny round beads inside.
Counting mandarin segments at snack and wondering if every mandarin has the same number.
A scent walk, gently rubbing a citrus leaf between fingers and smelling.
A blossom watch in early spring, noticing bees and the smell across the garden.
Helping spread frost cloth on cold evenings and wondering what frost does to leaves.
Weighing the harvest on a kitchen scale and keeping a chart through winter.
Observational drawing of a branch with leaves, blossoms and fruit at the same time.
Sharing the harvest with families in small bags children fill and label.

sections.text: Mandarin and finger lime trees have sharp thorns, so adults guide picking and finger limes are picked by adults. Citrus juice stings eyes and cuts, and lime juice left on skin in the sun can cause a burn, so hands are washed right after juicing. Citrus is cooked, squeezed and eaten, and peels go to the compost.

items: Decide which fruit is ready by color, feel and tasting.
Pick, carry and weigh the harvest.
Squeeze, measure and mix lemonade.
Serve at the Unicorn Café with real cups.
Help cover trees on frost nights.
Bag and label fruit to share with families.

sections.text: Children rinse the juicers, cups and pitchers in the wash bucket and stand them on the drying rack. They carry the peels and seeds to the compost bucket, wipe the sticky table with a damp cloth and wash their hands right away. Harvest baskets and the scale go back to their photo-labeled shelf, and an adult puts away the finger lime picker and any knife. It all happens on the floor as part of the work, so nothing waits for an educator later.

Sit at the table at child height and squeeze slowly with the children, showing the work takes time and strength. Let juice drip and seeds fall without hurrying to wipe. Narrate effort, such as You pressed with both hands and more juice came out.

items: I wonder why the lemons are ripe in winter.
Tell me about the smell when you rub the leaf.
How do you know when it is ready?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a visit to the citrus trees to look, touch the leaves and smell.
Harvest a few fruits and taste them.
Compare Meyer lemon, mandarin and finger lime.
Squeeze juice and make lemonade for the café.
Keep a weekly harvest chart through winter.
Watch for blossoms and bees in early spring.
Follow tiny green fruit through summer.
Make a citrus cookbook of children's recipes to share with families.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Harvesting happens in the garden with one adult to six children, and adults guide picking because of sharp thorns. Finger limes are picked by adults, and cutting fruit needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a hand reamer and a whole basket of lemons to squeeze, and the full harvest basket to carry to the piazza.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one leaf to rub and smell and a small cup to taste from, with the choice to smell only. A damp cloth nearby for sticky fingers helps.

Book collection, for Lemonade in Winter by Emily Jenkins

sections.text: Lemons or mandarins from your tree, a neighbor or the market, a hand juicer, a pitcher and cups.

items: Squeeze lemons and make lemonade together.
Peel a mandarin and count the segments.
Smell a citrus leaf or peel with eyes closed.
Taste a lemon and a mandarin and talk about the difference.

sections.text: Your child can squeeze, pour, stir, taste and serve. Your child can rinse the juicer and cups in a small tub, wipe the counter with a damp sponge and carry the peels to the compost. A low towel hook and a basket for the citrus help them finish on their own.

items: I wonder why lemons are sour.
How many segments do you think are inside?
What do you see that makes you say that?

cards.group: Across the year on our site
cards.title: Herbs and tea
cards.summary: Growing, harvesting and drying our herbs across the year and making simple tea together.

items: December to February. Rosemary blooms blue for bees. Mint dies back or slows in the cold, and lemon balm and oregano rest low.
March to May. Mint, lemon balm and catnip surge back. Lavender forms buds, and new soft growth is ready to pick.
June to August. Lavender is in full bloom. Herbs grow fast, and we pick in the morning and pinch tops so more leaves come before the plants flower.
September to November. Pineapple sage blooms red. The last big harvests are bundled and hung to dry for winter tea.
Year round. Rosemary, oregano, lavender and lamb's ear stay up for smelling and touching on garden walks.
A smell walk through the herb garden, rubbing a leaf gently and smelling fingers.
A smell match with eyes closed, using small cups of fresh picked herbs.
Harvesting herbs with child-size scissors into a basket, cutting just above a pair of leaves.
Herb bundles tied with string and hung upside down on a drying rack, with children checking when they crunch.
Tea making in the piazza culinary atelier with fresh mint and lemon balm, poured with real teapots and cups.
Cold mint and lemon balm tea made in a clear jar in the refrigerator, so children can watch the color change.
Hibiscus tea for color, served cool, with children wondering why it turns red.
Children make labels with drawings for each herb and the jars of dried herbs.
Lavender sachets sewn from fabric scraps and filled by children.
Rosemary and lavender sprigs pressed into homemade playdough.
Observational drawing of herbs with pencil and watercolor, noticing leaf shapes and square stems on mints.
A tea gathering at the Unicorn Café where children serve families or another class.

sections.text: Adults confirm every plant children pick, because poison hemlock can grow on our site and only herbs we know go into tea. Adults handle hot water, and tea is served cool or barely warm. Lavender and rosemary are strong, so only small amounts go into tea, and mint and lemon balm are our everyday tea herbs.

items: Choose which herbs to pick for tea.
Harvest, bundle and hang herbs to dry.
Decide when herbs are dry enough to store.
Make labels and keep the tea jars organized.
Measure, steep, pour and serve tea.
Teach friends how to smell a leaf gently.

sections.text: Children shake the leaf bits from the harvest baskets into the compost and rinse the cups and teapot in the wash bucket. They wipe the table with a damp cloth, tie any loose bundles onto the drying line and set the labeled tea jars back in their home. An adult empties and puts away the kettle. Everything closes on the floor as part of the work, so no educator needs time later to put it away.

Kneel in the herb bed and smell a leaf yourself first, slowly and with a calm face. Offer and wait, and accept a no thank you to any smell with the same ease as a yes. At tea, sit with the children and sip slowly so the table settles together.

items: Tell me what this smell reminds you of.
I wonder why mint smells so strong.
How do you think the leaves change when they dry?
What do you see that makes you say that?
Begin with a smell walk through the herbs.
Pick and taste fresh mint and lemon balm tea.
Add the smell match with eyes closed.
Bundle and dry herbs and check them daily.
Make labels and a tea shelf children manage.
Compare fresh tea and dried tea.
Sew lavender sachets and share them.
Host a tea gathering for families or another class.
Make a class herb book with drawings, smells described in children's words and tea recipes.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Picking herbs happens in the garden with one adult to six children, and adults confirm every plant. Hot water stays with an adult, and sewing lavender sachets needs an adult at the table.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer rubbing and crushing leaves firmly between the palms, a mortar and pestle for dried herbs, and carrying the bundles to the drying rack.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, start with soft lamb's ear or mild lemon balm, and let them smell from a small cup held at a distance. Saying no thank you to a smell is always fine.
connected: Recipe library, for mint, lemon balm and hibiscus tea
Elizabeth Blackwell on the Artists page, for A Curious Herbal, her drawings of hundreds of useful plants
Book collection, for The Tea Party in the Woods by Akiko Miyakoshi

sections.text: A pot of mint or another herb, scissors, string, a teapot or jar and cups.

items: Grow mint or lemon balm in a pot by the door.
Smell different herbs and spices from your kitchen with eyes closed.
Pick mint and make a cool tea together.
Hang a small bundle of herbs to dry and check it each day.
Have a small tea party with real cups.

sections.text: Your child can water, pick, smell, steep, pour and serve. Your child can rinse the cups and teapot in a small tub of water, wipe the table with a towel and put the jar of dried herbs back on its shelf. Leaf bits can go to the compost or the garden.

items: Tell me what this smell reminds you of.
I wonder what happens to the leaves in the water.
What do you see that makes you say that?

sections.text: Your child is using all their senses and learning that plants can feed and comfort us. Smelling herbs and sipping warm tea helps many children notice their bodies and feel calm.
Send in a cutting of an herb from your garden or a family tea recipe for our recipe collection. This counts toward your family participation hours.
Only use herbs you know well, and let an adult handle hot water. Serve tea cool for young children.

cards.title: Painting with water
cards.summary: Buckets of plain water and real brushes turn fences, walls and concrete into a huge surface that dries and invites more.

sections.text: Buckets or tubs of plain water, wide house painting brushes, small rollers and sponges. A fence, a wall, the outdoor piazza concrete or any dry surface in the yard.
Set the buckets along a fence or on open concrete with the brushes standing in them. Add nothing else and step back. On a hot day set some buckets in the sun and some in the shade.
Children tip the buckets onto the garden beds and stand the brushes, rollers and sponges bristle up in a crate to dry. The sun takes care of the wall.

Pick up a brush and paint a little yourself, then step back and stay nearby. Narrate what you see, such as Your line is drying from the top first. Let the water spill and the fence get wet without stopping the work.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: There is nothing to spill or ruin, and every mark fades so children can begin again. Big arm strokes and carrying full buckets give the body heavy work, and the drying is calm to watch.
Go to Water for spray bottles, droppers, pouring and rain. If children notice marks drying faster in the sun, Shadows through the year follows that question.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Painting with plain water is open to everyone. Keep an educator near the buckets when the 2s are painting.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer wide brushes, full buckets to carry along the fence, and a high wall to reach up and paint.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small brush and a small cup of water at a quiet stretch of fence. Plain water dries and leaves no mess.

cards.title: The covered table with one material
cards.summary: One whole table covered with one surface and one material in the middle, ready for many hands at once.

sections.text: One table and one surface to cover it, such as butcher paper, flattened cardboard, an old sheet or bubble wrap. Masking tape for the edges. One basket of one material, such as thick crayons, chalk pastels or pencils.
Cover the whole table and tape the surface down along the edges. Set the single basket in the middle. Move the chairs away so children can stand, lean and walk all the way around.
Children peel the tape, roll or fold the covering together and carry it to its drying spot or the recycling. They gather the material back into its one basket and set it on the shelf.

Stand at the edge of the table at children's height and stay there the whole time. Keep your hands slow in the material and leave the shared piece unfinished and uncorrected. Narrate what children add and let the busy middle be busy.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: One material asks for no explaining and no choosing. Many children can work side by side on the same surface, and the shared piece grows all day with no wrong place to begin.
Go to Studio and class ateliers to change the surface each week and add a second material slowly. Walls and documentation helps the finished piece go up with children's own words beside it.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Everyone can walk up and add to the shared surface. Nothing here needs extra attention.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, choose a textured surface such as bubble wrap or cardboard and invite both hands into the material across the whole table.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a corner of the table with a tool such as a brush or stick, and a moment to watch the busy middle first.

cards.title: Dance party
cards.summary: Music on, space cleared and everyone moving, with a slow song at the end to land together.

sections.text: A speaker and a few songs at different speeds. The basket of scarves or ribbon wands if it is close by.

Push back a table or step onto the outdoor piazza and turn on the music. Start dancing yourself and let children join, watch or move at the edges. Change the speed a few times and end with something slow.
Children fold the scarves and slide the ribbon wands back into their basket, then pull the table back to its place together. An adult turns off and puts away the speaker.

Dance with your whole body first, without worrying how it looks, because children borrow your ease. Watch for a child who needs a pause and move closer to them. Sit low with a soft voice for the slow song so the group lands with you.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Big energy gets a place to go and nobody needs to sit still. Children who only watch are still part of the group. The slow song at the end helps bodies settle before the next thing.
Go to Music and movement for freeze and melt, scarves, and dances children make up and teach each other.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Everyone can dance, watch or move at the edges. Keep the space clear of hard edges.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add spinning, jumping and landing on a pile of cushions, with a few faster songs.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, lower the volume and offer a spot at the edge to watch or tap along, with a scarf to wave while sitting.

cards.title: A clipboard walk
cards.summary: Every child carries a clipboard and a pencil on a slow walk through the yard or garden, stopping wherever someone stops.

sections.text: A clipboard for each child with paper clipped on, and a pencil tied to each one with string. A crate or bin to carry them out.
Hand out the clipboards at the door and walk the yard or garden together slowly. Stop when a child stops. Drawings, marks, a few letters or simply carrying the clipboard all count.
Children hang their pages on the documentation line or slip them into their folders. They stand the clipboards back in the crate with the pencils tucked under the clips.

Carry a clipboard of your own and walk slowly in the middle or back of the group. Stop when a child stops and crouch to look too. Narrate what you see on their page instead of praising it, such as You drew the fence with many lines.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A clipboard gives a restless child a job and a reason to look closely. It moves the group outside without a plan to follow, and each page holds what that child noticed today.
Go to Clipboards everywhere to keep them in every area for maps, lists, sign ups and observational drawing.

setting.why: An educator walks with the group. In the garden we keep one adult to six children.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, choose a longer route with slopes or steps, a thick pencil to press hard, and the bag of extra clipboards to carry.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, walk a short, quiet loop holding an adult's hand, and let carrying the clipboard be enough.

cards.title: Ice blocks on a hot day
cards.summary: Big blocks of ice on a tray in the shade with coarse salt and droppers of color, changing on their own as children watch.

sections.text: Blocks of ice frozen the day before in tubs or loaf pans, a tray or the sensory table, coarse salt in a small bowl, droppers, and liquid watercolor in a few small cups. Leaves or petals frozen inside add something to find. Adults choose these only from plants we know.
Turn the ice out onto the tray in the shade. Set the salt and the cups of color with droppers beside it. Wait to see what children do first.
Children carry the melted ice water to a thirsty plant and rinse the droppers and color cups in the wash bucket. They wipe the tray with a damp cloth and set the droppers on the drying rack.

Sit beside the tray in the shade and touch the ice yourself with a calm face. Let the colored water run and pool without wiping it. Narrate changes slowly, such as The salt made a little hole there, and leave space for children to notice more.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Cold is soothing on a hot afternoon. The ice changes by itself, so the material does the work. Children can stand and watch or stay with it for a long time.
Go to Ice for freezing children's own collections, melting questions and frosty mornings in the garden in winter.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: An educator stays near the tray because salt can sting eyes and cuts. Adults choose any leaves or petals frozen inside.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer bare hands on the ice, bigger blocks to push and turn, and a wooden mallet to tap the softened edges.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer gloves or a spoon for touching the ice and a dropper to add color from a little distance.

cards.title: Bubbles in the yard
cards.summary: A tub of soapy water and wands made from what is on hand, out in the open air.

sections.text: Dish soap and water in a wide tub, plus wands from what is around, such as pipe cleaner loops, slotted spoons, plastic berry baskets and string tied between two straws. A splash of glycerin if it is on the shelf.
Mix the soap and water in the tub on the grass or the outdoor piazza. Set the wands beside it and blow the first bubble yourself. Let the breeze take it.
Children dip the wands in a bucket of clear water and lay them in their basket to dry. Two children carry the tub together and pour it out on the grass away from the garden beds.

Blow the first bubble slowly and watch it all the way until it pops, so children see you care about small moments. Stay in one spot on the grass where children can come back to you. Let spills and soapy hands happen and keep your voice light and regular.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Bubbles float, drift and pop, and every age chases or watches. Outside there is almost nothing to clean up, and a tub can be ready in two minutes.
Go to Bubbles for giant wands, bubbles that last and bubble prints. If children follow where the bubbles go, Wind and air is next.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Bubbles are open to everyone. Keep an educator near the tub of soapy water with the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer giant wands that take the whole arm to swing, and chasing and popping bubbles across the yard.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small wand and a cup of their own, sitting in one spot to blow slowly and watch.

cards.title: A cloth over the table
cards.summary: A sheet draped over a table becomes a small room with walls, ready for quiet, stories or hiding.

sections.text: A large sheet, tablecloth or parachute, a table or two chairs, clothespins and a few cushions. A flashlight or a small stack of books if they are near.
Drape the cloth over the table so it reaches the floor on most sides. Pin it to the chairs. Put the cushions inside and leave one side open.
Children unclip the clothespins into their basket and fold the cloth together, each holding a corner. They stack the cushions and books back in their homes.

Sit at the open side of the cloth at floor level and stay there, close and calm. Keep your voice low and regular. If a child needs you, reach in with a hand or sit at the opening instead of crawling in.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A small space with walls gives a child somewhere to be held while still close to the group. It can be a quiet place, a house or a hideout, and children decide which.
Go to Hiding and enclosing for dens, crates, hammocks and the willow dome. If the fort keeps asking to stay, Quiet and cozy space is next.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator keeps sightlines into the fort and leaves one side open.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add heavy cushions and blankets to pile on and crawl under, and invite them to drag the cushions inside.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, keep one side open, limit it to one or two children at a time, and add a soft blanket and a book.

cards.title: A shade fort on a hot day
cards.summary: A sheet clipped to the fence makes cool shade and a hideout on a hot dry afternoon.

sections.text: A light sheet or parachute, clothespins or clamps, a few cushions or a blanket, and a fence corner, the edge of the willow dome or two trees.
Clip one edge of the sheet high on the fence and stake or weight the other edge low. Lay the blanket inside the shade. Invite children to help hold, clip and adjust it.
Children unclip the clamps into their basket and fold the sheet together, each holding a corner. They shake out the blanket and carry the cushions back to their home.

Ask for help and hold the sheet with the children, letting them clip and adjust even when it sags. Sit inside the shade once it is up so your body shows it is a place to rest. Keep your voice soft and your movements slow on a hot afternoon.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Shade cools bodies and slows the pace. Building it together is real work, and the space inside is calm and enclosed.
Go to Hiding and enclosing for bigger dens and covered spaces. Fabric follows children who want to sew, tie or dye their own walls.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator keeps sightlines into the shade fort and checks that clips and stakes hold.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry and place heavy stones or log rounds to weight the edge, and to pull the sheet tight.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a cushion in the cool shade with a book and a quiet place to rest away from the busy yard.

cards.title: Chalk on open concrete
cards.summary: A basket of thick chalk set down on bare concrete with nothing drawn first.

sections.text: A basket of thick sidewalk chalk and a bucket of water with a sponge or wide brush.
Set the basket down on open concrete in the outdoor piazza or the yard. Sit down and draw a little yourself, or just watch. Leave the water bucket nearby without explaining it.
Children drop the chalk back into its basket and carry it to the shelf. Anyone who wants to can wash the drawings away with the sponge and water bucket, or leave them for the rain.

Sit down on the concrete and draw a little yourself, then set the chalk down and watch. Narrate marks instead of praising, such as You pressed hard and the line got darker. Let the water bucket and the mess unfold without explaining.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Children can work big, lie down, crawl and travel across the ground. Dipping chalk in water changes it in a way they discover themselves. The next rain or a hose clears it all away.
Go to Chalk for grinding chalk, chalk paint, body tracing and long maps across the piazza.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Chalk on concrete is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer chalk dipped in the water bucket and pressed hard, long lines walked from one end of the piazza to the other, and hands to smear the color.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a chalk holder or a cloth wrapped around the chalk, and a small square of concrete at the edge.

cards.title: One big box
cards.summary: The biggest cardboard box on hand set out in an open space, with tape and nothing else said.

sections.text: The largest cardboard box available, masking tape and a few thick crayons. Child box cutters or scissors stay with an adult.
Set the box in an open spot, on its side or open end up, with the tape beside it. Say nothing about what it could be.

Children gather tape scraps and paper bits into the recycling and set the crayons back in their basket. The box stays as long as it is still in use, and when it is done children flatten and carry it to the recycling while an adult puts away any cutters.

Sit on the floor near the box and say very little. Let the box get torn, crushed or taped in odd ways without fixing it. Narrate what children do, such as You taped the flap shut from the inside, and stay in the space as ideas change.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A box becomes whatever children decide, which lets everyone in. Climbing in, pushing, hiding and decorating meet many needs with one object.
Go to Cardboard for cutting, joining and building houses and vehicles. If the box becomes a place to live, Castles, houses and homes is next.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: Everyone can climb in, tape and draw. Cutting doors and windows with box cutters or scissors stays with an adult.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to push and drag the box, climb inside and press against the walls, or flatten it together at the end.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, cut a small window to look in or out from, and offer a smaller box of their own.

cards.title: Tape on the floor
