cards.summary: A roll of masking tape and an open stretch of floor become roads, paths and shapes in minutes.

sections.text: A roll of masking or painter's tape, an open stretch of floor, and a basket of small cars or balls if one is near.
Tear a few strips and stick them along the edge of a table so they are ready to grab. Put down one line on the floor and leave the roll beside it.
Children peel the strips from the floor, roll them into a sticky ball and drop it in the trash. They return the cars or balls to their basket and the roll to its labeled home.

Kneel on the floor near the first line and tear tape with slow, careful hands. Let lines go crooked and cross each other without straightening them. Narrate what children make and stay on the floor at their level.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Tape is quick to start and quick to pull up. Children walk the lines, build roads and make shapes, and the floor is clear again in minutes.
Go to Tape for webs across doorways, tape resist painting and tape sculptures.

setting.why: Tape play is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, make a long tape line to walk, hop and jump along, and invite them to peel it all up and roll it into a big ball at the end.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, tear strips ahead of time and offer a small square of floor or a tray to tape on.

cards.title: Listening to the rain
cards.summary: Metal bowls and pots set at the drip line turn a rainy day into a shared sound to listen to.

sections.text: The covered porch or an open door, a few metal bowls, pots, pans and buckets, and rain gear for anyone who wants to go out.
Set the bowls and pots along the drip line where water falls from the roof. Sit down beside them and listen together before anyone talks.
Children carry the bowls and pots inside, tip the water into a bucket for the plants and stack them on a towel to dry. Rain gear goes back to the cubby hooks.
Sit down first beside the bowls and close your eyes for a moment, so children see that listening is the whole idea. Keep words few and your voice soft. Wait through the quiet without filling it.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Rain days can feel shut in. Sound brings the outside in and gives the group one calm thing to notice together. Children who want more can step out in rain gear.
Go to Weather, rain and wind for rain gauges, storms and drawing the rain. The rainy season follows the creek and the garden from November to March.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Listening is open to everyone. We come in if there is thunder or strong wind.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a hand or a bare foot under the drip line, and bigger pots to drum on after the listening.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a dry seat under the eaves with a blanket and one small bowl to listen to.

cards.title: Catching the rain
cards.summary: Clear containers of different shapes set out in the rain, with a line marked on each to check again later.

sections.text: Clear containers of different shapes and sizes, masking tape, a marker, and a rain gauge if one is on hand.
Set the containers outside where children can see them from the window. Put a strip of tape on each. Go back together after a while and mark the water line.
Children pour each container into the rain barrel or onto a plant, then stack the containers in their basket. The marked tape strips can stay on the window as a record.

Watch the containers from the window with the children, sitting at their height. When you go back out, let children read and mark the line themselves even if it is crooked. Narrate what you notice, such as This jar filled higher than the tall one.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A simple question to check again gives a stuck indoor day a reason to look out and step out. Children who arrive late can still join the next check.
Go to The rainy season to keep measuring through the winter and follow the creek as it rises.

setting.why: Catching and marking rain is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry the full containers inside with both hands and pour them all into one big tub.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, let them watch the containers fill from the window and help mark the tape line.

cards.title: Puddle time
cards.summary: Rain boots on and out into the yard after the rain to find, stomp, float and measure puddles.

sections.text: Rain boots and rain jackets from the cubbies, sticks, small boats from recycled lids or bark, and chalk.
After the rain, walk the yard together to find the puddles. Bring the basket of sticks and boats. Trace around one puddle with chalk so children can come back and look.
Children gather the sticks and boats back into their basket and set the chalk on the shelf. Boots go on the boot rack and jackets on the cubby hooks.

Wear boots yourself and step into the puddle first, so your body says getting wet is fine. Notice any wish to keep children clean and set it aside for this time. Narrate what you see, such as Your splash went higher than the fence.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Jumping, splashing and stomping use big energy fully. Puddles change shape and size, which brings questions with no setup at all.
Go to The rainy season for mapping puddles over weeks and following where water goes. Water travel and boats follows children who keep floating things.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: An educator walks the yard with the group and stays near deeper puddles.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, find the deepest puddle for big jumps and stomps, and offer a broom to sweep the water out of a puddle.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a stick to stir the edge of a puddle and a boat to float, with boots on and a dry spot to stand.

cards.title: Tracing shadows
cards.summary: Chalk and a sunny stretch of concrete for tracing shadows of objects and of each other.

sections.text: Chalk and a sunny piece of concrete. A few things to stand up, such as a block, a watering can or a toy animal.
Early or late in the day when shadows are long, stand one object on the concrete and trace around its shadow. Leave the chalk beside it. Come back later in the day to look again.
Children carry the block, watering can and toy back to their homes and drop the chalk into its basket. The traced shadows stay on the concrete to look at again tomorrow.

Kneel on the concrete and trace one shadow slowly, then hand over the chalk. Keep your body out of the light so you leave the shadows clear. Narrate plainly, such as Your shadow is longer than you are right now.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Shadows are always there and cost nothing. Tracing a friend's shadow is a calm way to be together, and a shadow that moves is a question that returns all day.
Go to Shadows through the year to trace the same spot across the seasons. Light and shadow follows the question indoors.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Shadow tracing is open to everyone. Children never look straight at the sun.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, trace whole bodies stretched out on the concrete and invite big poses and jumps to change the shadow.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer the shadow of a small object to trace alone, or the choice to hold still while a friend traces.

cards.title: A sitting spot outside
cards.summary: Each child chooses a place to sit quietly outside, alone and within sight, and the group shares what they noticed.

sections.text: A small mat, cushion or square of cloth for each child, and a place under a valley oak or at the edge of the garden.
Let each child choose a spot within sight of an adult and sit on the mat. Sit in your own spot too. Listen and watch for a few minutes, then gather to share what each child noticed.
Each child shakes out their own mat or cloth and stacks it in the basket. Children carry the basket back inside together.

Sit in your own spot within sight of every child and stay still and quiet the whole time. Let your breathing slow so the group can borrow your calm. When you gather, listen first and share one small thing you noticed yourself.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Sitting still outside settles busy bodies. Coming back to the same spot day after day builds the feeling that this place is ours.
Go to Birds through the seasons when children start hearing and naming birds, with Merlin Bird ID close by. Oaks and acorns follows the tree overhead.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Each child sits within sight of an adult, and an educator watches the whole group from their own spot.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, let them carry their own mat and a heavy cushion to the spot and lie on their belly in the grass.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, let them sit near an adult wrapped in a blanket, and keep the time short.

cards.title: A listening walk
cards.summary: A slow walk around the yard with eyes and ears open, collecting sounds in children's own words.

sections.text: Nothing for the children. A clipboard for the adult to write down what children hear.
Walk the yard slowly together and stop often. Close eyes for a moment and listen. Write down each sound the way a child names it.
There are no materials to put away. A child helps clip the list of sounds to the wall or slip it into the class book.
Walk slowly at the children's pace and stop with your whole body when you hear something. Close your own eyes when you ask children to close theirs. Write their words down exactly as they say them.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: It moves a group with no materials and no mess. Listening draws attention outward and quiets voices without asking for quiet.
Go to Sound and instruments to make the sounds children heard. If a bird call keeps coming up, Birds is next.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: A listening walk in our yard is open to everyone with an educator leading. Beyond our yards, each child holds an adult's hand.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add sounds children make on purpose, such as stomping on a deck, tapping a fence with a stick and crunching dry leaves.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, hold their hand, walk the quietest part of the yard, and offer cupped hands over the ears when a sound is too loud.

cards.title: Wheelbarrow hauling
cards.summary: A pile in one place, a spot across the yard where it needs to go, and wheelbarrows to move it.

sections.text: Wheelbarrows, wagons and buckets, shovels and rakes, and something to move, such as wood chips, sand, leaves, short logs or water.
Start a pile in one spot and choose a place across the yard where it needs to go. Ask who can help move it. Keep the shovels and rakes close.

Children rake the last spills into the pile and park the wheelbarrows and wagons in their row. They hang or stand the shovels and rakes in their labeled spots, and an adult moves any log too heavy to lift.

Work beside the children, lifting and pushing with them, so your body shows this is real work. When a barrow tips or spills, stay calm and reload together. Narrate effort, such as You pushed it all the way up the slope.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Big energy needs real work. Pushing a full load is heavy work that settles the body, and a real job builds the feeling of being capable.
Go to Carrying and transporting for bags, baskets, carts and moving things with purpose. If the load is mulch or compost, Garden is next.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: An educator stays close because loads get heavy and shovels swing. Adults lift short logs first to check for black widows.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, let them fill the barrow fuller, push it up a slope and dump it with a big tip.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a bucket or small wagon and a short route, or the job of choosing where the pile goes.

cards.title: Playdough already made
cards.summary: A ball of dough at each place and a small basket of natural parts in the middle of the table.

sections.text: A batch of playdough from the shelf, rolling pins or wooden tools, and a small basket of natural loose parts such as sticks, shells, pinecones and stones.
Set a ball of dough at each place with the basket in the middle. Sit down and press the dough with your own hands.
Children roll their dough back into a ball, pick out the loose parts and press the dough into its lidded jar. They wipe the table and tools with a damp cloth and set the basket back on the shelf.

Sit at the table at children's level with your own ball of dough and press it slowly. Keep your hands busy with your own dough instead of shaping theirs. Narrate what hands do, such as You squeezed it and it came out between your fingers.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Squeezing and pounding dough is heavy work for small hands and calms the body. Children can work alone at a shared table and talk or stay quiet.
Go to Playdough for children making their own dough, coloring it with chalk dust and a self serve tool shelf.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Playdough is open to everyone. Keep small loose parts away from the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a bigger, firmer ball to pound, squeeze and roll with the whole arm, and a heavy rolling pin.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a smaller piece of dough with a rolling pin or stick to press with, and time to watch first.

cards.title: Soup in the mud kitchen
cards.summary: Water, real pots and fallen petals set out in the mud kitchen for stirring, pouring and pretend cooking.

sections.text: The mud kitchen, a bucket or watering can of water, real pots, spoons and ladles, and a basket of fallen petals and leaves from plants we know.
An adult gathers or checks the petals and leaves first. Fill the bucket and leave it by the mud kitchen with a few pots out.
Children tip the soup into the garden bed and rinse the pots and ladles in the bucket. They hang or stack the pots back in the mud kitchen in their usual places.

Crouch by the mud kitchen and stir a pot yourself for a moment, then step back. Let mud and petals go everywhere without hurrying to tidy. Narrate the cooking in a regular voice, such as You poured slowly and the petals floated up.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Stirring, pouring and mixing are soothing and open, and every age joins in. Mud kitchen play holds stories, mixing and cooking for pretend with nothing to get wrong.
Go to Mud kitchen for menus, recipes and a café. Mud follows children who want the mud pit and mud slides.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Mud soup is open to everyone. An adult gathers or checks the petals and leaves first.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer bigger pots of water to carry and pour and thick mud to stir with a long spoon.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer clear water and petals only, a long spoon for stirring and a small cup to pour from.

cards.title: Wash day
cards.summary: Tubs of warm soapy water, scrub brushes and a line to dry things on, ready for real washing.

sections.text: Two tubs of warm soapy water and one of clear rinse water, sponges and scrub brushes, towels, and a drying rack or line with clothespins. Things to wash, such as dolls, doll clothes, play dishes, blocks or tricycles.
Set the tubs on a low table or the ground outside with the towels at the end. Begin washing something yourself.
Children hang the clean things on the line or rack and carry them back to their homes once dry. They tip the tubs onto the plants and drape the towels and sponges to dry.

Begin washing with slow, unhurried hands so the work feels calm. Stand at children's height and let water slosh and splash without stopping it. Narrate the work, such as You wrung it so hard the water ran down your arms.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Washing is real work with a clear beginning and end. Warm water soothes, and scrubbing and wringing are heavy work. The toys come out cleaner too.
Go to Home and dramatic play area for caring for babies and keeping house. If washing turns into bathing and caring, Family and babies is next.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays near the tubs of water, especially with the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavy wet towels to wring, a stiff scrub brush and full baskets to carry to the line.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small cloth, a smaller tub and the job of pinning dry things to the line.

cards.title: Stacking stones and sticks
cards.summary: A basket of flat stones and sticks beside a stump, for slow balancing that can fall and begin again.

sections.text: A basket of smooth flat stones, short logs and sticks, and a flat stump or board to build on.
Set the stump or board in the Log yard or on a table and pour the stones out beside it. Stack two stones and leave them.
Children take their towers apart stone by stone and set them back in the basket. They stack the sticks and logs beside the stump where they live.

Sit low beside the stump, stack slowly yourself, then leave your stack. When a stack falls, keep your face soft and calm, since falling is part of it. Narrate effort and balance, such as You turned that stone until it stayed.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Balancing asks for slow hands and close attention, which settles the body. When a stack falls the stones are ready again and nothing is lost.
Go to Building tall for towers, balance and knocking down. Natural materials follows children who begin making patterns and arrangements.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Stacking is open to everyone. Keep small stones away from the 2s and stack on a low surface.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavier stones and short log rounds to carry and stack, and let them knock the stack down on purpose before building again.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray and a few smooth stones of the same size to stack alone.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for balancing stones and sticks outdoors into works that stand for a while and then fall or wash away.

cards.title: Planks and balls
cards.summary: One plank leaned on a crate and a basket of balls at the top.

sections.text: A few wooden planks or rain gutters, crates or blocks to prop them on, and balls of different sizes.
Lean one plank on a crate and set the basket of balls at the top. Roll one ball down and watch where it goes.

Children gather the balls into their basket and carry the planks and gutters back to their stack in pairs. They return the crates and blocks to their spots, and an adult carries any plank too long or heavy to manage.

Sit at the bottom of the ramp at children's level and watch where the balls go. Let balls fly off and planks shift without fixing the set up. Narrate what you see, such as The heavy ball went farther than the small one.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Rolling and watching is easy to join at any age. Children carry planks, change the slope and try again on their own.
Go to Ramps and moving things for gutters, tubes, pulleys and water channels.

feeds: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: Ramps and balls are open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to carry heavy planks and crates to make steeper ramps, and to try bigger, heavier balls.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer one low ramp and a small ball to roll at a table.

cards.title: Rolling tires
cards.summary: Old tires from the yard and a clear lane for pushing, rolling and chasing.

sections.text: A few old tires from the yard, cones or crates to mark a lane, and a wide open stretch of ground.
Mark a lane with the cones away from the paths where others walk. Roll one tire down the lane and let it fall over. Agree together that everyone stays out of the lane while a tire rolls.
Children roll the tires back to their resting spot and stack the lighter ones together. They carry the cones and crates back to their home, and an adult lifts any tire too heavy to stack.

Stand at the side of the lane where you can see its whole length, with a relaxed body and soft knees. Keep your voice clear and regular when reminding the group of the lane agreement. Narrate effort and speed, such as You pushed and it rolled all the way to the cone.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Pushing a heavy rolling thing is strong work and a chase at the same time. Children can roll alone or work in pairs to send a tire back and forth.
Go to Spinning and rolling for wheels, tops and rolling on the hill. Tire swing yard follows children who want to swing and spin.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays by the lane because rolling tires are heavy, and everyone stays out of the lane while one rolls.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer the heaviest tire to push uphill and a longer lane to chase it down.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tire or hoop and a spot at the side of the lane to watch and cheer.

cards.title: Flashlights in a dark corner
cards.summary: A darkened corner with a few flashlights and a basket of things that make shadows and colored light.

sections.text: A few flashlights, a sheet to darken a corner or cover a table, and a basket of objects such as shells, translucent lids, colored film and a small toy animal.
Darken one corner with the sheet. Put the flashlights and the basket inside. Turn one light on to cast a shadow on the wall.
Children click off the flashlights and lay them in their basket with the objects. They unclip and fold the sheet together, each holding a corner.

Sit inside the dark corner at children's height and keep your voice low and calm. Notice whether the dark makes any child uneasy and stay close to them. Let children hold and point the lights, and narrate the shadows you see.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Dark and light draw children in on a rainy indoor day. A small dim space quiets voices, and shadows invite stories.
Go to Light and shadow for overhead projectors, shadow puppets and big shadow screens. Light table follows children who want to look through color.

feeds: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)

setting.why: An educator keeps sightlines into the dark corner and stays nearby for children unsure about the dark.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer brighter lights, colored transparent film and big body shadows made by moving close to the wall and far away.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, leave a soft light on inside, offer one flashlight of their own and keep the group to two or three.

cards.title: Books on a blanket
cards.summary: A blanket, a few cushions and a stack of books laid open, with an adult reading quietly.

sections.text: A blanket, a few cushions, and a stack of books from the shelf, including at least one with real photographs.
Spread the blanket in the shade outside or in a quiet corner. Lay the books open around the edge. Sit down and begin reading to yourself.
Children close the books and carry them back to the shelf with the covers facing out. They shake out and fold the blanket together and stack the cushions.
Sit on the blanket and read quietly to yourself, with a relaxed body and no rush. Let children come, go and lean in as they choose. When a child brings a book, read it in a regular, warm voice.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: An adult reading quietly draws children to sit close. Children can lie down, look alone or listen together, and late arrivals slip in easily.
Go to Books for favorite books returned to again and stories children tell. If the blanket wants a permanent home, Reading nook is next.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Books on a blanket are open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy lap blanket or cushion to hold, and books with flaps and textures to touch.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a spot at the edge of the blanket and a book of their own to look at with no group to join.

cards.title: Shakers and drums
cards.summary: A circle with shakers and drums in the middle and one steady beat to join.

sections.text: The basket of shakers, hand drums or buckets turned upside down, and wooden spoons.
Sit in a circle on the floor or outside and set the instruments in the middle. Start a slow steady beat and let children pick up an instrument and join. Stop together and wait, then begin again.
Children set each instrument back in its basket and turn the buckets over to stack them. The spoons go into their jar.

Sit low in the circle and keep a slow, steady beat with relaxed hands. Let the noise get big without hushing it, then bring the beat back with your own body. Pause together with a calm face so children can find the quiet.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A shared beat brings a scattered group together without words. Loud and soft, fast and slow give big energy a shape.
Go to Sound and instruments for making instruments and visits to the music shed.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Playing together is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big drum to play with both hands and a loud, fast part before coming back to the steady beat.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a soft shaker or a scarf, a spot a little farther from the drums, and the choice to cover ears or listen first.

cards.title: An obstacle course from what is out
cards.summary: Crates, planks and tires already in the yard become a course children help carry, build and change.

sections.text: Whatever is already in the yard, such as crates, planks, tires, stumps, hoops, cones and a tunnel.
Ask children to help carry and place the pieces. Walk the course together once, then let children change it. Stay close where a plank is high.

Children carry the crates, hoops, cones and tunnel back to their homes and stack them the way they found them. Two children carry each plank together, and an adult moves any stump or plank too heavy to lift.

Stay at the highest or trickiest spot with your hands ready and relaxed, without hovering. Notice any worry about heights in yourself and breathe so your face stays calm. Narrate what a child does, such as You held on with both hands and stepped across.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Climbing, balancing, crawling and jumping use big energy fully. Carrying and placing the pieces is heavy work, and children own the course they built.
Go to Climbing and high places for safe risk and growing confidence. Log yard follows children who want to balance on logs.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An educator stays close where a plank is high and watches how children change the course.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add a heavy tire to drag, a higher plank with an adult close and a crawl through a tunnel of crates.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a low path along the ground, their own pace with no one behind them, and the job of helping to set up.

cards.title: One object on the entry table
cards.summary: A single real thing from nature on the entry table with a magnifier and a question, ready for arrival.

sections.text: One interesting real thing, such as a large seed pod, a feather, a piece of bark with lichen or an oak gall. A cloth, a magnifier and a clipboard with a pencil.
Set the object on the cloth on the entry table with the magnifier and clipboard beside it. Write one wondering question on a card, such as I wonder where this came from.
A child carries the object back to the nature table or its collection box and folds the cloth. The magnifier and clipboard go back to their spots on the shelf.

Sit by the entry table as families arrive and look at the object yourself with real interest. Greet children at their level and let them look before you say anything. Write down what they say exactly.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Arrival is a big change. One quiet thing to look at gives a child and a family a reason to pause together, and an easy first step into the day.
Go to Entry and nature table for finds that change over time, children's own collections and labels in their words.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Looking and drawing are open to everyone. Small seeds and pods stay out of reach of the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, choose an object that is heavy, rough or strongly scented, such as a big stone, a piece of bark or a sprig of rosemary, and let them carry it to show a friend.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, invite them to look with the magnifier first and touch only when ready.

cards.title: A block of clay at arrival
cards.summary: One whole block of clay on a board, with nothing else, for hands to press as children arrive.

sections.text: A block of clay from the bag, a board, a spray bottle of water and a damp cloth to cover it after.
Set the whole block on the board in the middle of the table. Press your own hands into it as children come in.
Children press the clay back into one block, mist it and wrap it under the damp cloth in its bag. They wipe the board and table with a damp sponge and set the spray bottle on the shelf.

Sit at the table at child height and press your own hands into the clay as children come in. Keep your hands moving slowly and stay in the clay with them. Narrate what you see, such as You pushed with your whole palm and made a deep hole.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Pushing and pulling clay is heavy work that grounds the body. It asks for nothing in particular, and children can arrive and leave the table without breaking anything.
Go to Clay for adding tools, slabs, coils and pieces that dry on labeled boards.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Clay at arrival is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to push, pound and lean their whole body weight into the block, and to tear off big pieces.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a wooden tool to press into the clay and a small damp cloth for wiping hands.

cards.title: Helping in the animal yards
cards.summary: A small group goes with an adult to fill water, rake bedding or collect eggs, following the care chart.

sections.text: The water and feed buckets, a scoop, a rake or broom, the care chart, and one adult for every six children. Shoes on.
Bring a small group to the animal yards. Choose one job from the care chart and do it together, such as filling water, raking bedding or collecting eggs.
Children rinse the scoop and hang the rake or broom on its hook, then carry the buckets back to their home. They tick the job on the care chart and wash their hands.

Notice any tension you feel about the animals and breathe it out before going in. Move slowly and speak in a calm, regular voice in the yards, since animals and children both read your body. Work alongside the children on the same job.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Caring for animals is real and needed work. It gives an unsettled child a calm purpose and a quiet way to be near another living being.
Go to Animal yards for care charts, likes and dislikes and observational drawing. The goats through the year follows the herd across the seasons.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Animal care keeps one adult to six children with shoes on and handwashing before and after. Collecting eggs and raking bedding happen with an adult beside the child.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, choose heavy jobs such as carrying water, raking bedding and pushing the wheelbarrow.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, choose a light job such as collecting eggs or holding the chart, with the choice to watch from the gate first.
connected: The Image of the Child lens

cards.title: Watering the garden
cards.summary: Watering cans and a hose or rain barrel, and garden beds that truly need water on a hot day.

sections.text: Watering cans in a few sizes and a hose or rain barrel to fill them. Shoes on and one adult for every six children.
Fill one can and look together for the beds that are dry. Let children fill and carry their own cans and decide where the water goes.
Children empty the last of each can onto a bed and hang or stand the cans upside down in their spot. An adult turns off and coils the hose.

Fill a can yourself and walk slowly to the beds, pouring with care at the base of a plant. Let children decide where the water goes and let shoes get wet. Narrate what you see, such as The soil turned dark where you poured.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Carrying full cans is heavy work, and the garden really needs it. Water on dry soil is calming to watch and to smell.
Go to Garden for home beds, planting and harvest, with the Garden page close by. Seed to seed follows children who want to plant.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Garden time keeps one adult to six children. Filling cans at the hose works best with an adult close by.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer full watering cans carried with both hands and the hose to drag across the garden.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small can and one nearby bed, with a gentle sprinkle on the hands only if they want to feel the water.

cards.title: Boats in the long sink
cards.summary: The long yard sink or a tub of water with a basket of things that float, ready on a hot day.

sections.text: The long yard sink or a wide tub of water, and a basket of recycled lids, bark, corks, sponges, sticks and fallen leaves. Masking tape for joining.
Fill the sink or tub and set the basket beside it. Float one piece and blow on it gently.
Children fish out every boat and piece and lay them in the basket to dry. They pull the plug or tip the tub onto the garden and drop the tape scraps in the trash.

Stand at the sink at children's height and float a boat yourself for a moment. Let water spill over the edge without stopping the play. Narrate movement, such as Your boat drifted to the corner when you blew.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Water cools and calms on a hot day. Children float, sink, push and blow with no right answer to find.
Go to Water travel and boats for building boats, sails and testing how much a boat can hold.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Water play always has an adult watching closely.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer full jugs to pour and invite whole arms to push big waves for the boats.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tub of their own with a cup and a boat, and a towel nearby to dry hands.

cards.title: Looking under logs
cards.summary: A small group rolls over a log that has been lying on the ground to see who lives underneath.

sections.text: Magnifiers, a few clear containers with air holes, a soft paintbrush for moving small creatures, and a log or board that has been lying in the yard.
An adult tips the log first and checks for black widows. Then the small group rolls it over slowly together. Look first and touch gently, then put every creature and the log back where they were.
Children carry each creature back to where it was found and the small group rolls the log back slowly together. Magnifiers, containers and the brush go back into their basket.

Tip the log first with calm, careful hands, then crouch with the group close to the ground. Keep your face curious when creatures appear, since children borrow your feelings about bugs. Narrate gentle touch, such as You let the roly poly walk across your palm.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Small creatures pull attention outward and slow everyone down. Finding roly polys and worms is a shared joy, and children practice being kind to all beings.
Go to Bugs and small creatures for habitats, iNaturalist, drawings and books with real photos.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)

setting.why: An adult tips each log first to check for black widows before the small group looks. Creatures and the log go back where they were.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to help roll the heavy log with the group and carry stones to set back around it.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, invite them to watch from a few steps back and look at a creature in a viewing cup with a magnifier.

cards.title: Drawing at the window
cards.summary: A table pushed up to the window with paper and pencils for drawing the rain, fog or sky.

sections.text: Paper or clipboards, pencils, and a few gray, blue and white crayons or chalk pastels. A table that can move to a window.
Move the table to the window and set out the paper and pencils. Sit and draw the sky, rain or fog yourself.
Children slip the pencils and crayons back into their basket and hang the drawings on the documentation line. Together they slide the table back to its place.
Sit at the window and draw the sky yourself with slow, quiet marks. Speak little and let each drawing stay private. If a child shares, narrate what you see on the page instead of praising it.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Rainy days and foggy mornings give a changing view that is always ready. A quiet task by the window settles a busy room.
Go to Fog, sky and clouds to draw the same sky day after day and notice how it changes.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Drawing is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer thick soft pencils to press hard and a big sheet taped to the window to draw on standing up.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small sheet, one pencil and a quiet seat at the end of the table.
connected: John Constable on the Artists page, for painting the sky over and over in quick cloud studies from the same hill.

cards.title: Hammering into a stump
cards.summary: Real hammers, wide head nails and a big stump for strong, loud, purposeful work.

sections.text: A large stump or soft wood round, real hammers, roofing nails with wide heads, and safety glasses. One adult stays with the small group.
Start a few nails partway into the stump. Go over the agreements together, such as one hammer per person and glasses on. Hammer one nail yourself first.

Children hand each hammer and pair of glasses to the adult, who counts them and returns them to the tool shelf. Children pick up any dropped nails with a magnet and drop them in the jar, and the stump stays as it is for next time.

Stand within arm's reach of the stump with a calm, steady body and your own glasses on. Let the loud noise and bent nails happen without taking over. Narrate effort, such as You hit it three times and it went all the way in.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Hammering is strong, loud and purposeful heavy work. It gives big energy a safe target, and children feel capable using a real tool.
Go to Wood and tools for saws, drills and building with wood.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: Real hammers and nails need one adult staying with a small group and agreements about glasses and one hammer each. Starting nails is adult work.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavier hammer and longer nails to drive all the way in.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer ear protection and a spot a little away from the stump to watch, then a wooden mallet to tap golf tees into a thick piece of foam.

cards.title: Raking leaves into piles
cards.summary: Rakes and a tarp under the trees in fall, for raking one big pile and jumping in.

sections.text: Rakes in child and adult sizes, a tarp and a wheelbarrow. Fallen leaves under the valley oaks or the orchard trees.
An adult checks the area first for poison oak and sharp sticks. Lay the tarp and start raking toward it. Invite children to help make one big pile, then let them jump in.
Children rake the scattered leaves back to the pile and tip the tarp into the wheelbarrow to carry it to the compost or a garden bed. They hang the rakes in their labeled spots.

Rake with the children, then step back to the edge of the pile when the jumping begins. Keep your face relaxed as bodies crash in and stay close enough to check the pile is clear. Narrate what you see in a regular voice.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Raking and hauling are heavy work, and jumping into the pile is pure joy. The pile can be made again and again.
Go to Falling leaves for sorting, pressing, rubbings and composting.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)

setting.why: An adult checks the area for poison oak and sharp sticks first, then an educator stays close while children jump.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite them to rake a bigger pile, drag the full tarp and jump and roll in the leaves.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer gloves, a small rake and a corner of the tarp, with the choice to drop leaves on the pile instead of jumping in.
connected: Andy Goldsworthy on the Artists page, for gathering fallen leaves and laying them out by color on the ground where they were found.

cards.title: Breathing and marks
cards.summary: A few slow breaths together and then a mark on paper for how each body feels right now.

sections.text: Paper and a basket of oil pastels or crayons.
Sit together. Take three slow breaths as a group. Invite each child to make a mark that shows how they feel right now, then breathe again and make another mark.
Children set the pastels or crayons back in their basket and add their marks to a folder or the wall. One more breath together closes it.
Sit at children's level and breathe slowly yourself, letting your shoulders drop. Make your own mark too without explaining it. Narrate gently, such as Your second mark is softer than your first.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Breathing slows bodies down. Marks give feelings a place without needing words, and there is no wrong mark.
Go to Faces and feelings for mirrors, feeling words and stories about big feelings.

setting.why: Breathing and marking are open to everyone. A child who is very upset needs an adult close for calm first.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer big paper on the floor and thick pastels to press and scribble hard with both arms.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small card and one pencil, and let them breathe with eyes open or simply watch.

cards.title: A mirror on the table
cards.summary: A mirror laid flat with paper and pencils beside it, for quiet looking alone or with a friend.

sections.text: A hand mirror or a safe acrylic mirror, and paper and pencils.
Lay the mirror flat on a small table with the paper beside it. Look into it yourself and notice your own face.
Children set the pencils in their cup and wipe the mirror with a soft cloth. A child carries the mirror back to its home on the shelf.

Look into the mirror yourself with a soft, open face, so children see that looking is safe. Sit nearby and stay quiet, letting children look as long as they want. Name what you see without judging, such as You raised your eyebrows.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Children are curious about themselves. A mirror invites quiet looking and soft talk, alone or with one friend.
Go to Mirrors for mirror boxes, reflections and building on mirrors. Faces and feelings follows children who start drawing faces.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Mirror play is open to everyone. Use an acrylic mirror with the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a big mirror on the floor to move the whole body in front of, and to make big faces in.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small hand mirror and the choice to look at objects in it instead of their own face.

cards.title: Loose parts on a cloth
cards.summary: A cloth on the floor and a basket of loose parts for slow arranging at the end of the day.

sections.text: A cloth or tray and a basket of loose parts already on hand, such as wooden rings, stones, shells, bottle caps, spools and pinecones. For the youngest children choose pieces larger than a child's mouth.
Spread the cloth on the floor and pour the basket into one corner. Sit beside it and begin arranging slowly as families arrive.
Children gather the pieces back into the basket by the handful. They fold the cloth together and set both on the shelf.

Sit on the floor beside the cloth and arrange slowly with calm hands. Leave children's arrangements as they are, even when pieces move or fall. Narrate what you notice, such as You made a circle and then a line.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Arranging is quiet and absorbing. A child can stop at any moment for pickup, and a photo keeps the work.
Go to Loose parts for patterns, building and art that is arranged and then let go.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Loose parts are open to everyone. Choose pieces larger than a child's mouth for the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer heavier parts such as stones and log slices, and a bigger cloth to fill.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small tray of their own with a few smooth parts.

cards.title: Sorting a big basket
cards.summary: A big mixed basket of real things and a few smaller bowls for sorting in any way children choose.

sections.text: A big basket of mixed things, such as lids, spools, keys, shells, corks and wooden pieces, and a few small bowls or a recycled egg carton. For the youngest children choose pieces larger than a child's mouth.
Set the basket and the empty bowls on a table or the floor. Pick up one thing, look at it and put it in a bowl.
Children pour each bowl back into the big basket and stack the bowls or carton inside it. The basket goes back to its home on the shelf.
Sit beside the basket, sort one or two things slowly yourself, then stop. Let children sort in ways that make sense to them without correcting. Ask how they decided and listen closely.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Sorting is calm and orderly, and children decide what goes together. It works alone or side by side, with nothing to finish.
Go to Collecting and treasure for children's own collections, display and trading.

setting.why: Sorting is open to everyone. Choose pieces larger than a child's mouth for the 2s.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, offer a heavy basket to carry and pour out, and big objects such as pinecones and stones to sort into tubs across the room.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a small basket with a few kinds of objects and a quiet spot to sort alone.

cards.title: Looking back at today
cards.summary: A few photos or drawings from the day shared at meeting time to close the day together.

sections.text: A few photos taken today on a tablet or printed, or a drawing a child made, and the meeting time space.
Gather at meeting time near the end of the day. Show one photo and ask what children notice and remember. Write down what they say.
A child helps clip the words beside the photo on the wall or slip them into the class book. The tablet or prints go back to their basket.

Sit low in the circle with the photo at children's eye level and speak in a calm, regular voice. Wait through silences before writing down what children say. Read their words back exactly as they said them.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Ending together closes the day, even a hard one. Children see that their work matters, and their words become documentation.
Go to Walls and documentation for panels made with children. Meeting time follows routines that hold the group together.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Looking back is open to every child at meeting time. Photos of children's faces stay inside our walls.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, let them hold and pass the photo around the circle, or stand and show with their body what they did.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, let them sit close to an adult and listen, and talk later one on one if they wish.

cards.title: Streamers in the wind
cards.summary: Strips of ribbon or fabric and a windy day, for running, waving and watching where the wind goes.

sections.text: Ribbon or fabric strips, crepe paper or scarves, and string or tape for tying. A windy day.
Hand children a few strips and step out into the wind. Tie a few to the fence too so everyone can see the wind from inside.
Children untie their strips and wind them into the basket, leaving the fence streamers up if the wind still blows. Scraps of tape and string go in the trash.

Step out into the wind with your own streamer and let it fly, so your body shows the wind is good to feel. Stay in an open spot where children can see you. Narrate what the wind does, such as Your ribbon went straight up.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: Windy days bring wild energy. Running with streamers gives that energy a place and shows where the wind blows.
Go to Wind and air for windsocks, pinwheels and kites. Weather, rain and wind follows the bigger storms.

feeds: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)

setting.why: Streamers are open to everyone. Keep strips short and never tie them around a neck.

supports: Crossing the middle of the body (midline crossing)
cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, invite running, spinning and big figure eights with long streamers in both hands.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, offer a short streamer to hold while standing still, or the strips tied to the fence to watch from inside.

cards.title: The same song for moving
cards.summary: One song the group already knows, sung every time it is time to move from one place to the next.

sections.text: A song the children already know from the Song book.
Start singing at the door, softly, and keep walking while you sing. Children join the song and the line as they are ready.
The song ends where the group arrives, and there is nothing to put away. Children sit or set down whatever they carried right where it belongs.
Sing softly and keep walking at a calm, even pace, so your voice and body lead the move. Stay close to any child who finds moving hard. Keep the song the same every time so children can rely on it.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: The same song each time tells children what comes next without calling or counting. Singing together helps bodies move as one group.
Go to Music and movement for more songs and movement through the day. Meeting time follows the songs that open and close the day.

feeds: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Singing while moving is open to everyone. Nothing here needs extra attention.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, add marching, stomping or tiptoeing to the beat as the group walks.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, let them walk beside an adult and hum quietly or just listen.

cards.title: Something to carry
cards.summary: Each child carries one real thing from one space to the next, so moving becomes a job.

sections.text: Things that need to move anyway, such as cushions, baskets, a basket of balls, the water jug or the clipboard crate.
Before the group moves, hand each child one thing to carry. Walk together and have them set it down where it belongs.
Each child sets their thing in its home when the group arrives. That walk is the whole close.
Carry something yourself and walk at the children's pace. Hand each child their item with care and a calm word. Narrate the job, such as You carried the basket all the way to the shelf.

sections.h: Why it works on hard days
sections.text: A job in the hands helps a child leave one place and arrive in the next. Carrying is heavy work that settles the body on the way.
Go to Carrying and transporting for bags, baskets, carts and loads children choose themselves.

feeds: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)

setting.why: Carrying is open to everyone. Give heavier things to children who ask for them.

cards.seeks: For a child who seeks more, hand them something heavy, such as a full water jug, a crate or a stack of books.
cards.avoids: For a child who finds it too much, hand them something small and light, such as a basket or the song book, and let them walk beside an adult.

behaviors.label: Throwing things
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child throws blocks, toys, sand or materials across the room or yard. It may happen in play or when feelings are big.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about how far and how fast things travel and what happens when they land. Throwing may give the arms strong work and a push and pull feeling in muscles and joints (proprioception). It might also be a way to show a feeling that has no words yet.
needs: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "You are throwing the blocks far."
Offer a place where throwing is welcome, with soft balls, beanbags or a target outside.
Stay nearby and wonder together about where things land.
behaviors.keep_safe: Guide the throwing toward a space and objects where everyone's bodies stay safe.
behaviors.development: Throwing is one of the big body skills twos practice, along with running, jumping and kicking (gross motor skills). Twos and young threes often throw when a feeling is strong, because stopping an urge in the moment is still hard (impulse control). Through the threes and fours, children grow in managing impulses with less adult help, and many throw with more aim and purpose (gross motor manipulative skills). Throwing is common at two, and we still guide where it goes and what gets thrown. If throwing at people stays frequent past the threes, grows stronger, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
Toddlers and Challenging Behavior, Why They Do It and How to Respond, ZERO TO THREE
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Knocking down others' towers
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child knocks over a tower or building that another child made. They may watch the fall closely or laugh.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be fascinated by the moment things fall and change shape. The crash may bring strong sound and movement the child is hungry for (seeking sensation). It might also be an attempt to join the play when they are unsure how to ask.
needs: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and calmly protect the building that is still standing.
Describe what happened for both children.
Offer a tower of their own to build and knock down.
Invite the builder to say what they need.
behaviors.keep_safe: Hold the space around other children's work so both children can feel their work and their ideas are cared for.
from_us: A way into play with friends (peer entry)
A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
behaviors.development: Twos are fascinated by the moment things fall and change, and young children are still learning cause and effect (cause and effect). Joining another child's play is new for twos, so a crash can be an early way in (peer interaction). By three, many children notice other children and join them in play, and through the fours they grow in caring for shared work and asking to join (cooperation with peers). Threes still often need an adult to help them solve a disagreement, and fours begin to negotiate more on their own (conflict resolution). If knocking down others' work stays frequent past the fours, grows more intense, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.
