Milestones by 3 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Hitting
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child hits another child or an adult with a hand or an object. It often happens fast, during a disagreement or in close play.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be trying to say stop, mine, or come play, and the body speaks before words are ready. They may need strong input to the hands and arms (proprioception) to feel calm. A body that is tired, hungry or overwhelmed (interoception) might reach for hitting as the quickest way through.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move in quickly and calmly, and place your body between the children.
Check on the child who was hurt and keep the other child close.
Name the feeling you wonder about, such as "You might be frustrated."
Later, offer strong work for the hands, such as pounding clay or pushing a heavy cart.
behaviors.keep_safe: Gently block or hold the hand and keep both children close so everyone stays safe while feelings settle.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
behaviors.development: Hitting is common in toddlers and often peaks around age two, when feelings are strong and words are still coming (expressive language). Around two and a half, a child may know the rule and still not be able to stop in the moment (impulse control). Through the threes and fours, children build words for feelings and ways to handle conflict, often still with an adult's help (emotion regulation). Hitting is common at two, and we still keep everyone safe and show another way. If hitting happens often over weeks, comes with no clear trigger, grows more intense, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE
Aggressive Behavior in Young Children, UCSF California Childcare Health Program
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Pushing
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child pushes another child with hands or body, in a line, on the climber, or in play.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may need more personal space and push to make room. Pushing may give the arms and body the deep pressure they are looking for (proprioception). It might also be a way to claim a spot, a turn or a friend.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "You pushed and she fell."
Offer something heavy to push, such as a wheelbarrow, a wagon or a wall.
Help the child find words for space, such as "I need room."
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay near crowded places like lines and climbers so children have the space their bodies need.
from_us: A way into play with friends (peer entry)
A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Twos are still learning how close others are and how much room their bodies need, so pushing is common (spatial awareness). Twos and young threes may also push to claim a spot, a turn or a friend when words are slow to come (expressive language). Threes grow in using their own body and other people's space as a guide, and they often seek an adult's help with conflict (conflict resolution). Fours begin to negotiate and use words more often on their own. If pushing stays frequent or rough past the threes, grows over time, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE

behaviors.label: Biting
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child bites another child or an adult. It often happens in close, busy moments or when the child is upset.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may need strong input through the jaw and mouth (proprioception). Biting may be a fast way to say stop or mine before words are ready, or a sign of teething, tiredness or hunger (interoception). It might also come from crowded spaces that feel like too much.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move in calmly and care for the child who was bitten first.
Stay close to the child who bit and name the feeling you wonder about.
Notice when and where it happens, and write it down.
Offer crunchy snack at snack time and safe things to chew, such as a chewy tube.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close in busy moments and give children room so mouths and bodies stay safe for everyone.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Biting is common in toddlers and twos, often when feelings are big and words are still coming (expressive language). Teething can still play a part at two, since the back molars usually come in around this age (tooth eruption). Biting usually fades as children gain words and ways to solve problems with others, so it is less common in threes and fours (social problem solving). Biting is common at two, and we still keep everyone safe and show another way. Biting several times a week is more of a concern than an occasional bite, and if biting continues past the threes, grows, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE
Why Do Toddlers Bite? Educator's Version, ZERO TO THREE
Primary Tooth Development, American Dental Association MouthHealthy

behaviors.label: Kicking
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child kicks people, furniture or materials, often while upset or while lying on the floor.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The legs may be asking for strong work and pressure (proprioception). Kicking may be a way to say no or keep someone away when words feel far off. The child might also be exploring the power of their legs.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move a little back so you are out of reach, and stay calm.
Describe what you see in a quiet voice.
Offer a ball to kick outside, a stomping game or pushing feet against a wall.
Wait with the child until the body settles.
behaviors.keep_safe: Move people and breakables out of reach and stay present until the child's body is calm.
from_us: A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
behaviors.development: Many children can kick a ball by two, and twos love to test the power of their legs (gross motor skills). Twos and young threes may also kick when upset, since acting on a feeling comes faster than words (impulse control). Research with preschoolers finds that upsets (tantrums) are common, while upsets that happen every day or often include kicking or hitting are less typical (emotion regulation). Through the threes and fours, children grow in using words and strategies to cope, with less adult help. If kicking during upsets happens most days, lasts a long time, hurts others, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
Daily or Severe Tantrums May Point to Mental Health Issues, National Institute of Mental Health
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Spitting
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child spits at people, on the floor or on materials, sometimes in play and sometimes when upset.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be exploring what the mouth can do and how far spit can go. Spitting may bring a strong reaction that feels powerful. The child might also be telling us something is too much, such as a taste, a smell or a crowd (avoiding sensation).
needs: Moving things through the air (trajectory schema)
first_steps: Stay calm and keep your face neutral.
Describe what you see, such as "Spit is going on your friend."
Offer a sink, a bucket or a place outside for spitting games.
Offer water play, straws in water or blowing bubbles for the mouth.
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child move away from faces and food so everyone stays healthy and comfortable.
behaviors.development: Twos and threes are curious about what their bodies can do and what happens next, and spitting can be a test of both (cause and effect). Spitting at people often shows up when a child is upset or wants space and does not yet have the words (expressive language). Some children feel tastes, smells and textures more strongly, and spitting can follow something that feels like too much (sensory threshold). By four, many children change their behavior based on where they are, and they grow in managing impulses with less adult help (impulse control). If spitting at people stays frequent past the threes, grows, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE
Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University
Milestones by 4 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.

behaviors.label: Grabbing toys
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child takes a toy or material from another child's hands.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may want that exact object and not yet have the words or patience to ask. Grabbing may be a way to join the play. The child might also be drawn to how the object feels or moves (seeking sensation).
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see for both children.
Help the child who grabbed find words, such as "Can I have it next?"
Offer more of the same material when you can.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close so both children can be heard and the object can be handed back gently.
from_us: A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
A way into play with friends (peer entry)
behaviors.development: Under three, wanting something right now is typical, and seeing another child's point of view is still new (perspective taking). Twos often grab because waiting is hard and words are still coming (delay of gratification). Threes understand sharing and may still need a reminder, and fours share and treat others fairly more often on their own (fairness and turn taking). By five, many children follow rules and take turns in games. If grabbing stays frequent and forceful past the fours, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Sharing, ZERO TO THREE HealthySteps family handout
Toddlers and Challenging Behavior, Why They Do It and How to Respond, ZERO TO THREE
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Climbing on tables and shelves
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child climbs onto tables, shelves, counters or windowsills indoors.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking height and the thrill of being up high (vestibular). Climbing may give the whole body strong work (proprioception). The child might also want to see the room from a new view.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "You want to be up high."
Offer a place where climbing is welcome, such as crates, a climber or the Log yard.
Help the child climb down safely and go together to the new place.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close and spot the child while helping them down, and offer real places to climb.
behaviors.development: Climbing is a strong drive for twos, who are mastering stairs and getting ready for harder play structures (gross motor skills). Toddlers are still learning to judge distance and danger, so they may climb before they can tell what is safe (risk assessment). By four, many children avoid real danger, such as jumping from tall heights, while still seeking the thrill of being up high (risky play). Research suggests thrilling play with heights helps children master fear as their skills grow. Climbing is common at two, and we still offer safe places to climb and keep bodies safe. If climbing stays constant and unsafe past the threes, with little sense of danger, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
Milestones by 4 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.
Children's Risky Play from an Evolutionary Perspective, The Anti-Phobic Effects of Thrilling Experiences, Sandseter and Kennair 2011, Evolutionary Psychology

behaviors.label: Running away or off during transitions
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child runs away from the group when it is time to move, come inside or go on a walk.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may not want the play to end. Running may be a fast way to calm a body that feels too full (self-regulation). The child might also find the chase fun and connecting.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Stay calm and keep the child in sight.
Walk, and avoid chasing.
Give a warning before the change and a job for the move.
Hold hands on the way.
behaviors.keep_safe: Hold the child's hand on walks and near gates and keep an adult watching so everyone stays together.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
behaviors.development: Switching from one thing to another is hard for young children, especially without warning (transitions). Twos may run off in a game of chase, since running is new and joyful and stopping an urge is still hard (impulse control). Threes manage transitions with adult support, and fours begin to anticipate routines and move with less help (managing routines and transitions). Running off is common at two, and we still hold hands and keep everyone together. If running away from the group continues often past the threes, happens with little sense of danger, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Support Transitions for Infants and Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE

behaviors.label: Running inside
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child runs across the room or down the hallway instead of walking.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child's body may need fast movement to feel organized (vestibular). Running may be joyful energy that needs room. The child might also be heading somewhere important and in a hurry.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and walk beside the child.
Describe what you see, such as "Your legs want to go fast."
Offer a time and place to run outside.
Add heavy carrying jobs when moving between spaces.
behaviors.keep_safe: Guide running to open outdoor spaces where bodies have room to move.
behaviors.development: Running is new and exciting for twos, and they love speed (gross motor skills). Twos and threes are still learning to match how they move to the place they are in (impulse control). By four, many children change their behavior based on where they are, though a busy body still needs many chances to move each day. Some children are more active by temperament and need more movement than others (activity level). If running indoors stays constant past the fours, comes with many falls or bumps, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
Milestones by 4 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.
Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University

behaviors.label: Crashing into people
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child runs or falls into other children or adults, often with a big smile.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be looking for strong body pressure (proprioception). They may have trouble judging how close others are (visual-spatial). Crashing might also be a way to connect and play.
needs: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "You want to crash."
Offer a crash pad, a pile of cushions or a mound outside.
Play together with games that include stopping.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer a crash spot away from others so the child gets what they need and others stay steady.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Twos are still learning to judge distance and personal space, so bumping into others is common (spatial awareness). Twos and threes also love big, fast body play, and crashing can be a joyful way to make contact and connect (big body play). Through the threes and fours, children grow in using their own body and other people's space as a guide when they move. Seeking strong body input in ways that hurt others, often and over time, is a pattern worth a closer look. If crashing stays frequent and hard past the fours, grows, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE

behaviors.label: Rough play that goes too far
behaviors.what_we_might_see: Big body play starts with laughter and then someone gets hurt or upset.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: Children may be exploring power, strength and closeness. Rough play gives strong body input (proprioception) and practice reading others' signals. When it goes too far, a child might not yet notice when their body or their friend's body has had enough (interoception).
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and pause the play calmly.
Check that everyone is OK.
Describe what you see, such as "Her face looks scared."
Make agreements together, such as stop when someone says stop.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close and help children agree on safe big body play so it can keep going.
from_us: A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
A way into play with friends (peer entry)
behaviors.development: Chasing, tumbling and play fighting are common and valuable in the preschool years (rough and tumble play). Research finds that children signal play with smiles, laughter and trading roles, such as chaser and chased, and that this play builds social skills and control of strength (aggression regulation). Twos and threes are still learning to read these signals, and fours are growing in noticing when a friend has had enough (social cues). Play often goes too far when one child misses a signal or gets carried away by excitement. If play turns into real hurting often, a child seems unable to stop when others signal, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Children's Rough-and-Tumble Play in a Supportive Early Childhood Education and Care Environment, Storli 2021, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
Big Body Play, Why Boisterous, Vigorous, and Very Physical Play Is Essential to Children's Development and Learning, Carlson, NAEYC
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Chewing on clothes or objects
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child chews on shirt sleeves, collars, hair, pencils or other objects.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The mouth may be seeking strong pressure that helps the body feel calm (proprioception). Chewing may help the child stay focused or calm when things feel busy (self-regulation). It might also be a sign of teething.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Notice without drawing attention.
Offer a safe chewing tool and talk with the family.
Offer crunchy and chewy snacks at snack time.
Offer blowing games, such as bubbles or whistles.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer safe things to chew and remove small or broken objects from reach.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
Time to settle after a change (adjustment)
Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Many twos still use their mouths to explore and to soothe (oral exploration). The back molars usually come in around two, so chewing can still ease sore gums at this age (teething). From about two and a half, children explore more with their hands and fingers, and chewing that continues may help some children calm or focus (self-regulation). Some children keep chewing on sleeves or collars as a comfort habit when things feel hard. If chewing grows more frequent or intense, harms the mouth or teeth, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC
Primary Tooth Development, American Dental Association MouthHealthy
Pica, KidsHealth for Parents (Akron Children's)

behaviors.label: Mouthing toys
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child puts toys, materials or objects in their mouth, often past the age when most children stop.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The mouth may be a strong way to learn about objects, as it is for babies (tactile). The child may be seeking input that helps them feel calm (seeking sensation). It might also be a sign of teething or a habit of comfort.
first_steps: Notice without drawing attention.
Offer a safe chewing tool.
Wash mouthed toys before others use them.
Offer more hand play, such as clay or water.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep small parts out of reach and wash mouthed toys so everyone stays healthy.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Putting things in the mouth is a normal way to explore up to about age two (oral exploration). From about two and a half, children use their fingers and hands more to explore objects (fine motor skills). Some children keep mouthing toys during teething at two or as a comfort habit (self-soothing). Eating things that are not food can carry health risks, such as lead, so it is worth noticing closely. If a child past two often mouths or eats non-food items for a month or more, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at health and development may help.

sources.title: Pica, KidsHealth for Parents (Akron Children's)
Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC

behaviors.label: Putting sand or dirt in mouth
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child puts sand, dirt, mulch or small rocks in their mouth.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about how the earth tastes and feels (tactile). The mouth may be seeking a strong, gritty sensation (seeking sensation). It might also be a sign of hunger or thirst (interoception).
first_steps: Move close and calmly help the child spit it out.
Offer water to rinse.
Offer a safe chewing tool or a snack.
Offer hand play with sand and mud, such as digging and squeezing.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close and help the child rinse, and keep small rocks away from the youngest children.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Tasting the world is part of how young children learn, and putting sand or dirt in the mouth is common up to about age two (oral exploration). Twos are still learning which things are food and which are for play, and adults guide that learning (health and safety awareness). As children grow past two, eating non-food things is less expected. Eating dirt, sand or paint chips can carry health risks such as lead, and low iron can sometimes bring cravings for them (nutrition). If a child past two often eats dirt or sand for a month or more, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at health and development may help.

sources.title: Pica, KidsHealth for Parents (Akron Children's)
Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC

behaviors.label: Covering ears
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child covers their ears at loud sounds, music or when a group is busy.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be finding sounds too loud or sharp (auditory). Covering ears may help the body feel calm (self-regulation). They might also be using it to block out what feels like too much.
needs: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
first_steps: Notice and respect the child's choice.
Lower the volume where you can.
Offer a quiet spot or ear muffs.
Describe what you see, such as "The sound is big for your ears."
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer a quieter spot and ear muffs so the child can stay with the group.
from_us: Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Young children differ in how strongly they feel sound, and some are more sensitive to noise by temperament (sensory threshold). Covering ears at sudden or loud sounds is a sensible way for a child to protect themselves and manage the feeling (self-regulation). Threes make efforts to cope with stress with adult support, and fours use more of their own strategies, such as moving away or asking for quiet (coping strategies). Sensitivity is part of a child's temperament, and our part is to make a good fit between the child and the space. If sound sensitivity keeps a child from meals, meeting time or play, grows over time, comes with other changes, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Sensory Integration Therapies for Children With Developmental and Behavioral Disorders, AAP Policy Statement, Pediatrics 2012

behaviors.label: Hiding under tables
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child crawls under a table, behind a shelf or into a small space and stays there.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking a calm, enclosed space when the room feels too busy (avoiding sensation). Small spaces may give the body a feeling of safety and pressure (proprioception). The child might also be playing a game of hiding and being found.
needs: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
first_steps: Notice and let the child stay if it is safe.
Sit nearby and stay quiet.
Offer a cozy space with cushions and a blanket.
Wonder with the child about what they need.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep a cozy space open and safe so the child can rest and return when ready.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Young children often seek small, enclosed spaces, both in play and as a way to take a break (self-regulation). Threes make efforts to manage feelings and stress with adult support, and fours use more of their own strategies, such as choosing a quiet place (coping strategies). Children who feel noise, light or crowds more strongly by temperament may hide more in busy times (sensory threshold). Young children also seek comfort from trusted adults, so a child may hide and watch for us to come near (attachment). If hiding grows more frequent, lasts long stretches, keeps a child from play and friends, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University

behaviors.label: Avoiding messy materials
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child won't touch paint, glue, clay, mud or sand, or wipes their hands right away.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may find wet, sticky or gritty feelings too strong (tactile). Messy materials may feel unpredictable. The child might also be watching first to learn how it works.
first_steps: Respect the child's choice.
Offer tools, such as brushes, sticks or gloves.
Offer a smaller amount on a tray.
Invite them to watch first and wonder together.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep a cloth and water close so the child can wipe their hands whenever they need.
behaviors.development: Children differ in how strongly they feel touch, and some are more sensitive to wet, sticky or gritty textures by temperament (sensory threshold). Some children take longer to warm up to new materials and new situations (adaptability). Exploring with the senses is a strong part of learning through the threes and fours (sensory exploration), and a child can join through tools, gloves or watching first. If avoiding textures grows over time, gets in the way of eating, dressing or play, comes with other changes, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Sensory Integration Therapies for Children With Developmental and Behavioral Disorders, AAP Policy Statement, Pediatrics 2012

behaviors.label: Refusing shoes or clothing textures
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child takes off shoes, socks or jackets, or won't wear certain clothing.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may find tags, seams or textures too scratchy or tight (tactile). Bare feet may help them feel the ground (proprioception). They might also be warm or seeking freedom.
first_steps: Notice and describe without pressure.
Offer soft choices and talk with the family.
Offer time barefoot indoors where it is safe.
Offer warm-up rubs or pressure on the feet.
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child wear shoes in the garden, animal yards, piazzas and hallway so feet stay safe.
behaviors.development: Twos are working on undressing and dressing, and pulling off shoes and socks can be practice of a new skill (self-help skills). By three, many children can put on some clothes themselves, such as loose pants or a jacket. Between eighteen months and three, children are discovering they are their own person, so a no to a jacket can be about choice (autonomy). Some children feel tags, seams and tight fits more strongly by temperament (sensory threshold). If clothing refusal grows more intense, limits daily life such as going outside, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Milestones by 3 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.
Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers, ZERO TO THREE
Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University

behaviors.label: Not settling at meeting time
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child moves around, gets up or touches others during meeting time.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may need movement to stay alert and listen (vestibular). Sitting on the floor may feel uncomfortable (proprioception). The child might also find the topic hard to follow.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Offer a cushion, a wobble seat or a fidget.
Offer a job, such as holding the book.
Keep meeting time short and full of movement.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer a spot with room so the child can move without bumping others.
behaviors.development: Holding attention in a group grows slowly through the preschool years (attention). Threes often need adult support to stay with a group when distracted, and fours begin to manage this with less help (managing attention). By five, many children can pay attention for five to ten minutes during things like story time. Some children are more active by temperament and find sitting still harder, so moving while listening can help them stay with us (activity level). If a child cannot join even short, engaging gatherings past the fours, or the family has worries too, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Milestones by 5 Years, CDC Learn the Signs. Act Early.
Temperament Continuum, Handout 1.12, CSEFEL Vanderbilt University

behaviors.label: Rocking or spinning often
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child rocks back and forth or spins in circles often.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may be seeking movement that helps it feel calm or alert (vestibular). Rocking may be soothing when things feel like too much (self-regulation). The child might also enjoy the dizzy feeling.
first_steps: Notice without stopping it.
Offer a rocking chair, a swing or spinning games outside.
Describe what you see, such as "You are spinning."
Watch when it happens and write it down.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer clear space for spinning away from edges and others so the child can move safely.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Rocking and spinning are common in young children, and many enjoy the rhythm and the dizzy feeling of movement (vestibular input). Rocking is often soothing, and some children rock more when tired or stressed (self-soothing). Most children stop body rocking by about age five. Rolling and spinning are also part of big body play, which supports children's growth through the twos, threes and fours (big body play). If rocking or spinning fills long stretches of the day, gets in the way of play and friends, leads to injury, comes with lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Body-rocking, head-rolling and head-banging, Raising Children Network
Big Body Play, Why Boisterous, Vigorous, and Very Physical Play Is Essential to Children's Development and Learning, Carlson, NAEYC

behaviors.label: Flapping or bouncing
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child flaps their hands, bounces or jumps, often when excited or upset.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may be seeking movement and pressure to feel organized (proprioception). Flapping or bouncing may be a way to show big feelings, happy or upset. It might also help the child feel calm and focused (self-regulation).
first_steps: Notice and accept it as the child's way.
Offer a trampoline, a ball or jumping games.
Describe the feeling you wonder about.
Join the movement if the child likes.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer open space for bouncing so the child can move freely and safely.
behaviors.development: Many young children flap their hands, bounce or jump when they are excited, happy or deeply focused (repetitive movements). Research finds these movements usually begin before age three and are most often set off by excitement. They can continue for years and often do not get in the way of a child's play or learning. Jumping is also a growing body skill, and threes and young fours jump on two feet with more and more strength (gross motor skills). If these movements fill long stretches of time, get in the way of play or friendships, come with lost skills or changes in talking and play, or worry the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Nonautistic Motor Stereotypies, Clinical Features and Longitudinal Follow-Up, Harris, Mahone and Singer 2008, Pediatric Neurology
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education

behaviors.label: Lying on the floor
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child lies on the floor or ground during play, transitions or meeting time.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may be seeking pressure from the floor to feel calm (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). It might also be a way to say no or to rest when things feel like too much.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Notice and sit nearby.
Describe what you see, such as "Your body wants to rest."
Offer a cushion, a weighted lap pad or a cozy space.
Invite the child to join when ready.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep paths around the child clear so no one trips and the child can rest safely.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Twos and threes may drop to the floor when a feeling is bigger than their skills to handle it, and upsets (tantrums) are common in the preschool years (emotion regulation). A child may also lie down when tired, hungry or unwell, before they can name what the body needs (body signals, interoception). Through the threes and fours, children grow in managing feelings and transitions, still with adult support. Research with preschoolers finds that upsets that happen every day, last a long time or seem to come out of nowhere are less typical. If lying on the floor happens often, lasts long, comes with low energy or lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Daily or Severe Tantrums May Point to Mental Health Issues, National Institute of Mental Health
California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
Aggressive Behavior in Young Children, UCSF California Childcare Health Program

behaviors.label: Leaning on people
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child leans on adults or friends, or flops onto laps and shoulders.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may be seeking pressure to feel calm or steady (proprioception). The child may be tired or low on energy (interoception). Leaning might also be a way to connect and feel close.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Notice and offer a hug or a hand if the child likes.
Offer a cushion or a beanbag to lean on.
Offer heavy work, such as carrying.
Describe what you see, such as "You want to be close."
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child find something to lean on so friends feel comfortable too.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Young children seek closeness and comfort from trusted adults, and leaning in is one way to feel safe and connected (attachment). Threes seek security and support from the adults they trust, and fours begin to notice when they need support and ask for it more directly. Leaning can also come with tiredness, hunger or not feeling well, before a child has words for it (body signals, interoception). Twos and threes are still learning how much space other people want (personal space). If leaning or flopping grows, comes with low energy, weakness or lost skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: California Preschool/Transitional Kindergarten Learning Foundations At-a-Glance, California Department of Education
California Infant/Toddler Learning and Development Foundations, Appendix, California Department of Education
Tips for Keeping Children Safe, A Developmental Guide for Toddlers, Head Start ECLKC

behaviors.label: Tipping chairs
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child tips their chair back on two legs or rocks it during meals or work.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The body may be seeking movement to stay alert (vestibular). Tipping may help the child focus (self-regulation). The child might also be testing balance and risk.
first_steps: Notice and stay calm.
Offer a wobble seat or a chance to stand at the table.
Offer movement breaks before and after sitting.
Describe what you see, such as "Your chair is tipping."
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer steady seats and movement choices so the child can stay safe and focused.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Many children are drawn to a little thrill, and leaning, rocking and tipping are part of that healthy pull (risky play). Twos and threes are still building balance and a sense of where their body is, so a tipping chair can surprise them (gross motor development). Fours often tip on purpose to test how far they can go, since balance keeps growing through the preschool years. Tipping is common at this age, and we still keep everyone safe and offer another way to move. If tipping comes with frequent falls, balance that stands out as hard, or a need to move that never seems met, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Sandseter and Kennair (2011), Children's Risky Play from an Evolutionary Perspective, Evolutionary Psychology
HealthyChildren.org (AAP), Preschool Activity

behaviors.label: Constant touching of others
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child often touches, hugs or pokes other children and adults.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking touch to feel calm or connected (tactile). They may not yet notice others' signals about space. Touching might also be a way to join in.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Notice and describe what you see.
Offer touch with materials, such as clay, playdough or a fidget.
Offer a hug when the child likes.
Help the child ask, such as "Can I hug you?"
behaviors.keep_safe: Help children say and hear yes and no about touch so everyone's body is respected.
from_us: A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
behaviors.development: Twos explore people with their hands and are just starting to notice when others are upset (social awareness). Through threes and fours, children grow in reading others' signals and in caring for others (empathy), and the CDC lists comforting a hurt or sad friend as a milestone by age 4. Learning that every body can say yes or no to touch (body autonomy and consent) takes many small, gentle moments of practice. If touching stays constant well past the age it is common, comes with little notice of how others respond, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, High Five or Hug? Teaching Toddlers About Consent
CDC, Important Milestones by 2 Years
CDC, Important Milestones by 4 Years

behaviors.label: Big reactions to small changes
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child gets very upset when a plan, a cup, a seat or a routine changes.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may find changes hard to predict and feel unsafe. Sameness may help them feel calm (self-regulation). They might also have been holding many feelings already.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Stay close and calm.
Describe the change and the feeling you wonder about.
Offer a picture schedule.
Give warnings before changes.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay present and keep the space calm so the child and others feel safe.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
behaviors.development: Twos are building a sense of self in a world full of new people and things, and many hold tightly to sameness to feel secure (need for predictability). Shifting from one plan to another (cognitive flexibility) is part of a set of thinking skills that grows quickly between ages 3 and 5, so threes and fours usually bend a little more each year. Children with a more cautious nature may need more consistency for longer (temperament). If reactions grow more frequent or intense, last a long time, crowd out play and friendships, or worry the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, My 2-year-old always has to have her way
Harvard Center on the Developing Child, Executive Function InBrief

behaviors.label: Trouble at transitions
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child gets upset, refuses or melts down when it is time to change from one thing to the next.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may not want to stop what they are doing. The change may feel sudden or unclear. The child might also need more time to shift their body and attention (self-regulation).
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Give warnings before changes.
Offer a job or a choice.
Sing a transition song.
Stay close and help the child move.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close during changes so the child feels steady and the group stays together.
behaviors.development: Twos are not yet able to stop their impulses easily, so leaving deep play is hard (impulse control). Self-control grows slowly across the preschool years and keeps developing into school age (self-regulation). Threes often still lean on an adult to move through routines, and many fours begin to expect what comes next and move with less prompting, as the California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations describe. If transitions become harder over time, bring long or unsafe upsets, or worry the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, Toddlers and Challenging Behavior
California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations, Social and Emotional Development

behaviors.label: Excluding others
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child tells others they can't play or leaves others out.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be protecting their play idea. They may want a close friend all to themselves. It might also be a way to feel in charge.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "He wants to play."
Help the children find a role for the friend.
Wonder together about how it feels to be left out.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close and help everyone find a place in the play so all children feel they belong.
from_us: A way into play with friends (peer entry)
A skill to practice (social and emotional skills)
behaviors.development: Twos mostly play near other children more than with them (parallel play), so leaving others out is less common. Threes begin to choose one or two special friends, and fours build friendships that are more lasting and more exclusive, as the California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations describe (peer relationships). Using friendship as leverage, such as "You can't be my friend unless...", is common among fours as they test how friendship and power work (relational aggression). Leaving others out is common at four, and we still guide children toward kindness so everyone has a place. If excluding becomes a steady pattern, targets the same child again and again, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations, Social and Emotional Development
NAEYC, Preventing and Responding to Relational Aggression in Preschool
Zero to Three, Parallel Play in Early Childhood

behaviors.label: Wanting to be in charge
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child tells others what to do or wants to decide every part of the play.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking power and feeling capable. They may have a clear idea and want it to happen. They might also feel calm when things are predictable.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see.
Offer real jobs and choices.
Help the children take turns leading.
behaviors.keep_safe: Help children share ideas so every voice is heard in the play.
behaviors.development: Between two and three, children begin to see themselves as separate people, and wanting a say is part of that (autonomy). Threes and fours often hold big play ideas and want them to happen just so, while the skills to share control, such as negotiating and taking turns (cooperation), grow with practice and adult support. Older preschoolers begin to negotiate with peers more on their own, as the California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations describe. If the need to control every part of play keeps a child from playing with others, grows stronger over time, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, Toddlers and Challenging Behavior
California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations, Social and Emotional Development

behaviors.label: Destroying materials
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child breaks, rips or smashes materials, toys or other children's work.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about how things come apart. Breaking may give the hands and arms strong work (proprioception). The child might also be showing a big feeling.
needs: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see.
Offer things to take apart, such as old machines or cardboard.
Wonder together about how things are made.
behaviors.keep_safe: Guide the child toward things that are welcome to be taken apart so everyone's work stays cared for.
behaviors.development: Young children learn how the world works by acting on things and watching what happens (cause and effect). Twos often push, pull apart and test with little sense yet of what can break. Threes and fours grow in hand control (fine motor) and in understanding how others feel about their work (empathy), and a strong feeling can still come out through the hands before words arrive (emotional expression). Breaking things is common while children learn, and we still protect everyone's work and show another way. If destroying grows more frequent or intense, seems aimed at hurting others, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, Aggressive Behavior in Toddlers
Zero to Three, How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy

behaviors.label: Dumping bins
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child dumps bins, baskets or containers on the floor.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about filling and emptying. The sound and movement may be exciting (seeking sensation). They might also be looking for one thing at the bottom.
needs: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
first_steps: Notice and describe what you see.
Offer containers and things to fill and dump.
Invite the child to help put things back.
Wonder together about what they are looking for.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep dumping to open spaces so no one slips or trips.
behaviors.development: Filling and dumping is how toddlers learn about full and empty, in and out (cause and effect). Twos often dump again and again, since repetition helps them figure out how things work. By three and four, dumping usually grows into sorting, filling with purpose, carrying and building (constructive play). If a four or five year old still mostly dumps and rarely moves on to other ways of using materials, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Wandering without engaging
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child moves around the room or yard without settling into play.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be unsure what to do or how to join. The room might feel too busy (avoiding sensation). They might also be watching and learning before they join.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Notice and walk beside the child.
Describe what you see, such as "You are looking around."
Offer two choices.
Play alongside them for a while.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep the child in sight and close to the group so they feel safe and connected.
from_us: Their interests in the room (interest-based learning)
behaviors.development: Many young children watch before they join (onlooker play). Twos often play near others more than with them (parallel play), and the kind of play a child chooses can change in a new group or a new space. Children with a more cautious nature may stay at the edge for a while and learn a great deal by watching (slow to warm temperament). If wandering continues well into the year, the child rarely settles into anything, or seems to lose interest in play they once enjoyed, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Clinging to an adult
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child stays close to an adult, holds on or cries when the adult moves away.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may need to feel safe before exploring. They may be missing family. They might also find the room or group too much (avoiding sensation).
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Stay close and calm.
Describe the feeling you wonder about.
Offer a family photo or a comfort object.
Invite a friend to play nearby.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close and help the child feel safe while slowly inviting play.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Time to settle after a change (adjustment)
behaviors.development: Holding close to a trusted adult is a sign of a healthy bond (attachment). Toddlers grow more aware of separations as they become more independent, and these worries often continue into the preschool years (separation anxiety). The CDC lists settling within about ten minutes after a parent leaves, as at child care drop off, as a milestone by age 3. Pretend play often helps children work through goodbyes. If clinging grows stronger, returns after a change at home, keeps a child from play for long stretches, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Tantrums and big upsets
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child cries, screams, kicks or falls to the floor when upset.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be feeling something too big to manage alone. They may be tired, hungry or overwhelmed (interoception). They might also need help to calm their body (self-regulation).
first_steps: Stay close and calm.
Describe the feeling you wonder about in few words.
Offer a cozy space and wait.
Offer comfort when the child is ready.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep the child and others safe by giving space and staying present until the body is calm.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Tantrums are very common in twos and threes, when strong feelings arrive faster than words and self-control (emotional regulation). Daily tantrums become less common after age 3, though tantrums are still common among preschoolers. Fours usually have more words and more ways to cope, and they still need adult support (self-regulation). If tantrums are very frequent, very long or unsafe, include hurting themselves, or get in the way of play and friendships, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Not eating
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child refuses food, eats very little or eats only certain foods.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may find some textures, smells or tastes too strong (tactile, olfactory). They may not feel hungry (interoception). They might also want to feel in control.
first_steps: Notice without pressure.
Offer small amounts and choices.
Invite the child to help serve or prepare.
Talk with the family.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep mealtimes calm and pressure free so every child feels safe at the table.
from_us: Home and family in the room (cultural belonging)
Time to settle after a change (adjustment)
behaviors.development: Eating little or nothing at school is very common, especially in the first weeks, after a change or on a busy day. A table full of friends, new foods, new smells and a new routine can all take a child's attention away from eating (group setting). Picky eating is also a normal stage for toddlers, and some eat only one or two favorite foods for weeks (selective eating). It can take ten or more tastes before a child accepts a new food (repeated exposure), and appetite can change from one day to the next. Serving themselves with adult help can make the table feel more inviting (self-help skills). If a child eats very few foods at home as well, gags or struggles with many textures, seems low in weight or energy, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and the family can talk with the child's doctor.

behaviors.label: Overstuffing the mouth
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child puts too much food in their mouth at once or eats very fast.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The mouth may be seeking strong pressure (proprioception). The child may not notice when their mouth is full (interoception). They might also be very hungry.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Sit close and stay calm.
Offer small pieces and a calm pace.
Describe what you see, such as "Your mouth is very full."
Offer crunchy and chewy foods.
behaviors.keep_safe: Sit close at meals and offer small bites so every child can eat safely.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
behaviors.development: Young children are still learning to chew well and to notice when the mouth is full (oral motor skills). Babies and toddlers are at the highest risk of choking, so twos need close support and food cut small. Threes and fours grow in feeding themselves, using a fork by around three and serving themselves with adult help by around four, as CDC milestones describe (self-help skills). Overstuffing is common while children learn, and we still keep everyone safe by sitting to eat and showing small bites. If overstuffing stays a steady pattern, comes with frequent gagging or coughing at meals, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Toileting accidents during play
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child has a toileting accident while deep in play.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may not notice the body's signals in time (interoception). They may not want to stop playing. They might also be learning new routines. On our site the bathroom can be a long walk from the yards, the garden and the animal yards, so a signal that comes late leaves little time to get there.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Stay calm and help quietly, with no shame and no fuss.
Offer clean clothes privately, and let the child do what they can themselves.
Offer the bathroom before leaving for the yards, the garden, a walk or rest, and before deep play begins.
Notice where accidents happen. Plan bathroom trips around the longest walks.
Talk with the family, following our toilet learning policy.
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child change privately and calmly so they feel safe and cared for.
from_us: Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
Time to settle after a change (adjustment)
behaviors.development: Toileting accidents at school are very common and expected. A new place, a busy room, deep play and many friends nearby make it easy to miss the body's signals in time (interoception). Our bathroom is also far from many of the places children play, which makes the walk longer than at home. Learning to use the toilet takes time, and accidents are part of building new body habits (toilet learning). Many twos are just beginning, and accidents can continue for months after a child seems trained, even at three or four. A change at home or school can bring a return of accidents for a while (regression). If accidents are frequent and are not lessening over time, return after a long dry stretch with no change to explain them, or worry the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home and the family can talk with the child's doctor.

sources.title: HealthyChildren.org (AAP), Are accidents normal or the sign of a problem?

behaviors.label: Tearing paper or books
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child tears paper, pages of books or other children's drawings.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may enjoy the sound and feel of tearing (seeking sensation). Tearing may give the hands strong work (fine motor). It might also be a way to show a feeling.
needs: Knocking down and changing things (transformation schema)
first_steps: Notice and describe what you see.
Offer paper that is welcome to be torn.
Invite the child to help mend books.
Wonder together about the sound.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer paper that is welcome to tear so books and others' work stay cared for.
behaviors.development: Twos are learning to turn pages one at a time, a CDC milestone by about 30 months, and tearing is part of finding out what paper does (sensory exploration). Threes and fours grow stronger hand control, such as holding a crayon between fingers and thumb by around four (fine motor). Understanding that books and drawings matter to others grows along with caring about others' feelings (empathy). If tearing grows more frequent, seems tied to strong feelings much of the time, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: CDC, Important Milestones by 30 Months
CDC, Important Milestones by 4 Years
Zero to Three, How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy

behaviors.label: Hoarding objects
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child gathers many objects and keeps them close, hides them or won't share.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be collecting things that matter to them. Holding objects may help them feel safe (calm and grounding). They might also be exploring ideas of ownership.
needs: Enclosing and hiding (enclosure and enveloping schemas)
Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Notice and describe what you see.
Offer a basket or a bag for collecting.
Offer a place to keep treasures.
Wonder together about the collection.
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child keep a few treasures safely so others can use materials too.
from_us: Time to settle after a change (adjustment)
Home and family in the room (cultural belonging)
behaviors.development: Twos are building a sense of self, and holding on to things is part of it (possessiveness). Sharing takes a lot of time and practice, and it is not usually expected until between three and four (sharing). Threes and fours often gather treasures and argue over who had something first, and research in preschools shows these disputes over objects are part of learning social rules (ownership). If gathering and guarding objects becomes intense, brings deep distress when items are moved, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Repeating the same play every day
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child plays the same game, builds the same thing or chooses the same material every day.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be working through a question or an idea. Repetition may help them feel calm and capable. They might also be practicing a new skill.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Notice and describe what you see.
Offer a small change or a new material.
Wonder together about the play.
Document the play and share it.
behaviors.keep_safe: Support the play while gently offering new ideas so the child can grow at their own pace.
from_us: Their interests in the room (interest-based learning)
behaviors.development: Repetition is how young children figure out how things work and master new skills, which builds confidence (mastery). Twos love the same song, book or action again and again, since repetition helps them know what to expect (predictability). Threes and fours may return to the same play for days while they work through an idea or an experience, and pretend play helps children work through hard moments (symbolic play). If the play stays exactly the same for months, any change brings great distress, or play seems to narrow instead of grow, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, The Power of Play

behaviors.label: Silly or loud behavior at meeting time
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child makes loud noises, silly faces or jokes during meeting time.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking attention and connection. The body may need movement and sound to stay alert (seeking sensation). They might also find meeting time too long.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Offer a job or a role in meeting time.
Add songs and movement.
Keep meeting time short.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep meeting time short and full of movement so every child can take part.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
behaviors.development: Sitting, waiting and listening in a big group asks a lot of young bodies and minds (executive function). These skills grow quickly between ages 3 and 5, so twos and threes do best with very short group times. NAEYC suggests keeping circle time to about five or ten minutes and moving deeper learning into small groups. Silliness can also be a way to connect and be noticed (social bids). If a child cannot join any group time for long, the behavior grows over time, or it worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Harvard Center on the Developing Child, Executive Function InBrief

behaviors.label: Avoiding the group
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child stays away from group times or plays alone often.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may find groups too loud or busy (avoiding sensation). They may be watching and learning before joining. They might also prefer quiet play.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Notice and respect the child's choice.
Offer a spot at the edge of the group.
Invite one friend to play nearby.
Join the child in their play.
behaviors.keep_safe: Keep the child in sight and offer a calm spot near the group.
from_us: Their interests in the room (interest-based learning)
behaviors.development: Many young children watch from the side for a while before they feel ready to join (slow to warm temperament). Twos often play near others more than with them (parallel play). The CDC lists noticing other children and joining them to play as a milestone by age 3, and a child may play easily with familiar friends and still hang back in a new or busy group. If a child rarely joins others as the year goes on, pulls away from play they once enjoyed, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

CDC, Important Milestones by 3 Years

behaviors.label: Hurting animals
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child squeezes, chases, pulls or hurts animals or insects.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about how animals move and feel. They may not yet judge how strong their hands are (proprioception). They might also be exploring power.
needs: Heavy work and strong force (proprioceptive input)
first_steps: Move close and calmly protect the animal.
Describe what you see, such as "The rabbit is trying to get away."
Show gentle hands together.
Offer real care jobs, such as feeding.
behaviors.keep_safe: Stay close in the animal yards so every animal and child stays safe.
behaviors.development: Twos explore animals with their whole bodies and are still learning how strong their hands are (body awareness). Toddlers are just beginning to develop empathy, and understanding that an animal has feelings grows across the preschool years (empathy). The CDC lists comforting others who are hurt or sad as a milestone by age 4. Rough handling is common while children learn, and we still keep every animal safe and show gentle hands. If a child seems to hurt animals on purpose, keeps going when the animal shows distress, or this grows over time, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Picking plants
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child picks flowers, pulls leaves or uproots plants in the garden.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be curious about plants and how they feel or smell (tactile, olfactory). Picking may give the hands strong work (fine motor). They might also want to give a gift.
first_steps: Move close and stay calm.
Describe what you see.
Offer plants that are welcome to pick, such as clover or mint.
Remind gently, "Pick with purpose and leave some for others."
behaviors.keep_safe: Help the child pick only plants we know so everyone stays safe.
behaviors.development: Young children learn about living things by touching, smelling and gathering, and the California Preschool Learning Foundations build science on this natural curiosity (scientific inquiry). Twos often grab and pull what is in reach before they know what is welcome to pick. Threes begin to heed an adult's warning about danger, and fours begin to avoid danger more on their own, as CDC milestones describe (risk awareness). Picking with care, and knowing which plants are safe, grows with adult guidance and many visits to the garden. If picking stays rough and constant despite steady guidance, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Screaming or very loud voice
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child screams, shrieks or uses a very loud voice often.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may enjoy the sound and power of their voice (auditory). Screaming may help release big feelings. They might also not notice how loud they are.
first_steps: Notice and stay calm.
Describe what you see, such as "Your voice is very loud."
Offer a place outside for loud voices.
Play sound games together.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer outdoor spaces for loud voices so everyone's ears stay comfortable.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
behaviors.development: Twos often scream when feelings are big and words are still coming (expressive language). Screaming tends to grow louder when feelings go unnoticed, so naming the feeling often helps (emotion coaching). The CDC lists talking well enough for others to understand most of the time as a milestone by age 3, so threes and fours usually have more words to reach for. Many children also enjoy the power and play of a big voice. If screaming stays a main way to communicate, comes with few words, or a child seems not to notice sounds around them, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

behaviors.label: Saying no to everything
behaviors.what_we_might_see: A child says no to most requests or invitations.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child may be seeking power and choice. They may feel unsure about what will happen. They might also be tired or overwhelmed.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Stay calm and close.
Offer two choices.
Describe the feeling you wonder about.
Give time.
behaviors.keep_safe: Offer choices and stay present so the child feels respected and safe.
behaviors.development: Between two and three, children begin to see themselves as separate people, and "no" is one way to show it (autonomy). Toddlers often say no even when they do not mean it, while they learn to share likes and dislikes. Offering two or three real choices gives children a sense of control and builds confidence. If a child says no to almost everything for a long stretch, the refusals grow stronger with time, or the family is worried, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.

sources.title: Zero to Three, Toddlers and Challenging Behavior

behaviors.label: Out of balance in body and feelings (dysregulation)
behaviors.what_we_might_see: Dysregulation looks different in every child and can change from one moment to the next. Some children speed up. They run, crash, shout, grow very silly, hit or throw, or cannot stop moving. Some children slow down or shut down. They go quiet, stare, seem far away, hide, stop answering, go limp or seem sleepy. Some swing between the two. It can also show in eating, toileting, sleep, play that falls apart, tears over something small or a child who is suddenly not themselves.
behaviors.might_be_seeking: The child's nervous system may be out of its comfortable range, too revved up (hyperarousal) or too low (hypoarousal). Hunger, tiredness, illness, too much or too little sensory input, a change at home or school, a stressful moment or a big feeling can each tip the balance. The child is not choosing it and cannot think their way out of it. They may be seeking safety, connection, a steady adult to borrow calm from (co-regulation) and their body's needs met.
needs: Belonging and having a place (attachment and belonging)
first_steps: Regulate yourself first. Slow your breath, soften your face and lower your voice.
Come close and lower your body. Use very few words.
Notice which way the child is out of balance. A child who is revved up may need less noise and light and heavy work. A child who has shut down may need warmth, gentle movement and connection.
Check the body. Offer water, food, rest or a quiet spot.
Stay until the child is settled. Talk about it later, when the body is calm.
Write down when it happens and what came before. Patterns help the team understand.
behaviors.keep_safe: Move other children and objects away calmly if anyone could be hurt. Stay close and keep watching a child who has gone quiet or shut down, as closely as a child who is loud.
from_us: A calm adult to borrow from (co-regulation)
Rest, food, water or a body break (basic needs)
Less noise, light or crowding (lower sensory load)
behaviors.development: Every child moves in and out of balance, and young children need a steady adult to help them find their way back (co-regulation). Regulation means bringing energy and alertness down when they run high and up when they run low (arousal regulation), so dysregulation can look like speeding up, slowing down, shutting down or swinging between. Twos depend most on a trusted adult, and the skills to manage feelings and attention grow quickly between ages 3 and 5 (executive function). Fours still regulate best with some adult support, as the California Preschool/TK Learning Foundations describe. If dysregulation grows more frequent, intense or long, comes with loss of skills, or worries the family, the team talks with the family about what they see at home, and with the director about whether a closer look at development may help.
